Opinion at *22 (emphasis in original).The Chancellor: In a hearing like this, the well-pled allegations in the bill are accepted as true, and the plea is factually true. If the plea were negative, the rule regarding the bill's allegations would differ. The facts from the bill and plea are as follows. The defendant was incorporated under the

Delaware General Corporation Law on January 1, 1927. The capital stock included a 7% cumulative first preferred stock ($100 par value; 156,840 shares outstanding), an 8% cumulative second preferred stock ($100 par value; 18,554 shares outstanding), and common stock ($1 par value; 1,290,967 shares outstanding). The complainant owned 150 shares of first preferred stock before July 30, 1935. On that date, cumulative dividend arrears were $26.25 per share for first preferred and $30 per share for second preferred. The defendant's stock was reclassified via a charter amendment approved by two-thirds of each class. The complainant opposed and voted against it. Under the amendment, each old share was converted into new shares with altered rights. Key details include the first preferred

shares held by the complainant being converted into shares with different rights, and the accumulated $26.25 dividends being canceled. The complainant argues this violated his contractual rights and exceeded corporate authority. Keller, et al., v. Wilson & Co., Inc., 21 Del. Ch. 391, 190 A. 115. Before the reclassification vote, the complainant sued in New York Supreme Court to block the plan. His lawyer advised that this court had ruled against a similar claim (Keller, et al., v. Wilson & Co., Inc., 21 Del. Ch. 13, 180 A. 584) on May 24, 1935, which would bind the New York court.

Following this counsel, the complainant withdrew his injunction motion in the New York court. He claims he still objected to the reclassification plan. Almost a year later, on April 13, 1936, he submitted his first preferred shares to the corporation, requesting new certificates for the stocks he was due under the reclassification plan he had previously opposed. At that time, the new stocks he received were worth more than the old ones, including accrued dividends. The complainant asserts he acted under duress from the defendant, who allegedly threatened to pay dividends only on the new reclassified stock, not the old preferred shares. Such actions, however, do not legally qualify as duress.

The complainant exchanged 150 shares of old preferred stock for 150 shares of new 5% preferred, 150 shares of new 6% preferred, and 75 shares of common stock. Before April 13, 1936, the defendant had already declared dividends on the new preferred stocks. Upon exchanging, the complainant received back dividends on the 5% preferred and stock dividends on the 6% preferred. After April 1, 1936, he continued receiving cash dividends until another recapitalization on September 22, 1936, which included a cash dividend on common stock and scrip for fractional shares. It is unclear if he exchanged his holdings after the second reclassification, but he accepted subsequent dividends based on the 1935 reclassification.

The complainant argues the 1936 reclassification relied on the 1935 amendment, which he claims was invalid, rendering the later one void as well. His case hinges on challenging the 1935 charter amendment. After the Delaware Supreme Court reversed a related ruling on November 10, 1936, he demanded the reclassification be nullified and that no dividends be paid until arrears on the original 7% preferred stock were settled. The suit seeks both payment of accumulated dividends and invalidation of the reclassifications.

The bill requests payment of arrears for the old 7% and 8% preferred stockholders and demands the reclassifications be voided, restoring the original capital structure. The defendant argues the complainant is barred from suing due to his participation in the exchange and dividend acceptance, as well as laches. The complainant counters that the plea is improperly double, citing both acquiescence and laches as grounds for dismissal, though legal precedent allows multiple facts in a plea if they support a single defense.

All generally converge to a single point. 1 Daniel Chancery Practice, (4th Am. Ed.) 603, 607. However, there are instances where a dual plea is entirely appropriate. If the bill presents a claim that is inherently dual or alternative, it is acceptable to file a plea addressing each alternative. 1 Daniel Chancery Practice, (4th Am. Ed.) 609. This case exemplifies such a scenario. The complainant requests (a) full rescission of the two reclassifications and (b) payment of arrears on the old seven percent preferred stock. It is plausible that (a) could be denied while (b) is granted. The plea of laches suits (a), and the plea of acquiescence fits (b). The plea, as I see it, presents a unified defense against the two claims or alternatives in the bill. I now review the first alternative, (a), which seeks restoration of the defendant’s original capital structure. That the complainant is barred by laches from obtaining this relief seems indisputable.

The plea’s assertions, combined with the bill’s allegations, demonstrate that the original preferred shares were transformed through two reclassifications into numerous shares of a wholly different nature, which subsequently changed hands in an active market. New stockholders emerged through sales and purchases, stock dividends were issued, and the complexity of events has rendered the situation irreparable. The complainant delayed over a year and seven months before filing the bill, during which the entanglement worsened daily. Reclassifications, cash and stock dividends, and shifts in ownership during this delay made restoring the prior status increasingly difficult. Recovering paid dividends and reconciling the rights of innocent purchasers presents such an insurmountable challenge that attempting a solution would be extraordinarily impractical. No court, I dare say, has ever undertaken such a daunting task. The complainant’s argument that his delay resulted from a legal misconception, influenced by this court’s decision in the Keller Case, holds no merit.

The court deeply regrets when erroneous decisions mislead individuals. However, it is a well-established principle that courts do not rectify mistakes of law. Com'rs. of Lewes v. Breakwater Fisheries Co., 13 Del. Ch. 234, 117 A. 823. This rule remains applicable even if the legal error stemmed from a lower court’s reversed decision or a court overruling its prior rulings. Lyon v. Richmond, 2 Johns. Ch. (N. Y.) 51, 60; Pittsburgh, etc., v. Lake Superior, etc., Co., 118 Mich. 109, 76 N. W. 395; Baker v. Pool, 56 Ala. 14; Kelly v. Turner, 74 Ala. 513, 520; 10 R. C. L., p.

314, § 37. I now address the second alternative, (b), which seeks to compel the defendant to pay all arrears on the old first preferred stock. The July 1935 reclassification nullified these arrears. The Supreme Court’s opinion in Keller, et al., v. Wilson & Co., Inc., supra, states that a Delaware corporation formed before the 1927 amendment (35 Del. Laws, c. 85) cannot amend its charter to reclassify stock in a way that eliminates a dissenting preferred stockholder’s right to accumulated dividends. This ruling directly applies here, as the facts are analogous. However, the Supreme Court did not declare the reclassification amendment universally void under all circumstances or against all parties.

The court ruled that the amendment was invalid for a non-consenting stockholder, and nothing more. Had all preferred stockholders in the Wilson & Co. case approved the amendment, the court would not have voided it based on public policy. This issue concerned only the stockholders, and if they unanimously agreed, there was no reason for judicial interference. The Wilson & Co. case treated preferred dividends as a contractual right under the charter, ruling that a majority could not strip a dissenting stockholder of their rights. The general principle is that those who participate in or accept an action cannot later challenge it in equity, even if the action was legally impermissible, as seen in Finch.

In Finch et al. v. Warrior Cement Corp., a participant in an unlawful stock issuance was barred from contesting it. This principle has been upheld in numerous cases across various contexts. Equity typically refuses to entertain complaints from those who participated in or benefited from the actions they now oppose, especially when contractual rights are involved. As stated in Cook on Corporations, stockholders may be estopped from challenging an amendment if their actions or silence imply acceptance. Fletcher’s Cyclopedia of Corporations similarly notes that stockholders who benefit from an unauthorized act cannot later contest it, particularly if they accepted dividends derived from it.

Regarding stock reclassification, it is reasonable to assume that stockholders receiving new securities in lieu of cash dividends agreed to surrender their old rights. Accepting the new terms implies relinquishing prior claims. The complainant, however, seeks to retain old dividend rights while keeping all new benefits—a position that seems untenable. In reality, the complainant only joined the reclassification plan after market conditions favored the new securities over the old ones, suggesting speculative behavior rather than genuine objection.

Whether the complainant’s actions constitute acquiescence or estoppel is a semantic distinction. Here, it aligns more with acquiescence, compounded by speculative delay to maximize personal gain. Having chosen his course, a court of equity should not permit him to reverse his stance for opportunistic reasons.

The complainant should be bound by his choice. In this aspect of the case, which aims to recover the unpaid dividends on the old preferred stock, the complainant argues a previously mentioned point: that he acted under a legal misunderstanding, leading him to accept the new stock and various dividends. However, as previously noted, this error does not qualify for legal relief. Another procedural issue worth addressing is the complainant's claim that the defendant's plea should be dismissed since all objections could have been raised in a demurrer. While it is true that a plea cannot replace a demurrer, this case is unusual. The bill inadvertently includes facts supporting the defendant's argument of delay and acquiescence, creating an incomplete portrayal of the defendant's position. It would be unfair to force the defendant to defend based on an incomplete account.

The case presents a unique scenario where the complainant's bill partially outlines the defendant's facts, leaving gaps in the defense's narrative. It would be unjust to require the defendant to rely on a demurrer when the complainant's own pleading fails to fully present the defensive facts. Here, the defendant expanded on the incomplete facts provided by the complainant to ensure a fair representation of its defense. Pleading rules should not allow a complainant to deprive the defendant of its right to fully utilize legal procedures. This is not to suggest any intentional manipulation by the complainant's legal team, but rather to highlight the potential misuse of such an approach if accepted as standard practice.

The plea will be upheld. Additional details can be found in the Court's instructions. Lore, C. J., addressing the jury: Ladies and gentlemen, the plaintiff, William F. Heinel, alleges that on March 23, 1906, while assisting in loading furniture near his home at 213 West Second Street, he was struck by a negligently operated trolley car. He claims the car was speeding, lacked proper warnings, and that the motorman failed to avoid the collision, resulting in severe injuries. The defendant disputes these claims, asserting the car was operated carefully, with due warning and at a safe speed, and that the plaintiff's sudden movement caused the accident. The plaintiff bears the burden of proving the defendant's negligence caused his injuries.

This lawsuit hinges on the defendant's alleged negligence. To succeed, the plaintiff must demonstrate that his injuries resulted from the defendant's actions as described. Negligence is not assumed; it must be proven. Your task is to determine whether the defendant's negligence caused the harm. Both parties have outlined legal principles to guide your decision. West Second Street is a public roadway, and both the plaintiff and defendant had lawful access to it. Each party's rights must be exercised responsibly, with due consideration for the other's safety and legal entitlements.

Each party must respect the rights of others and act reasonably and cautiously to avoid unduly limiting or interfering with those rights. When using the highway, each person can assume others will behave as a reasonable person would under the circumstances, unless shown otherwise. The defendant company was required to exercise appropriate care regarding the speed of the car, sounding warnings, and stopping when danger arose, as dictated by the situation. The Court will not list specific actions but emphasizes that all parties must act with due regard for others' safety. If the company failed to meet this standard and injury resulted solely from this failure, it would be liable. Similarly, the plaintiff must also exercise reasonable care, and if their negligence contributed to the accident, they cannot recover damages.

In cases where the plaintiff is partly negligent, the Court will not quantify each party's contribution. However, the plaintiff may still recover if the defendant's negligence alone was the direct cause of the injury, provided the defendant could have prevented the accident with reasonable care. For instance, if the plaintiff negligently stood near the track but the motorman could have seen and stopped the car in time, the company would be liable. Conversely, if the plaintiff suddenly moved into danger, making it impossible for the motorman to avoid the collision, the defendant would not be held responsible.

If the motorman, upon seeing or being able to see the plaintiff in danger, took all reasonable steps to prevent the accident, the defendant would not be liable. The jury may consider the plaintiff's intoxication when assessing whether they exercised reasonable care for their safety. To weigh this, evidence must show the plaintiff was intoxicated and that this impaired their judgment. The defense's request for a directed verdict was denied, as the jury should decide the case based on the evidence. If the jury rules for the plaintiff, compensation should cover injuries, lost wages, pain, suffering, and future impacts.

The jury could also award damages for any future loss of earning capacity proven by the evidence. The jury failed to reach a verdict. CHRISTIE, Chief Justice: Defendant Crystal Robinson was indicted for emotionally abusing Jane Roe, a long-term care resident, under 16 Del.C. § 1136(a), and conspiring to commit this offense under 11 Del.C. § 511, both class A misdemeanors. After a May 16, 1990 trial, Robinson was convicted and fined $101 per offense, plus prosecution costs. She received 31-day sentences for each charge, to be served consecutively, but these were suspended for three months' probation per charge. Robinson appeals, raising five issues, including an alleged error in allowing the State to amend the indictment.

Include the 'knowingly' mens rea element as outlined in 16 Del.C. § 1136(a); 2) the Superior Court acted improperly by allowing evidence about Roe's physical and mental state during the offense; 3) the Superior Court erred by rejecting Robinson's mistrial motions due to the State improperly introducing testimony about her codefendant Yvette Jones' guilty plea; 4) the Superior Court legally erred by not incorporating the bill of particulars' recitals into the jury instructions; and 5) the patient abuse statute, 16 Del.C. § 1136(a), is unconstitutionally vague and overbroad under due process principles, particularly concerning the 'emotional abuse' element, 16 Del.C. § 1131(l)(b). We reject these arguments and uphold the Superior Court's judgment. FACTS FROM STATE'S WITNESS TESTIMONY The allegations against

Robinson stemmed from an event on a Sunday morning around 7:30 a.m. on August 13, 1989, in Room 400 of the Layton Home nursing facility. Robinson had worked there as a nurse's aide for over two years. Room 400, housing four elderly residents, measured 14 feet by 14 feet. Jane Roe, 85, was seated quietly in her wheelchair while two housekeepers cleaned and brought fresh linen. Robinson and codefendant Jones entered, ignored the others, and Robinson falsely claimed someone stole Roe's clothes, upsetting the possessive Roe. The exact sequence of

events is unclear, but the Court presents them as they might have happened. The defendants and Roe engaged in a loud, abusive exchange. Jones threw up to six towels at Roe, while Robinson flicked water droplets at her and mimicked spitting. Roe shouted for them to stop, and Robinson retorted with insults. Robinson also placed a small flowerpot on Roe's head, laughing when it fell. Roe screamed as Robinson provocatively shook her rear end and placed it on Roe's meal table. Roe pushed her away, yelling about divine punishment. The incident lasted 15-20 minutes. More facts will be provided as needed. Robinson claimed the exchange was brief and denied involvement in the described actions or having the statutory intent.

Robinson's first appeal argument is that the Superior Court erred legally by allowing the State to amend the indictment to add the 'knowingly' mens rea element to the patient abuse charge, omitted originally. She argues this was a prejudicial substantive amendment, warranting reversal of her convictions. See Keller v. State, Del.Supr., 425 A.2d 152, 154-55 (1981); Harley v

State, Del.Supr., 534 A.2d 255, 256-57 (1987); State v. Blendt, Del.Super., 120 A.2d 321, 322-23 (1956); Superior Court Criminal Rule 7(e). During Robinson's pretrial motion to dismiss the indictment on due process grounds, defense counsel highlighted that the original indictment omitted the necessary mental state for the patient abuse charge. Additionally, they pointed out that the charge was mistakenly filed under § 1131's definitional section instead of § 1136(a)'s violations section. The Superior Court permitted the State to amend the indictment to explicitly include the 'knowingly' mens rea element and to fix the citation from 16 Del. C. § 1131(a)(2) to § 1136(a). See Superior Court Criminal Rule 7(c) (citation errors do not warrant dismissal or reversal if they do not prejudice the defendant). This Court has held

repeatedly that a trial court may amend an indictment for formal issues but not substantive ones, provided no new or different charge is introduced and the defendant's substantial rights remain unaffected. Keller, 425 A.2d at 154-55; Harley, 534 A.2d at 256-57; Blendt, 120 A.2d at 322-23; Superior Court Criminal Rule 7(e). This rule ensures the accused is informed of the charges to prepare a proper defense. Keller, 425 A.2d at 155. Even if an indictment lacks explicit 'knowledge' or 'intent' language, it may still stand if other allegations imply the required mental state. See, e.g., United States v. Arteaga-Limones, 529 F.2d 1183, 1199 (5th Cir.) (an indictment for marijuana importation was valid despite omitting 'knowingly or intentionally,' as statutory references and jury instructions covered the element), cert. denied, 429 U.S. 920 (1976).

United States v. Martell, 335 F.2d 764, 765 (4th Cir.1964) (the 'knowingly' element for kidnapping could be inferred from allegations of seizing and abducting the victim); Hughes v. United States, 338 F.2d 651, 652 (1st Cir.1964). Although Robinson's original indictment did not explicitly state 'knowingly,' the Superior Court rightly noted that guilt required proof of the statutory mental state under 11 Del.C. § 251(a). Moreover, the allegations that Robinson emotionally abused Roe by 'ridiculing, demeaning, and making derogatory remarks' inherently imply the 'knowingly' requirement of 16 Del.C. § 1136(a). Terms like 'ridiculing' and 'demeaning' assume awareness of the conduct's nature or its likely outcome, per 11 Del.C. § 231(b).

The amended indictment did not introduce a new or different charge, and the original indictment sufficiently notified Robinson of the charges for defense preparation. Thus, we find no prejudice. We conclude the Superior Court acted lawfully in permitting the amendment to include 'knowingly' and correct the citation. B. Robinson's second appeal argument is that the Superior Court improperly exercised its discretion.

The court exercised its discretion by allowing evidence of Roe's physical and mental state during and after the offense. Robinson argues this evidence was irrelevant and inadmissible, as the case centers on the defendant's actions, not Roe's traits. Even if relevant, Robinson claims its value was outweighed by risks of unfair prejudice, confusion, or misleading the jury under D.R.E. 401, 402, and 403. These arguments are unfounded. The trial court is best positioned to assess such evidence, and reversal occurs only for clear abuse of discretion. Evidence of Roe's condition is crucial to determining whether Robinson knew her behavior would demean Roe.

The evidence indicates Roe was wheelchair-bound, often agitated, disoriented, and had memory issues. Knowing this, a jury could infer Robinson's actions—abusive remarks, false claims about stolen clothes, mock spitting, the flower pot incident, and lifting her uniform—were intended to provoke ridicule. While this evidence might evoke sympathy for Roe, the court properly balanced its probative value against potential prejudice. The Superior Court did not abuse its discretion in admitting evidence of Roe's condition during and after the incident.

Robinson's third appeal claim is that the court erred by denying her mistrial motions after the prosecution introduced hearsay about co-defendant Yvette Jones pleading guilty. This testimony was improperly elicited without establishing Jones's unavailability under D.R.E. 804(b)(3). Though the testimony was admitted erroneously, not every error warrants reversal. Often, a curative jury instruction suffices. To assess the error's impact, we apply the Hughes v. State test, considering the case's closeness, the issue's centrality, and mitigation efforts.

Given the strong evidence of guilt and the minimal prejudice from the improper testimony, the Superior Court acted within its discretion to deny the mistrial and issue a jury instruction. Robinson's defense relied on her claim of innocence, suggesting any wrongdoing was Jones's. The guilty plea aligned with this argument. The court promptly instructed jurors to disregard Jones's case, ensuring the error was harmless.

Beyond any reasonable doubt, the curative instruction effectively addressed any potential errors. D. Robinson's fourth appeal argument claims the Superior Court legally erred by not instructing the jury, as requested by the defense, that the State must prove the alleged acts in the bill of particulars for each charge. The defense objected to this omission, arguing it was reversible error. However, this claim lacks merit. In Taylor v. State, this Court ruled that a jury must be fully informed of all essential elements of the offense to ensure a fair trial. Here, the prosecution's evidence aligned with the bill of particulars, and the Superior Court provided standard jury instructions covering all statutory elements. Robinson cites no Delaware case mandating jury instructions on a bill of particulars.

The purpose of a bill of particulars is to inform the defendant of the charges they will face. In United States v. Francisco, the court noted that while submitting a bill of particulars to the jury isn’t reversible error, it is inadvisable. Other cases, such as United States v. Nathan and Pipkin v. United States, support this view, stating that reading the bill to the jury serves no purpose and could be erroneous. We agree with these findings and conclude the Superior Court committed no error by omitting the bill of particulars from jury instructions. E. Robinson's final appeal argument is that...

The Superior Court did not err in denying Robinson’s pretrial motion to dismiss the indictment, which argued the patient abuse statute was unconstitutionally vague and overbroad regarding emotional abuse. The court found the statute not vague, especially given the 'knowingly' requirement for abuse acts. We agree, as the statute does not reach constitutionally protected conduct. As the U.S. Supreme Court stated, a law must be examined for overbreadth first; if it doesn’t affect protected conduct, the vagueness challenge must show the law is unclear in all applications. Village of Hoffman Estates v. Flipside establishes this framework.

Thus, a law failing the overbreadth test may still face vagueness challenges under due process. We first assess the patient abuse statute’s legislative intent. In 1986, the General Assembly enacted it to address gaps in traditional criminal statutes, protecting long-term care facility patients from abuse, neglect, and mistreatment. 65 Del. Laws ch. 442 reflects this concern, ensuring comprehensive coverage for vulnerable individuals.

In 1986, the patient abuse statute was established under 16 Del. C. § 1136(a) (Supp.1990), aligning with prior laws aimed at safeguarding the dignity of nursing home and long-term care residents. See 16 Del. C. § 1121(1), which mandates treating patients with respect and recognizing their individuality. The statute targets vulnerable individuals who may be unable to report abuse due to dependency or disabilities, as highlighted in 65 Del. Laws ch. 442 (July 7, 1986). Victims often endure offensive language without recourse.

The patient abuse statute criminalizes knowingly abusing or neglecting residents in private or state facilities, as per 16 Del.C. § 1136(a). Abuse includes emotional harm, such as demeaning remarks or threats, outlined in 16 Del. C. § 1131(l)(b). This reflects the law's intent to protect vulnerable populations from mistreatment, as noted in Lehman v. City of Shaker Heights, 418 U.S. 298 (1974), where victims may have no escape from abusive speech.

Next, we examine whether the patient abuse statute infringes on protected speech under the First Amendment. While the First Amendment shields most speech, certain categories, like fighting words (Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire) or obscenity (Roth v. United States), are excluded. The Supreme Court has also limited speech inciting riots (Terminiello v. Chicago) or libel (Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc.), as noted in F.C.C. v. Pacifica Foundation, 438 U.S. 726 (1978).

Protected speech is not absolute; its permissibility varies by context, as stated in Cornelius v. NAACP Legal Defense Fund, 473 U.S. 788 (1985). The state may restrict offensive speech when a 'captive' audience cannot avoid it, as affirmed in Frisby v. Schultz, 487 U.S. 474. Thus, the patient abuse statute's limits on abusive language align with these legal precedents.

487, 108 S.Ct. 2495, 2503, 101 L.Ed.2d 420, 433 (1988); see, e.g., F.C.C. v. Pacifica Foundation, 438 U.S. 726, 748-49, 98 S.Ct. 3026, 3040-41, 57 L.Ed.2d 1073, 1093 (1978) (offensive radio broadcasts); Lehman v. City of Shaker Heights, 418 U.S. 298, 307-08, 94 S.Ct. 2714, 2719, 41 L.Ed.2d 770, 779-80 (1974) (ads on public transit); Rowan v. United States Post Office Dept., 397 U.S. 728, 736, 90 S.Ct. 14

84, 1490, 25 L.Ed.2d 736, 743 (1970) (unwanted mail); Kovacs v. Cooper, 336 U.S. 77, 86-87, 69 S.Ct. 448, 453-54, 93 L.Ed. 513 (1949) (loudspeaker vehicles); see also Cohen v. California, 403 U.S. 15, 21-22, 91 S.Ct. 1780, 1786, 29 L.Ed.2d 284, 291-92 (1971). In captive audience cases, the Supreme Court has weighed speakers' First Amendment rights against the State's duty to protect listeners' privacy. See, F.C.C. v. Pacifica Foundation, 438 U.S. 726, 748, 98 S.Ct. 3026, 3040, 57

L.Ed.2d 1073, 1093 (1978); Cohen v. California, 403 U.S. 15, 21-22, 91 S.Ct. 1780, 1786, 29 L.Ed.2d 284, 291-92 (1971); Rowan v. United States Post Office Dept., 397 U.S. 728, 736, 90 S.Ct. 1484, 1490, 25 L.Ed.2d 736, 743 (1970); Martin v. City of Struthers, 319 U.S. 141, 143, 63 S.Ct. 862, 863, 87 L.Ed. 1313, 1317 (1943). In F.C.C. v. Pacifica Foundation, 438 U.S. 726, 98 S.Ct. 3

026, 57 L.Ed.2d 1073 (1978), the Supreme Court affirmed the F.C.C.'s power to penalize broadcasters for obscene or indecent content, upholding its finding that the 'Filthy Words' monologue violated decency standards. See 47 U.S.C. § 326. The Court stated that 'indecent material broadcast into homes infringes on personal privacy more severely than it advances free speech rights.' F.C.C. v. Pacifica Foundation, 438 U.S. 726, 748, 98 S.Ct. 3026, 3040, 57 L.Ed.2d 1073, 1093 (1978). In Frisby v. Schultz, 487 U.S. 474,

In 108 S.Ct. 2495, 101 L.Ed.2d 420 (1988), the U.S. Supreme Court rejected an overbreadth and vagueness challenge to a content-neutral law banning targeted residential picketing in a public forum, citing the importance of safeguarding home privacy. The Court highlighted the State's compelling interest in maintaining domestic tranquility, noting, 'The home's sanctity as a refuge for the weary and vulnerable is paramount in a civilized society.' Frisby, 487 U.S. 474, 484, 108 S.Ct. 2495, 2502, 101 L.Ed.2d 420, 431 (1988). The ruling also affirmed protection for unwilling listeners, acknowledging that while people can often avoid unwanted speech elsewhere,

cf. Erznoznik v. Jacksonville, supra, 422 U.S. [205] at 210-211, 95 S.Ct. [2268], at 2273-74 [45 L.Ed.2d 125 (1975)]; Cohen v. California, 403 U.S. 15, 21-22, 91 S.Ct. 1780, 1786-1787, 29 L.Ed.2d 284 (1971), the home merits unique consideration. 'Being subjected to unwelcome speech in public spaces doesn’t justify similar intrusions at home.' Rowan v. Post Office Dept., 397 U.S. 728, 738, 90 S.Ct. 1484, 1491, 25 L.Ed.2d 736 (1970). Instead, the privacy afforded within one's residence, which the State may

legally safeguard, ensures freedom from unwanted intrusions. The Court has consistently upheld the right to exclude offensive speech from homes, as seen in cases like FCC v. Pacifica Foundation (1978) regarding radio broadcasts, Rowan (mailings), and Kovacs v. Cooper (1949) on loudspeakers. Frisby, 487 U.S. 474, 484-85, 108 S.Ct. 2495, 2502, 101 L.Ed.2d 420, 431-32 (1988). These precedents reinforce the State's authority to shield captive audiences from disruptive speech within their private spaces.

While residents may permit caregivers into their homes, this does not forfeit their privacy rights or expose them to offensive speech or behavior. Cf. F.C.C. v. Pacifica Foundation, 438 U.S. 726, 748, 98 S.Ct. 3026, 3040, 57 L.Ed.2d 1073, 1093 (1978) (even voluntary exposure to broadcasts doesn’t negate protections against indecent content). The State's interest in preserving residential tranquility remains paramount, ensuring individuals retain control over their personal environment.

The resident is protected against sudden and unexpected offensive intrusion. Additionally, we see no basis to differentiate between the privacy rights of patients and long-term care facility residents and those of homeowners, as established in Frisby. While the patient abuse statute is content-based regarding emotional abuse, covering speech that would otherwise be protected in public, we find that after balancing First Amendment rights against the state's interest in safeguarding the privacy of 'captive' individuals, the statute does not broadly infringe on protected speech. Thus, Robinson's overbreadth challenge is unsuccessful.

The patient abuse statute applies only within a 'facility.' Actions like ridiculing, demeaning, or cursing at patients or residents are punishable only if they occur in the facility, target a patient or resident, and are done knowingly. Liability is assessed objectively, based on whether reasonable people would view the conduct as derogatory or abusive in context, as noted in F.C.C. v. Pacifica Foundation.

With these guidelines, we assess Robinson's vagueness claim. A law must clearly define prohibited conduct to avoid arbitrary enforcement. Without proper standards, statutes risk allowing subjective enforcement, as highlighted in Kolender v. Lawson and Grayned v. City of Rockford.

In Colautti v. Franklin, the Court emphasized that vague statutes are less problematic if they include a mens rea requirement, ensuring individuals are not punished unknowingly. This principle, along with precedents like Village of Hoffman Estates v. Flipside, supports evaluating the statute's clarity.

455 U.S. 489, 499 n. 14, 102 S.Ct. 1186, 1193 n. 14, 71 L.Ed.2d 362, 372 n. 14 (1982). Considering the scope of the patient abuse statute and the specific circumstances of this case, we conclude that any reasonable individual would understand that Robinson's actions—such as the abusive language, falsely claiming Roe's clothes were stolen, mock spitting, the flower pot incident, and lifting her uniform to shake her buttocks while telling Roe to 'kiss her butt'—toward Jane Roe, an elderly wheelchair-bound patient, clearly meet the statutory definitions of 'ridiculing' and 'demeaning.' See Grayned v. City of Rockford, 408 U.S. 104, 112, 92 S.Ct. 2294, 2301, 33 L.Ed.2d 222,

230 (1972) (affirming an antinoise ordinance with clear, commonly understood terms). Furthermore, we find the State proved that Robinson acted 'knowingly,' meaning she was aware her conduct would likely subject Roe to scornful laughter and degradation. See 11 Del.C. § 231(b) (defining 'knowingly'); Webster's New World Dictionary (2nd college ed. 1986) defining 'ridicule' and 'demean.' Thus, Robinson, clearly covered by the statute, cannot argue it is vague for others whose conduct might edge toward its limits. Village of Hoffman Estates v. Flipside, Hoffman Est., 455 U.S. 489,

495, 102 S.Ct. 1186, 1191, 71 L.Ed.2d 362, 369 (1982). After thorough review, we hold the patient abuse statute defines emotional abuse clearly enough for ordinary people to understand prohibited conduct and provides adequate enforcement standards to prevent arbitrary application. Robinson's vagueness challenge therefore fails. Conclusion: The Superior Court's judgment is AFFIRMED. Jane Roe is a court-selected pseudonym. The original indictment stated: COUNT II. MISDEMEANOR PATIENT ABUSE under Title 16, Section 1131(a)(2) of the Delaware Code. CRYSTAL ROBINSON, on or about August 13, 1989, in New Castle County, Delaware, emotionally abused Jane Roe, a Layton Home patient, by ridiculing, demeaning, and making derogatory remarks toward her.

The Superior Court denied the motion to dismiss, stating: Denied. The charge is not vague, especially given the state of mind requirement. The State may amend the indictment to correct citations and clarify intent. This is over defense objection, as no prejudice exists—the State must prove intent regardless. See 11 Del.C. § 103(b), 251. Webster's Ninth New Collegiate Dictionary (1987) defines 'ridiculing,' 'demeaning,' and 'derogatory.' The State's bill of particulars detailed: Robinson placed a flower pot on the victim's head, lifted her dress, and said 'kiss my butt,' pretended to spit on her, and, with a co-defendant, threw towels and teased her using derogatory language.

The terms 'old hag' and 'bitch' are referenced. See earlier note 3. According to 16 Del.C. § 1131(4), a 'facility' encompasses any establishment mandated to be licensed under this chapter, as well as state-operated facilities offering long-term residential care. 16 Del.C. § 1136(a) specifies that knowingly abusing, mistreating, or neglecting a facility patient or resident is a class A misdemeanor. If such actions cause serious physical injury, it becomes a class D felony, and if they result in death, a class A felony. Refer to note 7. The U.S. Supreme Court has suggested stricter vagueness standards for laws impacting free speech rights, as seen in Village of Hoffman Estates v. Flipside, Hoffman Est., 455 U.S. 489, 499 (1982).

1 L.Ed.2d 362, 372 (1982). Legislatures often employ synonymous terms in criminal statutes without constitutional issues. Examples include 11 Del.C. § 1311(1), which defines 'harassment' as insulting, taunting, or alarming conduct, and Model Penal Code § 250.4(2). Similar rulings, like City of Seattle v. Huff, 111 Wash.2d 923 (1989), and State v. Cropley, Me.Supr. 544 A.2d 302 (1988), uphold statutes criminalizing harassment or torment. STIFTEL, President Judge. The City

of Newark filed a lawsuit against multiple defendant corporations for the costs of reconstructing a failed concrete drainage ditch. Defendant Edward H. Richardson Associates, Inc. ('Richardson'), an engineering firm, designed the sewer project using hydraulic data from the plaintiff. Richardson proposed four designs, and the plaintiff chose one requiring prestressed concrete planking. The construction contract was awarded to defendant Robert C. Peoples, while defendant Strescon Industries supplied the materials. Richardson delivered the plans in February 1966 and was paid by March 1966, with their final involvement ending in December 1966. The plaintiff paid for this last service in January 1967. The ditch collapsed in July 1975, and the complaint was filed on June 1, 1976. Richardson sought summary judgment under 10 Del.C. § 8127, a six-year statute of limitations, later also invoking 10 Del.C.

§ 8106, a three-year limitation. The plaintiff argued for the 'time of discovery' rule from Layton v. Allen, Del.Supr., 246 A.2d 794 (1968). The issue is whether the claim is time-barred. The Court ruled affirmatively, noting tort claims accrue at injury onset, as established in Freedman v. Beneficial Corp., D.Del., 406 F.Supp. 917 (1975). Here, Richardson allegedly caused harm by flawed design and material recommendations. The injury occurred when plans were finalized in 1966-1967, making 10 Del.C. § 8127 inapplicable.

This Act does not impact any legal claims that emerged or were established before its effective date, and for such claims, the limitations in place just before the Act's effective date will remain applicable. The Act took effect on June 18, 1970. Since the current case originated in the mid-1960s, it must be evaluated under the statute of limitations outlined in 10 Del.C. § 8106. This statute specifies that no action based on a promise or for damages from an injury without direct force or indirectly caused by the defendant can be filed more than three years after the cause of action arose. The plaintiff missed this deadline, filing the complaint on June 1, 1976, nearly a decade after the action accrued.

The plaintiff contends that the 'time of discovery' rule from Layton v. Allen and Isaacson, Stolper & Co. v. Artisan's Savings Bank governs this case. These rulings stated that in certain professional malpractice cases, where the injured party is unaware of the harm and the effects develop slowly, the statute of limitations only begins once the injury is detectable. The plaintiff argues the limitations period started in July 1975 when design flaws were revealed by a drainage ditch collapse. However, the Court disagrees, noting that Layton and Isaacson did not overturn the general principle that a plaintiff's lack of knowledge does not delay the accrual of a claim or pause the statute of limitations.

The Layton and Isaacson cases were narrow exceptions to the general rule, based on specific facts not present here. Layton involved a surgeon leaving a hemostat in a patient, with the Court explicitly limiting its ruling to such scenarios. Similarly, Isaacson extended the Layton doctrine to accountants and hinted at its applicability to attorneys, but emphasized that the 'time of discovery' rule is restricted and each case must be judged on its own merits. No precedents involving the defendant's type of service were cited, and related cases, such as Nardo and Lembert, rejected the 'time of discovery' rule. Unlike medical malpractice, the parties here could have contractually guaranteed design services for specific periods.

Given the above, the Court grants defendant Edward H. Richardson Associates, Inc.'s motion for summary judgment. IT IS SO ORDERED. HOLLAND, Justice: The defendant-appellant, Akbar Hassan-El, and Tyrone Guy, were indicted for Murder in the First Degree (intentional and felony murder) and Possession of a Firearm During Commission of a Felony.

The charges included ('PFDCF'), Attempted Robbery in the First Degree, and Conspiracy in the Second Degree. The State informed both defendants of its intention to pursue the death penalty if convicted of Murder in the First Degree. In November 2003, Hassan-El and Guy were jointly tried, but the trial resulted in a mistrial due to the jury's inability to reach a unanimous verdict. Subsequently, the State decided to try the defendants separately. Guy was retried first and found guilty on all counts. Hassan-El's retrial began on May 17, 2005, resulting in convictions for Murder in the First Degree (felony murder), Murder in the Second Degree, PFDCF, Attempted Robbery in the First Degree, and Conspiracy in the Second Degree. After a penalty hearing, the jury unanimously agreed on the felony-murder aggravating circumstance but voted 11-1 that mitigating factors outweighed the aggravating ones. On September 30, 20

05, Hassan-El received a life sentence for Felony Murder and an additional forty-five years at Level 5 for the other convictions. In his appeal, Hassan-El presents three arguments: first, that his felony murder conviction should be overturned as the homicide was not 'in furtherance of' the Attempted Robbery; second, that the jury instruction erroneously allowed a felony murder conviction if the death occurred during the robbery and was a 'foreseeable consequence'; and third, that the trial judge improperly admitted an out-of-court police interrogation of Robert Zayas, the State's key witness, which included officers' opinions on Zayas's truthfulness. While the first two arguments were deemed meritless, the third identified an error, though it was ruled harmless beyond a reasonable doubt. Thus, the Superior Court's judgments were affirmed.

On July 18, 2001, Wilmington Police responded to a 911 call reporting a shooting at 10th and Madison streets. They found Abdullah Alameri, who had been shot, unresponsive in an ice cream truck. He was pronounced dead shortly after being taken to Christiana Hospital. An autopsy revealed he died from a single gunshot wound to the chest. Police recovered a 9mm shell casing near the driver's seat and a 25-caliber casing under a floor mat, along with a 25-caliber projectile lodged in the passenger-side window track. After processing, the truck was returned to the Jack and Jill Company in Philadelphia, where an employee later found a 9mm bullet in a shirt at the back of the truck, which was handed over to the police.

Following the shooting, police conducted a neighborhood canvass and interviewed Keith Flowers, who mentioned Robert 'Whiteboy' Zayas. Investigators learned Zayas had bought a soda from the ice cream truck shortly before the shooting. Tracida Bailey also informed police that her boyfriend, Marcus Archy, might have information about the incident. Archy, who lived near the crime scene, was in jail by October 2001 and asked Bailey to relay his knowledge to the police.

During the trial, Archy stated that he was familiar with Zayas, Guy, and Hassan-El from the area. He recounted seeing the ice cream truck at 9th and Madison on the night of the shooting. Hassan-El mentioned that 'something crazy was about to happen' but didn’t elaborate. Archy observed Guy and Zayas on the sidewalk near Guy’s house on Madison, between 9th and 10th streets, and noticed Hassan-El approaching them. After hearing gunshots while walking home, Archy saw the three running toward 10th Street. Later, Hassan-El admitted to Archy that Guy had shot the ice cream man using a .25-caliber gun and that he had also fired a shot but missed.

Archy testified that he didn’t see any weapons on the three men that night and noted Hassan-El appeared shaken. Shortly after, Zayas also confirmed to Archy that Guy was the shooter. Keith Flowers, another witness, admitted during the trial that he initially avoided involvement but later disclosed he lived near Guy and Hassan-El. On the night of the incident, Flowers saw the three men near the ice cream truck before hearing gunshots. He didn’t witness the shooting but recognized the trio by their clothing as they fled east on 10th Street, prompting him to call 911.

Zayas testified that he had bought a soda and pretzel from the ice cream truck but found the soda frozen. While attempting to return it, he encountered Guy and Hassan-El hiding nearby. Hassan-El revealed a plan to rob the ice cream man, and Zayas noticed Guy had a .25-caliber gun. Reluctantly, Zayas flagged down the truck to exchange his soda. As he stood by the window, he saw Guy and Hassan-El approach with their faces covered, and Guy fired the shot that hit the victim.

Zayas described how Guy and Hassan-El, with t-shirts masking their faces, approached the truck. Guy was armed, and Hassan-El attempted to lift him through the window. After hearing two shots and seeing Guy shoot the ice cream man, all three fled down an alley. Zayas later checked on the victim and confided in Archy, expressing fear because he had flagged down the truck. The defense later moved to dismiss the felony murder charge, citing legal precedent from Williams v. State.

The trial judge rejected the motion. Hassan-El reiterates the same points in this appeal. At the time of the 2001 homicide, Delaware Code title 11, section 636(a)(2) defined 'felony-murder' as occurring when a person recklessly causes another's death during or in furtherance of a felony or attempted felony. This law was later revised. Hassan-El points out that while any felony or attempted felony qualifies, the statute mandated the death must occur 'in the course of and in furtherance of' the felony. Here, the attempted felony was robbery. Hassan-El admits the murder happened during the attempted robbery but questions whether it was 'in furtherance of' it. The 'in furtherance of' clause was interpreted by this Court in Williams, which stated the Delaware felony-murder statute requires the killing to both occur during and aid the felony.

The murder must not only happen during the felony but also advance it. The Chao opinion's claim that the 'in furtherance of' clause only identifies the killer is overruled. We uphold Weick's ruling that felony murder demands the killing helps progress the felony. Applying Williams, Hassan-El poses the appeal's central question: How did the murder advance the attempted robbery? The trial judge, denying acquittal, argued the killing met Williams' 'in furtherance of' standard: Mr. Alameri's death removed him as an obstacle, thus advancing the robbery. The defendants' decision to abandon the robbery afterward doesn’t negate this, as Williams doesn’t require the felony's completion.

Hassan-El claims the trial judge's interpretation of 'in furtherance of' relied on speculation that the killing enabled the robbery. He argues the judge ignored the fact that the perpetrators fled after shooting, questioning how the killing furthered the robbery. However, Hassan-El overlooks that the charge was based on attempted robbery, not its completion. His argument contradicts the statute, which explicitly includes homicides during attempted felonies. The opening brief's discussion on 'attempts' explains why the homicide furthered the attempted robbery, qualifying it as felony murder. Under the

Criminal Code, an 'attempt' occurs when the defendant takes a 'substantial step' toward committing the crime, defined as an act clearly demonstrating intent. Attempt laws aim to deter crime by punishing preparatory acts. The crime of 'attempt' is complete once a 'substantial step' is taken, regardless of the crime's completion. Hassan-El and Guy were clearly attempting robbery, as they took substantial steps: approaching the ice cream truck masked, armed, and firing immediately. The General Assembly accounted for incomplete felonies, and the felony-murder statute explicitly covers homicides during attempted felonies.

The act constitutes felony murder. When Hassan-El tried to rob the ice cream vendor, the resulting homicide was felony murder as it happened during and to advance the attempted felony, regardless of whether the robbery itself was completed. Hassan-El argues that the killing must have been accidental since the robbery wasn’t finished, claiming an accidental death doesn’t meet the intent required by the felony-murder law. While Hassan-El is right that an accident defense can argue for a lesser state of mind, it doesn’t automatically justify dismissing the felony-murder charge. The prosecution’s evidence strongly suggested Hassan-El’s guilt, as the killing occurred during an attempted robbery, leaving his intent for the jury to determine.

The trial record justifies the judge’s decision that the jury could reasonably find the shooting happened to advance the attempted robbery. Hassan-El admits in this appeal that, based on the evidence, he was an accomplice in the planned robbery. Though no evidence shows the participants intended a killing, Hassan-El carried a loaded gun and knew Guy had one when they approached the ice cream truck. Zayas testified both fired almost immediately. The defense asked the judge to instruct the jury that Hassan-El could only be guilty of felony murder if his intent matched the required state of mind, such as recklessness or criminal negligence regarding the risk of death. The defense also proposed an instruction conflicting with this Court’s ruling in Claudio v.

State. Following Claudio, the judge instructed the jury they could convict Hassan-El of felony murder as an accomplice if the killing was a foreseeable outcome of the robbery, even without specific intent. The jury was told that if they found a principal-accomplice relationship between Hassan-El and Guy to rob the victim, and if another crime in furtherance of the robbery was foreseeable, all participants were responsible, regardless of intent. Hassan-El now asks the Court to overturn Claudio, arguing the foreseeable consequence instruction was reversible error.

In Claudio, like here, the defendant was convicted of felony murder under accomplice liability. The Court ruled that under § 271, the focus isn’t on whether each accomplice intended murder, but whether they intended to aid the principal’s criminal conduct. The defendants didn’t need to specifically intend a killing—only that it was a foreseeable result of the felony. Delaware law requires the jury to agree a principal-accomplice relationship existed for the underlying felony, like robbery, but they don’t need to find the defendants specifically intended the consequential crime’s outcome.

For instance, in this scenario, the charges include murder and attempted murder. Id. In the Martin case, the defendants initially conspired to break into a home to steal firearms. Martin v. State, 433 A.2d [1025] at 1028. This Court ruled that both could be lawfully charged under 11 Del. C. § 271 for the murder carried out during the burglary. Hassan-El contends that this Court misapplied the accomplice liability statute in Claudio regarding felony murder. He asserts that in felony-murder cases, the 'offense' under section 271, which the accomplice aims to 'promote or facilitate,' is the murder itself, not the underlying robbery. This argument was dismissed in Hooks v. State, where the Court clarified that § 271 focuses on whether the accomplice intended to aid the principal’s actions, not whether they specifically intended the killing. The defendants need not have intended the fatal outcome.

The fatal outcome only needed to be a foreseeable result of their felonious actions for their intent as accomplices to encompass it. The facts in Hassan-El’s case align with the final ruling in Hooks: all defendants were aware guns would be used during the robbery. Thus, given the evidence, including the use of firearms, they could be convicted as accomplices to first-degree felony murder. Hassan-El further claims the 'foreseeable consequence' jury instruction, based on Claudio and Hooks, eliminates the need to prove mens rea for felony murder. This claim is unfounded. The 'foreseeable consequence' portion must be considered within the full jury charge, which included the trial judge’s instruction on mens rea: The third element requires the defendant to have acted recklessly, meaning they were aware of and disregarded a substantial risk of death. The risk must be so severe that ignoring it represents a gross deviation from reasonable behavior.

If someone 'is aware of and consciously ignores a substantial and unjustifiable risk of death resulting from their actions,' then death is a 'foreseeable consequence' of those actions. Conversely, if death is a 'foreseeable consequence' of certain conduct and the individual proceeds anyway, they act recklessly, as defined in the jury instructions. The principle in Claudio and Hooks is that an accomplice to a felony like armed robbery is also liable for any 'consequential crime,' such as murder, if it was a foreseeable result. In Claudio, the felony murder occurred during a knife-point robbery. In Hooks, it happened when the defendants, during an armed robbery, shot a store clerk. Here, the homicide took place during an attempted robbery by two masked individuals who fired their weapons. We uphold the rulings in Claudio and Hooks. The jury instructions in Hassan-El’s trial accurately reflected these established Delaware laws.

Section 3507 Violation Harmless Error Zayas testified for the State, stating that Guy and Hassan-El planned to rob the ice cream vendor. He claimed to witness the shooting and referenced a July 24, 2001, police interview. Before the jury heard Zayas’ out-of-court statement, the defense objected, arguing it violated 11 Del. C. § 3507 because it was a videotaped police interrogation, not a 'voluntary statement.' The trial judge overruled the objection but provided a limiting instruction. Hassan-El’s argument centers on whether a 'voluntary' statement under § 3507 includes a police-interrogation video. The trial court’s decision to admit the statement, with proper guidance to the jury, aligns with legal standards, rendering any error harmless.

A witness's statement under section 3507 encompasses the interaction between a police interrogator and a suspect or witness during an interrogation. Title 11, section 3507 of the Delaware Code states: (a) In a criminal case, a voluntary prior out-of-court statement from a witness who is present and cross-examined can serve as substantive evidence. This rule applies irrespective of whether the witness's in-court testimony aligns with the prior statement or if the introducing party demonstrates surprise. Hassan-El argues that the jury, upon viewing the full interrogation video of Zayas, could be improperly swayed by the police's expressed opinions on Zayas's truthfulness, which goes beyond the intended scope of section 3507.

Section 3507 permits a 'statement' as admissible evidence with a proper foundation, even if it would otherwise be excluded under Delaware's evidence rules. However, courts mandate a 'narrow interpretation' to protect a defendant's constitutional right to confront witnesses. An 'interpretive narrative' falls outside section 3507's scope—only the declarant's voluntary prior statement is admissible, not an officer's embellished retelling. Written statements are the best safeguard against misuse. Additionally, section 3507 prohibits including an officer's opinion on a witness's credibility.

In Holtzman, the jury saw a videotaped interrogation where an officer asserted her belief in the defendant's guilt and the victim's truthfulness. The court ruled such credibility assessments inadmissible under section 3507. Hassan-El claims his case mirrors Holtzman, as Zayas's interrogation contained repeated police assertions about knowing the truth and judging Zayas's honesty, which he argues improperly influenced the jury.

The officers' statements during Zayas's interrogation—claiming knowledge of events, other participants, and Zayas's involvement—exceeded section 3507's bounds. Phrases like 'We know what happened' and 'You have to be honest' inserted the officers' opinions on credibility, which the statute excludes. Hassan-El contends such narratives, akin to Holtzman, render the statements inadmissible under section 3507.

Both of them were involved, but we know who actually committed the crime. We’re aware of your actions, but you need to confess. POLICE OFFICER: Robert, who were those two men? Tell me, who were they? ZAYAS: I don’t know them, man! I don’t know them. POLICE OFFICER: We know them. You won’t reveal anything new, but we need to hear it from you. ZAYAS: I had nothing to do with it, man! POLICE OFFICER: Who were the two guys? Don’t say you don’t know—I know you do. POLICE OFFICER: Can you identify them? ZAYAS: No. POLICE OFFICER: You’re lying. POLICE OFFICER: What’s his name? ZAYAS: I don’t know... maybe ‘T.Y.’ or something. POLICE OFFICER: You’re doing fine, Robert... but you need to try harder.

help yourself. POLICE OFFICER: Give us his name. We know you know him. I’m tired of dropping hints. POLICE OFFICER: We know you’re more afraid of the other guy... because we know what he’s capable of. We know his nature... I understand the situation. We know who he is. POLICE OFFICER: Tell me their names. No more excuses—give me the names now. ZAYAS: It was T.Y. and someone named Ak, I think. POLICE OFFICER: Ak. Good. We’re getting somewhere. But you’re not done with Ak’s name. In this appeal, Hassan-El argues that these interrogation excerpts boosted Zayas’ credibility by implying his account matched what police ‘knew’ about the ice cream

vendor’s shooters. After the jury viewed the tape, the judge instructed them: Ladies and Gentlemen, regarding the tape, you heard detectives repeatedly say things like, ‘We know who was involved; we know who did it.’ These are common police tactics during interrogations. Such statements aren’t evidence and don’t indicate guilt. Disregard them entirely—they’re just investigative tools. However, you may consider the police’s actions when evaluating the witness’s credibility. Hassan-El accepts that curative instructions usually mitigate prejudice from inadmissible evidence but claims they failed here. Given the State’s strong case, we disagree. The police’s statements exceeded section 3507’s scope and should’ve been excluded. Recently, we dismissed the State’s argument that the full tape was needed for context as ‘unsubstantial.’ Section 3507 only allows ‘voluntary prior statements from a cross-examined witness.’ Admitting the police’s remarks warrants reversing Hassan-El’s convictions unless the error was ‘harmless beyond a reasonable doubt.’ The State must prove no prejudice occurred. Though the State didn’t argue harmless error in its brief, we may address it sua sponte. For this appeal, we asked both parties to brief the harmless error issue before en Banc oral arguments. The proper way to present section 3507 evidence is via the declarant’s written statement or a

redacted version. Hassan-El maintains the instructions couldn’t undo the prejudice. However, we find the State’s case strong enough to render the error harmless. We rule the police’s questioning violated section 3507 and should’ve been excluded. Our recent decision rejected the State’s ‘context’ argument as baseless. Only a witness’s voluntary prior statements, subject to cross-examination, are admissible under section 3507. Reversal is required unless the error was harmless beyond doubt, with the State bearing the burden of proof. Though the State didn’t raise harmless error, we may consider it independently. Pre-argument, we tasked the parties with briefing the issue en Banc. The ideal method for section 3507 evidence is a declarant’s written or redacted statement.

The recorded statement only included the declarant's exact words. However, given the limiting instruction and the strong evidence presented by the State, the inclusion of the police statements and questions was harmless beyond reasonable doubt. Thus, we conclude the error did not compromise Hassan-El's right to a fair trial. The Superior Court's rulings are upheld. See State v. Guy, 2005 WL 2436201, at *5, 2005 Del.Super.
