Rodney, J., delivering the Court's opinion: We will address these issues in order, as raised by the Relator. The Relator argues: 1(a) That under Art. II, Sec. 19 of the Delaware Constitution of 1897, the Act needed a two-thirds majority vote from all members elected to each House of the General Assembly, and (b) That under Art. VIII, Sec. 3, it required a three-fourths majority.

The Relator asserts that the Act did not meet either the two-thirds or three-fourths majority requirement and was thus invalidly passed. The defendants argue that the Court cannot review the vote count as recorded in the Legislative Journals, claiming the Enrolled Bill Doctrine, adopted by Constitutional Amendment, validates the Bill's passage upon enrollment. The Relator disputes this, maintaining that Courts can assess legislative votes when constitutional majority thresholds are at issue. This case does not require ruling on the Enrolled Bill Doctrine, as both parties agree the Act initially passed with a majority in each House and, after a gubernatorial veto, with three-fifths support. The first question is whether the Constitution mandated a higher initial vote for this Act, leading us to

The Relator's arguments, which we will address in sequence. (a) The Relator claims that Art. II, Sec. 19 required a two-thirds majority of all elected members in each House for the Bill's passage. The provision states: 'The General Assembly shall not enact any local or special law concerning fences; livestock straying; ditches; school district boundaries; or the establishment, modification, maintenance, or discontinuation of roads, highways, streets, lanes, or alleys; [however, the General Assembly may, by a two-thirds vote of all members elected to each House, pass laws related to roads or highways forming a continuous route through at least part of three state counties.]' The initial part, up to 'provided,' was the original 1897 text. The bracketed portion, starting with 'provided,' was proposed as an amendment in 19...

11 (Vol. 26, c. 2, Laws of Delaware), and enacted in 1913 (Vol. 27, c. 2). Before 1897, the Legislature held full authority to pass local and special laws on nearly any topic, with numerous examples in the Session Laws. Early on, many states recognized that unrestricted special or local legislation fostered legislative deals, favor-trading, and private over public interests. Today, most jurisdictions have constitutional restrictions on such laws. 25 R. C. L. 820; Note, 93 Am. St. Rep. 106. This led to Art. II, Sec. 19 of the Delaware Constitution, which barred the Legislature from passing special or local laws on certain matters, including roads and highways. The section explicitly prohibited laws concerning 'the laying out, opening, alteration, maintenance, or vacation, in whole or in part'

of any road, highway, street, lane, or alley.' The legislative majority—whether simple, two-thirds, or unanimous—was irrelevant. From 1897 to 1918, such laws were entirely forbidden. However, the Legislature retained full power to address these matters through general laws. This was the context when the Constitution was amended on March 17, 1913 (Vol. 27, c. 2). Defendants argue the 1911 amendment was tied to the duPont Highway's development, allowing special legislation if needed. Some history appears in Clendaniel v. Conrad, 3 Boyce (26 Del.) 549, 83 A. 1036, Ann. Cas. 1915B, 968. The timing lends credence

to this claim, but the amendment's effect, not its origin, is our focus. Defendants argue Art. II, Sec. 19 is irrelevant here, as the current Act deals not with 'laying out, opening, altering, maintaining, or vacating roads' but with reorganizing the Highway Department’s membership and related adjustments. Setting this aside, we examine the Constitutional Amendment. Defendants assert the Amendment solely permitted the Legislature, by a two-thirds vote, to pass special or local laws for roads or highways spanning portions of all three counties. They claim that before the Amendment, only general laws on roads were allowed; afterward, special or local laws for such continuous roads became possible. The current Act is acknowledged as general. The Relator agrees that pre-Amendment, only general road laws were permissible, and post-Amendment, special or local laws for cross-county roads required a two-thirds vote.

However, the Relator argues the Amendment restricts all laws, including general ones, for such roads, mandating a two-thirds vote. We disagree with this interpretation. The Relator concedes the Amendment grants power for special or local laws on cross-county roads but insists it also limits general laws, requiring a supermajority. We find this view unsupported. The Amendment’s language focuses on enabling special or local legislation, not constraining general laws. The Legislature’s authority to pass general road laws remains unchanged, while the Amendment merely adds an exception for specific cases.

There is no indication that the Constitutional Amendment was meant to restrict the Legislature's ability to enact general laws concerning roads or highways. It would be unreasonable to interpret the Amendment as requiring a two-thirds majority for roads spanning multiple counties while allowing simple majority votes for non-continuous roads. The Amendment's intent was to permit the Legislature, with a two-thirds vote, to pass local or special laws for continuous roads across three counties, not to limit general legislation on the matter. The Act in question did not necessitate a two-thirds vote under these provisions.

Article II, Section 19.1(b) addresses the Relator's claim that the Act needed a three-fourths majority vote under Article VIII, Section 3 of the Constitution, which mandates such a vote for borrowing money or creating state debt. The Act in question does not mention borrowing or debt, making this constitutional provision potentially irrelevant unless bonds or debt are issued. However, the Relator's arguments are examined thoroughly. The Act modifies the Highway Commission's membership and includes unrelated provisions, with no reference to debt creation.

The Relator argues that since the original State Highway Act allowed borrowing and debt creation, requiring a three-fourths majority, any amendment to it must also pass with the same majority. The Relator asserts that amendments or repeals of such Acts must meet the original voting threshold. While the term 'equal dignity' might imply similar formality, it does not inherently specify vote requirements, as seen in prior cases. If 'equal dignity' refers to procedural formality, we agree, but the Relator conflates repeal and amendment, focusing solely on the latter in this context.

The Relator contends that any amendment to a debt-authorizing statute, originally passed with a three-fourths majority, must also secure a three-fourths vote. No distinction is made between repealing and amending such laws. Our focus is on the voting requirement for amending an Act that initially needed a three-fourths majority. The broader question of whether debt-related Acts can only be repealed or amended with a similar majority remains unaddressed here, as it is not directly relevant to the current case.

A debt incurred by the State, which necessitates a three-fourths majority for approval, cannot be entirely revoked by a smaller vote. The rationale behind the higher vote requirement—to shield the State from potentially unwise debts and ensure broad public support—loses relevance when repealing the Act, as it eliminates any chance of the debt being imposed, reverting to the pre-authorization state. A simple majority is the standard legislative vote, with higher thresholds only mandated by the Constitution in specific cases. Article II, Section 10 of the Constitution affirms this by stating that no bill can pass without a majority vote in each House. A repeal Act is essentially new legislation and, unless it involves constitutional provisions needing more than a majority, a majority vote should suffice. No opposing authority has been presented or discovered through thorough research.

In Ohio, it was explicitly ruled that a two-thirds vote is not needed to repeal an act originally requiring such a vote under the constitution. Cases like State of Ohio v. Voris and Backenstoe v. State support this. Now, we must determine the vote threshold for amending the State Highway Department Act. The 1935 Revised Code’s Chapter 166, comprising five articles and forty-four sections, includes the Act in question, which amends three sections unrelated to debt or bonds. The original 1917 Act, with twenty sections, initially required a three-fourths vote due to debt-related provisions, though most sections were unrelated. Over twenty amendments followed, some requiring a three-fourths vote for debt-related changes, while others passed with a simple majority.

Many of the original Act’s sections did not involve debt creation, and subsequent amendments often required only a majority vote. For instance, amendments altering the Highway Department’s personnel, like replacing the Governor with the Secretary of State (Vol. 32, c. 52) or reversing this change (Vol. 36, c. 79), were passed without a three-fourths majority. The Relator argues that past amendments’ legality isn’t proven by their passage alone, as they might have been unlawful. Instead of relying on precedent, we analyze the principle: the original 1917 Act needed a three-fourths vote solely due to its debt provisions. Had it lacked such provisions, a majority vote would have sufficed.

If the 1917 Highway Act had passed without a three-fourths vote, only the debt-related portions would have been invalid, not the entire Act. The three-fourths requirement applied only to sections creating State debt, as mandated by the Constitution. Thus, amendments unrelated to debt, like those modifying the Department’s composition, could legally pass with a majority vote. The original Act’s validity hinged on the higher vote for debt provisions, while other sections required only standard majority approval. This principle underscores that amendments without debt implications need not meet the same stringent vote threshold.

If they had received it, the part of the law needing only a majority vote would have remained valid. A fundamental rule in interpreting statutes is that if a law includes separable provisions, with one unconstitutional and the other not, only the unconstitutional part is void, while the rest stands. Cases like Coleman v. Rhodes and State ex rel. Green v. Isaacs support this. While certain matters, like state debt creation, require a three-fourths vote and cannot be expanded by a lesser vote, separable parts of a statute needing only a majority vote can be amended by that same majority.

If a part of the law initially required only a majority vote, there’s no reason it can’t later be amended by that same majority, even if other sections needed a higher vote. This position is supported by logic and precedent. For instance, Mendelson v. Miller ruled that an act originally needing a two-thirds vote could be amended by a lesser vote if the changes were minor. Similarly, Dahlsten v. Anderson held that once a court is established, procedural adjustments can be made under standard legislative rules. The cited cases do not contradict this principle.

After reviewing the Relator’s references, such as Palmer v. Bank of Zumbrota and Cottrell v. Town of Lenoir, we find no conflict with our stance. Even if bond issuance or state debt were at issue here, the Act’s validity isn’t undermined by lacking a three-fourths vote per Article VIII, Section 3. Next, we address the Act’s title, which states it amends Chapter 166 of the 1935 Delaware Code regarding the State Highway Department’s reorganization.

It is claimed the title violates Article II, Section 16 of the Constitution, which mandates that a bill’s title must reflect its single subject. Critics argue that altering member terms and granting temporary vacancy-filling powers stray from the title’s focus on reorganization. Delaware precedents, like In re Cypress Farms Ditch, clarify that a title need not detail every provision but must reasonably indicate the bill’s purpose, which this one does.

If the title is structured to inform those concerned about the legislative subject matter, prompting a reasonable investigation into the Bill's contents. We believe that an Act titled 'Reorganization of the State Highway Department' adequately alerts legislators and the public that the Department's structure and operations may undergo changes, encouraging further scrutiny. We find the statute valid in terms of its title. 3. We now address the third and final issue raised by the Relator: whether the Act unlawfully encroaches on the executive powers constitutionally granted to the Governor. The Court, in its current composition, previously examined this matter in State ex rel. Morford v. Emerson, 1 Terry (40 Del.) 233, 8 A. 2d 154. We uphold the conclusions drawn there and will not elaborate extensively. Numerous precedents affirm that constitutional provisions generally constrain rather than confer legislative authority, unless explicitly stated otherwise. Citing additional sources for these principles is unnecessary, as they are widely accepted. However, since the current Relator, while seeking the same outcome, introduces a novel argument, we will briefly address this new perspective.

The current Relator does not argue that appointment powers belong solely to the Governor; they acknowledge that the Legislature can establish legislative or quasi-legislative offices and appoint individuals to them. However, the Relator asserts that legislative appointment authority is limited to legislative bodies, while the Governor holds the exclusive right to appoint officials in executive departments. Assuming the State Highway Department is an executive entity, the Relator concludes that the Governor should appoint its officers. Without deviating from our prior stance, we question when the management, upkeep, and jurisdiction over roads or highways shifted from legislative to executive control. In 1 Elliott on Roads and Streets, § 509, it is stated: 'Authority over roads and streets lies with the Legislature, and unless restricted by constitutional provisions, this power is nearly absolute.' This view is universally supported. Yet, one need not look beyond this State's history for evidence. Since its inception, the Legislature has exercised complete jurisdiction over roads and highways. Every volume of our statutes up to 1897 contains extensive general and special laws on public and private roads. The overwhelming volume of such legislation partly prompted the constitutional requirement that legislative control over roads be exercised through general laws, except under specific conditions requiring a two-thirds majority.

The 1897 Constitution acknowledges the Legislature's role in enacting general laws for roads and highways, and subsequent legislation has adhered to this mandate. Before 1897, the Legislature frequently passed special Acts designating commissioners for specific roads. While general laws have since empowered courts to appoint commissions and oversee highways, these measures have not stripped the Legislature of its jurisdiction. Today, it can legislate on roads and highways through general laws or special Acts meeting constitutional voting requirements. What evidence suggests the State Highway Department is an executive rather than a legislative body? Setting aside the voting requirements and the distinction between general and special Acts, we find no authority contesting that highway control is a legislative function. Highways are vital to the State, and the Legislature has always regulated their establishment, modification, maintenance, and discontinuation. This control is often delegated to local governments or, in some cases, to private or quasi-public entities like toll road operators.

Roads and highways serve as the State's lifelines, and their governance has historically been a legislative prerogative. The Legislature retains the authority to delegate this responsibility to local jurisdictions or private entities, but such delegation does not diminish its overarching control. The State Highway Department's classification as an executive body lacks substantiation, as no credible authority disputes the Legislature's inherent jurisdiction over highways. The constitutional framework and historical practice consistently affirm that highway management is a legislative function, whether exercised directly or through delegated mechanisms. Thus, the Relator's assumption that the Department is an executive entity is unfounded, and the Governor's exclusive appointment authority over its offices remains unsupported by legal precedent or historical practice.

Through legislative measures, the Legislature can oversee highways directly via entities like a State Highway Department, unless restricted by constitutional provisions. The Delaware State Highway Act mandates the Department to gather detailed information on current and required roads to create a cohesive, extensive, and enduring highway network that meets the public's needs. The Act also requires the Department to both construct and 'maintain' the highways, with maintenance encompassing repairs and ensuring the roads remain a functional public system. The Relator notes that the Highway Department's responsibilities extend beyond roads, including oversight of the State Police and Motor Vehicle Department, with the State Police tasked to prevent violence and enforce laws protecting people and property, as detailed in the Revised Code.

According to the Revised Code of 1935, the Department can appoint traffic officers, known as State Police, primarily responsible for enforcing laws on vehicle weight, speed, and operation on public roads. These officers possess police powers akin to sheriffs and constables, acting as peacekeepers statewide to curb violence and uphold safety laws. The Relator highlights that these powers and duties apply specifically under the 'traffic officers' designation, with their main role being highway traffic regulation. Additionally, the Relator points out that a 1939 legislative act placed the Motor Vehicle Department under the Highway Department's control, though its functions remain tied to highways and traffic regulation.

The Relator acknowledges the Legislature's authority to appoint officials for quasi-legislative roles. We conclude that the State Highway Department serves as a legislative, not executive, body, so its regulation does not infringe on executive powers. The statute's validity is upheld, and judgment is awarded to the respondents for their costs, as no constitutional violations were found.

HERLIHY, Judge. Defendant Joseph Taye ('Taye') faces multiple charges, including first-degree murder, stemming from a 2008 vehicle incident that killed Michelle Smith ('Smith'), a firefighter aiding an injured motorcyclist. Count I alleges Taye recklessly caused Smith's death while she performed her duties, mirroring 11 Del. C. § 636(a)(4). No fire was present, and Smith wasn't firefighting when struck. Since the Criminal Code lacks a 'firefighter' definition, Taye seeks dismissal, arguing the term should follow its common or dictionary meaning.

In this context, the dictionary defines a firefighter as someone who extinguishes fires. The key question is whether Smith was performing firefighter duties when she was hit. The Court rules that this issue cannot be resolved based on the current record and must be determined at trial. Background details reveal that on December 20, 2008, Edward Reiss was riding his motorcycle on Route 13 in New Castle County when he lost control near School Lane. Reiss and his bike came to a stop in the left lane. Emergency services arrived, and Smith, an ambulance driver, parked in the southbound lane with her emergency lights activated. She began treating Reiss, while Officer Jordan Miller positioned his police car behind the ambulance, also with lights flashing. Suddenly, a speeding silver BMW 760 struck the police car, ran over Reiss, and hit Smith, throwing her several feet down the road.

The damaged BMW sped away erratically before crashing on the shoulder of Route 13. A witness stopped behind the BMW and observed a light-colored Honda Accord pull up beside it. The Honda's driver dragged the BMW's occupant, who seemed unable to walk, into their car and fled. Police later identified the BMW as belonging to Tracey Young, who claimed her paraplegic boyfriend, Taye, never drove and she didn’t know his whereabouts during the incident. Fingerprints in the BMW matched Taye, and investigators found his license was revoked. They also discovered a wooden stick in the car, consistent with Taye’s known method of driving. Smith and Reiss were rushed to Christiana Hospital in critical condition; Smith died two days later, while Reiss survived but suffered severe injuries.

Reiss’s injuries resulted from both the motorcycle accident and the BMW’s impact. Discovery in Taye’s criminal case reveals his attorney claims Smith was driving an ambulance for the Delaware City Fire Department when struck. The affidavit states Smith had been a volunteer firefighter since 2004, completed basic firefighter and first responder training, but never actively fought fires. Instead, she primarily served as a first responder and planned to pursue EMT certification. Taye’s motion argues Smith’s legal status as a 'firefighter' at the time of her death is pivotal, as it could upgrade a manslaughter charge to first-degree murder. He notes the Criminal Code lacks a definition for 'firefighter' and urges the Court to adopt the common dictionary meaning: a fire department member who fights fires.

Taye argues Smith was providing medical care, not fighting fires, aligning with EMT duties. While acknowledging her firefighter training, he insists she never acted in that role for the fire department. Taye contends a 'firefighter' should be defined by their actual duties, not training. At the time, Delaware law did not protect EMTs under the relevant statute. Thus, Taye asserts the first-degree murder charge should be dismissed. The State opposes, arguing Smith’s firefighter status during the incident is a factual question for the jury, rendering the motion premature.

The issue may be considered premature and dismissed by this Court to be addressed during trial. Alternatively, the State counters the defendant's statutory interpretation claims, arguing that Taye's narrow definition of 'firefighter' is overly rigid and mistaken. The State emphasizes that it does not base its argument solely on Smith's firefighting training to invoke the aggravating language in 11 Del. C. § 636(a)(4). It argues that a firefighter's role extends beyond fire suppression, and Smith's responsibilities, such as ambulance operation and medical assistance, still qualify her for statutory protection. The case involves Taye, charged with first-degree murder for recklessly causing the death of Smith, a firefighter, who was providing medical aid at a vehicle accident with no fire present. The term 'firefighter' in this murder statute is undefined, serving as a key factor that elevates the charge from manslaughter to first-degree murder.

The Court must decide whether the State can presently demonstrate that Smith was a 'firefighter.' Both parties approach this as a matter of statutory interpretation, applying relevant legal principles. The Court's role is to discern and uphold legislative intent, especially under the Criminal Code, where statutes must be interpreted fairly to ensure justice and fulfill legal objectives. These objectives, outlined in 11 Del. C. § 201, include prohibiting harmful conduct, providing clear warnings of prohibited actions, defining offenses, distinguishing between major and minor crimes, and ensuring public safety through deterrence and rehabilitation. The Court must apply these principles to interpret the term 'firefighter' fairly.

Delaware precedent supports using dictionary definitions to clarify undefined statutory terms. Here, 'firefighter' is commonly defined as 'a person who fights fires,' which Taye relies on for his argument. The State agrees the term's common meaning applies but argues it broadly includes emergency responders, even those not directly involved in firefighting. Both parties cite Wikipedia to support their interpretations. A similar issue arose in Cephas v. State, where the Supreme Court had to define 'pregnant,' also undefined in the Criminal Code. The defendant, Cephas, was charged with assaulting a woman with a molar pregnancy, a non-viable condition lacking fetal tissue.

The State prosecuted Cephas for assaulting a 'pregnant female,' but the trial court did not define the term for the jury. On appeal, the Supreme Court rejected the State's argument, using a dictionary to define 'pregnant' as 'carrying unborn offspring.' Since a molar pregnancy does not meet this definition, the Court ruled that Cephas had not assaulted a pregnant woman, overturning the conviction.

The pregnant female as defined by the statute led the lower Court to err in denying Cephas's motion for acquittal. The Court agrees that the dictionary's definition of 'firefighter' may not be as broad as the State claims. While the State argues that the term now includes various duties beyond fire suppression, Delaware law requires undefined terms to retain their plain dictionary meaning. Absent legislative clarification, the dictionary offers 'fair warning of prohibited conduct.' Thus, Smith's classification as a firefighter under 11 Del. C. § 636(a)(4) hinges on her involvement in firefighting. However, the factual record is currently insufficient to determine her role, and Taye's affidavit states Smith only performed medical duties, never firefighting.

The State contends it will prove Smith was a firefighter but provides no details beyond her ambulance driving on December 20th. Both parties agree Smith handled medical tasks for the fire company. With unresolved factual disputes, dismissing the indictment is premature. Due to the incomplete record, the Court denies Taye's motion without prejudice, leaving the question open for reconsideration later in the proceedings. Additionally, the Court addresses statutory interpretation concerns, noting that killing a firefighter on duty is a death penalty aggravator in Delaware. Though the State opted against seeking the death penalty here, the undefined term 'firefighter' risks undermining the murder statute's intent.

Initially, the State debated pursuing the death penalty but declined. Yet, without a clear definition of 'firefighter,' the issue persists, potentially weakening the murder statute's aggravating circumstance. The Court also acknowledges the Governor's recent amendment to 11 Del. C. § 636(a)(4), adding EMTs, paramedics, and others as protected classes—though the amendment doesn't apply here. Regrettably, 'firefighter' remains undefined, leaving dictionary definitions as the default. HB 204 failed to define the newly added roles, and no Criminal Code definitions were provided. This omission may have worsened the ambiguity, as all protected persons except law enforcement officers lack clear definitions.

Smith's actions at the accident scene align with the protected duties these laws aim to safeguard. For contrast, 'law-enforcement officer' is meticulously defined in 11 Del. C. § 222(14). A similar definition for 'firefighter' would have clarified legislative intent beyond dictionary reliance. Given modern firefighting's complexity, statutory updates may be necessary to reflect firefighters' diverse responsibilities. The drafters recognized this need for clarity when defining 'law enforcement officer.' The Court notes Florida's broader statutory definition of 'firefighter,' which surpasses traditional dictionary interpretations.

The firefighter's role is broadened to include additional responsibilities, offering them protection. This could serve as a useful foundation, given that many firefighters often attend accident scenes without fires. For the reasons stated, the Defendant's Motion to Dismiss Count I of the Indictment is DENIED WITHOUT PREJUDICE. First-degree murder applies when someone recklessly kills a law-enforcement officer, corrections employee, or firefighter on duty. References include Cpl. William Nottingham's affidavit and other cited sections.

Del.2008 case citation and references to Delaware Code sections 203 and 221(c). Dickerson v. State is cited, along with dictionary definitions emphasizing firefighting. While Wikipedia can provide quick information, its open-editing nature makes it unreliable for legal purposes. Additional case law and statutory references are included.

Delaware Code section 612(a)(9) is mentioned. The doctor's testimony in the case was later deemed insufficient on appeal. References to Cephas and other cases highlight dictionary usage for undefined terms. The Court expresses concern over an affidavit containing discovery-based information.

State v. Carletti and Delaware Code section 4209(e)(l)c are cited. House Bill 204, signed in 2009, is discussed, noting Michele Smith's non-certified EMT status. The bill's synopsis clarifies her role as a firefighter, but retroactive application is unconstitutional. The definition of 'law-enforcement officer' is expanded.

The Attorney General along with their deputies, sheriffs and their deputies, agents from the State Division of Alcohol and Tobacco Enforcement, correctional officers, state and municipal fire marshals who are graduates of a Delaware Police Academy accredited by the Council on Police Training, sworn Wilmington Fire Department members who graduated from an accredited Delaware Police Academy, environmental protection officers, enforcement agents of the Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Control, and constables. The Court recognizes that Wilmington Fire Department members who graduated from an accredited police academy are law enforcement officers under 11 Del. C. § 222(14), though this does not apply to all firefighters statewide. 'Firefighter' here refers to any state public employee tasked with fire extinguishing, life or property protection, or enforcing fire prevention codes and related laws. Fla. Stat. Ann. § 784.

Under §.07(1)(b) (West 2007), Judge Keil's opinion outlines the procedural background of Christopher W. Albert (Father) filing for custody of Jason M. A. (Child, born 10/9/74), while Krystal R. Phillips (Mother) moves to dismiss, arguing Delaware lacks jurisdiction under the Uniform Child Custody Jurisdiction Act (13 Del.C. § 1901-1925). Father opposes the motion. The parties divorced in Missouri on May 28, 1981, with custody granted to Mother. The Child lived with her in Colorado and Alabama until June 30, 1989, when he moved to Delaware with Father. Disputes arise over when the Child left Delaware to return to Mother, with Father claiming September 21, 1990, and Mother asserting May 30, 1990, followed by a stay with his step-father in Alabama and a brief return to Delaware.

Mother states the Child permanently left Delaware in September 1990 and has been in various hospitals since December 1990 for emotional, behavioral, and medical treatment, including at the Desert Hills Center in Tucson, Arizona, where he remains. The core issue is whether Delaware has jurisdiction under the UCCJA (13 Del.C. § 1901-1925) to rule on Father's custody petition. Mother contends Delaware lacks jurisdiction and suggests Colorado as a more suitable forum, while Father argues Delaware has jurisdiction under the UCCJA and is the appropriate venue.

The Court's analysis begins with UCCJA Section 14 (13 Del.C. § 1914), which governs modifying another state's custody decree. Delaware may only modify if the original state lacks jurisdiction or declines to act, and Delaware has jurisdiction. Neither party claims Missouri retains jurisdiction, as no significant ties remain there. The Court finds Delaware has jurisdiction, satisfying § 1914's requirements, and thus may modify the custody arrangement.

Under the foreign decree, Section Three of the UCCJA outlines four specific 'tests' to establish a court's subject matter jurisdiction in custody disputes. Yost v. Johnson, Del.Supr., 591 A.2d 178 (1991); 13 Del.C. § 1903. Only two of these tests are relevant in this case. The first states that jurisdiction exists if: (1) This State (a) Is the child's home state when the proceeding begins; or (b) Was the child's home state within six months prior to the proceeding, and the child is absent due to removal or retention by a custodian, with a parent or guardian still residing here. 13 Del.C. § 1903. The key question is whether Delaware was the child's home state in the six months preceding the proceeding. Home state jurisdiction is typically favored over other grounds. Grayson v. Grayson, Del.Fam., 454 A.2d

1297 (1982); See also Comment UCCJA Section Three, reprinted in R. CROUCH, INTERSTATE CUSTODY LITIGATION: A GUIDE TO USE AND COURT INTERPRETATION OF THE UNIFORM CHILD CUSTODY JURISDICTION ACT (1981) (hereinafter CROUCH). If Delaware is not Jason's home state, no other state qualifies, as he hasn't lived in any single state for six consecutive months since leaving Delaware in September 1990. Accepting Father's timeline, Delaware barely meets the home state criteria. Under Mother's timeline, Delaware cannot be considered the home state, requiring jurisdiction to rely on other grounds. The Court, however, finds it unnecessary to resolve this dispute, as it determines Delaware may assert jurisdiction under 13 Del. C. § 1903(2), the 'significant connection' test. This test grants jurisdiction if: (2) It is in the child's best interest for the court to assume jurisdiction because

(a) The child and at least one parent or contestant have a significant tie to this State; and (b) Substantial evidence regarding the child's care, protection, training, and relationships is available here. 13 Del. C. § 1903. Jason resided in Delaware continuously from June 30, 1989, to at least May 30, 1990, and intermittently thereafter. Given his frequent moves, this represents a substantial period in one state. He attended school and worked in Delaware, and his Father still lives here. These facts meet § 1903(2)(a). However, the analysis continues. Section 1903(2)(b) requires substantial evidence about the child's welfare. Without such evidence, jurisdiction under § 1903(2) cannot be exercised. Father possesses records and reports on Jason's needs, as

well as employment and school records from Jason's time in Delaware. He can also testify about Jason's future care if the child returns. The Court finds sufficient evidence exists in Delaware to decide the custody dispute. With § 1903(2)(a) and § 1903(2)(b) satisfied, the Court rules Delaware has subject matter jurisdiction under the UCCJA. Mother contends Jason has strong ties to Colorado and that evidence about his care is available there, arguing Colorado, not Delaware, has jurisdiction under 13 Del.C. § 1903(2). The Court acknowledges Jason's connections to Colorado and the evidence there but disagrees with Mother's conclusion that only one state can have jurisdiction. The Court rejects this view, noting Subsection (2) explicitly allows concurrent jurisdiction. See Comment UCCJA Section Three, reprinted in

CROUCH, supra. Both Delaware and Colorado have jurisdiction under the 'significant connection' test in this case. Although multiple states can have jurisdiction, only one can act on it. This leads to Mother's alternative argument of forum non conveniens. After confirming this Court's jurisdiction, the Court evaluates Mother's claim that Delaware is an inconvenient forum under 13 Del.C. § 1907. The UCCJA allows a court to refuse jurisdiction if it finds another state more suitable, prioritizing the child's best interests. Key factors include: (1) whether another state is or was the child's home; (2) if another state has stronger ties to the child or family; (3) if substantial evidence about the child's welfare is more accessible elsewhere; (4) if parties agreed on another appropriate forum; and (5) if jurisdiction here conflicts with § 1901's purposes.

Subsection (c)(3) is particularly relevant here. The pleadings show Jason faces severe emotional, behavioral, and medical issues, leading to hospitalizations and youth center stays. This treatment began after he moved to Colorado, where Mother still lives and where Jason will likely return after discharge. The Court acknowledges that Father's petition hinges on Jason's health, requiring expert testimony on his condition, treatment, and prognosis. Reliable information is crucial for custody decisions, especially for children with special needs. Since Jason's treating professionals are in Colorado and Arizona, evidence about his health is more accessible there than in Delaware. Thus, the Court believes deferring to Colorado courts serves Jason's best interests.

Mother also seeks reimbursement for legal fees and travel costs under 13 Del.C. § 1907(g), which permits such awards if the forum is clearly inappropriate. A forum non conveniens ruling alone doesn’t mandate fee assessment. Here, Father’s choice of Delaware wasn’t unreasonable enough to justify this request. The Court’s ruling: (1) grants Mother’s Motion to Dismiss; (2) dismisses Father’s custody petition; and (3) denies Mother’s request for fees and expenses. IT IS SO ORDERED.

UPON REARGUMENT: The Court reviewed Father’s Motion for Reargument and Mother’s Reply, denying the Motion. The May 22, 1991, Opinion dismissed Father’s custody modification petition, deferring to Colorado’s jurisdiction under the UCCJA, particularly § 1907 on forum non conveniens. Father’s first argument reiterates facts without justifying reargument. His second claim—that Colorado is equally inconvenient—was already rejected in the May 22 decision, which deemed Delaware an inconvenient forum.

The evidence, both past and present, supports this conclusion. The Court also dismissed Father's final argument, ruling that both States had subject matter jurisdiction over the custody dispute and that Colorado was the more suitable venue. Finding no validity in Father's Motion for Reargument, the Court denied it. IT IS SO ORDERED. In reality, Father seeks a custody modification to have the Child primarily reside with him. Mother later filed a Response to Father's Response to the Motion to Dismiss, which was removed from the record as an unauthorized filing. Father filed his custody petition just before Delaware would no longer be Jason's home state (assuming Father's claims about Jason's residency were true). STEELE, Chief Justice. This case concerns a plea deal and a failed undercover operation. Edwin Scarborough, the defendant-appellant, was arrested on drug charges in 2004. Over a year, he repeatedly offered to assist police in investigating drug dealers in exchange for leniency. In September 2005, after previous efforts fell through, Scarborough sent a 'jail-house' letter to the prosecutor.

naming individuals he could inform on. This led to a plea agreement—part written, part oral. However, despite Superior Court Rule 11(c), which mandates at least an in-camera disclosure of the full plea deal, only the written portion was presented to the court. The written agreement required Scarborough to plead guilty and testify against his co-defendants. The oral part involved Scarborough acting as an informant and the State refraining from filing a habitual offender petition. When Scarborough's efforts failed to meet police expectations, the State moved to declare him a habitual offender. Scarborough then sought to withdraw his plea. A Superior Court judge denied the motion, citing the written agreement, Scarborough's court statements, and both parties' positions. The judge ignored the undisclosed oral terms and has since refused to acknowledge its existence. After oral arguments, we remanded the case, instructing the Superior Court to

determine the oral agreement's exact terms, whether Scarborough fulfilled or could have fulfilled them, and if any factual issues led to his misunderstanding of the plea's consequences. Despite these instructions, the judge's post-remand order skipped the first question entirely. During the appeal, both the State and Scarborough's attorney admitted the oral agreement existed but was never disclosed. Since neither disputed its existence, the judge's task was to clarify its terms and assess fulfillment. Instead, the judge ruled Scarborough never entered a performable contract. On remand, the judge again denied Scarborough's motion to withdraw his plea. Deciding Scarborough failed to perform without first defining his obligations is illogical. By ignoring our remand instructions, the judge abused his discretion. Now, we must reconstruct the oral agreement's terms from the remand hearing testimony. After reviewing the record, we find the oral agreement supplemented the written plea, requiring Scarborough to

provide information on other drug dealers ('work') and the State to avoid seeking habitual offender status. In prosecutorial terms, 'work' means cooperating with police to gather evidence on criminals, often for leniency. In Delaware's vague drug enforcement cooperation deals, 'work' is defined post-hoc by police, despite their absence during the agreement's formation. Here, the parties left 'work' undefined, leaving it to police who weren't part of the oral agreement's drafting. Regrettably, neither the prosecutor nor defense counsel ensured clarity, leading to this dispute.

A Superior Court judge was kept uninformed by the parties' counsel, either deliberately or negligently, due to their noncompliance with Superior Court Rule 11(e)(2). Here, we determine that the State, contrary to its implied obligation of good faith, unjustly dismissed the 'work' proposed by Scarborough, thereby releasing him from his duties. While Scarborough attempts to retract his guilty plea, the better solution is to uphold the State's commitment to refrain from pursuing habitual offender status. Thus, the Superior Court judge's ruling against Scarborough's plea withdrawal is AFFIRMED, his sentence is VACATED, and the case is REMANDED for resentencing.

In September 2005, Scarborough pled guilty to two counts of maintaining a vehicle for drug storage, one count of evidence tampering, and a misdemeanor charge of resisting arrest. His written plea agreement included two terms: truthful testimony against two co-defendants and participation in substance abuse treatment. During the plea hearing, the judge informed Scarborough of the possibility of a life sentence if habitual offender status was applied, which Scarborough acknowledged. The judge also clarified that the court was not bound by any pre-sentencing agreements with the prosecutor, and Scarborough confirmed his understanding. The plea form included a handwritten note about the potential for a life sentence if deemed habitual, and Scarborough affirmed that the written agreement encompassed all terms.

Scarborough missed his initial sentencing hearing, prompting the State to file for habitual offender status under 11 Del. C. 4214(a). At the subsequent hearing, Scarborough contested the State's petition and sought to withdraw his guilty plea. The judge assigned him new counsel and scheduled a hearing on the motion. Scarborough's new attorney argued that an undisclosed oral agreement existed, where the State promised not to pursue habitual offender status in exchange for Scarborough's cooperation in an investigation. The judge rejected this motion, citing the lack of any reference to such an agreement in the plea documents and Scarborough's sworn confirmation of the written terms.

During Scarborough's appeal in March 2007, both his counsel and the State admitted to an undisclosed oral side agreement, violating Superior Court Rule 11(e)(2). Given this admission, the ambiguous nature of the 'work' requirement, and the significant implications of habitual offender status, the case was remanded for further factual review. At the subsequent hearing, testimonies were heard from Scarborough, the prosecuting attorney, the involved police officer, and Scarborough's public defender. After the hearing, the judge denied Scarborough's motion to withdraw his plea.

To retract the guilty plea. In his ruling, the judge promptly asserts that 'if an agreement existed, and if fulfilling it would have led to a State recommendation for leniency, such as not seeking habitual offender status, there is absolutely no evidence it was carried out.' Despite our explicit instructions in the initial Opinion, the judge neglected to determine the specifics of the oral 'side' agreement. He concentrated only on his view that Scarborough did not deliver. The judge overlooked what both parties considered as 'work'—the key factor in Scarborough's performance. During Scarborough's counsel's cross-examination of O'Neil to clarify the agreement's terms, the judge remarked: '[t]his likely applies to both sides, but if the issue is whether Mr. Scarborough could and did fulfill the agreement, and the answer is he did nothing, isn’t this all theoretical?' Despite the judge's refusal to define the oral agreement's terms, the record reveals, and we conclude, that the testimony largely aligns on the agreement both parties believed they had.

Witnesses described two prior agreements where the State proposed leniency before the September 2005 plea deal. In the first, from February 2005, Scarborough agreed to share details on Louis Tolson, a significant drug trafficker, in return for a lighter sentence. While Scarborough provided some information, the State deemed it inadequate. The second agreement, spanning March to June 2005, involved Scarborough assisting Hake in capturing other major dealers for leniency. The State postponed multiple hearings to enable this cooperation, but Scarborough never acted. Meanwhile, he was arrested for a unrelated robbery and imprisoned. Notably, before September 2005, Scarborough had only committed to 'work,' not to plead guilty. Under these earlier agreements, his cooperation would lead to leniency upon any future guilty plea.

Scarborough wrote to his attorney, Dean, expressing his desire to resume 'work.' His letter mentioned an impending drug deal involving 'Willie Brown, Jermaine Brown, Pierre Down, and Robert Harris.' Hake recognized some names as Dover locals. O'Neil testified that Scarborough claimed he 'would expose these individuals and produce 17 ounces of powder the following week.' Contrary to the judge's doubts about an oral agreement, State witnesses O'Neil and Dean confirmed a verbal side deal alongside the written plea. The judge should have focused on this agreement’s terms during remand, not dismissed it due to perceived non-performance or unenforceability. Scarborough's letter to Dean led to a formal plea where he agreed to plead guilty, testify against co-defendants, and cooperate with Hake.

In exchange, the State reduced Scarborough's bail to aid his cooperation and refrained from pursuing habitual offender status. The written plea submitted to the judge only included the guilty plea, testimony agreement, and bail reduction. The oral side deal involved Scarborough's 'work' and the State's leniency pledge, but the judge was unaware of this. The State deliberately kept 'work' vague, as the prosecutor couldn’t predict Scarborough’s usefulness. Though his letter named targets, these didn’t limit the State; Hake would assess the value of his contributions. Dean, however, believed Scarborough had 'a new agreement to fulfill the outlined tasks.'

In his September 2005 letter, Scarborough did not comply exactly with police demands, leading them to claim he failed to meet their standards. The case hinges on Scarborough's attempts to cooperate with Hake and Hake's reaction. Hake testified that during a June 2005 call, Scarborough initially agreed to assist but changed his tone when pressed for substantial results, asserting the State lacked strong evidence against him and he could reverse his plea. The call ended abruptly after this shift.

Hake noted that Scarborough emphasized the State's weak case and his ability to overturn his plea. While no specific names were discussed, Hake insisted Scarborough provide significant assistance. Hake later received a letter with names of local drug dealers, which he deemed under Dover's jurisdiction. However, Dover police were unwilling to collaborate with Scarborough, prompting Hake to suggest targeting Woodside instead. Scarborough was never informed of this jurisdictional issue before the plea agreement.

The State acknowledged a discrepancy in Hake's testimony, as he claimed the June 2005 conversation included Scarborough mentioning a plea reversal—yet the plea wasn’t entered until September. Scarborough testified that post-plea, he and Hake discussed his list of Dover-based names, but Hake rejected them, insisting on Woodside. Scarborough argued this was unsafe, as he had no connections there. This attempt to cooperate ultimately failed.

Following a January 2006 hearing, Scarborough’s attorney sent a second list of names, but the State again rejected it due to Dover’s involvement. O’Neil stated no Dover detectives would work with Scarborough. The remand required the judge to examine the oral agreement’s terms, Scarborough’s ability to fulfill them, and whether they caused any plea misunderstanding. While factual findings are usually reviewed for competence, plea agreement interpretation demands closer scrutiny.

In accordance with contract principles, we refer to contract law to determine the proper standard of review. Thus, '[a] trial judge's interpretation of contract terms presents legal questions subject to de novo review for errors. On the other hand, a trial judge's decision on whether an oral contract exists is a factual matter reviewed for abuse of discretion.' I. Terms of the Oral Agreement For reasons unclear in the record, the trial judge treated our initial inquiry as purely theoretical, as shown by his remarks during the hearing and in his Order. In a revealing comment, the judge expressed doubt about our instructions by stating, 'if there ever were an agreement.' We interpret this as his belief that the oral agreement's terms were irrelevant. They were not. We sympathize with the judge's frustration. The parties deliberately excluded him by not following Superior Court Rule of Criminal Procedure 11(e)(2), which mandated disclosure of the oral agreement's terms, at least privately, during the plea entry. Yet, this frustration does not justify ignoring the existence of an oral side agreement—

no matter how vague its terms or challenging to fulfill due to third-party involvement. During the remand hearing, the prosecutor confirmed under oath that a side agreement existed: '[I] presented a written plea offer to Sandy Dean for Maintaining, Tampering, and Resisting Arrest. On September 15th, I emailed Sandy, stating, 'Ensure [Scarborough] understands he must work, or he’ll face a habitual offender petition.' Consequently, we must conclude the judge abused his discretion by neglecting the fact-finding and analysis we required. 'Plea agreements, based on contract principles, are mutually beneficial arrangements.' Under these principles, '[e]ven if the defendant and State agree, the plea remains executory pending court approval.' The contract stays executory until 'both parties fulfill remaining obligations.' As any law student knows, a contract must have reasonably clear terms to be enforceable. However, a contract demanding only

performance satisfactory to one party can still be valid. To safeguard the performing party from arbitrary rejection: Such a promise typically requires the promisor to meet the promisee's honest judgment. Yet, the promisee must evaluate the performance fairly. A refusal to assess the performance or rejecting it without genuine grounds constitutes preventing fulfillment and excuses the condition. After examining the testimony and concessions from oral arguments, we find the oral 'side' agreement enforceable, supplementing the written plea agreement. The full plea agreement was as follows: Scarborough would plead guilty, testify against co-defendants, and agree to 'work' with Hake. In exchange, the State would reduce his bail and refrain from seeking habitual offender status to aid his 'work.' The vague term 'work' let the State decide if Scarborough’s performance warranted this forbearance. The written plea submitted

to the judge only included Scarborough’s guilty plea, testimony agreement, and the State’s bail reduction. The undisclosed oral side agreement involved Scarborough’s promise to 'work' and the State’s pledge to avoid habitual offender status if he complied. 2. Did Scarborough Fulfill the Oral Agreement? By avoiding our first question, the judge’s assessment of whether Scarborough performed was flawed. Determining compliance is impossible without knowing the agreement’s terms. The judge’s analysis, therefore, was unhelpful. In his Order, he concluded Scarborough’s compliance was 'intrinsically unfulfillable [sic] . only concerning Jeff Tolson or others mentioned later.' This focus was misguided, however. The Tolson-related agreement occurred in February 2005, seven months before the plea deal. That avenue was exhausted long before the September agreement was considered. The February

The agreement concerning Tolson only sets the historical context for the parties' interactions. Scarborough's inability to supply adequate details about Tolson does not affect the September plea deal or the claimed unfeasibility of executing it. The judge misused his discretion by relying on issues entirely unrelated to the pertinent oral agreement when assessing Scarborough's actions. Evidence from the remand hearing shows that Scarborough tried to furnish information about the individuals mentioned in his September 2005 letter. Unchallenged testimony confirmed that Scarborough presented a list of targets, leading to the plea agreement with the State, which later hesitated due to the targets being in Dover. Testimonies from O'Neil, Dean, and Hake confirmed that Scarborough's September letter, containing a name list, initiated the plea agreement. Hake later saw this list and noted some names fell under Dover police's jurisdiction, but neither he nor O'Neil expressed discontent before Scarborough pleaded, despite the targets being in Dover. Still, both parties agreed Scarborough would 'work,' with Scarborough and his lawyer reasonably assuming the Dover targets in his letter would be the focus.

the foundation of his 'work.' However, when Scarborough reached out to Hake to meet his obligations, Hake told him he had to 'work' in Woodside, as his suggested targets were in Dover, outside Hake's jurisdiction. Scarborough refused, deeming Woodside too risky. After Hake threatened to pursue habitual offender status, Scarborough countered by threatening to withdraw his guilty plea. Following this, neither party made further efforts to collaborate. 3. Is Scarborough's Performance Excused? Given the plea agreement allowed the State to evaluate Scarborough's performance, we emphasize the State's obligations. The State must use 'honest judgment' and 'fair consideration' to assess if Scarborough's 'work' was adequate. If the State acted in bad faith or failed to fairly evaluate Scarborough's offer, his performance is excused. As noted in Cole, Scarborough rightly expected the State to avoid arbitrary or unreasonable actions denying him the agreement's benefits. Essentially, 'work' is a common term for a defendant's

proposed cooperation with law enforcement. In less detailed cases, it might simply reflect a policy-driven effort to 'use a thief to catch a thief.' Hence, Superior Court R. 11(e)(2). This rule ensures judges are fully engaged during plea entry, aiding in defining a clear, reasonable performance standard for 'satisfactory work.' Southerland, C. J.: In the lower court, Bennethum was indicted for breaching state income tax laws. He sought dismissal, arguing the indictment failed to allege an offense, but the motion was denied. Bennethum now seeks a writ of prohibition, claiming the Superior Court lacked jurisdiction.

The indictment alleges that on April 30, 1956, William H. Bennethum, III— 'Count I'—being a Delaware resident in 1955 with over $600 gross income, failed to file a state tax return as mandated by 30 Delaware Code, Section 1168, violating Section 1184(c). 'Count II' charges that under the same conditions, he neglected to pay owed income tax per 30 Delaware Code, Chapter 11, also breaching Section 1184(c). The relevant provisions of the state income tax law include: 30 Del. C. § 1168, requiring annual returns by April 30 for the prior year; 30 Del. C. § 1184(c), penalizing failure to file or pay as fraudulent; and 30 Del. C. § 1187(e)-(f), imposing fines or imprisonment for intentional evasion, false returns, or delayed compliance.

Section 1187(e) specifies that individuals or entities evading tax obligations by failing to pay, file, or providing false information face fines up to $500, six months’ imprisonment, or both, in addition to other penalties. Section 1187(f) penalizes taxables who delay filing or payment beyond 30 days after deadlines with similar sanctions. The indictment cites violations of § 1184(c). Bennethum contends (1) this section imposes only civil penalties, not criminal liability, and (2) if criminal, it unconstitutionally presumes fraud conclusively. These arguments necessitate interpreting §§ 1184(c), 1187(e), and 1187(f) harmoniously, as they address related matters and must form a coherent legal framework.

This interpretive challenge requires reconciling the statutes to avoid inconsistency. Bennethum’s claims hinge on whether § 1184(c) is civil or criminal and if its presumption of fraud is valid. The court must analyze these provisions in context, ensuring they align with legislative intent and constitutional standards. The task involves nuanced statutory construction to determine if the penalties under § 1184(c) are standalone or supplementary to § 1187’s sanctions, and whether their combined application is justifiable under Delaware law.

The challenge lies in the poorly drafted statutes, with the precise interpretation of § 1184(c) being unclear. Delaying the analysis of § 1184(c), we observe that § 1187(e) broadly addresses evading the Tax Department's 'requirements' (i.e., the law and regulations) through actions like not paying taxes, failing to submit or verify returns, withholding information, or submitting false details. These acts become criminal offenses if intent to evade is proven. So, what role does § 1184(c) play? It specifically targets the refusal or failure to file a return or pay taxes—raising questions about labeling such acts as 'fraud,' a term undefined in the statute and not a common-law crime. How can mere failure to file a return conclusively imply fraud?

It seems unreasonable to interpret the statute as defining 'fraud' solely based on failing to file a return or pay taxes. Such a failure could stem from various reasons—tax avoidance, absence, illness, oversight, or neglect. This interpretation would raise constitutional concerns, as legislatures cannot enforce irrebuttable presumptions against factual evidence (see Appeal of Brown, 4 Terry (43 Del.) 608, 49 A. 2d 618). Thus, § 1184(c), while framed as a criminal statute, does not establish a distinct crime separate from § 1187(e). At most, it might create a prima facie presumption of intent to defraud the state by failing to file or pay, supporting an indictment under § 1187(e).

In this interpretation, § 1187(e) and § 1184(c) could jointly define two offenses: (1) fraudulent returns and (2) refusal or failure to file or pay taxes. Both require proof of intent to evade. For the first, intent is inferred from circumstances; for the second, § 1184(c) might provide a prima facie presumption of intent. Regardless, any indictment must rely on § 1187(e), with intent to evade being a critical element. The Attorney General argues that § 1184(c)'s phrase 'shall be guilty of fraud' is redundant, suggesting it merely imposes penalties for fraudulent returns without defining a new crime.

The State's argument that § 1184(c) penalizes delays in filing or payment, irrespective of intent, faces a major flaw: it renders § 1187(f) meaningless. § 1187(f) explicitly targets failures to file or pay within 30 days, requiring no intent to defraud. If § 1184(c) allowed immediate prosecution for delays, the 30-day grace period in § 1187(f) would serve no purpose. This untenable interpretation must be rejected. Consequently, the indictment is flawed for omitting the essential charge of intent to evade under § 1187(e).

Section 1187(e) should have been dismissed. While our interpretation doesn't perfectly align all statutes, it's unavoidable that §1187(f) carries the same penalty as §1187(e) despite differing fraud involvement. The jurisdictional issue remains - though the indictment is flawed, dismissing the petition would waste time as prosecution can't refile due to the two-year limit, warranting the writ's issuance.

The limitations statute prevents reindictment, but a lawyer's alleged ethical breach remains concerning. Regardless of criminal outcomes, such professional misconduct may warrant disciplinary action. Previously, the Court's Censor Committee investigated tax irregularities among lawyers but paused during this case. Now with charges resolved, the Committee will resume its investigation into the petitioner's conduct.

Justice Moore: Deloris Slingwine appeals the Superior Court's denial of a prohibition writ against medical tests ordered by the Industrial Accident Board. We examine whether 'examination' under 19 Del. C. §2343 includes imaging and conduction studies. The Board correctly interpreted 'examination' to encompass necessary, non-redundant diagnostic tests, so we affirm the denial.

On April 4, 1986, Slingwine suffered a work injury. After receiving disability benefits, her employer's insurer petitioned to review her status and arranged Dr. Barsky's examination. When requested to undergo additional tests (X-rays, EMG, etc.), Slingwine refused, supported by her physician's opinion that they were unnecessary and exposed her to excessive radiation.

However, the Board concluded that § 2343 authorizes any reasonable tests needed to assess the worker's injury. Slingwine sought a writ of prohibition in the Superior Court, claiming the Industrial Accident Board overstepped its authority by permitting these medical tests. The Superior Court rejected the writ, ruling that § 2343 permits such physical examinations. Slingwine now appeals, asserting the statute's plain language restricts 'examinations' to non-invasive inspections. II. As this case involves an appeal from the denial of a writ of prohibition, our review focuses on a legal question and is conducted de novo. Fiduciary Trust Co. v. Fiduciary Trust Co., Del.Supr., 445 A.2d 927, 930 (1982). Consequently, the Board's decision itself is not under review. The Workmen's Compensation Law allows employers or the Board to require medical examinations to assess injuries or monitor recovery: (a) After an injury and during the

period of disability, the employee must, upon request by the employer or order by the Board, submit to examinations at reasonable intervals and locations by a licensed physician chosen and paid by the employer. The employee may have a personal physician, qualified under this section, attend the examination at their own expense. For subsequent examinations, the employer must cover the employee's reasonable travel costs and lost wages. (b) Refusal or obstruction of the examination under subsection (a) forfeits the employee's right to compensation during such refusal, and this period is deducted from eligible compensation time. (c) Information obtained by any physician during examinations is not privileged and may be used in hearings or legal actions. 19 Del. C.

§ 2343 (1985). Slingwine argues that 'examination' in § 2343 only refers to visual or sensory inspections, excluding imaging or invasive procedures. She claims this interpretation reflects the term's 'plain meaning' and that unambiguous statutes must be construed accordingly. See 2A Sutherland, Statutes and Statutory Construction, § 46.01 (4th ed. 1984); Trans-Americas Airlines, Inc. v. Kenton, Del.Supr., 491 A.2d 1139 (1985). This argument fails for two reasons. First, plain meaning isn't strictly dictionary-defined; in medical contexts, 'examination' includes tests like X-rays or bloodwork, which go beyond sensory observation. Routine physicals often involve such procedures, yet they are universally termed 'examinations.' Delaware Code's interpretation provisions acknowledge that technical terms may carry legal-specific meanings. 1 Del.C. § 303. Here, 'examination' in 19 Del. C. § 2343 is clearly such a term.

Even if we accepted Slingwine's narrow definition of 'examination,' we wouldn't be constrained by it if it conflicted with the Workmen's Compensation Statute's intent. Cf. Home Insurance Co. v. Maldonado, Del.Supr., 515 A.2d 690 (1986); Burpulis v. Director of Revenue, Del.Supr., 498 A.2d 1082 (1985); Oney v. State, Del.Supr., 446 A.2d 389 (1982). The statute's overarching goal is to provide fair and timely compensation to injured workers. Allowing restrictive interpretations would undermine this purpose.

It is neither reasonable nor fair to make an initial injury determination, or to assess whether an injury continues, based solely on a superficial examination. Additionally, the balance of rights between employees and employers under the Workmen's Compensation Act would be disrupted if employees could use X-rays to demonstrate an injury's existence or severity, while employers were restricted to superficial exams to refute such claims. Therefore, to maintain fairness under the Act, the term 'examination' should encompass all appropriate medical techniques and tests needed for an informed diagnosis, provided they are not excessively invasive.

While Slingwine had the chance to present evidence and cross-examine witnesses to argue that the requested medical tests were unnecessary or overly invasive, she opted not to do so during the hearing. Nonetheless, determining the 'reasonableness' of such tests under 19 Del.C. § 2343 is a factual matter best resolved in an evidentiary proceeding. Given today's ruling on the definition of 'examination,' and considering any shortcomings in Board Rule Number 8, the Industrial Accident Board should implement additional safeguards to prevent employees from undergoing inappropriate, risky, or unnecessary medical procedures.

The Industrial Accident Board must establish procedures allowing employees to contest proposed medical tests or procedures they deem unreasonable or unnecessary. The Superior Court's decision to deny the writ of prohibition is upheld. Delaware statutes mandate that words be interpreted in context and according to common usage, with technical terms understood in their legal sense. In replevin cases where a third party is called to testify about property ownership, objections to their competency are common but often unfounded. Waples, where a witness with balanced interests was deemed admissible. Despite judicial disagreement, the witness was sworn in and confirmed the defendant's partnership claim.

Judge Houston J. informed the jury that upon reconsideration after the witness's testimony, he realized he had mistakenly referenced the Mears & Son v. Waples case too hastily, overlooking key differences between that case and the current one. The true criterion for a witness's interest is whether they stand to gain or lose directly from the judgment's legal effect, or if the record could serve as evidence in another case. This interest must be immediate, definite, and vested, not speculative or distant. Even a minor direct interest disqualifies a witness, regardless of its scale. Citations: 1 Greenl. Elizabeth, now married to Pennington, serves as the executrix of Jacob Vanhorn's last will and testament. John Vanhorn, represented by his guardian, initiated a writ of scire facias, which is currently under review by this court. This scire facias is a legal process designed to comply with the twelfth section of the Act for establishing Orphans' Courts, 1 Del. Laws 87. The Act stipulates that judgments on specified bonds must retain their original nature, with no execution issued until the aggrieved party uses a writ of scire facias to summon the judgment holders to appear and justify why execution should not proceed. If the aggrieved party demonstrates damages and secures a verdict, the Court of Common Pleas will authorize execution for the awarded amount plus costs. In this case, the plaintiff detailed the original judgment and the terms of the testamentary bond, which required Elizabeth, as executrix, to provide an accurate account of her administration and distribute the remaining assets according to the will.

Additionally, the record indicates that a distributive account of Jacob Vanhorn's estate was filed in the Register's office by Pennington and his wife on June 14, 1802, revealing a sum of £25.18.10½ owed to John Vanhorn, one of Jacob Vanhorn's heirs. The grievance cited is the nonpayment of this amount, including interest, prompting the summons for Pennington and wife to justify why execution should not be issued for the said $6000. The central issue is whether John Vanhorn has presented adequate grounds to claim the £25.18.10½ specified in the distributive account. Assuming John Vanhorn is a legatee of Jacob Vanhorn, the court finds he has not established a valid claim to this sum through the scire facias. Elizabeth, as executrix, was obligated by the bond's terms to distribute the residual personal estate according to the will's intent. However, the plaintiff has not demonstrated his entitlement to any residual share of Jacob Vanhorn's estate.

If John Vanhorn is considered a legatee of Jacob Vanhorn, the court concludes he has not proven his right to the £25.18.10½ mentioned in the distributive account. Elizabeth, the executrix, was bound by the bond's conditions to distribute the residual personal estate as per the will's directives. The plaintiff has not shown he is a residuary legatee or has any claim under Jacob Vanhorn's will. The personal estate was either disposed of by the will or remained with the executrix if not allocated. If the estate was distributed, the legatees were entitled to it; if not, the executrix retained it, leaving John Vanhorn no claim except through the will. The will or the specific bequest to John Vanhorn should have been cited in the scire facias to substantiate his claim. Instead, the scire facias notes the distributive account identifies £25.18.10½ due to John Vanhorn as an heir, which conflicts with any claim under the will and thus fails to establish his right to the funds.

The scire facias states that the distributive account found £25.18.10½ owed to John Vanhorn as an heir, but this contradicts his potential claim under the will, undermining his right to recovery. This inconsistency is fatal to his case, as he shows no valid title to the money. The account's nature—whether judicial or extrajudicial—is irrelevant without the will's inclusion, as it alone could grant the legatees rights to the residual estate. The account, at best, could serve as evidence but does not authorize recovery. The scire facias correctly follows the Act's requirement to summon the party to justify why execution should not proceed, but the plaintiff's failure to present a valid claim renders the writ ineffective.

The term 'the said judgment' refers to the total amount for which judgment is given on the bond. This interpretation aligns with the procedural guidelines set by the Act of Assembly for such bonds. The judgment serves as a safeguard to compensate any others who may suffer harm, and the scire facias must be issued for the amount specified in that judgment. Rape is defined as sexual intercourse with a woman by force and without her consent. Legal force, whether direct or implied, is a necessary component of rape. Historically, rape prosecutions required proof of both penetration and emission, but current law only mandates proof of penetration. While minimal penetration suffices, it must be proven beyond doubt that the male organ entered the female’s genitalia without her consent. If the jury concludes beyond reasonable doubt that the defendant had non-consensual intercourse with the prosecuting witness as charged, they must consider all evidence, including the credibility of both parties. If the sexual intercourse was forced and against the prosecuting witness's will, your verdict must be guilty. You may also recommend mercy for the defendant if appropriate. In criminal cases, the accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt. QUILLEN, Justice: We outline the case based largely on the appellants' brief. Robert Golson, Sterling Hobbs, Clarence Hooks, and Wilbur Johnson were indicted for Murder in the first degree, Robbery in the first degree, and Conspiracy in the second degree. Hobbs also faced a charge for Possession of a Deadly Weapon during a Felony.

Hooks and Johnson sought separate trials, but the Superior Court refused. Arraignment and jury selection followed promptly. After a prolonged trial, all defendants were convicted. Their motions for a new trial were denied. Robert Golson received a death sentence for Murder in the first degree, thirty years for Robbery in the first degree, and seven years for Conspiracy in the second degree. Sterling Hobbs was sentenced to death for Murder in the first degree, thirty years for Robbery in the first degree, seven years for Conspiracy in the second degree, and thirty years for Possession of a Deadly Weapon during a Felony. Clarence Hooks was sentenced to death for Murder in the first degree, thirty years for Robbery in the first degree, and seven years for Conspiracy in the second degree. Wilbur Johnson received a death sentence for Murder in the first degree and thirty years for Robbery in the first degree.

He received a thirty-year prison term for first-degree Robbery and a seven-year sentence for second-degree Conspiracy. This Court reviewed an appeal concerning a death penalty for first-degree Murder. In State v. Spence, Del.Supr., 367 A.2d 983 (1976), the Court determined that the death penalty in these cases violated the Eighth Amendment as cruel and unusual punishment. The Court decided that life imprisonment without parole under 11 Del.C. § 4209(a) (1974) would apply for first-degree Murder. The incident leading to these charges occurred on May 5, 1975, when Ridge Liquors in Claymont, Delaware, was robbed of around $200, resulting in the fatal shooting of clerk Philip Whiteman by a .22 caliber handgun. Five individuals were arrested for the crime.

Four of the men were charged and convicted, with their appeals now before this Court. The fifth, Gregory Payne, pleaded guilty to First Degree Robbery and was sentenced to twenty years in prison. He testified for the State against the other four defendants during the trial. The defendants raise multiple issues in this appeal, which the Court addresses in two parts: pre-trial matters and trial-related legal issues. The convictions are upheld. The appellants argue that the Trial Court mishandled the voir dire process, particularly in excluding jurors opposed to capital punishment, which they claim violated the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments. They also contend the Court inadequately screened jurors for racial or religious bias against Blacks and Black Muslims. They argue that even if individual errors were minor, their combined effect warranted reversal. The case of Parson

v. State, Del. Supr., 275 A.2d 777 (1971), affirms the Trial Judge's broad discretion in voir dire, with reversible error only if this discretion was abused to the appellants' detriment. The Delaware statute on voir dire in capital cases aligns with Witherspoon v. Illinois, 391 U.S. 510 (1968), which outlines when jurors opposing capital punishment may be dismissed for cause. In Witherspoon, the death penalty was overturned because all jurors with such scruples were removed, resulting in a biased jury favoring the death penalty, violating the Sixth and Fourteenth Amendments. The Illinois statute allowed the exclusion of all scrupled jurors, even those who could still judge guilt impartially. Thus, the Witherspoon standard permits excusing only jurors who cannot remain impartial due to their opposition to capital punishment. This standard was reaffirmed in Lockett v. Ohio, 438 U.S. 586 (1978), and Delaware's statute was upheld in Steigler v. State, Del.Supr., 277 A.2d 662 (1971).

After reviewing the voir dire, the Court found the Trial Judge meticulously followed the Witherspoon standard. Each juror was questioned to determine if their stance on capital punishment would hinder their ability to decide based on evidence. Those who admitted they could never return a guilty verdict if the death penalty applied were excused. The process ensured an impartial jury, adhering to constitutional requirements.

Dismissed for cause. Refer to Parson v. State, supra, 275 A.2d at 784-785. Certain jurors with unclear responses were targeted by the State's peremptory challenges, yet no misconduct was found in how the State applied these challenges. Appellants urge this Court to expand the Witherspoon criteria to address an unresolved issue from that ruling. They contend that excluding individuals opposed to capital punishment inherently creates a jury predisposed to convict. The Witherspoon Court declined to conclude that such a jury was biased toward conviction, despite acknowledging that removing death penalty opponents might increase the likelihood of a death sentence. The Court noted the evidence suggesting a conviction-prone jury was preliminary and incomplete. Appellants assert that current evidence is more robust and unified, warranting a fresh review of this argument. They reference newer studies not available during the Witherspoon case, which have since been presented to various courts as proof.

Due to these and other methodological flaws, the studies have been dismissed as unreliable. See, e.g., Spinkellink v. Appellants' additional objections to the Trial Court's voir dire process concern its handling of potential jurors biased against Blacks or Black Muslims. They argue the Court's approach was cursory and insufficient. Although opinions may differ on the matter, we find no misuse of discretion by the Trial Judge. The Trial Court's authority during voir dire is limited only by fundamental fairness requirements. Shields v.
