The Town of Seaford is prohibited from selling or otherwise disrupting the burial ground, ensuring the trust's purpose remains intact. The original trustees are deceased, and the court overrules objections, admitting the record as evidence. After the plaintiff's testimony, the defense moved for a directed verdict, citing lack of title proof, but the court instead directed a guilty verdict for the plaintiff due to the defendant's lack of evidence.

The appellant was convicted of assault with intent to rape without legal representation during trial. An appeal argues the judge erred by not instructing the jury that a guilty verdict requires unanimity, despite no such request. Delaware law mandates unanimous jury verdicts, rooted in common law and the state constitution, as affirmed in prior cases and legal texts.

While unanimity is undisputed, the appellant claims the judge should have instructed the jury on this requirement without prompting. Federal law does not mandate such instructions, and Delaware assumes jurors know this, as they receive a handbook explaining unanimous verdicts before service. The court found no error, as jurors are presumed aware of this rule.

Each juror is expected to consider the views of others but is not obligated to abandon their own firmly held beliefs. The instructions are presumably read by every potential juror, and the appellant has provided no evidence to challenge this assumption. After reaching a verdict, the jury returns to the courtroom, where the Prothonotary inquires about the decision from the foreman, who declares it. The Prothonotary then asks the jury collectively, 'And so say you all?' allowing any juror to dissent if they disagree. This procedure was followed in this case without objection from the appellant. Additionally, any party or the court can request a jury poll, where each juror confirms the verdict individually, as guaranteed by Criminal Rule 31(d). The appellant did not request such a poll. Given the lack of evidence to the contrary, we conclude the verdict was unanimous and find no error in the absence of a specific unanimity instruction.

We believe, however, that future cases should eliminate any ambiguity by routinely instructing juries, as per Criminal Rule 31(a), that their verdict must be unanimous. This imposes minimal burden on the trial judge and reinforces the defendant's constitutional right to a unanimous decision. The appellant cites Coby v. State, 225 Md. 293, which interpreted Article 21 of the Maryland Declaration of Rights to mandate a unanimity instruction. We choose not to adopt this strict requirement. Although this issue was not raised earlier, we address it due to its constitutional significance. We decline, however, to review the appellant's other arguments, as they were not presented in the lower court.

The appellant's counsel did not raise these issues previously, and none involve plain error or constitutional violations warranting our independent review. Rule 5(7); Pepe v. State, 3 Storey 417; Robinson v. Meding, 2 Storey 578; Richards v. State, 6 Terry 573. The lower court's conviction is affirmed. Article 21 of the Maryland Declaration of Rights guarantees a speedy trial by an impartial jury, requiring unanimous consent for a guilty verdict. OPINION AND ORDER LAMB, Vice Chancellor. A major shareholder of a Delaware corporation seeks access to company records under 8 Del. C. § 220, citing concerns over mismanagement and for use in a proxy contest.

The shareholder's demand letter, spanning 25 single-spaced pages with 47 categories, requests extensive documentation. The corporation denied the request, leading to a lawsuit filed on April 24, 2006. After expedited proceedings and a one-day trial on June 2, 2006, the shareholder revised its demand, though it remained overly broad. The court must determine whether the demand was proper or excessively sweeping, constituting misuse of statutory inspection rights. For the reasons outlined, the court will deny the plaintiff's request in its entirety.

Highlighting the restricted nature of the books and records remedy compared to the wider discovery allowed under Rule 34. Section 220 is a crucial stockholder right, which the court must address promptly as mandated by statute. Its significance demands vigilant oversight to prevent misuse, particularly when stockholders make demands during an active proxy contest. I. A. Parties The plaintiff, Highland Select, is a Delaware-based limited partnership headquartered in Dallas, Texas. Highland Select and its affiliates hold combined investments in Motient Corporation valued at around $230 million. James Dondero, a former Motient director, is a key figure at Highland Capital Management, L.P., the main advisory firm for various Highland entities, including Highland Select. Collectively, Highland Capital oversees roughly $20 billion in investments. Motient is a publicly traded Delaware corporation previously involved in wireless data and internet services. Its current main assets are its stakes in Mobile Satellite Ventures, L.P. and TerreStar Networks, Inc.

which are working to establish satellite-based communication systems using U.S. government-allocated spectrum segments. Steven G. Singer serves as Motient's board chairman. B. Highland's Concerns About Mismanagement Only a concise summary of Motient's operations is pertinent to the court's ruling. Motient manages a wireless communications business primarily through TerreStar Networks, Inc., in which it holds a majority stake, and Mobile Satellite Ventures (MSV), where it is a minority investor. The complexity of this setup prompted Motient to propose two consolidation deals. Highland has strongly opposed these transactions—the 'roll-up' and TerreStar deals—arguing they misvalue Motient's assets and may involve self-interest. Highland has also questioned consulting agreements between Motient and Communications Technology Advisors (CTA), as well as CTA's parent, Tejas investment bank. Notably, Tejas and CTA executives have close ties to Motient's leadership, and Motient has paid both firms substantial fees annually for various services.

These potentially conflicted transactions also involve payments to Gary Singer, brother of Steven Singer, who is barred from holding executive roles in public companies due to past financial crimes. Motient has faced ongoing challenges with financial reporting, disclosing internal control weaknesses multiple times. It has frequently revised quarterly filings and, in 2003, terminated its independent auditor amid disputes over accounting practices for 2000–2001 transactions. Additionally, Motient risks classification under the Investment Company Act of 1940, which could severely impact its operations. In mid-2005, Dondero urged Motient's audit committee to probe these issues and provide details on questionable transactions. The board initiated an investigation with independent counsel, but the resulting report, while clearing the board, was never fully shared with Dondero. Highland suspects the inquiry may have been inadequate or compromised by conflicts.

This books and records dispute is one facet of a broader conflict between Motient and Highland Select. On August 16, 2005, a Highland affiliate filed a derivative suit in this court, accusing Motient's directors and officers of fiduciary breaches. The court dismissed the claim on March 17, 2006, for failing to demonstrate demand futility under Rule 23.1. The same day, Highland affiliates sued Motient in Texas state court seeking to void a $90 million transaction.

The company's Series A preferred stock was sold to Highland affiliates for a million dollars. On October 7, 2005, Highland Select affiliates, holders of Motient's Series A preferred stock, filed a class action in this court to block an exchange offer for that stock. In response, Motient has sued Highland affiliates twice. On October 19, 2005, Motient sued Dondero for breach of fiduciary duty in a Texas state court, with allegations tied to the same facts as this case. Motient's claims in Texas hinge on whether Dondero was justified in opposing the board. The same day, Motient filed another lawsuit in a Texas federal court, accusing Dondero of making misleading statements and violating federal proxy rules while soliciting proxies to replace Motient's board and management. The suit argues Dondero's accusations against the board are false.

Motient asserts that Dondero's claims of self-dealing in the roll-up transaction are 'objectively false,' citing an independent audit committee investigation. The truth of Dondero's accusations is central to Motient's argument in both state and federal cases. All suits, except the dismissed Delaware derivative action, remain pending. Notably, Dondero and Highland entities in the federal securities case have invoked a litigation stay under the Private Securities Law Reform Act and Securities Litigation Uniform Standards Act, halting discovery until the motion to dismiss is resolved. Dondero also tried to use these laws to stay discovery in the state fiduciary duty case, but the motion was denied on May 1, 2006.

On February 14, 2006, Dondero resigned from Motient's board, and Highland announced a proxy contest against the board in a press release. Highland expressed concerns over 'continued mismanagement,' citing financial control weaknesses, disclosure issues, a flawed April 2005 stock issuance, and the failed roll-up transaction. Highland stated it would nominate independent candidates for a new board. Highland later filed a proxy statement with the SEC for Motient's July 12, 2006, annual meeting, expanding on the concerns from the press release.

On April 12, 2006, after the court dismissed Highland's derivative complaint, Highland Select sent a 25-page Section 220 demand for Motient's books and records, listing eight purposes and 47 broad demands. The request, resembling an overbroad Rule 34 discovery demand, sought extensive documents on financial control issues. Motient refused on April 20, 2006, calling the demand improperly broad and lacking proper purpose. Highland Select sued on April 24, seeking an expedited schedule to use obtained documents in the proxy contest. Motient's counsel opposed the request.

Given their readiness to proceed with the trial within the proposed timeline, the court scheduled the hearing for June 2, 2006. C. Discovery And The Ongoing Litigation The discovery phase encountered significant difficulties. On May 4, 2006, Motient issued a deposition notice for a corporate representative of Highland Select to testify on specific subjects under Court of Chancery Rule 30(b)(6). Highland Select appointed Michael Minces, an attorney who was Highland Capital's chief compliance officer and, since April, the sole officer of Highland Select. Motient also scheduled Dondero's deposition, and after negotiations, May 15 was set for both depositions. Early in Minces's deposition, it was evident he was unsuitable as a Rule 30(b)(6) witness. He frequently failed to provide meaningful responses to key questions about Highland Select's rationale for its Section 220 request. For instance, when questioned about the public disclosure of the demand in an SEC Form 14A, Minces cited privilege and declined to answer.

Minces further stated that, apart from himself, no one else at Highland Select could address the matter. Similarly, when asked if Highland Select had reported Motient to the SEC for a potential 1940 Act violation, Minces avoided answering directly, suggesting Motient contact the SEC instead. When Minces did respond, his answers often referred to Highland Select's demand letter or public filings. For example, when questioned about the intended use of the documents from the Section 220 request, Minces merely reiterated the purposes outlined in the demand letter. Additionally, Minces frequently declined to testify on topics he seemed personally aware of or that Highland Select as an entity would know, particularly those predating his April appointment as sole officer. Highland Select argued such testimony was beyond Minces's role as an officer, though this did not prevent him from

discussing matters outside his official capacity when it benefited Highland. For instance, when asked how Highland Select knew Dondero was denied a fair chance to voice his objections at an October 6, 2005 board meeting, Minces stated it was the 'general consensus and opinion from the participants afterward.' How Minces knew this, given his April appointment, remains unclear. Yet he answered this question while avoiding others involving similarly acquired knowledge. Despite this, Motient's counsel continued Minces's deposition for nine hours, a futile effort that left no time to depose Dondero. The trial on June 2, 2006, featured Minces testifying on issues he had previously avoided during deposition. He expanded on

Highland Select's suspicions about Motient, which the court found credible, supporting the conclusion that Highland Select had reasonable grounds to suspect misconduct. Minces also elaborated on the purpose behind the Section 220 demand, revealing it was prompted by the dismissal of Highland's earlier derivative suit and prepared once new counsel was hired. However, the court was perplexed by Minces's ambiguity regarding Highland Select's decision to proceed with its proxy contest. He repeatedly stated no final decision had been made, initially citing the unfiled proxy and plans to review corrective action after obtaining Section 220 documents. Later, he claimed the decision to mail the proxy was still pending.

The proxy statement was 'not entirely up to me, and a decision has not been finalized yet.' However, at the trial's conclusion, Highland Select's legal team disputed Minces's statement, asserting that any notion the proxy contest decision was undecided was 'contrary to the evidence.' As mentioned earlier, Highland Select officially filed its proxy statement shortly after the trial. Moreover, the trial's approach seemed to trigger significant modifications to Highland's initial Section 220 request. The first adjustment appeared in Highland's opening brief, which cited a 'significant reduction' in its original demand. Later, just before trial, Highland further refined its document request, slashing the initial 47 categories down to 10. The court instructed Highland Select to outline the differences between these two versions to clarify if the demand had genuinely been narrowed. Highland complied with a letter explaining the revisions, seemingly further curtailing its request. Yet, a thorough review of Highland Select's evolving demands reveals that

the revised demand submitted on the eve of trial remains as overly broad as the original. Highland's modifications primarily fall into three categories. First, six of the new demands specify date ranges or topics that inherently restrict the scope of responsive documents. Second, Highland Select imposes 'creator/recipient' constraints, targeting documents shared or prepared by the board, executive committee, audit committee, SEC, or external auditors, unlike the original blanket request for all Motient-held documents. Lastly, Highland Select removed eight categories from the initial 47, leaving 39. Highland Select maintains that it is entitled to all documents in its latest demand, citing its goal of probing mismanagement to either initiate another derivative lawsuit or wage a proxy battle to replace Motient's board. It argues that the presented facts establish credible grounds to suspect mismanagement,

and that every requested document is vital for its broad objectives. Motient weakly counters that Highland has not substantiated any suspicion of corporate misconduct. More critically, Motient contends that the plaintiff's demand and its pursuit reveal an ulterior motive—using the Section 220 claim to undermine Motient's leadership in anticipation of the proxy contest, irrespective of obtaining information. Under Delaware law, shareholders have a statutory right to inspect corporate books and records under 8 Del. C. § 220, provided the demand meets procedural requirements and serves a proper purpose. A 'proper purpose' is defined as one 'reasonably tied to the shareholder's interest.' A Section 220 plaintiff must also present credible evidence of wrongdoing to justify further investigation. Merely meeting the proper purpose and credible suspicion criteria is insufficient;

the scope of inspection is typically restricted to documents strictly necessary for the stated purpose, a burden the plaintiff must prove. These requirements emphasize good faith, with courts closely scrutinizing demands to prevent misuse of inspection rights. Recent cases highlight the risk of abuse, particularly when Section 220 demands coincide with proxy contests. While Section 220 actions are expedited proceedings, processing them within a proxy fight's tight timeline can be challenging, especially if the shareholder seeks to publicly disclose confidential materials obtained post-trial. In such scenarios, the court faces added pressure to prevent exploitation of the inspection process.

only tasked with attempting to resolve the case within a few weeks, but also anticipated to address the inevitable disputes stemming from the corporation's need to protect confidential information and the stockholder's desire to use such information for proxy solicitation. In such situations, a stockholder must necessarily submit a precise request, asking for only a limited set of specific documents. Section 220 is not a means to bypass discovery processes, nor is it intended to serve as a venue for extensive document requests allowed under Rule 34. The Supreme Court highlighted this in Security First Corporation v. U.S. Die Casting and Development Company, where it addressed a broad, eight-category demand. While the Court mandated some document production, to be decided upon remand, the crucial takeaway from Security First is its commentary on the permissible scope of a Section 220 request. The Court clarified that Section 220 and Rule 34 discovery are distinct processes, with Section 220 inspections intended to be narrowly focused.

scope: The production scope ordered by the Court of Chancery here resembles a broad discovery order under Rule 34 more than a Section 220 directive. These procedures differ and should not be conflated. A Section 220 proceeding should yield an order defined with exact precision. Rule 34 production orders, by contrast, often align with the broader discovery scope under Rule 26(b). Our Section 220 precedents affirm that while stockholders have a significant right to access books and records, it is not without limits. Any Section 220 demand must be scrutinized for legal appropriateness. The demand in this case, both in wording and intent, conflicts with the Security First ruling. Notably, the plaintiff submitted an excessively broad Section 220 request, dwarfing even the lengthy demand in Security First. Furthermore, this demand was filed despite the plaintiff (or its affiliates) having the opportunity to pursue full

discovery on the same mismanagement claims in other Texas federal and state court cases, yet opted to avoid this by invoking the PSLRA and SLUSA stay provisions. While exercising federal rights to delay discovery is permissible, it should not precede a Section 220 demand that effectively seeks unilateral discovery on the same issues. After submitting this clearly improper demand, Highland Select filed suit in this court and requested expedited handling to prepare for a proxy contest scheduled just a month after trial. Had the court granted the document request, it would have spent June resolving confidentiality disputes arising from the production. Despite seeking expedited review and forcing Motient to mount a rapid defense, Highland hindered Motient's efforts by presenting a Rule 30(b)(6) witness who was constrained by attorney-client privilege, limited tenure at the plaintiff corporation, and insufficient knowledge, raising serious concerns about

Highland's adherence to the rule. The court was especially troubled by Highland's narrow interpretation that a Rule 30(b)(6) witness can only testify based on information gained in their corporate role. Such a designee is expected to familiarize themselves with the entity's knowledge and testify within the designated bounds. The trial also revealed that the urgency for resolution was largely Highland's own doing. Highland Capital and its affiliates had known about the alleged mismanagement for months. Dondero could have resigned and advocated for change at any time but waited until February to act. This pattern began in August 2005 when, instead of using Section 220 to gather information as courts advise, a Highland affiliate filed an inadequately pleaded derivative suit, later dismissed by this court. Meanwhile, Highland repeatedly publicized its excessive Section 220 demand. Finally confronted with

Highland started to reduce its demands gradually, first slightly in its initial brief, then significantly the night before the trial. The court had to request further explanations as Highland Select failed to clarify how the new demand differed from the original. Highland's subsequent response altered the demand once more, none of which resolved the court's concerns about the original demand's scope or the relief sought. These actions demonstrate an abuse of the Section 220 process, seemingly aimed at something other than protecting stockholder rights, with evidence suggesting Highland's intent was to leverage the demand for its proxy battle.

Highland appears to have used the demand primarily as a rhetorical tool, not for legitimate purposes as outlined in Disney. The court is not obligated to sift through the disorganized demand to find a few justifiable documents. Section 220 is meant for focused investigations into potential mismanagement, but Highland's demand starkly contradicts this framework, leading to its denial. Consequently, the complaint is dismissed, and judgment is awarded to Motient Corporation, with costs.

The plaintiff corporation filed a replevin action to recover forty-one 40 x 16 Harmer 4x4 box looms delivered to defendant James G. Knowles under four agreements dated between 1894 and 1895. The agreements, except for the number of looms, price, and payment terms, followed a standard format. Knowles acknowledged receipt of the looms as property of Knowles Loom Works, agreeing to pay in installments with interest. The agreements stipulated that title would remain with Knowles Loom Works until full payment was made and required insurance coverage for the looms.

Each agreement specified that failure to meet payment terms allowed Knowles Loom Works to reclaim and sell the looms, with any surplus returned to the defendant. The first agreement covered eleven looms priced at $2,200, payable in four installments with interest from November 1, 1894. The second agreement involved ten looms and twenty warp beams (the latter not in dispute) for $2,032.50, due in four installments with interest from February 15, 1895. The third agreement included twelve looms at $2,400, payable in installments.

The agreements emphasized that Knowles Loom Works retained ownership until full payment, with no title transfer until then. The defendant also agreed to insure the looms for the benefit of Knowles Loom Works. Default on payments permitted Knowles Loom Works to repossess and sell the looms, refunding any excess proceeds to the defendant. The case details are drawn from the court's opinion, which outlines the terms of the agreements and the dispute over the looms.

This opinion confirms our stance on two issues: (1) the appropriateness of the writ for the plaintiff's aims; and (2) the Speaker's authority to call the election. The Superior Court disagreed, stating prohibition can restrain administrative actions based on disputed legal authority.
