In 1934, it was also established that the Superior Court can issue a writ of prohibition to an administrative agency when it is engaged in a judicial or quasi-judicial role. This was affirmed in Family Court v. Department of Labor & Industrial Relations, Del.Ch., 320 A.2d 777, 779 (1974). While some jurisdictions allow such writs to limit election-related actions, we had reservations about applying this extraordinary remedy to the routine task of scheduling a special election, as dictated by higher authority. Given time constraints and limited opportunity for thorough analysis, we provisionally accepted the writ of prohibition as a valid recourse for the plaintiff, acknowledging the challenges faced by their legal team due to existing case law. See Starnes v. O'Grady, Del.Ch. Civil Action No. 4766 (April 4, 1975). Consequently, we proceeded under the assumption that the writ was appropriate and addressed the case on its merits.

The plaintiff contended that the Speaker lacked authority to issue the writ of election under § 7101, as the House was not 'in session' on July 30th, when the vacancy arose. They argued that the July 28th session had effectively ended when it was 'recessed to the call of the Chair' without a set reconvening date, equating this to an 'adjournment without day.' This would invoke 15 Del.C. § 7103, requiring the Governor to summon the General Assembly before a writ could be issued. We found these claims unconvincing. Article II, § 4 of the Delaware Constitution explicitly designates the July 28th session as a 'recall' of the regular session, which typically concludes on June 30th. The section states: 'The General Assembly may extend its session annually as deemed necessary, but no session shall go beyond June 30 unless recalled by the Governor or the joint action of both Houses' presiding officers.' (emphasis

added.) The Governor invoked his Article II, § 4 recall authority through a proclamation under Del.Const. Art. III, § 16: 'I, Sherman W. Tribbitt, Governor of Delaware, under Article III, Section 16 of the State Constitution, hereby call the House and Senate of the 128th General Assembly into Special Session on July 28, 1975, at 1:00 p.m., to address, among other items, an Omnibus Amendment to the 1976 Budget Appropriation Act (Senate Bill 431) and related matters.' Evidently, the agenda for this recall session pertained to standard legislative business: budget and taxation. We noted that the phrase 'recessed to the call of the Chair' is commonly understood in Delaware’s General Assembly. Established practice dictates that these words, used during a regular session by a presiding officer, do not signify an adjournment

without day or session termination, even absent a specified return date. Customarily, adjournment without day requires a formal motion and vote; a mere recess does not. Given the significance of the General Assembly members' perception of their session status, and considering the July 28th meeting was a 'recall' under Article II, § 4, the term 'recess to the call of the Chair' must carry the same meaning as in a regular session—a temporary pause without a fixed return date, not a final adjournment. No compelling evidence was presented to justify interpreting this phrase differently in a recall session versus a regular session. To further affirm that the July 28th recall remained active, Del.Const. Art. II, § 12 must be considered, which stipulates that neither House

Neither chamber may pause for over three days unless the other agrees. There is no evidence that the Senate approved the House's break on July 28th. Determining if the July 28th 'recall' session concluded isn't just about wording—whether the Speaker said 'recessed' or 'adjourned.' What matters is whether the session ended according to standard House practices. On July 28, the House followed procedures for a recess, not a final adjournment. Thus, the session remained active on July 30, 1975, when Representative Jornlin's death created a vacancy. The Speaker had the authority to issue the election writ, and the prohibition writ was correctly denied.

Affirmed. Under 16 Del.C. § 7101, if a vacancy arises in the General Assembly due to lack of election, ineligibility, death, resignation, or other reasons, the presiding officer of the affected house must issue an election writ within 30 days. If the Assembly isn't in session, the Governor may issue the writ. Section 7104 states that special elections for the General Assembly must be scheduled within 10-11 days of receiving the writ if the vacancy occurs during or within 20 days before a session. For vacancies occurring 20+ days before a session, the election must be held within 30-40 days, allowing time for voter registration.

If a House vacancy occurs after the General Assembly adjourns indefinitely, no election writ can be issued under § 7101 unless the Governor also calls the Assembly back. Since the Department of Elections only challenged the prohibition writ—not the Speaker's authority to issue the election writ—the Superior Court allowed the Speaker to intervene and defend the case on its merits.

The Superior Court cited precedents like State ex rel. Newell v. Brown, where a writ barred ineligible names from ballots, and State ex rel. Higgins v. Brown, which prohibited an ineligible candidate's name from appearing. Similarly, State ex rel. Corrigan v. Perk upheld a writ preventing county officials from counting invalid referendum petitions. These cases support the court's decision to allow the prohibition writ.

In contrast, Wyman v. Durkin, N.H.Supr., 330 A.2d 772 (1974) (a writ of prohibition is unsuitable to prevent, among other things, the Ballot Law Commission from certifying a winner in a disputed U.S. Senate election when the Commission was acting within its legal authority); see also Moore v. Smith, Ky., 307 S.W.2d 191 (1957) (a writ is improper to stop a lower court from incorporating a city due to the Court's dismissal of unregistered voters). In Starnes, the Court of Chancery ruled that because the authority to conduct an election is political, equity lacks jurisdiction to prevent election officers from exercising such power. Del.Const. Art. III, § 16 states in part: 'Section 16. [The Governor] may call the General Assembly into special session by proclamation during emergencies; and if the two Houses disagree on adjournment timing, the Governor may adjourn them for up to three months.'

We observe that the Governor's Article III authority does not pertain to recalling a regular session when used for emergencies or between Election Day and the second Tuesday of the following year, the date set by Article II, § 4 for the General Assembly's convening. Del.Const. Art. II, § 12 states: 'Section 12. Neither House may adjourn for more than three days or to a location other than where both Houses are sitting without the other's consent.' Boyce, J.: The inquiry to Mr. Barrall and his response did not demonstrate any effort to locate the document or confirm its absence. Proof of search or loss was not provided. The objection is upheld. Later, the plaintiff was questioned again about whether he had contacted Mr. Barrall during the recess regarding the missing document, and he confirmed this.

He was then asked: 'What did Mr. Barrall tell you during that phone call about any search he conducted for the contract between Mr. Morgan and Mr. Cleaver?' The question was challenged as hearsay. Boyce, J.: Such responses are not admitted as hearsay evidence of the document's loss but to show a reasonable effort was made to locate it. 1 Greenleaf on Evidence (16th Ed.) § 563B., note 9. For this reason, we reject the objection. The witness may answer. 'A. I informed Mr. Barrall I was calling about the document mentioned by Mr. Handy last week. He said he had searched thoroughly but could not find it and had not written to Mr. Handy because he had promised to send it if found. He offered to testify if needed.'

'Q. Did you draft the contract for Mr. Morgan and Mr. Cleaver? A. Yes. Q. What were its terms?' An objection was raised, arguing insufficient effort to locate the original before allowing secondary evidence. Boyce, J.: The court finds the search reasonable. The objection is denied. Proceed with the answer. 'A. I prepared the agreement between Mr. Morgan and Mr. Cleaver, with the farm's purchase price set at $15,000. Mr. Morgan paid $500 upfront, and the balance was due by a specified date—now forgotten. Both parties signed, with Mr. White as a witness.' The defendant acknowledged agreeing to pay the plaintiff a 3% commission upon successful sale but understood payment was due only after receiving the purchase price. He also confirmed accepting Mr. Morgan as the buyer, deeming him financially capable of meeting the contract's terms.

Boyce, J., instructing the jury: This case involves John Heldmyer, Jr., a real estate agent, suing Henry Cleaver for payment regarding services purportedly provided by Heldmyer in selling a farm. Heldmyer seeks $450, or 3% of the sale price, claiming he facilitated the transaction. If someone hires another to perform a task and the worker fulfills the agreed terms, they are owed the predetermined amount or, if unspecified, a reasonable fee. For a real estate broker to claim compensation, they must have acted as the seller's agent and either finalized the sale or advanced negotiations to a point where the deal hinged solely on their efforts. Here, if Heldmyer connected Morgan and Cleaver, leading to a sale agreement, his right to payment is valid unless he misrepresented the buyer's ability to meet the terms, even if the buyer later backs out.

If the plaintiff, as the defendant's agent, introduced a buyer willing and able to purchase the farm at the agreed price, his role was fulfilled, and he earned his fee. The buyer's later refusal, absent any fault by the plaintiff, doesn’t negate this entitlement. The jury must assess whether the buyer could meet the sale terms and if the plaintiff misrepresented facts. If the evidence shows the plaintiff fulfilled his agreed duties, the verdict should favor him for the agreed sum or, if no amount was set, a reasonable value for his services. Tebo v. Mitchell, 5 Pennewill 356, 63 Atl. 327. Verdict for the plaintiff.

WALSH, Justice: This appeal stems from a criminal trial in the Superior Court. Richard Jackson was convicted on two counts of Unlawful Sexual Intercourse in the First Degree, along with one count each of Possession of a Deadly Weapon During a Felony, Unlawful Imprisonment in the First Degree, and Assault in the Third Degree. He received a 38-year sentence. Jackson now raises multiple unobjected-to claims of error, arguing each constitutes plain error. We find no merit in his arguments and affirm the lower court's decision. At trial, the state presented evidence that the victim, after attending night school on October 9, 1989, assisted her teacher, Veronica Clark, with her car before visiting the Clark residence. There, they met Jackson and later accompanied him to his home.

At Jackson's residence, the group played cards, ate, and drank. The victim stated she did not flirt with Jackson nor consider it a date. When the Clarks prepared to leave at 11:30 p.m., Jackson asked the victim to stay briefly. After a short conversation, he became emotional, and as she tried to leave again, he physically restrained her, tearing her jacket. He then assaulted her, pulling her hair, throwing her onto a couch, and biting her breasts despite her resistance.

However, he struck her face, brandished a knife, and threatened her life, causing her to cease resistance. Jackson let her use the bathroom before taking her to the bedroom. Later, he returned and forced her into sexual intercourse for thirty minutes. After the assault, she fled, drove home, contacted Mrs. Clark, and reported the incident to police the next day. Jackson's testimony contradicted hers, claiming consensual intimacy and denying the knife threat.

Jackson argues the trial court erred by misstating an element of Unlawful Sexual Intercourse in the First Degree to the jury, permitting unsupported guilty verdicts for both that and the Weapons charge, and allowing the State to repeatedly call the complainant 'victim.' Since these issues weren’t raised at trial, they are reviewed only for plain error. Appellate courts typically ignore claims not presented below, as failure to object usually waives appellate rights. However, under Delaware Rule 103(d), plain errors affecting substantial rights may still be considered.

Under plain error review, the error must severely prejudice substantial rights, undermining the trial's fairness. This doctrine applies only to glaring, fundamental flaws apparent in the record that deny the accused a critical right or cause manifest injustice. Constitutional claims may still be reviewed despite trial omissions. Jackson contends his conviction must be overturned because the trial court improperly instructed the jury on an essential element of First Degree Unlawful Sexual Intercourse, alleging plain error.

Jackson faced two counts of First Degree Unlawful Sexual Intercourse for nonconsensual intercourse (Third Degree) involving a deadly weapon. Delaware law elevates the offense to First Degree if a weapon is displayed. The trial judge emphasized this distinction to the jury, though not verbatim from the statute. Since the instructions accurately conveyed the law without confusion, no plain error occurred. Proper jury instructions that clarify the law and avoid confusion uphold the verdict's validity.

The decision made under the instruction will not be overturned for plain error. Probst v. State, Del.Supr., 547 A.2d 114, 119 (1988). The trial court's instruction accurately reflected Delaware law and included all elements of the offense. Therefore, we dismiss Jackson's argument that the jury was improperly instructed. Jackson's second appeal claim is that the trial court made a plain error by permitting a guilty verdict on the Unlawful Sexual Intercourse in the First Degree charge. Jackson asserts there is inadequate evidence to prove he brandished a deadly weapon 'during the commission' of the rape. As mentioned earlier, displaying a deadly weapon during a rape is a required element for a first-degree unlawful sexual intercourse conviction. 11 Del. C. § 775(a)(3). 'When a defendant argues that the evidence is insufficient to sustain a guilty verdict, the key issue is whether, after examining the evidence in the prosecution's favor, any reasonable fact-finder could have determined the crime's essential elements beyond a reasonable doubt.' Davis v. State, Del.Sup

r., 453 A.2d 802, 803 (1982) (citing Jackson v. Virginia, 443 U.S. 307, 317, 99 S.Ct. 2781, 2788, 61 L.Ed.2d 560 (1979)). The record contains ample evidence to uphold the jury's verdict. The victim testified that she complied with Jackson's sexual assault after he showed her a knife and that he kept the knife within reach throughout the attack. Additionally, physical evidence indicated some of her hair had been forcibly removed, supporting her claim of a violent, non-consensual assault. The jury had sufficient grounds to conclude Jackson used a knife, fulfilling all elements of Unlawful Sexual Intercourse in the First Degree. We find no plain error and deny this claim. Next, we address the defendant's argument that the trial court erred in allowing a guilty verdict for Possession of a Deadly Weapon During the Commission of a Felony.

Applying the Davis standard, we must determine whether all crime elements were proven. 453 A.2d at 803. Evidence indicates Jackson subdued the victim's resistance to his sexual advances by threatening her with a knife. This supports a weapons conviction. Since Jackson employed the knife to force compliance during the rape, the jury rightly found him guilty of Possession of a Deadly Weapon During the Commission of a Felony. We find no plain error. Jackson's final claim is that the trial court committed prejudicial error by allowing the prosecutor to call the complainant 'the victim.' Jackson argues this term biased the jury, as his defense rested on consent. He contends that labeling her a 'victim' presumes a crime occurred, undermining the jury's impartiality. The term 'victim' is fitting when the crime's occurrence is undisputed, and only the perpetrator's identity is contested. We concur with the defendant that the word

'victim' should be avoided when the crime itself is disputed. However, the defendant did not object when the prosecutor used the term. Failing to object typically waives the right to appeal the issue. Supreme Court Rule 8; Michael v. State, 529 A.2d at 762. Given Jackson's lack of objection, he must prove plain error. The term 'victim' was used during the direct examination of a police officer and an FBI hair expert. The trial court did not commit plain error by permitting its use, as law enforcement often employs 'victim' interchangeably with 'complaining witness.' Furthermore, the indictment itself used 'victim,' as is standard in criminal charges read to the jury. While the term should be avoided in consent-dispute cases, its unopposed use here does not amount to plain error. The Superior Court's judgment is AFFIRMED. Before

CHRISTIE, C.J., HORSEY, MOORE, WALSH, and HOLLAND, JJ. (sitting en banc). REQUEST FOR CLARIFICATION OR REHEARING EN BANC Despite prevailing in this appeal, the State seeks clarification or a rehearing en banc, arguing that the Court's critique of the term 'victim' in Jackson's trial amounts to prohibiting its use. This interpretation is an exaggerated misreading. The principal opinion specifically addresses the prosecutor's repeated use of 'victim' in a case where consent was the sole defense, potentially biasing the jury. The Court did not suggest that the term 'victim' cannot be used by witnesses or in general discourse.

In instances where the defense of consent is raised, labeling the complainant as a 'victim' prematurely assumes a crime occurred, undermining the presumption of innocence. This parallels referring to the defendant as a 'criminal' before guilt is established. If no crime is proven, the complainant cannot be deemed a victim. While the term is acceptable when a crime is undisputed, its use in contested cases like this is inappropriate. The prosecutor must avoid implying disputed facts as proven. Absent an objection, such conduct does not rise to plain error. The motion for rehearing en banc is DENIED. Appellant contends the trial court erred by allowing the State to call the complainant a 'victim' when the core issue was whether a crime happened.

Now that the defendant has been convicted, the presumption of innocence no longer applies, and referring to the complainant as the victim is permissible. Jackson's current attorney was not his trial counsel. OPINION ON PROPOSED SETTLEMENT AND DISMISSAL; COURT REJECTS PROPOSAL QUILLEN, Chancellor: The Court has been asked to approve a settlement and dismissal with prejudice in this consolidated appraisal action under Section 262 of the Delaware General Corporation Law, without notifying other dissenting shareholders. The Court declines. Counsel is commended for their transparency. While detailed facts are unnecessary, key points must be noted.

The defendant, LTV Aerospace Corporation, survived a 1972 merger with LTA-II Corporation. Shareholders were informed of the merger, their right to object, and to seek payment for their shares. Although the merger was approved, petitioners and others filed timely objections. On May 25, 1972, dissenting shareholders were notified of the merger's effective date and their right to demand payment under § 262. This notice included relevant proxy excerpts and the full text of § 262. The plaintiffs and the Company could not agree on share value, leading to timely petitions under § 262(c).

) requesting an appraisal process in this Court. Herbert D. Raynor initiated Civil Action No. 4044, while Borden B. Price filed Civil Action No. 4052, and Harris E. and Glenn Mary Phillips brought Civil Action No. 4053. On January 4, 1973, Chancellor Duffy issued an order merging these three cases into a single action, Civil Action No. 4044. On November 13, 1972, following § 262(d), the defendant submitted a verified list to the Register in Chancery, detailing the names and addresses of LTV Aerospace Corporation stockholders who sought payment for their shares but had not reached valuation agreements with the company. Over forty dissenting stockholders were included. However, due to immediate settlement talks between the plaintiffs and the Company, no appraisal hearing was scheduled or announced by the Register in Chancery. The parties involved in Consolidated Action No. 4044 now seek Court approval of

a settlement agreement where, in return for dismissing their appraisal claim with prejudice, the Company will compensate each plaintiff (Raynor, Price, and the Phillips) at a rate per share higher than the $9,125 paid to certain dissenting stockholders who agreed on valuation under § 262(b). Additionally, the parties request that no notice of the settlement and dismissal be sent to the forty-plus other dissenting stockholders who did not file suit in the Court of Chancery by November 14, 1972 (the deadline, four months after a thirty-day period following the twenty-day window after the merger notice was mailed). The parties argue that these stockholders' failure to file individual appraisal suits eliminates any further recourse under the General Corporation Law. The Court finds the proposed approach inconsistent with both the wording and intent of the appraisal statute. Section 262(c) (cited in footnote 2, supra) does not mandate that every dissenting stockholder must petition

the Court to appoint an appraiser. Instead, it explicitly permits any such stockholder to petition the Court and 'request a valuation of the stock of all such stockholders by a court-appointed appraiser.' (Emphasis added). Requiring each dissenting stockholder to file a separate petition would be impractical and excessive. The drafters of § 262 likely did not envision forty separate petitions, only to consolidate them into a single case with one appraiser determining the stock value for all dissenters. The statute anticipates a hearing, with mailed and published notice to all dissenting stockholders [§ 262(d)], before appointing an appraiser. Furthermore, § 262(e) clarifies that only one petition is needed to prompt the Court to hold such a hearing, after which it will 'identify the stockholders who have met the section’s requirements and are entitled to share valuation and payment.' Only then will the Court appoint an appraiser to 'provide interested parties a fair opportunity to

present relevant evidence on share value.' The plaintiffs here claim they alone have satisfied § 262’s conditions and are the only ones entitled to payment. While § 262(e) does not require the Court to determine which stockholders have secured their appraisal rights until after a hearing, the Court highlights Professor Folk’s summary: 'Dissent formalities. Revised § 262(b) (1967, amended 1969) requires: (1) a written objection filed with the corporation before the merger vote; (2) shares either non-voting or voted against the merger; and (3) a written demand for cash payment within 20 days of merger notice.' Folk, The Delaware General Corporation Law, § 262, p. 374. Since the Company’s verified list of dissenting stockholders suggests these requirements were met, and a timely appraisal petition was filed with this

The Court currently sees no basis to assume that stockholders not involved in the proposed settlement are ineligible for notice and inclusion in the settlement. This stance is supported by the statute's wording, legal precedents, and the case's specifics. For over two decades, the appraisal statute has been understood to offer a unified process for all dissenting stockholders who have secured their appraisal rights. In Southern Production Company v. Sabath, Chief Justice Southerland noted that the Court of Chancery oversees appraisals in a class-action-like proceeding, involving the corporation and all dissenting stockholders under the court's jurisdiction. This principle was reaffirmed in Levin v. Midland-Ross Corporation, where it was stated that dissenting stockholders have a statutory right to appraisal without needing legal or expert representation, ensuring they receive full value minus statutory costs.

In Levin v. Midland-Ross Corporation, Vice Chancellor Marvel emphasized that dissenting stockholders in Delaware corporations have a statutory right to appraisal during mergers, without the obligation to hire legal or expert representation. This ensures they receive the full appraisal value, less any statutory costs. He noted the unfairness of dissenting stockholders benefiting from others' efforts in engaging counsel or experts, often to the advantage of all. Thus, in the current case, dissenting stockholders who are not petitioners will not lose their rights under § 262 merely for choosing not to actively participate. The Court also observes that while formal notice of an appraisal hearing has not been sent, court records show correspondence from dissenting stockholders aware of the proceedings, indicating their reliance on the ongoing consolidated lawsuit.

The Register in Chancery has responded to inquiries from dissenting stockholders by confirming their inclusion in the verified list and directing them to the plaintiffs' attorney. These stockholders are depending on the pending consolidated lawsuit. Given § 262's language, prior precedents, and statutory notices, the Court concludes these stockholders believed their appraisal rights were secured without filing separate petitions. The Company cannot now argue that these stockholders lack appraisal rights due to not filing individual petitions. Once a petition was filed, other dissenting stockholders could rely on § 262, expecting their shares to be valued in the appraisal. The Company cannot undermine their rights by settling with current plaintiffs at a premium.

Under § 262(d), a hearing will be scheduled to determine which stockholders are entitled to share valuation and payment. These stockholders will then share equally in any settlement of the consolidated appraisal action. The Court rejects the proposed dismissal and directs counsel to submit an order per 8 Del.C. § 262(d) and (e). Section 262(b) requires the surviving corporation to notify dissenting stockholders within 10 days of the merger's effective date. If a stockholder demands payment within 20 days of the notice, the surviving corporation must comply with the appraisal process.

The company must, within 30 days after the 20-day period ends, pay the stockholder the value of their shares as of the merger's effective date, excluding any value linked to the merger itself. Section 262(c) states that if the corporation and the stockholder cannot agree on the stock's value within the following 30 days, either party may petition the Court of Chancery within four months to appoint an appraiser for valuation. Section 262(d) requires the corporation to file a verified list of stockholders who demanded payment but haven’t reached an agreement within ten days of being served.

Three plaintiffs appeared to support an interpretation of § 262(e) similar to the Court's. Raynor and the Phillips requested in their petitions that the Court issue a summons for the corporation to comply with § 262 by filing a list of stockholders who demanded payment but lacked agreements. They also sought Court determination of eligible stockholders, appointment of an appraiser, and a decree for payment of stock value with interest from the merger date.

The corporation's response does not admit liability, citing 8 Del.C. § 262(e) and In Re Universal Pictures Co. The defendant argued for a tenancy in common, while plaintiffs cited trespass laws for boundary removal. The Chancellor noted that trespass applies to ouster or destruction but not to reclaimable actions. The complainant acknowledged no binding contract existed without formal acceptance of the bid.

The complainant argued that the City Council was equitably bound to award him the contract, but the Chancellor found no grounds to interfere. The Council rejected all initial bids and sought new proposals under revised specifications. While preferring a higher bidder might be questionable, the Council had the authority to modify terms and restart the bidding process, absent specific regulatory constraints.

Contrary to any claims, the complete authority of any individual or entity remains intact even after receiving and reviewing bids for a proposed project, allowing them to entirely abandon the work, modify its design, or revise the specifications and issue new ones; without this, there would be no safeguard against collusion or excessive bids surpassing the budget—nor any solution for flaws in the project plan or specifications revealed during bidding. This discretion, exercised fairly and honestly, is widely accepted. A comparable 1867 New York case, The People vs. The Croton Aqueduct, Boards 49 Barb. Sup. Ct. Repts. 259, mirrors this situation. There, the Croton Aqueduct Board solicited bids for construction, received offers including the lowest from the relator, but awarded no contract. Later, the Board revised the project plan and re-advertised for bids. The initial lowest bidder sought mandamus relief, which was denied.

The Court upheld the broad discretionary authority of those issuing proposals, even after bids are submitted and opened, until a contract is finalized. The Court stated: 'The notice did not bind them (the Board) to award the project to the lowest bidder; issuing proposals alone did not impose such an obligation. It was merely an invitation for bids, and if those bids were excessive or beyond the budget, the Board typically had the right to reject them entirely.' This ruling was endorsed by Brewster J. in Wiggins vs. The City of Philadelphia, 2 Brews. Repts. 144. As long as this discretion to reject original specifications and restart is used in good faith, courts cannot intervene. The charter grants this discretion to the Council, and courts will only ensure it is exercised fairly and honestly. The Council's integrity

in this matter is unchallenged in the case record. Additionally, a key aspect of this case solidifies the City Council's right to reject Keogh's bid or even favor a higher bid under the original advertisement. His bid explicitly acknowledged the Council's right 'to reject any or all bids' under that notice. By submitting his bid under these terms, he implicitly agreed to this condition. The reservation effectively framed his bid as an offer to perform the work at a specified price, contingent on the Council's approval. His acceptance of the advertisement's terms binds him, preventing him from later contesting whether the street committee's reservation conflicted with a city ordinance mandating contracts be awarded to the lowest bidder. The ordinance is not a statutory requirement but an internal directive for the Council's agents,

governing discretionary matters. Any deviation from it can be ratified by the Council as effectively as if pre-authorized. Compliance with the ordinance is an internal issue between the Council and its officers, irrelevant to the bidder. By bidding under the reserved terms, Keogh waived any objection. This case does not address whether the Council, absent statutory constraints, could reject the lowest bid without reservation, provided it acts in good faith for the public interest. That broader question remains unanswered and inappropriate here. Lastly, the complainant amended his bill to assert his status as a Wilmington citizen and taxpayer, though this does not alter the core legal issues at hand.

In that role, he requests the injunction to safeguard public interest from extra costs and higher taxes that might arise from the City Council's actions. I set aside the debate over who can legally challenge municipal misconduct and will address this case as properly presented. Both attorneys agreed to resolve the motion based on merits, avoiding technicalities. Here, the key is defining judicial limits over municipal discretion. Courts may intervene to protect private rights, prevent unauthorized powers, or stop corrupt misuse of authority. However, if no private right is harmed and the City acts in good faith, courts won’t question their decisions' expediency.

This straightforward rule is practical, protects the public, and respects discretionary powers, supported by legal precedents like People vs. New York and Reynolds vs. Mayor of Albany. Applying this to Wilmington’s street paving—a discretionary power granted to the City Council—arguments framed it as a trustee duty, but the distinction is irrelevant. Whether legislative or fiduciary, the power remains discretionary, covering plans, contracts, and funding. The Council’s shift from macadamizing Fourth Street to new bids violated no rights nor showed bad faith, making judicial interference unwarranted.

Whether viewed as legislative or strict trusteeship, the power is inherently discretionary, involving plans, contracts, and funding. The Council’s rejection of initial bids for Fourth Street and adoption of new specifications breached no legal or equitable rights of Mr. Keogh, nor implied corruption. It was a good-faith exercise of charter-granted discretion, beyond judicial review. If discretionary powers are overly broad or prone to abuse, legislatures, not courts, must impose limits. Citizens address officer qualifications through elections. Courts only step in to protect private rights or curb unauthorized or corrupt power misuse.

Where charter-granted discretion is excessive or abuse-prone, legislatures must set limits. Citizen elections address officer fitness. Courts intervene solely to protect private rights or prevent unauthorized or corrupt power use. The injunction motion is denied. In a later case, Attorney General vs. Detroit, Michigan’s Supreme Court echoed these principles, allowing injunctions only for substantial public interest violations. A ‘lowest bidder’ sought to block a contract award to the highest bidder, but courts upheld interference only where public rights were at stake.

The law requires the contract to be awarded to the lowest bidder, yet certain decisions inevitably remain within the City Council's discretion. While not identical, the Michigan case offers valuable insights on this matter. Dillon, in the most recent edition of his work on Municipal Corporations, Section 470, argues that a contract remains incomplete until the bid is accepted. Furthermore, in Section 832, he asserts that the discretion of municipal authorities cannot be overruled, even by mandamus, which he notes cannot compel the awarding of a contract to the lowest bidder (note 3).

No relationship between the father and his illegitimate child was established. The father argued that the mother had continually prevented him from seeing the child since birth. The Family Court dismissed his visitation petition, noting he had the chance to amend it to demonstrate a relationship formed after April 2, 1970, but failed to do so. The Superior Court upheld this decision, citing the factual circumstances. The father contends that neither court allowed him a hearing to present evidence of the mother's refusal, claiming a denial of due process.

In determining custody or visitation rights for a child, whether legitimate or not, the court's primary consideration must be the child's best interests and welfare, not the parents' wishes. Modern law recognizes the father's right to custody or visitation if it benefits the child. The parents' interests are never paramount in such decisions. The record indicates the father was unjustly denied the opportunity to prove that the mother's refusal prevented him from establishing a relationship with his child.

The summary denial of a hearing by both the Family Court and Superior Court deprived the father of due process and fundamental fairness. This contradicts procedural rules, and we disapprove of such actions. We reverse the Superior Court's decision and remand the case for a hearing—either in the Family Court or a trial de novo in the Superior Court—to determine if visitation rights would serve the child's best interests. We refrain from prejudging the outcome but emphasize the error in denying the father a hearing. The judgment is reversed.

Wright, Jr. was found guilty of first-degree rape, attempted first-degree rape, first-degree kidnapping, possessing a deadly weapon during a felony, and being a prohibited person in possession of a deadly weapon. On appeal, he contends that his constitutional right to confront and cross-examine the complainant was violated because the trial judge excluded evidence of the complainant's prior sexual conduct. He also claims ineffective assistance of counsel, though this issue was not raised during the trial. We find no reversible error in the judge's refusal to hold an in camera hearing or exclude the evidence, and thus affirm the conviction. On November 19, 1984, the complainant, a 15-year-old student, left home at 7:40 a.m. for school. While walking near the soccer field, she noticed a man who seemed to be jogging. He called to her, and she quickened her pace.

He called again, and when the student realized he was pursuing her, she ran. The man chased her, caught her, and held her in a headlock with a knife to her throat. He ordered her to stay quiet and led her into tall grass, where he cut his sweatpants' drawstring and removed them along with his gym shorts. He forced her to perform oral sex, then attempted vaginal intercourse at knifepoint but failed. Afterward, he let her go, returning her belongings. As she fled, he gestured for her silence. She reached school by 8:00 a.m. and told her boyfriend, who took her to the assistant principal. Police were called.

Delaware State Police Corporal Susan Brady interviewed the victim at school and visited the crime scene. She then took the victim to the hospital for an examination, where the victim’s clothes were collected for evidence. Though visibly distressed, the victim recounted the attack to the doctor but was uncertain about vaginal penetration. Based on her description, police created a photo lineup, and she identified Wright. Another student also picked Wright from a lineup. A search of Wright’s home near the school uncovered clothing matching the victims' descriptions, including sweatpants with a cut drawstring, and a knife resembling the one described. These items were sent to the FBI lab.

The FBI found two hairs on Wright’s sweatpants microscopically consistent with the victim’s. At trial, Wright presented an alibi, claiming he was jogging near the school but returned home by 7:55 a.m. A neighbor testified she saw him after 8:00 a.m., contradicting his parents' account. Defense counsel questioned the victim about prior sexual activity, but the state objected, arguing this was an improper credibility attack without following statutory procedures. The state also maintained that such evidence was irrelevant to the case.

The act was considered a crime as the defendant was under the age of consent. The State argued that the defense forfeited its chance to introduce evidence about the complainant's sexual history by not adhering to the proper process. The defense countered that the rules about admitting a rape victim's prior sexual activity aim to avoid unexpected revelations. They claimed that since the prosecution was already aware of this history, there could be no surprise, rendering the statute irrelevant. The defense sought to present the victim's past sexual conduct for two reasons: first, they found the complainant had unprotected sex with her boyfriend before the alleged rape, which could suggest a motive for a false accusation due to pregnancy fears. Second, they wanted to question her understanding of sexual activity, as her statement showed uncertainty about penetration. The trial judge sided with the State, barring the evidence, stating the rape shield law wasn't just about preventing surprise.

The trial judge ruled that even if the statutory process could be bypassed, the defendant hadn't shown enough relevance to justify attacking the victim's credibility with her sexual history. The defense then requested a mistrial, arguing they were barred from presenting key evidence to support their claim that the rape didn't happen. The court denied this, noting that even with proper procedure, the evidence was too weak to allow questioning about the victim's past. The next day, the defense again asked to cross-examine the complainant on her sexual history, but the judge refused due to insufficient proof. The defense, worried their failure to follow the rape shield law had limited their cross-examination, moved for another mistrial, implicitly admitting inadequate investigation into the victim's past. The judge denied this motion as well.

Under the U.S. and Delaware Constitutions, a defendant has the right to confront witnesses against them. The main goal of this right is to allow cross-examination. However, this right isn't unlimited and can be restricted when it clashes with other trial needs. The Confrontation Clause ensures a chance for meaningful cross-examination, not unlimited questioning as the defense desires. Judges can limit cross-examination on marginally relevant topics unless there's a clear basis for bias or prejudice. They may require an offer of proof to assess if the evidence is relevant enough to justify discrediting a witness.

The trial court must balance these factors, as required by Delaware law. Evidence of a rape victim's prior sexual conduct is only admissible if the statutory process is followed and the court deems it relevant. Before presenting such evidence to challenge the complainant's credibility, the defense must submit a written motion with an offer of proof. If the court finds the proof sufficient, it may allow the evidence. This ensures that only relevant and properly vetted evidence is used during the trial.

The court must hold a hearing without the jury present and permit the complaining witness to be questioned about the defendant's offer of proof. After the hearing, the court may authorize the defendant to introduce relevant evidence. 11 Del. C. § 3508. The rape shield law is not unconstitutional, as it balances the defendant's right to confront accusers with protections for victims from unnecessary humiliation, while promoting societal interests in victim cooperation.

If the defendant's offer of proof is inadequate, the court need not hold an in camera hearing. Here, the trial judge reviewed an oral offer but found it insufficient to challenge the complainant's credibility, so no hearing was required. The record supports this decision, as the defendant's claims—inconsistent statements and potential fabrication due to pregnancy fears—lacked sufficient factual basis.

The complainant had fully disclosed her history to the physician, and her reporting of oral sex contradicted any pregnancy-related motive. The trial focused on identification, not the specifics of the acts. The defendant's impeachment attempt was irrelevant, and the trial judge correctly deemed the offer of proof insufficient for an in camera hearing.

A claim of ineffective counsel must first be raised below and requires proof of prejudice, not just deficient performance. Here, counsel’s failure to file a required motion does not alone establish incompetence. Without a full record, this Court cannot assess the claim on direct appeal. The Superior Court's judgment is affirmed under 11 Del. C. § 3508, which governs rape case evidence procedures.

The procedure for the complaining witness is as follows: (1) The defendant must submit a written motion to the court and prosecutor, detailing the defense's offer of proof regarding the relevance of evidence about the complaining witness's sexual conduct and its impact on their credibility. (2) The motion must include an affidavit outlining the offer of proof. (3) If the court deems the offer sufficient, a hearing will be held without the jury, where the complaining witness may be questioned about the defendant's offer. (4) After the hearing, if the court finds the evidence relevant and admissible, it may issue an order specifying what evidence can be presented and the scope of questioning. The defendant may then proceed as per the court's order. (b) 'Complaining witness' refers to the alleged victim of rape, attempted rape, conspiracy, or assault.

WALSH, Justice: This interlocutory appeal examines a Superior Court ruling favoring insurers in a dispute over liability coverage for tobacco-related injuries. Liggett Group, Inc. ('Liggett') sued its general commercial liability insurers, seeking coverage and a defense for numerous tobacco liability lawsuits. The Superior Court, citing policy exclusions, ruled the insurers had no obligation to cover or defend Liggett in these cases. We affirm. Liggett, a Delaware-based tobacco manufacturer, faces over a thousand lawsuits alleging negligence, defective design, failure to warn, misrepresentation, emotional distress, conspiracy, and concerted action. Liggett's suit against thirty-three insurers seeks to determine coverage under policies issued from 1970 to 2000.

Liggett seeks defense coverage for tobacco lawsuits nationwide. Partial summary judgment was granted to Primary Commercial General Liability Insurers due to tobacco exclusions in their policies. Seven Primary CGL Insurers are involved: Transportation Insurance Company (1979–1981), Federal Insurance Company (1981–1985), National Union Fire Insurance Company (1985–1986), Zurich Insurance Company (1986), The Home Insurance Company (1986–1988), Hartford Accident and Indemnity Company (1988–1990), and Twin City Fire Insurance Group (1990–1993). The Superior Court directed the parties to select twenty representative complaints to assess the duty to defend. These complaints involve plaintiffs claiming diseases from smoking, seeking damages for physical symptoms, mental distress, and loss of consortium.

Many plaintiffs also seek compensation for tobacco-related illnesses. Third-party payors, like state governments and health insurers, file claims for reimbursement of treatment costs. The Primary CGL policies include broad tobacco exclusions, barring coverage for claims linked to tobacco use. Exclusions vary but commonly address injuries 'arising from tobacco product use' or 'caused by tobacco.' These exclusions apply to 'bodily injury' and sometimes 'property damage,' but not 'personal injury.' The Superior Court also ruled in favor of the insurers, reinforcing the exclusions' validity.

The court ruled in favor of Royal Indemnity Company and Royal Insurance Company of America (together 'Royal') by granting summary judgment, citing the products-hazard exclusion in their policies, which removed their obligation to defend Liggett's claims. Liggett had bought a series of consecutive CGL insurance policies from Royal, covering bodily injury incidents from 1993 to 1997. These policies excluded injuries falling under the 'products-completed operations hazard,' which includes all bodily injuries stemming from 'your product.' 'Your product' refers to goods or products made, sold, or distributed by the insured. Summary judgment was also awarded to Continental Casualty Company ('Continental') since the complaints did not claim 'advertising injury,' a requirement under Continental's Media Special Perils ('MSP') policies. Continental had issued five annual MSP policies to Liggett from 1981 to 1986, with the 1981 and 1983 policies specifying coverage for defamation-related claims in advertising.

Continental's policies from 1981 and 1983 stated they would cover losses the insured owed due to claims from defamation in advertising. The term 'emotional distress' was absent in these policies. The 1984 MSP policy retained similar wording but added 'infliction of emotional distress' to the listed offenses. The 1985 MSP policy expanded coverage further with a defamation perils endorsement, including claims related to harm to reputation or emotional distress. The Superior Court also partially ruled in Royal's favor, stating Liggett was not a Named Insured under an umbrella CGL policy issued to Intercontinental Hotels Corporation. This policy lacked a tobacco or products-hazard exclusion and broadly defined 'personal injury' coverage.

The umbrella policy listed Intercontinental Hotels Corporation as the Named Insured, with Endorsement No. 1 adding other corporations, including Grand Metropolitan Public Limited Company ('Grand Met'). The policy defined Named Insured to include subsidiaries and companies under the insured's management. Liggett was not a direct subsidiary of Grand Met due to multiple corporate layers. Grand Met, a large conglomerate, owned Grand Met Holdings, Inc., which in turn owned Grand Metropolitan (USA) Holdings, followed by Grand Met USA, Inc., and finally Liggett. Intercontinental Hotels was a subsidiary of Grand Met Holdings, Inc., and operated independently from Liggett.

Each Grand Met entity was distinct, with its own leadership. Intercontinental Hotels managed its operations and insurance separately from Liggett. The Superior Court's summary judgment ruling is reviewed de novo, as is its interpretation of the insurance policies. The court applied North Carolina law to this dispute, a decision unchallenged on appeal. Insurers can secure summary judgment by proving the claimant cannot establish a key element of their claim or overcome a valid defense.

In 79 N.C.App. 688, 340 S.E.2d 510, 512 (1986), and Oakley v. Little, 49 N.C.App. 650, 272 S.E.2d 370, 372 (1980), it was noted that summary judgment facilitates swift resolution of claims where no genuine issue exists regarding the plaintiff's recovery or when the defendant has proven a complete defense. Liggett contends that the Superior Court misapplied the duty to defend by interpreting it too restrictively and expansively reading policy exclusions. Insurers respond that the policies explicitly exclude tobacco-related claims and accuse Liggett of cherry-picking policy language to justify unjustified exceptions. The duty to defend is typically broader than the duty to indemnify and is assessed based on the allegations in the pleadings. Waste Management v. Peerless Ins. Co., 315 N.C. 688, 340 S.E.2d 374,

377 (1986). However, if the pleadings present facts showing no coverage and the insurer lacks contrary knowledge, no defense is required. Waste Management, 340 S.E.2d at 377. North Carolina courts use the 'comparison test' to evaluate the duty to defend, as seen in Smith v. Nationwide Mut. Fire Ins. Co., 116 N.C.App. 134, 446 S.E.2d 877, 878 (1994). This test involves comparing the underlying suit's pleadings with the policy to ascertain coverage. If the pleadings reveal covered injuries, the insurer must defend, regardless of ultimate liability. The focus is on the factual allegations, not their legal characterization. Holz-Her U.S., Inc. v. U.S. Fidelity and Guar. Co., 141 N.C.App.

127, 539 S.E.2d 348, 350 (2000). While the duty to defend is extensive, it does not extend to risks insurers explicitly excluded. See Waste Management, 315 N.C. 688, 340 S.E.2d 374; Holz-Her U.S., 141 N.C.App. 127, 539 S.E.2d 348; Smith, 116 N.C.App. 134, 446 S.E.2d 877. After reviewing the complaints and policies, the Superior Court found that all claims sought damages for health effects from tobacco use, which the policies plainly excluded. In construing the policies, the court aimed to discern the parties' original intent, as emphasized in Woods v. Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co., 295 N.C. 500, 246 S.E.2d 773, 777 (1978).

We concur with the trial court that the complaints allege injuries from Liggett's tobacco products, which the primary CGL policies exclude, relieving insurers of defense obligations. This outcome aligns with the parties' intent. Liggett previously acknowledged lacking coverage for such claims, while insurers priced premiums assuming tobacco-related exclusions. Interpreting the policies to cover these claims would defy the parties' contractual intent and grant Liggett unearned benefits.

Liggett criticizes the trial court for not differentiating among 'bodily injury,' 'sickness,' and 'disease.' They note that tobacco exclusions differ in scope, with some blocking claims for 'sickness or disease' but not 'bodily injury,' and others excluding 'disease' but not 'bodily injury' or 'sickness.' Liggett contends that the complaints include claims of bodily injury, like migraines, back pain, tooth decay, poor circulation, and pregnancy issues, which don't qualify as 'disease' or 'sickness.' The Superior Court ruled that 'disease' and 'sickness' cover all 'unhealthy conditions,' whereas sudden injuries like burns or fractures are bodily injuries, not diseases.

Liggett's argument that sickness, disease, and bodily injury are stages of the same harm would undermine the tobacco exclusions, allowing coverage for excluded diseases until diagnosis. This interpretation is unreasonable. Similarly flawed is Liggett's claim that sickness is distinct from disease as a 'condition disrupting daily activities.' If accepted, tobacco exclusions would be meaningless, as diseases like cancer eventually interfere with daily life. Liggett suggests the exclusions only apply to conditions with diagnosed symptoms but no activity disruption, a reading unsupported by the policy's clear language.

Liggett asserts the policies include personal injury coverage separate from bodily injury coverage with tobacco exclusions. They argue the complaints allege personal injuries like mental harm and humiliation, covered under CGL policies. However, the Superior Court ruled that personal injury coverage doesn't extend to emotional distress from excluded bodily injuries or diseases. Under North Carolina law, 'personal injury' in CGL policies is restricted to listed torts, such as false arrest or defamation, and doesn't cover mental anguish claims.

The policies define personal injury liability as covering specific torts like false arrest, libel, slander, and wrongful eviction, along with 'injury to feelings or reputation.' These don't include the mental anguish claims Liggett seeks to cover. The plaintiffs' emotional distress stems from physical ailments caused by tobacco use, and the claims are based on negligence in producing a harmful product. The policies explicitly exclude negligence claims, and the 'injury to feelings' clause doesn't apply to these cases.

Liggett's argument must be understood in context. Gaston County Dyeing Mach. Co. v. Northfield Ins. Co., 351 N.C. 293, 524 S.E.2d 558, 563 (2000) (stating that insurance policy terms should be 'construed harmoniously'). Here, it should be interpreted alongside the preceding list of torts, which broadly includes libel, slander, and defamation. It cannot be viewed as a standalone expansion of coverage to all mental anguish claims in products liability or negligence cases. Liggett also contends that Royal's products-hazard exclusion does not cover bodily injury claims unrelated to its product, such as those from secondhand smokers, third-party payors, or government actions. The Superior Court ruled these claims 'arise from' Liggett's tobacco products, citing Eon Labs Manufacturing, Inc. v. Reliance Insurance Co., 756 A.2d 889 (Del.2000), where claims against a manufacturer for fen-phen injuries were deemed to fall under the products-completed operations hazard exclusion.

Claims for injuries from the fen-phen drug combination were linked to the manufacturer's product and fell under the CGL policy's exclusion, even if other products were involved. Liggett tries to dismiss Eon Labs by arguing it wasn't based on North Carolina law, but the Court emphasized its reliance on 'general insurance contract principles.' Id. at 892. The arguments dismissed in Eon Labs closely resemble Liggett's here. Both cases involve claims where the defendant's product, combined with others, caused harm. The Court rejected the idea that such claims hold the defendant liable for others' products, stressing that the suits centered on the defendant's product and its role in the injuries. Id. at 893. North Carolina law does not mandate a different outcome.

In State Capital and related cases, the North Carolina Supreme Court ruled that excluded liability sources must be the sole cause of injury to deny coverage. State Capital, 350 S.E.2d at 73. The Superior Court found tobacco use to be the sole cause here, barring coverage. We concur. The complaints target Liggett because its product allegedly caused harm. Moreover, State Capital involved motor vehicle or homeowners insurance, which serve public policy and consumer protection goals. This case concerns a commercial policy between sophisticated parties, a distinction North Carolina courts acknowledge, showing less protection for commercial insureds. See Wake Stone Corp., 995 F.Supp. at 617 (noting 'arising out of' in CGL policies doesn't widen coverage).

Liggett argues the Superior Court erred in finding the complaints didn't allege damages 'arising out of' its advertising, which would trigger Continental's Media Special Perils policy. Liggett claims the Court applied the wrong causation standard, requiring injuries to stem directly from the advertising's content rather than being a foreseeable result. Continental asserts the MSP only covers defamation against competitors in advertising, not consumer injury claims. Liggett counters that the complaints allege emotional distress caused by its ads. While the complaints cite intentional or negligent infliction of emotional distress, their core allegation is that Liggett hid its products' addictiveness and misrepresented their safety. See Holz-Her, 539 S.E.2d at 350 (focusing on pleaded facts, not claim labels). Plaintiffs relied on these misrepresentations. The claim that Liggett's ads targeted youth or encouraged product use could apply to all advertising—indeed, the very purpose of ads is to influence behavior.

The primary goal of all commercial advertising is to encourage the purchase of products. While the plaintiffs use terms like emotional distress, their case fundamentally involves allegations of fraud and misrepresentation. Additionally, the emotional distress claimed stems from physical injuries caused by using Liggett's product. Even the broadest Continental MSP policy mandates a link between the claimed offense and the insured's advertising efforts, covering claims that arise from emotional distress inflicted during the dissemination of Liggett's ads. Liggett cites the State Capital case to argue that emotional distress claims are covered if they naturally result from advertising. However, the court in State Capital clarified that the 'arising out of' clause requires proximate cause, contradicting Liggett's interpretation.

The Superior Court correctly ruled that for coverage to apply, the advertising itself must be legally actionable. As this Court has observed, most courts agree that claims under advertising injury provisions need a causal link between the injury and the advertising activities. The McDonald's Corp. case, which involved similar policy terms, is also relevant. The court there decided that coverage only applies if the offense was directly caused by promotional efforts. The trial court rightly noted that broadening this interpretation would extend coverage to all product-related claims merely because the product was advertised, which would be an overreach.

Expanding coverage as Liggett suggests would unjustly include all claims tied to a product simply due to its advertisement, as highlighted in the McDonald's case and supported by Frog, Switch & Mfg. Co. The Superior Court also determined that Liggett is not a 'Named Insured' under Royal's umbrella policy. Liggett disputes this, arguing the court misapplied the term 'subsidiary' by limiting it to direct subsidiaries and overlooking standard contract interpretation principles favoring coverage. Liggett further contends the court underestimated the impact of the word 'any' on the term 'subsidiary' and the scope of the duty to defend.

Royal asserts the policy was designed for hotel operations, and the parties never intended to cover Liggett, which is six corporate levels removed from the named insured, Grand Met. Interpreting the policy requires understanding the parties' intent at the time of issuance, not a fragmented analysis. The contract must be evaluated in its entirety, with a construction that is logical, practical, and aligned with the policy's overall risks and objectives, as emphasized in Blake v. St. Paul Fire and Marine Ins. Co. and supported by established legal principles.

Any uncertainty in the wording of the policy should be interpreted in favor of the insured, with the plain and ordinary meaning of terms being the preferred approach. C.D. Spangler Constr. Co. v. Industrial Crankshaft & Engineering Co., 326 N.C. 133, 388 S.E.2d 557, 568 (N.C.1990) (noting that unless the policy provides a specific definition, terms like 'damages' should be understood in their everyday sense). To determine the ordinary meaning of contested terms, the North Carolina Supreme Court has relied on standard, nonlegal dictionaries. C.D. Spangler, 388 S.E.2d at 568, citing Jamestown Mut. Ins. Co. v. Nationwide Mut. Ins. Co., 266 N.C. 430, 146 S.E.2d 410, 416 (1966). Here, the disputed language involves the inclusion of 'any subsidiary company' in the Named Insured definition.

According to The American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language 1283 (4th ed.2000), a subsidiary company is 'a company with over half its stock owned by another.' Other dictionaries, like Random House Unabridged Dictionary 1896 (2nd ed.1993) and Webster's Third New International Dictionary 2279 (1993), similarly define it as a company controlled by another through majority ownership. The Superior Court correctly interpreted the Royal insurance policy to cover only subsidiaries directly owned or controlled by Grand Met, the named insured. Since the policy does not define 'subsidiary company,' the term must carry its ordinary meaning, which refers to direct subsidiaries, despite potential variations in corporate law.

Interpreting 'subsidiary company' as direct subsidiaries aligns with Grand Met's structure as a holding company with numerous direct and indirect subsidiaries globally. This interpretation also reflects the intent of the contracting parties, Intercontinental Hotels and Royal, to cover hotel and food operations, not tobacco litigation. While ambiguous policy terms are typically resolved in favor of coverage, this case supports a reasonable and logical reading. Liggett's argument that the ruling implicates corporate law is misplaced, as the court focused solely on the term's ordinary meaning in an insurance contract, not corporate governance. The Superior Court's summary judgment in favor of the insurers is upheld.

LEIN, Judge. Defendant Joseph Walls has filed a motion in limine to exclude evidence of his prior robbery conviction. On May 18, 1986, Walls and co-defendant Efrain Hernandez were indicted on 24 counts, including the 'Hailstone' and 'Pancoast' robberies. Defense attorneys sought to sever the offenses, arguing they were unrelated and trying them together would prejudice the jury. The Superior Court agreed and severed the charges. Walls and Hernandez were jointly tried for the Pancoast robbery (Counts I-X), resulting in Walls' conviction on October 15, 1986, for crimes similar to those in the current case.

The conviction included one count of Burglary First Degree, two counts of Robbery First Degree, one count of Possession of a Deadly Weapon During a Felony, one count of Terroristic Threatening, and one count of Conspiracy Second Degree. The jury failed to reach a verdict for Hernandez, leading to a mistrial on October 15, 1986. The State aims to present testimony from the Pancoast robbery victim and a certified copy of Walls' conviction to demonstrate a common scheme or plan and identity in Walls' trial for the Hailstone offense. The defense argues this evidence would be highly prejudicial, risking jury bias, and that a curative instruction would not suffice. Walls also fears testifying if it reveals his 1986 conviction.

The State highlighted factual parallels between the current charges and the 1986 conviction, claiming a modus operandi. Common elements include two men burglarizing a home, one wearing a ski mask, threats with a handgun, instructing victims not to look, physical abuse, and attempts to disable communication. The defense counters that these traits are generic to robberies, noting discrepancies like the use of a baseball bat in one case but not the other.

In criminal cases, evidence of prior crimes is generally inadmissible to prove guilt for the current charge, per D.U.R.E. 404(b) and 608(b). Exceptions exist if the prior crimes are relevant to identity, intent, motive, or a common scheme. Such evidence risks biasing the jury, as it may imply the defendant's criminal propensity. The State argues the Pancoast robbery evidence is admissible to establish identity and a shared plan.

To admit evidence of other crimes, clear and substantial proof is required, as seen in Renzi v. State and Benson v. State. For modus operandi, the similarities must significantly exceed typical crime traits. Cases like State v. Harding and State v. Allen emphasize this high standard. The State contends the robberies' unique similarities justify admitting the evidence, while the defense disputes their distinctiveness.

N.W.2d 200 (1976). The Court must evaluate both similarities and differences. Refer to State v. Harding, supra. Here, the similarities significantly exceed those typical in a home robbery, outweighing any discrepancies. Defendant claims insufficient evidence in the Pancoast case, where the jury failed to agree on Hernandez, leading to a mistrial. Walls and Hernandez were both convicted based on testimony from the Pancoasts. The trial Court found the lineups for Walls and Hernandez improperly suggestive. Other victims, not exposed to these lineups, did not identify Walls. Walls has filed a motion for a mistrial or new trial in the Pancoast case, which remains pending. The State argued orally that there is ample evidence beyond witness identification to convict Walls for the Pancoast robbery. Defendant contends the evidence against him is weak and compromised. Nevertheless, the jury convicted him, and the verdict stands.

This Court previously allowed evidence of the Pancoast robbery to demonstrate modus operandi and identity. This decision was made during a May 25, 1987, office conference when defense counsel requested discovery on alleged misidentifications by the Pancoast victims. Defendant has since changed lawyers and tactics, now seeking to exclude all Pancoast-related evidence. Additionally, this Court’s earlier ruling to sever the three robbery-burglary cases noted potential prejudice from introducing evidence of other alleged crimes. (Only Hernandez was charged in one.) Thus, one might infer this Court initially deemed Pancoast evidence inadmissible for the other cases. Cf. Bates v. State, Del.Supr., 386 A.2d 1139 (1978). However, the situation changed as charges against Hernandez were dropped, and he was acquitted in the third case.

The Pancoast robbery resulted in this defendant’s conviction, providing clear proof of his involvement. See Benson, supra. Consequently, the Court permits testimony from the Pancoast victims solely to establish identity via modus operandi. This evidence is restricted to testimony; the conviction itself is inadmissible in the State’s case. The Pancoast jury’s verdict is highly prejudicial to a fair trial here, offering minimal probative value while causing significant bias. Under D.U.R.E. 403, the Court excludes the conviction from the State’s case. However, if the defendant testifies, impeachment becomes relevant. Under D.U.R.E. 609(a), prior felony convictions may be used to challenge credibility if their probative value outweighs prejudice.

The Court rules that the defendant’s felony conviction may be introduced for impeachment. A defendant’s right to testify is not unduly hindered by the State’s ability to question prior felonies. Wilson v. State, Del.Supr., 414 A.2d 208 (1980). Details of the conviction may also be admitted if the defendant denies involvement in the Pancoast robbery. The motion in limine is partially granted and denied. The Court also notes the mistrial motion in Pancoast stems from alleged juror bias, including a remark about the defendant avoiding a murder charge. Balancing probative value and prejudice, the Court does not bar the defendant’s testimony but ensures he does not gain undue advantage.

the advantage of giving false testimony.Speakman, Judge: The Statute (3550 of the Code of 1935, as revised by Chap. 207, Vol. 43) states that 'a married couple residing in this State (if not legally separated) may jointly petition the Orphans' Court of their county for an order permitting them to adopt a minor child not biologically theirs. A properly acknowledged written consent must be provided by each known living parent who is not mentally incapacitated, addicted to drugs or alcohol, has not abandoned the child, or lost custody through a court order. The child's father argues that custody granted to the mother in a divorce does not constitute a court-ordered loss of custody under the adoption statute. This argument need not be addressed here, as under statute 3551 of the 1935 Code, as

amended by Chap. 187, Vol. 41), the court must be, in the statute's wording, 'convinced at a hearing where all involved parties may attend or be represented, that the biological parents have valid reasons to relinquish care and support of the child, have abandoned the child, or are morally unfit to retain custody.' When a statute like ours mandates the court to determine that parents are morally unfit to keep custody, this cannot be proven solely by a foreign divorce decree granting custody to one parent. At the hearing, both petitioners, the respondent, and their lawyers were present. Since the father withheld consent, the petitioners needed to present evidence meeting the statute's jurisdictional criteria, which they failed to do, leading to the petition's dismissal. The Court ruled that in

line with rulings under the small debt recovery act, this law mandates a ten-day notice period, excluding the day of service and return. In another case, Joseph Chandler and others petitioned for a public road, but the order was denied because the notice omitted the application's location. The Court upheld this, noting the law requires notice of both time and place, a standard also applied in Orphans' Court proceedings.HERRMANN, Justice: This case involves a plaintiff seeking repayment of a check for which payment was unsuccessfully stopped, leading the defendant bank to issue a cashier's check. The undisputed facts are: The plaintiff, a used car dealer, held a checking account with the defendant bank. The plaintiff's president, Samuel Woloshin, issued a check to Solomon Klein for a car purchase. After Klein left, Woloshin, suspecting the car was stolen, called

the defendant's nearby branch to halt payment. This call occurred between 2:00 and 2:20 P.M. Klein was at the branch during the call and was told the check wouldn’t be cashed as he wasn’t a bank customer. After Klein left, the branch manager informed Woloshin and advised him to contact the main office’s bookkeeping department to stop payment. Woloshin did so, explaining the urgency. Shortly after 2:30 P.M., Klein presented the check at the main office, over a mile away, and was directed to the assistant cashier, who phoned the

The supervisor of the bookkeeping department (located in the same building) was contacted to verify if the check was valid. The response confirmed sufficient funds in the plaintiff's account and no stop payment order. The assistant cashier then informed the supervisor that the check would be paid and instructed to reserve the amount against the account. Following Klein's request, the assistant cashier issued a cashier's check to Klein. Around 2:45 P.M., after Klein left, the bookkeeping supervisor discovered Woloshin's stop payment order through standard banking procedures. The next day, Klein cashed the cashier's check at the defendant's Smyrna branch, leading to this lawsuit. The plaintiff argues the defendant failed to honor the stop payment order and should have canceled the cashier's check to prevent payment to Klein. The Superior Court ruled in favor of the defendant, prompting the plaintiff's appeal.

The first part of the plaintiff's claim centers on negligence, questioning whether the defendant acted with appropriate care and if any lapse caused the plaintiff's loss. Key cases cited include National Dredging Co. v. President, etc., of Farmers Bank of State of Delaware and Thomas v. First National Bank of Scranton. The appeal focuses on whether the defendant proved, with reasonable certainty, that no factual issue exists which could hold it liable. Reference is made to Williamson v. Wilmington Housing Authority. The court cannot conclude

that no such issue exists. The core question is whether the defendant's bookkeeping staff acted with due care regarding the plaintiff's stop payment order, especially since the order wasn't recorded when the assistant cashier inquired before issuing the cashier's check. Based on the current record, the court cannot definitively rule in the defendant's favor or declare its employees free of negligence. The outcome may depend on trial evidence about standard banking practices and whether they were followed—details absent from the record. Thus, the court finds the defendant failed to meet its burden for summary judgment, deeming its grant erroneous and remanding the case for trial on negligence and proximate cause. Resolving the negligence issue

will likely determine whether the defendant had the right or duty to revoke the cashier's check to protect the plaintiff. If negligence and proximate cause are proven, the second part of the case may become irrelevant. Conversely, if the defendant prevails, the plaintiff's argument that the cashier's check lacked consideration—and thus should have been countermanded—fails. Relevant cases include Polotsky v. Artisans Savings Bank and Dakota Transfer and Storage Company v. Merchants National Bank and Trust Company, along with legal references like Michie 'Banks and Banking' and Johnson v. The New Castle County Levy Court is involved, with plotted lots, a park area, and trees marked. The park and streets are noted as 'Dedicated by this Plat,' including Llangollen Boulevard.
