Interpreting the Delaware rule this way would align it with the Federal rule. The Chancellor noted that the first step is to determine whether Hannah M. Darlington properly executed the power of appointment in her conveyance to Thomas Darlington. Since the property is in Delaware, Delaware law governs the execution, even though the will was made in Pennsylvania.

In 1903, the Supreme Court of Delaware, in Lane v. Lane, adopted the common law principle from Davis v. Vincent, which states that executing a power of appointment requires a clear intention, demonstrated by referencing the power or the property involved. A general power of appointment allows for the sale and distribution of proceeds. Hannah M. Darlington's will makes no mention of the power of appointment, the deed to Thomas Darlington, or the trust it established. She only refers to 'my property' or 'my estate,' indicating she was disposing of her absolute ownership without acknowledging any trust or power. There is also no clear reference to the property described in the deed to Darlington.

The deed described a specific lot on the west side of Shipley Street between Ninth and Tenth Streets. The will bequeaths 'my house and lot in Wilmington on the west side of Shipley Street between Ninth and Tenth' to Anna and Emily Webb. However, evidence confirmed that the testatrix owned only one house and lot in that location. This lack of explicit reference to the power of appointment or the deed suggests she did not intend to exercise the power, focusing instead on her personally owned property.

The street located between Ninth and Tenth Streets. The connection between the property described in the deed and that mentioned in the will was confirmed, with the will referencing the property under the power, ensuring proper execution by the appointor, Hannah M. Darlington, in the sixth clause of her will. The issue now is determining who should manage the conversion of the property and distribution of proceeds. Should it be the administrator c.t.a. of Hannah M. Darlington, or a new trustee replacing the deceased Thomas Darlington? The defendant argues that since the legal title belonged to Thomas Darlington and passed to his heir, the executrix of Hannah’s will couldn’t have handled the sale, nor can the current administrator c.t.a.

The case can be clarified by first examining the scenario as if both Thomas Darlington and Hannah’s executrix were alive, with the will explicitly instructing the executrix to convert and divide the property. While Thomas held the legal estate until his death, as shown by the deed transferring it to him 'his heirs and assigns, in trust,' this doesn’t resolve who should fulfill the appointor’s intent. Powers of appointment are complex and rarely addressed, but certain principles can guide the solution. Before the statute of uses, such powers were mere directives to trustees on conveying the estate, but afterward, they allowed the appointee to gain the legal estate directly upon execution.

According to Washburn’s Real Property (4th Ed.), the donee’s power, when exercised, creates a use that merges with the legal estate under the statute. Similarly, Sugden on Powers explains that executing a power invests the appointee with the use, instantly granting them the legal estate. A power is an authority to dispose of property for others’ benefit, creating a use at the discretion of the holder. These principles, as noted in Williams’ Real Property and Washburn’s works, show powers operate as executory limitations, with the appointee taking the land as if originally designated in the instrument.

For instance, if property is conveyed to A. with the grantor retaining appointment power, and later appointed to C., C. gains a fee simple as if originally named. If the power follows a life estate, it functions as a remainder. The execution of a power makes the appointed estates effective as if written in the original deed. However, if the legal estate is held in trust for A. with a remainder subject to appointment, A.’s exercise of the power in favor of C. transfers the interest accordingly.

The equitable interest in B. will be transferred to C., though the legal ownership remains with the trustee, who is obligated in equity to hold it for C.'s benefit. According to 1 Tiffany on Real Property, §276, referencing Sugden on Powers, 200, and Farwell on Powers, 2, Thomas Darlington, if alive, would retain legal title for the beneficiary designated by the executrix, had she been alive and instructed by Hannah M. Darlington's will. The applicability of this to the current scenario, where the executrix is deceased and no will-mandated converter exists, will be addressed later. After reviewing relevant authorities, it is clear that the executrix, not the deed's trustee, would have held the sale authority if the will had specified conversion. When property is entrusted to a trustee under a power of appointment, and the appointor's will directs the executor to sell, the executor, not the original trustee, gains the sale authority.

In Cowx v. Foster, 1 Johnson and Hemming (70 Eng. Reprint) 30, a testator exercised a power to appoint realty among children, delegating sale and distribution to new trustees. The court upheld the testamentary trustees' authority to convey title and receive payment, enforcing specific performance against a buyer. Similarly, in Hayes v. Watley, L. R. 14 Eq. Cas. 1, a married woman with a general power appointed an executor, and the settlement trustees properly transferred the fund to the executor, despite subsequent losses, absolving them of liability. This aligns with In re Hoskin's Trusts, L. R. 6 Ch. Div. 281, and Olney v. Balch, 154 Mass. 318, 28 N. E. 258, as well as Humphrey v. Campbell, 59 S. C. 39, 37 S. E. 26.

In Harker v. Reilly, 4 Del. Ch. 72, the power's donee instructed the original trustee to convey to a new testamentary trustee for sale and proceeds distribution. While the original trustee complied, the sale was conducted by a sheriff under a levari facias writ to satisfy a mortgage. Notably, the remaining proceeds went to the testamentary trustee, who also served as the power donee's administrator c. t. a., handling the funds accordingly. Here, however, no designated seller exists, and the defendant argues the administrator c. t. a. lacks sale authority—a position I reject. Even without implied power, Delaware statutes provide the necessary authority.

Under Delaware's 1871 Act (Rev. Code 1852, amended to 1874, c. 90, §17), if a will devises real estate for sale without naming a seller, the executor(s) gain sale authority. The 1907 Act (24 Del. Laws, Chap. 235) extends this to life-tenancy scenarios, permitting the executor(s) at the sale-directed time to act. Both statutes are consolidated as Section 19, affirming the administrator c. t. a.'s authority to sell in such cases.

Section 99 of the 1915 Revised Code addresses a scenario where land is to be sold per a will, but no individual is designated to conduct the sale. The original trustee lacked such authority, and the complainant, as administrator c.t.a., now oversees the will's execution. This situation falls under the statute's broad provisions. However, the defendant references Chandler v. Delaplaine (1872), where Chancellor Bates interpreted the statute differently, ruling that an administrator c.t.a. could not execute a sale if the will did not specify a seller. This case differs from the current one.

In Chandler v. Delaplaine, Chancellor Bates noted that the statute did not apply when the executor, as the life tenant, could not fulfill the sale directive until after their tenure. The Chancellor reasoned that the statute could not override the will's terms, as the sale was contingent on the life tenant's death. This interpretation, while somewhat unclear, suggests the statute's applicability hinges on the executor's role and timing. The court concluded that the statute did not authorize a sale under such circumstances.

The Chancellor's decision might imply that the statute only applies when the will directs the sale proceeds to be distributed as part of the personal estate by the executor or administrator d.b.n.c.t.a. If so, this narrow interpretation is inconsistent with the statute's remedial intent. Historically, executors lacked clear authority to sell land unless the will explicitly linked the proceeds to their duties. This limitation created legal uncertainties, prompting the 1871 and 1907 statutes to clarify and expand such powers.

These statutes, designed to facilitate testators' wishes, should be interpreted broadly. They apply whenever a will mandates a sale without appointing a seller, even if the proceeds are not explicitly tied to the executor's duties. In cases like this, the sale proceeds form part of the estate. Notably, if a power of appointment is exercised via will, equity rules dictate that the proceeds may first cover the appointor's debts, as established in legal precedents and scholarly works.

In the case of 28 N. E. 258 and Johnson v. Cushing, 15 N. H. 298, 41 Am. Landowners Cunninghams appeal an interlocutory judgment valuing their 5.46-acre tract residentially due to a restrictive covenant. The land, part of a 15.630-acre parcel, is being taken to relocate Governor Printz Boulevard for Interstate Route 1-495 construction.

Originally part of Joseph S. Keen’s 200-acre estate acquired in 1901, the land lay between River Road and the Delaware River. Keen developed a country estate with a manor house and farmland. Later acquisitions in 1910 and 1912 expanded the property. Keen’s conveyances included sales to William C. Newport Co. (unrestricted), Richard Sellers, and his son (with manufacturing prohibitions). Sales to Helen Baer Coxe in 1916 and 1921 included restrictions against commercial or industrial use.

These deeds prohibited certain uses, such as offensive or undesirable activities, and included a clause mandating that Keen include the same restrictions in any future sales of adjacent land. After Keen's death in 1935, his trustees transferred a strip of land next to the Cunningham property to the State, which later became part of Governor Printz Boulevard. Initially a two-lane road in 1935, it was widened to four lanes by 1941, disrupting the Keen Estate's landscaping. Between 1935 and 1952, more Keen lands were sold without restrictions, and in 1952, the Cunninghams received their land free of any limitations. The Cunningham property stretches about 1000 feet along the Boulevard, with varying depths.

The Cunningham land measures roughly 400 feet deep at the north end and 630 feet at the south end. In 1954, this land and other adjacent properties were zoned M-l up to 400 feet deep, with the State acquiring portions within this classification. The nearby Kynlyn Apartments agreed to this zoning. Governor Printz Boulevard has primarily seen commercial or light industrial development, with no recent residential construction nearby. The Cunningham land borders the Kynlyn development, part of which is zoned M-l but never developed residentially due to its proximity to the Boulevard. The Coxe tract, subject to restrictive covenants, is now separated from the Cunningham land by unrestricted property sold in 1952. The Coxe mansion now serves as an institution, while the Keen mansion has been demolished.

Along this stretch of Governor Printz Boulevard, the land to the west, including the Cunningham property, is level for about 400 feet before rising 30 feet. Residential development has occurred on the higher ground, while commercial or light industrial uses dominate near the Boulevard. The key issue is how to value the Cunningham land for condemnation. The State argues it must be valued as residential due to the Coxe deed restrictions, while the Cunninghams claim these restrictions are irrelevant or unenforceable, advocating for industrial-use valuation. The trial judge upheld the restrictions, but we disagree, citing precedent where changed conditions rendered such restrictions unenforceable.

In Welshire, Inc. v. Harbison, we acknowledged that land restrictions could become void under significant neighborhood changes, such as a shift from residential to commercial or industrial use. Here, the evidence suggests the area's character has changed enough to render residential restrictions ineffective. Even if not conclusive, the record strongly supports this view, especially when considering other factors. Additionally, the only enforceable restriction on Keen and his successors was to impose similar covenants when selling adjacent land, further weakening the State's argument for residential valuation.

The term 'adjacent' land is not specified in the restrictive covenant. In reality, Cunningham's land is separated from Coxe's land by property acquired by Finnacchaico in 1952 from Keen's trustees, though this acquisition appears to have occurred after Cunningham's. It seems unreasonable to assume that Keen intended to restrict all his land as 'adjacent' to Coxe, regardless of its actual proximity, as this would extend the covenant beyond its likely intent. A plausible interpretation is that the restriction, if enforceable, applies only to the Finnacchaico land, which is directly contiguous to Coxe's and thus clearly 'adjacent.' While this is not the only possible conclusion, it is a reasonable one. The ambiguity in the restrictions would require judicial interpretation if enforced against the Cunninghams, and given the legal preference against land alienation restrictions, such enforcement would be strictly construed against the claimant. Norris v. Williams, 189 Md. 73

, 54 A.2d 331, 4 A.L.R.2d 1106. Another consideration is the land's M-l industrial zoning, which prohibits residential construction under the Zoning Code. If the Coxe deed restriction were applied to the Cunningham land, it would render the land unusable—barred from industrial use by the restriction and from residential use by zoning. This would create an impractical deadlock, which the law disfavors. Considering these factors, we conclude the Cunningham land is unrestricted except by zoning, and its valuation should reflect this. The lower court's interlocutory judgment is reversed. ON PETITION FOR REARGUMENT The State's petition for reargument, citing seven points, was reviewed but denied. We address the sixth point, which challenges our stance that enforcing the deed restriction would result in a stalemate due to M-l zoning prohibiting residential use. The State notes no precedent where zoning ordinances override deed restrictions, but we find this irrelevant. Both parties acknowledged at oral argument that M-l zoning validly prevents residential use, creating the stalemate. Our opinion is supported by authorities like the Restatement of Property and Rathkopf's Zoning and Planning. Without deciding whether intervention is a right, permissive intervention under Rule 24 requires a shared legal or factual question with the main action and no undue delay or prejudice. and the main action involve common questions, justifying permissive intervention. This decision aligns with the principles of Chancery Rule 24, balancing the interests of the original parties and the intervener. The case will proceed with Tomlinson as a party plaintiff, and the corporate defendant's procedural concerns will be addressed as the litigation progresses. The court retains discretion to manage the proceedings to avoid redundancy or prejudice.

The intervener's participation will not complicate the case but rather ensure a comprehensive resolution of the disputed issues. The corporate defendant's opposition, while noted, does not outweigh the benefits of allowing Tomlinson to intervene. The shared legal and factual questions between the claims justify this outcome, and the court is satisfied that intervention aligns with the rules of equity and procedural fairness. The motion is granted, and the case will move forward with the intervener's inclusion. Given the preliminary nature of this matter, the Court should address this procedural hurdle if feasible. As such, I exercise discretion to allow Tomlinson to intervene concerning the complaint's subject matter. The Court explicitly stated in Campbell v. Loew's, Inc. that this issue was not before it and would not be decided. The question is whether permissive intervention under the rule is appropriate, specifically whether Tomlinson's claim shares a legal or factual question with the main action. While the Court did not rule on the Tomlinson faction's entitlement to corporate-funded proxy expenses, it affirmed the other faction's right to do so. The facts, if not the law, surrounding this issue overlap with the Tomlinson group's claim.

The Court refrains from delving too deeply into the matter at this stage to avoid prejudging the merits of the pleading. However, the proposed claim is not legally frivolous, as seen in cases like Young v. Janas and Schiff v. RKO Pictures Corp. This later ordinance establishes a three-member Printing Committee to oversee city printing needs and manage advertisements for public contracts, granting the committee discretion over ad placement and method. Section 5 repeals all conflicting prior ordinances.

The argument is that Section 3 of this ordinance, which allows the printing committee of the Council to decide how, when, and where advertisements for sealed proposals for public works or contracts should be made, conflicts with the 1870 ordinance mandating public bidding and awarding to the lowest bidder, effectively repealing it. This claim is unfounded. The two ordinances do not clash. The 1870 ordinance mandates public bidding but does not specify the details of how, when, or in what manner bids should be invited. The 1883 ordinance merely supplements the 1870 one by granting the Council committee authority to determine the specifics of publicizing bids. However, I need not rule on whether the 1883 ordinance affects the 1870 one.

The defendants also argue that one City Council cannot bind a subsequent Council to a public bidding ordinance passed by its predecessors. Cases like Bunker v. City of Hutchinson and Keogh v. Mayor of Wilmington are cited, but even if this principle is accepted, it doesn’t resolve this motion. Here, the Department of Public Safety, not the Council, made the purchases, so the principle doesn’t apply. (c) Another contention is that the Department of Public Safety wasn’t bound by the 1870 ordinance because Section 5 of the General Assembly’s Act suggests the department had discretion to acquire property as it saw fit, overriding the city’s bidding requirement.

This argument hinges on the idea that municipal legislative power, exercised through the Council, is subordinate to state legislative authority, which is indisputable. The key issue is whether this principle applies here, requiring interpretation of the legislative language in Section 5. If the section grants the Department of Public Safety discretion over purchasing fire equipment, then any conflicting city ordinance mandating public bids must yield. The question is whether such a conflict exists in this case.

Previously, this court overlooked the current argument, which focuses on Section 5’s implications. Earlier, the debate centered on Section 9, suggesting the ordinance wouldn’t apply until the department was fully established. Now, the motion to dissolve the injunction argues that Section 5 renders the competitive bid ordinance inapplicable to the fire hose purchases, a point not previously emphasized or addressed in the opinion.

Engines and trucks. The prior opinion does not oppose this argument, and even if it did, the court should not hesitate to reject it if further reflection reveals a mistaken perspective. I return to the issue at hand: Does Section 5 of the General Assembly's Act establishing the Department of Public Safety suggest an intention to grant the department unrestricted authority to enter into such contracts, bypassing the limitations set by the 1870 ordinance? The ordinance prohibits city officials and committees from making contracts without publicly soliciting sealed bids and awarding them to the lowest bidder. Section 5 of the 1921 Act states that starting May 1, 1921, the Mayor and Council of Wilmington may use the Department of Public Safety to develop a fire department plan and acquire necessary property.

For the city, the plan and its estimated cost involve acquiring property from Wilmington's fire companies, either through purchase, negotiation, condemnation, or other means, as deemed suitable by appraisers for a city of its stature. If the Council approves the plan, the Department of Public Safety will proceed to obtain the required property. Fire companies may reserve the right to accept or reject the appraisers' valuation. The City Solicitor, representing the defendants, argues

That Section 5 exempts the Department of Public Safety from the 1870 ordinance for two reasons. First, the directive that the Mayor and Council act through the department implies it operates independently of city legislative constraints, particularly in purchasing property for the new fire department. Two cases support this claim—Greene v. Mayor of New York and Guidet v. Mayor of New York. The Greene case ruled that New York's charter provisions for sealed bids applied only to contracts authorized by the common council, not those by the public works commissioner, who was state-appointed for specific tasks. The decision hinged on interpreting Section 104 of the charter, where general language about advertising was limited by the clause restricting it to council-authorized contracts. Guidet appears to align with this interpretation.

These cases are irrelevant here. Had the 1870 ordinance been a charter provision explicitly or implicitly applying only to council-made contracts, the New York cases might be useful. But that is not the case. I cannot conclude that merely because the Legislature specified the agency for establishing the paid fire department, it intended that agency to operate free from all restrictions.

The regulation should not be governed by the Council's ordinance in question. If this were the only argument, I would oppose it, as doing otherwise would overemphasize the simple act of assigning a city agency. A more reasonable perspective is that the Legislature, when establishing city offices or departments, intends them to integrate smoothly into the existing municipal legal framework. If this does not happen in a specific case, the reason must be found elsewhere. Does Section 5 suggest that the 1870 ordinance should not apply to the Department of Public Safety when creating the new fire department? This leads to the City Solicitor's second argument. The fire hose, engines, and trucks under restraint do not belong to existing companies and fall under 'necessary property.' How should such property be obtained? The ordinance requires public bidding and selecting the lowest bidder, while the General Assembly permits purchase, compromise, or other methods at agreed prices. The legislative language is broad, allowing any pricing method. If competitive bidding were mandatory, the Legislature would not have used such general terms. The department can set prices through negotiation or agreement, which would be impossible under the ordinance's strict rules.

The court finds a conflict between the state's legislative intent in Section 5 and the city's 1870 ordinance, with the latter yielding to the former. The complainants' solicitor argued that the ordinance could still require public bidding while allowing negotiation with the lowest bidder, or that bids could be invited but the contract awarded to a higher bidder if beneficial. These arguments are flawed. If bids are invited and the lowest bidder identified, they would unlikely negotiate a lower price. The Legislature did not intend this scenario when drafting Section 5. The ordinance cannot be partially applied; if bidding is required, the contract must go to the lowest bidder. Once applicable, the ordinance operates fully, preventing awards to higher bidders.

Given these considerations, the preliminary injunction blocking the purchase of fire hose, engines, and trucks is dissolved. An order will be prepared accordingly. Comegys, C.J., instructing the jury: Gentlemen of the Jury: The requests from the Attorney General and the defendant's counsel necessitate a more formal charge than usual, despite the presented testimony.

Before you are two cases, each with unique facts not previously seen in this State. Without delving into the testimony extensively, it’s enough to note that it reveals a conflict between the prisoner and the deceased near the intersection of Front and Market streets. This altercation began either verbally, physically, or both, either on the sidewalk by the prisoner’s store and peanut stand or inside the store itself. What’s clear is that a fight occurred, initiated by one party—state witnesses claim the prisoner struck first, while the defense asserts the deceased started it by grabbing the prisoner’s throat in his store after hurling an insult.

The struggle escalated into mutual combat, with the State arguing the prisoner was the sole aggressor, while the defense maintains the deceased attacked first and the prisoner acted in self-defense. This conflicting testimony, like all aspects of the trial, is for the jury to resolve, as the Court’s role is only to guide how such disputes should be weighed. When testimony diverges on a key issue, jurors must scrutinize the evidence, considering witness credibility, impartiality, observational accuracy, and consistency. Greater weight should be given to the side with more reliable testimony, but this principle doesn’t apply to the totality of evidence, as a conviction requires proof beyond reasonable doubt, not just a preponderance of evidence.

Jurors must remember that a defendant cannot be convicted solely based on the weight of testimony; they must be fully convinced of guilt beyond reasonable doubt. The evidence against the prisoner must so outweigh the defense’s case that no reasonable uncertainty remains. During the fight, the deceased and prisoner moved into the street, where the deceased overpowered the prisoner, slamming him onto the pavement and an iron gutter cover with such force that, according to some witnesses, multiple men were needed to pull him away. After separation, it was discovered the deceased had been fatally stabbed by the pick the prisoner used in his store and held during the altercation.

There’s little doubt the prisoner carried the pick throughout the fight outside his store, as he never reentered after the conflict began. Defense witnesses describe the deceased as a large, strong man, far more powerful than the prisoner. State witnesses, however, portray the deceased as defending himself from the prisoner’s attempts to stab him, backing away to avoid the pick. The defense counters this, claiming the deceased was the aggressor and the prisoner only used the pick’s handle to push him away, except when, as Mr. Scott testified, the deceased repeatedly kicked the prisoner.

When he appeared to be trying to avoid further conflict by retreating to his shop, only then did he turn and hit him on the head with the pick. With this brief, and I trust adequate summary of the facts presented to you—since they are still fresh in your minds and require no repetition from me—I will now explain the legal principles governing homicide, allowing you to apply the relevant portions to the facts you find sufficiently proven and reach your verdict. I will address the law in the reverse order of the Attorney General’s requested instructions, as I believe this approach allows for clearer explanation in this instance. Any act where one person kills another constitutes homicide, which may or may not be criminal depending on the context. Some homicides are justifiable, others excusable, and others are neither, instead being felonious and punishable based on their nature. Justifiable homicides are irrelevant here, so I will focus on felonious homicides and those excusable due to self-defense. Felonious homicides include murder and manslaughter.

These are further categorized as malicious and non-malicious acts. Malice is fundamental to murder, meaning no homicide qualifies as murder unless it is carried out with malice. Manslaughter, however, lacks malice, which is the key distinction between the two. Initially, our legal system recognized only one type of murder, but the 1852 Code divided it into two classes: first-degree murder, explicitly defined, and second-degree murder, encompassing all others. Murder (covering both degrees) involves the unlawful and felonious killing of one person by another with malice aforethought—meaning premeditated malice. If the malice is explicit, the crime is first-degree murder; if it is implied by law based on the act’s nature, it is second-degree murder. Express malice occurs when someone kills another with a calm, deliberate mind and premeditated intent. This mindset is often demonstrated by the intentional choice and use of a lethal weapon, a prearranged

confrontation—whether in a formal duel or a street fight agreed upon by both parties, or one announced and threatened by the accused—lying in wait, a prior dispute or grudge, preparing poison, or other methods likely to cause severe harm. Implied malice, in legal terms, is a conclusion drawn by the jury from the facts, with the accused’s actual intent being a critical factor. Even if the accused did not intend to kill or harm, their involvement in another felonious or unlawful act may lead the law to presume malice. For example, if someone attempts to kill or injure Person A but accidentally kills Person B, a loved one or bystander, or if during a riot or street fight, a participant unintentionally kills a peacekeeper trying to intervene—the law infers malice, rendering the killer guilty of murder. Additional examples exist in legal texts, but suffice it to say, all malicious homicides not involving express malice aforethought are second-degree murders. Legally, malice is defined as

a general disregard for human life and safety, stemming from a heart devoid of social responsibility and intent on harm. Whenever a fatal act is committed deliberately or without sufficient provocation, the law presumes malice, and the burden falls on the accused to demonstrate through evidence or circumstances that the offense is less severe and not murder. I have already explained how express malice is proven; implied malice, as noted, arises differently. Manslaughter, as mentioned earlier, is not malicious. It typically arises from a sudden altercation or fight where one party, in the heat of passion, kills the other. If the fatal blow is struck with a deadly weapon, the homicide may be deemed murder if evidence shows the attacker brought the weapon in preparation for the encounter. All homicides involving a deadly weapon or an instrument capable of causing death are legally presumed malicious; to counter this presumption, the accused must convince the jury that their possession of such a weapon was not premeditated.

Preparing for the conflict, the principle of self-defense states that if someone is suddenly attacked in a way that threatens their life or causes severe bodily harm, and they cannot escape without killing the assailant, they may do so. However, they must first attempt every possible means to escape and only resort to lethal force as a last resort when no other options exist. This also applies when two individuals are fighting, and one tries to withdraw but is prevented by the other, leading to potential death or serious injury. The court has provided all relevant legal guidance to assist in deciding this case, affirming the key points raised by the Attorney General, with no dispute over the law.

The defense proposed by the prisoner's counsel suggests the deceased might have accidentally fallen onto the prisoner's weapon rather than being struck by it. However, no evidence supports this claim. Even if proven, it would only help the prisoner if the weapon was used lawfully in self-defense; otherwise, it would constitute unlawful use, resulting in manslaughter charges. The case is now left to the jury to deliberate based on the presented law and witness testimonies, with confidence that their verdict will align with their consciences. The jury must be convinced beyond a reasonable doubt of the prisoner's guilt for any conviction. In first-degree murder cases, the jury may convict for first-degree murder, second-degree murder, or manslaughter, depending on the evidence.

If the evidence does not support a conviction for any offense, the jury must acquit entirely. Verdict: not guilty. Judge Taylor. In the case of Use-plaintiff, S. M. Aronow Co., which provided labor and materials for Friendly Ice Cream Corporation at Concord Mall, the contractual chain involved Friendly contracting with Carr Construction, Inc., which then contracted with Andrew E. Mitchell & Sons, Inc., which in turn contracted with Aronow. Aronow's only direct contract was with Mitchell. Carr seeks dismissal, arguing no contractual relationship exists with Aronow. Aronow claims third-party beneficiary rights based on an affidavit from Carr to Friendly, stating all laborers and subcontractors hired by Carr were paid in full and no liens could be filed.

The affidavit included two key representations: first, that all parties hired by Carr were fully paid, which does not apply to Aronow as they were not hired by Carr. Second, that no entity could impose liens related to the project. If Aronow supplied materials and the lien period was still active, this representation would be false. Aronow connects this affidavit to the precedent set in Royal Indemnity Company v. Alexander Industries, Inc., Del.Supr., 211 A.2d 919 (1965), arguing it establishes their right to assert a claim.

) The ruling stated that a subcontractor providing labor and materials could recover as a third-party beneficiary under a payment bond issued by the general contractor, as per the contract with the owner. The bond ensured the contractor would fulfill all contractual obligations, including paying for materials and labor. Key differences from the Royal case include: the affidavit-certification was not an agreement or future commitment, it did not specify fund usage, it described existing conditions at the time, it limited payment references to Carr’s hires, and it did not suggest the lien waiver benefited anyone beyond the property owner. Based on these points,

the analysis concludes Carr has no contractual liability to Aronow under third-party beneficiary principles. Aronow also argues Carr negligently failed to ensure his payment, citing Murphy v. Godwin, which requires a pre-existing duty. Aronow claims Carr’s representation to Friendly about payments imposed a duty to verify. Murphy ties negligent nonfeasance to a definite relationship justifying a duty. There, the court assessed a doctor’s inaction within a doctor-patient relationship. Here,

liability under this theory hinges on a direct Aronow-Carr relationship, which hasn’t been shown. The record reveals no prior dealings. Lastly, Aronow asserts Carr held funds as a trustee under 6 Del.C. § 3502, requiring disbursement to laborers and material providers. Section 3503 mandates contractors prioritize these payments before other uses. Section 3504 deems non-payment within 30 days as prima facie misuse. Aronow doesn’t dispute Carr paid its direct obligations but argues Carr should have ensured Mitchell paid him. While Mitchell owed Aronow under the statute,

no authority supports extending Carr’s duty to track funds through Mitchell. The statute places payment obligations on the contractor receiving funds, not upstream parties like Carr. Aronow’s claim lacks legal basis for imposing such a duty on Carr under the cited provisions.

Mitchell's subcontractor ensured that the subcontractor received payment from Mitchell. Section 3503 seems to address the obligation that the contractor or their agent must allocate funds to cover 'all amounts owed by the contractor to all parties' [emphasis added]. If this obligation includes subcontractors, the statute's mention of funds 'owed by the contractor' would exclude a trust relationship here, as Carr owed nothing to Aronow. This suggests the trust principle applies only to direct obligations of the fund recipient. As previously stated, Carr had no direct obligation to Aronow. Relevant Delaware cases, such as State v. Tabasso Homes, Maull v. Stokes, and State v. Pierson, do not resolve this issue.

This remedy is specifically established by legislative act, and the petitioner must meet its requirements. The petitioner must demonstrate, through their petition and evidence if contested, that the dam in question was built within six years. This is a legal constraint. The writ is not automatically granted, nor is this process ex parte. The petitioner claims the dam was recently erected, causing harm, and must provide at least prima facie evidence to justify the court's involvement. Revised agreements between the corporate defendant and Menzies and Wall were challenged by Sam Achsel’s attorney, who argued the settlement isn’t a true compromise but a dismissal with prejudice. The objector seeks to intervene and litigate the amended complaint’s claims. Servel, founded around 1930, initially made gas refrigerators but faced post-WWII competition. After the Korean War, despite diversification, its civilian business declined.

After WWII and the Korean War, Servel’s civilian business continued to decline despite ventures into air conditioning and freezers. By 1954, the company was struggling, leading to the hiring of Mr. Menzies, a renowned industrial turnaround expert, as president and director. The amended complaint alleges that Servel’s officers, including Menzies, received salaries, pensions, and options, plus 'percentage compensation' tied to operational improvements in civilian and defense divisions. From 1955 to 1957, this deferred compensation totaled $790,434, with Menzies claiming $664,850. The complaint highlights this arrangement despite the company’s worsening sales.

Servel’s net sales dropped from $87,067,080 in 1954 to $16,623,346 in 1957, while civilian losses decreased annually. The disputed 'percentage compensation' clause, based on pre-tax operational improvements, allowed officials like Menzies to receive substantial credits despite declining business activity. This 'improvement' stemmed from scaling down operations, eventually leading to asset sales. The clause’s application during this downturn raises questions about its fairness and alignment with the company’s actual performance.

The removal of significant civilian division losses. Refer to Treves v. Menzies, ante p. 330, 142 A.2d 520. Key sections of the original Menzies agreement (Achsel Ex. 1) stated, page 3: 'For computation purposes (operational results),

the 'adjusted consolidated operating net results' for a Percentage year will be the consolidated net profit or loss, before federal and state income taxes and before deducting amounts payable under subparagraph (b)' (the percentage compensation formula), excluding specified extraordinary income and expenses. Paragraph 8 of the agreement affirmed: 'Servel confirms it is not contemplating any merger, substantial asset sale, or business discontinuation.' However, paragraph 10 stipulated that the formula would remain applicable despite a merger or major asset transfer. While Mr. Menzies may have been legally entitled to his substantial compensation through fiscal year 1957, Servel’s directors recognized by autumn 1956, following partial asset sales, that applying the compensation formula to periods with minimal or no production deviated from its original intent.

In March 1958, the Menzies agreement was revised following discussions between Mr. Menzies and other directors, with changes outlined in a June 3, 1958 notice to stockholders as per the Court's order. The modifications included extending Mr. Menzies' full-time employment until October 31, 1961, with provisions for early termination under specific conditions related to Servel's acquisition of a new business.

If Servel acquired a new business before December 31, 1958, Mr. Menzies could terminate his employment within 30 days. Termination under certain clauses would void restrictions on Mr. Menzies working with competitors. His Percentage Compensation post-October 1957 was set at 5% of Servel's pre-tax net income, but this would cease if employment ended early under specified terms.

The option price for 150,000 Servel shares granted to Mr. Menzies in 1955 was reduced from $7,625 to $4,875 per share and made exercisable only after acquiring a new business or by February 1, 1959. Pacific Eastern Corporation, 21 Del.Ch. 81, 180 A. 604), the compromise here resulted from negotiations that the plaintiffs, at best, only initiated. The amended agreements will stay in effect regardless of this Court's decision on dismissing the plaintiffs' action. The Rule

Defendant Richard Snavely faces charges of Rape First Degree involving his stepdaughter, Jeanette Kelly Snavely. The State has filed a motion in limine to assess the admissibility of the victim's statements, as she may not be available to testify. A hearing on this motion began on July 7, 1986, and concluded on July 10, 1986, with further testimony scheduled for August 11, 1986. Subpoenas for Linda Snavely, the defendant's wife, and John Wills, his father-in-law, were not served, as their locations are unknown. Both are considered material witnesses for the State's motion.

The hearing evidence linked both witnesses to the victim's initial disappearance and her later appearance in St. Maarten, Kingdom of the Netherlands. During the disappearance, the Court had to compel their testimony before the New Castle County Grand Jury under immunity. This is documented in the Court's records. In July, the State detailed efforts to serve subpoenas, including visits to their homes and surveillance. The State sought a capias for each witness, which the Court approved after further service attempts. Linda Snavely and John Wills hired an attorney to quash the warrants, arguing the Court lacked jurisdiction without prior subpoena service.

Their attorney contended that the Uniform Law to Secure Witnesses From Out of State (11 Del.C., Ch. 35, Subchapter II) is the sole legal basis for arresting a material witness. They claimed the Court could only act via subpoena or the Uniform Act. This argument is unfounded. The Superior Court, as a court of general jurisdiction (Art. IV, Section 7, Delaware Constitution), holds broad authority, including issuing writs and warrants. Under 10 DelC. § 562, the Court can issue necessary process, and under 11 Del.C. § 5102, it can summon witnesses in criminal cases.

The authority in 11 Del.C. § 5102 includes issuing warrants to compel testimony, distinct from the Uniform Act, which applies only to out-of-state witnesses. Here, the witnesses are unwilling but material. To ensure their appearance, the Court authorized their custody. The motions to quash the capias for Linda Snavely and John Wills are DENIED. IT IS SO ORDERED. The State asserts that

The victim was persuaded to leave the area to avoid testifying against her stepfather, who is accused of arranging her absence. The Court issued a warrant for the arrest of these individuals as key witnesses in an ongoing case. It is important to note that the witnesses' legal representation, by filing this motion to challenge the Court's jurisdiction without prior subpoena service, might be seen as a general appearance. In Delaware, the difference between general and special appearances no longer exists, as established in Brainard v. Canaday. By effectively making a general appearance, the witnesses have submitted to the Court's jurisdiction.

Service of process is deemed equivalent to a general appearance, granting the Court personal jurisdiction, as noted in 6 C.J.S. Appearances § 39. This eliminates the need for formal service. Even without statutory support, the Court retains common law authority to issue warrants for uncooperative witnesses, as seen in Barry v. United States ex rel. Cunningham. The Court also reminds the witnesses' counsel of Rule 3.3(a)(2) regarding honesty to the tribunal, as aiding a client in obstructing justice may breach this rule, per Fellerman v. Bradley. No order for the witnesses' addresses has been issued yet, but the Court would consider such a request if made by the State.

VAUGHN, Justice: I. INTRODUCTION Arthur Stoner appeals a Family Court ruling that found him delinquent for Second-Degree Robbery and Conspiracy. He raises three issues: first, that his due process rights were violated as the conspiracy charge was based on an uncharged statute subsection; second, insufficient evidence for the robbery charge, arguing the Court misapplied the statute's 'in the course of committing theft' clause; and third, that the conspiracy statute, 11 Del. C. § 512(1), is unconstitutionally vague for lacking an overt act requirement. The State acknowledges the error in charging Stoner under an unlisted subsection and agrees the conspiracy adjudication should be overturned.

The State concedes that Stoner’s conspiracy adjudication should be vacated, making his first and third arguments moot. Only his robbery charge remains for review. II. FACTS AND PROCEDURAL HISTORY On November 16, 2017, around 7:30 p.m., Jessica Halloran left a Trolley Square restaurant in Wilmington and noticed 'two guys' across the street acting suspiciously.

Standing near the Fed Ex box, one individual, later known as Tayshaun Gibbs, faced her while the other, Arthur Stoner, had his back turned. As she approached, Gibbs repeatedly glanced up from his phone, which lit up his face distinctly. Finding this behavior strange, Halloran deliberately locked eyes with him, prompting him to look away. Gibbs wore a black hoodie and blue jeans, while Stoner, whose face she didn’t see, had on a black hoodie and khaki pants. Moments after she passed them, Gibbs snatched her wristlet bag, tearing it from her strap. Both fled, with Stoner slightly ahead, disappearing from view. Though neither spoke to her or each other, Halloran testified they seemed to be acting together. Police were alerted, and Gibbs and Stoner were apprehended ten blocks away by Corporal David Simmons.

About twenty minutes post-robbery, Halloran was brought to the location and identified Gibbs and Stoner as the perpetrators. She recognized Gibbs’s face as the one who stole her wristlet and identified Stoner by his clothing. Her wristlet was recovered near where they were detained. At trial, Stoner moved for acquittal, arguing no evidence showed he aided the robbery beyond being present and fleeing. The court denied the motion, citing sufficient evidence. During closing arguments, the court noted Stoner’s role, stating robbery includes acts during immediate flight, and found him complicit despite not being the one who grabbed the bag.

The court emphasized that under 11 Del. C. § 831(b), robbery encompasses acts during immediate flight, not just the theft itself. It concluded Stoner was aware of and agreed to the robbery, as evidenced by his simultaneous flight with Gibbs. The judge stated there was no indication Stoner was surprised; his actions showed intent to facilitate the crime. Though Gibbs performed the physical act, the court found Stoner guilty of both conspiracy and robbery, citing their coordinated escape as proof of involvement.

After the verdict, Stoner received an indefinite commitment to youth rehabilitation, suspended for community supervision. On appeal, Stoner argued the evidence was insufficient to prove he was Gibbs’s accomplice, claiming the court misapplied § 831(b) by treating flight as part of the robbery in all cases. He contended the robbery ended when Gibbs took the bag, an act he didn’t participate in, and that fleeing alone shouldn’t constitute guilt. The State disagreed, maintaining the court correctly interpreted the law and that Stoner’s flight demonstrated his complicity in the crime.

The response addresses Stoner's argument about the court's reading of the second-degree robbery statute but focuses on the claim that there was enough evidence to show Stoner acted as an accomplice under 11 Del. C. § 271(2)(b). Beginning with the petition's wording, it mirrors 11 Del. C. § 831(a), charging Stoner with using force against Jessica Halloran during a theft to overcome resistance. Section 831(b) clarifies that 'in the course of committing theft' encompasses acts during immediate flight after the theft attempt. Thus, under § 831(b), actions during flight can be considered part of the theft. The Family Court ruled that the robbery act extends beyond the initial snatch to include immediate flight, repeatedly citing Stoner's flight as part of the robbery itself.

The court specifically noted that Stoner participated in the immediate flight following the forceful robbery by Gibbs and was 'part of the act itself.' However, we find the Family Court's ruling unclear. Based on the facts, the robbery concluded when Gibbs took Halloran’s wristlet, making the flight separate from Gibbs's robbery act. Section 831(b) defines 'in the course of committing theft,' meaning if force is used during flight after a theft, it can be deemed part of the theft. Here, Stoner's flight alone did not constitute part of Gibbs's robbery. The Family Court's statement that the robbery act continues into immediate flight is ambiguous, leaving uncertainty about its interpretation.

Ambiguity also arises in the Family Court's findings on accomplice liability. In bench trials, judges must provide specific findings for each element of the offense. The court concluded Stoner was delinquent as an accomplice, citing his awareness, agreement, participation in flight, involvement in the act, and intent to facilitate. To establish accomplice liability, Stoner must have intended to promote the robbery and aided or agreed to aid Gibbs. While the court found intent, mere awareness and agreement do not equate to aiding or counseling. Additionally, the conclusions about Stoner's flight and role in the act remain unclear, as previously discussed, with no explicit finding that he aided Gibbs in planning or committing the robbery.

Knowing about a crime and agreeing to it does not necessarily involve aiding or assisting. The Family Court's findings that Stoner participated in flight and was 'part of the act' are ambiguous, as the robbery's endpoint is unclear. Without clear evidence that Stoner aided Gibbs, the case may need remand for clearer findings. We recommend returning the case to the Family Court for specific findings on the second-degree robbery charge. The judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded. The Family Court must vacate Stoner's conspiracy adjudication and provide clearer findings on the robbery charge before reinstating or vacating the decision.
