This issue, being novel in the state's courts, required a principled and accurate resolution, especially given discrepancies between legal and equitable rulings. Legal courts had stricter rules on this matter. Key facts were minimal: the sale terms designated the highest bidder as the purchaser, yet the seller, Miller, secretly enlisted Captain Thompson to bid for the estate without informing other bidders.

After bids exceeded eighty dollars per acre, only Captain Thompson and George H. Baynard competed, with Baynard ultimately winning. Thompson, acting as a 'puffer,' was hired to inflate the price covertly. The central question was whether such secret bidding at a public sale is lawful. The court ruled it is not, deeming the practice contrary to public policy and fraudulent. Public auctions implicitly promise fair and honest participation, and any clandestine arrangement undermining this trust constitutes unfair dealing. If the price is artificially raised, it deceives the buyer to the seller's benefit. Morally, such tactics are indefensible, and neither law nor equity should reward gains from deception. The sale terms explicitly stated the highest bidder would win, reinforcing this principle. Lords Mansfield, Kenyon, and Tenterden had affirmed this stance, emphasizing good faith as the foundation of all transactions.

Lord Mansfield, in Bexwell v. Christie, asserted that public sales rely on trust that the highest bidder will prevail. Secretly using a puffer to drive up prices violates this trust. The court agreed, ruling that such practices undermine fairness and invalidate the sale. The seller's covert actions misled bidders, rendering the transaction fraudulent. The principle of good faith is paramount, particularly in public auctions where participants expect equal footing. Any hidden scheme to manipulate prices breaches this trust and harms the buyer. The court's decision aligned with historical precedents, reinforcing that honesty must govern public sales to maintain their integrity and legitimacy.

Lord Kenyon in Howard v. Castle, 6 T. R. 642, explicitly stated that Lord Mansfield's doctrine on by-bidding at auctions was based on 'the highest principles of morality and justice.' This principle has been upheld in cases like Wheeler v. Collier, 1 Moody Malk 126, and others, including Crowder v. Austen and Thornet v. Haines. The rule is fair, as sellers can set a minimum price or bid themselves, provided they give clear notice to avoid deception.

The 1776 case of Bexwell v. Christie set a precedent in England for over twenty years until Lord Loughborough questioned its validity in Conolly v. Parsons, advocating for secret bidding. This view was later supported by Sir Richard Pippin Arden and Sir William Grant in Bramley v. Ault and Smith v. Clark. However, Steel v. Ellmaker, once cited by the plaintiff, was overturned by Pennock's Appeal, weakening their argument.

Despite the equity cases cited, subsequent rulings in England and the U.S. have reaffirmed Lord Mansfield's original doctrine, which aims to prevent buyer deception through seller manipulation. Cases like Crowder v. Austin and Veazie v. Williams support this view. Chancellor Kent praised these earlier rulings as 'just and salutary,' emphasizing that secret bidding by the owner is fraudulent unless disclosed in sale conditions.

Therefore, employing Thompson to bid secretly for the seller without notice was deemed illegal and fraudulent, warranting judgment for the defendant. 880, 14 L. R. A. 33, 41, 27 Am. St. Rep. 487. These provisions primarily concern creditors and assignees. The clear intent was to protect both the trust corpus from mismanagement and the life beneficiaries from their own imprudence. The trustee's role extended beyond safeguarding remainders. As previously stated, the doctrine of coalescing does not apply here. During the re-hearing, more significant issues were raised and extensively argued by the solicitors for the intervening

complainants. Initially, the court determined that Joseph W. Donner properly exercised his power of appointment under Delaware law via the October 9, 1929, instrument, effective until the life estates of his children ended. Now, it is argued that New York law, not Delaware law, should govern the validity of the power's exercise. The record includes relevant New York statutes and court interpretations. Only one statute was previously considered—stating that a will's general bequest of personal property includes assets under a power of appointment unless the will indicates otherwise. N. Y. Personal Property Law, (Consol. Laws, c. 41), § 18. This was disregarded in the prior opinion because the power had already been exercised through the 1929 instrument.

However, the validity of the October 9, 1929, instrument, upheld under Delaware law, is now challenged on the basis that it must meet New York law's standards, under which it would be invalid. Quoting all the presented New York statutes is unnecessary; suffice it to say that the instrument cannot stand if judged by them. New York law limits the suspension of the absolute right of alienation, calculated from the power's creation (Genet, et al., v. Hunt, et al., 113 N. Y. 158, 170, 21 N. E. 91; Hillen v. Iselin, 144 N. Y. 365, 39 N. E).

Section 368 and § 11 of the Personal Property Law restrict the suspension of absolute ownership of personal property to no more than two lives existing at the time the instrument is created. These statutes must be interpreted together, and when done so, they invalidate trusts for the lives of Joseph W. Donner's children who were not alive when William H. Donner's deed established the power. Cases like Fargo v. Squires and Cheever v. Cheever support this. There is no dispute that under New York law, these life estates are invalid. The key question is whether New York or Delaware law applies—Delaware law would uphold the interests, while New York law would void them.

The law of the testator's domicile determines whether a testamentary power over personal property has been properly executed, as established in Lane v. Lane. Here, the issue is not the execution but the legality of the power's operation—whether the appointed interests are legally valid. The principle of mobilia sequuntur personam generally requires that testamentary trusts of personal property be evaluated under the law of the testator's domicile. Since executing a power is seen as the donor's act through the appointee, the validity of trusts created by such appointments should follow the same rule.

However, this general rule is not absolute. Cases like Chamberlain v. Chamberlain and Hope v. Brewer show exceptions where bequests of personal property to non-residents for administration in another state are upheld if they align with that state's public policy, even if they violate the domicile's laws. This is based on the idea that public policy concerns, such as perpetuities or mortmain statutes, only apply to property held within the relevant jurisdiction. While some authorities disagree, this approach is reasonable and principled.

This case does not involve a testamentary trust or power, which has unique considerations. Cases involving testamentary powers must be distinguished from those arising from inter vivos agreements when addressing conflicts of law. The distinction is critical in determining the applicable legal framework.

In an inter vivos agreement, the significance of domicile is less critical than it is in the law of wills, allowing greater emphasis on the donor's intent. There is no justification for restricting a donor's choice of jurisdiction to determine the validity of an inter vivos trust, as long as the trust property is transferred to a trustee within the chosen jurisdiction and managed there. Even in testamentary trusts, intent has been recognized as a decisive factor, as implied by recent case law, even if not explicitly stated. The notion that allowing individuals to apply foreign laws to their personal property grants them legislative power is unfounded, as domicile should not rigidly confine one's legal status.

If a New York resident travels to Delaware with cash and establishes a trust there, it would be unreasonable to apply New York law instead of Delaware's. Domicile should not act as a constraint, preventing individuals from completing arrangements in another state. In this case, the governing law for the trust created by Joseph W. Donner depends on the donor's intent, which was not explicitly stated but can be inferred from the circumstances. At the time of creation, the donor, trustee, beneficiaries, and trust assets were all in New York, strongly suggesting an intention for New York law to apply.

Given that the donor, trustee, and beneficiaries were all domiciled in New York, the trust assets were located there, and the transfer occurred there, New York law clearly governed the trust from its inception. This conclusion aligns with multiple factors, including the donor's domicile, the trustee's location, and the place of asset delivery. Even if beneficiary domicile is considered irrelevant, the evidence overwhelmingly supports New York as the intended jurisdiction. In Mercer v. Buchanan, a similar scenario involving a New York resident and Pennsylvania trustees still resulted in New York law applying, reinforcing this principle.

The case here is even more compelling, as the trust deed was executed and delivered in New York by a New York resident, with the trustee also based there. This suggests the trustee's duties were to be performed in New York unless changed. Later, when the Wilmington Trust Company became trustee, additional assets were deposited in Delaware, but this does not necessarily shift the governing law to Delaware. The original intent and circumstances still favor New York law, as the donor remained a New York resident and the trust's foundational elements were established there.

In all respects, this argument is untenable primarily because the trust, as established in 1920, applied its provisions uniformly to all property under its terms, whether existing then or added later. Accepting this contention would disrupt this uniformity, subjecting parts of the property to different rules. The trust instrument not only lacks support for this idea but actively contradicts it. Even if New York law initially governed the trust, the selection of a Delaware-based trustee and the relocation of assets to Delaware do not justify shifting the governing law, as this would imply the donor's intent was unstable.

The argument that Delaware law now governs the trust suggests the donor's intent was fluid, lacking a firm foundation. Altering the applicable law would effectively rewrite the trust's terms. While the donor reserved the right to modify the trust, he never did so formally. His approval of a trustee change does not equate to modifying the trust's terms, as such changes require a formal instrument under the trust deed. Interpreting this approval as a modification inflates its significance beyond its intended purpose.

Elevating the donor's approval of a trustee change to the status of a formal modification instrument is unjustified. If the donor intended to amend the trust, he would have done so explicitly. A simple written approval for a trustee change does not qualify as a modification instrument, as it solely addresses the trustee's identity, not the trust's terms. Relocating the trustee and assets to Delaware does not alter the trust's legal status, as established by precedent. The original governing law would still apply even if the trustee moved.

Appointing a new trustee in Delaware with the settlor's approval does not fundamentally alter the trust's terms. The trust instrument specifies that successor trustees adhere to the original conditions. Choosing a Delaware trustee cannot shift the governing intent to Delaware law, as this would allow the trust's terms to fluctuate with each administrative relocation. Such an interpretation would create instability, with the trust's meaning changing based on the trustee's location, contrary to the donor's original intent.

This scenario is less likely to be accepted as the trustor's intention when considering that, although his approval was required to change the trustee to a trust company from another state during his lifetime, the adult beneficiaries had full authority to make such changes after his death. This means the beneficiaries could significantly alter the trust's terms by choosing the jurisdiction of administration. It is unlikely the trustor intended such fundamental consequences simply because he allowed a majority of adult beneficiaries to replace his wife as trustee with any trust company in the U.S. This provision seems aimed solely at administrative convenience, not at selecting the governing law for the trust's core terms. There is no conflict in having one jurisdiction determine the trust's validity while another governs its administration.

Management issues are to be addressed in the jurisdiction where the trust is administered. Cases like First National Bank v. National Broadway Bank and others support this principle. When a validity dispute arises during administration, the overseeing tribunal must resolve it according to the applicable foreign law. Since New York law governs the validity of the trusts under Joseph W. Donner's appointment instrument, the assumed interests created by it are invalid, as previously stated.

What follows from this? The guardian of Joseph W. Donner's children argues that the property allocated to his share should pass to the children free of trusts, as per their grandfather's original settlement. This claim holds unless the executor of Joseph W. Donner's will can prove the residuary clause executed the conferred power. Whether the will executed the power depends on New York law, which states that a general bequest passes property under a power unless the will shows a contrary intent, expressly or by implication.

The statute only considers intent negatively, requiring evidence within the will itself to override the default rule. If the ineffective 1929 deed could be consulted, it clearly shows the power's donee did not intend his will to execute it. However, some argue the deed cannot be used for intent evidence, as the statute limits such evidence to the will's contents. The statute does not demand affirmative proof of intent to execute the power. In Lockwood v. Mildeberger, the New York Court of Appeals interpreted the statute, stating it does not require such affirmative proof.

As we have observed, it is not required for the testatrix to have intended to execute the power, since the statute intervenes and directs the property subject to the power in the same manner as her own property. The same ruling notes that any intent to reject the power’s exercise must be evident within the will itself, as explicitly stated by the statute. Additionally, refer to Speir v. Benvenuti, 197 N. Y. App. Div. 209, 189 N. Y. S. 885. While reviewing the statute, I questioned whether the clause restricting evidence of negativing intent to the will alone applies strictly when the power can be executed by deed or will. I considered that, since a deed holds equal validity under the power’s terms, it might also serve as evidence of such intent. This thought stemmed from the statute’s focus on cases where execution is solely by will. However, the decision

in McLean v. McLean, (Sup.) 158 N. Y. S. 59, affirmed 174 App. Div. 152, 160 N. Y. S. 949, affirmed 223 N. Y. 695, 119 N. E. 1056, renders my earlier query irrelevant. This is because, even if the October 9, 1929, instrument were considered in interpreting Joseph W. Donner’s residuary clause as an execution of the power, it would carry no more weight than if its terms had been included directly in the will. Viewed favorably, as though part of the will, the cited case—which was affirmed by New York’s highest court—clearly establishes that the residuary clause’s effect as an execution of the power is not undermined by any negativing intent suggested elsewhere in the will, such as through an invalid exercise of the power with differing terms. The reasoning in that case builds on the principle from Lockwood v. Mildeberger, supra, that under New York law, a general residuary clause directs the power’s property in the same way as the testator’s own assets. It treats ineffective attempts to exercise the power like any failed disposition of the testator’s property, funneling it into the residuary gift. The trial court in McLean v. McLean, supra, and the reviewing courts rejected the idea that the appointee’s belief in having validly exercised the power could negate the residuary clause’s operation. This case, which

underwent thorough judicial review up to the highest court and remains unchallenged, definitively resolves the issue for New York. Since New York law governs, as previously noted, the decree here must align with that state’s law as outlined, even if the outcome might differ under Delaware law. Joseph W. Donner’s power extended to the full interest in the trust portion from which he received lifetime income. However, his authority over three-fourths of this portion was limited in terms of permissible appointees, excluding his wife. For the remaining one-fourth, his power was unrestricted, allowing him to appoint his wife as a beneficiary in whole or in part. Given that the residuary clause did not explicitly restrict its application to just one-fourth of the appointive estate, the

outcome hinges on New York’s interpretation of such clauses. The McLean case’s precedent confirms that the residuary clause’s broad language encompasses the entire appointive property, regardless of partial restrictions elsewhere in the will. This aligns with the statutory framework treating powers of appointment under a unified rule, ensuring consistency in disposition. Thus, the decree must reflect New York’s stance, even if alternative interpretations might arise under different jurisdictions like Delaware.

It is contended that since Joseph W. Donner’s residuary clause could not transfer the three-fourths interest to his disqualified widow, we should infer he did not intend for her to receive the one-fourth interest either. This reasoning ignores the donor’s explicit division of the estate into two distinct portions: three-fourths under a special power and one-fourth under a general power, akin to separate properties with different powers. Under New York law, a general devise to an ineligible appointee for the special power does not imply an intent to exclude them from the general power’s portion.

There is no logical difference between two separate properties under different powers and two fractional parts of an estate treated as distinct entities by the donor. Had the donor only created a general power over the one-fourth, the residuary clause would have validly passed it. The donee’s failure to properly dispose of the three-fourths does not negate the clause’s effectiveness for the one-fourth, as argued in Lockwood and McLean.

The briefs mistakenly treat the residuary clause as an attempt to appoint the three-fourths to the wife. However, since the clause operates under New York statute and the widow is barred from receiving the three-fourths, the statute cannot imply an intent to execute the power for that portion. If Joseph W. Donner had intended to exceed the power’s scope, the disposition would be invalid only for the excess, as per § 177 of the New York Real Property Law and related cases.

Even if the residuary clause attempted an invalid appointment of the three-fourths, the one-fourth’s disposition would remain valid. However, this assumption is unfounded. Thus, the one-fourth passes under the residuary clause, while the three-fourths appointment in trust for the children is void under New York’s perpetuities law.

The grandchildren are unconditionally entitled to three-fourths of the estate as per the original trust established by their grandfather. According to the trust's conditions, since their father did not exercise his appointment rights, the children gain full entitlement. The decree aligns with this ruling. Objections were raised regarding restitution, personal interest, and past practices, referencing Gilb.Evid. 135, 1 Salk. 283, 2 Hawk.P.C. 433, [2] Str. 728, 1043, 1104. In response, the State cited 2 Str. 1229, 4 Burr. 2252, and [1] Dall. 110. The Court sought the Bar's opinion, with most, except Miers Fisher, opposing admission. However, the majority overruled the objection. Note: While 2 Str. 1043, 1104, 1229 allows an interested party to testify in forgery or perjury cases,

earlier laws, as seen in 1 Morg.Ess. 271 and 1 Term 296, suggest this was not permitted before Chief Justice Lee's era (see 2 Hawk.P.C. 610, 611 and 1 Morg.Ess. 438). Even now, a witness with a financial stake in the case's outcome is barred. Before 21 Hen.VIII, c. 11, theft victims could not testify and reclaim stolen goods, per 4 Bl.Comm. 356. The Court instructed the jury that a well-maintained account book, alongside the plaintiff's oath, is valid evidence for accountable matters, with credibility left to the jury. Discrediting one entry does not invalidate the entire book, though the jury may choose to disregard it entirely. Falsified entries may discredit the whole or part of the account, depending on

the jury's assessment of conflicting evidence, while also considering corroborating proof, such as a promise to pay the balance after reviewing the items. This evidence supports a plaintiff's claim under an account-stated count if the jury deems it sufficient. The verdict favored the plaintiff. HOLLAND, Justice. Defendant Joseph Walker faced charges including two counts of Second-Degree Rape, two counts of Third-Degree Rape, First-Degree Reckless Endangering, and Distributing Alcohol to a Minor. The State dropped the latter charge before trial. The Superior Court presented the Third-Degree Rape counts as lesser offenses under the Second-Degree charges. After trial, Walker was convicted of one count of Attempted Second-Degree Rape, acquitted of one Second-Degree Rape charge, and cleared of Reckless Endangering. The State then sought to

have Walker declared a habitual offender under Delaware Code sections 4214(a) and 4214(b). Following a hearing, the Superior Court ruled him a habitual offender and sentenced him to life without parole under section 4214(b). Walker appeals his conviction on three grounds: first, challenging the admission of prior drug felonies for impeachment under Delaware Rule 609(a), claiming it deterred his testimony; second, alleging prosecutorial misconduct in closing arguments; and third, contesting his habitual offender designation. We find the prosecutorial remarks issue requires further review.

The initial consideration for rebuttal summation should be addressed in a Superior Court Criminal Rule 61 motion regarding ineffective assistance of trial counsel. We find Walker's remaining two arguments lack merit. Thus, the Superior Court's judgment is upheld. On October 3, 1998, Walker, a 32-year-old man, drove Jessica Johnson, a 16-year-old girl, to her friend's house. They collected Crysta Adkins, Johnson's 15-year-old friend, and visited a liquor store where Walker purchased gin. The trio then went to a park, consuming the gin and later buying more alcohol and marijuana. Adkins became severely intoxicated, unable to walk. Walker then took the girls to his friend John Diaz's trailer in Dover, where Adkins was placed on a sofa, either asleep or unconscious. Johnson requested a ride to a phone booth, leaving Adkins with Walker and Diaz.

After Diaz left to check on Johnson and Jenkins, Adkins testified that Walker exposed himself and attempted to remove her pants while she resisted. Diaz heard shouting and Adkins yelling, 'Stop! I don’t want to do this.' Upon returning, Diaz saw Walker standing over Adkins on the couch. Walker then left briefly before reentering to offer Adkins a ride to meet Johnson. Adkins couldn’t locate Johnson but went with Walker, who later dropped her at a pay phone in an unfamiliar area. After returning to offer her a ride home, Adkins claimed Walker again exposed himself and forced her into sexual intercourse in the car despite her protests. She was later dropped near her grandmother’s home, where she reported the rape to her mother, who contacted the police and took her to Kent General Hospital.

The medical examination indicated signs consistent with sexual intercourse, though the doctor couldn’t confirm it occurred before the exam. Adkins filed a police complaint that night, stating Walker had raped her twice—once in Diaz’s trailer and again in his car. Walker contests the trial judge’s decision to allow his prior felony drug convictions as impeachment evidence under Delaware Rule of Evidence 609(a), claiming it deterred him from testifying. However, the record doesn’t substantiate this claim. We cannot conclude his decision not to testify was solely due to the ruling. The State sought pretrial approval to use Walker’s 1991 and 1992 felony convictions to challenge his credibility. Walker’s choice not to testify limits our ability to assess the ruling’s impact, making any harm speculative.

Walker’s challenge to the impeachment evidence ruling lacks sufficient support in the record. The trial judge permitted the State to introduce Walker’s prior felony convictions under Rule 609(a) to question his credibility if he testified. Walker asserts this influenced his decision not to testify, but without his testimony, evaluating the ruling’s effect is impossible. The State’s pretrial motion sought clarity on the admissibility of Walker’s past convictions. The judge allowed their use for impeachment, leading Walker to forgo testifying. However, without his testimony, any claim of prejudice remains speculative, as the record provides no basis to confirm the ruling’s adverse impact.

This Court lacks testimony to assess and cannot determine if the trial court would have altered its decision based on the presented evidence. The State might have chosen not to use Walker's prior felony convictions for impeachment. While Walker claims the ruling discouraged him from testifying, a defendant's choice to testify rarely hinges on one factor. A reviewing court cannot presume the ruling influenced his decision. Additionally, a defendant must testify and then appeal to challenge a ruling on prior conviction admissibility. Since Walker did not testify, he offers no factual basis for this appeal claim. In his second argument, Walker asserts the prosecutor's closing and rebuttal summaries were improper, violating his right to a fair trial and warranting reversal. He specifically objects to comments criticizing his counsel's cross-examination of Crysta Adkins.

Walker highlights the prosecutor's request for the jury to note the tone of defense counsel's cross-examination of Adkins compared to other witnesses. He challenges the prosecutor's depiction of the cross-examination as 'very loud,' 'rapid-fire,' and aimed to 'intimidate' and 'confuse' Adkins. Additionally, he disputes the prosecutor's remarks that defense counsel's reactions made it hard for jurors to process Adkins' answers and that counsel treated her 'without respect,' urging the jury not to let this affect their evaluation. All contested statements focus on defense counsel's cross-examination style. In our adversarial system, defense counsel must zealously advocate for the defendant, exercising the right to confrontation through cross-examination. The core of a fair trial allows reasonable leeway for cross-examiners to test witness credibility, enabling jurors to assess it fairly.

While prosecutors have broad latitude in summation, they must not undermine defense counsel's role by expressing personal frustration with defense tactics. This latitude does not extend to urging the jury to consider matters beyond trial evidence. This Court endorses the American Bar Association's Standards for Criminal Justice, which state that closing arguments should avoid diverting the jury from evidence-based decisions. Prosecutors must not attack defense counsel's integrity or role. Here, the prosecutor's closing and rebuttal remarks collectively disparaged defense counsel's strategy. Defense counsel's duty to vigorously represent Walker included scrutinizing unfavorable testimony through cross-examination. A prosecutor's closing argument cannot restrict the defendant's due process right to a robust defense.

Such statements risk prompting the jury to penalize the defendant for exercising the right to cross-examine the alleged victim. The prosecutor's comments implicated Walker's confrontation right and disparaged his counsel for using it. The State argues the prosecutor's remarks were proper, aiming to: highlight Adkins' testimony endured tough cross-examination, remind jurors that defense counsel's reactions were not evidence, and ensure counsel's treatment of Adkins did not undermine her credibility. However, prosecutorial arguments should center on trial evidence, not extraneous issues.

Expressing views about defense counsel's character or courtroom tactics is inappropriate. Prosecutors must not undermine defense attorneys in the jury's presence. Even corrective jury instructions later may not undo the damage caused by such remarks, potentially compromising a fair trial. During Walker's trial, his defense lawyer did not object to the questionable statements but addressed them in the closing argument. While the attorney explained his role to the jury, improper remarks should be challenged immediately. Typically, not objecting during closing arguments forfeits the right to appeal the issue. However, the court can review for plain error if the prosecutor's comments severely harmed Walker's rights. Here, the court chose not to apply plain error review, believing the defense's strategy of responding to the statements, rather than objecting, should be evaluated in context. The effectiveness of

this strategic choice by the defense can only be assessed with a full record. Regarding Walker's habitual criminal status, he received a life sentence without parole under Delaware Code section 4214(b). Walker claims the court lacked sufficient evidence for this designation. At his hearing, the state proved he had over three prior felonies using certified court dockets, arrest records, attorney general files, a thumbprint match, and his criminal history. These documents covered convictions like Possession with Intent to Deliver Marijuana and Trafficking Cocaine. The state

linked Walker's past felony convictions by cross-referencing arrest records, attorney general files, and court dockets. A fingerprint expert confirmed the thumbprint on his arrest records matched the one taken during the May 2000 hearing. Based on this, the court found beyond a reasonable doubt that Walker had four prior felonies in 1985, 1989, 1991, and 1992. Combined with his Attempted Rape conviction, he met the criteria of section 4214(a). The court also ruled that section 4214(b) applied, as the Attempted Rape conviction, along with prior drug offenses, counted as his third qualifying felony. Since the statute mandates life imprisonment, Walker was sentenced accordingly. The court's habitual offender finding must be

supported by substantial evidence and free from legal or procedural errors. The state provided ample proof linking Walker to his prior felonies. The court correctly admitted the attorney general's files under evidence rules and verified each offense by comparing arrest reports, official records, and court transcripts. Where court records were unclear, the judge referred to Walker's criminal history. The court's conclusion that Walker qualified as a habitual offender under sections 4214(a) and 4214(b) was well-founded. Thus, the Superior Court's judgment is upheld. See Luce v. McNEILLY, Justice: On August 15, 1981, Hunter Betts was fatally shot in the chest during an armed robbery at his home. On September 21, 1981, the defendant was indicted for First-Degree Murder under the felony murder statute outlined in

11 Del.C. 636(a)(6). The defendant did not shoot Betts; her role was limited to involvement in the robbery during which Betts was killed. She pleaded not guilty to the charges. During a pretrial conference on March 31, 1981, the defendant requested the Superior Court to permit her to undergo psychiatric evaluation by two experts to assess her mental state. Arguing that she might rely on the defense of extreme emotional distress under 11 Del.C. § 641, she asked the State to cover the costs. The Superior Court denied the motion, ruling that the extreme emotional distress defense only applies to violations of 11 Del.C. § 636 involving intentional acts. On April 15, 1982, the defendant filed a Motion for Reargument or, alternatively, a Motion to Certify Questions to the Delaware Supreme Court. The Superior Court, under Supreme Court Rule 41, certified four legal questions to this Court on April 15, 1982. On May 6,

1982, certification was accepted. The four questions for review are: 1. Is the mitigating factor of extreme emotional distress under 11 Del.C. § 641 applicable to a defendant charged with first-degree murder under 11 Del.C. § 636(a)(6)? 2. If the answer to Question 1 is no, does the mitigating factor of extreme emotional distress under 11 Del.C. § 641 apply if the State proves criminal negligence under 11 Del.C. § 253 by showing the defendant acted intentionally? 3. If either Question 1 or 2 is answered affirmatively, does the extreme emotional distress defense under 11 Del.C. § 641 extend to a participant [in the underlying felony under 11 Del.C. § 636(a)(6)] who did not fire the fatal shot?

? 4. If the answer to Question 3 is no, does 11 Del.C. § 641 violate the Fourteenth Amendment of the U.S. Constitution and Article I, Section 7 of the Delaware Constitution by denying due process to a co-defendant charged under 11 Del.C. § 636(a)(6) who did not fire the fatal shot? II 11 Del.C. § 636(a), defining first-degree murder, states: (a) A person commits Murder in the First Degree when: (1) They intentionally cause another's death; (2) During a felony or attempted felony, they recklessly cause another's death; (3) They intentionally force or coerce another to commit suicide; (4) They recklessly cause the death of a law enforcement officer, corrections employee, or firefighter while the officer is performing lawful duties

(5) He kills another person by using or setting off a bomb or similar explosive device; (6) He negligently causes another's death while committing or attempting rape, kidnapping, arson, robbery, or fleeing from such crimes; (7) He causes death to evade lawful arrest or during an escape attempt. 11 Del.C. § 641 addresses extreme emotional distress as a mitigating factor, reducing first-degree murder to manslaughter if proven by the accused with sufficient evidence.

The accused must also demonstrate a valid reason for the extreme emotional distress, judged from the perspective of a reasonable person in their situation. The defendant argues that extreme emotional distress applies to felony murder, but the court finds that the requirement of a reasonable explanation under § 641 bars its use in such cases.

Extreme emotional distress, replacing the older 'provocation' defense, was intended to broaden mitigating circumstances but not to excuse distress without a reasonable cause. The distress must stem from an external, justifiable trigger, not the accused's own actions, as ruled in Boyd v. State.

Since felony murder involves self-induced mental disturbance due to criminal activity, extreme emotional distress cannot apply under § 636(a)(2) or (6). The court rejects arguments linking distress to the felony itself, answering certified questions in the negative. The defendant also faces charges for burglary, conspiracy, weapon possession, and theft.

VEASEY, Chief Justice: This case primarily addresses the correct application of 11 Del.C. § 3507 and the trial court's discretion in allowing out-of-court statements from a child victim of alleged sexual abuse. Additional concerns include the child's competency to testify and constitutional confrontation rights. We find no abuse of discretion or constitutional violation, affirming the conviction. FACTS After a Superior Court jury trial in New Castle County, defendant/appellant Abraham Feleke ('

Feleke') was found guilty of two counts of First-Degree Unlawful Sexual Intercourse under 11 Del.C. § 775, one count of Third-Degree Unlawful Sexual Penetration under 11 Del.C. § 770, and one count of Second-Degree Unlawful Sexual Contact under 11 Del.C. § 768. Feleke received fifteen years' mandatory imprisonment for each First-Degree charge, fifteen months for the Third-Degree offense, and two years for the Second-Degree count. The victim was Feleke's nine-year-old daughter. Feleke, an Ethiopian national, was a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Delaware, studying molecular and atomic physics since 1985. His wife joined him a year after his arrival, while their three children stayed in Ethiopia until

December 1990, when the daughter came to Delaware amid her parents' marital struggles. By January 1991, the couple divorced under Ethiopian custom but continued living together in a one-bedroom apartment due to financial constraints. Feleke's relationship with his daughter was tense, and he showed little affection. However, before his arrest, the Mother observed a sudden shift in his behavior, as he began engaging positively with the girl. Six months after the daughter's arrival, the incidents leading to this appeal occurred. On May 28, 1991, the Mother returned from her McDonald's shift, and the daughter came home from school. At dinner, the child refused to eat and cried in her room. Upon questioning, she revealed that Feleke had sexually assaulted her the previous day, a Memorial Day holiday when she was home from school. After hearing the details, the Mother

took the daughter to her workplace, McDonald's, and called the police. Newark Police officers arrived and interviewed only the Mother, as the daughter did not speak English. At the station, a detective conducted a taped interview with the Mother translating. The daughter alleged that Feleke led her to the bedroom, used his fingers and oil for penetration, and claimed he did not want to hurt her. A medical exam at Christiana Medical Center found no physical evidence of trauma or semen, though the child's account detailed the assault.

The likelihood of detecting semen in the daughter's vagina was greatly diminished as she had bathed after the assault. A digital examination of the child's vagina was conducted to assess for any internal irregularities, deformities, or tenderness. The doctor noted, 'I observed unusually minimal resistance when inserting a finger...' He also testified that the hymenal ring was absent. When given anatomically correct dolls, the child positioned the female doll on its back and the male doll, knees bent, on top. On June 13, 1991, the daughter provided a second tape-recorded statement to the police, facilitated by a translator from the Philadelphia Nationalities Service Agency, without her mother present. This account echoed the mother's earlier allegations but included more detail, with the daughter adding that Feleke had sexually abused her multiple times before May 27, though she kept it secret after he promised to buy her underwear.

Feleke's trial began on September 25, 1991, roughly four months after the alleged May 27 incident. The daughter testified in English without an interpreter, though her limited proficiency necessitated leading questions. Despite this, she affirmed that Feleke 'did something bad' to her, pointing at him when asked who it was. She identified him as Abraham (Feleke) but gave inconsistent responses, later denying that the 'bad thing' involved 'bad touching.' She also couldn't demonstrate what happened using dolls. When questioned about truth versus lies, she claimed to know the difference. The State then moved to admit her taped statements under 11 Del. C. § 3507, but the defense objected, citing hearsay, lack of confrontation, and competency issues. The judge overruled, admitting the tapes after deeming the child competent.

On appeal, the issues were: (1) whether the judge erred in finding the child competent to testify; (2) whether the taped statements met the foundational requirements of 11 Del.C. § 3507; and (3) whether the defendant's constitutional rights, including confrontation under the Sixth Amendment and Delaware Constitution, were violated. The court upheld the judge's decision, finding no abuse of discretion in the child's competency ruling or the admission of the tapes. The child had affirmed the statements' truthfulness and touched on the events, satisfying § 3507. The Confrontation Clause was not violated, as the child testified and was subject to cross-examination.

The court concluded that the trial judge acted within his discretion in both the competency determination and the admission of the out-of-court statements under 11 Del.C. § 3507. The defendant's constitutional rights under federal and state law were not infringed. The child's acknowledgment of truth versus fiction supported her competency, and the tapes were properly admitted after she testified to their accuracy. The Confrontation Clause was satisfied, as the child was available for cross-examination, and the judge's actions aligned with legal standards.

Constitutions ensure the chance for meaningful cross-examination, but not necessarily in the exact manner or to the degree the defense desires. As the defense had ample opportunity to challenge any weaknesses in the child's testimony, there was no breach of the Confrontation Clause. Additionally, even if the trial judge's interpretation of the child's gestures was incorrect, the mistake was insignificant. THE COMPETENCY ISSUE Under Delaware Rule of Evidence ('D.R.E.') 601, nearly everyone is deemed competent to testify unless specified otherwise. Furthermore, 10 Del.C. § 4302 states that no child under 10 can be barred from testifying solely due to a lack of understanding of the oath's obligation, though their age and comprehension may influence credibility assessments.

D.R.E. 601 reflects the principle that most individuals are fit to testify, with concerns about mental or moral capacity affecting credibility rather than admissibility. Ricketts v. State, Del. Supr., 488 A.2d 856, 857 (1985). D.R.E. 603 mandates that witnesses must pledge to testify truthfully, either by oath or affirmation, to emphasize their duty. This Court has acknowledged the need for flexibility with child witnesses, as seen in Ricketts, where a six-year-old rape victim was deemed competent after promising to tell the truth. Although the nine-year-old in this case did not make such a promise, the adaptable competency rules support the trial judge's decision that she was fit to testify.

The daughter in this case lacked strong English proficiency, unlike the child in Ricketts. Despite initially struggling with questions about truth and lies, she asserted she could distinguish between fabricated and true stories. When asked if she was coached, she replied, 'I told what happened to me.' While her responses were unclear at times and her English skills limited, the trial judge reasonably concluded, within the flexibility of competency rules, that she was competent. We respect the judge's discretion, as there was sufficient testimony to meet D.R.E. 603's standards, aligned with 10 Del.C. § 4302. A child's age and oath comprehension may influence credibility but do not bar testimony.

ADMISSIBILITY OF OUT-OF-COURT STATEMENTS In Ray v. State, Del. Supr., 587 A.2d 439 (1991), this Court ruled that two conditions must be met for admitting out-of-court statements under 11 Del. C. § 3507. First, the witness must affirm the statement's truthfulness. Second, they must testify about the events they witnessed or heard. As stated in Ray, such statements are tied to the witness's ability to recount perceived events. Keys v. State, Del.Supr., 337 A.2d 18 (1975) further requires the declarant to be an in-court witness, subject to cross-examination. The use of hearsay under § 3507 must be strictly controlled.

This applies to scenarios where a proper foundation is set, preventing instances where the sole direct evidence of an offense comes from third parties recounting the victim's prior statements. 587 A.2d at 444. Here, the State introduced two prior out-of-court statements as evidence. Under § 3507, the child testified to confirm these statements. Meeting the first part of the foundation, she affirmed their truthfulness despite her young age and English language challenges. When questioned, 'Did anyone instruct you on what to say to [the detective], or did you tell her the truth?' she replied, 'I told her what happened.' Thus, while her testimony lacked detail, the trial judge could reasonably conclude it addressed the events, minimally fulfilling the first § 3507 requirement. Likewise, though her testimony was fragmented and mostly from direct examination, the judge could find the second foundational part satisfied.

Her testimony described the events she witnessed. The child stated that Fe-leke did something inappropriate involving touching. Key parts of her direct examination included: By Mr. Letang: Q. Can you tell me who did something bad to you? A. Yes. Q. Who was it? A. It was him. (The record notes she pointed to the defense table.) Q. Who exactly did this? A. Abraham. Q. Can you repeat that louder? A. Abraham. Q. Is Abraham your father? A. (She nodded.) Mr. Letang: The record confirms she said yes. Later, the prosecutor asked: Q. What bad thing happened? Did it involve touching? A. Huh? Q. Was it touching? A. (She nodded.)

State, 587 A.2d at 444. We see no abuse of discretion. CONFRONTATION RIGHTS The Sixth Amendment and Delaware Constitution’s Article I, section 7 grant the accused the right to confront witnesses. However, this guarantees only 'an opportunity for effective cross-examination, not unlimited cross-examination as the defense might prefer.' U.S. v. Owens, 484 U.S. 554, 559 (1988) (emphasis in original).

Id. at 1123 (quoting Burke v. State, Del.Supr., 484 A.2d 490, 495 (1989)). Aligning with these principles, this Court ruled that while § 3507 mandates the declarant be cross-examined, 'it doesn’t explicitly specify any particular requirements.'

The effectiveness of cross-examination or the acceptance of an out-of-court statement does not hinge on the witness's specific memory during trial.' Johnson v. State, Del.Supr., 338 A.2d 124, 127 (1975). Here, the daughter underwent both direct and cross-examination, with the defense recalling her after her recorded statements were presented to the jury. Thus, even if Feleke was unhappy with the cross-examination, the Confrontation Clause was met as 'the defense had ample opportunity to explore and highlight any weaknesses through cross-examination.' This case involves a claim for unpaid workers' compensation benefits. Plaintiff William Kelley ('Kelley') moves for summary judgment, which is granted under Huffman v. C.C. Oliphant & Son, Inc. ('Huffman'). BACKGROUND: On April 29, 1988, Kelley, an ILC Dover, Inc. ('ILC') maintenance worker, was injured in an industrial accident. He received temporary total disability benefits from ILC's insurer, Liberty Mutual Insurance Company ('Liberty'), which later filed a petition.

request to end proceedings with the Industrial Accident Board ('IAB'); Kelly additionally submitted a petition to the IAB requesting a rise in permanent partial disability. On November 9, 1995, the IAB approved Liberty's request to terminate and lowered Kelley's benefits from $242.13 weekly in temporary total disability to $82.13 weekly in temporary partial disability. The IAB also granted Kelley fees for medical witnesses and legal representation. Later, Kelley appealed the IAB's decision to reduce compensation to the Superior Court. On October 31, 1997, the Superior Court overturned the IAB's ruling, restoring Kelley's benefits to $242.13. The Supreme Court upheld this decision on June 25, 1998. After the Supreme Court's ruling, Kelley, via his attorney, sent a letter on July 18, 1998, requesting payment of all owed workers' compensation benefits. The plaintiff's attorney received payment for the reinstated total disability benefits on August 27, 1998. The fees for medical witnesses and legal representation remain outstanding. The plaintiff initiated this lawsuit seeking compensation

for delayed payment of total disability benefits, along with unpaid medical witness fees, attorney's fees, and additional penalties. The plaintiff has requested summary judgment. II. ARGUMENTS OF THE PARTIES Supporting his motion for summary judgment, the plaintiff asserts there are no genuine disputes of material fact concerning the awarded total disability benefits, medical witness fees, and attorney's fees. Kelley contends he is legally entitled to judgment under Huffman, as the defendants did not promptly pay the owed amounts after proper demand. The defendants counter that (a) Kelley's Huffman demand was unclear and inadequate; (b) they had valid reasons to withhold payments; (c) the Superior Court's reversal eliminated their obligation to pay medical witness and attorney's fees; and (d) Kelley's acceptance of the back total disability benefits check resolved the entire debt. III. SUMMARY JUDGMENT CRITERIA Summary judgment will only be issued if, after reviewing the record favorably to the non-moving party, no genuine material facts are in dispute, and the moving party is legally entitled to judgment. The moving party must prove no material facts are contested. The non-moving party cannot rely solely on pleadings but must present specific facts, via affidavit or other means, showing a material issue for trial exists.

IV. ANALYSIS A lawsuit 'to recover unpaid wages and additional damages can be filed in any court with proper jurisdiction.' The plaintiff seeks summary judgment under 19 Del. C. § 2357, which states, '[i]f an employer fails to pay any owed amount under this chapter within 30 days of demand, the amount can be recovered like wage claims.' Wage claims against an employer can be pursued under the Wage Payment and Collection Act (WPCA). To enforce Section 2357, the term 'wages' in Section 1113(a) must be interpreted to 'cover claims for unpaid workers' compensation benefits after proper demand.' In other words, if an employer does not pay owed amounts under the Workers' Compensation statute within 30 days of demand, the debt can be recovered like claims under the Wage Payment and Collection Act.'

The plaintiff also seeks additional damages under 19 Del. C. § 1103(b), which states, '[i]f an employer, without reasonable grounds, fails to pay required wages under this Chapter, the employer shall also owe the employee 10% of the unpaid wages for each day, excluding Sundays and holidays, the delay continues after the due date, or the full unpaid amount, whichever is less....' The defendants argue Kelley's Huffman demand is invalid due to lack of specificity about the compensation sought. Kelley's letter demanded 'payment of all owed workers' compensation benefits' because the 'Board award remains unpaid.' The wording in Kelley's demand closely resembles that in MacDonald v. Smalls Insurance Co. In MacDonald, the Court dismissed the defendants' vagueness claim, ruling the demand provided sufficient notice as 'both parties knew payments were due.' Similarly here, the original

The IAB award and subsequent appellate decisions adequately informed the plaintiff of what was owed. Section 2357's demand requirements aim to notify defendants of their default, allowing them 30 days to rectify the issue and avoid WPCA liquidated damages. The defendants' duty to pay benefits stemmed from the Superior Court overturning the IAB's termination order, not the demand letter, which simply served as a notice of default. Thus, the plaintiffs demand letter didn’t need to restate the relief sought, as both parties were aware of the payments due after the appeal. In Holden v. Gaico, the Supreme Court deemed a demand for 'all workers' compensation benefits due' as timely, reversing and remanding the case to allow Holden’s Huffman claim. The defendants claim the letter was only deemed timely, not proper, but the Supreme Court’s ruling implicitly rejected this argument, affirming the letter’s validity.

The defendants also claim a factual dispute exists over the dates demand or payment letters were sent, postmarked, and received. Regardless of the dates selected, all scenarios exceed the 30-day window. They further argue a 'reasonable justification' for non-payment, asserting they were unsure of Kelley’s owed benefits and whether he received Second Injury Fund payments post-IAB termination. However, Huffman v. Supreme Court ruled that an employer’s good faith belief in a claimant’s ineligibility is irrelevant without an IAB termination order. The Board, not the employer or insurer, determines compensation eligibility. Thus, ILC and Liberty had no right to withhold payment unilaterally; their recourse was to petition the IAB. Additionally, the Second Injury and Contingency Fund under 19 Del. C. § 2347 does not extend benefits post-IAB termination, even during appeals, rendering the 'reasonable justification' argument legally invalid.

The defendants argue the Superior Court’s reversal of the IAB’s decision also nullified ancillary awards like attorney’s and medical witness fees. However, Superior Court Civil Rule 72(c) allows partial appeals of agency decisions. In Johnson v. General Motors, the Court upheld limited appeals while permitting payment of uncontested IAB award portions. Similarly, in Keeler v. Metal Masters, Huffman damages were granted for unappealed IAB award segments during an appeal. Here, Kelley only appealed the disability benefits reduction, and the defendants filed no cross-appeal, leaving the rest of the IAB award binding and final after the appeal period lapsed.

The defendants raise an accord and satisfaction defense, requiring: 1) a good-faith dispute over the owed amount, 2) a tender intended as full debt satisfaction, and 3) creditor acceptance. The burden of proof lies with the party asserting it. They claim this defense applies to liquidated damages from delayed back disability payments. However, 19 Del. C. § 2805 prohibits any agreement relieving employers of Chapter 28 liabilities without IAB approval. Since defendants lack such approval, this defense is unavailable. Y. CONCLUSION The plaintiff is entitled to judgment as a matter of law under these circumstances.

In England, the probate of wills under the old system persisted until recently, influencing legal decisions. The law of real estate was rooted in medieval feudal tenure, with the heir at law remaining significant even after the underlying institutions faded. Unlike England, which lacked a registry, here a registry and Register's Court were established by the 1792 Constitution, with judicial power confirmed in 1832, requiring written depositions as part of the record.

The Register's jurisdiction is broad, allowing examination of a will's validity, with appeals to the Superior Court for final decisions. This integrates the Register into the state judiciary. The Legislature ensures its effectiveness, but the key question is whether granting an issue is mandatory or discretionary. Some argue it’s a duty, but this interpretation conflicts with the Constitution and law. The Register of Wills has the authority, but not the obligation, to grant an issue, exercising legal discretion. Under the Duke of York's laws, wills were proved at assizes and sent to New York. After 1682, William Penn established a legal code with Registers, including a Register General in Philadelphia. The 1706 and 1769 statutes validated wills proved here or in English Chancery, transferring land title effectively.

In 20 & 21 Viet, there was no Court of Probate for real estate. Chancery had long held jurisdiction to validate wills, as evidenced by cited cases. If the heir-at-law was in possession, a bill could be filed in Chancery to establish a will, with the Chancellor having authority. In Rash vs. Purnell, 2 Harring. 448, Clayton, C.J., noted that the process resembled the Chancery Court's practice in England when a devisee sought to validate a will.
