Pearson, Vice-Chancellor: The complainant seeks a decree to cancel 700 shares of the corporation's stock issued in 1944, arguing that the directors' primary motive was improper, aimed at maintaining corporate control.

Until late 1944, the corporation had 500 outstanding shares of $10 par value capital stock. The complainant held 150 shares; defendant Waltman, 10 shares; and French residents owned the remaining 340 shares. Before the war with Germany began, the French shareholders provided Waltman with proxies to vote their shares at meetings from 1941 to 1944. Once the war started, communication with the French shareholders was prohibited, and the proxies were used without their direct input at annual meetings through 1944. These proxies represented a majority of shares, effectively controlling director elections during those years. The proxies expired in November 1944. At a May meeting that year, an amendment to the certificate of incorporation was approved, increasing authorized capital stock from 500 to 2000 shares. Shortly after, the directors voted to issue 700

shares at $10 each. The corporation issued 14 shares to Waltman, reflecting his pre-emptive rights. It also issued 476 shares—the total available to French shareholders if communication had been possible—in blocks to individual defendants Waltman, Trammell, and Grant, three of the four directors. These shares were issued under subscription agreements, described later. The corporation offered the complainant 210 shares, matching his pre-emptive rights. Although the complainant objected to the issuance, he subscribed to his allotment 'to protect his shareholder position.' The complainant argues that the directors' sole intent in issuing additional shares was to retain control after the French shareholders' proxies expired in November. He notes that in May 1944, when the directors authorized the share issuance, it was uncertain whether communication with France would resume in time to secure new proxies for the annual meeting.

At the stockholders' meeting in March 1945, new proxies were submitted and voted upon. The election outcome remained unchanged regardless of whether the newly issued shares were counted, leading the complainant to drop all requests except for the cancellation of the 700 shares. The complainant cited the legal principle from Kingston v. Home Life Ins. Co., which prohibits issuing new shares for improper purposes like maintaining corporate control, a point also addressed in Yasik v. Wachtel. The defendants argued the share issuance was prompted by the complainant's actions.

During the March 1944 annual meeting, the complainant was represented by his attorney, Mr. Holmes, and solicitor, Mr. Cronan. Their objections, including protests against proxy considerations and election inspectors, were noted but not pursued. The chairman presented a balance sheet revealing a $7,000 deficit, sparking extensive discussion. Complainant's representatives questioned the directors' inaction but none of their motions passed.

Questions arose about the corporation's prolonged insolvency and the directors' failure to address it. Proposals for shareholder contributions to rectify the deficit were rejected, as was a motion to censure the directors. A protest against re-electing the directors cited their mishandling of the company's financial decline, but these objections were unsuccessful.

The complainant's representatives maintained until the 1945 trial that he was unaware of the deficit. However, evidence showed his secretary received a similar balance sheet in 1937. Post-meeting, the corporation's president responded to inquiries, acknowledging the long-standing deficit but asserting sufficient U.S. funds negated the need for additional capital contributions.

Any potential demands here; and it was highly likely that a 'hidden reserve' beyond the deficit existed, as some claims on outstanding coupons or talons (linked to deposits of Franco-Wyoming Oil Company shares) were time-barred. While the complainant initially found these reasons acceptable at the hearing, their attorney responded differently on April 4 to Waltman's letter, stating: 'I don’t understand why you use quotes around 'deficit.' The deficit is real and acknowledged in your letter. Liabilities have surpassed assets significantly for years. Had Mr. Aldridge or I known, we would have acted sooner, despite the Gaillochets' control, to rectify this. Your claim that the corporation has sufficient U.S. funds to meet demands here avoids the issue. Unpresented claims don’t justify insolvency or misuse of coupon funds.'

The corporation’s funds for coupon payments should only be used for that purpose. Your argument about lost or destroyed dividend talons being time-barred is misleading, as the Oil Company’s agreement requires barred dividends to be returned. Thus, the idea of a hidden reserve is baseless. Post-war political changes in France may trigger immediate coupon payments, and Franco-Wyoming Securities Corporation’s stockholders can only be protected by urgent financial reforms. Your letter and the financial statement reveal management’s disregard for non-controlling interests, with directors—whether French nominees or your appointees—negligent in restoring financial stability.

Directors show no intent to address the situation. Please confirm if your stance remains unchanged after reviewing this.' The April 4 letter prompted the May 2 stockholders' meeting, where a capital increase was approved. Complainant’s representatives opposed it without explanation, save for a vague claim about maintaining control. As French owners held most shares, issuing new stock required a license under Executive Order 8389. The directors applied to issue 700 shares, citing the need to align assets with liabilities. Complainant and Waltman were offered shares proportional to their holdings, while U.S. citizens would subscribe for French shareholders’ allotments due to wartime restrictions.

The Treasury rejected the application, citing a need to defer until French stockholders could participate. A revised application proposed issuing 700 shares: 224 to complainant and Waltman, and 476 via subscription agreements with individual defendants. These agreements allocated blocks of shares to French shareholders, allowing them to purchase post-war. Each agreement tied a block to a specific shareholder, with terms for purchase once communication was restored.

The transaction with the shareholder was deemed lawful, allowing the purchase of shares at cost price plus interest, with the stock certificate including a reference to the agreement. Following a subsequent application, the Treasury Secretary issued a license on September 18, 1944, permitting the sale of 476 shares under the subscription agreements. The proceeds were to be placed in a blocked account, and the share certificates were similarly restricted. Defendants argued that the complainant's remarks about the deficit suggested potential insolvency proceedings, citing past litigation involving the complainant and the defendant corporation, as well as Franco-Wyoming Oil Company.

Complainant has not demonstrated an 'improper purpose' in the issuance of the shares. The deficit, acknowledged by the complainant's attorney as genuine, justified the issuance of new shares to address it—a solution proposed by the complainant's own representatives. The directors' purchase of a significant portion of the shares, under the agreements, was not seen as improper, as the Treasury Department likely would not have approved an issuance without safeguards for French shareholders. The complainant was offered his full pre-emptive rights, and the disposal of remaining shares was a fair arrangement to protect absent shareholders during wartime.

The complainant's evidence fails to establish an improper purpose beyond the directors' desire to retain control while addressing the deficit through new share issuance. This does not constitute misconduct. The bill lacks merit and should be dismissed. A decree to this effect will be advised. BERGER, Justice: This appeal examines whether the Superior Court overstepped by dismissing a 'trip and fall' case due to the appellant's failure to submit an expert report. While medical records were provided, the court insisted on a formal report, despite counsel's argument that it was redundant. Dismissal was excessive, as the claim had merit, there was time to file the report, and no lesser sanctions had been attempted.

Factual and Procedural Background: James Hill, Jr. sustained a left knee injury after stepping into a pothole in a parking lot owned by Dover Medical Center Condominium Association and others. The injury required surgery and rehabilitation. Hill filed suit in May 2010, alleging negligence in maintaining the premises. A Trial Scheduling Order in December 2010 set deadlines, including expert reports by February 22, 2011. Hill notified the Medical Center via email on that date, identifying treating physicians as his only experts.

The testimony aligns with their medical records, which you have... The Medical Center responded: Regarding your expert disclosures, consider this email as formal notice that defendants deem your expert disclosure inadequate and non-compliant with Superior Court Civil Rule 26... Defendants urge the plaintiff to promptly submit the expert's identity, qualifications, opinions, and their foundations. Shortly after, Hill conceded: Fine, you win. I’ll comply in two weeks, though you’ll find nothing new. Despite this, Hill took no action. On March 10, 2011, the Medical Center filed a motion to compel, demanding the discovery within seven days. By March 28, 2011, with no response from Hill, the court ordered the expert disclosures within seven days, warning of exclusion from testimony if unmet. Surprisingly, the order extended the Medical Center’s expert deadline to July 3, 2011, if disclosures weren’t provided by April 8.

2011.' This addition was handwritten by the court on the Medical Center’s proposed order. Hill failed to comply. On April 29, 2011, the Medical Center moved to bar Hill’s expert testimony and dismiss the case. Hill countered, stating the case was straightforward and no liability expert was needed, arguing the Medical Center never contested his injury or its cause. The Superior Court granted both motions, leading to this appeal. Discussion: Hill’s counsel severely failed his client. An experienced personal injury lawyer, he deemed the case 'simple,' providing medical records but neglecting expert disclosures. Despite the Medical Center’s demands for expert details, Hill’s counsel ignored both informal requests and the court’s order to compel. Only when faced with a motion to preclude and dismiss did he respond.

At the hearing, Hill’s counsel argued causation was indisputable—Hill twisted his knee in a pothole, and the medical records sufficed. He claimed any seasoned lawyer would grasp the case’s simplicity. His inaction on the motion to compel and dismiss likely stemmed from expecting resolution without court involvement. He admitted, 'I’ve never had to fuss over such things in similar cases, but I’m learning.' The court, however, deemed expert disclosures critical. Hill’s counsel then requested leeway to expand on the medical records: 'If the Court finds my submission lacking, I ask for a chance to elaborate in the interest of justice.' The court questioned, 'Elaborate how?' Counsel conceded uncertainty but insisted no new meaningful information would emerge.

The court concluded counsel had rejected its implicit offer for extra time to submit an expert opinion linking defendants’ negligence to Hill’s injuries. In Drejka v. Hitchens Tire Service, this Court faced a comparable scenario, ruling it was an abuse of discretion to exclude expert testimony and dismiss. Drejka was injured by a falling truck wheel. Though her expert report was delayed until May 5, 2009, her medical records were timely. The trial court excluded the report, citing insufficient time for rebuttal. This Court reversed, emphasizing the undue harshness of preclusion.

The court emphasized that dismissal should only be considered as a final option. It evaluated how the trial court assessed six key factors: (1) the individual's accountability; (2) the impact on the opposing party; (3) past delays; (4) whether the actions were intentional or malicious; (5) the viability of lighter penalties; and (6) the validity of the claim. Drejka's claim had merit; no signs of bad faith were found; she wasn't to blame for her lawyer's delays; the other side had time for discovery; and no lighter sanctions were tried. While Drejka had a record of delays, this alone didn't warrant the harshest penalty. The trial court noted parallels between Drejka's case and the current one. Hill wasn't responsible for the delay, and there was ample time for discovery before trial. No lighter sanctions were applied, and his lawyer acted in good faith. Though the court didn't address the claim's merit, the evidence supports it. These factors collectively opposed dismissal.

However, the trial court deemed dismissal fitting 'under the circumstances.' It highlighted three reasons: First, the lawyer ignored the trial schedule and a subsequent deadline. Second, he refused to guarantee an expert report. Third, his behavior warranted strong punishment to deter others. This Court agrees his conduct was unacceptable. Even if he mistakenly thought medical records sufficed under Rule 26(b)(4), that didn’t excuse disregarding court orders. While severe sanctions were justified, dismissal wasn’t. The trial court claimed lesser sanctions wouldn’t work, assuming the lawyer would never submit a report. This isn’t backed by the record, as he offered to provide a 'more explicit' report if dismissal was the alternative, though he admitted it wouldn’t add meaningful information.

The Court recognizes the trial court's frustration with the lawyer's dismissive attitude. Regardless of its usefulness, a formal report was required by the rules and ordered by the court. Hill's lawyer wasted time and deserves personal sanctions. The trial court didn’t attempt sanctions before dismissal, and the record doesn’t show they’d have failed. In short, the Drejka factors show dismissal was unjustified. Conclusion: The Superior Court’s ruling is reversed, and the case is remanded for further proceedings. Jurisdiction isn’t retained. References: Appellant's Appendix (A-37, A-50, A-51, A-66, A-67), Super. Ct. Civil R. 26, and Hill v. DuShuttle (2011 WL 2623349).

15 A.3d 1221 (Del. 2010). Hill v. DuShuttle (2011 WL 2623349 at *5). HOLLAND, Justice: Keith L. Thompson was convicted by a Superior Court jury in New Castle County of Rape First Degree, Kidnapping First Degree, and Assault First Degree. He received life sentences for rape and kidnapping, plus two years for assault. The appeal centers on whether his warrantless arrest had probable cause, specifically whether the court erred in denying a motion to suppress evidence from the arrest. After reviewing the record and the forensic hair analysis used by police, we find probable cause existed. Thus, we uphold the denial of the motion to suppress and affirm Thompson’s convictions. Background: On July...

On October 28, 1984, an eight-year-old girl was asleep in her grandmother's home on Bowers Street in Wilmington. Around 5:00 a.m., a black male intruder took the girl outside, undressed her, and tried to rape her. When she screamed, he hit her and moved her to a dump site, where he raped her. After pretending to be dead, she escaped and returned home. Her uncle called the police, who arrived by 5:20 a.m. A doctor confirmed her injuries were consistent with rape. Investigators found a mattress with a red stain, along with shoe and barefoot prints, which they cast in plaster. They also collected a blanket and sofa cushion from the home.

Police gathered hair samples from the mattress cover, blanket, and sofa cushion. On September 9, 1984, a similar crime occurred at Royal Oaks Apartments near Wilmington, where a black male intruder took a nine-year-old girl from her bedroom but fled when she woke up. Police stopped Thompson nearby, as he matched the suspect's description. Though the girl couldn’t identify him initially, she later picked his photo in a lineup, saying he 'might be the one' and rated his resemblance as a ten.

On September 21, 1984, Thompson voluntarily went with detectives for questioning in the Royal Oaks case. After providing hair and fingerprint samples, Detective Godek took them to the FBI lab. Agent Warren compared Thompson’s hair to evidence from the Bowers Street case and found matching characteristics. While hair analysis can’t confirm identity, Warren noted he had never seen such similarities between different individuals. Godek relayed the findings to his superiors and Wilmington police.

After Thompson’s warrantless arrest on September 21, 1984, the Bowers Street victim identified him in a lineup as resembling her attacker. His shoes were seized for comparison with the plaster casts. Thompson argues his arrest lacked probable cause, relying solely on hair analysis, which he claims is insufficient for identification.

He suggests that while microscopic analysis can serve as pertinent evidence, it is not a dependable method for confirming identity and thus should not be the sole basis for establishing probable cause. Thompson asserts that his arrest was unlawful and that any evidence gathered during this illegal detention is inadmissible under the 'fruit of the poisonous tree' doctrine, referencing Wong Sun v. United States. The State counters that probable cause was based on the overall circumstances, including Thompson's status as a suspect in the Royal Oaks case. Delaware law permits warrantless felony arrests only if the offense occurs in the officer's presence or if there is reasonable belief that the person committed a felony.

A comparable federal statute aligns with the constitutional mandate that arrests require probable cause, as noted in Henry v. United States. The Court in Henry highlighted that probable cause is a fundamental principle in Anglo-American law, preventing arbitrary arrests based on mere suspicion. Historical abuses like general warrants and writs of assistance underscore the necessity of judicial oversight. The Court emphasized that rumor or strong suspicion alone has never sufficed to justify an arrest warrant, let alone a warrantless arrest.

Delaware's statute authorizing warrantless arrests demands 'reasonable ground to believe' a felony has been committed. Since suspicion alone is inadequate, the statute must be interpreted as requiring probable cause to remain constitutional. This Court has previously equated 'reasonable grounds to suspect' with probable cause in State v. Cochran. We now affirm that 'reasonable ground to believe' carries the same legal weight as probable cause, consistent with prior rulings such as Thomas v. State.

Identifying probable cause as the standard for warrantless arrests is just the starting point. Probable cause is a nuanced concept, difficult to define precisely, as acknowledged in State v. Cochran. It exists between mere suspicion and conclusive evidence, as described in United States v. Thompson. The U.S. Supreme Court emphasizes that probable cause is a practical, flexible standard, not a rigid technical rule, as outlined in Illinois v. Gates.

7 (1983) (citing Brinegar v. United States, 338 U.S. 160, 176, 69 S.Ct. 1302, 1311, 93 L.Ed. 1879 (1949)). The Gates Court held that probable cause should be evaluated based on the totality of circumstances, rejecting a rigid test in favor of a flexible approach grounded in 'the factual and practical considerations of everyday life on which reasonable and prudent individuals, not legal experts, act.' Id. (quoting Brinegar v. United States, 338 U.S. at 175, 69 S.Ct. at 1310)). While no single test defines probable cause, certain standards apply. For instance, warrantless arrests must meet the same probable cause threshold as those with warrants. Wong Sun v. United States, 371 U.S. at 479, 83 S.Ct. at 412. 'Otherwise, a key motivation for securing arrest warrants would be undermined.'

Id. at 479-80, 83 S.Ct. at 413 (footnote omitted). In Garner v. State, Del.Supr., 314 A.2d 908 (1973), Chief Justice Herrmann outlined the probable cause standard. Valid arrests, whether warrantless or not, require officers to have information that would lead a reasonable person to believe a crime occurred. Assessing probable cause involves balancing effective law enforcement against citizens' constitutional rights to avoid arbitrary police actions. Id. at 910-11 (citations omitted). When challenged, the factual basis for a warrantless felony arrest must be presented to the court. Thompson contends his arrest lacked probable cause. See Wong Sun v. United States, 371 U.S. at 479, 83 S.Ct. at 412. The Superior Court found that reasonable officers in the Wilmington police's position would have

believed they had probable cause to arrest Thompson for the Bowers Street rape. Cf. Henry v. United States, 361 U.S. at 102, 80 S.Ct. at 171. 'The amount of information needed for probable cause—evidence sufficient to lead a cautious person to conclude a felony was committed—depends on the specific case's facts.' Wong Sun v. United States, 371 U.S. at 479, 83 S.Ct. at 413 (citation omitted) (quoting Carroll v. United States, 267 U.S. 132, 162, 45 S.Ct. 280, 288, 69 L.Ed. 543 (1925)). Thus, we must now assess the facts of this case. Forensic Hair Analysis in This Case Thompson's arrest stemmed from an FBI comparison of his voluntarily provided hair samples from the Royal Oaks case with evidence from the Bowers Street incident. Our analysis begins by examining why Delaware police sought the FBI's

hair analysis. Wilmington police were investigating the Bowers Street case when the Royal Oaks attack occurred outside the city in New Castle County. Collaboration between law enforcement revealed both crimes involved a nighttime burglary by a Black male and the sexual assault of a young female victim taken from her bedroom. Hair evidence was collected in both investigations. The Royal Oaks case also led to the victim's tentative identification of Thompson, found jogging near the crime scene shortly after the incident. Due to the similarities, Delaware police suspected a link between the cases. Testimony at the suppression hearing showed that on September 21, 1984, Thompson's hair samples were sent to the FBI Lab in Washington, D.C., by Detective Godek. There, Special Agent Warren compared them with hair evidence from both cases, with Detective Godek present during the examination.

While Special Agent Warren conducted the microscopic hair examination, Detective Godek recounted his observations during the suppression hearing. He noted that Agent Warren analyzed three distinct hairs from the Bowers Street case—one on a blanket, one on a green seat cushion, and one on a mattress cover. These were compared to Keith Thompson's head hairs, with Agent Warren concluding they shared enough similarities to suggest they likely originated from Thompson. Although hair analysis isn't as definitive as fingerprints, Agent Warren testified that he could distinguish hairs from different individuals, including twins, and affirmed the hairs matched Thompson's characteristics. Detective Godek emphasized the significance of finding three hairs in separate locations.

Detective Godek promptly called his superior, Lieutenant Thomas Gordon, to relay Agent Warren's findings. Lieutenant Gordon coordinated with Wilmington police to arrange a meeting between Detective Godek and the investigators handling both Delaware cases. Returning to Delaware that evening, Detective Godek arrived at the Wilmington police station around 10:00 p.m., where Thompson was already being questioned. Godek shared the FBI hair analysis results, and after reviewing additional case similarities, Thompson was arrested for the Bowers Street rape by 11:00 p.m. The history of forensic hair analysis dates back over a century, with courts widely accepting such evidence, as seen in cases like Knoll v. State (1882) and numerous scholarly discussions on its admissibility and limitations.

Forensic hair analysis has been extensively debated in legal and academic circles, with publications like Imwinkelried's and Gaudette's works highlighting its role and challenges. While fingerprint matches are deemed conclusive for arrests, hair comparisons lack the same precision, as noted in Miller's research and FBI guidelines. This distinction was acknowledged by courts, including in Parson v. State (1966), which recognized hair analysis as less definitive than fingerprints. Despite this, courts have upheld the admissibility of hair evidence, leaving its weight to the trier of fact, as demonstrated in cases like Brown v. State.

The admissibility of hair analysis testimony has been upheld in trials, such as when an FBI expert testified that hairs found on a victim's clothing matched the defendant's characteristics. While the expert couldn't definitively state the hairs were the defendant's, the court ruled the testimony admissible, leaving its evaluation to the jury. This aligns with broader legal recognition that hair evidence, though not as conclusive as fingerprints, remains a valid forensic tool when presented with appropriate caveats about its limitations.

In 329 A.2d 153, 154 (1974), the issue Thompson raises is not about the weight of hair identification evidence at trial, but its role in assessing probable cause for arrest. The relevance of hair comparison evidence is clarified by examining prior rulings that discuss its use. Notably, denying access to hair analysis results has been deemed grounds for overturning a conviction, as seen in Ayres v. State, Del.Supr., 436 A.2d 800, 802-03 (1981). See also Deberry v. State, Del.Supr., 457 A.2d 744, 751 & n. 5 (1983); Fensterer v. State, Del.Supr., 509 A.2d 1106, 1109-11 (1986). In Ayres, an FBI report included two exculpatory hair comparisons in a rape case.

In a rape case, the FBI report contained two hair comparisons favorable to the defendant. 436 A.2d at 802 & n. 1. The Court determined this report was Brady material and 'clearly relevant to whether intercourse occurred.' Id. at 802. Additionally, the Court ruled the report had 'enough probative value (due to its objectivity) to raise reasonable doubt about the defendant’s guilt.' Id. at 803. Similarly, in Deberry, another rape case, the absence of the victim’s hair on the defendant’s clothing undermined the claim of intercourse. 457 A.2d at 751 & n. 5. From the prosecution’s perspective, hair analysis has been deemed sufficient to link a rape victim and the defendant. Parson v. State, 222 A.2d at 331. Hairs found in a discarded ski mask also tied the defendant to a robbery. Buckingham v. State, Del.Supr., 482 A.2d 327, 330 (1984).

The legitimacy of Thompson’s arrest hinges on whether officers had probable cause at the time—whether the facts known to them justified a reasonable belief that Thompson had committed a crime. Beck v. Ohio, 379 U.S. 89, 91 (1964). The Superior Court found probable cause for Thompson’s warrantless arrest, citing his status as a suspect in a similar case (Royal Oaks) and the hair comparison similarities. The trial judge noted that while hair analysis isn’t definitive, as a scientific test, it allowed police to infer probable cause—a middle ground between suspicion and proof beyond doubt.

We agree with the Superior Court’s reasoning. Hair analysis alone was insufficient for probable cause in Thompson’s warrantless arrest for the Bowers Street rape. Cf. Thomas v. State, 467 A.2d at 956-57. However, it did connect Thompson to the case. Parson v. State, 222 A.2d at 331. The FBI’s hair analysis provided the objective link needed to elevate police suspicion to probable cause, justifying Thompson’s arrest. Carroll v. United States, 267 U.S. 132, 162 (1925).

543 (1925). See United States v. De Larosa, 450 F.2d 1057, 1067 (3d Cir. 1971), cert. denied, 405 U.S. 927 (1972). Additionally, In re Grand Jury Proceedings: Cecil Mills, 686 F.2d 135, 140 (3d Cir. 1982), cert. denied, 459 U.S. 1020 (1982). The seizure of Thompson's tennis shoes and his lineup identification by the Bowers Street victim were lawful as they followed his valid felony arrest. Thus, the Superior Court correctly denied Thompson's Motion to Suppress, and his convictions are AFFIRMED. The life sentence included a mandatory minimum incarceration of twenty years.

The incident leading to Thompson's convictions is known as the Bowers Street case. The victim required hospitalization for several days due to her injuries. Another incident, referred to as the Royal Oaks case, also occurred. In 1776, Section 17 of the Delaware Declaration of Rights stated that warrants without oath to search or seize property or persons are oppressive, and general warrants lacking specificity are illegal. 1 Del. The court deemed the testimony admissible and relevant. See also Dutton v. State, 452 A.2d 127, 133 (Del. 1982). Legal scholars acknowledge hair analysis's value despite limitations. Defendants have criticized investigations neglecting hair evidence. Brady matter refers to evidence favorable to the defendant regarding guilt or punishment. Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83, 87-88 (1963).

OPINION McNEILLY, Judge. This case, filed on November 5, 1971, involves E. I. duPont deNemours & Company and Liberty Mutual Insurance Company (collectively 'duPont') seeking recovery of unpaid royalties from En-jay Chemical Company (now Exxon) and Johnson & Johnson. The dispute centers on royalty payments under licensing agreements allowing defendants to use duPont’s proprietary processes. While the contract terms are uncontested, the core issue is whether payments made via checks from 1962 to 1969—later embezzled by a duPont employee—fulfilled defendants’ obligations.

The records show that over nine years, royalty checks totaling $135,000 were fraudulently endorsed and deposited into the personal account of C. H. D., a duPont accountant. Responsible for processing incoming checks, C. H. D. intercepted quarterly payments, altered checks, and concealed transmittal letters to hide his theft. His role granted him access to these checks, which he exploited by forging endorsements and diverting funds to his Bank of Delaware account, systematically covering his tracks to avoid detection.

The next follow-up letter should specify that the time frame mentioned in the subsequent letter includes the period related to the misused check. By falsifying regular letters to show a six-month duration instead of three months, he managed to avoid being caught. An examination of duPont's royalty payment records would show a letter covering six months and a correctly credited check, with no visible inconsistencies. Around September 13, 1971, a standard audit of duPont checks during bank reconciliation uncovered a suspicious endorsement, leading to the discovery of C. H. D.'s involvement in preparing the voucher and endorsing the check. Further probes revealed more fraudulent checks and discrepancies totaling nearly $135,000.

The checks issued by Johnson & Johnson from their Chase Manhattan Bank account to duPont were as follows: Dates and amounts: March 1962 - $1,872.50; June 1962 - $1,998.15; September 1962 - $1,129.45; December 1962 - $1,462.30; March 1963 - $1,030.05; June 1963 - $1,016.40; September 1963 - $140.35; December 1963 - $1,925.00; March 1964 - $1,575.00; June 1964 - $1,065.75; September 1964 - $700.00; December 1964 - $350.00; March 1965 - $2,625.00, summing to $16,889.95.

Checks drawn by Enjay from their Citibank account payable to duPont included: July 20, 1965 - $5,521.41; October 29, 1965 - $9,029.34; August 2, 1966 - $17,576.08; May 5, 1967 - $26,935.67; May 3, 1968 - $27,617.88; November 6, 1968 - $15,379.80; February 4, 1969 - $12,043.75; August 8, 1969 - $1,549.26; July 31, 1969 - $554.75; October 30, 1969 - $596.40, totaling $116,804.34.

Upon receiving these checks, C. H. D. altered them by adding 'Account of C. H. D.' under the payee's name before endorsing them for deposit into his personal Bank of Delaware account. For nine years, royalty checks were sent to duPont’s Elastomer Chemicals Department under C. H. D.'s directive. Enjay sought summary judgment, while Johnson & Johnson moved to dismiss, citing full payment to duPont and the statute of limitations under 10 Del.C. § 8106 as defenses.

They withdrew from opposing this motion as they had agreed to a similar motion filed by other defendants, arguing that the complaint against Johnson and Johnson is so baseless it warrants dismissal and an award of attorney fees to the defendant. duPont asserts: (1) Legally, no 'Payment' has been made to duPont; (2) This case falls outside the scope of 10 Del.C. § 8106, as it stems from a sealed contract exempt from the Statute of Limitations; (3) There is absolutely no grounds for claiming estoppel. The record lacks any proof that employee C. H. D. had explicit authority to receive and endorse checks sent to his office in the normal course of business. Conversely, substantial evidence suggests he had both implied and apparent authority to handle checks from defendants for the Company. Over nine years of dealings, C. H. D. routinely received and endorsed defendants' checks, sometimes depositing them into his personal account and other times into duPont's. At no point did duPont question or revoke his authority.

C. H. D.'s authority to receive and endorse checks properly deposited into duPont's account was never contested by duPont, nor did duPont instruct defendants to avoid dealing directly with him. In standard business practice, an Agent may have three forms of authority: express (given orally or in writing), implied (inferred from the principal's conduct), or apparent (where the principal's actions suggest the Agent has authority, preventing denial). Implied authority is genuine authority demonstrated through the principal's behavior, which could lead a jury to conclude the Agent had actual authority. This can be proven by the principal's silent approval of the Agent's actions over time. Floyd R. Mechem's 'Outlines of the Law of Agency,' 4th Ed., page 29, supports this. Similarly, apparent authority arises when the principal's actions lead a reasonable person to believe the Agent has certain powers, as noted in Agency 2A C.J.S. § 157 and 3 Am.Jur.2nd, pages 470–481.

duPont acknowledges that C. H. D. frequently received and endorsed checks from defendants, sometimes diverting them to his personal account and other times to duPont's. This practice continued for nine years without duPont ever challenging his authority to handle checks rightfully deposited into its account. duPont also never directed defendants to interact with anyone else at the Company. By failing to disavow C. H. D.'s authority for properly handled checks, duPont cannot now reject the same authority when checks were misdirected. The California Supreme Court in Navrides v. Zurich Insurance Co., 5 Cal.3d 698, ruled that a principal cannot selectively ratify an Agent's actions—approving beneficial acts while rejecting harmful ones. Ratifying part of a transaction implies ratification of the whole. Likewise, in Crumlish v. Price, the Delaware Supreme Court denied a seller-principal's claim to recover the purchase price, reinforcing this principle.

The Court in Navrides v. Zurich Insurance Company emphasized that a principal cannot ratify an Agent's beneficial actions while disclaiming the detrimental ones, as partial ratification implies full acceptance. This aligns with the ruling in Crumlish v. Price, where the Delaware Supreme Court barred a seller-principal from reclaiming the purchase price, underscoring the fairness of holding principals accountable for their Agents' authorized conduct. These precedents highlight the legal expectation that principals must consistently acknowledge or reject their Agents' actions, preventing selective enforcement based on outcomes.

The buyer when he submitted his payment via check to the seller's legal representative. 'A principal is liable for an agent's apparent authority if the principal allows the agent to act with such authority or represents the agent as having it'. Id., 183-184. The Supreme Court acknowledged a decision between two innocent parties was necessary, but concluded the principal should bear the loss: 'Such situations are regrettable, but when one of two innocent parties must suffer, the loss should fall on the one whose actions led to the issue. Here, Errigo, as the plaintiff's agent, had apparent authority to accept payment. The defendant acted reasonably in paying, so the plaintiff must bear the loss.' Id., 184. Other jurisdictions' laws support the defendants' claim that C. H. D. had authority and that payment to duPont was valid. A key consideration was how long the agent had performed similar tasks for the employer. In Federal Land Bank of Omaha v. Union Bank & Trust Co. of Ottumwa, 228 Iowa 205, 290

N.W. 512 (1940), the plaintiff's attorney received checks payable to the plaintiff banks over four years, endorsing and depositing them into his personal account. The Court ruled the plaintiff could not deny the attorney's authority to accept the checks. While the Ottumwa case spanned four years, here C. H. D. acted for duPont for nine years. Likewise, in A. G. Spalding & Brothers v. Contra Costa County, 12 Cal.App.2d 262, 55 P.2d 520 (1936), it was determined that since the agent had acted for the plaintiff over several years, the plaintiff was presumed to know the agent received and endorsed checks in his own name. Here, C. H. D. routinely received checks from multiple companies, including the defendants, endorsing them sometimes to his personal account and sometimes to his employer's. Because C. H. D. occasionally endorsed checks to duPont's account, duPont cannot deny his authority to endorse checks made out to it.

An essential factor in assessing apparent authority is whether the debtor, when sending payments to the creditor's agent, had any reason to suspect misconduct. New Jersey, citing other jurisdictions, affirms the principle 'that when a debtor pays a duly authorized agent without notice or reason to suspect wrongdoing, the debt is discharged once the agent receives the funds'. Gross v. Grimaldi, 64 N.J.Super. 457, 166 A.2d 592 at 596 (1960). Similar rulings include May v. Ackerman, 235 Minn. 273, 51 N.W.2d 87, 91 (1951); Haynes Petroleum Corp. v. Turlington, 261 N.C. 475, 135 S.E.2d 43 (1964); and Strickland Transportation Co. v. First State Bank of Memphis

, 147 Tex. 193, 214 S.W.2d 934 (1948). The record shows nothing in the nine-year dealings between duPont's employee and the defendants suggested misconduct. It is clear the employer-creditor is accountable for its employee's actions. It is also evident the employer-creditor is better positioned to implement safeguards against check mishandling than the debtor sending the checks. In this case, years passed before duPont discovered the fraud. Now duPont argues the debtor defendants should have reviewed their canceled checks from the bank for fraudulent endorsements. However, large companies like the defendants receive thousands of returned checks monthly, making it impractical and costly to inspect each endorsement. Determining whether an endorser had authority for a specific check would be even more challenging. If

The burden was duPont's, not the defendants', as established in Crumlish v. Price. The defendants fulfilled their royalty obligations to duPont by sending timely checks to C. H. D., duPont's authorized agent, which were duly processed. The fraudulent conversion of these funds by duPont's employee, C. H. D., does not necessitate the defendants paying twice. References include Restatement (2d) of Agency, § 178, Mechem on Agency (2d ed.) § 953, p. 687, and cases such as Navrides v. Zurich Ins. Co. and Haynes Petroleum Corp. v. Turlington.

Additional cases supporting this principle include Strickland Transp. Co. v. First State Bank of Memphis, Zidek v. West Penn Power Company, and Mills v. Hurley Hardware & Furniture Co. Further precedents like McFadden v. Follrath, Sage v. Burton, and annotations in 49 A.L.R. 843 (1973) reinforce the rule outlined in § 178 of the Restatement (2d) of Agency.

Section 178 of the Restatement (2d) of Agency states that if an agent authorized to receive checks forges the principal's endorsement, the maker is absolved of liability if the bank honors the check. Mechem's treatise clarifies that wrongful endorsement by the agent does not negate the check's validity as payment. Comment C to § 178 places the loss risk on the payee (duPont), even if the bank cannot recover the funds, subrogating the creditor to the debtor's rights against the bank.

In Haynes Petroleum Corp. v. Turlington, the debtor's checks were converted by the creditor's agent, yet the court ruled no second payment was due. Similarly, in Strickland Transportation Co. v. First State Bank of Memphis, the Texas Supreme Court dismissed Strickland's claim, stating the drawer (White Auto) had no recoverable rights against the bank to assign.

The land had been compensated, White incurred no loss, and thus Strickland had no valid claim: 'The predicament faced by the petitioner stems not from any action or negligence by White Auto Store but solely from the dishonesty of the petitioner’s own agent. In such a scenario, it would be unjust to require White Auto Store to repay its debt, whether based on recourse against the bank or the petitioner’s potential lack of remedy against the bank. White Auto Store should not endure the hassle and cost of legal proceedings due to the petitioner’s agent’s breach of trust; these consequences rightly fall on the petitioner. We conclude that White Auto Store’s obligation was fulfilled upon delivering the checks to Akard and their subsequent payment by the bank, leaving no grounds for White Auto Store to pursue a claim against the bank or assign one to the petitioner.' (214 S.W.2d at 939) Similarly, McCook v. First State Bank, 367 S.W.2d 66 (Tex.Civ.App.1963). The rationale here is that paying a check handed to an authorized agent is as valid as paying

cash directly to the principal. In both scenarios, the principal is considered paid, even if the agent later misappropriates the funds. As noted in Burstein v. Sullivan, 134 App.Div. 623, 119 N.Y.S. 317 (1909): 'Paying Melle (the agent) in cash would have constituted payment to the plaintiffs, even if he had stolen the money. The defendant should not face double payment or legal disputes with the bank simply for safeguarding the plaintiffs by issuing a check in their name. While a check or note alone doesn’t settle a debt, delivering a check to the creditor or their authorized agent—with sufficient funds to cover it—should be treated as payment, just like cash, even if the agent forges an endorsement and steals the funds.' (119 N.Y.S

. at 319) Ruling that the defendants hadn’t made payment would unfairly compel them to pay twice and place the loss on a party without control over the wrongdoer. C. H. D. was duPont’s employee, not the defendants’, and no action by the defendants could have guaranteed his honesty. Burstein v. Sullivan, supra; Strickland Transportation Co. v. First State Bank of Memphis, supra. In McFadden v. Follrath, supra, the loss was assigned to the party directly accountable for and overseeing the dishonest agent. The Uniform Commercial Code’s drafters argue that losses from employee fraud should be a business expense, particularly in cases like 'padded payrolls.' When an employee adds a fictitious payee (as C. H. D. did with the 'Burton Rubber Company' checks drawn by duPont), the drafters assert the business, not the bank, should absorb the loss: 'The guiding principle is that the loss should

fall on the employer as a business risk rather than on subsequent parties. The employer is better positioned to prevent such fraud through careful hiring and supervision or to mitigate losses via fidelity insurance. This cost is a rightful business expense, not one for others to bear.' Official comment 4 to § 3—405. This logic extends to third-party checks payable to duPont but diverted by C. H. D. duPont should have exercised diligence in hiring and oversight. The defendants shouldn’t be liable for the misconduct of duPont’s employee, whom they couldn’t control, especially over nine years. By properly delivering royalty checks to duPont’s authorized agent, C. H. D., and having those checks honored by the defendants’ banks, the defendants fulfilled their obligation to duPont under the royalty agreements and shouldn’t be forced to pay again. This conclusion resolves the plaintiff’s case.

OPINION COOCH, J. INTRODUCTION This case arises from a July 6, 2000 car accident in Delaware involving a rental car owned by Budget Rent A Car and rented to Stacie Frazier, which struck pedestrian George E. Green. Green's complaint seeks a declaration that Delaware law governs his PIP claim against Budget, entitles him to PIP benefits under Budget’s self-insured policy per 21 Del. C. § 2118, and allows stacking of PIP benefits. Budget has filed a motion for summary judgment in response.

Budget argues that its rental car was registered in Pennsylvania, not Delaware, and thus falls under Pennsylvania insurance law, not Delaware’s. It also claims Green is ineligible for additional PIP benefits from Budget, as he has already received them from his personal State Farm policy. Budget maintains there are no disputed material facts. Green counters that material facts are in dispute, making summary judgment premature. He asserts Budget, as a Delaware corporation operating rental agencies in Delaware, must comply with 21 Del. C. § 2118. Green further argues the statute applies to Budget’s rental car, allowing him to claim PIP benefits and stack them under Delaware law. The Court now rules that 21 Del. C. § 2118 does not apply

to out-of-state registered rental cars that meet their home state’s minimum insurance requirements, even if occasionally used in Delaware as part of a larger fleet. For these reasons, Budget’s motion for summary judgment is GRANTED. FACTS On July 6, 2000, Green was struck by a Budget rental car driven by Tomorrow M. Monroe, a Delaware resident, while crossing Philadelphia Pike near Claymont. The car, rented by Stacie Frazier from Budget’s Wilmington agency, was registered in Pennsylvania and self-insured under a Pennsylvania certificate. Green filed a PIP claim with State Farm, which paid the $50,000 policy limit. When Budget refused to cover the remaining medical expenses, Green filed a complaint

seeking a declaration that Delaware law applies to his PIP claim, entitling him to benefits under Budget’s self-insured policy per 21 Del. C. § 2118, and permitting PIP stacking. Under Pennsylvania law, Green would be barred from further PIP recovery, as 75 Pa.C.S.A § 1713 prohibits stacking. STANDARD OF REVIEW Summary judgment is appropriate only if no genuine material facts are disputed and the movant is entitled to judgment as law. The Court must view facts favorably to the non-movant, whose evidence must suffice to defeat a directed verdict motion and support a jury verdict. All reasonable inferences favor the non-movant. Budget's argument is that its rental car was registered and self-insured under Pennsylvania's motor vehicle laws, meaning it was not obligated to provide PIP benefits as per Delaware's PIP statute. They assert that § 2118(a) only applies to vehicles mandated for Delaware registration, excluding out-of-state registered vehicles like theirs, and thus Delaware PIP coverage should not apply.

The court must decide whether § 2118 applies to out-of-state-registered rental cars occasionally used in Delaware. This novel issue involves a Pennsylvania-registered, self-insured rental car. While § 2118(a) specifically addresses vehicles 'required to be registered' in Delaware, Green acknowledges it does not explicitly cover this unique scenario. Delaware's PIP benefits are governed by § 2118, and both its language and case law suggest it only applies to Delaware-registered vehicles.

In Nationwide Insurance Co. v. Battaglia, the Delaware Supreme Court ruled that § 2118's PIP benefits hinge on the vehicle being 'required to be registered in this State.' In Swezey v. The Home Indemnity Company, a Delaware resident was injured in Delaware while riding in a Pennsylvania-registered car. Self-insurance requires proof of reliable financial arrangements to cover benefits and judgments, ensuring compliance with Pennsylvania’s motor vehicle code.

C. § 2904(b) holds self-insured vehicle owners to the same standards as insurers).Ridgely, Chancellor, and ex officio Judge of the Orphans' Court.— The marriage agreement stipulated that the petitioner would receive one-third of her husband Joseph Farrow's personal estate upon his death, 'in lieu and full satisfaction of her third or portion of his real or personal estate.' At the time of marriage, Joseph Farrow was heavily indebted, exceeding his personal estate's value. He died around December 12, 182

1. On January 1st and 2nd, 1822, his entire personal estate was sold by the sheriff under an execution issued on September 8, 1818, the marriage day, leaving none for the contract's fulfillment. The wife was 21 at marriage. Respondents argued two points: I. The Act of Assembly did not grant this Court jurisdiction in all dower cases; complex legal issues might arise, better settled by the High Court of Errors and Appeals. They suggested the fraud allegation should go to a jury. II. They claimed a wife could, pre-marriage, agree to forfeit dower rights, regardless of the agreement's uncertainty. First, this Court's jurisdiction is unquestionable under the Act concerning land devises and joint estates.

The law (5 Del. Laws, 174) states that a widow entitled to dower may have it assigned by the Orphans' Court in the county where the property is located. This is done through a petition, following procedures similar to those for intestate estates. Costs are to be paid by relevant parties based on their land interests. The Legislature's intent is clear: this Court can assign dower in all cases unless Chancery Court intervention is needed, mirroring practices for intestate estates.

The law applies uniformly, whether the widow's right stems from intestacy or other circumstances. It aims to streamline dower assignments, reduce costs, and fairly distribute expenses among involved parties. However, the Act doesn’t restrict the widow from seeking other courts with prior jurisdiction. In complex cases, such as missing title deeds or legal obstacles, Chancery Court may step in to ensure her dower rights, provided the facts are not disputed.

Dower is a significant claim, and the widow’s primary remedy lies in legal proceedings. While some argue fraud allegations should go to a jury, this Court is equally capable of evaluating facts and witness credibility. Sending the case to a jury would not bind this Court, especially on appeal. The Assembly’s Act and intestate laws do not support such a step, and no precedent exists for it. The widow’s claim is time-sensitive, and delays should be avoided.

The respondents’ plea cites a pre-marriage agreement as a bar to dower. At common law, jointure didn’t preclude dower, as collateral satisfaction couldn’t override inheritance rights. However, Statute 27 H. 8 altered this. The petitioner’s claim, limited to her lifetime, shouldn’t face unnecessary delays, especially given the Act’s alignment with intestacy procedures. The core issue revolves around the respondents’ defense, which challenges traditional dower rights.

A jointure established under the Statute serves as a legal bar. While collateral satisfaction cannot be pleaded in law, it may still act as a valid bar in equity. Cases like Lawrence vs. Lawrence (2 Vern. 365) and others illustrate how equitable bars often stem from legal obstacles or challenges in pursuing claims at law. The question here is whether this Court should accept such an equitable plea, assuming it holds weight in equity.

The nature of this Court and its procedures determine the answer. The Constitution and related laws describe its jurisdiction as purely equitable, with proceedings like petitions and summonses typical of equity courts. While some functions, like partitioning intestate estates, resemble common law, they remain exceptions. This Court’s authority is fundamentally equitable, allowing pleas from either legal or equitable bars.

This Court operates as a equity court within its jurisdiction, permitting any bar—legal or equitable—to be pleaded. The Act mandates that dower assignments require proof of the widow’s entitlement. If no legal right or an equitable bar exists, the Court cannot proceed. The issue then hinges on the widow’s claim, particularly the enforceability of the marriage contract.

The marriage contract, if valid, would bind the petitioner. Precedents like Lawrence vs. Lawrence (2 Vern. 365) show equitable bars to dower, though reversals sometimes occur on technical grounds. Cases such as Davila vs. Davila (2 Vern. 724) and Glover vs. Bates (1 Atk. 439) further confirm that marriage agreements can bar claims under statutes, provided they clearly intend to replace such rights.

Notwithstanding any city regulations, laws, or customs, in the case of Caruthers vs. Caruthers, 4 Bro. Ch. Rep 500, it was ruled that a female infant could not be held to a marriage settlement due to the uncertain provisions for the wife. The Master of the Rolls noted that an adult woman could have accepted provisions from the personal estate or taken a chance in lieu of dower, provided she acted knowingly, but an infant cannot be bound by such uncertain terms. As summarized in 1 Madd. Ch. Pr. 355, any agreement by an adult before marriage, even if inadequate or precarious, to accept provisions in place of dower constitutes valid equitable jointure. This holds if she is fully informed, acts with open eyes, and has equal knowledge of the facts as her husband.

If she is fully aware of all circumstances and enters the contract without deception, she should be bound by it. However, any concealment or omission of material facts constitutes fraud and invalidates the contract. This principle applies universally, as seen in cases like Jervois vs. Duke, 1 Vernon 19, and Broderick vs. Broderick, 1 P. Wms. 239. Even in dower cases, fraudulent assignment by the sheriff warrants equity court intervention, as in Hoby vs. Hoby, 1 Vern. 218. In Harvey vs. Ashley, 3 Atk. 607, Lord Hardwicke found the husband guilty of fraud for hiding judgments and debts from his infant wife, justifying partial relief by using the husband’s unsettled estate to clear undisclosed encumbrances.

The petitioner’s reference to 2 Com. Dig. 469 illustrates that when a widow’s agreed annuity in lieu of dower fell short, the deficiency was covered by the real estate. This demonstrates that if the expected compensation fails, alternative satisfaction is due. This does not contradict the earlier principle that an adult woman may accept any precarious provision knowingly in lieu of dower, as an unreasonable contract stands if entered into freely and without deception. The current contract, however, is unenforceable in Chancery due to the husband’s concealment of debts binding his real and personal estate.

On September 8, 1818, the marriage contract date, two writs of execution were issued against the husband’s assets, which were later sold insufficiently to cover his debts. Evidence shows no proof that Mrs. Farrow knew of these debts, as no witnesses confirmed her awareness. The contract’s validity hinges on full disclosure of his financial plight, which he withheld despite knowing she would likely receive nothing in lieu of dower. Justice demands such disclosure, and an order for dower assignment must therefore be considered.

In January 2000, Michael P. Jackson pleaded guilty to cocaine trafficking. His sentencing was postponed under DeLCode Ann. tit. 11, § 6705 and 6712, allowing him to join a boot camp program. After finishing the initial six-month military-style training, Jackson breached probation, marking him as a program failure. Despite this, the Superior Court granted him another chance, permitting him to restart the boot camp instead of imposing the mandatory Level V sentence. However, Jackson violated boot camp order number five during retraining, leading to his removal and referral to the Superior Court for final sentencing.

Jackson was subsequently ordered to serve the remaining three-year mandatory Level V sentence for cocaine trafficking, with the Superior Court's decision upheld. Records show that during his retraining, Jackson made a remark about wanting to escape while working at the boot camp farm. Another cadet had recently escaped, and the instructor interpreted Jackson's comment as a threat, violating boot camp order five, which mandates speaking and acting with good purpose. A counselor's letter to the Superior Court cited Jackson's statement as a security risk, resulting in his dismissal and a hearing.

On July 3, 2002, Jackson faced trial for violating boot camp rules. He claimed his escape remark was a joke, but the instructor described his demeanor as sullen and took the comment seriously. The Superior Court likened the statement to a bomb threat, ruling it a breach of boot camp rules. Jackson received a five-year Level V sentence, suspended after the mandatory three years. On appeal, Jackson argued no specific rule barred his statement, but precedent requires probation violations to involve clear conditions.

Section 6707 mandates that boot camp participants agree to a written contract outlining program rules and consequences. Delaware's boot camp has ten general orders, including order five, requiring cadets to 'speak and act with good purpose.' Jackson admitted knowing the rules and acknowledged his escape remark, even in jest, violated this order. He testified that the comment was irresponsible, undermining his appeal argument. The court found his own testimony contradicted his claim, affirming the violation.

The record thus confirms the Superior Court's finding that Jackson's mention of escaping breached boot camp general order five. Jackson further contends on appeal that this order infringes upon his First Amendment rights under the U.S. Constitution. The U.S. Supreme Court has noted that probationers do not possess the full liberty granted to ordinary citizens. Restrictions on probation, including limits on speech and association, are permissible if they serve rehabilitation and public safety. Such conditions are valid if they reasonably align with probation objectives. Here, the boot camp's initial phase is not probation but intensive incarceration, making such restrictions even more justified. The Superior Court rightly compared Jackson's escape remark to a bomb threat, as prohibiting such speech in a boot camp setting supports rehabilitation and public protection. Therefore, Jackson's First Amendment claim fails.

The court rules that Jackson's 'escape' remark violated boot camp general order five, which mandates speaking and acting with good purpose. The relevant statute requires sentencing on deferred charges if an offender violates boot camp terms. Thus, the Superior Court correctly sentenced Jackson for his original charges. The judgment is affirmed, and the time for reargument is shortened to three days per Supreme Court Rule 18.

The ten general orders include: following staff orders, avoiding violence, abstaining from drugs/alcohol, truthful communication, speaking with good intent, active participation in Network, adhering to group contracts, maintaining positivity, upholding military demeanor, and engaging in ASAT, Education, and Recreation sessions.

See also cases like United States v. Ritter and United States v. Turner, which uphold probation conditions that reasonably relate to sentencing goals. Similarly, Commonwealth v. Lapointe affirms enforceable probation terms even if they limit constitutional rights, provided they align with rehabilitation and public safety. During the hearing, the chancellor dismissed the complainant's bill with costs, prompting an appeal. The case was argued in writing by Mr. J. A. Bayard for the appellant and Mr. Rogers for the respondents. The complainants sought reversal of the decree and two forms of equitable relief: First, that Samuel Carlisle’s will, though invalid as a will, should be upheld as an agreement with David Carlisle, supported by valuable consideration and performance. Second, if the agreement was deemed too vague, David Carlisle deserved compensation for his services and sacrifices under the agreement. The first argument framed the case as one for specific performance, requiring proof of the agreement’s terms, consideration, and the complainant’s performance or readiness to perform. While no written agreement existed, the complainant had fully performed his obligations. It was argued that Samuel Carlisle agreed to leave the farm to David in exchange for his assistance during Samuel’s lifetime, a valid agreement despite their familial relationship.

The absence of a written agreement is offset by the complainant’s full performance. Samuel Carlisle’s agreement with David, supported by consideration (David’s labor and care), was enforceable, even if it involved a will. Equity courts can compel heirs to honor such agreements, as heirs inherit subject to the ancestor’s valid obligations. The case of Goilmere v. Battison, 1 Vernon 48, supports this, even with weaker evidence or consideration than the present case. Heirs, as volunteers, are bound by the ancestor’s agreements, just as debts bind inherited property. The cited case enforced an agreement against a husband, who holds stronger rights than heirs. Specific performance hinges on the receipt of consideration, binding all successors who claim as volunteers. These principles apply here: Samuel Carlisle’s promise to will the farm to David is undisputed, as is his capacity to make it. The adequacy of consideration and partial performance to substitute for a written agreement remain key questions.

How do these equitable principles apply here? Samuel Carlisle’s promise to will the farm to his son is clear, as is his legal capacity to make it. Is the consideration sufficient, and has partial performance compensated for the lack of a written agreement? The latter hinges on David’s fulfillment of his duties under the agreement. Equity intervenes when one party, having received consideration, must fulfill their promise, binding all voluntary successors. The case of Goilmere v. Battison illustrates this, even with less compelling facts. Heirs, taking property voluntarily, inherit subject to the ancestor’s valid agreements. The same applies to Samuel Carlisle’s promise, regardless of whether the will was unmade due to intent, neglect, or accident. The core issue is whether David’s performance justifies enforcing the agreement against Samuel’s heirs.

It is generally accepted that David Carlisle stayed with his father and helped him farm until his father's death; he was the most capable worker on the farm until 1820, after which he took full responsibility for it. He dedicated his and his wife's efforts to farming, supporting his father's household, and settling his father's debts. This demonstrates the complainant's full compliance with the agreement. Is the consideration not adequate? In our society, both legally and practically, a hardworking individual's time and effort are valued beyond mere subsistence for himself and his family. Regardless, the agreement deemed these services worthy of the land upon the father's death. A relevant precedent supports both the adequacy of consideration and the right to equitable relief: Scotis Ex'r. vs. Osborne's Ex'rs. 2 Munf. 413. 'A father-in-law promised his son-in-law assistance in purchasing land by providing funds from a specific bond once collected, and the son-in-law acted accordingly, establishing a legally binding agreement based on sufficient consideration.

The objection in the lower court that the complainant's remedy should be at law lacks merit. While legal action is possible in cases of specific performance, it often falls short. Equitable relief is justified when compelling heirs to convey land based on a valid agreement with their ancestor. Damages are insufficient when the contract can be specifically enforced, especially after full performance by the complainant. This objection is untimely; it should have been raised earlier. The case of Underhill vs. Van Courtlandt, 2 Johns. Ch. Rep. 369, established that once a defendant answers instead of demurring, jurisdictional objections based on legal remedies are too late.

Regarding specific performance, the absence of a direct plea for conveyance by Samuel Carlisle's heirs is inconsequential. A general relief prayer allows the court to grant appropriate remedies based on the case's circumstances, as seen in Johns. Rep. 529 Bebee vs. Bank of New York. If the agreement's existence is disputed, the court may refer the matter to a legal trial. Secondly, equitable relief can be sought independently of an explicit agreement when one party's actions or omissions cause another to suffer a loss they wouldn't have otherwise incurred. Equity prevents benefiting from such misconduct, even if no legal damages apply.

This principle is inherent in equity and supported by numerous cases, including 2 Vern. 506, Oldham vs. Litchfield, and others. The defendants argued that no formal agreement between Samuel and David Carlisle was proven, only vague promises or intentions. However, equity recognizes obligations arising from conduct and fairness, not just explicit contracts. Thus, the complainant is entitled to an account as requested in the bill, based on the broader principles of equity and justice.

The individual intended to leave the farm to David, but such promises were made voluntarily and lacked consideration; David's stay on the farm was for his own benefit, as he enjoyed the profits from a valuable property in exchange for his and his wife's labor, which left him indebted to his father's estate. He remained there for personal gain, trusting his father's voluntary intentions regarding the will. The request for specific performance of the alleged agreement was opposed, as it was not mentioned in the initial complaint or brought before the chancellor during the hearing. Had it been included, the defense strategy would have differed significantly, possibly involving objections based on jurisdiction or the statute of frauds.

The defendants could have demurred or pleaded the statute of frauds if the bill had sought specific performance, as the alleged agreement was merely verbal and unenforceable under the statute. No written evidence or clear terms supported the claim, and no precedent exists for enforcing such parol agreements without written documentation. The defendants were disadvantaged by the late introduction of this claim, as they lost the opportunity to challenge it on grounds of lack of consideration or statutory noncompliance. The agreement's vague terms and lack of mutual obligation further weakened the case for specific performance.

Specific performance cannot be granted unless the complainant's situation would be fraudulent without enforcement, and the agreement's terms must be clear and definite. Here, the alleged promise was too uncertain—David's obligations, the nature of his services, and the farm's financial details were unspecified. The father's will was voluntary, and equity does not enforce such agreements without fraud or clear obligation. Even under a general relief plea, specific performance was unjustified, especially given the father's power to revoke his decisions, as established by legal precedents.

The second relief request argued that equity should prevent someone from benefiting from their own misconduct, even if no legal damages apply. However, cited cases involved personal property or clear fraud, whereas here, no fraud was alleged or proven. Samuel Carlisle's promise, if it existed, was a matter of honor, not legal obligation. While equity principles can be nuanced, enforcing such a vague and voluntary agreement would overstep judicial boundaries, especially without evidence of deceit or binding terms.

confused by the intricate issues surrounding the evaluation of a purely moral commitment. Even if the promise could form the basis of a legal duty, there was no consideration to validate it. David's contributions, in nature and scope, were voluntary and could be discontinued at any time; they were more than offset by the sustenance he and his family received from the farm. If they were not, and he still has a claim against his father's estate for services provided, this is not a matter for equity but a legal remedy, which fully addresses this aspect of the case, whether raised by demurrer or at trial, as equity cannot intervene in purely legal matters. Only equitable claims warrant equitable relief.

argued in rebuttal that specific performance need not be explicitly requested in the pleading, citing precedents like Bebee vs. Bank of New-York and Hollis vs. Carr. Equity courts disdain technicalities; the rule is that if the evidence supports relief beyond what is requested, it may be granted under a general plea. The validity of a will is not solely a legal issue; while its existence is a legal question, its interpretation or effect can be addressed in any court where it arises. We concede the will is invalid but assert that Samuel Carlisle's agreement to create a valid will, whether breached by accident, neglect, or intent, binds his heirs, compelling them to convey the land. Defendants could have demurred if they chose; objecting to the prayer for lack of equity is unheard of in equity practice. If the bill shows any equitable grounds, a demurrer fails; relief is determined at trial.

irrelevant whether the defendants lose the statute of frauds defense due to the bill's general prayer, as the burden lies with the complainant to prove an agreement either outside the statute or exempted by part performance or fraud. Here, the exemption is argued first through David Carlisle's labor, which constituted the promise's consideration, and second, if not seen as an agreement, through the unjust retention of benefits from his labor under an unfulfilled promise to a child, warranting enforcement to prevent fraud. The cited case of a bare, unperformed agreement is inapplicable; here, David fully performed, and we accept the opposing principle that relief is due only if non-performance would fraudulently harm the complainant. On this basis, we seek specific performance.

contend the agreement bound both parties. David's continued involvement was ensured by his reliance on compensation for his services, and while will-making is typically voluntary, Samuel Carlisle's agreement to do so for valuable consideration made it binding and irrevocable. Contrary to the complainant's assertion, cited cases like Oldham vs. Litchfield and others involve real estate, not just personal property. The claim that legal relief suffices was previously addressed, and the high authority cited then remains unchallenged, implying the counsel's opinion outweighs even James Kent's. We are prepared to accept the outcome, confident in our position.

Based on a contractual agreement that allows us to demand specific performance, the remedy lies solely in equity. If it involves Samuel Carlisle's unfulfilled promise, leading to mutual claims as outlined, then there is adequate justification to seek an accounting in equity. In June 1835, Judge Robinson rendered the court's opinion. After summarizing the case (see ante pp. 421, etc.), he noted that the appellants' argument, crafted with considerable expertise, urged the court to overturn the chancellor's decree and grant one of two forms of equitable relief to David Carlisle, the sole appellant with an interest in the disputed farm, as others had transferred their stakes to him. The first relief sought involves enforcing an agreement, specifically treating Samuel Carlisle's will—though invalid as a will—as binding due to a prior agreement with David, supported by consideration and performance.

The second form of equitable relief mirrors the bill's request for an accounting. The primary issue is whether the alleged agreement, denied in the defendants' responses, has been substantiated. Mary Carlisle, Samuel's widow and David's witness, testified that upon David reaching adulthood, he expressed the farm's poor condition necessitating a lime quarry purchase for improvement. Samuel repeatedly assured David that if he stayed to enhance the farm and help settle debts, he would inherit it, though Samuel retained control during his lifetime. In response to another query, Mary stated Samuel lamented David's toil to clear debts, acknowledging David's efforts and his intent to leave him the farm as earned.

Sarah Wilson, another witness for the complainants, testified that when David came of age and considered leaving, Samuel repeatedly promised him the farm if he stayed and improved it. These testimonies form the crux of David Carlisle's evidence. Additional testimony reveals David turned 21 in October 1809, meaning he had worked for his father two years before the alleged agreement. Notably, the bill claims David agreed to stay, but witnesses neither confirm this nor any explicit commitment. David's sole condition for remaining was the acquisition of a lime quarry, as recounted by his mother, who cited his statement that the farm's poor state required this purchase.

Samuel's repeated assurances to David about inheriting the farm if he stayed and improved it undermine the likelihood of a binding mutual agreement. The lack of mutuality is evident: while Samuel made promises, David faced no obligation to remain or enhance the farm. He could depart anytime without breaching any contract. In Bromley vs. Jeffries, 2 Vern. 415, Sir Rowland Berkley covenanted that if the plaintiff outlived him and had children by his daughter, the plaintiff would acquire a manor at a reduced price compared to other buyers.

The court declined to enforce a specific execution for two reasons, one being that the agreement lacked mutuality, as the plaintiff was not obligated to accept it at any price. David Carlisle was not proven to be bound to stay and enhance the farm. Similarly, in Cook vs. Oxley, 3 Term Rep. 652, it was ruled that the agreement was nudum pactum due to its one-sided nature at inception. The document from December 30, 1830, intended to enforce the agreement, was questioned as to whether Samuel Carlisle was obligated to execute it or if it sufficed to bypass the assembly's requirement for written contracts concerning land sales.

Courts of equity enforce specific performance of oral agreements primarily due to fraud, such as one party reneging after the other has fulfilled their part. However, no fraud was attributed to Samuel Carlisle; instead, he believed the written instrument fulfilled his promise and was valid as a will. Relief based on fraud is sometimes denied if not raised in pleadings. This appeal seeks not just specific performance for fraud but to rectify a mistake in the will's execution, such as lacking required witnesses, as Samuel Carlisle assumed the document was legally sufficient to transfer property as intended.

Had the agreement been proven and the instrument aligned with its terms, equity could enforce its provisions. However, the agreement stipulated David would inherit the farm unconditionally as a purchaser, while Samuel Carlisle's intended will included voluntary gifts to family members, such as portions to his wife, daughter, and grandson, along with other provisions like a road, firewood, and annual payments. These discrepancies mean the will could not be deemed fulfillment of the agreement, and equity could not correct its execution due to mistake.

It was argued that David's actions—improving the farm, supporting his father, paying debts, and constructing buildings—constituted part performance of the alleged agreement. The chancellor in Ambler 586 noted that part performance requires clear proof of the agreement's terms and acts solely indicative of its fulfillment. Here, the acts might have had other purposes, undermining the claim of part performance.

We have previously mentioned that there is no proof David agreed to stay on the farm to enhance it or perform any tasks; however, even if the agreement had been proven, do David's actions necessarily indicate they were done as part performance? Handing over possession is seen as part performance, particularly if funds are spent on construction per the agreement, but the possession must be given as part performance. If it can be linked to a separate title, it won’t exempt the case from the statute. For instance, a tenant remaining in possession isn’t considered part performance, as tenants typically stay unless given notice to leave, and their continued presence alone has no legal impact. The bill’s claims about the agreement’s terms show no expectation for David to have sole possession before his father’s death, build expensive structures using farm profits, pay his father’s debts or taxes similarly, or provide financial support. Thus, these actions cannot be deemed part performance.

Similarly, David’s ongoing management and dedication to farming and improving the land since the alleged contract cannot be seen as part performance, as he merely maintained the same relationship with his father as he had for years prior, starting from adulthood. Mary Carlisle’s testimony reveals the old man’s goal was farm improvement to settle debts, referencing his statements when David turned 21 in 1809. Yet, the bill admits that by 1820, the farm remained largely unimproved, depleted from prolonged use without fertilization, with poor fences and much of it as common land—despite the lime quarry being bought earlier and David’s efforts from 1811 to 1820. This lack of progress occurred despite David having sufficient resources to improve the farm significantly.

Additionally, David’s marriage in 1814 and raising a family in his father’s household, owning livestock paid for by farm proceeds, and coming and going as he pleased—along with the key fact that his father sold part of the farm to Fleming, who built a home at his own expense without David’s objection—collectively justify the chancellor’s refusal to grant specific performance. As for compensating David for his and his wife’s services, the court notes that if entitled, he has adequate legal recourse, making further opinion on this matter unnecessary or inappropriate.

J. A. Bayard represented the appellants; Rogers, the appellees. The decree was upheld with costs, and the record was remanded. Justice Rice, delivering the Court’s opinion, addressed the defense’s argument against admitting an X-ray photo taken by Dr. Evans without his testimony.
