Dr. Phillips, a plaintiff’s witness, confirmed his presence during the X-ray, assisting in positioning the plaintiff and observing the plate’s development, and attested to its authenticity. X-rays of bone structures, when properly identified, are widely accepted in courts nationwide, leaving no doubt about their admissibility.

The admission of such photographs in this case is not in dispute; the objection pertains to allowing the photograph into evidence based on Doctor Phillips' testimony, despite him not being the one who took it. The trial court believed that Doctor Phillips' testimony sufficiently verified the photograph's accuracy, making its inclusion appropriate, and upon further review, the court maintains this stance. In Prescott & N. W. R. Co. v. Franks, 111 Ark. 83, 163 S. W. 180, Ann. Cas. 1916A, 773, the appellate court ruled that admitting an X-ray photograph of the plaintiff's injury, supported by a physician's testimony who was present during the process but not an X-ray expert, was not erroneous. Similarly, in State v. Matheson, 142 Iowa, 414, 120 N. W. 1036, 134 Am. St. Rep. 426, an X-ray photograph was admitted

based on a physician's testimony who, although not operating the machine, was present when the photograph was taken. The court noted: 'This physician would understand, just as well as the operator, that the radiograph resulted from the X-ray machine depicting the body's bony structure.' For these reasons, the court declines to overturn the jury's verdict and denies a new trial. BALICK, Judge. Summit Aviation, Inc. has moved to dismiss a certiorari action filed by Elcorta, Inc. and Sebastian R. Ciotti, challenging proceedings in a Justice of the Peace Court to enforce a garageman's lien under 25 Del.C., c. 39. The justice of the peace approved the sale of Elcorta's Mitsubishi aircraft, in which Ciotti held a security interest. The aircraft sold for $190,000, with Summit's $170,000 lien paid from the proceeds. Elcorta and Ciotti argue they lacked proper notice of the sale, the justice of the peace wrongly refused to recuse himself, and other procedural errors occurred during

the proceedings. Summit asserts that the plaintiffs failed to fulfill procedural requirements for the Superior Court's jurisdiction, claiming these prerequisites apply to certiorari as they do to appeals from Justice of the Peace Courts under 10 Del.C. § 9571. Summit contends that since certiorari is a type of appeal, the statute's jurisdictional requirements apply, citing Williams v. Singleton, Del.Supr., 160 A.2d 376 (1960). However, this premise is flawed. While certiorari is a common law appellate review mechanism, it differs fundamentally from an appeal. Certiorari examines the record, whereas an appeal is de novo. 1 Woolley on Delaware Practice § 900. Consequently, the procedures must differ, as seen in Landis Supply, etc. v. Joseph A. Capaldi, Inc., Del.Super. 415 A.2d 497 (1980). For instance, the certiorari statute requires

'sufficient surety to be approved by the Prothonotary,' while the appeal statute mandates 'security in such sum as the justice deems sufficient.' 10 Del.C. § 3918, 9571(b). Despite both remedies coexisting for years, no ruling has applied the appeal statute to certiorari. Neither statute nor court rule imposes a time limit for filing certiorari, unlike Superior Court Criminal Rule 37. Common law also lacks such a limitation, likely because the writ's discretionary nature meant timeliness influenced the court's decision. Woolley § 903. Delaware's constitution once set a five-year limit for writs of error, later reduced to six months before repeal. Art. VI, Del. Const. 1792 § 13, Art. VI, Del. Const. 1831 § 20, Art. IV, Del. Const. 1

Section 28, previously numbered as 897, was modified by 40 DeLLaws, c. 2 (1935), later renumbered to Section 25 under 48 DeLLaws, c. 109 (1951), and ultimately repealed by 51 DeLLaws, c. 78 (1957). The constitutional clause also covered certiorari, a type of writ of error, regardless of the issuing court. Wool-ley § 895. The repeal amendment specified it would take effect once the General Assembly passed a law addressing the constitutional provision's subject. The subsequent statute set a 60-day window for filing a praecipe in the Supreme Court, later shortened to 30 days. 10 Del.C. § 148, 51 DeLLaws, c. 346 (1958), 58 DeLLaws, c. 21 (1971). Since this statute only pertains to praecipe filings in the Supreme Court and not writs of error broadly,

the unintended outcome was the absence of any time limit for filing a praecipe for certiorari in the Superior Court. Without a specific statute or court rule, courts often analogize to appeal notice or writ of error filing deadlines. 14 Am Jur 2d, Certiorari, § 30 (1964). As noted by one court, '[tjhere seems no justification, barring unusual cases, for allowing more time to request certiorari than for filing an appeal or writ of error in standard cases.' Eigner v. Geake, N.M. Supr., 52 N.M. 98, 192 P.2d 310, 310-11 (1948). This aligns with Delaware's trend to reduce appellate review timelines. Thus, I believe the court should refer to appeal statutes by analogy. I also hold that the 30-day period for Supreme Court praecipe filings is the most fitting benchmark.

This aligns with the legislative background mentioned earlier and mirrors the 30-day certiorari filing window for county Board of Adjustment decisions. 9 Del.C. § 1353. Due to distinctions between certiorari and de novo review, the timelines for appeals de novo from Justice of the Peace Courts are unsuitable for comparison. The 15-day appeal allowance period from a justice of the peace doesn’t allow sufficient time for record transcription, which is necessary for the Prothonotary to process recognizance and issue certiorari. Woolley § 902. Similarly, the 20-day period under Rule 3(c) for praecipe and transcript filing is inappropriate, as it starts from appeal allowance rather than the lower court's judgment. Since the 30-day period is based on the Superior Court's common law authority over certiorari, it isn’t jurisdictional but subject to the court's discretion to waive delays when warranted.

Refer to Rule 6(b). Now, examining this case's timeline: Lower court judgment entered May 6, 1986; Praecipe filed May 20, 1986; Record transcript filed June 5, 1986; Security amount set June 10, 1986; Recognizance filed June 19, 1986; Writ issued July 3, 1986; Lower court record received July 17, 1986; Dismissal motion filed July 28, 1986; Certiorari exceptions filed August 12, 1986. Several procedural shortcomings arose. While the praecipe was filed within 30 days of the judgment, it lacked the record transcript. Instead, counsel notified the Prothonotary of pending transcript submission to determine recognizance amount. Although filed within 30 days, the transcript arrived later.

Initially, the recognizance was absent, and the writ was delayed 58 days post-judgment. Additionally, process wasn't initiated immediately per Rule 4(a), and certiorari exceptions missed the 10-day filing deadline under Rule 12(aal). Despite these procedural shortcomings, dismissal is unwarranted. Correspondence shows counsel's efforts to adhere to statutes, rules, or Woolley’s guidance, with some delays caused by the court itself. The Prothonotary’s role in setting recognizance was bypassed for a civil office judge, and the writ took 14 days post-filing. The praecipe’s 30-day deadline post-judgment remains critical, as seen in Chadwick v. Janaman.

742 (1975). Here, opposing counsel received the praecipe—a courteous but non-mandatory step that facilitates early dismissal motions. This act mirrors a notice of appeal under modern practice, per Supreme Court Rule 7 commentary. Yet, rules mandate immediate process issuance, contingent on timely transcript filing, security determination, and recognizance entry. Counsel must proactively ensure writ issuance to avoid dismissal risks, as in Russell v. Olmedo. Unexplained is the 9-day lag post-security setting.

Post-judge’s security determination, the 9-day recognizance delay is presumed due to securing corporate surety. Certiorari exceptions were late because counsel was absent when the record arrived; he filed them upon return. While delegating this task might have helped, his prompt action mitigates the delay’s severity. The security amount is now disputed: Ciotti’s appeal required $170,000 for the aircraft lien, which was unmet. Summit’s claim that statutory bond adequacy is jurisdictional under 10 Del. C. §§ 9571–9572 is rejected; a motion to adjust security, not dismissal, is the remedy.

10 Del.C. § 3918(c) and Woolley § 904 guide security adjustments. This opinion clarifies certiorari procedures, eliminating future delays like this case’s praecipe-to-writ gap. Access to Superior Court for reviewing Justice of the Peace rulings is vital, especially given their exclusive garagemen’s lien jurisdiction under 25 Del.C. § 3909. The bond requirement’s rigidity, as shown here, underscores procedural tensions in lien enforcement.

A jurisdictional requirement for a de novo appeal can be prohibitive. In such instances, certiorari serves as the sole viable method to review the legality of proceedings in Justice of the Peace Courts. Today, I have signed an order rejecting the motion to dismiss. Per Curiam. An assault occurs when there is a forceful attempt to harm another, provided the attempt is accompanied by the capability to inflict harm. Regarding the notice from Coxe's wife to Fleetwood barring entry into the house: a wife lacks the authority to prohibit entry when her husband is present. It is well-established that an officer cannot justify breaking an outer door to execute civil process, nor can a landlord to distrain; however, if a levy or distress has been made peacefully, it is equally clear that an outer door may be broken to access goods for sale. Breaking an outer door to sell goods is akin to breaking it to recapture someone who escaped after an arrest on a copias ad respondendum, which is permissible even on Sunday. (See Francomb v. Pinche, 1 Esp.N.P. 382). Verdict, guilty.

Court Below—Superior Court of Delaware, C.A. No. N13C-12-218 AFFIRMED. VEASEY, Chief Justice. This appeal examines whether the Superior Court erred in admitting evidence of a 1979 juvenile adjudication of defendant Charles H. Trowbridge, III ('Trowbridge') during his trial for a 1991 murder. We conclude that admitting such evidence was reversible error, as the juvenile adjudication was too distant in time to be relevant to the current charges. Thus, we REVERSE Trowbridge's convictions and REMAND for a new trial. I. FACTS. In the early hours of June 30, 1991, Trowbridge was heavily drinking near the Heartbreak Hotel in Bowers Beach. Trowbridge had grown up next to the hotel but had not lived there since its 1974 sale to Harry Warner (the 'Warner House').

In June 1991, the Warner House was occupied by Margaret Wyman, who ran the Heartbreak Hotel, and her son, Chad Wyman ('Chad'). Trowbridge resided three blocks away. Around 12:45 a.m. on June 30, 1991, Trowbridge had a drink at the hotel and lingered outside by a fence. He later entered the Warner House, mistakenly believing he still lived there. Harry Warner testified that Trowbridge had previously attempted to enter the house while drunk. Trowbridge's fingerprints were found on the door. Trowbridge claimed he fell inside, picked up a wet knife, saw a body, and fled. The knife, bearing his fingerprint, was found in his uncle William Jackson's vehicle. Margaret Wyman returned after 2:00 a.m. and saw Chad seemingly asleep on the floor.

Though some items were out of place, there was no sign of forced entry or a struggle. Margaret left Chad on the floor and went to bed. At 4:00 a.m., she woke and found Chad still there. Removing an afghan, she discovered he was dead. The autopsy revealed multiple stab wounds, scrapes, and bruises. During trial, Trowbridge's counsel argued the State lacked motive evidence. After Trowbridge's testimony, the State sought to introduce evidence of a 1979 juvenile act: Trowbridge setting fire to the Bowers Beach Fire Company. When questioned in 1979, Trowbridge said, 'I don't know.' The State contended this evidence was relevant.

The evidence was pertinent to demonstrate that Trowbridge had acted without motive in the past. The court allowed this evidence under Delaware Rule of Evidence ('D.R.E.') 404. The jury convicted Trowbridge of first-degree murder, first-degree burglary, and possessing a deadly weapon during a felony. He was sentenced to life without parole for the murder. Trowbridge appeals on three grounds: (1) improper admission of his 1979 juvenile adjudication under D.R.E. 404(b); (2) failure to grant a new trial due to alleged Brady violations; and (3) overruling his objection to a prosecutor's comment about witness testimony. We find the admission of the 1979 adjudication erroneous, necessitating reversal of his convictions. The other issues may become moot on remand.

We do not address the remaining issues in this appeal. II. ADMISSION OF TROWBRIDGE'S 1979 JUVENILE ADJUDICATION. The court admitted the 1979 adjudication under D.R.E. 404(b), applying the standards from Getz v. State, which outlines criteria for prior bad acts evidence: (1) materiality to a disputed issue; (2) a permissible purpose under D.R.E. 404(b); (3) clear and conclusive proof; (4) temporal proximity; (5) probative value outweighing prejudice; and (6) jury instructions on limited use. The trial judge deemed the 1979 conviction relevant to Trowbridge's lack of motive, not overly remote, and more probative than prejudicial.

The 1979 adjudication occurred 12 years before the current charges, raising concerns about relevance. This Court has noted that the required similarity between incidents decreases as time between them increases. A long gap can diminish probative value, potentially rendering evidence irrelevant. As stated in Allen v. State, acts from 12 years prior may lack relevance, with courts often referencing Rule 609(b)'s 10-year limit for impeachment evidence.

We conclude the Superior Court erred in finding the 1979 adjudication not too remote. As in Allen, an act from 12 years ago is less relevant than a recent one and may be irrelevant altogether. While no strict rule exists, courts often align with Rule 609(b)'s 10-year benchmark. See also Loper v. State, where similar temporal concerns were raised.

In 994 WL 10820 (Jan. 3, 1994) (ORDER), it was ruled that D.R.E. 609(b) was breached as more than 10 years had elapsed since the prior convictions, and the State neglected to request the trial court to assess whether the probative value of these convictions outweighed their prejudicial impact, nor did it provide adequate written notice of its intent to use such evidence. The 12-year gap has entirely nullified the relevance of Trowbridge's 1979 juvenile adjudication and his related statement to the current charges. Thus, the Superior Court's oversight in evaluating the impact of this lengthy delay on the adjudication's relevance is a reversible error, leading to the REVERSAL of Trowbridge's convictions and a REMAND for a new trial in line with this opinion. OPINION AND ORDER by LAMB, Vice Chancellor. I. These cases stem from a proposed merger ('Merger') between NCS Healthcare, Inc. and a Genesis Health Ventures, Inc. subsidiary, where each share of NCS

Class A and Class B Common Stock would convert into the right to receive 0.1 share of Genesis common stock. While Class A and Class B shares are largely similar, key differences include: (i) Class A shares grant one (1) vote per share, whereas Class B shares grant ten (10) votes, and (ii) Class B shares face transfer restrictions triggering automatic conversion to Class A shares upon non-permitted transfers. The Merger Agreement, approved by the NCS board of directors ('Board') on July 28, 2002, also led to the execution of two Voting Agreements with Genesis, NCS, and key executives Jon H. Outcalt and Kevin Shaw. These agreements required Outcalt and Shaw to vote their shares in favor of the Merger and granted Genesis officers an irrevocable proxy to vote their shares accordingly. At the time, Outcalt and Shaw collectively controlled over 65% of NCS's voting power through their Class B shares, ensuring Merger ratification.

Omnicare, Inc., the plaintiff in Civil Action No. 19800, had its merger proposal with NCS rejected by the Board. Omnicare subsequently acquired NCS shares, filed this lawsuit, and launched a cash tender offer for all outstanding NCS shares. Civil Action No. 19786 was initiated by NCS stockholders on behalf of a class. Currently, motions for partial summary judgment are pending, seeking a declaration that the Voting Agreements and irrevocable proxies triggered the automatic conversion of Outcalt and Shaw's Class B shares into Class A shares. If successful, these motions could jeopardize the Merger's approval, especially since the Board has withdrawn its prior endorsement. II. NCS Healthcare, Inc., incorporated in Delaware in 1995 as a subsidiary of Ohio-based Aberdeen Group, Inc., was controlled by Outcalt and Shaw through their majority ownership of Aberdeen's high-vote Class B shares. Following a 1996 merger with Aberdeen, NCS's charter was amended, and it later went public. Key provisions in the NCS Charter, particularly Article IV, Section 7, are central to this case.

Section 7(a) of the NCS Charter outlines transfer restrictions, stating that no holder of shares may transfer them under certain conditions. This provision, along with others in Section 7, plays a critical role in the ongoing litigation regarding the validity of the Voting Agreements and the potential conversion of Class B shares. The outcome of these legal proceedings will significantly impact the proposed Merger's feasibility, given the Board's withdrawn support and the contested voting power dynamics.

Shares of Class B Common Stock cannot be transferred, and the Corporation will not register such transfers, unless the recipient is a 'Permitted Transferee.' According to Section 7(d) of the Charter, any Class B shares transferred to a non-Permitted Transferee will automatically convert into Class A shares on a share-for-share basis. Additionally, Section 7(c)(5) clarifies that granting a proxy in a proxy solicitation under Section 14 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 does not count as a transfer of Class B stock.

Omnicare and the stockholder-plaintiffs claim that Outcalt's and Shaw's Class B shares converted to Class A shares upon signing the Voting Agreements. They base this argument on Sections 2(b) and 2(c) of the agreements, which require the stockholders to vote their shares in favor of the Merger and against competing proposals, and grant an irrevocable proxy to Parent representatives to vote the shares accordingly.

The Voting Agreements also prohibit actions like mergers, liquidations, or capital structure changes outside the Merger Agreement. Omnicare and the plaintiffs argue that these agreements effectively transferred an interest in the Class B shares to non-Permitted Transferees, as they restricted Outcalt and Shaw from freely alienating or encumbering their shares.

Plaintiffs further assert that Section 7(c)(5) does not apply to the proxy created by the Voting Agreements, as it was not part of a Section 14(a) proxy solicitation. Defendants counter that the agreements did not transfer any ownership interest in the Class B shares, maintaining that Outcalt and Shaw retained full control over their shares.

The Voting Agreements simply document that Outcalt and Shaw, to encourage Genesis's involvement in the Merger Agreement, pledged to vote all their shares in favor of the Merger (and against anything that could hinder or stop it), reinforcing this commitment by giving Genesis proxies to vote those shares as agreed. Since Outcalt and Shaw determined how their shares would be voted, and the proxies only allow Genesis to vote them accordingly, it is argued that the Voting Agreements did not transfer any Class B shares or related interests to Genesis. Additionally, the defendants claim the proxies in Section 2(c) of the Voting Agreements were 'provided as part of a proxy solicitation' under Section 14(a) of the Exchange Act. Therefore, Section 7(c)(5) of the NCS Charter mandates the conclusion that no share or share interest transfer occurred.

When considering a summary judgment motion, the court must evaluate the facts in the most favorable light for the non-moving party, with the moving party required to prove no material factual disputes exist. 'If the moving party meets this burden, the non-moving party must present admissible evidence to create a trial-worthy issue or face an unfavorable ruling.' Furthermore, the court may grant summary judgment to the opposing party, even without a motion, if the undisputed facts clearly justify such a decision.

Extrinsic evidence will not be used for interpretation if the contract's language is clear; instead, the terms will be enforced as written. Comparing Sections 7(a) and 7(d) shows a wording difference that may restrict Section 7(d) to share transfers, not just share interests. Section 7(a) explicitly mentions 'any interest' in shares, while Section 7(d) refers only to 'purported transfer of shares.' Standard contract interpretation principles require giving effect to all Charter provisions, suggesting Section 7(d) covers both full share transfers and significant interest transfers, though not minor ones.

Section 7(d) is triggered only when a substantial interest in Class B shares is transferred, not a minor one. This interpretation acknowledges the differing language in Sections 7(a) and 7(d) while ensuring Section 7(d) remains effective in preventing significant share interest transfers. Applying this reasoning, the issue is whether Outcalt and Shaw transferred their Class B shares or a major portion of the associated ownership interests.

When they signed the Voting Agreements, the court will initially examine this matter without taking into account the irrevocable proxies outlined in Section 2(c) of those agreements or the impact of Section 7(c)(5) of the NCS Charter on those proxies. Omnicare starts by claiming that Outcalt and Shaw relinquished all their 'voting power' over the Class B shares. It further contends, oversimplifying the situation, that since the Merger's approval is assured by this transferred voting power, Outcalt and Shaw have effectively surrendered 'all present and future interests in their Class B shares.' Omnicare asserts this is inevitable because the eventual transfer or loss of economic and other rights tied to these shares is a certainty. Omnicare states, 'The Voting Agreements marked the final step.' These claims misrepresent the proper legal analysis by wrongly assigning to the Voting Agreements terms or outcomes more accurately linked to the Merger Agreement. For instance, the voting commitment in the Voting Agreements is narrowly defined and does not broadly hand over Outcalt's or Shaw's voting authority to Genesis.

Likewise, the Voting Agreements contain no provisions for canceling the Class B shares or selling Outcalt's and Shaw's Class B shares to Genesis. The court cannot determine that the mere pledge to vote the shares, as stated in Section 2(b) of the Voting Agreements, equates to transferring any portion of Outcalt's or Shaw's ownership stake in the shares. On July 28, 2002, both Outcalt and Shaw retained the authority to vote their shares as they chose, as well as the ability to commit contractually to exercise that authority. Section 2(b) of the Voting Agreements merely reflects their commitments to vote the shares in a specific way to persuade Genesis to join the Merger Agreement with NCS. Genesis did not gain any of their voting power through this arrangement. At most, Genesis secured a legal right to enforce Outcalt's or Shaw's compliance with their contractual obligations. The Garrett v. Brown case strongly supports the view that agreeing to vote did not constitute transferring an interest in the Class B shares. Brown dealt with a restriction on transferring stock or

any 'interest' in it that was, if anything, more expansive than Section 7(a), though it appeared in a stockholders' agreement rather than the certificate of incorporation. Additionally, similar to this case, the dispute centered on whether a secondary agreement among certain stockholders, which imposed strict limits on transferability and voting rights, violated the terms of the stockholders' agreement by constituting a prohibited transfer. The Brown court easily determined that no transfer of an 'interest' had taken place. The court observed: Provisions dictating how La Cadena votes its stock cannot reasonably be interpreted as a transfer under the Stockholders' Agreement. As previously mentioned, the Stockholders' Agreement does not restrict stockholders' freedom to vote their shares as they wish. Given this, it would be incorrect to classify a voting agreement as a transfer. The logical outcome in Brown applies here as well. Outcalt and Shaw retained full voting authority over their shares when they executed the Voting Agreements on July 28, 2002. By agreeing to Section 2(b) of these agreements, they were simply deciding to vote their shares

in support of the Merger. Casting their votes or agreeing on how to vote at a future meeting does not imply that Outcalt or Shaw transferred their voting power to another party. For these reasons, referencing the Brown decision, the court rules that Section 2(a) of the Voting Agreements did not grant Genesis an 'interest' in the Class B common shares covered by the agreement. C. Section 7(c)(5) Further Demonstrates That The Voting Agreements Did Not Transfer An 'Interest' In The Class B Shares The remaining questions are whether the irrevocable proxies in Section 2(c) of the Voting Agreements involved transferring such a significant portion of Outcalt's and Shaw's ownership interests in their Class B shares as to activate the automatic conversion clause in Section 7(d), and if so, whether Section 7(c)(5) of the NCS Charter exempts such transfers from conversion. The court finds that the proxies did not cause the Class B shares to convert for two reasons. First, the proxies simply serve as a practical means to enforce the Voting Agreements' terms.

Under Section 2(b), these proxies are restricted in scope to the issues addressed within that section and can only be used as the shareholders originally agreed to vote. Consequently, the proxies alone do not constitute a significant transfer of Outcalt's or Shaw's voting authority. The court recognizes that the combined proxies represent a majority of NCS voting power, meaning their use under Section 2(b) will lead to the Merger Agreement's ratification unless it is abandoned beforehand. While this outcome is significant for NCS, resulting in the conversion of all NCS common stock into Genesis shares—potentially on less favorable terms than Omnicare's tender offer—the substantial effect of the proxies' exercise does not imply that their initial grant transferred a major portion of Outcalt's

or Shaw's ownership stake in the Class B shares. Additionally, the finding that Outcalt and Shaw did not activate Section 7(d) of the Charter's automatic conversion is supported by Section 7(c)(5). This section states that granting a proxy 'in connection with' a solicitation under Section 14 of the Exchange Act does not count as a 'transfer of interest in the Class B shares.' Omnicare contends that Section 7(c)(5) has a narrow purpose, allowing NCS to solicit proxies for routine matters at annual meetings, not to enable Outcalt and Shaw to transfer beneficial ownership to Genesis for imposing the Merger Agreement on Class A shareholders. However, this restrictive interpretation is not reflected in Section 7(c)(5)'s explicit wording, and their

'purpose' argument is as logically flawed as their claims about Section 7(d). If the Merger Agreement is finalized, it will be due to the NCS board's approval and a majority vote of NCS shareholders, not because Outcalt and Shaw 'transferred ownership' to Genesis or because Genesis forced the agreement on Class A shareholders. Omnicare and the plaintiffs also argue that Section 7(c)(5) does not cover the Section 2(c) proxies because they were not given 'in connection with' a Section 14 solicitation. They raise two points: first, Section 14 only applies to securities registered under Section 12, and since Class B shares are not registered, the proxy solicitation cannot fall under Section 7(c)(5).

their second argument is that the July 28, 2002, proxies could not relate to any future NCS solicitation, as it had not yet begun. The plaintiffs' first claim is too broad and would render Section 7(c)(5) meaningless. Class B shares are not and will likely never be registered under the Exchange Act, given the transfer restrictions in Section 7(a) of the NCS Charter. Therefore, Section 7(c)(5) must apply when Class B shareholders grant proxies linked to solicitations targeting Class A shareholders. This interpretation aligns with common sense and Article IV's provisions.

Under Section 2(c) of the NCS Charter, Class A and Class B shares generally vote together as a single class for director elections and other matters presented to stockholders. Consequently, any proxy solicitation at NCS would target both share classes. The key issue is whether the proxies given by Outcalt and Shaw on July 28, 2002, were linked to a solicitation of Class A shareholders. Plaintiffs note no such solicitation had occurred by then, nor does the record indicate one has since. A strict interpretation of Section 7(c)(5) requiring simultaneity between proxy grants and solicitations would exclude these proxies from its exemption, but such a narrow reading is unsupported by the text. The phrase 'in connection with' suggests a broad, not close, relationship.

Legal scholars describe 'in connection with' as inherently vague and broad, a interpretation consistent with its use in federal securities laws. The Voting and Merger Agreements demonstrate Outcalt and Shaw’s Section 2(c) proxies were tied to an expected Class A proxy solicitation. The Voting Agreements state they were signed to persuade Genesis to proceed with the Merger Agreement, which required NCS to convene a special stockholder meeting for merger approval and distribute a compliant proxy statement. Section 2(b) of the Voting Agreements further links the voting commitment to this anticipated meeting, confirming the necessary connection.

The court rejects Omnicare and the stockholder-plaintiffs’ claim that Outcalt and Shaw’s July 28, 2002 voting agreements violate Article IV, Section 7 of the NCS Charter. There is no evidence the Charter’s drafters intended to bar Class B shareholders from using their majority voting power to approve a board-authorized merger. Accordingly, the motions for partial summary judgment in these cases are DENIED. Partial summary judgment is GRANTED for defendants on Count I of both complaints. Defendants include Outcalt, Shaw, NCS, Genesis, Geneva Sub, Inc., Boake Sells, and Richard Osborne.

In an October 25, 2002 opinion, the court partially granted a motion to dismiss Omnicare’s complaint in C.A. No. 19800, citing Omnicare’s non-stockholder status on July 28, 2002. The court dismissed claims challenging the Board’s merger approval as a fiduciary breach but preserved Count I, which seeks a declaratory judgment on the status of Outcalt and Shaw’s Class B shares. Omnicare also cites Section 7(g) of the Charter, defining 'beneficial ownership' as the power to vote or direct voting, to argue Genesis acquired full ownership of the shares.

To control the vote or manage the disposition of Class B Common Stock shares, a 'beneficial owner' is defined as the individual with beneficial ownership. This definition is much more restrictive than under federal securities laws. Unlike Regulation 13d-3 under the Exchange Act, Section 7(g) does not include those who merely 'share' voting or disposal power. This narrow scope aligns with Section 7(g)'s limited role in the Charter, where 'beneficial ownership' only appears in Section 7(e), granting registration rights. Given this, the court finds Section 7(g) irrelevant to the summary judgment motions. The parties agree Genesis was not a 'Permitted Transferee.'

The term 'Permitted Transferee' is defined in Sections 7(a)(1)-(a)(7) of the NCS Charter. The argument hinges on Section 2(a) of the Voting Agreements, prohibiting share transfers before the Effective Time. An agreement not to transfer shares cannot be interpreted as a transfer itself. See Williams v. Geier, 671 A.2d 1368 (Del. 1996) and Tanzer v. Int'l General Indus., Inc., 402 A.2d 382 (Del. Ch. 1979). The court also references Chancery Court Rule 56(e) and Continental Ins. Co. v. Rutledge & Co., 2000 WL 268297 (Del. Ch. 2000).

Chancery Court Rule 56 allows sua sponte summary judgment if the record clearly favors the non-moving party, as stated in Stroud v. Grace, 606 A.2d 75 (Del. 1992). Citing Elliott Assocs., L.P. v. Avatex Corp., 715 A.2d 843 (Del. 1998), plaintiffs argue ambiguities in Section 7 of the NCS Charter should favor Class A shareholders. This misreads Elliott, which only applies to 'hopeless ambiguities' misleading investors. No such ambiguity exists here, and Outcalt and Shaw should not be treated as drafters.

Kaiser Aluminum Corp. v. Matheson, 681 A.2d 392 (Del. 1996), and McIlquham v. Feste, 2002 WL 244859 (Del. Ch. 2002), alongside Eagle Indus. v. DeVilbiss Health Care, Inc., 702 A.2d 1228 (Del. 1997), and Harrah's Entm't, Inc. v. ICC Holding Co., 802 A.2d 294 (Del. 2002), are referenced. The court finds no basis to treat Outcalt and Shaw as drafters of Article IV, Section 7, given their stakeholder interests.

2d 294, 309 (Del.Ch.2002). See note 11, supra. During oral argument, Omnicare's counsel contended that Outcalt and Shaw had effectively transferred 'beneficial ownership' of their shares to Genesis, and that Genesis could compel NCS to register the shares under its name per Section 7(e) of the NCS Charter. However, this claim lacks backing in Section 7(g)'s definition of 'beneficial ownership' or Section 7(e)'s provisions. In fact, Section 7(e) explicitly states that only one 'beneficial owner' can exist per share of Class B Common Stock at any time. 1986 WL 6708, at *10 (Del.Ch. June 13, 1986), aff'd, 511 A.2d 1044 (Del.1986). See id., at *2. Brown dealt with a stockholders' agreement rather than a charter provision, yet

the stockholders' agreement clause closely mirrored the NCS Charter's terms. It stated, '[N]o Shareholder or their legal representative may Transfer any shares of Common Stock or any rights therein.' Id. See Id., at *9-10. Id., at *10. Under federal securities laws, an irrevocable proxy holder with an interest (unlike a revocable proxy holder) may be considered a 'beneficial owner' of the shares, even if the proxy is time-bound or limited in scope. Calumet Indus., Inc. v. MacClure, 464 F.Supp. 19, 30-31 (N.D.Ill.1978). Yet, this does not imply that the proxies under Section 2(c) of the Voting Agreements constituted a 'transfer' under Section 7(d) of the NCS Charter. See discussion, supra, at note 14. Biyan A. Gardner, A

Dictionary of Modern Legal Usage (2d Ed.) at 434. See, e.g., Manhattan Casualty Co. v. Bankers Life and Casualty Co., 404 U.S. 6, 12-13, 92 S.Ct. 165, 30 L.Ed.2d 128 (1971) (interpreting Rule 10b-5's 'in connection with' broadly as 'touching'). HOLLAND, Justice: In July 1980, defendant Coy Edward Bailey, Jr. was initially convicted by a Kent County Superior Court jury of first-degree murder and possessing a deadly weapon during a felony. This Court overturned the 1980 convictions on appeal and ordered a retrial. Bailey v. State, Del.Supr., 440 A.2d 997 (1982). The second trial occurred in October 1983, also in Kent County. During this trial, three State witnesses mentioned

Bailey's first trial, with the third witness also referencing his prior conviction. After the third mention of the 1980 trial and conviction, the Superior Court Judge declared a mistrial sua sponte. Bailey's third trial in Kent County commenced on September 10, 1984, but the jury deadlocked, leading to another mistrial. On October 18, 1984, Bailey's motion for a venue change was approved. His fourth trial began on April 1, 1985, in New Castle County, resulting in convictions for first-degree murder and a weapons offense. Bailey received a life sentence without parole for murder and an additional fifteen years for the weapons charge. He now appeals these convictions. The facts of the case are detailed in this Court's prior opinion. Bailey v. State, Del.Supr. 440 A.2d 997 (1982). We will only reiterate the

Here are the fundamental facts. Although the evidence in the fourth trial differed from previous trials, the core arguments about the crime stayed largely unchanged. The defendant was found guilty of deliberately killing Frank Dukes by shooting him on June 10, 1978, at an improvised shooting range. Michael Sponaugle, the State's key witness, was present with Bailey during the incident. Sponaugle testified that he, the defendant, and the victim were shooting glass bottles off a log behind his parents' home. He claims Bailey intentionally shot Dukes with a .44 revolver while Dukes was placing more bottles on the log. After the shooting, Sponaugle says he went back to his parents' house and heard another gunshot. Bailey strongly disputes this account, alleging Sponaugle was the one who shot Dukes twice—once from a distance and again in the head as he lay injured. There is also disagreement about what happened afterward.

Bailey appeals his 1985 conviction on multiple grounds. His attorney argues: 1) double jeopardy protections under U.S. and Delaware Constitutions barred his 1985 retrial after jeopardy attached in his second trial; 2) his right to a speedy trial under both constitutions was violated; 3) state interference with attorney-client communication denied him effective counsel; 4) the State's failure to preserve evidence breached his due process rights; and 5) the trial court erred by not instructing the jury on second-degree murder. In a September 17, 1986 order, the Court allowed Bailey to supplement his attorney's brief with his own affidavit, treated as a pro se 'Supplemental Brief,' but limited review to issues raised in trial court filings where his arguments were clear.

In his 'Supplemental Brief,' Bailey addresses two issues from his attorney's brief—double jeopardy and speedy trial claims—and raises three additional points: 1) the State withheld that Sponaugle received immunity before testifying and didn't disclose immunity hearing details; 2) the 1985 jury wasn't informed about Sponaugle's immunity, unlike in Bailey's 1980 trial; and 3) his 1985 trial lawyers were ineffective. Other issues he raises mostly illustrate his counsel's incompetence, such as failing to file motions or challenge the arrest warrant. The Court will review all properly raised arguments.

Bailey's first claim is that prosecutors intentionally provoked a mistrial during his 1983 retrial by having a witness mention his prior conviction, barring further trials under double jeopardy protections. To assess this, the circumstances leading to the mistrial must be examined. During the 1983 retrial, three witnesses referenced Bailey's first trial, with one also noting his prior conviction. The first was Patricia Bailey, his ex-wife and a prosecution witness, who testified in 1980. Under cross-examination in 1983, she was asked about statements made at 'a prior proceeding,' prompting the mistrial.

She was asked if she had given sworn testimony, to which she replied, 'Are you referring to the previous trial?' Neither the defense nor the prosecution requested any corrective measures from the judge. The following day, Jerry Price, an acquaintance of the defendant, testified for the prosecution. Price mentioned that after hearing about the defendant's arrest and incarceration, he had visited him multiple times. He claimed Bailey expressed a wish to have Sponaugle, the key witness for the prosecution, killed. During cross-examination, defense counsel questioned Price about when the defendant first asked for his assistance in eliminating Sponaugle. They also inquired when Price first reported these discussions to the authorities, to which he responded it was around the start of the new trial proceedings, two or three months prior. The jury was then excused, and the defense argued for a mistrial or at least a warning to the jury. The prosecutor noted that Price had been instructed not to mention the first trial and highlighted that the defense had encountered a similar response during their cross-examination of Patricia Bailey.

The judge expressed willingness to issue a cautionary instruction or to question the jury about their awareness of the prior trial but warned that this might further complicate matters by revealing the existence of the previous trial. Defense counsel reiterated their motion for a mistrial, which was denied, and no warning was given to the jury. The prosecution then called Gary Lee Hastings, who had been jailed with the defendant in late 1981 and early 1982. The prosecution aimed to use Hastings' testimony to demonstrate Bailey's intent to undermine his murder case by eliminating Sponaugle. During questioning, Hastings confirmed discussing Bailey's charges, noting it was common knowledge in the facility that Bailey was serving a life sentence for murder. The court immediately halted proceedings and removed the jury.

After the jury left, the judge stated, 'We’ve spent nearly two weeks on this, but I think this seals it.' The prosecutor agreed, and the judge declared a mistrial, scheduling a new trial for a later date. Defense counsel did not object to this decision. The principle of avoiding double jeopardy dates back to ancient Greek and Roman law, as referenced in legal precedents like Bartkus v. Illinois and United States v. Jenkins. This concept was explicitly incorporated into the U.S. and Delaware Constitutions to prevent individuals from being tried twice for the same offense.

Bailey argues that the interruption of his second trial under these circumstances violates the Double Jeopardy clauses of the Fifth Amendment and Delaware’s Constitution. The analysis of his claim under both provisions is the same. These clauses reflect a policy of finality to protect defendants from the strain of multiple trials. Courts recognize the balance between the government’s need to enforce laws and the defendant’s right to avoid repeated prosecutions. However, double jeopardy does not ensure the government will always resolve a case in a single trial.

For a specific offense, a defendant may face retrial if their conviction is overturned on appeal. Cases like United States v. Ball and Green v. United States illustrate this principle. However, the issue arises when a retrial is barred after a trial is aborted before a verdict. Generally, if the defendant requests and is granted a mistrial, reprosecution is allowed, as seen in Oregon v. Kennedy. The most complex double jeopardy questions emerge when proceedings are halted without the defendant's request.

When a trial court declares a mistrial on its own before a verdict, the situation differs significantly from cases where the defendant moves for a mistrial. The defendant has a vested interest in whether the case is taken from the jury under questionable circumstances. References like United States v. Jorn highlight this distinction. Courts have avoided creating rigid rules for retrial in such scenarios, as seen in Rentoul v. State and other cases, preferring instead to evaluate each situation individually.

A blanket rule against retrial when a jury is dismissed without the defendant's consent would undermine the pursuit of justice. While protecting defendants from harassment is important, the public interest in fair trials must also be considered. As noted in Wade v. Hunter, the right to a trial by a specific tribunal may sometimes yield to broader justice concerns. Appellate review of a judge's sua sponte mistrial declaration hinges on the 'manifest necessity' standard, a doctrine with deep roots in legal history.

The 'manifest necessity' doctrine, first articulated in United States v. Perez, grants courts discretion to discharge a jury when justice demands it. Justice Storey emphasized that this power must be used cautiously, particularly in capital cases, to avoid depriving defendants of fair opportunities. The doctrine balances judicial discretion with public trust, ensuring that mistrials are declared only for compelling reasons, as further elaborated in Perez and subsequent rulings.

The duty of the Judges, as per their sworn oaths, is emphasized here. Id. at 580. Without a defendant's motion for a mistrial, the Perez doctrine of manifest necessity directs trial judges to preserve the defendant's right to proceed with the trial, unless a careful judicial evaluation determines that continuing the trial would not serve public justice. Cf. United States v. Jorn, 400 U.S. 470, 91 S.Ct. 547; United States v. Perez, 22 U.S. 579. Reviewing the specifics of Bailey's case confirms that the trial court's spontaneous mistrial declaration in 1983 was justified and necessary. The 1983 trial records indicate the mistrial was prompted by the jury's exposure to details about the defendant's 1980 trial. See Arizona v. Washington, 434 U.S. 497, 98 S.Ct. 824, 54 L.Ed.2d

717 (1978). The jury discovered not only that the defendant had faced prior charges but also that the 1980 trial resulted in a conviction. Such information is inherently prejudicial, especially when revealed during trial. Hughes v. State, Del.Supr., 490 A.2d 1034, 1044-47 (1985). The Hughes court recognized that a jury's knowledge of a prior conviction, later overturned, in a subsequent trial would warrant a mistrial. Id. In Hughes, it was stated: 'It is difficult to imagine anything more damaging to a defendant than a jury knowing he was previously convicted of the same crime. Expecting jurors to disregard such knowledge during deliberations is unrealistic, as the state's repeated efforts might lead an average person to assume guilt.'

Hughes, 490 A.2d at 1044. The Hughes ruling also emphasized that jurors acquiring prejudicial information during trial poses a significant risk to the defendant. 'This scenario demands stricter scrutiny than pretrial exposure to such information.' Hughes v. State, 490 A.2d at 1045. U.S. Supreme Court rulings on juror bias align with this view. In Arizona v. Washington, 434 U.S. 497, 98 S.Ct. 824, the Court upheld a mistrial due to highly prejudicial evidence. A dissenting opinion by Justice Marshall noted the 'manifest necessity' doctrine requires the record to show either no viable alternatives to a mistrial or that the court thoroughly evaluated alternatives before halting proceedings.' Id. The record here confirms no practical alternatives existed and that the court had previously

examined and dismissed all options. When a witness mentioned Bailey's prior trial and conviction, the jury was promptly removed. Defense counsel did not oppose the mistrial at the time, though Bailey later contested the court's statement, 'That about locks it up.' The lack of an explicit 'manifest necessity' finding is not decisive. If an error guarantees an appeal reversal, the necessity can be inferred from the mistrial declaration. See Illinois v. Somerville, 410 U.S. 458, 464, 93 S.Ct. 1066, 1070, 35 L.Ed.2d 425 (1973). Since the record justifies the ruling, the absence of a detailed explanation does not violate State or Federal Constitutional standards. Cf. Arizona v. Washington, 434 U.S. 4

97, 98 S.Ct. 824. The trial court's rationale for declaring a mistrial is clearly documented in the record, which includes discussions with counsel and evaluation of other options. The record demonstrates the judge's careful decision to ensure the defendant receives a fair trial by an unbiased jury. Cf. Rentoul v. State, 301 A.2d 284 (Del.Supr.1973). Neither side is entitled to a trial by a potentially prejudiced jury. In such cases, the societal need for fair and just outcomes takes precedence over the defendant's right to continue with the originally selected jury. Cf. Arizona v. Washington, 434 U.S. 497, 98 S.Ct. 824. If a mistrial halts a trial that might have led to a conviction later overturned on appeal, the defendant's desire for a verdict is outweighed by the broader interest in public justice. Illinois v. Somerville, 410 U.S.

458 at 464, 93 S.Ct. 1066 at 1070, citing Wade v. Hunter, 336 U.S. 684, 69 S.Ct. 834. Continuing Bailey's 1983 trial would not have served public justice. The record justifies the judge's sua sponte mistrial declaration due to manifest necessity. However, finding manifest necessity does not end the double jeopardy inquiry. Even when such necessity exists, as here, double jeopardy protections shield defendants from prosecutorial or judicial misconduct aimed at forcing a mistrial to gain an unfair advantage. United States v. Dinitz, 424 U.S. 600, 96 S.Ct. 1075, 47 L.Ed.2d 267 (1976). Retrials are prohibited if 'bad-faith actions by the court or prosecution harass the defendant through repeated trials or mistrials designed to improve the prosecution's chances.' United States v. Dinitz, 424 U.S. at 611, 96 S.Ct. at 1081.

In Oregon v. Kennedy, the Supreme Court clarified Dinitz, ruling that double jeopardy bars retrial only if the mistrial resulted from intentional misconduct by the prosecutor or judge. 456 U.S. at 679, 102 S.Ct. at 209. Justice Powell agreed, stating that prosecutorial intent determines whether a mistrial precludes retrial. He added that courts should focus on objective evidence rather than subjective intent when assessing double jeopardy claims. Id. Reviewing the facts of Bailey's case reveals no intentional provocation of the mistrial by the prosecutor.

As noted earlier, this exchange between the prosecutor and Hastings occurred just before the mistrial: 'Q. Did you discuss Bailey's charges while he was jailed? A. Yes, but not specifics—it was common knowledge he was serving life for murder.' Earlier, Hastings testified Bailey offered a contract to kill Sponaugle. The State claims the questioning aimed to show Bailey's intent to obstruct justice, while Bailey alleges prosecutorial misconduct. Evidence of the murder plot was admissible to demonstrate guilt. See Goldsmith v. State, Del.Supr. 405 A.2d 109, 114 (1979). Prior

Regarding the questioning that resulted in the mistrial declaration, Hastings stated that Bailey wished for Sponaugle's death and sought to enlist Hastings for the act. Hastings' awareness of Bailey's charges was crucial to show Bailey's motive in desiring Sponaugle's demise and to offer evidence for the jury to infer Bailey's guilt. Although the State's questions could have been phrased better to obtain pertinent testimony, Hastings' response was irrelevant. Deliberate prosecutorial misconduct to incite a mistrial isn't proven by spontaneous witness statements or unanticipated answers to seemingly appropriate questions. Cf. Commonwealth v. Yost, 305 Pa.Supr. 316, 451 A.2d 549 (1982); Commonwealth v. Miele, 300 Pa.Supr. 197, 446 A.2d 298 (1982); State v. Blanks, 190 N.J.Super. 269, 463 A.2d 359, 364

-365 (1983). In Oregon v. Kennedy, Justice Powell noted the lack of prior prosecutorial overreach before the prejudicial question. During Bailey's 1983 trial, no other misconduct occurred before its termination. In fact, the prosecution had previously warned witnesses not to reference the first trial. Bailey's claim that the prosecutor aimed to provoke a mistrial lacks support. In his brief, Bailey admits that 'one can only guess whether the prosecution sought delay or another advantage from a mistrial.' For the reasons stated, the Superior Court's sua sponte mistrial declaration was justified. The record doesn't substantiate Bailey's claim that the prosecutor's final questions were in bad faith or meant to cause a mistrial. Given these circumstances, neither state nor federal double jeopardy clauses, nor Delaware law, prevent Bailey's retrial. Cf. United States v. Perez, 22 U.S. 579; Oregon v. Kennedy, 456 U

.S. 667, 102 S.Ct. 2083. SPEEDY TRIAL Bailey's second argument is that his Sixth Amendment and Delaware Constitution Article I, Section 7 right to a speedy trial was violated. He argues the delay from his arrest on June 11, 1978, to his trial on April 1, 1985, deprived him of this right. Delaware's Constitution guarantees the same speedy trial rights as the U.S. Constitution, so Bailey's state claim mirrors his federal one. See Fensterer v. State, Del.Supr., 493 A.2d 959 (1985) and Shockley v. State, Del.Supr., 269 A.2d 778 (1970). What qualifies as a speedy trial depends on case specifics. Stacey v. Delaware, Del.Supr., 364 A.2d

819, 820 (1976) (citing Beebe v. State, Del.Supr., 346 A.2d 169 (1975)). To assess a speedy trial violation, courts balance the conduct of both prosecution and defendant. Barker v. Wingo, 407 U.S. 514, 92 S.Ct. 2182, 33 L.Ed.2d 101 (1972). Barker outlined factors like delay length, its cause, the defendant's assertion of rights, and prejudice. Id. This Court adopted this approach in Fensterer, 493 A.2d at 965. We now examine Barker's factors. 'Delay length acts as a trigger; only once it’s presumptively prejudicial must other factors be analyzed.' Barker, 407 U.S. at

530, 92 S.Ct. at 2192. Bailey was taken into custody for the killing of Frank Dukes on June 11, 1978. His latest trial, which is the focus of this appeal, began around seven years later, on July 1, 1985. Eighteen months of this duration covered the time from Bailey's initial conviction in July 1980 until the overturning and return of the case to the Superior Court in February 1982. For assessing Bailey's assertion of a denied speedy trial, the appeal period is rightly excluded from our review. See Tramill v. State, Del.Supr. 425 A.2d 142, 143 (1980); see also United States v. Ewell, 383 U.S. 116, 121, 86 S.Ct. 773, 777, 15 L.Ed.2d 627 (1966). The State acknowledges that the remaining span of five years and eight months is enough on its own to warrant an examination of all the

Barker criteria. On the surface, a delay of five years and eight months raises significant concerns. With the Barker balancing test activated by the prolonged delay, we now evaluate all pertinent factors. The defendant contends that the state's actions violated his right to a speedy trial. Given our deep unease about the extensive delay, we will scrutinize the entire history of Bailey's prosecution. To begin, we observe that since his arrest, Bailey has undergone four trials (three concluded and one halted) or one trial per fourteen months while his case was pending in the Superior Court. The longest continuous pre-trial delay was the twenty-five months between his arrest in June 1978 and his first trial in July 1980. Much of the initial six months involved routine pre-trial procedures, largely initiated by the defendant. For example, his suppression motion, filed in July, proceeded to a hearing in September, required briefing in October and November, and was resolved in December. The need for briefing and oral argument on Bailey's motions cannot be held against the State. 'The State is not obligated to abandon its valid

legal positions merely to expedite a defendant's trial.' Cf. Fensterer, 493 A.2d at 965-966. Beyond pre-trial preparations, much of the remaining delay before the first trial also stems from the defendant's actions. At that time, Bailey was represented by private counsel. While the Motion to Suppress was under review in the Superior Court, his lawyers also filed a motion to appoint a ballistics expert. Despite having private representation, Bailey sought a court order to compel the Public Defender's office to fund or provide a ballistics expert at no cost. This motion was also briefed and argued, resulting in a favorable ruling for Bailey. After losing the payment dispute in the Superior Court, the Public Defender's office appealed to this Court in March 1979. Following briefing and oral arguments, this Court upheld the Superior Court's decision on December 26, 1979. The prosecution was not involved in this ancillary litigation, and the resulting delay cannot be attributed to the State. Over the next six months leading to the first trial, the defendant

submitted multiple motions, including one for personal transport to the crime scene and another requesting a private investigator at the Public Defender's expense. Both motions were approved. Bailey's first trial began on July 7, 1980. Before this trial, he did not file a motion claiming a speedy trial violation. As we conclude that the prosecution was not accountable for any part of the twenty-five-month delay between Bailey's arrest and his first trial, this delay will not count against the prosecution. Excluding the appeal period for the first conviction, we now address the eighteen-month delay between this Court's reversal of the conviction in February 1982 and the second trial in October 1983. Again, we find the delay was caused by the defendant's actions. During this time, Bailey had new defense counsel who pursued habeas corpus relief and other extraordinary remedies in both the Superior Court and this Court. Bailey also submitted several pro se applications during this period. On May 23, 1983, the defense requested a continuance

The continuance requested by the defense was approved despite the state's opposition, leading to a trial date in the fall to allow adequate preparation time. On October 19, 1983, Bailey's second trial was halted as the judge declared a mistrial on their own initiative, citing reasons previously mentioned. None of the eighteen-month period between this Court's reversal of Bailey's initial conviction and his second trial can be attributed to prosecutorial misconduct. The eleven-month gap following the 1983 mistrial until Bailey's third trial on September 10, 1984, involved the appointment of new counsel, who suggested the September trial date. This period also saw the court handling defense motions related to speedy trial dismissal, habeas corpus, change of venue, and bail. No delays during these eleven months were due to improper state actions. The third trial resulted in a hung jury, leading to a mistrial and a new trial being set.

The next trial was planned for January 1985. We now assess the eight-month span between the third and fourth trials. During this time, Bailey was assigned new attorneys again. A defense motion to move the trial to New Castle County was approved, as was a request to postpone the trial from January to March 1985. The defense also sought bail reduction, filed a habeas corpus petition, and requested an investigator, with the latter being granted. Additionally, the defense was permitted to visit the crime scene, and a hearing on a Rule to Show Cause motion occurred on March 29. However, a defense request for another continuance that day was denied. Once more, we find no prosecutorial delays during this eight-month interval. In speedy trial evaluations, the reason for delay is pivotal, often determining the outcome of such claims. United States v. Loud Hawk, 474 U.S. 302, 106 S.Ct. 648, 655 (1986). Our thorough review concludes Bailey did not succeed in proving prosecutorial delay.

The third factor in speedy trial analysis is the defendant's assertion of their right. Timely and consistent claims are crucial in determining violations, as seen in Whalen v. State, 492 A.2d 552, 568-69 (1985). Both timing and frequency carry significant weight. Bailey first raised speedy trial concerns after his initial conviction was overturned. He later filed similar motions before his third and fourth trials. However, records show no such claim before his first trial. While his initial omission isn’t decisive, his subsequent motions were timely. Yet, Bailey’s assertions resemble Penelope’s Tapestry, as referenced in Loud Hawk. Despite his repeated speedy trial dismissal requests, his simultaneous filings for interlocutory appeals and other relief contributed to trial delays. Merely filing motions doesn’t alone demonstrate proper assertion of rights.

When reviewing Bailey’s speedy trial motions in context—including his numerous pro se and counsel-filed requests for extraordinary relief—it’s clear they compounded trial delays. Although Bailey consistently sought dismissal on speedy trial grounds, this alone doesn’t prove he properly asserted his right, per Loud Hawk. The record reflects a pattern where his actions, while ostensibly advocating for a speedy trial, paradoxically prolonged proceedings. Thus, his claims lack the consistency and clarity required to establish a violation, particularly when weighed against the broader procedural history of his case.

After reviewing various motions, petitions, and interim appeals, we determine that Bailey deliberately chose to pursue his defense through alternative strategies, some of which conflicted with his stated goal of a speedy trial. The fourth and final factor in our speedy trial evaluation is the defendant's prejudice. In Fensterer, this Court clarified that prejudice must be evaluated based on the defendant's interests, which the speedy trial right aims to safeguard. These interests include preventing undue pretrial detention, reducing the accused's anxiety, and ensuring the defense is not weakened. The defendant did not argue the first two points, but we will examine all three. Aside from the period from July 22, 1980, to January 20, 1982, when Bailey was serving a sentence later overturned by this Court, Bailey

was held in custody without bail or unable to post bail since his arrest. Throughout his detention, records show Bailey was either ineligible for bail or couldn't afford it. His repeated requests for bail reduction or a certificate of reasonable doubt were thoroughly reviewed. We find no evidence that his pretrial detention was oppressive. The second interest, minimizing the accused's anxiety, is inherent in any criminal case. The record provides no indication that Bailey experienced undue anxiety beyond what is typical for someone facing first-degree murder charges. The third interest, preventing impairment of the defense due to delay, is central to the speedy trial right. Bailey argues his defense was prejudiced because the judge delayed approving a private investigator until two weeks before his fourth trial, denied a continuance, and allegedly confiscated trial materials from his cell. He also claims his attorney calls were restricted. These issues, however, do not directly relate to his speedy trial claim. Bailey further asserts that some witnesses became unavailable due to the prolonged delay, though their prior testimony was preserved and could be presented at trial. While live testimony is preferable, the preserved records ensured his defense remained intact.

Bailey acknowledges that the testimony from his first trial could be read into the record and provides no reason to believe the witnesses' accounts would differ in his fourth trial. Although live testimony is often more compelling, the sworn statements from his initial trial were available for the jury. Thus, we find no prejudice to Bailey's defense attributable to the trial delay. After assessing all relevant factors, we conclude the balance weighs against Bailey. The delays were largely due to his defense strategy, including numerous motions, some repetitive but all within his procedural rights. We find no significant harm to his ability to present his defense at his fourth trial. Cf. Fensterer v. State, 493 A.2d at 967.

INTERFERENCE WITH COUNSEL Bailey next argues that state interference violated his Sixth Amendment right to effective counsel. He claims prison officials disrupted his attorney calls and destroyed trial preparation materials. The right to counsel is fundamental, ensuring fairness in criminal proceedings. Denial of this right violates due process, as established in Gideon v. Wainwright, 372 U.S. 335 (1963).

Under the principles of due process in both federal and Delaware constitutional law, as established in Merritt v. State, Del.Supr., 219 A.2d 258 (1966), courts have acknowledged valid claims where government actions undermine the effectiveness of legal counsel. Referencing Massiah v. United States, 377 U.S. 201 (1964), while upholding the critical right to effective counsel, courts also recognize society's stake in fair criminal proceedings. Dismissing an indictment is deemed unjustified without clear prejudice, even if there was intentional infringement on counsel rights, as noted in United States v. Morrison, 449 U.S. 361 (1981).

Referencing United States v. Morrison, 449 U.S. 361 (1981), remedies for counsel interference must align with the harm caused and avoid undue disruption to criminal justice processes. With these guidelines, we assess the trial court's handling of the case, citing Chapman v. California, 386 U.S. 18 (1967). Before his fourth trial, Bailey was held in maximum security at Delaware Correctional Center, which he argued hindered his trial preparation.

Bailey contended that his maximum security confinement obstructed his defense efforts, leading him to file for relocation. On March 12, 1985, the Superior Court rejected his request but granted extensive privileges, including attorney access and legal materials. However, issues emerged quickly, with Bailey alleging in letters on March 22 and 23 that his legal documents were seized, phone access was restricted, and officials disrupted a call with his lawyer. His attorneys echoed these claims in a March 25 motion to dismiss, citing state interference.

The Superior Court promptly scheduled a March 29, 1985 hearing to address these motions. Bailey testified that essential defense documents were confiscated during a cell search, his posted court order was removed, and materials were scattered. He also reiterated phone access denials. A correctional officer denied taking any papers. After Bailey's testimony, the state urged the court to reject his motions without presenting evidence, leading the court to rule against Bailey.

If materials had gone missing from Bailey's prison cell, they were not unknown and could likely be restored or reorganized into a usable state within a week. The court decided it was 'not convinced the case should be dismissed based on the evidence presented, nor that a rule to show cause should be issued or the trial delayed.' However, right after this decision, the Superior Court instructed the State to promptly provide Bailey with previously requested photos to aid his trial preparation, confirming it had already coordinated with prison staff to ensure the return of Bailey's sketch pad. The prosecutor also assured the court that Bailey's calls to his lawyer would not be interrupted. The court warned the State that further issues would lead to potential contempt charges. Additionally, the court acknowledged Bailey and his lawyers' vested interest in their defense strategy, praising the trial judge's handling of the interference claims as exemplary.

The Superior Court reviewed Bailey's claims by not only voicing deep concern over the allegations but also quickly setting a hearing. Bailey attended, testified, and presented witnesses, though their accounts conflicted. The trial court ruled against Bailey, rejecting his requests. This court upholds factual decisions by trial judges when backed by credible evidence, as seen in State v. Rooks, Del.Supr. 401 A.2d 943 (1979). While the Superior Court denied Bailey's specific requests for dismissal or contempt, it properly evaluated the harm done and devised a suitable remedy. The court acknowledged the disappearance of materials but found they could be quickly restored without significant prejudice, ordering prison officials to return Bailey's items and ensure unimpeded attorney access or face contempt.

Bailey contended that reconstructing lost materials just a week before trial hindered his defense, leaving his attorney unprepared for witness examinations. The Superior Court was informed of this concern pre-trial and offered to grant extra preparation time if needed during proceedings. The trial judge adeptly tailored a solution, but the defense never requested additional time. Without clear irreparable harm, dismissing charges is unwarranted despite interference with counsel rights, per United States v. Morrison, 449 U.S. 361 (1981). The trial court determined the missing materials did not severely prejudice Bailey, though interference with counsel rights is unacceptable, especially if it defies a court order.

We disapprove of any obstruction of a defendant's counsel access, particularly the alleged misconduct here, which would be egregious given the Superior Court's explicit order. Nonetheless, the court's response—including contempt measures—was justified. We uphold the decision not to dismiss charges, as the record supports the Superior Court's conclusions and corrective actions. Regarding the March 29, 1985 hearing, the denial of a trial continuance was also affirmed, as the court found no undue prejudice to Bailey's defense.

The Superior Court rejected Bailey's plea to drop the charges and his petition for a Rule to Show Cause, as well as his motion for a case continuance. Bailey's continuance request was made verbally for the first time during a meeting about his written motions. The court postponed ruling on all defense motions until after the March 29, 1985 hearing. At the hearing's end, the judge inquired if the continuance request still stood, leading to a discussion where Bailey's attorney argued for its necessity due to preparation challenges.

Early trial preparation involves extensive material, and the defense attorney only learned about the trial a few weeks prior. The attorney noted that the defendant found certain testimony more relevant than initially thought, justifying the continuance request. Additionally, access to specific photos for Bailey's drawings was expected, though they weren’t ready by the hearing date. The prosecutor confirmed the photos were completed but not delivered in time for the hearing.

During the exchange, the judge asked how long the continuance would last, and Bailey's attorney suggested a week. The prosecutor opposed the request, citing witness scheduling issues. The defense offered flexibility in witness order, but the prosecution declined. The judge then deliberated on the request, weighing both sides' arguments.

The judge ruled against the continuance, noting the State's case would take at least four days, potentially filling the first week. He proposed starting the trial immediately, with the option to reconsider if the defense needed more time later. The judge emphasized that delaying the case would inconvenience the State, witnesses, and the court, and saw no grounds for dismissal or a continuance based on the arguments presented. This Court has previously addressed continuance applications.

The decision is left to the trial judge's discretion, and their ruling will only be overturned on appeal if it is clearly unreasonable or arbitrary. Riley v. State, Del.Supr. 496 A.2d 997, 1018 (1985), cert. den. — U.S.-, 106 S.Ct. 3339, 92 L.Ed.2d 743 (1986). In Riley, the court agreed with the U.S. Supreme Court's view that no fixed rules exist to determine when denying a continuance violates due process, and each case must be evaluated based on its specific circumstances and the reasons given to the trial judge at the time of the request. Ungar v. Sarafite, 376 U.S. 575, 589, 84 S.Ct. 841, 850, 11 L.Ed.2d 921, reh. den. 377 U.S. 925, 84 S.Ct. 1218, 12 L.Ed.2d 217 (1964).

In Riley, the Court ruled that when deciding on a continuance, the trial court must weigh the defendant's reasons and the case's circumstances. Here, the trial judge properly used his discretion in denying Bailey's continuance request. Bailey's attorney argued that State interference had caused the loss or damage of legal materials, hindering his defense, citing Merritt v. State, Del.Supr., 219 A.2d 258 (1966). In Merritt, the court found an abuse of discretion when new counsel was given only 30 minutes to prepare. Bailey's case differed, as his attorneys were appointed months before trial on December 6, 1984.

Bailey's initial continuance request was approved, moving the trial from January 21, 1985, to March 11, 1985, and later to April 1, 1985. His attorneys had months to prepare, and their motions for a private investigator and a crime scene visit were granted in March 1985. The only continuance issue on March 29, 1985, concerned missing materials. After a hearing, the court concluded the materials could likely be reassembled within a week, minimizing prejudice to Bailey. Even if the request included all potential issues, it sought only a one-week delay.

The trial court acknowledged that a one-week delay would cause significant disruption but denied the continuance, stating it would reconsider if the defense needed more time during trial. No further continuance requests were made. The court properly weighed Bailey's reasons and the case's circumstances before denying the one-week postponement. Cf. Riley v. State, 496 A.2d 997. The court left open the possibility of a future request during trial, emphasizing the broad discretion trial courts have in such matters.

Regarding the request for a continuance, the court's response was entirely justified given the context. Refer to Riley v. State, 496 A.2d 997, and Raymond Heartless, Inc. v. State, Del.Supr. 401 A.2d 921 (1979), as well as Ungar v. Sarafite, 376 U.S. 575, 84 S.Ct. 841. The defendant claims a due process violation due to the State's failure to preserve evidence, citing a missing Pepsi can, a lost paper bag containing a gun, and an uncollected metal bucket allegedly used to conceal blood.

The defense further argued that the State neglected to investigate a potential eyewitness, as mentioned in Sergeant Collison's statement. The defense contended this omission prejudiced their case, requesting a judgment of acquittal. The court inquired for clarification, and the defense maintained that the State's explanation for the third party's presence was inadequate.

The State is obligated to disclose exculpatory evidence under Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83 (1963), and United States v. Agurs, 427 U.S. 97 (1976). Failure to do so risks an unfair trial or wrongful conviction. Superior Court Rule 16 mandates evidence production, extending beyond Brady to include preservation, as established in Deberry v. State, Del.Supr., 457 A.2d 744 (1983).

the defense did not request to examine. Defendants often argue they cannot specify items without knowing what was gathered. We assumed the defendant planned to use this list for a detailed follow-up request under Rule 16(b). A request for all crime scene evidence would have been reasonable for Bailey's defense. Here, no pretrial request was made that would have required the State to list or produce the Pepsi can. Had such a request been made, the can would have been identified and provided, as the State retained it and had it at trial. Regarding the evidentiary issues raised by Bailey about items not collected or preserved: For the items not kept by the defense, one—the Pepsi-Cola can—is still accessible and can be used if desired. The paper bag and metal bucket, however, were not addressed previously, as recalled by Miss Brady’s remarks. These items were more prominent earlier due to extensive testimony, but nothing in this case highlights their relevance. I doubt they were even mentioned in this trial. The State has repeatedly explained the third-party theory, which the defense struggles to grasp, alleging it was fabricated by Collison. However, no proof exists of a third party’s involvement or the State’s awareness of one, and Collison has denied it. Failing to investigate an unsubstantiated claim isn’t grounds for dismissal. The Superior Court, after reviewing arguments about missing evidence, denied the motion, aligning with the balancing test. The court found no negligence by the State in handling the paper bag or metal bucket or considering them as key evidence.

The trial judge explicitly stated that nothing indicated the paper bag or metal bucket held significance, nor were they referenced in the trial. Concerning the alleged missing eyewitness, the Court found no evidence of a third party or State knowledge of one, and the officer denied the claim. Not investigating a nonexistent issue doesn’t justify dismissal. Bailey’s conviction stands as he didn’t meet the balancing test’s first two prongs.
