The Chancellor: The corporation’s charter grants exclusive voting rights to Class A common stock. Preferred stock holds no voting rights unless dividends are unpaid for two semi-annual periods or sinking fund payments are missed for two periods, in which case preferred stockholders gain voting rights until all arrears are settled. The complainant claims such arrears existed during the 1933 director election by Class A stockholders, but evidence only supports unpaid dividends, not sinking fund defaults. The key issue is whether preferred dividends were unpaid for two periods before the meeting. The

annual director election meeting was scheduled for March 1, 1933, with notice sent only to Class A stockholders. A preferred dividend had been paid on January 1, so preferred stockholders lacked voting rights. At the March 1 meeting, disputes over the treasurer’s financial statement led to adjournment without electing directors. The meeting reconvened on May 15, 1933, but lacked a quorum and adjourned again. The president called another meeting for June 26, 1933, but no quorum attended. Discussions focused on purchasing Harry Ades’s shares, the president and controlling Class A stockholder. The minutes note the meeting was postponed after reaching an agreement.

The terms of these agreements could be 'executed.' An adjournment was then approved, pending the president's call. Up to this point, only Class A common stockholders had convened. Following the June 26, 1933 meeting, preferred stockholders began to participate, likely due to preliminary plans discussed in June to acquire Harry Ades' shares. On June 30, 1933, both common and preferred stockholders were notified of a special and extraordinary meeting scheduled for July 10, 1933. The agenda included five items, all seemingly related to finalizing the purchase of Ades' holdings and removing him from the company. The notice also mentioned that the annual meeting, adjourned on June 26, 1933, would resume immediately after the special meeting. Thus, two stockholders' meetings were planned.

On July 10, 1933, two meetings took place—one joint session for common and preferred stockholders and another for common stockholders, adjourned from June 26th. Separate minutes were recorded for each. The special meeting lacked a quorum and was adjourned to July 17, 1933, as noted in the minutes. The Class A common stockholders' meeting, however, had a quorum, and the individual defendants were elected directors. This election is contested in the bill, arguing that the Class A common stock lost its voting rights due to two unpaid preferred dividends. Had the vote occurred on March 1, 1933, when the Class A meeting first convened, the voting rights would have been uncontested, as only one default (assuming the January 1, 1933 dividend was unlawful) would have existed.

However, if the January 1, 1933 preferred dividend was indeed unlawful and counted as a default, by July 10, 1933, a second default occurred when the July 1 dividend was missed. The complainant argues that the Class A common stock's voting rights should be assessed as of July 10, 1933, when the vote occurred, not March 1, 1933. This hinges on the claim that the January 1 dividend was illegal, making the July 1 omission a second default. The complainant asserts that by July 17, 1933, two preferred dividend periods had been missed. The defendants counter that even if the January 1 dividend was unlawful, its payment satisfied the charter's wording, which transfers voting control only if dividends 'shall not have been paid' for two periods.

A strict interpretation of the charter cannot be upheld. The term 'dividends' in this context must refer to legally permissible payments. Any other reading would be unreasonable and risk harming the corporation's capital. It is also questionable whether preferred stockholders could immediately elect new directors upon gaining voting rights, bypassing the annual meeting. Regardless, if voting rights shift to preferred stockholders between the original meeting and an adjourned session where voting occurs, I believe the preferred stockholders' rights should prevail. The charter's intent must align with legal and equitable principles, not just literal wording.

Common stock lacks voting rights. Given this, it is appropriate to assess whether the January 1, 1933, dividend was legally valid. The defendant corporation was established to operate a loan and investment business. Such entities may distribute dividends either from net assets exceeding capital or, absent such excess, from net profits of the current or prior fiscal year. Section 34 of the General Corporation Law (Revised Code 1915, § 1948, amended by 36 Del. Laws, c. 135, § 16) outlines this. The defendants do not claim the 1933 dividend came from current or prior-year profits, as none existed. Instead, they argue it was paid from surplus assets. The complainant contends no such surplus existed. Extensive testimony and time have been devoted to this matter.

The dispute centers on whether a sufficient surplus existed to justify the dividend. The key disagreement is whether assets for dividends can be valued at cost without considering current worth. The defendants argue in favor, while the complainant insists assets must reflect present value through write-downs or reserves. While unrealized gains on fixed assets like real estate cannot be counted as profits until sold (Kingston et al. v. Home Life Insurance Co., 11 Del. Ch. 258, 101 A. 898), this does not mean loans and investments—core to the defendant’s business—can ignore value declines when determining surplus. Worthless receivables must be excluded from net assets for dividends (American Steel & Wire Co. v. Eddy, 138 Mich. 403, 101 N.W. 578).

The Pennsylvania Supreme Court, in Loan Society of Phila. v. Eavenson (248 Pa. 407, 94 A. 121), similarly treated worthless loans as non-viable assets. Partially impaired assets should likewise be reduced proportionally. The Iowa case Hubbard v. Weare (79 Iowa 678, 44 N.W. 915) ruled that dividends from excess assets require deductions for collection losses on receivables. Good accounts, however, should be valued at face (Quinn v. Quinn Mfg. Co., 201 Mich. 664, 167 N.W. 898). The legality of a dividend depends on conditions at the time of declaration (Main v. Mills, Fed. Cas. No. 8,974, 6 Bliss. 98).

Authorities and statutes agree that dividend assets must account for depreciation. Section 34 of the amended General Corporation Law prohibits dividends if capital is diminished by property depreciation or losses. The defendant’s December 31, 1932, balance sheet listed loans receivable at $86,580.09—full cost. Testimony revealed many loans were unsecured, delinquent, or backed by junior liens, yet they were carried at cost. This raises doubts about the corporation’s ability to recover the full amount.

Out of $86,580.09 in loans issued, some backed by collateral and others not, the management displayed a financial acumen unmatched by similar firms. The plaintiff argues for a $22,000 depreciation on receivable loans, roughly 27%, which may or may not be excessive. A 10% write-off seems more reasonable, though an accountant might deem it insufficient, suggesting at least an $8,650 reduction in loans receivable.

The $42,315.03 listed as loans to an affiliated company refers to a fully owned subsidiary, Home Realty Company. When the defendant foreclosed on properties, titles were transferred to Home Realty, with costs recorded as loans. Only $36,195 reflects actual real estate investments; the remaining $6,120.03 is unrealized interest, essentially capitalizing unearned income, which cannot justify dividends.

An expert testified that the defendant’s real estate, valued at $36,195, was actually worth only $24,750, indicating an $11,445 overvaluation. The expert’s credibility was strong, yet the directors recorded no depreciation by December 31, 1932, despite market declines. Summarizing, loans receivable should be reduced by $8,650, affiliated loans by $6,120, and real estate by $11,445, totaling $26,215 in overvalued assets.

The company reported a $6,306.84 surplus and a $10,680 'reserved surplus,' totaling $16,986.84. However, with assets overstated by $26,215, no net assets existed to justify the $4,508 preferred dividend paid on January 1, 1933. Thus, this dividend should not count under the charter’s voting rights clause, nullifying the Class A common stock’s director election rights on July 10, 1933. The plaintiff’s challenge to these votes, however, faces objections.

He asserted that he attended the meeting and did not oppose the voting of that stock. In the case of Triplex Shoe Co. et al. v. Rice & Hutchins et al., the Delaware Supreme Court suggested in dictum that a stockholder present at a meeting, who consents to others voting no par value common stock (claimed to be unlawfully issued) and votes such stock himself, might be barred from contesting the stock's validity. This dictum, if upheld, extends the consent doctrine beyond what this case requires, as the validity of the stock issuance is not in dispute. The issue here is the less significant matter of voting rights for lawfully issued stock. A general principle holds that election legality will not be challenged based on illegal votes cast at the behest of stockholders who attended the meeting and raised no objections.

In cases like In re United Towns Bldg. & Loan Asso. and others, the rule states that stockholders cannot contest wrongdoing if their own inaction or tacit approval prevented timely correction. However, as noted in Wiltz v. Peters, this rule does not apply if the complaining party was unaware of the illegality and had no means to discover it at the time. This exception aligns with the reasoning in In re United Towns Bldg. & Loan Asso., where the court emphasized that the petitioner could have checked the stock books to verify voting eligibility.

The general principle that a stockholder's silence at a meeting bars later objections to improper votes must reasonably include the condition that they either knew of the votes' flaws or could have discovered them through reasonable diligence. Here, the disputed votes' invalidity hinged on whether the January 1, 1933, preferred dividend was unlawful, meaning two charter-mandated dividends had not been paid by the meeting date. Stockholders could reasonably assume the directors acted lawfully in declaring the dividend, especially since the directors' circulated statement indicated the company's financial health supported it.

It would be unreasonable to expect stockholders to independently investigate the directors' dividend declaration or the accuracy of the provided statement. This case is even more compelling than Cahall, Rec'r., v. Lofland et al., where the Chancellor ruled stockholders had no obligation to review corporate books available at the meeting. Thus, the complainant is not barred by his failure to object to the common stock votes at the meeting. However, the claim that his proxy raised no objection is disputed, creating a factual question unnecessary to resolve here. The preferred stockholders attempted to elect directors on July 17, 1933, after adjourning from the failed July 10, 1933, special meeting.

A quorum was not met as no notice for a meeting of preferred stockholders to elect directors was issued. Out of 1,127 outstanding preferred shares, 627 were present at the July 17th meeting, but the remaining 500 were entitled to notice. The June 20, 1933, notice did not inform preferred stockholders of the director election, implying it was for common stockholders. Thus, the July 17th election is invalid, and prior lawfully elected officers remain in place until successors are duly elected.

Since 1933, no annual meeting has been held, and one is now due. Unless preferred dividend defaults are resolved, only preferred stockholders may vote. The Chancellor noted that the Washington Fire Company of Wilmington was incorporated in 1841, with a defective 1849 act reincorporating it for 20 years. In 1866, deeds referenced the grantee as 'Washington Fire Company of said city,' raising identification issues.

The deeds described the grantee as 'Washington Fire Company of said city,' not its full name, leading to disputes over corporate identity. In 1869, an act reincorporated the company under a slightly different name for 20 years. Critics argue this did not renew the original corporation’s lifespan due to the name discrepancy.

An 1889 act reincorporated the company 11 days after the prior act’s expiration, raising claims that its property reverted to grantors. A 1895 amendment renamed the company to 'Washington Fire Company No. 7 of the City,' addressing prior inconsistencies in its legal identity.

In Wilmington, Delaware, Section 2 states that the company's charter and all related amendments are revised by replacing 'the Washington Steam Fire Engine and Hook and Ladder Company No. 7, of the City of Wilmington, Delaware,' with 'the Washington Fire Company No. 7 of the City of Wilmington, Delaware.' Three objections challenge the complainant's title as a marketable fee simple. These will be addressed in order. First, it is argued that the complainant is no longer a valid corporation due to discrepancies in the re-incorporation acts of 1869 and 1889, which refer to 'Washington Steam Fire Engine and Hook and Ladder Company,' while the original name was simply 'Washington Fire Company of the City of Wilmington.'

The Washington Fire Company of the City of Wilmington's corporate existence is not disputed in this proceeding. The court concludes that the complainant is indeed a lawful corporation, originally named Washington Fire Company of the City of Wilmington, which held title to the land in question. Legislative acts concerning this corporation's charter show carelessness, creating confusion about its status. However, based on the stipulations and a review of the acts, the conclusion is clear. The parties agree: '1. Since February 9, 1841, an organization known as the Washington Fire Company of the City of Wilmington, later renamed, has existed for fire prevention. This corporation initially received its charter under the original name.'

Fire Engine and Hook and Ladder Company, No. 7, of the City of Wilmington, Delaware, and later as the Washington Fire Company, No. 7, of the City of Wilmington, Delaware. The answer in the case confirms that this corporation was first chartered as the Washington Fire Company of the City of Wilmington. '2. The original corporation was intended to be renewed through legislative acts and is the complainant in this case. '3. Since 1841, only one corporation, the complainant, has continuously existed for firefighting, relying on these legislative acts. '6. No other corporation in Wilmington has used the same or a similar name or claimed benefits under these acts.' The acts mentioned in the stipulations are those referenced earlier in this opinion.

The admissions in the stipulations resolve the dispute between the parties. Names primarily serve identification purposes, and in legal documents, their importance lies in clarifying intent. The law prioritizes uncovering the intended meaning, even using external evidence when necessary. Legislative acts follow the same principle, with intent being paramount. Here, the parties agree that despite varying names in legislative acts, the same corporation was always intended. This agreement should settle the matter. Beyond the stipulations, the evidence further supports this conclusion.

It is quite evident from the actions of the parties that when considered collectively, these acts demonstrate the Legislature intended to refer to the same corporation in each instance. The initial act was enacted on February 9, 1841, naming the entity the Washington Fire Company of the City of Wilmington. A subsequent act in 1849 explicitly referenced the same corporation using its proper name. The 1869 act introduced a different name, but the reference to the original incorporation date of February 9, 1841, strongly suggests the same corporation was intended. Additionally, a review of published laws shows no other act from that date or prior to 1869 incorporating a company under the name used in the 1869 act. The 1889 act aligns with the 1869 act, clearly referring to the same corporation. The 1895 act then followed.

The 1895 act demonstrates the Legislature's recognition of the earlier error in the corporation's name. This act corrected the mistake by amending all prior acts and assigning the corporation the name it currently uses in this filing. The only reasonable interpretation of the 1895 act is that the Legislature sought to rectify a mistake. Given the interconnected nature of these acts, it is clear they were the ones the Legislature aimed to amend. Thus, the acts themselves provide sufficient evidence that the complainant corporation was the intended subject in all legislative acts, regardless of name variations. Names should not override intent, as they are merely tools to discern intent. If the intent is clear, errors in naming should not undermine the intended purpose.

In analyzing the legislative acts pertaining to this corporation, I have reviewed and endorse the following authorities, which support my conclusions: 2 Kent's Com., par 292; 2 Fletcher's Cyc. of Corporations, par. 742, p. 1696; A tty. Gen. v. Railroad Companies, 35 Wis. 425, 556; Cotton v. Miss. & Rum River Boom Co., 22 Minn. 372. It is also worth noting that since 1895, the complainant has been recognized as a de jure corporation, assuming it was one before that date. I affirm that it was, despite the name difference. Therefore, the defendant's argument—that he should not be obligated to fulfill the purchase contract because the complainant is not the same corporation that acquired the title from the Taggarts in 1866—is invalid.

The defendant further argues that the corporation, if it ever held title to the land, lost it by failing to reincorporate within the 20-year period specified in the 1869 act, resulting in the title reverting to the grantors' heirs. This argument is incorrect, as established in Diamond State Iron Co. v. Husbands, 8 Del. Ch. 205, 68 Atl. 240. Another contention is that the 1866 deeds did not transfer title to the complainant, then named 'The Washington Fire Company of the City of Wilmington.' The use of 'its successors and assigns' in the deeds confirms the grantee was a corporation. The name 'Washington Fire Company of said city' referred to Wilmington, Delaware, as indicated earlier in the deeds. Thus, the corporate name was sufficiently provided. However, unlike typical cases, the deeds did not explicitly state the grantee was a corporation.

However, this was not a significant oversight because, as previously mentioned, the deeds clearly indicate that the grantee was indeed a corporation. It is evident from the deeds that the Washington Fire Company of the City of Wilmington, a corporation, was the intended grantee. Furthermore, the stipulations filed in the case confirm that this corporation, albeit slightly misnamed, was the complainant and the intended recipient of the property.

The corporation, which has continuously existed under the same legislative acts, took possession of the land, paid taxes, leased it, and exercised ownership for fifty-five years, now seeks to transfer title. Given the deeds and stipulations, there is no doubt the complainant was the intended grantee in the 1866 conveyances. No objections to the title’s validity remain, and a decree will be issued granting the requested relief, with costs to be paid by the defendant within thirty days.

PER CURIAM: We uphold the trial court’s decision to deny the petition for the return of property seized during a search of the petitioner’s home. The Superior Court barred the petitioner from challenging the search’s legality, as these issues were already resolved in his criminal trial. The court found the petitioner failed to prove the property was not forfeitable and rejected his claims regarding jury trial waiver and due process violations.

On August 15, 1995, parole officer David Santobianco visited Brown’s home and witnessed drug activity, leading to a struggle and arrests. Later, a search uncovered drugs and money tied to drug dealing. Brown was convicted and sentenced to thirty years. His attempts to suppress the evidence and reclaim the property were denied, with the court ruling the seizure was justified and his claims were barred by collateral estoppel.

Revisiting the illegal search and seizure claims from his criminal trial, collateral estoppel is examined to confirm if these issues were fully litigated in prior court proceedings. This doctrine holds that factual determinations made in a final judgment are binding in subsequent cases involving the same parties, even under different legal claims. Delaware law extends this principle to criminal defendants in civil forfeiture cases, requiring only that the party against whom estoppel is asserted was previously involved. Under Delaware Superior Court Civil Rule 71.8(f), a convicted defendant cannot deny the core allegations of their offense in related proceedings, regardless of pending appeals. Brown’s petition, filed under Rule 71.3(e), is barred by collateral estoppel from challenging the search and seizure’s legality in this civil context, as these issues were already addressed during the suppression hearing in District Court.

The 1995 search of Brown’s residence was thoroughly examined during the suppression hearing, and the District Court’s failure to address every specific claim does not negate the fact that Brown had sufficient opportunity to raise them then. With competent legal representation, Brown cannot now use this Court to revisit claims he neglected to pursue earlier. Nevertheless, he retains the right to argue that the seized funds were lawfully obtained and thus not subject to forfeiture. Regarding the burden of proof, forfeiture decisions are reviewed for clear error. While this Court has not previously defined the parties’ burdens under Delaware’s Forfeiture Act, the Superior Court has consistently ruled that the State must first establish probable cause, after which the petitioner must rebut the forfeiture presumption. The Act presumes money found near controlled substances is forfeitable, and since the funds in question were discovered close to cocaine, the State met its initial burden, shifting the onus to Brown to prove otherwise.

Brown’s evidence of legitimate income resembling the seized amount was insufficient to overturn the trial court’s finding that he failed to rebut the forfeiture presumption. He also contested the trial court’s denial of a jury trial, a legal issue subject to de novo review. Under Rule 71.3, non-jury trials are standard unless a jury is explicitly demanded under Rule 38(b). Brown initiated the action, received notice of the non-jury trial, and never objected, later claiming ignorance of Rule 38(b). However, unawareness does not excuse the waiver of jury rights, and untimely demands are deemed forfeited. Brown’s due process claims, reviewed de novo, include the trial court’s refusal to provide a state-funded transcript. Despite his in forma pauperis status, Brown bore the responsibility for securing transcripts and offered no justification for his request, rendering the court’s denial proper.

Brown further alleged due process violations due to inadequate trial date notice and unissued witness subpoenas. The Sixth Amendment’s compulsory process right does not extend to civil cases, placing the onus on Brown to ensure witness attendance. Although the Prothonotary supplied subpoena forms and instructions, Brown presented no evidence of attempting to use them, failing to show prejudice from the court’s actions. Thus, his due process claims lack merit, as he neither demonstrated harm nor fulfilled his obligations as a civil litigant.

Brown claims the court did not provide adequate notice, an issue this Court can resolve. He also contends his due process rights were violated when the trial court did not force the State to respond to his discovery request. Although Brown filed his production request with the Prothonotary, he offers no proof it was served to the State. The Superior Court Civil Rules distinguish between filing and serving documents. Additionally, Brown raises due process and equal protection concerns about the trial judge. His claim about lacking notice of a judge change is baseless, as the trial had not started when the new judge was assigned. Brown had no right to know which judge would preside, so no notice was required. He also argues he should have been informed the new judge used hearing aids, but he fails to show any prejudice beyond speculation. Thus, his claim fails. Based on these reasons, we uphold the Superior Court's decision to deny Brown's property return petition. United States of America v.

Speakman, J., delivering the Court’s opinion: The central dispute is whether garnishment attached any of Mr. Warrick’s assets held by the garnishee. The garnishee argues commercial paper couldn’t be seized under common law, so checks—even if accepted by Mr. Satterthwaite—weren’t attachable. The plaintiff counters that (1) seizure via execution isn’t at issue here (though it might arise later), and (2) common-law rules don’t apply to certified checks like those involved. We address these points sequentially: (1) Commercial paper’s seizure via execution isn’t pertinent to garnishment if checks are viewed merely as tangible property. Such issues pertain to the initial attachment, not garnishment. However, since checks allegedly passed through Mr. Satterthwaite’s possession before being taken by the Deputy Sheriff, these details require brief examination.
The statute (Revised Code 1935, Section 4612) mandates: 'The sheriff or officer shall, under such writ [of attachment], seize all the...'

The defendant's real and personal property, along with his rights and credits, shall be located and seized. The officer must take control of these assets, inventory and appraise them, and be held accountable. If physical possession isn't possible, the officer must notify whoever holds these items, declaring them attached for the plaintiff's case and summoning the holder as a garnishee to appear as required. Evidence clearly shows Mr. Satterthwaite never had actual possession of the checks when the writ was served. They were on his desk, and he stated multiple times in the deputy's presence that he hadn't accepted them. The deputy could have taken them easily, as Mr. Satterthwaite's behavior made clear. Shortly after the writ was served, the deputy took possession under Mr. Logan's orders, confirmed by the sheriff's return and the checks being in custody by trial time.

After the writ was served, the deputy sheriff took possession of the checks under Mr. Logan's direction, as shown by the sheriff's return and the checks being held at trial. Given this, the sheriff had no legal grounds to notify Mr. Satterthwaite of the attachment. The validity of garnishing the checks or their related credits hinges on whether Mr. Satterthwaite had accepted them, which is disputed. We'll summarize the evidence on this alleged acceptance and explain why it doesn’t merit the initial attention it seems to warrant. On April 5, 1938, the chancellor denied a bill of review regarding Mr. Warrick's allowance and ordered the receivers to pay him. An appeal to the Supreme Court resulted in an affirming opinion on October 11, 1938. Before this, the receivers had prepared checks for Mr. Satterthwaite as Mr. Warrick's attorney, anticipating the court's decision.

Prior to the Supreme Court's October 11, 1938, order, the receivers had issued checks to Mr. Satterthwaite as Mr. Warrick's attorney. Delays in obtaining a receiver's signature from Chicago prompted early preparation. Mr. Logan, representing both the receivers and the plaintiff, received the checks before October 11. On that day, while in Dover, he instructed his secretary to certify the checks. Returning to Wilmington by 2 PM, he found them certified. The lawsuit began around 3 PM, and he scheduled a 4:15 PM meeting with Mr. Satterthwaite to exchange the checks for documents, with a deputy sheriff ready to serve the writ. Mr. Satterthwaite arrived on time, and the exchange occurred just before the deputy entered.

Mr. Satterthwaite arrived as scheduled, and the checks and documents were exchanged. Immediately after receiving the checks, he placed them on the desk and stated he hadn’t accepted them. The deputy sheriff then served the writ. Before leaving, Mr. Logan told Mr. Satterthwaite in the deputy's presence that the checks were attached. The deputy’s subsequent seizure, approved by Mr. Logan and reflected in the sheriff's return, confirmed the checks were in custody by trial. This sequence raises questions about the checks' acceptance, but the evidence suggests this issue may not be as critical as it initially appears.

The Sheriff advised, 'You should take these checks,' but Mr. Satterthwaite responded, 'No, I refuse to take them.' He frequently reiterated this refusal in front of the Deputy Sheriff, stating, 'I did not accept the checks.' After Mr. Satterthwaite departed, Mr. Logan told the Deputy Sheriff, 'You may as well take them since Mr. Satterthwaite clearly didn’t want them.' Mr. Logan also testified about his concerns regarding the Sheriff’s return to the writ of attachment, noting he was worried about the proper handling given the unusual situation of the checks being left in his office and the Sheriff taking them on his instruction. He confirmed he gave no specific directions on preparing the return but was content with the outcome. If the garnishee’s claim that Mr. Satterthwaite never accepted the checks is true, yet the Sheriff seized them, this would not justify garnishment proceedings against Mr.

Satterthwaite. However, if Mr. Satterthwaite had accepted the checks from Mr. Logan, which were then taken by the Deputy Sheriff, the issue remains whether Mr. Satterthwaite held any money or credits belonging to Mr. Warrick at the time of the writ’s service or before the 'Nulla Bona' plea. Whether he possessed such funds, even if he accepted the checks, hinges on whether the checks’ acceptance acted as an assignment of the underlying funds. For uncertified ordinary checks, acceptance would not constitute such an assignment, as clarified by Sec. 3313 of the Revised Code of 1935. The plaintiff argues that certified checks follow different rules regarding fund assignment, which may be true, but this discussion requires first examining

who initiated the certification, as this is critically important. Regarding the checks’ certification, Henry T. Bush, a receiver, testified: 'Q. Did you personally certify these checks? A. I did not. Q. Were you aware of their certification? A. I knew nothing about it, as I was away when it happened. Q. Do you know who arranged the certification? A. I do not. Q. Could it have been Mr. Logan? A. Possibly; he might have instructed it. Q. Did you order anyone to certify the checks? A. No. Q. So, you were unaware they were certified? A. Correct, due to my absence. Q. Was certification required by the court? A. No. Q. Then the certification was unauthorized by the receivers? A. Yes, though the bank likely acted on the receivers’ counsel’s instructions, which seems standard. Q. But the receivers never directed the certification? A. No.' The evidence shows neither Mr. Warrick nor his representatives requested certification, nor did the makers authorize it. It appears Mr. Logan sought certification as the plaintiff’s attorney, not for the receivers, making him a stranger to the checks. Thus, we must now analyze the legal principles governing fund assignment via certified checks, particularly when certification was initiated by a third party.

The plaintiff acknowledges that Section 188 (Section 3312, Revised Code of 1935) of the Negotiable Instruments Law pertains to the rules surrounding certified checks, especially when the certification was not requested by the payee but by an unrelated party. This distinction is vital for determining whether the acceptance of such checks transfers the funds they represent. The evidence confirms that the certifications were not authorized by the receivers or the makers, raising questions about their validity and legal effect. The focus now shifts to applying the relevant legal standards to assess whether the checks’ acceptance under these circumstances constitutes an assignment of funds, a key issue in resolving the dispute.

impact of a certification obtained by the recipient. The plaintiff bases their argument on Section 189 (Section 3313, Revised Code of 1935) of the law, which states: 'A check alone does not transfer any portion of the drawer's bank funds, and the bank is not responsible to the holder unless it accepts or certifies the check.' Clearly, the National Conference aimed to alter the law in adopting states, ensuring that holders of uncertified checks would no longer be considered assignees of the underlying funds. This aligns with the stance of the State Supreme Court, as seen in Polotsky v. Artisans Savings Bank, where it was ruled that an uncertified check is merely a revocable order.

The focus is on interpreting the phrase 'and the bank is not liable to the holder, unless and until it accepts or certifies the cheque' in the cited section. According to legal understanding, when a bank certifies a check—whether requested by the drawer or holder—it enters into a contractual agreement that significantly alters its relationship with the involved parties. It is unclear how a third party's request could justify such a change. The certifications in question, obtained by an unrelated party, do not affect the contractual ties between Mr. Warrick or his attorney and the drawers or the bank. This perspective was upheld in Central Hanover Bank & Trust Co.

v. The Mirror, where the court noted: 'Certification by an unauthorized party does not constitute acceptance or reassign funds.' This was supported by Gasper v. Security State Bank, a case under the Uniform Negotiable Instruments Law. However, the plaintiff argues that the receivers authorized the certifications. Regarding pre-delivery certification, 7 Am. Jur. states, supported by multiple precedents, that certification by the drawer before delivery does not alter the drawer's liability to the holder. It merely enhances the check's credibility by binding the bank.

responsibilities, and commitments between the drawer and payee or holder remain unchanged. A drawer who certifies a check before delivery remains liable to the holder until payment. Certification only boosts the instrument's credibility by involving the drawee bank's obligation, without altering its legal standing. The plaintiff heavily references Mclntire v. Raskin, where the court affirmed that certification or acceptance of a check effectively assigns the drawer's funds to cover the check, consistent with the principle that uncertified checks do not transfer funds unless certified.

The court distinguishes between certification at the payee's request and the drawer's request, noting that certification by the payee makes the bank the absolute debtor, while certification by the drawer assures the check's validity, leaving both the bank and the drawer liable, with the bank primarily responsible.

This distinction is supported by various legal cases, including Railway Express Agency v. Thomas and Florida P. & L. Co. v. Tomasello. The Mclntire case is interpreted as holding that a certified check acts as an assignment to the bank, aligning with Downey v. Citizens' State Bank, where certification by the drawer assigns the check amount to the bank.

Accepting the plaintiff's argument would imply the funds were assigned to Mr. Satterthwaite, satisfying the chancellor's order, which we reject. Whether certification constitutes acceptance, freezes funds, or assigns them to the bank, the drawee bank remains a debtor to the check holder, with no debtor-creditor relationship between Mr. Satterthwaite and Mr. Warrick until payment.

The correct rule, as stated in Commercial Inv. Trust v. Windsor, is that delivering a pre-certified check maintains the same obligations between drawer and payee as under the Uniform Negotiable Instruments Law, which had been in effect in North Carolina for about two decades by 1929.

II. IMPACT OF A PANEL DECISION BY THIS COURT ON A CERTIFIED LEGAL QUESTION IN A CAPITAL CASE The statutory aggravating factor in question, 11 Del.C. § 4209(e)(l)s., mandates that the victim be 'a child aged 14 or younger.' This law took effect on July 14, 1994. No prior Delaware court has interpreted this specific language, making it a matter of first impression. The Court is convened as a panel to address this certified legal question. It is fitting for a panel to resolve such a certified question before trial, even in a death penalty case. According to Del. Const. Art. IV, § 12, and Supreme Court Rule 4, the Court must sit en banc in cases involving a death sentence. However, since the defendant has not yet been convicted or sentenced, no trial has occurred. The trial's outcome hinges on the resolution of the certified question. We need not speculate on the implications of a potential death sentence based on this aggravating factor, as that would be addressed by the en banc Court if such a scenario arises.

this statutory aggravating circumstance. In such an event, the en banc Court would determine the impact of this decision on the certified question. III. ARGUMENTS OF THE PARTIES The State argues that the phrase '14 years of age or younger' includes any child who has not yet reached their fifteenth birthday. The defendant counters that this aggravating factor ceases to apply once a child has passed their fourteenth birthday. As framed in the certified question, the defendant cites Farrow v. State, Del.Supr., 258 A.2d 276 (1969), where this Court interpreted 'over the age of 16 years' under former 11 Del.C. § 468A(c) (felony firearm possession). In Farrow, the Court ruled that the defendant was correctly tried as an adult for firearm possession during a felony because he had already turned sixteen. The Court stated: In everyday language, a child turns one year old on their first birthday and sixteen on their sixteenth birthday. Before this anniversary, they are under sixteen; after, they are over sixteen. Farrow, 258 A.2d at 277.

IV. RELEVANT STATUTORY INTERPRETATION PRINCIPLES A detailed discussion of statutory construction principles is unnecessary here. Per 1 Del.C. § 303, statutes, including criminal ones, must be interpreted according to standard English usage. Under 11 Del.C. § 221(c), criminal statutes should carry their ordinary meaning, aligned with the purposes outlined in § 201 of the Criminal Code. Whenever possible, statutes should be construed sensibly, in line with constitutional principles, and to avoid unreasonable or absurd outcomes. See Snell v. Engineered Sys. & Designs, Inc., Del.Supr., 669 A.2d 13, 20-21 (1995).

V. APPLYING CONSTRUCTION PRINCIPLES TO THE CERTIFIED QUESTION The defendant's interpretation implies the statutory aggravating factor only applies if the victim is murdered on or before their fourteenth birthday. Under this view, the statute would not cover a victim killed even one day after turning fourteen. This interpretation contradicts common sense. In everyday usage, a person is considered a certain age from one birthday until the next. Thus, a child who has turned fourteen remains fourteen until their fifteenth birthday. Therefore, the aggravating factor applies here, as the victim had turned fourteen but not fifteen. Farrow does not dictate otherwise, as it addressed the phrase 'over the age of sixteen,' which differs significantly from the current statute's language regarding a victim 'fourteen years old or younger.'

The statute in question differs from the one in Farrow, which functioned as a 'threshold' statute, taking effect once a defendant turned sixteen. The Farrow court interpreted it as applying to the defendant's age for the rest of their life. In contrast, the current statute, 11 Del. C. § 4209(e)(l)s., ceases to apply once the victim turns fifteen. Here, the victim was fourteen, placing them between their fourteenth and fifteenth birthdays. Farrow is irrelevant as it addresses a different statutory framework. Thus, we answer the certified question negatively and remand the case to the Superior Court with immediate effect, retaining no further jurisdiction. The former statute, now 11 Del.C. § 1447(d), states that individuals over sixteen charged under this section will be tried as adults.

This case is before the Court en Banc following a remand to the Family Court, as directed by the decision in *In the Interest of Kelly Stevens* ('Stevens I'). The background involves efforts to terminate Thomas P. Dillard's parental rights over his daughter, Kelly Stevens. In *Stevens I*, we affirmed the Family Court's application of Delaware's termination statutes but remanded for an assessment of Dillard's litigation conduct and his failure to pursue visitation. After remand, the Family Court heard extensive testimony, including psychological evidence, and concluded that Dillard had not made meaningful efforts to establish a relationship with Kelly, delaying visitation petitions and refusing to cooperate with evaluations.

The Family Court's report detailed several findings: (i) Dillard delayed seeking visitation until termination proceedings resumed; (ii) he refused to communicate with the assigned social agency; (iii) he ignored court directives to plan for reintroduction into Kelly's life and missed a key hearing; (iv) he engaged in federal litigation to delay state proceedings, exposing Kelly to undue publicity; (v) he avoided discussions with Kelly's Court Appointed Special Advocate; and (vi) his psychological profile revealed an obsessive focus on parental rights at the expense of a genuine relationship. The court found his conduct demonstrated abandonment of any caring parental role.

After establishing statutory grounds for termination, the Family Court evaluated Kelly's best interests, finding she had formed a strong bond with her long-term caregivers. The petition was granted to facilitate her adoption by them. Our review is limited to ensuring the factual findings are logical and legally sound, as outlined in *Stevens I*. The Family Court properly applied the law, and the evidence overwhelmingly supported termination to secure Kelly's stable future with her de facto parents.

In A.2d at 23, Dillard argues in this appeal that the Family Court violated procedural fairness during the remand proceedings. He claims the court-appointed psychologist's independence was compromised due to information from opposing counsel, though the expert testified her evaluation relied on objective tests and personal analysis, unaffected by external materials. Additionally, Dillard's complaint about denied access to Kelly for hearing preparation lacks merit, as the court reasonably denied a face-to-face meeting with his estranged daughter but granted access to her medical and school records.

The Family Court's decision to withhold a confrontation between Dillard and his young daughter, given potential psychological harm, was within its discretion. The court provided sufficient discovery by releasing Kelly's medical, school, and Division of Family Services records, ensuring Dillard had necessary information for his case. Dillard further alleges procedural error, claiming the court prematurely applied the 'best interests' test before confirming abandonment. However, the court’s report shows it addressed abandonment first under 13 Del.C. § 1101(1), and presenting evidence out of sequence was not improper given judicial discretion in managing trials.

Dillard’s assertion that the Family Court’s findings lack substantial evidence or logical consistency is unfounded. On remand, the court reassessed his 'good faith and subjective intent,' concluding his parental efforts were superficial and insincere. The record supports that Dillard prioritized litigation over genuine engagement with his daughter, meeting the legal definition of abandonment. Furthermore, evidence overwhelmingly favors Kelly’s best interests being served by remaining with her adoptive parents, the only family she has known.

SYNOPSIS The Plaintiff has filed a Motion for Reargument seeking to alter the Court’s January 3, 2013, Order. The Motion challenges three aspects: the Order’s description of the DSM as non-peer-reviewed, an alleged mix-up between 'suppression' and 'repression,' and the characterization of the police encounter as 'trauma.' These claims lack merit, and none affected the Order’s outcome, leading to the Motion’s denial.

DISCUSSION The description of the DSM as non-peer-reviewed has been misunderstood. 'Peer-reviewed' refers to academic work evaluated by independent experts selected by a journal, not by the authors themselves. It is a technical term, not a judgment. Notably, the former DSM editor declined inclusion in the latest edition due to disagreements, highlighting the lack of unanimous consensus. However, this is irrelevant here, as the DSM and related materials only peripherally address repression timing. None reliably establish when repression occurs, justifying the exclusion of this testimony, as detailed in the prior decision.

Addressing the claim that the Order confused 'suppression' with 'repression,' Dr. Tavani explicitly acknowledged conscious suppression leading to traumatic amnesia (T: p.1061.23). Additionally, while dissociative amnesia differs from normal forgetting (T: p.28 1.7 & p.196 1), this distinction does not alter the prior ruling. The Motion’s arguments, even if technically correct, do not impact the Order’s validity, reinforcing its denial.

At times, she alternated between discussing Plaintiff's condition using two distinct mechanisms. For instance, she stated: 'whether he forgot immediately or .' (T: p.104 1.12); and 'a portion of individuals who forget, experiencing traumatic dissociative amnesia .' (T: p.79 1.11); and most explicitly, 'I believe he forgot during that period .' (T: p.105 1.10) (all emphasis added). The reality is that the distinctions made between 'repression,' 'suppression,' and 'forgetting' often became unclear or interchangeable throughout the testimony. Nonetheless, these nuances are irrelevant. The key takeaway is that there isn't enough scientific basis to allow expert testimony on the timing of repression. Additionally, Plaintiff mentions the Court's misinterpretation of 'the trauma.' Two distressing events were repeatedly mentioned: the alleged sexual actions and the police encounter. While the rape would undoubtedly be traumatic if it occurred as Plaintiff claims, the hearing's focus is on evaluating the timing of repression, not distinguishing between two events likely happening within weeks of each other.

Despite this, the testimony frequently emphasized that Plaintiff was deeply unsettled by the police's presence on the boardwalk. According to Dr. Tavani, this realization triggered a chain of thoughts leading to fear of arrest and Ferris School, which troubled Plaintiff. Dr. Tavani suggested this mental process might have caused the repression—or it could have been the sexual incident itself. Either event could theoretically lead to repression. Whether one labels these events as trauma, shock, or concern is unimportant. The phrasing holds no significance, as Plaintiff's expert cannot scientifically determine the exact timing of memory repression. She admits she cannot definitively pinpoint whether repression occurred during the assault or the police encounter, only that it happened within a certain timeframe. This is her opinion, clearly stated. However, her clinical experience and references (like the DSM) lack the scientific rigor needed to support her claims about repression timing for admissible jury testimony.

The complexities of memory—its persistence or fleeting nature—remain imprecise, as noted by Dr. Tavani, Dr. Toborowski, the DSM, and other cited texts. Friedrich Nietzsche, a philosopher unrelated to psychology, once remarked: 'The existence of forgetting has never been proven; we only know some things elude recall when needed.' Over a century later, little progress may have been made. Regardless, Plaintiff's Motion for Reargument does not change the Court's January 3, 2013, decision. The Motion is DENIED. Clendaniel's counsel contested the Associate Judge's authority, arguing the enabling statute, Chapter 189, Volume 26 of Delaware Laws, was unconstitutional and thus invalid.

Clendaniel's objection was dismissed by the Associate Judge, who denied the motion to reject the petition and postponed further proceedings until May 11, 1912. Later, on May 3, 1912, Clendaniel petitioned the court for a writ of prohibition to halt the Associate Judge's actions. His petition questioned the constitutionality of Chapter 189 and alleged the corporation lacked a genuine plan to dedicate the entire 200-foot-wide boulevard to public use, except for a vehicular road. Six identical affidavits accompanied the petition, claiming Thomas Coleman du Pont admitted no concrete plans existed for public use of the remaining land.

These affidavits, signed by William I. Simpson and others, asserted that du Pont acknowledged no definite plans for the unused boulevard portion, only vague future intentions. The court then issued a rule for the defendants to justify why the writ should not be granted, returnable by May 11, 1912. On the return date, the Associate Judge submitted a certified copy of the proceedings, while other defendants filed a sworn response affirming their intent to dedicate the entire boulevard to public use, presenting a development plan.

The defendants' response included Thomas Coleman du Pont's affidavit refuting the six affidavits and additional statements denying the petitioner's claims. Beyond the constitutional debate, a factual dispute arose outside the record. The defendants also argued the statute conflicted with Section 16, Article 2 of the state Constitution.

By modifying Chapter 273, Volume 21 of Delaware's Laws, which is titled 'An act providing a general corporation law,' this amendment includes provisions unrelated to the chapter's subject and not mentioned in its title. Additionally, the amendatory act, Chapter 189, Volume 26, violates constitutional requirements by addressing multiple subjects. The Constitution states that no bill, except those appropriating public funds, should cover more than one subject, which must be clearly stated in its title. Many states have similar constitutional rules, and court decisions largely agree on the provision's intent and scope. As seen in Monaghan v. Lewis, the courts emphasize preventing unrelated matters in a single act and avoiding deceptive provisions not hinted at in the title.

The purpose of this constitutional rule is to avoid combining unrelated topics in one act and to prevent hidden provisions not reflected in the title. While the provision should be enforced to prevent misuse, it shouldn't hinder legitimate legislation that substantially complies. The act should be upheld if its parts relate directly or indirectly to the main subject. The title need only broadly state the act's purpose without detailing every aspect. As Judge Cooley notes in Constitutional Limitations, such provisions should be interpreted liberally to avoid unnecessarily obstructing legislation.

A broad title isn't problematic unless it hides unrelated or incongruous laws. In People v. Gaslight Co., the court ruled that a general title can encompass many specific topics. Applying this to the current case, the amendatory act's title is very general, as is the act it modifies. The plaintiff argues that the amendment includes provisions unrelated to the original act's subject and not mentioned in its title, violating the single-subject rule. To prove this, they examine legislative records and the bill itself.

Legislative records, including the Governor's message, can sometimes clarify a bill's intent, but here, they reveal nothing beyond what the bill itself shows. The plaintiff cites State v. Ferschke, emphasizing that a bill's title should fairly notify the public and lawmakers of its content. They argue that neither the original title, 'An act providing a general corporation law,' nor the amendment's title adequately conveys the unrelated provisions included in the act.

The title of the amendatory act would suggest that the state's highway system was involved, proposing a new state road, creating a new state official, and introducing public expenses. Critics argue that the title of the amendatory act is no clearer than the original, with the added phrase 'by authorizing the organization of boulevard corporations' misleadingly implying the bill's purpose was to form street construction companies. While it’s acknowledged that boulevard corporations could have been included in the general corporation act, opponents stress that the amendatory act includes provisions unrelated to boulevard corporations. The key issue is whether authorizing such corporations conflicts with the constitutional provision, hinging on the definition of 'boulevard.'

Originally, 'boulevard' meant 'a promenade on a demolished fortification,' but it later came to mean 'a broad street or walkway lined with trees.' Today, it carries an even broader meaning, suggesting an attractive, wide highway for transporting people and goods by various means. A boulevard from Wilmington to the state’s southern border implies a state highway adorned with trees and landscaping. The bill’s general subject aligns with its title—a broad public highway—and the legislature could reasonably include provisions for modern transportation methods like railways, telegraphs, and pipelines, which are not incongruous with boulevard corporations.

The act’s provisions do not represent separate subjects but are interconnected ideas related to boulevard corporations. For constitutional purposes, distinct subjects only arise if they are incongruous. Authorities agree that if provisions relate to the same subject, are naturally connected, and align with the title, they are constitutional. An act may include pertinent details under one general subject, and provisions for a corporation’s operation, regulation, and maintenance are permissible under a title authorizing its organization. As Chief Justice Parker noted, regulations for a completed railroad are germane to its construction, and such provisions can be added by amendment without violating the constitution.

In some cases, courts have ruled that provisions allowing towns to subscribe to a railroad company’s stock and issue bonds were not foreign to the title, rejecting claims that such statutes unconstitutionally combined distinct subjects. Critics argued these laws improperly merged railroad incorporation with municipal powers, but courts found them valid if the provisions were germane to the general subject. Similarly, amendments to the boulevard corporation act are constitutional if they relate to the original subject and could have been included initially.

It is evident that the oversight and governance of boulevard corporations, along with the creation, oversight, and regulation of the public utilities referenced in the act, can all be reasonably considered part of the definition of a boulevard and are relevant to its broader purpose. [6] However, some argue that the statute addresses multiple subjects by mandating that a portion of the boulevard be transferred to and maintained by the state, while the rest remains under private corporate control. This requirement does not diminish the conveyed portion's role as part of the boulevard, which encompasses the entire land strip authorized for acquisition. The act envisions a unified public improvement plan, where the entire strip forms an indivisible boulevard entity. While certain utilities or amenities like walks and trees may occupy areas outside the vehicular road, the entire strip must remain accessible for public use.

The argument posits that assigning a thirty-foot strip to the state’s care and the remaining one hundred seventy feet to a private corporation creates a complete separation, as if they were on opposite state boundaries. However, the act specifies that all corporate actions must occur on land acquired for the boulevard, reinforcing the strip’s indivisibility. State ownership of the thirty-foot strip is inherently tied to the boulevard corporation’s formation. The legislature had the authority to impose this transfer as a condition for the corporation’s right to build and manage the boulevard. If constructing the vehicular road aligns with the act’s purpose, its maintenance logically does as well. Thus, requiring the road’s transfer to the state does not detach it from the overarching subject.

How does transferring the road to the state disconnect it from the boulevard’s general purpose? It remains the most critical component. While the statute addresses multiple elements like railways and utilities, these are integral parts of the boulevard’s broader framework. In State v. Electric Co., a provision requiring profit-sharing with the state was deemed valid under an act titled for canal construction, as it was a reasonable condition tied to the grant. Similarly, the boulevard act’s provisions for utilities and state compensation are not extraneous. The title encompasses canal and lock construction, and the act appropriately includes operational terms, including state compensation, without violating constitutional rules.

The act’s provision exempting boulevard company property from taxation does not breach constitutional requirements. This issue was addressed in National Loan & Investment Co. v. City of Detroit, where a tax exemption for building and loan associations under a similarly titled act was upheld. The court emphasized a broad interpretation of the title-subject alignment. The boulevard act’s primary aim is to establish state boulevards featuring vehicular roads, with remaining land serving ancillary purposes. The exemptions and provisions are germane to this objective, ensuring compliance with constitutional standards.

Its sensible design and function could be enhanced with trees, pathways, and other parking amenities, or allocated partly to these uses and partly to public utilities referenced in the act. None of these purposes, we believe, conflict with the bill's central theme of state boulevards, as indicated in the title. Thus, it is irrelevant that the bill includes state maintenance of the road, introduces a new state official, and incurs extra public costs. These are regulatory details, secondary to the primary goal of establishing and managing a statewide boulevard. Any uncertainty about the term 'boulevard' encompassing the bill's provisions would have been dispelled by public knowledge during the legislative process. References to the Governor's message and public debates show that the bill's comprehensive scope was understood.

The plaintiff's cited cases do not contradict our conclusion. Their argument hinges on viewing the bill's provisions as separate subjects, treating the road and other utilities as unrelated. We see the boulevard as a unified concept, encompassing both the road and ancillary utilities or landscaping. The cited cases mostly involve misleading or overly narrow titles, unlike this bill's broad and transparent title, which adequately informs legislators and the public of its intent. The title's generality ensures it meets the requirement of providing reasonable notice of the proposed legislation.

The General Corporation Law aimed to establish a comprehensive framework for forming, regulating, and managing corporations, including classification and varying powers. If the original act complies with constitutional requirements despite covering diverse corporations, an amendment adding boulevard corporations should not be deemed unconstitutional. The amendment, like the original act, addresses a single subject and clearly expresses it in the title. We find no grounds to invalidate it for violating constitutional constraints on legislative scope.

The plaintiff argues the statute breaches constitutional bans on special acts for creating corporations or regulating roads. While the act could not authorize a special corporation or road via special legislation, the question is whether it is inherently special or local. Emphasis was placed on the law's impetus from Mr. T. Coleman du Pont, who pledged to fulfill its mandates. However, the act's validity depends on its general applicability, not the circumstances of its proposal.

They were unique, but this does not inherently define the nature of the act—whether specific or broad. Numerous, and possibly most, general laws are proposed to the Legislature, and their enactment, in a way, ensured due to particular circumstances at the time. Frequently, the need for a general law only becomes apparent when individual interests or desires are impacted or stimulated. Someone might request legislation favoring their own benefit, and the Legislature may decide such a law would serve the public good, leading to a general statute. Using the defendant’s counsel’s fitting example: Imagine our General Corporation Law excluded electric railways. It’s highly probable that soon after its passage, an amendment would have been proposed to include this utility, driven by someone’s intent to build and run an electric railway. The key trait of a general law is its uniform application to all similarly situated individuals. We find no need to revisit the numerous cases cited on this matter.

The rulings across states on this topic are vast, yet the core principles remain consistent, as clearly outlined in Lewis' Sutherland Statutory Construction (2d Ed.) §§ 195, 196. 'A statute addressing a class of persons or things is general; one targeting specific members of a class is special. The boundary between general and special laws may appear blurred, but adhering to the underlying principles reduces the complexity. A law is constitutionally general if it uniformly applies to all members of a class needing distinct legislation, whereas a special law pertains to particular members of a class, either explicitly named or selectively distinguished.' The same source in Section 203, citing Van Riper v. Parsons, 40 N.J. Law, states: 'A law phrased broadly, not limited by location, and affecting all members of a group defined by significant traits is general, even if only one such member or place exists.'

Further, the same authority (Section 215) notes: 'The count of individuals impacted by a law doesn’t dictate its validity; it suffices that the law addresses a general subject and operates uniformly on all meeting its criteria.' Applying these principles here, can there be any question that the statute is general? It is framed broadly, allowing any five individuals to form a boulevard corporation. The boulevard envisioned isn’t confined locally but spans the state. The act’s benefits are equally accessible to all, with no restrictions based on location or time.

Over six months passed after the act’s approval before the 'Coleman du Pont Road, Incorporated' was formed, during which any five persons could have organized such a corporation. Doubt arises only if the classifications under the statute are artificial or unreasonable. As Clark and Marshall on Corporations (Vol. 1, p. 105) states: 'An act enabling corporate formation or granting privileges isn’t special merely because it doesn’t apply universally, so long as it operates uniformly for all in similar circumstances. Classification is permissible if reasonable and inclusive of all qualifying persons or corporations.'

The classification must not be arbitrary or without reason. It should be a genuine classification, based on differences that have a fair and logical connection to the purpose for which the classification was created. The statute in question categorizes corporations, specifically boulevard corporations. The legislative intent focused on boulevards, and we believe this classification is neither artificial nor unreasonable, given the definition of 'boulevard.' Existing state laws already recognized classes like electric railway and pipeline corporations. The new statute introduces boulevard corporations, which may encompass not just roads but also utilities like walks and trees, distinguishing them from ordinary highways.

The classification of boulevard corporations is valid and distinct. It is not unreasonable simply because it is a newer concept arising from modern conditions, absent from earlier laws. As stated in State ex rel. v. Parsons, a law applying uniformly to a well-defined group with clear characteristics is general, not special. We find no constitutional conflict in this statute.

It is argued that the statute's land-taking authority for eminent domain does not serve public use, violating the state Constitution. The objection centers on the optional nature of utility construction by the private corporation. However, as noted in Attorney General v. Williams, public use evolves with societal progress. Similarly, Tuttle v. Moore highlights that public use expands as community needs grow.

Courts disagree on 'public use,' but we believe taking land for boulevards—which may include highways, railways, and other utilities—qualifies. If highways are public uses, so are boulevards, which encompass them and more. Precedent, like Whiteman v. R. R. Co., supports delegating eminent domain to private corporations for public projects like highways.

The right of eminent domain may be invoked when the state's interest or convenience is at stake, such as acquiring land for roads, canals, or other public projects. This authority can be exercised through corporations or private initiatives for public benefits. As noted in Mills on Eminent Domain (2d Ed.) § 21, 'public use' is adaptable and not limited to historical definitions. It includes any improvement serving public needs, like travel, communication, or commodity transport. Each component of the boulevard—roads, railways, utilities, and landscaping—has been recognized as serving a public purpose. However, the plaintiff argues the statute fails to mandate public use for the taken land.

The court acknowledges this as the most challenging issue in the case, warranting thorough scrutiny. The core question is whether the Legislature can permit individuals or corporations to condemn land for public use without ensuring its actual public benefit or use over an extended period. While 30 feet of the strip must serve as a road, the remaining 170 feet lacks specific public-use requirements, leaving its use to the corporation's discretion. The plaintiff's concern about potential private use is dismissed, as the statute permits non-road portions to be used for any lawful purpose. However, the delegation of eminent domain implies only public uses are intended.

The phrase 'any other purpose' in the statute should be interpreted narrowly, referring to purposes similar or incidental to the boulevard's public functions. It does not grant broader privileges than those explicitly stated. This interpretation aligns with legal precedents, such as In re Barre Water Co. and Slingerland v. Newark, which emphasize that such terms must be construed in context. The statute's language likely limits uses to those consistent with the boulevard's public objectives, ensuring no deviation from its intended purpose.

The argument that the statute is unconstitutional for not explicitly guaranteeing public access or benefits lacks merit. While a distinction exists between public use and public benefit, courts recognize both. Even without explicit statutory language, a corporation exercising eminent domain implicitly commits to serving the public. Legal authorities, like Lewis on Eminent Domain and Nichols on the Power of Eminent Domain, affirm that public service obligations need not be expressly stated but are inherent in the exercise of such powers. Thus, the public's right to the boulevard's benefits is presumed.

A corporation that accepts a charter from the state implicitly agrees to provide the public with adequate and suitable facilities for transporting passengers and goods. It can be mandated to fulfill this duty, and if more land is necessary, it may be compelled to acquire and compensate for it. In Thoroughgood v. Georgetown Water Co., 77 Atl. 720, the Court of Chancery stated that when a private corporation engaged in public utilities receives public benefits like franchises or eminent domain rights, it assumes an obligation to serve the public purpose behind those grants. Often, the law granting eminent domain doesn’t explicitly require public service, but the corporation implicitly accepts this duty by exercising the power. This principle was echoed in Borden v. Irrigation Co., 98 Tex. 494, 86 S. W. 11, 107.

In modern times, it is widely accepted that accepting a franchise to operate railways, telegraphs, or similar utilities, along with eminent domain rights, entails public duties. This was affirmed in Turnpike Co. v. News Co., 43 N. J. Law, 381, where the court ruled that telegraph companies, by accepting legislative benefits and eminent domain, must allow public use of their lines under reasonable rules. The court emphasized that such acceptance implies a public obligation, justifying eminent domain. Similarly, in this case, the company’s acceptance of the act’s benefits and eminent domain power obligates it to public service. The act’s provisions further clarify that the boulevard and its components are intended for public use, with all elements serving public utilities and benefits.

The statute clearly designates the boulevard’s elements as public utilities, all aimed at public benefit. The state’s agents determine its location, and the state owns and maintains the vehicular travel portion. This underscores that the land taken is for public use, with the public entitled to its benefits, and the company obligated to dedicate it to such use. The plaintiff argues that land taken for public use must be strictly necessary, questioning whether a 200-foot strip is reasonable for a boulevard requiring only a 30-foot road. While 30 feet might suffice for the road alone, additional space is needed for construction and operation. However, the land is being acquired not just for the road but for the entire boulevard, which encompasses more than just vehicular travel.

The plaintiff’s claim that a 200-foot width is excessive for a boulevard is not strongly supported. While 30 feet may suffice for the road itself, extra land is necessary for ancillary purposes. The boulevard, as a whole, includes more than just the road, justifying the broader land requirement. The entity in question is the boulevard itself, with the road being only one component. Thus, the taking of the plaintiff’s land under eminent domain is justified for the broader public use of the boulevard, not merely the narrower road.

While the corporation is explicitly mandated to build only the road on the entire strip of land to be acquired, it is implicitly obligated to utilize the entire strip for public benefit, as dictated by the act's intent. Given this, can it be argued that a 200-foot-wide strip is excessive for a boulevard featuring a 30-foot vehicular road, with the remainder legally dedicated to public uses under the statute? Since these uses are public, both the necessity of eminent domain and the land quantity required are legislative decisions, as noted in legal texts.

The welfare and necessity of invoking eminent domain rest solely with the Legislature, as affirmed by legal authorities like Tiedeman, who states that courts cannot challenge the taking's necessity if it serves a public purpose. This principle is echoed in Delaware's judicial rulings, such as Wilson v. B. & P. R. R. Co., where the Legislature's exclusive authority to determine the expediency of eminent domain was upheld.

The Legislature's discretion in determining the amount of land taken for public use is nearly absolute, barring extreme abuse or fraud, which is not alleged here. As emphasized by Mills and McGehee, legislative judgment on the scope of eminent domain is final, with compensation being the sole constraint. This aligns with U.S. Supreme Court rulings affirming Congress's authority to decide land width for public projects.

Precedents like Northern Pac. R. R. Co. v. Smith demonstrate that legislative decisions on land width for public works, such as railroads, are conclusive. The courts defer to such determinations, reinforcing the principle that the Legislature's judgment on necessity and extent of eminent domain is binding, provided just compensation is ensured.

In Stark v. Railroad Co., 43 Iowa 501, the Supreme Court ruled that land designated by the Legislature for a railroad right of way is deemed essential without question. Similarly, Penn. R. R. Co. v. Nat. Docks, etc., 57 N. J. Law, 86, 30 Atl. 183, and Croley v. Railroad Co., 56 S. W. 615, affirmed that legislative authority over right-of-way width negates judicial interference, as seen in Coe v. Aiken (C. C.) 61 Fed. 24 and other cases.

It is not unusual for legislatures to permit railroads to condemn strips of land up to 200 or even 400 feet wide, given their need for space. While boulevards differ from railroads, the Legislature’s determination of a 200-foot width for a boulevard is similarly beyond judicial challenge. Historical precedents, like turnpike condemnations of 60 to 100 feet, further support legislative discretion in such matters.

The critical issue is whether land can be taken for public use when the statute implies it may remain unused beyond a 30-foot road for up to 50 years. Section 168 allows tax exemption for unused land, raising concerns about compulsory public use. The plaintiff argues the corporation might never utilize the additional 170 feet, undermining the public use requirement.

While Sections 158 and 161 grant the corporation authority to build railways or other utilities on unused boulevard land, Section 142 defines a boulevard as primarily a vehicular road with optional additions. The plaintiff contends these uses are speculative, but courts have recognized them as more than mere possibilities, though eminent domain requires timely public use.
