Has Hallock considered a corpus provision for his grandchildren after Elizabeth's death, regardless of whether his ex-wife remarried or not? However, there's more. If Eve and Hallock pass away before Elizabeth, and Eve leaves descendants who outlive Elizabeth, the corpus is allocated to those descendants irrespective of Elizabeth's marital status. Sections E and H are interconnected in this regard. The agreement addresses four scenarios involving the corpus: two concerning remarriage or non-remarriage of Elizabeth, and two others. In three cases, the corpus clearly goes to Eve's descendants; in the fourth, it reverts to Hallock's estate if Eve dies childless. The implication that Eve's descendants should inherit in this case too seems undeniable. Thus, Section H's wording, when read alongside the agreement's other clauses, should be interpreted to establish an implied remainder. This is the most logical interpretation, as construing a resulting trust for Hallock would suggest an arbitrary intent.

The plaintiffs contend that an implied remainder is unwarranted because the agreement, unlike others such as in Brock v. Hall, does not show the settlor's intent to fully relinquish the trust property. They note the settlor explicitly included reversions in some cases. While there's no presumption against intestacy here, this argument holds some merit and underscores the need for caution in applying implied remainder rules. However, our review finds the argument irrelevant. The settlor provided for reversions in two scenarios (Sections F and H), both contingent on Eve dying without descendants. These provisions don't contradict an implied remainder under Section H; rather, they support it.

Little significance should be given to the agreement's omission of a clause addressing Hallock outliving both Elizabeth and Eve with Eve leaving descendants. This scenario is improbable. Sections A-F and G-H were meant to align, and the omission applies to both. Thus, it doesn't affect our analysis. If the descendants only inherit after surviving both Hallock and Eve, the remainder is doubly contingent but doesn't weaken the inference from Section H, supported by Sections D and E, that they receive the corpus if they outlive both. The lack of a provision for Hallock if he survives Elizabeth and Eve, with Eve leaving no descendants or descendants predeceasing Elizabeth, also doesn't imply otherwise, as the corpus would revert to him via resulting trust.

The plaintiffs emphasize that the agreement's main goal was supporting Elizabeth and Eve, with benefits to descendants being secondary. They point out the agreement lacks income provisions for Eve's descendants if Eve dies before turning 21 or survives Elizabeth but later dies leaving descendants. While the second claim isn't entirely accurate—since descendants would receive corpus (and thus income) under Section D if Eve outlives Hallock and Elizabeth—it's generally true that the descendants' income rights are limited. Still, the intent to grant the corpus to Eve's descendants if she survives Elizabeth and Hallock is clear, resolving this issue. The plaintiffs also critique the Chancellor's broad statement that Sections D and E award the corpus to the descendants, though it might be conditional.

Only claim the corpus if they outlive Hallock. However, it remains accurate that if they do survive him, they indeed claim it. Plaintiffs further argue that the Chancellor used interpretive rules suitable solely for a will. While he did so, it was only partially. For instance, he mentions the settlor's lack of intent to penalize his grandchildren and the potential for a resulting trust to the settlor if no implied remainder is identified—an outcome he seemed to presume should be averted if feasible. While these factors are more fitting for will interpretation than this trust agreement, we believe this does not undermine the Chancellor's sound conclusion, which, like ours, hinges mainly on Section H's wording backed by other agreement terms. Plaintiffs emphasize the context of the agreement's signing. During its drafting and execution, Hallock was experiencing a severe nervous breakdown. His mother and brother-in-law handled negotiations with Elizabeth. The agreement was drafted by attorneys whom the Chancellor explicitly determined represented both parties. Plaintiffs acknowledge the agreement's validity but contend that Hallock, under these conditions,

lacked any 'intent,' and none can be ascribed to him. This, we believe, merely suggests that someone who signs an agreement drafted by another, without intending to agree to all its terms or without comprehending them, is not bound by the intent reflected in its language, even if its validity is unchallenged. This argument is clearly flawed. If accepted, it would upend the established principle that a valid written contract binds the parties, regardless of their understanding, barring exceptional circumstances not present here. We agree with the Chancellor's ruling that Hallock's health when the agreement was prepared and signed holds no relevance in this case. II. Having determined that Section H's wording implies a remainder to Eve's descendants if she outlives Elizabeth and Hallock, we must assess whether this implied remainder has lapsed. Plaintiffs argue as follows: Section H's language, like Section D's, plainly assumes Hallock's death must occur before Eve's for any corpus transfer to happen. They assert this is due to

the life estate reserved for Hallock under Section G. The corpus distribution specified in Section H's paragraph (2) and the initial part of paragraph (3) is set for Elizabeth's death, and these clauses presume Hallock's prior death. If Hallock outlives Elizabeth, no corpus distribution can occur, as the trust will persist to provide Hallock his reserved income for life. (Plaintiffs likely reference the principle that a trust continues as long as needed to fulfill its purposes. Cf. 4 Bogert, Trusts and Trustees, § 991.) Additionally, paragraph (3)'s distribution is not to Hallock if he is alive then, as stipulated in the corresponding Section F, but to his residual estate. The allocation to Hallock's estate upon Elizabeth's death also presumes his prior death. Building on this, plaintiffs claim the implied gift to Eve's descendants in the survival clause assumes not only Hallock's (and Elizabeth's) death before Eve's but also Hallock's death before Elizabeth's. Their reasoning proceeds thus: Paragraph

(2) of Section H and the opening clause of paragraph (3) set the corpus distribution date at Elizabeth's death, with Hallock predeceasing her. The second clause, starting with 'or,' includes the implied remainder to Eve's descendants if she survives her mother. Thus, this clause, part of the same sentence as the first and separated only by commas, also implicitly requires Hallock to have died before both Eve and Elizabeth. Since Hallock survived Elizabeth, the implied remainder fails. For argument's sake, let's assume the implied remainder to Eve's descendants depends on Hallock (and Elizabeth) dying before Eve. But must Hallock also predecease Elizabeth? The immediate query is: Why should an implied remainder to descendants hinge on the order of Hallock and Elizabeth's deaths? What does it matter who dies first, as long as both precede Eve? Plaintiffs' initial reasoning step, as noted, is proving Hallock must die before Elizabeth for the explicit terms

The remaining provisions concerning Eve's issue are to be enforced. This conclusion arises because the trust is designed to end upon Elizabeth's death. Due to Hallock's life estate, terminating the trust and distributing its assets can only occur if he dies before Elizabeth. However, this logic does not apply if Eve outlives her mother. The survival clause's wording indicates the trust persists after Elizabeth's death, as she (and Hallock, if alive) continue receiving income under Section G. The restriction on Hallock's income to Elizabeth's lifetime, stated in Section H(1), is irrelevant here. The transfer of assets to Hallock (or by implication to Eve's issue) occurs after Elizabeth's death. The term 'then surviving' in the first clause does not pertain to the survival clause, where the trust ends upon Eve's death. Thus, the requirement for Hallock to predecease Elizabeth to terminate the trust, as argued by plaintiffs for Section H(2) and the first part of Section H(3), does not apply to the survival clause in Section H(3). To end the trust under this clause, Elizabeth and Hallock need only predecease Eve, regardless of the order of their deaths. This interpretation yields a far more reasonable outcome than the plaintiffs' claim.

We previously noted the arbitrary intent attributed to the settlor if the implied remainder for Eve's issue hinged on Elizabeth's remarriage, an unrelated event. Similarly, interpreting the document to tie the implied remainder to a specific sequence of deaths between Hallock and Elizabeth—a factor unrelated to any logical distribution plan—would again suggest capriciousness by the settlor. While a settlor may act arbitrarily if their intent is clear, this convoluted document lacks clarity. Courts must strive for a reasonable interpretation consistent with the overall distribution scheme. For instance, Section D specifies that if Eve survives both Elizabeth and Hallock and dies with issue, the issue inherits the assets, irrespective of the order of deaths between Elizabeth and Hallock. The parallel between Sections D, E, F and Sections G, H, while imperfect, supports construing Section H's survival clause to mirror Section D's explicit outcome.

CHRISTIE, Chief Justice. Defendant/appellant Wallace A. Zimmerman ('Zimmerman') was found guilty of first-degree arson, possessing a deadly weapon during a felony, possessing a destructive weapon, and criminal mischief. The Superior Court imposed consecutive prison sentences totaling eight and a half years for the first three charges, followed by six months of probation for the last. All convictions stemmed from an incident involving a homemade pipe bomb thrown into the victim's home. On appeal, Zimmerman argues the trial court erred by: (1) admitting testimony about prior bad acts without a jury instruction; (2) instructing the jury on accomplice liability despite the prosecution not raising it; (3) allowing prejudicial prosecutorial remarks during closing arguments without correction; and (4) imposing multiple sentences for the same offense, violating double jeopardy. We find these claims lack merit and affirm the Superior Court's decision, though we remand for resentencing adjustments.

Our conclusions are: (1) Section H implies a remainder for Eve's issue (whether vested or contingent), and (2) this remainder is not invalidated merely because Hallock outlived Elizabeth. Consequently, the plaintiffs are not the sole beneficiaries and cannot terminate the trust. The Court of Chancery's judgment is upheld.

The sentencing was in accordance with 11 DelC. § 1447(c). On September 16, 1986, a pipe bomb detonated on the second floor of Sistilio Popo's ('Popo') home. Zimmerman, the appellant, was apprehended for hurling the bomb that led to the blast into the victim's residence. Earlier in 1986, Cindy Marta ('Marta') had been in a relationship with Popo. By July 1986, Marta had started dating the defendant. Popo had bought a car for Marta during their relationship. After Marta began seeing Zimmerman, Popo tried to transfer the car's title, which was jointly under his and Marta's names, solely to his name. However, before he could complete this, Marta managed to have the title transferred exclusively to her name. The car dispute fueled tensions between Popo and Zimmerman. Popo stated that weeks before the bombing, Zimmerman had tried to assault him with a crowbar. Popo dodged the attack and was unharmed, but the incident prompted a police call. Additionally, Popo

testified that his role as a police informant worsened the animosity between him and Zimmerman after Zimmerman's brother was arrested on drug-related charges. During the trial, Popo recounted that on September 16, 1986, he was at home with his family, girlfriend, and two friends when he heard glass shattering on the second floor. Popo and his friends rushed outside to identify the culprit but found no one. Moments later, the bomb exploded upstairs. The device, made from a plumbing pipe filled with black powder, shattered two windows in Popo's bedroom. Despite several people being inside, no injuries occurred. Edward Foraker ('Foraker'), a neighbor, testified that after hearing the explosion, he went outside and spotted two white males walking away from Popo's house. Upon noticing Foraker, they began jogging, entered a car matching Zimmerman's, and sped off without headlights. Around the same time, one of Popo's friends was driving nearby and, right after the explosion, turned onto Popo's street. Both the friend and his companion saw a car identical to Zimmerman's driving away and were certain Zimmerman was behind the wheel.

James R. Hedrick ('Hedrick') of the New Castle County Police testified that he phoned Marta after the incident. Marta claimed she hadn't seen Zimmerman all day or evening. Zimmerman was arrested the following day. At trial, both Marta and Zimmerman testified he was with her during the explosion. The bomb was constructed from a pipe filled with black powder. A neighbor of Zimmerman's brother stated that in September 1986, while Zimmerman lived with his brother, she frequently heard loud explosions in a vacant lot behind a shed where Zimmerman's brother stored plumbing materials. The Superior Court jury convicted Zimmerman on multiple charges, leading to the aforementioned sentences. I. Zimmerman argues the trial court erred by permitting testimony about his prior misconduct. He also claims the court's failure to issue a limiting instruction regarding this evidence was prejudicial. During the trial, defense counsel did not object to the introduction of the prior bad acts evidence, which included threats Zimmerman made to the victim with a crowbar.

Under Supreme Court Rule 8, this issue is not properly before the Court unless plain error is established. See Bowe v. State, Del.Supr., 514 A.2d 408, 411 (1986). Evidence of a defendant's prior misconduct is inadmissible to prove criminal conduct. Del.R.Evid. 404(a); Johnson v. State, Del.Supr., 311 A.2d 873, 874 (1973). However, Delaware Rule of Evidence 404(b) allows such evidence for other purposes, such as demonstrating motive, intent, plan, or absence of mistake. Del.R.Evid. 404(b); Diaz v. State, Del. Supr., 508 A.2d.

861, 865 (1986). In this case, the prosecution's use of prior misconduct falls within the allowable scope under Rule 404(b), as it pertains to the defendant's motive. The admission of this evidence did not amount to plain error, and a limiting instruction was unnecessary. Additionally, the defendant challenges hearsay testimony presented during Popo's trial examination over counsel's objection. The trial court correctly determined the testimony reflected Popo's state of mind rather than the truth of the statement. The defendant further argues the trial court erred in instructing the jury on accomplice liability, claiming the prosecutor did not rely on this theory or request such a charge. Since the defendant did not object, this issue is reviewable only for plain error under Supreme Court Rule 8. Jury instructions aim to precisely outline the factual disputes and legal principles for the jury to apply.

Substantial clarity is required in defining factual issues and instructing the jury on applicable legal principles, as noted in United States v. Anderton, 629 F.2d 1044, 1048 (5th Cir. 1980). Parties are entitled to instructions on their case theories if timely requested, evidence-supported, and legally accurate, per United States v. Jerde, 841 F.2d 818, 820 (8th Cir. 1988). Generally, parties must submit written requests for jury instructions to preserve arguments for appeal, as per Super. Ct. Crim.R. 30(a). However, the instruction here was prompted by a jury question, not a party request. A trial court may provide additional instructions post-submission if the jury requests them, as stated in 76 Am.Jur. 2d Trial § 1046 (1975). The decision to give supplemental instructions lies within the court's discretion, per Sheeran v. State, 526 A.2d 886, 893 (Del. 1987).

Testimony indicated the defendant fled the crime scene with another individual, making accomplice liability foreseeable. A trial court must instruct the jury based on evidence and law, regardless of party requests, as held in United States v. Cooper, 812 F.2d 1283, 1286 (10th Cir. 1987). Lovett v. State, 516 A.2d 455, 468 (Del. 1986), further supports that the trial court's accomplice liability instruction was justified by trial evidence and caused no prejudice, even if not detailed in the bill of particulars. Given these circumstances and no demonstrated prejudice, the supplemental instruction on accomplice liability does not constitute reversible error. The defendant also argues the trial court erred by not reiterating a unanimity instruction with the supplemental instruction. This Court has ruled that a specific unanimity instruction is unnecessary when a defendant may be convicted as either a principal or accomplice, per Probst v. State, 547 A.2d 114, 122 (Del. 1988).

Absent a specific request or unusual circumstances, a general unanimity instruction suffices. Thus, the trial court's failure to provide a second unanimity instruction alongside the accomplice liability instruction was not improper. The defendant further contends that the trial court erred in other respects, but these claims lack merit under the applicable legal standards. The court's rulings were consistent with precedent and the evidence presented, ensuring a fair trial. The defendant's arguments do not demonstrate plain error or prejudice, and the jury instructions adequately addressed the legal and factual issues. Therefore, the defendant's claims are without grounds for reversal or further review under the established legal framework.

The prosecutor inappropriately included his personal views in the closing argument, yet no objections were raised during the trial. This Court has consistently stressed the importance of timely objections to potentially improper closing statements by opposing counsel. Michael v. State, Del.Supr., 529 A.2d 752, 762 (1987) (citing Hooks v. State, Del.Supr., 416 A.2d 189 (1980)). Generally, 'not objecting means the defendant forfeits the right to appeal the issue.' Goddard v. State, Del.Supr., 382 A.2d 238, 242 (1977). Without an objection during trial, this Court can only overturn the verdict if the remarks constituted plain error. Id.; Supr.Ct. R. 8. Plain error is assessed based on 'whether the prosecutor's comments were so fundamentally wrong as to clearly deny the defendant a substantial right or result in manifest injustice.'

In Michael v. State, 529 A.2d at 762 (quoting Ward v. State, Del. Supr., 366 A.2d 1194, 1197 (1976)), the defendant argues the prosecutor's use of 'I' introduced personal bias, creating prejudice severe enough to qualify as plain error. This Court has warned that 'first-person arguments are highly risky and should be strictly avoided.' Brokenbrough v. State, Del.Supr., 522 A.2d 851, 859 (1987) (per curiam). However, while such language is improper, it doesn’t automatically warrant reversal. Id. When evaluating prosecutorial misconduct claims, the Court applies the three-part test from Hughes v. State, Del.Supr., 437 A.2d 559 (1981), which considers 'the case's closeness, the significance of the issue impacted by the alleged error, and measures taken to lessen the error's effect.'

affected by the claimed mistake, and any actions taken to reduce its impact.' Id. at 571 (quoting Dyson v. United States, D.C.App., 418 A.2d 127, 132 (1980)). Applying this test, we conclude the case was not closely contested, and sufficient evidence supported the jury's decision. The prosecutor's improper comments were not pivotal, and the defendant did not seek remedies to counteract them. Thus, we rule the remarks do not justify reversal. IV. Lastly, the defendant argues that convicting and sentencing him for three charges from one incident amounts to unconstitutional 'multiple punishments' for the 'same offense,' violating the Fifth Amendment's double jeopardy clause. Here, the defendant was found guilty of first-degree arson, possessing a deadly weapon during a felony, having a destructive weapon, and criminal mischief. He claims the first three charges stemmed from a single event involving a homemade bomb, so he should only face sentencing for one offense.

The U.S. Supreme Court's Blockburger v. United States, 284 U.S. 299, 52 S.Ct. 180, 76 L.Ed. 306 (1932), established the test for determining whether two convictions are the same offense under double jeopardy. 'A single act can be charged and punished as separate crimes under distinct statutes if each requires proof of an element the others lack.' See also State v. Skyers, Del.Supr., 560 A.2d 1052 (1989) (citing Jefferson v. State, Del.Supr., 543 A.2d 339 (1988) (ORDER)). Additionally, if 'a legislature explicitly permits cumulative punishment under two statutes, regardless of whether they cover the 'same' conduct under Blockburger, courts must allow cumulative penalties in a single trial.' LeCompte v. State, Del.Supr., 5

16 A.2d 898, 901-02 (1986) (referencing Missouri v. Hunter, 459 U.S. 359, 368-69, 103 S.Ct. 673, 679, 74 L.Ed.2d 535, 544 (1983) (footnote omitted)). Here, we examine the arson and weapons charges in relation to one another, as well as the two weapons offenses independently of the arson charge, to assess potential double jeopardy violations. For a first-degree arson conviction under 11 Del.C. § 803, the prosecution must demonstrate that the defendant 1) deliberately damaged a structure by igniting a fire or causing an explosion, and 2) was aware that another individual, not an accomplice, was inside. To secure a conviction for possessing a destructive weapon under 11 Del. C. § 1444, the State must establish the defendant had specific prohibited items.

To convict for possessing a deadly weapon during a felony under 11 Del.C. § 1447, the State must prove the defendant had such a weapon while committing the felony. The arson and weapons charges demand distinct evidence, making them separate offenses eligible for separate penalties. The destructive weapon statute targets those owning hazardous devices, with no necessity for their use. The deadly weapon charge necessitates proof of additional felonious behavior, a criterion absent in other charges. Arson focuses on outcomes, requiring evidence of intentional damage via fire or explosion, but not proof of weapon possession. Imposing separate sentences for the weapons offenses does not breach double jeopardy protections.

Clearly, the legislature intended cumulative penalties under both 11 Del.C. § 1444 and § 1447, as they address different threats. Section 1444 bars the public from acquiring 'highly dangerous weapons,' as there is typically no valid reason for their possession (Delaware Criminal Code with Commentary, Commentary on sec. 1444 at 464 (1973)). Section 1447 aims to reduce the availability of deadly weapons during felonies, thereby minimizing risks to victims (Mack v. State, Del.Supr., 312 A.2d 319, 321 (1973)). It reflects legislative intent to impose harsher penalties for felonies involving weapons, deterring such acts and enhancing victim safety (DeShields v. State, Del.Supr., 534 A.2d 630, 647 (1987); LeCompte v. State, Del.Supr., 516 A.2d 898, 902 (1986)). Since the legislature defined these offenses separately with unique elements and sentencing intent, no double jeopardy exists.

The trial court correctly allowed convictions on four charges and imposed separate sentences. The State notes an unraised issue: the Superior Court ordered three years for the deadly weapon charge, followed by four years for arson, contrary to 11 Del. C. § 1447(c), which mandates serving the felony sentence first. Thus, the convictions are AFFIRMED, but the case is REMANDED for resentencing compliance. Supreme Court Rule 8 limits appellate review to issues presented at trial, though exceptions exist for justice. 11 Del.C. § 1444 criminalizes selling, transferring, buying, receiving, or possessing destructive weapons.

Regarding a bomb, bombshell, firearm silencer, sawed-off shotgun, machine gun, or any other firearm or weapon that can be modified to function as a machine gun. Stiftel, J.: This is a condemnation case where the State Highway Department of Delaware (State) sought to overturn the award given by a condemnation jury, arguing that the defendants, Harvey and Shirley Mintzer (lessees), failed to provide valid evidence regarding the value of their leasehold, Toppers Drive-in Restaurant, a luncheonette they operated on the southbound lane of duPont Highway (Route 13), near the junction of the western controlled highway from the Delaware Memorial Bridge. The State's sole contention concerns the admissibility of Harvey Mintzer's testimony about the leasehold's fair market value. The restaurant occupied a 525-square-foot building leased by Sidney Bicow to the Mintzers for $175 monthly. While the lease did not explicitly include land for access, it was understood that the land previously leased to Socony-Vacuum Company could be used by the luncheonette's patrons for parking and entry.

The defendants' attorney presented Mr. Mintzer as their sole witness on the leasehold's value. The lease stipulated a $175 monthly rent, but Mintzer estimated the fair market value at $275, claiming the leasehold was worth $100 more than the agreed rent. Before providing his estimate, Mintzer noted his decade of experience in related businesses and hinted at familiarity with rental values along duPont Highway. He also testified, without objection, about the business's gross receipts and expenses from June 1956 to September 1958. The State called two real estate experts: Robert E. Hickman, president of Emmett S. Hickman Company, who estimated the leasehold's fair market value at $175 monthly, and Arnold Goldsborough, a realtor, who pegged it between $150 and $175. Hickman based his valuation on comparisons with properties on Kirkwood Highway, miles away, while Goldsborough used commercial rentals in Fairfax, also distant from the defendants' location.

The jury was instructed that the lessees' compensation depended on the fair market value of the leasehold exceeding the reserved rent at the time of taking. If the fair market value was higher, they could recover the difference; otherwise, they would receive nothing. As per the State's experts, the leasehold's value matched or fell below the reserved rent, meaning the defendants were entitled to no damages. However, the jury awarded $1,650, which could only have been based on Mintzer's testimony. The maximum recoverable amount would have been derived from his valuation.

The State's experts, Hickman and Goldsborough, relied on comparisons with distant properties—Kirkwood Highway and Fairfax—to estimate the leasehold's value. Hickman doubled the square footage value of Kirkwood Highway properties to approximate duPont Highway rentals, while Goldsborough deemed Fairfax rentals twice as valuable as those on duPont Highway. The jury's decision hinged on whether the leasehold's fair market value surpassed the reserved rent. Since the State's witnesses concluded it did not, the award to the defendants must have stemmed solely from Mintzer's testimony, as no other evidence supported a higher valuation.

The owner's testimony regarding the market value was $3,300, calculated as $100 per month for the remaining 33 months of the lease term. The jury granted the defendants half of this sum, $1,650. The State Highway Department objected, claiming the leasehold owner's testimony should have been dismissed, arguing he lacked the expertise to provide a valid opinion simply because he owned the leasehold. However, legal precedent supports that an owner of property is inherently qualified to estimate its value, as noted in 37 A. L. R. 2d 967 and affirmed in Ligon v. Brooks, where this Court upheld an automobile owner's right to testify about its market value.

The rule, as cited from Chamberlayne's Modern Law of Evidence, allows an owner to estimate the value of common personal property, given their inherent familiarity with it. While the jury determines the weight of such testimony, no specialized expertise is typically required. Similarly, in Fidanque v. American Maracaibo Co., the Chancery Court affirmed that ownership alone qualifies an individual to estimate value, though the credibility of their testimony depends on their knowledge. The Highway Department, however, argued this principle should not apply to leasehold owners, insisting they must demonstrate specific valuation expertise.

The State contended that the leasehold owner testified solely based on ownership, without showing specialized knowledge. Generally, a lessee running a business on the property should be allowed to estimate the leasehold's value, as they are typically aware of its market worth. This awareness stems from daily exposure to local market conditions and competition. Like an automobile owner, a lessee-operator gains practical knowledge of their leasehold's value, making it rare for them to lack such insight. Exceptions may arise if a lessee proves unfamiliar with valuation, but the court retains discretion in assessing witness competency.

In rare cases, a lessee—whether as owner or operator—may lack sufficient knowledge of value, prompting the court to deem them incompetent to testify. However, competency standards are flexible, and the distinction between witness eligibility and testimony credibility remains crucial. Here, Mr. Mintzer provided more than ownership claims; he justified his $275 valuation by detailing his leasehold's history, including its initial state as an empty shell, his business operations from June 1956 to September 1958, and the circumstances of its loss to the State.

He stated that there were no customers or potential customers. He noted that he made lasting improvements to the property to better operate his business. Additionally, Mintzer provided uncontested testimony about his gross income and expenses for part of 1956, all of 1957, and part of 1958. This data showed a business generating modest but increasing profits. Mintzer also highlighted his decade of experience in similar businesses, suggesting some understanding of leasehold property values. While he lacked precise knowledge of local luncheonette rental rates, his testimony hinted at general awareness of a few comparable rentals. Thus, his testimony about the business's profitability and operations was relevant for assessing the leasehold's value, as seen in Eisenring v. Kansas Turnpike Authority, 183 Kan. 77.

4, 332 P. 2d 539; State Roads Commission of Maryland v. Novosel, 203 Md. 619, 102 A. 2d 563. The agreed rent, the improvements he made, and other mentioned factors suggested a potential rise in the property's fair market value. See Minsk v. Fulton County, 83 Ga. App. 520, 64 S. E. 2d 336, 338. The State emphasized the lack of testimony on comparable rents or sales nearby. While such evidence is valuable for determining market value, it isn't the sole method, and its absence doesn't bar recovery if other valid testimony on value exists. Mintzer, as the leasehold operator, was permitted to demonstrate increased rental value since the lease's signing and seek compensation for this rise.

I conclude that the jury's verdict is backed by substantial evidence and must be upheld. Generally, property or leasehold owners in the U.S. may testify about their property's value, though competency standards vary. Some jurisdictions allow owners to testify based solely on ownership, leaving the weight of their testimony to the jury. Kinter v. United States, 3 Cir., 156 F. 2d 5, 172 A. L. R. 232; Salt Lake & Utah R. Co. v. Schramm, 56 Utah 53, 189 P. 90; Bailey v. Ford, 151 Md. 664, 135 A. 835; Pennsylvania Threshermen & Farmers' Mut. Casualty Ins. Co. v. Messenger, 181 Md. 295, 29 A. 2d 653; Harold v. Pugh, 174 Cal.

App. 2d 603, 345 P. 2d 112. Other jurisdictions require owners to understand value-determining factors beyond mere ownership. Nichols, Eminent Domain, Vol. 5, Sec. 18.4[2], pp. 139-40; Village of Lapwai v. Alligier, 69 Idaho 397, 207 P. 2d 1025; Chicago, R. I. & G. R. Co. v. Martin, Tex. Civ. App., 37 S. W. 2d 207; Rotge v. Murphy, Tex. Civ. App., 198 S. W. 2d 932. In these cases, ownership alone doesn't qualify someone unfamiliar with value or location to testify. 32 C. J. S. Evidence 545 D (3), and owners follow standard witness rules without special status. Sgar

In Lat Estate v. Commonwealth, 398 Pa. 406, 158 A.2d 541, 545, comparable value testimony was deemed admissible, as seen in Wilmington Housing Authority v. Harris, 8 Terry 469, 93 A.2d 518. A few jurisdictions remain reluctant to allow such testimony despite fair market value being in question. Refer to Walnut Street Federal Savings & Loan Ass'n v. Bernstein, 394 Pa. 353, 147 A.2d 359, 361, and generally, 118 A.L.R. 869; 174 A.L.R. 386. Per Curiam. (In their charge.) A fundamental principle is that a plaintiff must have standing to sue when the action is initiated, which the plaintiff here lacked. Nonetheless, the jury ruled in favor of the plaintiff, with the defendant agreeing not to appeal on the condition of his release from jail and covering the suit's costs. LONGOB

ARDI, Judge. This appeal challenges the Industrial Accident Board's denial of Anthony F. Taimo's claim for compensation benefits. The Board concluded that his myocardial infarction on July 17, 1980, while lifting a manhole cover, stemmed from a pre-existing condition rather than work-related strain. It noted that lifting manhole covers was a routine task for Mr. Taimo, performed with a coworker's assistance, and did not involve unusual exertion. The court's role is to assess whether the Board's decision was legally sound or supported by substantial evidence, per Olney v. Cooch, Del. Supr., 425 A.2d 610 (1981). The record shows Mr. Taimo had worked for New Castle County's Department of Public Works since 1972.

as a maintenance and construction worker. Due to his age and weight, his supervisor assigned him lighter tasks within his role. Regularly, he lifted manhole covers with a coworker using a pick, raising and sliding them aside for resealing. He estimated handling around 100 covers weekly. Dr. Constantine W. Michell, his physician, noted chest pain complaints starting in October 1979, prescribing nitroglycerine and recommending light duty, which Mr. Taimo declined to avoid reduced hours. On July 15, 1980, he reported recurring chest pain and knee issues, prompting increased medication and a follow-up on July 17.

On July 17, 1980, while lifting his second manhole cover of the day, Mr. Taimo experienced sharp chest pain. After finishing the task, he informed the workplace nurse and visited Dr. Michell, who hospitalized him until August 29, 1980, diagnosing an acute myocardial infarction. This condition involves narrowed heart arteries reducing oxygen supply. Since the incident, he has been unable to work. Dr. Michell testified that the lifting likely triggered the infarction, though he later expressed uncertainty about whether the activity directly caused it.

The infarction did not happen on July 15th or earlier, and lifting a manhole cover might have triggered or worsened it. During hospitalization for the heart attack, the Claimant was diagnosed with cancer, leading to blood loss and anemia. Combined with diabetes, age, and weight, these factors narrowed the heart's blood vessels, reducing oxygen supply. Dr. Michell stated that lifting the cover demanded more oxygen, but the heart couldn't meet this need due to the existing conditions, making the heart attack inevitable under any strain. The Board relied on Dr. Lombardi's video testimony, who, without examining the Claimant, concluded that a preexisting cardiac condition made the heart attack unavoidable. The Claimant argues the Board's findings contradict its benefit denial.

The Claimant argues that the Board cannot deny benefits after acknowledging that lifting the manhole cover on July 17, 1980, caused the heart attack. The case Chicago Bridge & Iron Co. v. Walker outlines four legal grounds for compensation: (1) a clear work-related incident, (2) unusual exertion aggravating a preexisting condition, (3) a compensable occupational disease, or (4) cumulative work-related harm. In heart attack cases, Delaware courts prioritize the 'unusual exertion' theory, requiring proof that the exertion exceeded normal job duties. Mere occurrence at work doesn’t qualify. The Claimant’s chest pain during the lifting was diagnosed as a heart attack, but the act was part of his routine.

The evidence shows lifting manhole covers was routine for the Claimant, who did it about 100 times weekly. In General Motors Corp. v. Veasey, the Supreme Court ruled that 'unusual exertion' must exceed normal job duties to justify compensation. The Claimant’s only argument was that he received lighter tasks due to age and weight, but no proof showed the exertion was beyond his usual duties. The County’s accommodations don’t meet the legal standard for 'unusual exertion.' Thus, the heart attack, while work-related, doesn’t qualify for compensation under the cited precedent.

Lifting the manhole cover could have triggered the infarction, but it was part of the Claimant’s regular duties. The Supreme Court emphasized that compensation requires exertion beyond ordinary job demands. The Claimant’s case lacked evidence of such exceptional strain, despite his health challenges. The Board’s decision aligns with legal precedents, as routine work activities, even strenuous ones, don’t meet the 'unusual exertion' threshold unless they exceed the claimant’s typical responsibilities. Therefore, the denial of benefits was consistent with established law.

The manhole cover was part of the Claimant's regular job responsibilities. Even though the County was aware that the Claimant was older and overweight and attempted to assign him lighter tasks, this does not alter the reality that moving manhole covers was a routine part of his duties. After oral argument, the Claimant cited a Supreme Court case decided shortly thereafter, Petera and Son Oil Company v. Moore, which involved a truck driver exacerbating his heart condition while lifting a snow-covered truck cab. The Supreme Court did not address whether the lifting was 'unusual exertion' under Veasey, as the employer conceded the point. The Court found substantial evidence to support the Board's ruling that the Claimant's injury did not stem from unusual exertion.

The decision is affirmed. The Claimant also contends that his work had a cumulative negative impact on his health, a theory outlined in Chicago Bridge & Iron Co. v. Walker. However, this argument was not presented to the Board, and the Claimant's attorney admitted that the work did not worsen the heart disease but merely triggered the heart attack. The record lacks any evidence supporting the cumulative effect claim, so the Board's decision is upheld. IT IS SO ORDERED. An infarction-related heart condition implies a pre-existing vulnerability. To Governor Elbert N. Carvel: The Supreme Court Justices acknowledge your letter dated January 16, 1952, seeking their opinion on specific matters.

The questions posed are: 1. Would the Attorney General be disqualified from investigating Mr. Reichert's allegations? 2. If disqualified, can the Governor appoint a special prosecutor? 3. Can the complaint reach the Grand Jury without the Attorney General's involvement? The letter requests an investigation into alleged vote-buying in Blackbird Hundred and a special prosecutor due to the Attorney General's alleged conflict. The Justices sought counsel to address these questions and additional ones, including the constitutionality of Paragraph 374 of the 1935 Delaware Code and its applicability to the Supreme Court.

After reviewing the questions and additional issues, the Justices provide their opinions. On the first question, Paragraph 374 of the 1935 Code permits advisory opinions only on constitutional interpretation or the constitutionality of state laws. The first question falls outside this scope. The Justices conclude that advisory opinions are limited to the statute's specified subjects and no others.

No issue pertains to the interpretation or construction of any clause in the State or U.S. Constitution, nor to the validity of any state legislation, and thus falls outside the statute's scope. The State Constitution lacks any provision addressing the disqualification of the Attorney General due to personal interest or bias, nor does any clause offer guidance on this matter. Disqualification is a factual determination to be resolved by a court in appropriate proceedings, not unilaterally by the Governor. Consequently, answering this question is unnecessary for the Governor's duties. We conclude the first question does not align with Paragraph 374 of the 1935 Revised Code and respectfully decline to respond.

The second question involves the unconfirmed disqualification of the Attorney General, rendering it hypothetical. Courts in other states with advisory opinion mandates uniformly reject addressing speculative inquiries. Such questions must relate to an immediate constitutional duty of the executive. Precedents like *In re Opinion of the Justices* (217 Mass. 607) support this view. Our statute permits opinions only when the Governor needs them for public clarity or official duties. Since the Attorney General's disqualification remains unproven, no pressing public issue or executive obligation exists. Thus, the second question also lies beyond Paragraph 374's purview, and we respectfully decline to answer.

The third question examines the Governor's authority, under his constitutional duty to enforce laws (Article III, Section 17), to direct a grand jury complaint regarding election bribery without the Attorney General's involvement. It requires interpreting Delaware's Constitution, particularly Article I, Section 4, which mandates grand jury composition and voting thresholds in New Castle, Kent, and Sussex Counties. Article I, Section 8 further prohibits criminal proceedings by information except in military cases. These provisions enshrine the grand jury as a constitutional entity, preserving its traditional role as a protective legal mechanism, albeit with constitutional modifications. The grand jury operates as a judicial body tasked with investigating crimes and issuing indictments.

The grand jury, as an arm of the court, retains its common-law functions unless altered by the Constitution. Its primary role is to examine alleged legal violations and issue indictments, as noted in *State v. Lyons* (40 Del. 77) and *In re Opinion to the Governor* (62 R.I. 200). This historical institution remains vital for safeguarding citizens against unfounded prosecutions. Its procedures and powers, rooted in tradition, are upheld unless explicitly revised by constitutional amendments or statutes.

2. The issue of whether the entity can utilize its investigative authority to address complaints from any origin, as seen in Brack v. Wells, 184 Md. 86, 40 A. 2d 319, 156 A. L. R. 324, or if it is limited to matters brought forward by the prosecutor, as in In re Charge to the Grand Jury, Fed. Cas. No. 18,255, 2 Sawy. 667, is not one we need to resolve. This is because the response to the Governor's third question hinges on the specifics of constitutional provisions concerning arrests and prosecutions for election bribery. Article V, Section 7, outlines offenses related to offering or accepting bribes for voting or withholding votes in various elections, along with other violations affecting electoral integrity, and specifies the corresponding penalties.

Section 8 of the same article states that prosecutions for offenses under Section 7 must be initiated by the Attorney-General following an examination and commitment or bail by a judge or Justice of the Peace. The case is to be tried by the court without a grand or petit jury. If convicted, the accused has three months to appeal to the Supreme Court. The lower court or a judge must grant the appeal upon request, but it does not act as a stay unless the appellant posts a bond approved by the court. The Supreme Court will promptly review the evidence and proceedings, delivering a final judgment to affirm or reverse the lower court's decision. Failure to pursue the appeal as per the rules results in the Supreme Court upholding the lower court's judgment.

If the lower court's sentence includes imprisonment and an appeal bond is posted, the Supreme Court, upon affirming the judgment, will impose a sentence equal to the original minus any time already served. The bond's surety may apprehend the appellant and deliver them to the sheriff within specified timeframes, using the bond as a warrant. If the Supreme Court overturns a fine and the accused has paid it, the amount will be refunded via a warrant from the lower court to the county treasurer.

No individual can be convicted of a Section 7 offense without unanimous agreement among the judges trying the case. On appeal, the lower court's judgment cannot be affirmed without unanimity among the Supreme Court judges, with dissent resulting in reversal. However, unanimity is not required if the appellant fails to follow appeal procedures. The alleged offenses involve vote-buying in primary or general elections in Blackbird Hundred, New Castle County, falling under Section 8. We believe the outlined procedures apply to prosecuting and punishing such offenses.

This is as specified in Section 8, and it excludes any other process. The thorough constitutional provisions necessitate this outcome. Every critical stage of prosecution, from bail to the Supreme Court's final ruling, is outlined. The process is unique in many ways, bypassing both indictment and petit jury trials. Unanimous Supreme Court agreement is needed to uphold a conviction, with judges reviewing facts and law. The appeal window is shortened from five years to three months, with special appellate rules included. These requirements are compulsory, not optional. Regarding grand jury powers, the Constitution's framers clearly intended to replace them, as indicated in legal references. The Convention Debates show no intent to retain grand jury involvement for Section 7 offenses.

Concerning the grand jury's investigative authority, evidence suggests the framers meant to completely exclude both grand and petit juries from Section 7 cases. References from Vol. 3 support this view. While the grand jury can no longer indict for these offenses, some argue it retains investigative powers. However, it would be illogical to allow investigations into crimes where legal action is barred. Moreover, common law likely doesn't grant grand juries investigative authority over offenses where they lack indictment power, as noted in Maryland's Court of Appeals ruling that grand jury inquiries should solely aim to bring accused individuals to trial.

We conclude that Section 8 of Article V removes all grand jury powers—investigative, presentment, and indictment—related to Section 7 offenses. Our response to the Governor's third question is negative. Additional questions raised by the Supreme Court Justices about Paragraph 374 were also addressed. Their stance on the third question aligns with the Governor's answers, while their views on the other two are detailed below. The first concerns whether Paragraph 374 applies to current Supreme Court Justices, with the Chief Justice and Justice Wolcott providing opinions on advisory opinions in light of recent constitutional changes establishing a separate Supreme Court.

How should this statute be interpreted post-amendment? Should it be read literally or aligned with its intent despite wording? Basic statutory construction principles apply: clear, unambiguous language reflecting legislative intent requires no interpretation, as established in Nigro v. Flinn. Conversely, literal meanings shouldn't prevail if they contradict the statute's purpose, leading to outcomes inconsistent with the act's objectives, as noted in Darling Apartment Co. v. Springer.

3. The challenge, as usual, is in applying these principles. We should review the statute's history considering the judiciary's structure and evolution, noting that advisory opinions are non-judicial and lack binding authority. State ex rel. Satterthwaite v. Highfield, 4 W. W. Harr. (34 Del.) 272, 152 A. 45. 'The Duty of Judges as Constitutional Advisers', 24 Am. Law Rev. 369. The current law originates from an 1832 Act (8 Del. Laws, Ch. 106) implementing the 1831 Constitution. Section 9 states: 'The chancellor and judges must provide written opinions when the Governor requests them for public guidance or to fulfill his duties, addressing the interpretation of state or federal constitutional provisions or the constitutionality of state laws.'

Under the 1831 Constitution, judicial power was vested in multiple courts, including a Court of Errors and Appeals, Superior Court, and others. Five judges were appointed for general jurisdiction: a Chancellor, a Chief Justice, and three Associates. (Art. VI, Secs. 1–2.) Unlike the 1792 Constitution, the 1831 version omitted a clause specifying the High Court's composition. However, Section 7 allowed law questions from the Superior Court to the Court of Errors and Appeals, where the Chancellor and four judges would serve.

The 1897 Constitution added an associate judge but maintained the Chancellor and judges' dual trial and appellate roles, avoiding ambiguity in the advisory opinion statute. The 1951 amendment, however, introduced a complication: the Chancellor and judges now primarily handle trials, while a separate Supreme Court handles appeals. Which group should provide advisory opinions? The 1951 General Assembly did not clarify this or address similar statutes assigning non-judicial duties to judges, leaving the question of how these laws fit the new judicial structure.

Delaware statutes reveal a long history of assigning non-judicial duties to judges, with varying designations. Some laws specify judges by court (e.g., 'judges of the Court of General Sessions'), others by court name alone (e.g., 'The Superior Court'), and some by title (e.g., 'The Chief Justice'). The statute in question uses 'the Chancellor and Judges,' showing no consistent pattern in such designations. Nonetheless, it is clear that the language for assigning these duties has been inconsistent, though certain conclusions can still be drawn.

It can be stated that in certain instances where the duty is local (see notes 3 and 5) or relates to trial judge responsibilities (see notes 5 and 7), the reference is to a trial court or its judges; in other cases involving state-wide functions or duties suited to the highest court (see note 4), differing wording reflects the function's nature. Notably, two statutes (see note 4) refer to 'Judges of the Supreme Court,' despite the 1897 Constitution not explicitly defining a Supreme Court. This clearly denotes the judiciary's highest-ranking members. The phrasing in these statutes aligns with 'the Chancellor and Judges' in Paragraph 374, indicating the General Assembly's consistent intent. Given statutory variations, interpreting Paragraph 374 requires aligning with the act's clear intent, especially if a literal reading yields anomalies.

The constitutional amendment's adoption necessitates resolving statutory interpretation issues by adhering to the original legislative intent, provided it is evident and a literal interpretation would lead to unreasonable outcomes. The statute mandates advisory opinions from 'the Chancellor and Judges,' reflecting the 1832 Act's intent that the highest-ranking judiciary members advise the Governor. Similar requirements exist or have existed in other states, where advisory opinions typically come from the highest judicial authorities. It would be illogical for the executive to accept advice from lower-ranking judiciary members. As noted, such advisory opinions lack judicial authority, deriving persuasiveness solely from the stature of the state's top judicial officers.

The General Assembly's intent in the 1832 Act was clearly to grant the Governor access to advisory opinions from the state's highest judicial officials. Thus, 'the Chancellor and Judges' in Paragraph 374 should be interpreted as 'the members of the state's highest court,' ensuring alignment between the Constitution and the older statute. This conclusion acknowledges that the court's role here differs from typical litigation, as it involves administrative duty allocation rather than adjudicating private rights. While departing from a statute's literal wording is rare, especially in private rights cases, this situation warrants it to avoid anomalous results without expanding judicial power.

This task merely involves assigning an administrative duty and does not constitute an inappropriate judicial power grab. Since advisory opinions establish no legal rights or consequences, they exert no authority over individuals, serving only an advisory role. For the current court to refuse this duty would prioritize legal technicalities over the law's spirit. Precedents exist, even in private rights cases, where courts adjust statutory language to reflect intent. For example, in Murray's Lessee v. Baker, the U.S. Supreme Court interpreted 'beyond seas' in a Georgia statute as 'outside the state,' aligning with the underlying purpose. Such examples support interpreting statutes to fulfill their intended role.

In Sutherland's Statutory Construction, Section 4925, it is noted: 'Most cases allow replacing one word with another when necessary to fulfill legislative intent.' This principle is especially relevant here, as refusing to answer the Governor's questions might mean neglecting a duty the General Assembly intended for us. We believe Paragraph 374 applies to the current Supreme Court Justices. Justice Tunnell's opinion states: While I acknowledge that justices can broadly be called 'judges,' I disagree that we are 'The Chancellor and Judges.' When the state's highest court was restructured, the legislature did not amend the advisory opinion statute, possibly due to oversight or intent. If it was oversight, no other entity can amend it; only the General Assembly holds that power.

If the omission was intentional, and the legislature meant to retain the advisory role for the Chancellor and judges, the answer remains the same. We still have judges who could be called 'the Chancellor and Judges.' There’s no reason they shouldn’t advise the executive if the legislature wills it, and no legal principle would be violated. Perhaps it was thought that, freed from appellate duties, the Chancellor and judges should retain this function. Our advisory opinions are no more binding than theirs would be. However, I support giving advisory opinions, as the function is non-judicial, allowing personal discretion, unlike judicial duties. Given the circumstances, providing an opinion seems appropriate.

The Governor directed his questions to us, and significant time has passed since then. We’ve thoroughly examined all aspects of the issue, with input from skilled counsel. While I don’t believe Paragraph 374 applies to us, my colleagues disagree. If we decline to answer, trial judges might also refuse, believing the statute refers to us. Clearly, the legislature intended the Governor to receive advisory opinions from some judicial branch. Since the advisory role is non-judicial, I see no strong reason to withhold an opinion, especially given practical considerations. Though not compelled by statute, voluntary action seems expedient and courteous here.

Thus, except for the point discussed, I fully concur with the advisory opinion submitted by our Chief Justice and endorsed by Justice Wolcott. On the constitutionality of Paragraph 374, all Justices agree: The answer hinges on how Delaware’s Constitution interprets the separation of powers—the division of government into legislative, executive, and judicial branches, with no overlap. The 1897 Constitution, like its predecessors, lacks explicit separation language, unlike some states. Still, the separation of powers is a cornerstone of American constitutional law, as noted by Cooley in Constitutional Limitations, Chapter V, page 175.

Our courts have confirmed that state government has always been structured into three branches: legislative, executive, and judicial. State ex rel. Biggs v. Corley (Ct. in Banc 1934), 6 W. W. Harr. (36 Del.) 135, 144, 172 A. 415, 419. However, the separation of powers principle has not been strictly followed in practice. The Constitutions of 1792 (art. VIII, Sec. 3) and 1831 (art. II, Sec. 16) allowed the General Assembly to perform some executive functions, and the current constitution permits legislative appointments to office. State ex rel. Morford v. Emerson, 1 Terry (40 Del.) 233, 8 A. 2d 154, affirmed on opinion below, 1 Terry (40 Del.) 496, 14 A. 2d 378. Additionally (and more relevant here), the Constitution

of 1897 explicitly assigns the judiciary the administrative task of reviewing election results. Art. V, Sec. 6. This suggests that the public does not oppose some flexibility in the separation of powers, implying that restrictions on the General Assembly’s authority should not be overly rigid. While some cases reject the legislature’s power to demand advisory opinions from judges without constitutional backing, most rulings support this view. See In re Constitutionality of House Bill No. 222, 262 Ky. 437, 90 S. W. 2d 692, 103 A. L. R. 1085; In re Opinion of the Justices, 1949, 115 Vt. 524, 64 A. 2d 169; In the matter of the Application of the Senate, 10 Minn. 78, 10

Gil. 56. Conversely, Alabama upheld such a statute. In re Opinions of the Justices, 209 Ala. 593, 96 So. 487. These differing outcomes do not stem from disputes over the nature of advisory opinions. There is consensus, as stated in State ex rel. Satterthwaite v. Highfield, supra, 4 W. W. Harr. (34 Del.) 272, 152 A. 45, that this is a non-judicial role. However, interpretations vary. Kentucky’s Court of Appeals ruled that granting such powers to judges violated the constitution’s limit to appellate jurisdiction. Other cases base their reasoning on separation of powers. Vermont’s constitution explicitly mandates this division, stating that no branch may exercise another’s powers

.' Ch. II, Sec. 5; 64 A. 2d 172. A similar provision likely influenced Minnesota’s decision, 10 Minn. 78, 10 Gil. 57. In contrast, Alabama’s Supreme Court justices, despite their constitution’s ban on interdepartmental power exercises (Constitution of Alabama of 1901, Secs. 42 and 43), distinguished between non-judicial duties assigned to judges and those conferred on courts as constitutional entities. They concluded that such assignments do not violate separation of powers. Rejecting Minnesota’s stance, the Alabama justices endorsed Fox v. McDonald, 101 Ala. 51, 13 So. 4, which supported their position.

In 16, 21 L. R. A. 529, 46 Am. St. Rep. 98, the constitutionality of a law mandating a county probate judge to appoint a police commission for Birmingham was upheld. This decision acknowledges, unlike opposing views, that the roles of the three branches of state government have historically overlapped, and the strict theoretical separation has never been rigidly enforced. Which approach aligns better with Delaware's constitutional and legislative evolution? Reviewing Delaware's laws assigning non-judicial tasks to judges reveals a long-standing practice of judicial officers handling diverse executive and administrative responsibilities. For instance, since colonial times, courts like the Quarter Sessions or General Sessions have evaluated tavern license applications and advised the Governor. See 1 Del. L. Ch. 75 (13 Geo. II); 2 Del. L. Ch. 20 (1793); 8 Del. L. Ch. 208 (1833); 1852 Code, Ch. 53.

Another early example is the 1814 Act (5 Del. L. Ch. 23), authorizing Sussex County's Court of General Quarter Sessions to appoint trustees for Cape Henlopen lands. Numerous other cases, detailed earlier in this opinion, demonstrate a centuries-old tradition under Delaware's constitutions of judges performing non-judicial tasks, often unrelated to their judicial roles. No Delaware court has ever challenged the General Assembly's authority in this matter. Notably, past Governors have sought advisory opinions from the Chancellor and judges, which were provided without constitutional objections. For example, In re School Code of 1919 involved arguments before the Chancellor and judges, with extensive legal briefs, and the resulting opinion was published (7 Boyce 406, 108 A. 39).

The long history of such legislative actions reflects a practical interpretation by Delaware's citizens and lawmakers of the separation of powers doctrine, further supported by the judiciary and legal community's tacit acceptance. While the doctrine may limit legislative power in some cases, it cannot invalidate Paragraph 374. The policy behind such laws, often criticized elsewhere, is not our concern here. However, the risks to democratic governance from blending governmental functions seem least significant when judges perform minor administrative duties, given the judiciary's traditionally weaker role among the three branches.

Considering this, the Alabama Supreme Court's reasoning appears more convincing than rulings in Minnesota and Vermont. The Kentucky case's objection to advisory opinions as conflicting with appellate jurisdiction assumes the statute expands the court's judicial authority, which we find incorrect. Advisory opinions are not judicial acts but executive advice, as members of the court do not exercise judicial power in such cases. Additionally, the argument that the statute infringes on the Attorney General's constitutional role (Art. Ill, Sec. 21) as the state's legal advisor and representative merits attention but does not undermine the statute's validity.

Other state officials and agencies may request legal advice from the Attorney General. The legislative branch has the authority to modify the common law powers and responsibilities of the office, as acknowledged in Darling Apartment Co. v. Springer, particularly in Judge Rodney's concurring opinion. We find the statute does not unconstitutionally infringe on the Attorney General's role. Therefore, we uphold the constitutionality of Paragraph 374 of the 1935 Revised Code. Respectfully submitted, Clarence A. Southerland, Chief Justice, and Associate Justices Daniel F. Wolcott and James M. Tunnell, Jr. Unrelated sections regarding Supreme Court rules are omitted.

In 1935, the period was reduced to six months. References include the 1852 Code, Sec. 924 on tavern licenses, and Sec. 878 appointing trustees for the indigent blind. Additional sections cover the Superior Court judges, trustees for the New Castle County Workhouse, the State Library, and the Board of Parole. Further provisions address Cape trustees, slave import/export licenses, and fence viewers.

Additional statutes include jury commissioners, the Medical Council, and the Old Age Welfare Commission. Other sections pertain to deputy judges of the Municipal Court and county law libraries. Cited authorities include 'The Federalist,' No. 78. Justice Boyce delivered the court's opinion on a demurrer challenging charges against Samuel Burris for violating Delaware's Constitution. Several demurrer grounds were raised, with some withdrawn during arguments.

The demurrer challenges the sufficiency of the charges, alleging vagueness and legal conclusions. The counts accuse Burris of unlawfully influencing election officers during a 1915 primary in Wilmington, urging them to close polls prematurely. Counsel focused on the latter allegations, arguing they fail to specify the offense clearly.

alleging that Samuel Burris, during the specified primary election, unlawfully urged election officers to close the polls between one and seven o'clock in the afternoon, thereby attempting to make them neglect their duties; this charge is part of the second count, which similarly accuses him of trying to influence the officers to shut the polls during the same timeframe; the third count reiterates these allegations, emphasizing his unlawful actions to disrupt the election process.

further accusing Burris of compelling election officers to close the polls during the primary election by instructing and advising them to do so, as detailed in the fourth count; this count also notes that the officers followed his directives, keeping the polls closed for over an hour, which violated their official responsibilities; the indictment lacks specific details about the steps taken beyond mere preparation, which is deemed insufficient under the statute.

the offense, as defined by the Constitution, involves causing or attempting to cause election officers to breach their duties, which is a distinct crime rather than an attempt to commit another offense; the charges clearly outline the accused's actions and the specific duties the officers were allegedly pressured to violate, meeting the legal requirement for reasonable certainty in the description of the offense.

the court overruled the demurrer, affirming that the charges in the information align with the state's constitutional provisions; the case also involves a divorce proceeding, where the petitioner seeks child support and legal fees from the respondent, with both parties having previously reached a temporary agreement on these matters during a pre-hearing conference.

1. The Court has ordered the Respondent to pay the Petitioner $75.00 weekly for child support until further notice. Temporary custody of their child, Jennifer Lucy H...., is granted to the Petitioner. The Respondent is allowed unsupervised visitation as agreed by both parties. The child must not be taken out of Delaware without Court approval, and both parties are prohibited from doing so. Violating this order may result in the violator forfeiting all property rights to the non-violating party. The Court endorsed this agreement on December 27, 1978.

2. The Petitioner, born in Norway in 1948, held a Norwegian passport for herself and her child. The Respondent, born in the U.S. in 1939, had taken her passport and refused to return it. On January 19, 1979, his attorney sent the passport to the Court, arguing it should not be released to her without a hearing. Her attorney countered on January 24, stating the December 27 order’s restrictions negated the Respondent’s claim. The Court discussed the matter on January 31, acknowledging the Respondent’s fears but ruling it had no grounds to retain the passport, though warning the Petitioner against leaving Delaware without permission.

3. During the January 31 conference, the Court dismissed the Respondent’s custody application with his consent. This case involves testamentary trustees seeking guidance on whether shares distributed by the Delaware Railroad Company belong to the life tenant or should remain part of the estate's corpus. Key facts about the new shares include: (1) They were part of an increased stock issue representing earnings reinvested in the company's railroad infrastructure; (2) These earnings were generated and reinvested after the testator's death; (3) The old shares' market value remains unaffected by the new shares and can be sold for more than their original cost. The central question is the proper allocation of these shares, as clearly presented in this case.

This case is being heard in Delaware courts for the first time, leaving this court unbound by any local precedents in its decision. The will of James C. Aikin instructs trustees to pay the net income, interest, and dividends to the life tenant, but this wording does not clarify the testator's intent regarding the disputed issue. The term 'dividends' alone does not universally imply such intent. Additionally, while some shares held by the trustees were owned by the testator, there was no specific mention or bequest of these shares in the will. The distribution in question occurred long after the testator's death, making it unlikely he anticipated or addressed it in his will. Despite varying opinions on corporate earnings distribution, certain principles are accepted: corporations may choose to distribute or reinvest earnings, expand operations, or capitalize them by issuing new shares, all within reasonable bounds of good faith without judicial interference.

Corporations are prohibited from distributing capital as dividends or reducing their capital stock. Dividends must come from earnings or profits. The rights of life tenants and remaindermen in unusual corporate distributions have long challenged courts, leading to several established rules. These rules hinge on whether the distribution stems from earnings or capital, and sometimes on the nature of the distribution even if derived from earnings. Courts must determine whether the distributed funds represent past or current earnings, a change in capital structure, or an increase in capital value unrelated to earnings. While earnings may be divided differently, distributions labeled as dividends but sourced from non-earnings are generally treated as capital. The resolution often depends on the company's declared intent and the nature of the distribution.

When a distribution to shareholders results from capital reduction during dissolution or reflects increased asset value due to market conditions rather than earnings accumulation, it is typically allocated to the corpus, not income. Courts generally agree to examine corporate actions to determine whether a distribution originates from earnings or other sources, and if earnings, whether they were converted into capital. In this instance, the company's resolutions clearly specify the distribution's source, acquisition period, and usage. The appreciation in stock value from accumulated earnings is considered part of the corpus; if sold, the proceeds augment the principal, with the life tenant receiving income from reinvested funds while the remainder beneficiary retains the preserved principal.

Similarly, the right to subscribe to new shares at par value, when marketable above par, is deemed a capital accretion, not income for the life tenant. If trustees sell these subscription rights (often called 'warrants'), the proceeds belong to the principal. Legal precedents such as Stewart v. Phelps and Perry on Trusts support this principle. However, conflicting rulings exist on the specific issue raised in this case, with divergent underlying rationales. For example, the treatment of the shares in question varies widely, reflecting the lack of consensus among courts on this matter.

The Chancellor noted the initial oral agreement between the complainant and his father treated the conveyance as loan security, with no repayment deadline. A later written agreement set a three-year limit for reconveyance, but an unwritten extension followed. The complainant’s claims rely on an oral agreement, a written contract, and a subsequent oral amendment. The defendant demurred, arguing: (1) the oral modification was invalid post-sealing and lacked consideration; (2) it violated the statute of frauds. Neither argument holds, as the defendant misinterprets the case’s nature.

The defendant incorrectly frames the case as a standard land sale contract requiring specific performance, invoking the parol evidence rule and statute of frauds. However, the bill actually involves a deed meant as mortgage security for a $2,000 loan, entitling the complainant to reclaim the land. In such cases, parol evidence is admissible to reveal the true intent behind seemingly absolute written instruments. This aligns with established precedent where oral proof has been used to impose trusts or convert deeds into mortgages, without violating the parol evidence rule or statute of frauds.

Parol evidence is permissible to demonstrate that a deed appearing absolute was intended solely as loan security. Precedents like Walker’s Adm’x v. Farmers’ Bank, Hall v. Livingston, and others support this principle, allowing oral evidence to alter the interpretation of formal documents. Such evidence does not breach the parol evidence rule or statute of frauds, as it clarifies the parties’ true agreement rather than contradicting written terms. Thus, the bill’s claim—that the deed functioned as a mortgage—can be substantiated through parol evidence without legal conflict.

The defendant argues that the clause in the May 27, 1924 agreement, which set a three-year limit for the complainant to reclaim the land, nullifies his rights since he failed to pay within that period. This argument is invalid for two reasons. First, it is evident that the defendant's president, whose authority is undisputed, assured the complainant he could pay anytime, leading him to delay payment. It would be unjust to now deny the complainant's reliance on these representations. The defendant's actions prejudiced the complainant, creating an estoppel. The agreement merely granted the complainant the right to redeem the land, and under these circumstances, the time limit was effectively waived.

The right to redeem persists until foreclosure, as affirmed by the Court of Errors and Appeals in Walker's Adm'x. v. Farmers' Bank. Judge Grubb noted that an equity of redemption is inherent in a mortgage and cannot be waived, even by contractual agreement. A similar case, Jackson et al. v. Lynch, involved an absolute deed with a repurchase agreement tied to debt repayment. When the time lapsed, the Illinois court ruled that the mortgagor's right to redeem cannot be forfeited by contract, as equity courts always protect this right.

In Jackson v. Lynch, the Illinois court emphasized that a mortgagor cannot lose the equity of redemption through any contractual terms, no matter how explicit. The court held that chancery courts will intervene to uphold the mortgagor's right to redeem if the transaction was intended as security. Mooney v. Byrne echoed this principle. Thus, regardless of estoppel, the complainant retains the right to reclaim the land upon repayment, even after the three-year period, as his redemption right was never foreclosed.
