Is this a case of set-off under the statute, or can it be done under the Court's equitable power independently? These were the questions argued. First, is it a set-off within the statute? I believe it is not. The statute (Rev. Code 380, Sec. 21) specifically limits set-off to 'mutual debts' between parties due 'in the same right.' This means a debt owed by A alone can only discharge a debt owed to A alone, ensuring debts of the same nature are matched. The provision aims to protect claims with attached rights from unjust discharge.

A joint debt cannot offset a several one, as it would unfairly extinguish the joint creditor's rights. Similarly, an executor cannot set off a debt owed to the estate against a personal debt, as it would misuse assets belonging to beneficiaries. The same principle applies to discharging a husband's debt with his wife's legacy, as she retains a survivorship right in the legacy, protected by law. The exact nature of this right varies, but its legal recognition as a substantial interest is undisputed.

The wife's survivorship right is safeguarded with the same rigor as joint creditors or estate beneficiaries. The law favors her interest in choses in action, requiring the husband's explicit action to extinguish it. Creditors generally cannot interfere unless specified by statute. For instance, attaching a wife's chose in action is limited to the husband's rights, leaving her interest intact unless possession is achieved.

Even if a creditor attaches the husband's right to the wife's chose in action, her survivorship interest remains unless the creditor takes possession. The law is strict about what extinguishes her right, requiring clear action by the husband. Creditors' claims do not override her interest unless explicitly allowed by statute, emphasizing the protective stance of the law toward the wife's rights.

For actual and positive reduction, the husband taking possession, or a release or assignment for valuable consideration, is enough to prevent the wife's survivorship rights to her choses in action. A voluntary assignment by the husband without consideration does not affect her. 2 Kent (137). There has been long debate over whether an assignment, even for consideration, should transfer more than the husband's ability to claim the chose in action, subject to the wife's survivorship if he dies first. It is now settled that a paid assignment bars the wife's right to a presently claimable chose in action, but not reversionary interests. 2 Kent (137)-(138) note (a). Courts have required clear and deliberate acts by the husband to change ownership and override the wife's rights.

Setting aside a specific fund, like a mortgage, from a testator's estate to pay a legacy to the wife, along with interest payments to the husband, was deemed insufficient to override her survivorship rights. Blount vs. Bestland, 5 Ves. 515. Similarly, a husband proving his wife's debt in bankruptcy and paying contributions did not alter ownership to deny her dividends. Anon. 2 Vern. 707. Depositing the wife's legacy in court under a decree, without an order for payment to the husband, is also inadequate. Bond vs. Simmons, 3 Atk. 20; Macaulay vs. Philips, 4 Ves. 17; Clancy on M. W. 119. Partial payments of interest or principal to the husband do not constitute full possession of the remaining balance.

Nash vs. Nash, 2 Madd. 133 (1 Dan. Ch. Pr. 149). Even if the husband receives money owed to the wife, it does not suffice if his possession can be linked to any right other than marital authority. In Baker vs. Hall, 12 Ves. 497, an executor marrying a residuary legatee did not alter her legacy until he actively converted it for his use. See also Wall vs. Tomlinson, 16 Ves. 413. A joint lawsuit for the wife's chose in action, whether pre- or post-marriage, does not affect her rights, nor does a judgment alone—only execution suffices. Clancy on M. W. 113; 2 Kent 127; 2 Ves. Sr. 676; 6 Johns. Ch. R. 132; 9 Paige 283.

In a suit filed solely by the husband, the debt is only reduced to his possession upon judgment, not before. Clancy on M. W. 113. Further examples are unnecessary, as it is clear that the wife's survivorship rights to her choses in action are carefully protected and can only be overridden by the husband's clear intent to change ownership. Exceptions include involuntary assignments due to bankruptcy or creditor attachments under state law. This perspective aligns with Chancellor Kent's opinion in Schuyler vs. Hoyle, 5 Johns. Ch. R. 625, and is reinforced by Judge King in Miller's Case, 1 Ashmead 323, C.J. Gibson in Timbers vs. Katz, 6 W. & S. 290, and C.J. Parker in Marston vs. Carter & Trustee, 12 N.H.

159. Our courts have consistently protected the ydfe's interest in her chose in action with strict vigilance. The Court of Appeals ruled that a husband's equitable assignment of his wife's distributive share to settle his debt does not nullify her rights if he dies before the creditor obtains possession, as seen in State vs. Robertson & Burton, 5 Harring. 201. Similarly, Lendeman vs. Lendeman's Ex'r., 1 Houst. 523, affirmed that a promissory note given to the wife during marriage remains hers if unpaid at her husband's death. This ruling favored the wife more than some precedents, which treat such instruments as wholly the husband's property, akin to cash. Lightbourn vs. Holy day, 1 Eq. Ca. Ab. 1; Nash vs. Nash, 2 Mad. 135 (n); 1 Dan. Ch. Pr. 149; Shuttlesworth vs. Noyes.

8 Mass. 229; Com. vs. Manley, 12 Pick. 172. The 1 Houston decision aligns with Nash vs. Nash, 2 Mad. 133. This analysis reveals that the wife's survivorship right in the contested legacy is significant enough that, while active, the legacy cannot be considered the husband's sole property under the statute. Offsetting her claim would undermine the statute's intent and the protective policy safeguarding her choses in action, which are only divested by the husband's deliberate conversion, release, or assignment for value. It was argued that the Court should consider the proceeding's substance, subjecting it to claims against the husband. However, no such outcome is guaranteed or should be presumed.

Execution may not occur during the husband's lifetime, leaving the wife's survivorship right intact until then, and it must be fully honored. The law will not preemptively strip her of this right to appease the husband's creditor. Burrough vs. Moss, 10 B. & C. 558, directly supports this: when a husband sued alone on a note given to his wife during marriage, the defendant tried to offset a debt from her pre-marriage days. The Court rejected this, citing the husband's election evidenced by his solo suit. They stated the husband could treat the note as joint or separate property; choosing the latter allowed his debts as offsets, but not both. 1 Roper, on H. & W. (212.).

The claim that the executor's offset right should not hinge on the lawsuit's form or the husband's choice to sue alone or jointly is untenable. The husband's right to convert the wife's chose in action is exercised through his litigation choices, which reflect his intent. No act of his constitutes possession against his will. This principle underpinned Wall vs. Tomlinson, 16 Ves. 415, where a husband, as executor, handling stock owed to his wife, was deemed not to have claimed it, as the transfer had a different purpose. Similarly, Timbers vs. Katz, 6 W. & S. 290, illustrated this doctrine.

The husband accompanied his wife in a receipt for funds owed on a bond issued to her while single, but without collecting the money, was deemed not to have taken possession of the bond. C. J. Gibson states, 'ownership aligns with his intent; the law will not impose it on him against his will.' This is echoed in Dennison vs. Nigh, 2 Watts 90. Thus, since the husband can choose to nullify his wife's claim to her legacy, he can safeguard her interest by including her in the legal action until recovery and execution, thereby unavoidably limiting the creditor's right to set-off based on the lawsuit's structure. In Pennsylvania, despite some rulings treating the wife's survivorship right as an active title rather than a mere possibility, it has been ruled in three instances that it can be offset against the husband's debt, including one case involving a joint claim. Yohe vs. Barnett, 1 Binn. 358; Wishart vs. Downey and wife, 15 S. & R.

77; Lowman's Appeal, 3 W. & S. 349. See also Brockenridge J.'s opinion in Murray vs. Williamson, 3 Binn. 135. These cases, however, hinge on interpretations of state statutes and are explicitly contrasted with English legal precedents. In Yohe vs. Barnet, 1 Binn. 358, which influenced later rulings, the wife held an interest in real estate undergoing partition in the Orphans' Court. The property was appraised, and her portion of the proceeds was secured by a bond, seemingly issued in the husband's name per statutory requirements. He owed a debt to the intestate via a judgment, and the administrators successfully petitioned to offset the bond's owed amount against this debt. The ruling centered on the bond being under the husband's name as mandated by law. The case in 3 Binney, Murray vs. Williamson, does not directly address the issue, though Brockenridge J. notes in his opinion that Pennsylvania's broader statutory interpretation of set-off overrides the English doctrine barring the use of the wife's claim against

the husband's debt. In the subsequent case of Wishart vs. Downey & wife, 15 S. & R. 77, involving a sci.fa. filed jointly by husband and wife over a recognizance securing the wife's inheritance share, the court permitted offsetting the husband's debt, citing Binney cases as establishing a more expansive set-off rule than English law. They remarked, 'In England, since the suit is in the wife's right and would survive to her, this claim couldn’t be offset. Our law differs, and this, if proven, was a valid set-off.' Lowman's Appeal, 3 W. & S., concerning a wife's legacy, adhered to prior Pennsylvania rulings. Thus, the state's legal trajectory openly diverges from the general rule, rooted in its statutes. Notably, these decisions clash with Pennsylvania's otherwise robust stance on the wife's retained ownership of her claims until the husband formally takes possession, as emphasized by C. J. Gibson in Timbers vs. Katz, 6 W. & S. 290, where he states the husband lacks even a 'semblance of ownership' until such conversion. In Ferguson vs. Lathrop, 15 Wend. 625, where the couple jointly leased the wife's property and distrained for rent, the tenant was allowed to offset a claim against the husband alone. The court broadly asserted that 'a lawful

claim against him shouldn’t be thwarted by unnecessarily involving his wife’s name'—since he could voluntarily collect rent or settle it against his debt without infringing her rights, the law could enforce this without violation. This principle fit the case, as rents from the wife’s real estate wholly belonged to the husband, with no spousal claim, making her inclusion in the lease improper.

The argument regarding rent action lacks support from authority or principle, particularly concerning the wife's choses in action, where her interest remains until the husband or his assignee decides otherwise. Notably, this reasoning, based on the husband's potential to sue alone, wouldn't apply in equity cases, where the wife must always join to safeguard her interests. A conflicting New York case, Mollan vs. Griffith, 3 Paige 402, involved a suit by a couple to recover rents from the wife's estate, where executors attempted to offset an overpayment to the husband for a legacy. The Chancellor rejected this, stating the debts were not in the same right.

The Chancellor denied the set-off, ruling that the rents and profits claim belonged to the wife and would pass to her by survivorship, while the overpayment to the husband was his personal debt. English cases similarly distinguish between debts owed to or by the wife before marriage and those involving the husband, barring set-off unless the husband converted her choses in action or assumed her liabilities. For instance, Paynter vs. Walker (4 Geo. III) and Wood vs. Akers (2 Esp. Rep. 594) emphasize that a husband cannot offset debts owed to him in his wife's right against his own liabilities, as the wife's pre-marital debts remain distinct.

In Burrough vs. Moss (10 B. & C. 558), the husband sued alone on a promissory note given to the wife during marriage, making it his separate property. The court barred the defendant from offsetting a debt owed by the wife before marriage. The decision highlighted that if the husband had treated the note as joint property, the wife's debts might have been considered, but not both her and his debts. These cases demonstrate that common law courts prohibit offsetting joint or separate spousal debts, with equity courts further protecting the wife's interests by requiring her inclusion in all suits.

Equity cases align with this principle but offer additional protection for the wife, mandating her joinder in all suits, unlike common law where it's optional for post-marriage claims. Lady Elibank vs. Montolieu (5 Ves. 737) was cited to support offsetting a wife's share against her husband's debt, but the case only ruled that an administrator couldn't offset the husband's debt against her settlement claim. The court left unresolved how to handle the remaining share, as this issue wasn't before them and wasn't thoroughly examined.

It has been subject to action or any issue of offset against the balance has emerged, except in disputes between the administrator and the husband or, as in the next case, between the administrator and the husband's assignees. In Carr vs. Taylor, 10 Ves. 575, the same issue arose and was resolved. The wife filed a bill against an administrator for a distributive share, seeking its full settlement due to the husband's bankruptcy. The administrator sought to retain a debt owed by the husband. With the bankruptcy assignees involved and claiming the entire share, the offset question affected both the wife's equity and the assignees' surplus. Sir Wm. Grant, the Master of the Rolls, denied the offset entirely, awarding the share to the assignees, subject to a settlement for the wife.

Sir Wm. Grant's wording is unequivocal: 'Concerning the administratrix of Taylor's offset claim based on the plaintiff’s husband’s debt to the intestate’s estate,' he stated, 'regardless of any dispute over the husband’s right to sue for his wife’s legal choses in action, he could not sue for this fund without her. Had he obtained a decree in her right and died before securing it, it would have survived. Thus, no offset for the husband’s debt is permissible.' This principle applies equally here, even if a statute allows the husband to sue alone for a legacy at law. In equity, the parties’ rights remain as they were under Sir Wm. Grant, and even at law, the husband can preserve his wife’s rights by including her in the suit. The matter was briefly addressed, though not decided, in McMahon vs. Burchell, 3 Hare 97 and 5 Hare 322, before Vice Chancellor Sir James Wigram.

In a case involving legacies payable to both husband and wife, the executors sought to offset rent owed by the husband for shared premises with the testator. The Vice Chancellor allowed the offset against the husband’s legacy but noted, as recorded in 3 Hare, that it ‘does not apply to the wife’s legacy.’ When the case reappeared in 5 Hare, the Master found no rent due applicable to the legacies, resolving the matter. However, the Vice Chancellor clarified that his earlier remark in 3 Hare was misreported: he had not entirely barred offsetting the husband’s debt against the wife’s legacy but only to the extent it harmed her equity to a settlement.

The Vice Chancellor’s clarification negated the initial report’s authority against offsetting the husband’s debt from the legacy’s balance after the wife’s settlement, though it did not endorse such an offset. A strong precedent protecting the wife’s legacy from her husband’s debts emerged in Harrison vs. Andrews, 13 Simons 595 (1843). There, a £100 legacy to the wife was offset against the husband’s debt, with both signing a receipt. However, the executors had not surrendered the promissory note. After the husband’s death, the wife was awarded the legacy, with the Vice Chancellor ruling that only the husband’s release or payment could discharge it against her. McNEILLY, Justice: Defendant Robert H. Saunders appeals his first-degree murder and conspiracy convictions.

The defendant was charged with possessing a deadly weapon during a felony, third-degree burglary, theft, and second-degree conspiracy. He also appeals the Superior Court's decision to classify him as a habitual offender, resulting in a life sentence without probation or parole. The defendant presents ten arguments for reversal, which we address in order. Finding no grounds for reversal, we uphold the conviction. The victim, Joseph L. (Spoon) Johnson, was killed on Delaware Route 9 near Delaware City. Three accomplices, who pleaded guilty to lesser charges in exchange for testifying, stated that the victim was murdered shortly after they and the defendant robbed a small bank. According to their testimony, the defendant shot Johnson at close range with a .38 caliber revolver while in a car near Red Lion Creek. The bullet fragmented, causing immediate death by destroying the victim's brain.

After the shooting, the defendant instructed the accomplices—Eron M. Davis, Joseph F. Wood, and William McK. Jones—to each fire a shot into the victim's body. He then ordered them to dispose of the body in Red Lion Creek before proceeding to Wilmington, where they destroyed the weapon and divided the stolen money. The defendant argues that the inconsistent and uncorroborated testimony of the accomplices, along with his own denials and an alibi witness, should overturn the conviction. Citing Bland v. State, he highlights twelve inconsistencies in the accomplices' accounts. While their testimonies varied in details, all three agreed that the defendant murdered Johnson with a .38 caliber revolver after the bank robbery. Unlike Bland, where discrepancies involved the number of participants and the defendant's presence, here the inconsistencies were minor. The court in Bland emphasized caution when evaluating accomplice testimony, a principle followed in this case. We find no merit in the defendant's argument.

The defendant claims the trial court erred by admitting five statements from the accomplices under 11 Del.C. § 3507(a). He argues these statements violated his Sixth and Fourteenth Amendment rights, were involuntary due to plea bargaining, were cumulative and prejudicial, and breached the Bruton rule. However, each accomplice testified that their statements were voluntary, and they were cross-examined extensively. No Bruton or Blodgett issues arose, and the statements were properly presented to the jury. We reject this contention.

The defendant asserts that the trial court violated his constitutional rights under Brady v. Maryland and Jenkins v. State by not declaring a mistrial after learning new information post-trial. He argues the withheld evidence was material and prejudicial. However, the court determined the evidence would not have altered the verdict. Given the lack of prejudicial impact, we find no error in the denial of a mistrial.

The State's case involves accomplices Davis and Wood making exculpatory statements not shared with the defense despite a pre-trial discovery motion. These statements reportedly address a 'critical issue' of motive for someone other than the defendant to kill victim 'Spoon' Johnson. The defense argues the statements, by introducing new motive evidence, were relevant for cross-examining Wood and Davis, making them subject to Brady rule disclosure. Under Brady, prosecutors must share evidence 'material' to the defense. In U.S. v. Agurs, the Court ruled that unless nondisclosure severely compromises the defendant's right to a fair trial, it doesn’t breach constitutional disclosure duties. The potential usefulness of undisclosed evidence alone doesn’t establish materiality unless it could have introduced reasonable doubt.

The trial's outcome isn’t constitutionally affected by undisclosed evidence unless it would have created 'reasonable doubt of guilt' that wasn’t present otherwise. Here, the defendant knew of the statements for at least five months before revealing them to his attorney during the State's case. In fact, he had used these statements for an unrelated bank robbery case in Pennsylvania. His current attorney, the prosecutor, and the chief investigator were unaware of the statements, though the latter witnessed one without knowing its content. After hearing testimony from Wood and Davis, the Trial Judge deemed the statements non-critical and immaterial under Brady, a ruling we uphold. The defendant also claims his trial was unfair due to racial bias, citing underrepresentation of blacks on the petit jury panel, the peremptory challenge of the sole black juror, limited peremptory challenges, and being barred from discussing race in closing arguments.

The defendant’s reliance on People v. Wheeler to support his jury selection claim is misguided. In Wheeler, black defendants were convicted of murdering a white victim, and the State used peremptory challenges to exclude all black jurors despite their passing cause challenges. The defense objected, proving a prima facie case of systematic exclusion, shifting the burden to the State to justify its actions. The State failed, leading to reversed convictions. Here, only one black juror was challenged, with no record of impropriety. As Wheeler states, peremptory challenges aren’t scrutinized unless a prima facie showing of group bias exists. None of the defendant’s other claims hold merit: his case wasn’t capital, so he wasn’t entitled to twenty challenges, and with no racial overtones, the judge rightly barred race from closing arguments.

The defendant argues the Trial Judge’s active involvement—questioning witnesses and advising the prosecutor on evidence admissibility—compromised judicial impartiality in the jury’s eyes. The judge’s remarks when overruling defense objections clarify this issue: 'The jury is absent during this voir dire examination to determine the admissibility of photographs and the doctor’s expertise before allowing his testimony. My role is to ensure proper legal standards are met, not to sway the jury.' This underscores the judge’s duty to manage trial proceedings fairly, without bias, while maintaining procedural correctness.

During my questioning of Mr. Wood, I believed the questions aimed to uncover the truth, some even favoring the defense. The Court called a sidebar to address potential prejudice, emphasizing the need for factual accuracy in the record and rejecting irrelevant claims. We see no misuse of discretion in the Judge's actions or in denying the defendant's request for an investigator at state expense in this criminal case.

The defendant argues the Trial Judge erred by not instructing the jury on assault, given the victim died from multiple gunshot wounds and others were involved. This claim lacks merit, as the defendant's alibi defense contradicted assault, and eyewitnesses testified he fatally shot the victim at close range. No assault instruction was warranted, nor was there error in omitting conspiracy instructions, as the given charges were proper.

Newly discovered evidence, including inmate affidavits, suggested the accomplices framed the defendant for the murder. However, the Trial Judge deemed this evidence cumulative and unlikely to alter the trial's outcome. We agree, as the evidence either repeated trial testimony or was impeaching, failing to justify a new trial.

The defendant challenges his sentencing as an habitual criminal, citing the Attorney General's selective prosecution and a prior 1962 sentencing claim. The prosecutor cited the defendant's extensive criminal record as justification. The record shows no prior habitual criminal sentencing, and we accept the State's assertion. After reviewing the evidence, the Trial Judge correctly ruled the defendant met the habitual criminal criteria.

The Court determines the following: In State's Exhibit 13, which contains the business records of the Presentence Office under tab sixteen, the defendant, Robert H. Saunders, born December 2, 1939, a Black male, pleaded guilty to four felonies—Indictments No. 526, 527, 528, and 529—three for burglary and one for motor vehicle theft. These facts are supported by State's Exhibits No. 1 and 2. Additionally, the presentence reports and State's Exhibit No. 3 confirm guilty pleas to two counts of forgery under Title 11, Section 543, Subsection 5 of the former Delaware Code. Exhibit 13, under tab fourteen, shows Robert H. Saunders Jr., of 449 South Buttonwood Street, born December 2, 1939, pleading guilty to two forgery charges.

On April 27, 1961, the defendant pleaded not guilty, stood trial, and was convicted on January 5, 1962, of fourth-degree burglary in Criminal Actions 413, 414, and 415 of 1961, under the prior version of 11 Delaware Code, Section 395. Specifically, in Criminal Actions 414 and 415, he was found guilty of two counts of fourth-degree burglary, felonies under state law, as verified by State's Exhibit No. 6. State's Exhibit No. 9 further confirms his guilty pleas to two counts of fourth-degree burglary under the original statute (Indictments No. 157 and 158). State's Exhibit 12 reflects a guilty plea to robbery under 18 U.S.C. Section 4205(2), a federal felony.

State's Exhibit No. 10 documents a guilty plea by Robert Harlum Saunders to a felony under 18 U.S.C. Section 1001. Based on trial evidence, the Court concludes that the State met the requirements of Sections 4215 and 14 of the Delaware Code, proving the defendant had prior felony convictions exceeding three before his 1976 first-degree murder trial. The Trial Judge's findings are substantiated by the record, showing no legal error or abuse of discretion in the habitual offender proceedings.

The defendant's final claims of error include: (1) the jury not receiving written instructions; (2) denial of a mistrial after an accomplice referenced the defendant's incarceration; (3) alleged bias due to the Trial Judge and prosecutors' prior involvement in his cases; and (4) refusal to allow examination by his private psychiatrist. The record lacks evidence or legal authority supporting these claims. The Court finds no legal error or abuse of discretion in the Trial Judge's rulings. AFFIRMED. Under 11 Del.C. § 3507(a), a witness's prior voluntary statement may be used as substantive evidence if they are available for cross-examination.

Section 4(a) states that an individual with three prior felony convictions in this or any other state, U.S., or its territories—excluding those listed in subsection (b)—who is later convicted of another felony in this state may be deemed an habitual offender. The court handling the fourth or subsequent conviction has the discretion to sentence the individual to life imprisonment.

Section 4(b) specifies that a person with two prior convictions for certain named felonies or attempts, whether in this state or elsewhere, who is later convicted of another such felony or attempt must be sentenced to life imprisonment, unless capital punishment applies. This sentence is exempt from probation or parole under Chapter 43. Listed felonies include arson, burglary, murder, kidnapping, assault, rape, sodomy, and robbery.

In this shareholders' derivative suit for Shell Oil Company, defendants—past/present directors and corporate entities owning 69% of Shell's stock—seek dismissal of claims predating June 17, 1966, citing the statute of limitations. They also aim to strike later allegations as sham. The original 1969 complaint alleged Shell suffered losses due to coerced inter-corporate transactions favoring defendants.

The court previously ruled that plaintiffs' evidence—a 1964 lecture and 1962-63 articles—only supported claims about crude oil transactions during those years, not the broader allegations. The amended complaint now focuses solely on crude oil. Defendants argue the statute of limitations bars pre-1966 claims and that no evidence supports post-1966 wrongdoing, seeking dismissal of those allegations as sham.

The argument is that all claims are either barred or fraudulent. A. First, I examine the statute of limitations in this case. It is well-established that the three-year statute, 10 Del.C. § 8106, governs shareholder derivative actions seeking damages or similar legal remedies, as seen in Bokat v. Getty Oil Co., Del.Supr., 262 A.2d 246 (1970). However, plaintiffs argue for an exception here, presenting two theories: (1) the case falls under the Bovay v. H. M. Byllesby & Co. rule, which denies statute protection to fiduciaries who breach duties, and (2) defendants concealed the cause of action, tolling the statute.

In Bovay, the Supreme Court stated that equity courts handling constructive trusts due to fiduciary breaches may adjust the statute of limitations based on case specifics. The key issue is determining when corporate officers lose statute protections. Plaintiffs advocate a broad interpretation, arguing the statute should not shield defendants in derivative suits involving serious trust violations. Defendants, however, insist Bovay is narrowly applicable, limited to unique facts and strictly confined by later rulings. I side with defendants, as Bovay involved extreme misconduct, and its application has been consistently narrow. The case involved a bankrupt corporation’s creditors suing officers who fraudulently diverted funds, causing insolvency.

Brown v. Dolese, 38 Del.Ch. 471, 154 A.2d 233 (1959), is the only other Delaware case applying Bovay to suspend the statute, involving a director accused of fraudulently misusing assets. Conversely, courts have upheld the statute where directors did not personally profit, as in Mayer v. Adams, Del.Supr., 36 Del.Ch. 466, 174 A.2d 313 (1961), and Schleiff v. B. & O. R.R., 36 Del.Ch. 342, 130 A.2d 321 (1956). Merely alleging fiduciary self-dealing is insufficient; fraud must be charged. Schleiff’s Chancellor Seitz clarified that Bovay treats officials as trustees only if they divert assets.

Summarizing Bovay and related cases: the statute generally applies to derivative suits, but in rare cases involving fraudulent self-dealing, officers who profit may lose its protection. Here, plaintiffs have not shown personal profit by individual defendants, so Bovay’s exception does not apply. For corporate defendants, even if Bovay extends to controlling entities, the complaint lacks fraud allegations. Thus, neither individual nor corporate defendants are exempt from the statute under Bovay.

Defendants cannot depend on it. Next, I need to evaluate if the statute should be paused due to defendants fraudulently hiding the action. B. Fraudulent concealment of a claim is a separate reason to pause a statute of limitations. Lieberman v. First Nat'l Bank, Del.Supr., 8 Del.Ch. 519, 45 A. 901 (1900); 51 Am.Jur.2d, Limitations of Actions § 147. If a plaintiff is misled, the statute is paused until they discover their rights or could have discovered them with reasonable effort. Giordano v. Czerwinski, Del.Supr., 216 A.2d 874 (1966). Fraudulent concealment involves affirmative actions by a defendant, such as deliberate deception to hide facts or misrepresentations meant to mislead the plaintiff. Nardo v. Guido DeAscanis & Sons, Inc., Del.Super., 254 A.2d 254

(1969); 51 Am.Jur.2d, Limitation of Actions § 148. Simply not knowing the facts, without concealment, does not stop the statute. Mastellone v. Argo Oil Corp., Del.Supr., 7 Terry 102, 82 A.2d 379 (1951). If a plaintiff claims fraudulent misrepresentation to pause the statute, they must detail the fraud under Chancery Rule 9(b), Mayer v. Adams, supra; Klein v. Lionel Corp., 130 F.Supp. 725 (D.Del.1955). The allegations must be specific enough to inform the defendant of the claim’s basis, and merely using the term 'fraud' is insufficient. Dann v. Chrysler Corp., 40 Del.Ch. 103, 174 A.2d 696 (1961). Here, plaintiffs rely on the following

section of the amended complaint as proof of fraudulent concealment: '...Defendants tried to hide the alleged acts by mixing related and unrelated revenues and costs in Shell’s records, among other reasons, requiring them to provide a full accounting.' I note this allegation lacks any mention of fraud or specific deceptive acts by defendants to conceal the claims. These are broad statements without concrete evidence of concealment. Thus, the complaint fails to meet the required specificity for fraudulent acts to pause the statute. Therefore, the statute of limitations, 10 Del.C. § 8106, bars claims arising more than three years before the original complaint, i.e., before June 17, 1966. With that settled, I now assess whether plaintiffs have valid claims of wrongdoing after June

17, 1966. C. Plaintiffs argue this Court’s May 10, 1971, decision allowing the amended complaint established its sufficiency against motions to dismiss. Defendants disagree. In that unpublished opinion, the Court noted the original complaint’s overbreadth covered both time and subject matter, alleging wrongdoing in various inter-corporate transactions beyond crude oil and continuing until the lawsuit’s filing. See Hai-pern v. Barran, supra. The amended complaint narrowed the claims to crude oil. The Court stated: 'For now, plaintiffs can infer that the Gripaios speech and Symonds articles implicated Shell (and others) in crude oil practices and that these practices persisted after 19'

64. Referencing McFarland v. Gregory, 425 F.2d 443 (2d Cir. 1970), the court noted that the duration of the period in question was not critical to resolve at this stage, as only 'good cause' for the pleading was being considered. The language suggests plaintiffs could infer the complained-of practices persisted after 1964, but the exact timeframe was unnecessary to determine. Defendants, in their renewed motion to strike, emphasized the period, arguing the inferences should not extend beyond June 17, 1966. While the statute of limitations applied to pre-1966 events, the court avoided specifying the inference's duration, as it leaned toward evidentiary matters rather than pleading. Pleadings allow for inferences, but evidence requires case-by-case evaluation.

The nature of the issue and specific circumstances dictate the approach, as seen in McFarland v. Gregory and Wigmore on Evidence § 437 (3d ed.). Here, the focus is on pleading, and the court previously treated the submission under Rule 11, noting no judgment on defenses except the Rule 11 motion resolved in the opinion. Thus, the current motion to strike is effectively a third Rule 11 request, possibly due to the opinion's ambiguity rather than counsel's persistence. Regardless, the motion is excessive. While the 1971 ruling settles this motion, additional remarks on Rule 11 are warranted: it aids litigation but isn't suited for nuanced pleading comparisons or early Rule 12(b) motions.

Though 'good ground' can be objectively assessed, Rule 11 primarily sets standards for attorneys signing pleadings. It applies when pleadings vastly exceed available information or lack a reasonable basis, but attorneys need not preemptively defend against summary judgment. While bound by the prior decision, the amended complaint meets Rule 11's minimum requirements, supported by inferences (e.g., Gripaios speech, Symonds articles, Shell's affiliate transactions post-1966, and Ralph L. Ellis's affidavit data). The court emphasizes this is the bare minimum; no further conclusions are drawn. Defendants' motion to dismiss is granted for pre-1966 claims (time-barred) but denied for post-1966 claims.

Plaintiffs also moved under Chancery Rule 37 to compel answers to interrogatories, addressed in a separate decision. Under 10 Del.C. § 8106, injury claims without force or indirect effects must be filed within three years. Plaintiffs argued corporate defendants held a 'fiduciary' role akin to Shell's directors, but this need not be resolved here. In Bolcat, self-dealing allegations didn't suspend the statute, barring claims filed over three years post-complaint. Thus, the statute of limitations applies accordingly.

Simply claiming self-dealing is not enough. Whether this statutory exception extends to individuals in fiduciary roles beyond officers and directors remains uncertain, as noted in n. 3 supra. It is noteworthy that (1) the Bovay rule specifically targeted corporate officers and directors, (2) later applications of the rule, like Brown v. Dolese, involved an officer-director, and (3) other versions of the rule typically mention officers and directors, as seen in Mayer v. Adams and Schleiff v. B. & O. R.R. However, see Wise v. Delaware Steeplechase & Race Ass'n for a differing view. Bovay v. H. M. Byllesby is occasionally referenced for this point, but a detailed review of the case indicates otherwise.

Defendants were not granted the statute's protection; no tolling occurred for fraudulent concealment. FARRELL, Associate Judge: Petitioner was hurt on January 24, 2000, while working for Flippo. After a brief leave, he was reassigned to light-duty work at full pay. However, Flippo fired him on March 22, 2000, for breaking attendance policies. Petitioner then filed for workers' compensation from March 20 to October 9, 2000, when he started a new job. An ALJ rejected the claim, stating his post-March 20 wage loss resulted from violating company rules, not his injury. The DOES Director upheld this decision. In such cases, 'we accept the Director’s ruling if it is logically derived from the facts and supported by substantial evidence,' per Upchurch v. District of Columbia Dep’t of Employment Servs., 783 A.2d 623, 627 (D.C. 2001).

The ALJ concluded that while petitioner was injured, his post-March 20 wage loss stemmed from his refusal to comply with Flippo’s light-duty offer at full pay, not his injury. Petitioner was terminated after missing work on February 14, March 15, and March 21, 2000, despite warnings. He does not dispute the ALJ’s finding that Flippo provided suitable light-duty work. In Upchurch, the court addressed a similar employer argument that the worker was fired for failing to update his status and follow procedures. 783 A.2d at 625.

The court outlined the legal framework: Disability is economic, not medical, and requires wage-loss proof. The statutory presumption of compensability (D.C.Code § 32-1521) can be overturned if the employer proves with substantial evidence that the disability wasn’t work-related. Thus, the claimant must ultimately show by a preponderance of evidence that their economic disability resulted from the injury. Id. at 627-28. The court remanded to assess whether the claimant’s wage-loss arose from personal choices, like failing to inform the employer of his status or attend school. Id.

At 628, the Director correctly applied the Upchurch framework, concluding that Flippo had rebutted the presumption of compensability and the petitioner failed to demonstrate a causal link between the injury and wage loss, supported by substantial evidence. Flippo provided evidence, accepted by the ALJ, that the petitioner was terminated due to three unauthorized absences and ignoring two warnings, the second of which included a suspension and indicated further violations would lead to dismissal. A Flippo supervisor testified this progressive discipline aligned with company policy. While the petitioner explained the first two absences—such as being unable to locate the worksite on March 15 despite instructions—he offered no justification for the third absence, only claiming he couldn’t recall being suspended. The Director rightly found these explanations inadequate to prove the injury, rather than the disciplinary violations, caused his wage loss.

The petitioner cites no legal basis for his claim (Br. for Pet. at 8) that only 'gross misconduct,' as defined under D.C.Code § 51-110(b)(l) (2001), can sever the link between injury and wage loss. His additional argument (Br. for Pet. at 12) that a lesser standard than 'willful' misconduct incentivizes employers to terminate injured employees overlooks the employer’s burden to rebut compensability and statutory protections against retaliation (D.C.Code § 32-1542). The petitioner raised no claim of pretextual discharge here. Given these safeguards, the Director reasonably held Flippo could enforce its attendance policy uniformly, even for an injured employee on light duty. This aligns with Larson’s Workers’ Compensation § 84.04[1], stating discharge for misconduct unrelated to impairment doesn’t support compensable disability.

The Director implicitly found the petitioner’s violation of attendance rules was voluntary, unrelated to his injury. Larson acknowledges the severity of losing all workers’ compensation benefits for minor misconduct (e.g., a brief altercation) but suggests legislative remedies, like unemployment compensation penalties, might mitigate this. Courts, however, cannot enact such changes. The case doesn’t address unemployment eligibility, and Flippo conceded it remained liable for the petitioner’s ongoing medical treatment post-termination. The supervisor confirmed issuing warnings both in writing and verbally. The petitioner admitted not calling Flippo after failing to locate the worksite, and Stelma testified to contacting him at home that afternoon.

By 'regular employment,' Larson likely includes suitable light-duty work. JACOBS, Justice. The plaintiffs, former owners of Digital Imaging & Technologies, Inc. ('DIT'), sold the company to Lason, Inc., later revealed to have fraudulent accounting practices. Lason paid only part of the purchase price at closing and, after filing for bankruptcy, defaulted on the remainder. The plaintiffs then sued Lason’s accounting firm, PricewaterhouseCoopers, LLC ('PWC').

The case was filed in the Superior Court on February 21, 2008. The plaintiffs alleged that PWC negligently missed uncovering fraud during its audit of Lason's financial statements, which the plaintiffs relied on before selling DIT. PWC argued that the accounting malpractice claim was invalid due to the three-year statute of limitations, citing an email sent to the plaintiffs on January 6, 1999, which they claimed served as notice. The Superior Court agreed and dismissed the case, but this decision was later deemed incorrect and reversed.

Lason expanded its data/image capture services and acquired several companies between 1996 and 1999 to strengthen its market position. In 1998, Lason executives proposed acquiring DIT from the plaintiffs. PWC, which had handled Lason's financial audits and due diligence for previous acquisitions, prepared financial statements that the plaintiffs reviewed before finalizing the sale. The plaintiffs also met with PWC’s Timothy Molnar, who assured them the financial documents were accurate.

The parties signed a letter of intent in mid-1998, setting the base purchase price for DIT at $18 million, with adjustments for debt and future earnings. The payment was structured as 85% cash and 15% Lason stock. The merger closed on November 25, 1998, with an initial $6.5 million payment and the rest scheduled over three years. Before closing, DIT renegotiated a $1.9 million loan, resulting in an $800,000 debt forgiveness recorded as an 'accrued expense.'

After the merger, DIT and Lason exchanged emails regarding balance sheet adjustments. On January 6, 1999, Lason’s assistant comptroller, Robert Bassman, emailed DIT’s CFO, suggesting an aggressive accounting approach for the $800,000 debt forgiveness. He advised recording half as income discreetly and saving the rest for future use, explicitly avoiding auditor scrutiny. This email later became central to the legal dispute over the statute of limitations.

Upon receiving the email, Mr. Lydon grew worried about the appropriateness of Bassman's directive. Lydon alerted plaintiff Coleman, who then reached out to Lason's CEO, Gary Monroe, seeking clarification. Monroe apologized for the email's phrasing and assured Coleman that the transaction's accounting would be approved by PWC. Reassured, Coleman instructed Lydon to proceed with the adjustment as per the January 6, 1999 email. By December 1999, Lason's stock price had plummeted. On December 9, Monroe publicly claimed unawareness of any reason for the decline. On December 17, Monroe held a conference call with plaintiffs and others who had sold businesses to Lason, assuring them of the company's strong financial health despite the stock drop. However, by the next trading day, Lason's stock had fallen sharply from its yearly high.

On February 1, 1999, the stock was at $64.94 per share but dropped to $11.88 by December 20, 1999. In May 2000, Lason notified plaintiffs and other sellers that it was reviewing each earn-out agreement. By June 2000, Coleman and Lydon, alarmed by Lason's questionable practices, traveled to Detroit to meet with newly-appointed independent director Bill Brooks. Brooks promised to investigate but never followed up. In July 2000, Lason's board launched an internal probe into potential accounting irregularities, forming a Special Committee with legal counsel and initially hiring PWC. After eight months, on March 23, 2001, the Committee filed an SEC Form 8K disclosing major accounting issues in prior financial statements.

On December 5, 2001, Lason filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. Later, its top executives were indicted for securities fraud. Plaintiffs sued PWC on February 21, 2003, alleging accounting malpractice and negligent misrepresentation. They argued that proper auditing by PWC would have exposed Lason's irregularities and GAAP violations, preventing the sale of DIT. The Superior Court granted PWC summary judgment, ruling that the January 6, 1999 email should have alerted plaintiffs to potential issues, prompting further investigation. Had they acted, they would have discovered the facts before the three-year limitation expired around January 6, 2002.

The complaint, filed in February 2003, was deemed time-barred. This Court reviews summary judgment de novo, which is appropriate only when no material facts are disputed. The key issue is whether the trial court correctly applied the three-year statute of limitations under 10 Del. C. § 8106. The statute states that tort actions accrue when the wrongful act occurs, with limitations beginning at that time. Ignorance of the claim does not toll the statute unless concealment, fraud, or inherently unknowable injuries exist, in which case the clock starts when the injury is discovered.

The identification of facts 'forming the foundation of the cause of action or the presence of facts adequate to alert a person of average intelligence and caution to investigate further, which, if followed, would reveal' such facts. This Court has utilized the aforementioned 'discovery rule' in cases involving accounting and attorney malpractice, due to the unique nature of the professional-client relationship and the layperson's inability to recognize professional negligence. The rule's application depends on the specifics of each case. There is no disagreement that this case involves the discovery rule. The professional relationship between PWC and the plaintiffs; the plaintiffs' lack of alternative means to obtain information about La-son's financial statements' accounting treatment, which they relied on during DIT's acquisition; and the necessity for individuals in the plaintiffs' position to depend on PWC's accounting work, all support this conclusion. The appeal's central question is whether the January 6, 1999 email was legally sufficient to place the plaintiffs on inquiry notice of a potential claim that PWC negligently overlooked Lason's improper accounting practices during its audit.

This Court determines that the answer must be no, for two reasons. First, it is factually uncertain whether the 1999 email should have raised the plaintiffs' suspicions enough to require further investigation. Second, the current record does not allow a conclusion that a more thorough investigation would have revealed facts enabling the plaintiffs to identify the basis of their accounting malpractice claim. Regarding the first point, this Court cannot legally assert that the January 6, 1999 email alone was enough to obligate the plaintiffs to investigate further. A reasonable person could interpret the email and Lason CEO Mr. Monroe's response in conflicting ways. The plaintiffs testified that Monroe assured them PWC would be notified of the email and would endorse its accounting treatment. Furthermore, Messrs. Coleman and Lydon (both certified accountants) and expert witness William N. Easton, III, CPA, all stated that the entries fell into accounting's 'gray area' and were not outright prohibited under GAAP. Mr. Easton's affidavit also noted that the email alone would not have made him 'suspicious of Lason's accounting practices.' Thus, no clear 'red flag' would have prompted a prudent person to suspect PWC's negligence in failing to identify GAAP violations in Lason's pre-acquisition accounting. While one could draw such an inference, opposing interpretations are equally plausible. The issue is therefore a factual dispute requiring trial resolution. The trial court erred in legally concluding that the plaintiffs were on inquiry notice upon receiving the email.

The trial court also erred in granting summary judgment to PWC for another reason. Even assuming the plaintiffs were on inquiry notice, the record does not establish whether a diligent investigation would have uncovered sufficient facts to support an accounting malpractice claim. After receiving the January 6, 1999 email, the plaintiffs promptly inquired about its contents. DIT's CEO contacted Lason's CEO, Mr. Monroe, to express concerns. However, Monroe provided false reassurances and withheld accurate information about the later-discovered accounting irregularities at Lason. Notably, even Lason's Special Committee, which had full access to the company's records, took eight months to uncover the irregularities after starting its investigation. The plaintiffs, unlike the committee, had limited access to information, primarily through Lason executives later indicted for securities fraud. These facts alone prevent a legal determination that a more diligent inquiry by the plaintiffs between January 1999 and January 2002 would have revealed the irregularities. Thus, the trial court erred in concluding as a matter of law that such an inquiry would have been successful.

Additionally, Mr. Easton's testimony emphasized that the accounting entries in question were not clearly prohibited under GAAP, further supporting the plaintiffs' position. The lack of a definitive 'red flag' in the email undermines the argument that the plaintiffs should have been put on immediate notice of potential malpractice. The trial court's decision to grant summary judgment overlooked these nuanced factual disputes, which are essential for a fair resolution. The plaintiffs' reliance on Monroe's reassurances and the absence of clear warning signs justify their lack of further investigation at the time. Therefore, the trial court's ruling was premature and must be reconsidered in light of these unresolved factual issues.

The findings have disclosed information that would have allowed them to file their malpractice claim within the three-year statute of limitations. This matter must also be decided during the trial. Consequently, the Superior Court's decision to grant summary judgment to PWC is overturned. As per the complaint, following PWC's due diligence, the purchase price was renegotiated to $13 million, with an 'earn-out' possibility (structured as a repurchase of the former DIT owners' Lason stock by Lason) amounting to $25 million over the three years post-merger. Appellants' Appendix, at A000013, ¶ 55. Whether this actually happened is irrelevant to our ruling on this appeal. Coleman v. PricewaterhouseCoopers, LLP, C.A. No. 03C-02-137, 2003 WL 22765851, at 19-20 (Del.Super.Ct. Nov. 18, 2003). Kaufman v. C.L. McCabe & Sons, Inc., 603 A.2d 831, 8

33 (Del.1992). Super. Ct. Civ. R. 56(c), Burkhart v. Davies, 602 A.2d 56, 59 (Del.1991). Isaacson, Stolper & Co. v. Artisan's Sav. Bank, 330 A.2d 130, 132-33 (Del.1974) (citing Mastellone v.
