Conditional vendors are privileged creditors, possessing not only the remedies of ordinary vendors but also the retention of title.

The conditional vendor's right to reclaim goods and later recover a purchase price deficiency is not absolute. Section 24 reaffirms this right but imposes limits and clarifies the compatibility of certain remedies. To recover the remaining purchase price after repossession, the vendor must resell the goods, and their right to the deficiency is governed by Section 22. We will not further discuss Section 24, as it is agreed that the goods were resold after repossession. Section 22 (supra) grants the seller the right to recover the deficiency from the buyer after resale and application of the proceeds. The Uniform Conditional Sales Act, particularly Section 22, adopts the principle that the buyer uses the goods until default, after which they are repossessed, resold, and the proceeds credited to the buyer's account, allowing the seller to recover any shortfall.

The buyer has fully benefited from the goods, while the seller suffered a loss due to the resale. It is agreed that the plaintiff can claim the shortfall in the purchase price from the buyer, Charles F. L. Hutchinson, one of the defendants. However, it is disputed whether this claim can be based on the promissory note for the purchase price or if the other defendant, Selena S. Hutchinson, is liable. The resale of the goods by the vendor and the subsequent credit of the resale proceeds on the note did not release Charles F. L. Hutchinson from liability beyond the credited amount. The resale proceeds did reduce the primary liability of both defendants on the note. Selena S. Hutchinson might have had more grounds to object if the plaintiff had pursued the note initially without reclaiming the automobile and crediting the resale proceeds, which the defendant acknowledges could have occurred. Since there was no inconsistent remedy chosen by the plaintiff, the defendants' liability must be assessed under the applicable law.

Under the Uniform Negotiable Instruments Act, Section 2836 of the 1915 Code (Section 192 of the Act) states that a person 'primarily' liable on an instrument is one who is unconditionally obligated to pay it. This makes Selena S. Hutchinson, as a co-maker, primarily liable on the note. Section 2763 of the 1915 Code (Section 119 of the Act) outlines how a negotiable instrument can be discharged, including the discharge of a primarily liable party, and excludes other discharge methods. The affidavit mentions no discharge of the note except through the retaking of the automobile, which has already been addressed. Although courts in this state hesitate to issue judgments based on demand affidavits, they must do so when no valid defense is presented. Finding none here, the motion for judgment despite the defense affidavit is granted. TAYLOR, Judge. This case concerns the sale of a purportedly faulty automobile to the plaintiff, Norman Gershman's Things

to Wear, Inc. [Gershman's]. The vehicle was distributed by Mercedes-Benz of North America, Inc. [Mercedes] and sold to Gershman's by I.G. Burton & Co., Inc. [Burton]. Gershman's complaint alleges breaches of multiple warranties, failure of warranty purposes, violations of Delaware's 'Lemon Law,' consumer fraud, deceptive trade practices, negligent repairs, and breaches of the Magnuson-Moss Act by both defendants. Both defendants have filed for summary judgment on several claims. Burton has also sought summary judgment against Mercedes, demanding indemnification for potential damages and attorney fees. Gershman's bought a new 1984 Mercedes-Benz 500 SEC from Burton, a Mercedes-Benz dealer. Six months post-purchase, the engine overheated and required repairs. Burton inspected the car and found a hairline crack in the short block, which Mercedes authorized to replace at no cost to Gershman's. Within two years, the engine overheated again, causing severe damage. Burton, with Mercedes' approval, replaced the entire engine under warranty. Gershman's then revoked acceptance of the car, demanding a refund, which was denied, leading to this lawsuit. The car was later sold at auction by mutual agreement.

Count I of the complaint accuses both Burton and Mercedes of breaching express warranties. Count II alleges a breach of the implied warranty of merchantability. Burton seeks summary judgment, arguing it disclaimed all express and implied warranties in its 'Sales Contract' with Gershman's, governed by Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code, 6 Del. C. Subtitle I. 'Any factual assertion or promise made by the seller to the buyer...'

The buyer's statement regarding the goods, which forms part of the agreement's foundation, constitutes an express warranty under the contract. 6 Del. C. § 2-313. Furthermore, the contract includes an implied warranty that the goods are merchantable unless explicitly excluded or altered. 6 Del.C. § 2-314. Goods are deemed 'merchantable' if they are suitable for their typical uses. 6 Del.C. § 2-314(2)(c). To exclude or modify the implied warranty of merchantability, the language must explicitly mention merchantability and, if written, must be prominent. 6 Del.C. § 2-316(2). 'Conspicuous' is defined under 6 Del.C. § 1-201(10) as terms or clauses written in a manner that would reasonably draw attention. For example, a heading in capital letters (e.g., NON-NEGOTIABLE BILL OF LADING) is conspicuous. Language within a form is 'conspicuous' if it stands out through size or color contrast.

A term or clause is considered 'conspicuous' if it is highlighted by larger or contrasting type or color. The determination of conspicuousness rests with the court, focusing on whether the disclaimer language would reasonably catch a person's attention. Lecates v. Hertrich Pontiac Buick Co., Del.Super., 515 A.2d 163, 169 (1986). The sales contract between Burton and Gershman was a single-page document with text on both sides. The back side included a paragraph stating that the only warranties were those provided by the Manufacturer, with the Dealer disclaiming all other warranties, including merchantability or fitness for a particular purpose. The Dealer also denied liability for consequential or incidental damages. This paragraph was among eight others on the back, printed in smaller type.

The back page of the document featured text in a significantly smaller font compared to other sections. On the front, the phrase 'DISCLAIMER OF WARRANTIES — SEE REVERSE SIDE' was bolded and slightly larger than some other text. This was the sole reference to warranty disclaimers on the front. The back included a bold heading 'ADDITIONAL TERMS AND CONDITIONS'. The Court ruled that the disclaimer failed to meet the statutory requirement of being conspicuous. The front-page notice did not specify which of the eight paragraphs contained the disclaimer, nor was the disclaimer highlighted in larger or contrasting type. Thus, the Court found that a reasonable person might not notice it, rendering Burton's disclaimer of express and implied warranties ineffective. Consequently, Burton was denied summary judgment for Counts I and II.

Mercedes sought summary judgment on Counts I and II, arguing that its express written warranty limited its liability to repairing or replacing defective parts. It claimed compliance with 6 Del. C. § 2-719, stating it had met its obligations by repairing the car. Under 6 Del. C. § 2-719, parties may agree to remedies beyond or instead of those in the Article, such as limiting the buyer's recourse to refunds or repairs. If an exclusive remedy fails, alternative remedies may apply. Consequential damages can be restricted unless deemed unconscionable. Mercedes asserted that its warranty was exclusive and fulfilled, but the Court examined whether the remedy's limitation was valid under the circumstances.

Injury to an individual involving consumer goods is clearly unconscionable, whereas limiting damages for commercial losses is not. Mercedes' written warranty states that any authorized dealer will perform necessary repairs or replacements for defects in materials or workmanship within 48 months or 50,000 miles at no cost. The warranty also specifies that no compensation will be provided for indirect or consequential damages, including personal injury, property damage, or lost revenue. This warranty replaces all other implied warranties, including those of merchantability or fitness for a particular purpose.

Under 6 Del.C. § 2-719(2), if a limited remedy fails to serve its essential purpose, the buyer can seek remedies under the Uniform Commercial Code. A repair or replacement remedy fails if the warrantor refuses repairs, takes too long, or requires excessive attempts. Gershman argues that Mercedes' warranty failed because the car was not fixed properly or timely after multiple repair attempts, leaving it unusable for weeks.

Gershman testified that after the initial repair, the car still overheated and stalled, especially in traffic. Despite returning the car for service, the overheating issue persisted. Mercedes claims it fulfilled the warranty by repairing the engine in 21 days and disputes the overheating claims, noting Gershman did not report further issues during subsequent visits. This conflicting evidence creates a material dispute over whether the warranty's purpose was met.

Count III alleges violations of Delaware's Lemon Law, which requires manufacturers to repair nonconforming vehicles within a reasonable time or provide a refund or replacement. If the manufacturer fails to fix the issue, the consumer can return the vehicle for a new one or a refund. The court does not need to address Gershman's other arguments due to the unresolved factual dispute over the warranty's effectiveness.

The automobile warranty requires repairing or fixing any issues after a reasonable number of attempts. Burton seeks summary judgment on Count III, claiming that 6 Del C. § 5002 applies only to manufacturers, not dealers, placing the repair responsibility on the manufacturer. Gershman interprets the statute as holding both the dealer and manufacturer accountable. Neither party has provided supporting legal authority. Under 1 Del. C. § 303, the Court must interpret the Delaware Code according to common language usage, concluding that the statute assigns repair duties solely to the manufacturer. Since Burton is not the manufacturer, Gershman's Lemon Law claim against Burton lacks merit, and Burton is entitled to summary judgment on Count III. Mercedes also seeks summary judgment, arguing it fulfilled its repair obligations under the warranty.

Mercedes asserts that the warranty was honored by promptly addressing vehicle defects and that Gershman's remedy is restricted to the exclusive repair or replacement warranty, barring a Lemon Law claim. The court found a factual dispute regarding whether the vehicle met warranty standards post-repair and whether Mercedes' warranty failed its essential purpose, denying summary judgment on Count III. Count IV alleges violations of the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act against Burton and Mercedes, with Gershman claiming Burton unlawfully waived its implied warranty of merchantability. Burton argues the Act doesn’t apply as it provided no written warranty. The Act aims to curb deceptive warranty practices and allows consumers to sue suppliers or warrantors for violations or warranty breaches.

Under 15 U.S.C. § 2310(d)(1), a 'supplier' is defined as any entity involved in providing consumer products, while a 'warrantor' includes anyone offering a written warranty or bound by an implied warranty. Section 2308 prohibits suppliers from disclaiming implied warranties if they provide a written warranty or service contract. The statute states that no supplier may modify or disclaim implied warranties when a written warranty exists or within 90 days of sale if a service contract is established. Implied warranties can only be limited in duration if clearly stated and reasonable, with violations rendering disclaimers ineffective under federal and state law.

The Act defines a written warranty as a written commitment to repair, replace, or refund a product failing to meet specified terms, and a service contract as a written agreement for maintenance or repair services over a fixed period. Gershman argues Burton violated § 2308 by attempting to waive its implied warranty of merchantability and failed to honor its implied warranty under the Act.

2310(d). Burton argues that § 2308 does not apply to them because they did not provide Gershman's with a written warranty or enter into a service contract related to the car, as mandated by the Act. The sole document from Burton regarding the sale was the sales contract, which disclaimed all warranties. Additionally, Burton provided the Mercedes Owner's Manual, which included a warranty from Mercedes-Benz, not Burton. Gershman's has not shown that Burton's disclaimer qualifies as a 'written warranty' under the Act, but instead claims that Burton's delivery of Mercedes' warranty brings them under the Act's scope.

The consumer argues that the dealer is covered by the Act due to the delivery of Mercedes' warranty. Burton references Henderson v. Benson-Hartman Motors, Inc., where a dealer-lessor was bound by the Act after delivering a manufacturer's warranty that obligated them to perform repairs. However, in this case, the Mercedes warranty applies to any authorized dealer, not specifically Burton, unlike the Henderson case. The court concludes that Burton's delivery of the warranty does not imply an obligation to repair, granting Burton summary judgment on Count IV.

Gershman's alleges that Mercedes breached its express and implied warranties under 15 U.S.C. § 2310 and improperly waived the implied warranty under § 2308. Mercedes seeks summary judgment, stating their warranty limits remedies to repair or replacement and that they have addressed all defects. The court notes conflicting evidence about the car's performance post-repair, preventing summary judgment on compliance. Mercedes also argues its implied warranty limitation complies with § 2308(b), as it is clearly stated and conscionable, lasting 48 months or 50,000 miles.

The warranty explicitly limits implied warranties to 48 months or 50,000 miles, complying with § 2308(b). The court rules in favor of Mercedes on Count IV regarding the Magnuson-Moss Act. Count V accuses Burton and Mercedes of consumer fraud under 6 Del. C. § 2513, alleging false claims about the car's condition and post-sale misrepresentations. The Delaware Consumer Fraud Act prohibits deception, fraud, or misrepresentation, which Gershman's claims defendants engaged in.

Hiding, suppressing, or leaving out any key fact with the intention that others depend on such concealment, suppression, or omission, related to the sale or promotion of any goods, regardless of whether anyone was actually misled, deceived, or harmed, is illegal. [Emphasis added.] The Act aims to 'safeguard consumers and honest businesses from unfair or deceptive sales tactics,' and for this reason, the Act should be interpreted broadly. 6 Del. C. § 2512. See In Re: Brandywine Volkswagen Ltd., Del. Super., 306 A.2d 24 (1973). To demonstrate fraud, the buyer must show that the seller knowingly made a false claim or negligently misrepresented the facts. Stephenson v. Capano Development, Inc., Del.Supr., 462 A.2d 1069, 1072 (1983). 'A person can be held accountable for a false statement if it was made in a way that suggests they knew it was untrue.' In Re: Brandywine Volkswagen, Ltd.,

306 A.2d at 27. Burton has requested summary judgment on this matter. First, Burton contends that the statute explicitly excludes post-sale statements. Gershman's argues that including post-sale statements aligns with the legislature's directive for a broad interpretation of the Act. While Gershman's correctly states that the Consumer Fraud Act should be interpreted liberally, this Court cannot disregard the statute's explicit language limiting its scope to deceptive acts 'related to the sale or advertising' of goods. Given this restriction, post-sale statements unconnected to the sale or promotion of the car do not qualify as consumer fraud under the Act. Thus, Burton is entitled to summary judgment regarding Count V of the complaint concerning alleged post-sale statements. Regarding Gershman's claim of fraudulent pre-sale statements by Burton that the car had no defects, the record includes a sworn statement from David G. Burton, Burton's president, affirming that the car sold to Gershman's was inspected by trained mechanics and no defects were found. Mr. Burton also stated that Burton had no

awareness of any issues with the car at the time of sale. Archie L. Carey, Jr., a Burton mechanic, testified via affidavit that 'it would have been nearly impossible to detect the hairline crack in the engine block during a standard pre-sale inspection.' Gershman's will need to prove the alleged fraudulent pre-sale claims at trial. Under these conditions, Gershman's must 'go beyond the pleadings and provide affidavits, depositions, interrogatory responses, or admissions to demonstrate a genuine dispute requiring trial.' Celotex Corp. v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 324, 106 S.Ct. 2548, 2553, 91 L.Ed.2d 265, 274 (1986). Gershman's has not presented any evidence indicating Burton knew of the defect or negligently misrepresented the car's condition. Therefore, Burton is entitled to summary judgment on Count V regarding alleged fraudulent

pre-sale statements. Gershman's further alleges that Burton breached the Consumer Fraud Act by falsely claiming that any car defects would be quickly repaired due to readily available parts. Gershman's asserts that the required parts were unavailable, causing unreasonable delays. Burton has not addressed this claim in its motion briefs. Consequently, summary judgment is inappropriate for this portion of Count V concerning fraudulent pre-sale claims about part availability. Mercedes has moved for summary judgment on Count V, arguing its 'repair or replacement' warranty was exclusive, and any evidence of false statements contradicting this warranty made before or during the sale is inadmissible under the parole evidence rule (6 Del.C. § 2-202). As previously mentioned, a factual dispute exists over whether the exclusive warranty failed its core purpose. Since Mercedes' argument hinges on this warranty, summary judgment is unwarranted. VI Count VI of the complaint claims Burton and Mercedes violated Delaware's Deceptive Trade Practices Act, 6 Del.C

Under § 2531 et seq., both defendants argue that consumers cannot seek remedies under the Act. The Deceptive Trade Practices Act offers relief, including injunctions and attorney's fees for willful violations (6 Del. C. § 2533). It also allows treble damages if awarded under common law or other Delaware statutes (6 Del. C. § 2533(c)). Burton and Mercedes seek summary judgment, claiming Gershman's lacks standing as a consumer. However, in Roberts v. American Warranty Corp., the court ruled consumers do have standing under the Act, emphasizing antifraud protections apply to deceived individuals.

Mercedes further argues Gershman's cannot claim relief under the Act, as the deceptive practices allegations mirror breach of warranty claims. Citing Whitehurst v. Crisp R.V. Center, Inc., they contend no separate violation exists. However, 6 Del.C. § 2533(c) clarifies that the Act's remedies supplement common law or statutory claims. Thus, even if conduct breaches warranty and constitutes deceptive practices, the injured party may pursue both claims, including treble damages or injunctive relief under the Act.

Count VII alleges negligent repair against both defendants, claiming Burton's faulty engine rebuild caused overheating. Gershman's seeks damages for the car's diminished value and consequential losses. Burton counters that Gershman's suffered no damages, as repairs were free and the car sold above 'Blue Book' value. In Chambers v. Hassell A. Van Dyke, the court defined negligent repair damages as the difference between properly and defectively repaired vehicle values.

Gershman's delayed selling the car until 1987 due to disputes over remedies, arguing for a purchase price refund or new car, while Burton cited warranty limitations. Gershman's also claims Burton agreed to provide a new car, which Burton denies. Whether Gershman's can pursue negligent repair depends on the jury's resolution of warranty limitations, as discussed in Section II of the Opinion.

or if Gershman's has the right to a refund or a replacement vehicle. If Gershman's qualifies for a refund or a new car, it cannot also claim damages for negligent repairs. Thus, deciding whether Gershman's can recover damages for negligent repair and the amount owed should be deferred until these connected matters are resolved at trial. Regarding Gershman's claim for consequential damages from loss of use and inconvenience, there is a factual dispute about whether the car was adequately repaired after the initial engine overheating and the duration it was unavailable for repairs related to this case. Consequently, Mercedes cannot obtain summary judgment on Count VII of the complaint concerning consequential damages.

The warranty explicitly states that Mercedes is responsible for addressing defects in the vehicle. While authorized dealers perform the repairs, Mercedes remains ultimately accountable for ensuring defects are fixed. Therefore, Mercedes should bear liability for any damage caused by a dealer's negligent repair, regardless of whether it oversaw the repairs. Additionally, there is ample evidence suggesting Mercedes did supervise the repairs in this case. Records show Burton performed the relevant repairs under Mercedes' guidance after inspections were communicated to Mercedes. Thus, Mercedes is not entitled to summary judgment on this matter.

Burton seeks summary judgment against Mercedes, arguing that under 6 Del.C. § 4905 and their franchise agreement, Mercedes must indemnify Burton for any damages and legal fees from this lawsuit. The statute mandates that manufacturers indemnify dealers for judgments or settlements related to defects or negligence in manufacturing, design, or assembly, beyond the dealer's control. Mercedes agrees to indemnify Burton for Counts I through VI but disputes liability for Count VII (negligent repair), arguing the second overheating may not stem from a vehicle defect.

Evidence indicates the car was inspected after the second overheating, and a Burton mechanic found a faulty thermostat, which Mercedes authorized as a warranty repair. The only counterevidence is testimony from Mercedes' specialist, who admitted uncertainty about the overheating's cause but acknowledged engine defects likely caused the damage. Since no evidence points to non-defect-related damage, summary judgment is unwarranted where the opposing party fails to establish a critical factual issue.

77 U.S. at 322-23, 106 S.Ct. 2548 at 2552-53, 91 L.Ed.2d at 273. Consequently, Burton is eligible for indemnification for any damages awarded in this case, making summary judgment suitable. Regarding Burton's request for attorney's fees under 6 Del.C. § 4905, Mercedes contests this, arguing the statute mandates indemnification only with a 'judgment or written settlement by the manufacturer,' neither of which exists here. As Burton's right to damages hinges on Gersh-man securing a judgment or written settlement, the issue of attorney's fees cannot be resolved now. In summary judgment motions, the Court's role is not to assess evidence or determine truth but to identify genuine issues for trial. Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 10

6 S.Ct. 2505, 91 L.Ed.2d 202 (1986). Per the foregoing analysis, defendant Burton's summary judgment motion for Count I (breach of express warranty) is DENIED. The motion for Count II (breach of implied warranty of merchantability) is also DENIED. However, Burton's motion for Count III (Delaware's Lemon Law) is GRANTED. The motion for Count IV (Magnuson-Moss Act) is GRANTED. For Count V (fraudulent post-sale and presale defect claims), the motion is GRANTED, but DENIED for presale parts availability claims. Burton's motions for Counts VI (Deceptive Trade Practices Act) and VII (negligent repair damages) are DENIED. Burton's indemnification motion for damages is GRANTED, but the motion for attorney's fees is DENIED. Mercedes' summary judgment motion for Counts I (express warranty) and

II (implied warranty) is DENIED. Mercedes' motion for Count III (Delaware's Lemon Law) is also DENIED. For Count IV (Magnuson-Moss Act breach of express warranty), the motion is DENIED, but GRANTED for improper limitation of implied warranty. Mercedes' motions for Count V (consumer fraud) and VI (Deceptive Trade Practices Act) are DENIED, as is the motion for Count VII (negligent repair). Under Delaware's Lemon Law, a 'manufacturer' includes entities distributing at least 10 new automobiles annually. 6 Del.C. § 5001(3). Similarly, the Motor Vehicle Franchising Practices Act defines 'manufacturer' to encompass distributors selling or distributing new vehicles to dealers. 6 Del.C. § 4902(l)(a).

Seitz, Chancellor: Plaintiffs aim to prevent defendants from using adjacent land for a sanitary landfill, colloquially termed a dump, near Llangollen Estates. The Levy Court acts under statutory authority (9 Del.C. §2401 et seq.), allowing it to acquire or use land for landfills 'deemed advisable' and to contract operators, such as Land-Fill, Inc. The court, addressing this last-minute application, provides general conclusions. Plaintiffs argue the landfill violates zoning codes, but these codes govern private land use and do not apply to the Levy Court, which derives authority from a separate statute enacted June 21, 1951, shortly after the zoning statute.

The text does not mention any zoning restrictions. In fact, a 1959 amendment to the waste management law allowed the Levy Court to take the contested action. This amendment also does not include any zoning constraints. The plaintiffs argue that the dump will become a nuisance, but the defendants promise precautions will prevent this. The issue is that the Levy Court legally has the authority to proceed, and the court cannot override its decision, even if the choice seems unwise. Whether the plaintiffs can seek redress if the dump actually causes a nuisance remains undecided. The plaintiffs also claim the State Board of Health's approval was needed, but the cited laws do not apply here, as they concern transporting waste into the state or unauthorized dumping.

The court acknowledges the plaintiffs' concerns but finds their request for an injunction lacks merit, as the Levy Court acted within its legal authority. The court cannot question the wisdom of this authority, and no constitutional issues are raised. Justice Holland then shifts to a medical negligence case involving Heather Turner, who sued Dr. Conway, Dr. Kalish, and their practice, Delaware Surgical Group, alleging substandard care in two bowel obstruction surgeries. The jury ruled in favor of the defendants.

Turner appeals, challenging two trial rulings. First, she argues Dr. Kalish improperly testified as an expert on his own liability without proper disclosure. Second, she claims the court unfairly barred her from questioning Dr. Conway about his delayed surgical report, which allegedly violated hospital policy requiring reports within 24 hours. She contends this evidence should have been allowed to impeach Dr. Conway's testimony.

The appellate court finds Dr. Kalish's undisclosed expert testimony was reversible error and orders a new trial. It also addresses the 24-hour rule issue for the retrial. The background details Turner's multiple surgeries, including procedures by Dr. Kalish and Dr. Conway for bowel obstructions, and a later liver mass removal by Dr. Bennett.

008, via a laparoscopic surgical intervention. In correspondence to Turner's gastroenterologist, Dr. Bennett noted that the mass 'suggested the possibility of spillage from previous surgeries.' Subsequently, on January 10, 2012, Turner had a final operation to address a significant ventral incisional hernia, purportedly resulting from two prior laparoscopic procedures conducted by Dr. Kalish and Dr. Conway. Expert Testimony Disputed Turner argues that the 'trial court erred by allowing Dr. Kalish to provide expert testimony and opinions during the trial, as his attorney failed to provide adequate notice to Turner in his expert disclosure or deposition.' Turner maintains that Dr. Kalish's trial testimony did not align with the notice mandates under Superior Court Civil Rules 16(e) and 26(e) or this Court's ruling in Barrow v. Abramowicz. Consequently, Turner asserts that the expert testimony was erroneously admitted, materially prejudicing the trial, necessitating a remand for a new trial. Disclosure Obligations The requirements for disclosing an expert and their

opinions are clearly outlined in the Superior Court Civil Rules. Initially, the identification of Dr. Kalish as an expert and his associated opinions must adhere to the Superior Court Civil Rule ('Rule') 16(e) trial scheduling order. Additionally, these disclosures must meet Rule 26(e)(1), which mandates that parties promptly supplement responses regarding the identity of expert witnesses, the topics they will address, and the essence of their testimony. In Bush v. HMO of Delaware, Inc., this Court ruled that parties must fulfill discovery requirements related to expert identification and the 'substance of their anticipated opinions' before presenting such testimony at trial. A physician-defendant must meet the same criteria as any expert witness. In Barrow v. Abramowicz, we outlined these prerequisites: '(i) timely identification as an expert; and (ii) timely disclosure of opinions and their foundations.' This Court emphasized that 'a defendant doctor must notify the opposing party to ensure a fair opportunity to counter the expert opinion, as without such notice, proper trial preparation is compromised.' Inadequate Disclosure Turner concedes that Dr. Kalish was identified as both a fact and expert witness, satisfying the first Barrow prerequisite. However, Turner contests the second prerequisite, claiming that 'the defense failed to disclose any details about Dr. Kalish's alleged expert opinions, including his assertion that the post-surgery pathology report exonerated him from negligence.' The defendants' disclosure of Dr. Kalish as an expert, dated April 12, 2011, stated: 'C. Eric Kalish, M.D.: To the extent required by Court rules for expert witness disclosures, he will testify as an expert, consistent with his deposition and medical records.' Trial Objections Turner objected to Dr. Kalish's

testimony during the trial, arguing it was not previously disclosed in his deposition or medical records. Specifically, Turner contested Dr. Kalish's remarks about the 'post-surgery pathology report and his interpretations of its findings.' The pathology report, dated August 8, 2007, analyzed a one-inch bowel segment removed by Dr. Kalish. When defense counsel questioned Dr. Kalish about the report at trial, Turner's counsel promptly objected. During a sidebar, the following exchange occurred: Plaintiff's Counsel: I object to this line of questioning. Dr. Kalish is here as a fact witness, not an expert. There was no prior disclosure in interrogatories or his deposition about his opinions on the pathology report. I assumed he wouldn't be interpreting its findings. Defense Counsel: Your Honor, he was disclosed as

an expert witness, and his testimony falls within the scope of that disclosure. The pathology report is part of the medical records, and Dr. Kalish is qualified to discuss its implications. Plaintiff's Counsel: But the defense never specified he would opine on the report's meaning, depriving us of the chance to prepare a rebuttal. The court must exclude this testimony. Defense Counsel: The disclosure was sufficient under the rules, and Dr. Kalish's testimony is relevant to the case. The trial court's decision to allow the testimony is now under review.

In line with the rules outlined in my disclosure, as an expert, I confirm that he is not only a defendant but also listed as an expert. This is noted in the pretrial conference order, and he has the right to explain the pathology report from his surgery. The Court: He is a defendant who conducted the surgery. It’s typical for a treating physician, as he was, to provide expert opinions when they pertain directly to their knowledge and the case’s relevance. Therefore, I overrule the plaintiff’s objection and permit the doctor to discuss the pathology report as he sees fit. Plaintiff’s Counsel: Your Honor, to clarify, I may have misspoken earlier regarding their identification of him as an expert. The expert disclosure only lists his name without any details on opinions or other information, leaving me with no insight into Dr. Kalish’s testimony. The Court: I’ll consider this a motion.

for reconsideration. Any response? Defense Counsel: No additional arguments. The Court: I maintain that the witness can testify about the pathology report. As the treating physician, it’s within his expertise, and you may challenge this during cross-examination. [Objection overruled.] The record shows plaintiff’s counsel was worried Dr. Kalish would interpret the pathology report, including its microscopic findings. Shortly after the objection was overruled, Dr. Kalish testified, clarifying that 'microscopic' refers to visible sections under a microscope, not minuscule details. He further explained abnormalities like 'transmural,' indicating all bowel layers were affected.

Defense Counsel then questioned Dr. Kalish about terms like 'ischemic change' and 'liquefaction' from the pathology report. Dr. Kalish explained that ischemic means loss of blood supply, which necessitated the surgery. Defense Counsel asked if delaying surgery would lead to necrosis, to which Dr. Kalish confirmed, describing how the tissue would darken and soften, a condition called liquefaction, indicating irreversible damage. Testimony Admitted Erroneously. Pretrial, both parties agreed one claim was that Dr. Kalish’s bowel resection surgery was unnecessary and improperly performed, breaching the standard of care.

Thus, Dr. Kalish’s surgical decision was central to the case. Despite not being deposed about the pathology report, he testified at trial as an expert, asserting his surgery was justified. He argued the report confirmed the bowel abnormality, which could have worsened without intervention. Delaware law mandates pretrial disclosure of experts and their opinions. The trial judge overlooked this, ruling that as the defendant and surgeon, Dr. Kalish could provide expert opinions relevant to his knowledge and the case.

Therefore, I will overrule the plaintiff's objection and permit the doctor to address the pathology report as much as he can. This decision conflicts with Rules 16(e) and 26(e) and the Court's earlier ruling in Barrow v. Abramowicz. The record shows the trial judge misused his discretion by allowing Dr. Kalish to give an expert opinion on the pathology report without prior disclosure, violating procedural rules. Given this error, we must assess whether it caused substantial prejudice, denying the appellant a fair trial. Dr. Kalish's testimony was pivotal, as it challenged Turner's claim about the surgery's necessity using post-operative findings he lacked initially.

The testimony from Dr. Kalish conflicted with Turner's expert, Dr. Beaton, yet Turner was unaware of these opinions due to inadequate pre-trial disclosure under Rules 16 and 26. The improper admission of this testimony severely disadvantaged Turner, preventing her from preparing cross-examinations, refining her expert's testimony, or securing another expert to counter Dr. Kalish. Allowing Dr. Kalish to testify unfairly gave the defense two experts against Turner's one, undermining her right to a fair trial.

Christiana Care Hospital's 24-hour rule mandates surgeons to complete operative reports promptly, ideally within a day post-surgery. Turner argues the trial court wrongly barred testimony on this rule, claiming it was relevant to proving negligence or impeaching Dr. Conway's denial of awareness. While we agree the rule was inadmissible as direct proof of negligence, the court failed to properly evaluate its use for impeachment purposes.

Turner asserts the 24-hour rule evidence should have been admitted to demonstrate negligence, citing Dr. Conway's 52-day delay in filing the operative report. She contends this delay could imply incomplete reporting, faulty memory, or an attempt to conceal negligence. The defense moved to exclude this argument, preventing Turner from questioning key witnesses about the delay, which she believed supported her negligence claim.

Turner acknowledged that Dr. Conway's delay in dictating the operative report did not directly cause physical harm but contended that his breach of the 24-hour rule, along with performing 27 surgeries in 52 days, suggested he rushed through Turner's procedure, resulting in abdominal spillage and necessitating further surgery. The trial judge permitted evidence of the report's 52-day delay but barred linking it to negligence, citing lack of causation.

The judge noted hospital guidelines for timely operative reports but ruled under Rule 403 that the probative value of testimony on report timing was outweighed by potential jury prejudice. While the jury could consider the 52-day delay, no reference to the 24-hour rule or hospital violations was allowed, as plaintiffs lacked a causation claim tied to the report.

The judge allowed the operative report's date into evidence but prohibited mention of the 24-hour rule, fearing jury confusion under Rule 403. Turner argued the rule's relevance under DRE 401, which defines relevance as evidence affecting the probability of a consequential fact. The court acknowledged relevance but excluded it due to disproportionate prejudice.

The trial judge admitted the operative report's timing had probative value but excluded it under DRE 403, as prejudice and confusion outweighed its relevance. He referenced hospital guidelines for prompt reports but upheld the exclusion, emphasizing no causation claim tied to the report and Rule 408's balancing test.

The value is significantly outweighed by concerns of prejudice and jury confusion. I intended to rule, and believe I did, that defendants cannot be proven to have completed the operative reports improperly or late. While no hospital rules were introduced, the jury may question an operative report prepared 52 days later. This fact can be admitted as evidence without commentary or violation of my stated reasons. Plaintiffs initially noted no causation claim tied to the report, which is significant, though they argued it showed negligence. The absence of a causation claim justifies excluding the report, among other reasons. Plaintiffs can inform the jury about the report's date, and the jury may interpret it, but references to the so-called 24-hour rule, admitted in this motion, are barred under Rule 40.

Rule 403 acknowledges some probative value, but here, it is greatly outweighed by prejudice and potential jury misguidance. Turner admits Dr. Conway's delayed dictation didn’t cause physical harm but still questioned medical witnesses on whether the delay hinted at surgical negligence. The trial judge correctly applied Rule 403’s balancing test and rightly excluded evidence of a 24-hour rule violation as proof of negligence. Turner later argued the rule was relevant for impeachment, citing Dr. Conway’s deposition. She contended that even if the rule couldn’t prove negligence, it should have been admitted to challenge Dr. Conway’s credibility, as he denied knowing the rule under oath.

Turner argued the jury should have heard Dr. Conway’s deposition testimony, where he denied awareness of any 24-hour rule at Christiana Care Hospital, stating operative reports were often dictated later. Turner was barred from using these statements to impeach him at trial, which she claims was an abuse of discretion. DRE 607 and 616 allow attacking a witness’s credibility, including through bias or interest evidence. Turner aimed to cross-examine Dr. Conway using his deposition, but while trial judges have discretion over such evidence, they cannot undermine effective cross-examination. This Court has outlined factors for discretion, including the witness’s importance, the relevance of impeachment, and risks of prejudice or delay.

Turner’s impeachment argument focused on the 24-hour rule in a reargument motion after the judge excluded it as proof of negligence. Though the judge deemed the argument untimely, he addressed its merits, noting impeachment was scarcely raised in plaintiffs’ initial response or oral arguments but became central in the reargument. The judge emphasized that while impeachment is a valid tool, its late introduction and minimal earlier mention weakened Turner’s case. The ruling upheld the exclusion, balancing the need for fair cross-examination against procedural fairness and avoiding undue prejudice or confusion.

The main point of impeachment is argued too late, as it wasn't raised initially. The trial judge noted that plaintiffs could present the operative report's date to the jury, but barred any reference to the 24-hour rule, stating there was no evidence to question the report's credibility or bias. The motion for reargument was denied.

Turner aimed to challenge Dr. Conway's overall credibility, particularly in accurately preparing the report, by highlighting his unawareness of the 24-hour rule. Dr. Beaton would have testified about the rule's establishment at Christiana Care Hospital, undermining Dr. Conway's testimony. The trial judge failed to apply the Snowden v. State factors when excluding the 24-hour rule evidence for impeachment.

The 24-hour rule's admissibility for impeaching Dr. Conway's credibility can be relitigated on remand, as its exclusion isn't binding under the law of the case. The Superior Court's judgments are reversed, and a new trial is ordered. The hernia and liver mass surgeries weren't cited as negligent.

The defendants' harmless error claim lacks merit, as the trial judge's failure to limit expert testimony caused significant prejudice. Exceptions to evidence admissibility include marginal relevance, as noted in Weber. References to Barrow v. Abramowicz and Snowden v. State support the ruling.

v. State, 457 A.2d 674, 682 (Del.1983). See id. Snowden v. State, 672 A.2d 1017, 1025 (Del.1996). Compare Cede & Co. v. Technicolor, Inc., 884 A.2d 26, 38 (Del.2005) ('An appellate court's remand requires the trial court to adhere to its mandate and the established law of the case.'). Snowden v. State, 672 A.2d at 1025. HERRMANN, Chief Justice: This appeal involves Delmarva Power and Light Company, the defendant in a personal injury case where the plaintiff hit her head on a metal box affixed to a utility pole. The incident occurred around 9:30 p.m. during a rainstorm after the plaintiff left her brother's house on the southern side of 14th Street in Wilmington.

14th Street, near Union Street, in Wilmington. After leaving, the plaintiff crossed 14th Street to her sister’s car, parked on the northern side and facing west. While stepping onto the curb and moving around the pole to enter the passenger side, she struck her head on the box, causing her to be stunned. The box, housing an electrical-load meter, was mounted 70' high, measuring 20' in height and 10.5' in depth. Post-accident, the plaintiff suffered nausea, severe headaches, and blurred vision. Her left eye recovered, but her right eye’s vision worsened, leaving her only light-sensitive. Previously employed as a licensed practical nurse, she has not returned to work. The plaintiff sued for negligence in the box’s placement, seeking damages for medical costs, lost earnings, and blindness. The jury awarded her $145,000.

The defendant moved for a new trial, which the Trial Court denied, leading to this appeal. We uphold the decision. I. The first issue is whether the Trial Court erred in not directing a verdict for the defendant. A. The defendant argues the plaintiff failed to prove negligence, claiming the standard of care for box placement was not demonstrated through customary practices or expert testimony. We reject this. The plaintiff’s duty was to show the defendant did not act as a reasonably prudent person under the circumstances. Without a fixed legal or legislative standard, the jury must define and apply this standard. Restatement, Torts II § 285. In Robelen Piano Company v. DiFonzo, 169 A.2d 240, 244-5 (Del.1961), this Court noted the standard of care is not rigid but must be tailored to each case’s unique facts, determined by what a reasonable person would do.

In close cases, the jury decides the reasonable person’s actions. Custom or expert testimony may aid in establishing this standard, as seen in Suburban Propane Gas Corp. v. Papen, 245 A.2d 795 (Del.1968), or Fitzmaurice v. Flynn, 356 A.2d 887 (Conn.1975), and Densler v. Metropolitan Edison Co., 345 A.2d 758 (Pa.Super.1975), but such evidence is not always required or definitive.

We maintain that such evidence was neither required nor decisive in this case. Evidence of industry practices is not definitive, as seen in Honolulu Limited v. Cain, Md.Supr., 244 Md. 590, 224 A.2d 433 (1966), and expert testimony is pertinent only when the issue is beyond common understanding. See Robelen Piano Co. v. DiFonzo, supra, Ginn v. Penobscott Co., Me.Supr., 334 A.2d 874 (1975); Cutroneo v. F. W. Woolworth Co., R.I.Supr., 112 R.I. 696, 315 A.2d 56 (1974). Given the absence of industry-wide standards for box placement on utility poles and the lack of specialized knowledge needed to locate a meter box in a residential area, we find such testimony unnecessary for the plaintiff's case. When considering a directed verdict motion, the evidence must favor the plaintiff.

The Trial Court, supported by our agreement, identified a factual dispute regarding whether the defendant took all reasonable steps to protect the public. The evidence sufficiently suggested the defendant failed to act prudently in placing the box: positioned near a pedestrian sidewalk, below standard height, under dense foliage, and without proper warnings. Thus, the plaintiff demonstrated a breach of the reasonable-care standard, justifying the denial of a directed verdict. The defendant further argued the plaintiff was contributorily negligent, citing her forehead striking the box as proof she failed to look ahead. However, the plaintiff testified the box was hidden by the pole and darkness, making her actions a jury question.

The plaintiff testified she was looking forward but could not see the box due to its concealment behind the pole and the area's darkness. Whether she acted prudently was a factual matter for the jury, which found her not contributorily negligent. The Trial Court correctly denied the directed verdict. The defendant also challenged the $145,000 verdict as excessive, given $43,000 in special damages. The jury likely awarded damages for permanent eyesight damage, which the defendant contested, claiming no credible evidence of blindness was presented. The Court will only overturn a verdict if it is shockingly unjust, which we do not find here.

A verdict will only be overturned if it is grossly excessive and clearly unjust, per Riegel v. Aastad, Del.Supr., 272 A.2d 715 (1970). Credible evidence of blindness supports the verdict, so we find no injustice. The dispute centers on Dr. Heather's testimony linking the accident to the plaintiff's eye issues. He attributed her blindness to circulatory insufficiency from the injury. The defendant argues his opinion lacked basis, as he was not an ophthalmologist and relied on hypotheticals without examining her eyes or consulting specialists. They contend the circulatory finding, made by an ophthalmologist, was unrelated to blindness.

Heather's opinion evidence should not have been presented to the jury. The defendant argues that the only admissible evidence on blindness should have been the testimonies of the two ophthalmologists, who attributed the plaintiff's blindness to glaucoma, a progressive condition. However, Dr. Heather's lack of specialization in ophthalmology is irrelevant. Delaware law, consistent with other jurisdictions, recognizes that an experienced physician qualifies as an expert, regardless of whether they specialize in the specific condition at hand. Precedents such as Drucker v. Philadelphia Dairy Products and Board of Public Education in Wilmington v. Rimlinger support this. Dr. Heather, a specialist in physical medicine, had extensive knowledge of trauma's effects on the nervous system, including the optic nerve. Evidence showed the plaintiff suffered blurred vision and temple pain post-accident, with vision deteriorating to light perception in one eye.

Dr. Heather, who treated the plaintiff from the injury's onset, testified that the trauma stretched the optic nerve, damaging its blood supply and causing vision loss. Submitting this evidence to the jury was not erroneous. The defendant also argues the Trial Court erred by excluding 13 photographs of utility boxes on poles in Wilmington, intended to demonstrate community and industry care standards. The Court excluded them because the photographed boxes were in more visible street corners than the one in question. Photograph admissibility is typically at the Trial Court's discretion, and reversal requires a clear abuse of that discretion, as seen in Killary v. Burlington-Lake Champlain Chamber of Commerce. No such abuse occurred here. The defendant further claims error in barring testimony on industry standards, but the witness admitted no such standards existed, rendering the claim baseless.

The defendant also challenges the Trial Court's jury instructions, alleging errors in: (1) the standard of care instruction regarding the box's height; (2) refusing the 'step-in-the-dark' instruction; and (3) rejecting the 'urban impediments' charge. First, sufficient evidence supported the height-related instruction. Second, Maher v. Voss, cited by the defendant, mandates the 'step-in-the-dark' instruction only when someone enters a completely dark, unfamiliar space—unlike this case, where the plaintiff knew the premises and no such entry occurred.

Lastly, the defendant's reliance on Hagan v. Washington Suburban Sanitary Com'n for the 'urban-impediments' charge is misplaced, as that case involved a plaintiff tripping over a conspicuous fire hydrant near a lit restaurant entrance—a scenario vastly different from this case. The defendant failed to show reversible error in the jury instructions. The Trial Court's charge included: '. . . if you find Delmarva placed the metal box in a location, height, or lighting condition that created a hazardous situation for pedestrians, such actions could constitute negligence.' The judgment is affirmed.

It would be careless. If you find that this carelessness directly led to the Plaintiff's injuries, and if the Plaintiff herself is not at fault, then your decision should favor the Plaintiff, Mrs. Stout.' The defendant objected: 'I disagree with your Honor's instruction to the jury about the Defendant's responsibility regarding the box's height. The Plaintiff must provide expert testimony to establish this duty, which was not done, so the instruction was unfounded.' The defendant's 'step-in-the-dark' request stated: 'Every person must watch where they walk and stay alert for their safety. This includes seeing what is clearly visible. However, testimony indicates this incident happened at night during rain. The law states that if darkness limits visibility, a person should not proceed without knowing their path and potential obstacles, and must move carefully.'

If you find Mrs. Stout's vision was hindered by darkness and rain, and she failed to proceed cautiously, and this directly caused the accident, she cannot recover, and you must rule for the defendant.' The defendant's 'urban impediments' charge read: 'A prudent person should expect obstacles like public fixtures, fire alarms, and hydrants in public areas.' Citing Hagan v. Washington Suburban Commission, 'Mrs. Stout could not assume the area near her sister's car was free of obstacles. While she didn’t have to expect negligence, she should have anticipated possible objects near utility poles.'

Justice Harrington, delivering the Court's opinion: It is agreed that William Schwartz, as administrator, received over $152,000 from Benjamin J. Schwartz's estate and paid it to himself as trustee for his mother, Sarah K. Schwartz, the sole beneficiary. It is also agreed that the debt owed to William Beadenkopf remains unpaid. The issue is whether the defendant, as surety for William Schwartz's bond, is liable for this debt. Schouler's treatise on executors states: 'An executor or administrator must lawfully distribute the estate, paying debts and claims in order before any distribution. This duty is imposed by law, oath, and public policy, treating the estate as liable for all valid debts and expenses.'

When letters for Benjamin J. Schwartz's estate were issued to David J. Reinhardt, Sarah K. Schwartz, and William Schwartz, each published creditor notices as required by Code Section 3398. This section mandates: 'The register shall order executors or administrators to publish notices of the letters' issuance, requiring creditors to submit claims.'

or comply with the law in this matter.' After detailing specific requirements regarding the number of notices, their content, the timeframe for posting and publishing, and the locations for such actions, the section further states: 'If an executor or administrator follows the order’s instructions and, one year after letters are granted, pays out the estate to legatees or distributees without notice of a claim against the deceased, such payment is valid. The executor or administrator can use this as a defense against any unnoticed claims by pleading full administration. The notice need not be a legal action but must be written.' Aligning with Section 3398, Section 3373 of the 1915 Code also states: 'If an executor or administrator, six months after letters are granted, pays a lower-grade claim without notice of a higher-grade demand, such payment is permissible.' Unlike Section 3398, this section specifies that 'Such notice need not

be a legal action.' Section 3376 of the 1915 Code further requires: 'Before paying any debt of the deceased, the creditor must swear that no payments have been made toward the debt except as stated, and that the amount claimed is justly owed.' Mr. Beadenkopf did not meet this requirement until late November or early December 1931, when legal action was taken on the bond tied to his mortgage. Section 3398 clarifies that 'demand' refers to a debt or claim, and the validity of such a claim is unaffected by whether it was probated under Section 3376 before the estate’s distribution. While notices to creditors under this section protect the executor if the estate is distributed after one year,

the personal representative is relieved of liability if, without the required notice, the estate is distributed to legatees after one year from the grant of letters. Given the need to settle estates promptly for the benefit of creditors and other parties, it would be unreasonable to interpret Section 3398 as preventing William Schwartz from relying on prior creditor notices issued by David J. Reinhardt and Sarah K. Schwartz if he distributed Benjamin J. Schwartz’s estate as early as October 1928. See 2 Woerner’s Amer. Law of Admr. 1165, 1175. The notices given by Reinhardt and Schwartz were lawful under Section 3346 of the 1915 Code, which validates the acts of a removed executor or administrator if done lawfully. This section also states that any administrative act remains valid until proven erroneous, even if the executor is later removed.

Both bonds and mortgages are primarily settled from the deceased’s personal estate (Section 3372, 1915 Code), but Section 3398 specifies that notice to the personal representative need not be a legal action but must be written. This section must be interpreted alongside Section 3374 of the 1915 Code, which is titled 'Of What Debts Notice Presumed.' It states: 'An executor or administrator is presumed to have notice of recorded judgments, decrees, recognizances, and mortgages in the county where letters were granted, unless they were omitted from the docket index—except for justice of the peace judgments and recognizances, of which

Regarding debts recorded in another county, an individual is not considered to have notice unless actual notice is provided. The claim essentially states that William Schwartz did not meet the terms of the administration bond, where he acted as the principal and the defendant company as the surety, by failing to settle the outstanding amount on Benjamin J. Schwartz's bond to William Beadenkopf, dated November 12, 1913. Bonds themselves are not explicitly covered under Section 3374 of the 1915 Code, which imputes notice to executors or administrators. However, mortgages in the county where letters are issued fall under this section. In this instance, since the bond was linked to a properly recorded and indexed mortgage and referenced within it, the obligation qualifies as a mortgage debt under Section 3374, with the mortgage serving as collateral. This principle is well-established in state law, as seen in Ellison v. Dolbey and Stanert, 3 Penn. 45, 49 A. 1.

In Malsberger v. Parsons, 1 Boyce 256, 75 A. 698, it was noted that when William Schwartz, acting as administrator for Benjamin J. Schwartz's estate, transferred the remaining personal property to himself as trustee for Sarah K. Schwartz, he was aware of the debt owed to William Beadenkopf. Consequently, the defendant, as surety on his bond, is accountable for Schwartz's failure to pay the debt as administrator. This renders it unnecessary to determine whether the estate's personal property was distributed in October 1931 or, as the plaintiff argues, as early as October 1928. While a lien creditor may primarily seek payment from a deceased's personal estate, this right can be waived through explicit actions. Despite Benjamin J. Schwartz's death in 1925, Beadenkopf's delay in probating his claim until 1931 and securing judgment in 1932 does not forfeit his right to claim payment from the estate.

The delay until 1931 for probating the claim and until March 1932 for obtaining judgment does not constitute a waiver of William Beadenkopf's right to seek payment from Benjamin J. Schwartz's personal estate. Therefore, judgment must be awarded to the plaintiff for the remaining balance owed, as executor of Beadenkopf's estate, plus interest. HOLLAND, Justice: The defendant-appellant, Michael R. Smith ('Smith'), was convicted by a Superior Court jury of Felony Murder, Second-Degree Murder, two counts of First-Degree Robbery, four counts of Possession of a Firearm During Commission of a Felony ('PFDCF'), and Second-Degree Conspiracy. Smith received a life sentence plus an additional 142 years. His convictions and sentences were upheld on direct appeal. Smith later filed a timely Motion for Post-Conviction Relief ('Rule 61 Motion'), alleging ineffective counsel during trial and appeal. His former attorneys responded to these claims, but no evidentiary hearing was held, and the Superior Court denied the motion.

Smith raises three issues in this appeal. First, he argues his trial attorneys were ineffective under Strickland v. Washington for not requesting a jury instruction on accomplice testimony credibility, per Bland v. State. Second, he claims they were ineffective for not challenging the lack of a self-defense instruction and the inclusion of a 'negative self-defense' instruction, violating his constitutional right to a fair trial. Third, he asserts they failed to address potential juror bias after some jurors witnessed him and others in restraints. We find Smith was prejudiced by his attorneys' failure to request the accomplice testimony instruction under Strickland's Sixth Amendment standards, making it unnecessary to address the other claims. Consequently, Smith's convictions must be overturned. The facts leading to his conviction are summarized in the following.

In this Court's ruling on Smith's direct appeal, the evidence was interpreted in the light most favorable to the State. The Indictment claimed that on April 17, 2003, Smith was involved in a robbery with Shane DeShields, leading to George Coverdale's death. The State conceded at trial that DeShields fired the fatal shot. In this appeal, the State admits it prosecuted Smith as DeShields' accomplice. The prosecution's case relied heavily on testimonies from two alleged eyewitnesses—DeShields, Smith's supposed accomplice, and Shawn Blackwell. Their accounts of the events were inconsistent and contradictory but both implicated Smith. Smith provided his own version of events in his defense. The Court noted in Smith's direct appeal that the trial's outcome hinged on the jury's assessment of credibility between Smith and the other witnesses.

The credibility of DeShields and Blackwell was central to the case: The Court acknowledged that their testimonies were often inconsistent and contradictory, both internally and with prior statements. For this opinion, the facts are primarily drawn from their direct testimonies. By convicting Smith, the jury favored DeShields' and Blackwell's accounts over Smith's, despite the inconsistencies highlighted by the defense. The Court concluded that once the jury resolved the credibility issue, the case was no longer close. Smith's Rule 61 Motion argued his trial attorneys were ineffective for not requesting a jury instruction on accomplice testimony credibility, as established in Bland v. State and Cabrera v. State. Smith contends that uncorroborated statements from DeShields were pivotal to the State's case, as they formed the basis for key charges.

All evidence regarding the plan to steal drugs from Coverdale and the actual theft came solely from DeShields' uncorroborated testimony. DeShields admitted at trial that he took drugs from Coverdale before the shooting and claimed Smith was part of the plan. Blackwell and Smith, however, denied any discussion or theft of drugs. DeShields' testimony, unsupported by other evidence, underpinned charges like Felony Murder and Robbery. The determination of whether Smith was DeShields' accomplice, and thus liable for Coverdale's murder and Blackwell's robbery, relied almost entirely on DeShields' credibility versus Smith's.

During Smith's trial, the jury heard conflicting accounts of his involvement in the gunfire that killed Coverdale. DeShields and Blackwell testified that Smith fired a .32 automatic at Coverdale, with differing details about the shot's trajectory. Smith, however, denied bringing or using any weapon, stating he disarmed Coverdale when the gun accidentally discharged. The evidence also conflicted regarding Smith's role in stealing property from Coverdale and Blackwell, further complicating the jury's assessment of his culpability.

According to DeShields, once the shooting ceased and Coverdale was fatally injured near the van, he witnessed Smith striking Coverdale in the face with the .32 handgun. DeShields did not observe or know if Smith stole any jewelry or belongings from Coverdale. Blackwell stated that after the shooting, DeShields forced him back into the van, held a gun to his head, and robbed him of all his possessions. Smith, however, denied taking anything from Coverdale and claimed he saw DeShields searching Coverdale's pockets and taking money while Coverdale was on the ground. The Strickland Standard governs ineffective assistance of counsel claims, requiring proof that counsel's performance was unreasonable and caused prejudice to the defendant.

Under Strickland’s first prong, the defendant must show that counsel’s actions were unreasonable by professional standards at the time. The second prong requires demonstrating a reasonable probability that counsel’s failures harmed the defendant’s case, undermining confidence in the trial’s outcome. Courts must assess counsel’s conduct without hindsight bias, reconstructing the circumstances and evaluating decisions from counsel’s perspective at the time. Counsel’s actions are presumed reasonable, and the defendant must prove they were not sound trial strategy.

In Smith’s case, defense counsel did not request a specific instruction on accomplice testimony credibility. To assess if this was reasonable under Strickland, the merits of the claim must be examined. Competent attorneys are expected to know the applicable law, and at the time of Smith’s trial, Delaware law entitled defendants to such an instruction when the State relied on accomplice testimony. The Bland case endorsed a jury instruction urging caution and suspicion when evaluating uncorroborated accomplice testimony.

In Cabrera, the court approved a modified version of the Bland instruction, using 'with caution' instead of 'with suspicion and great caution.' Cabrera did not argue this wording was misleading or incorrect, so his appeal failed. Later, in Bordley, the court rejected a claim that omitting the 'with caution' instruction was error, as the judge used a revised pattern instruction instead. This instruction emphasized the jury’s role in assessing witness credibility, including that of an alleged accomplice.

You may evaluate the credibility of each witness by considering various factors, such as potential self-interest, agreements with the State, personal stakes in the case, bias against the Defendant, and whether their testimony aligns with other evidence. In Bordley, we noted that while the judge didn’t explicitly advise caution when reviewing Cry’s testimony, judges have broad discretion in crafting jury instructions. Additionally, instructions are not grounds for reversal if they accurately convey the law and are clear and non-misleading. While Bordley upheld an accomplice credibility instruction without the 'caution' wording from Bland and Cabrera, it didn’t overturn those cases, emphasizing judicial flexibility in instruction phrasing.

Smith’s situation differs from Bland, Cabrera, and Bordley, as his defense didn’t request a specific accomplice credibility instruction. Smith contends his attorneys should have known such an instruction was legally necessary, given DeShields’ pivotal yet conflicting testimony and lack of corroboration. His trial lawyers admitted in an affidavit to overlooking this but provided no strategic justification. Despite their admission, this Court must independently review for error, as it hasn’t previously addressed such omissions under Strickland claims.

Other courts have ruled that neglecting to request cautionary accomplice instructions constitutes deficient performance under Strickland, as no tactical benefit justifies the omission. Smith was legally entitled to a Bland-style instruction, which would have aided jurors in evaluating DeShields’ uncorroborated, critical testimony. Thus, we find Smith’s counsel’s failure to request this instruction meets Strickland’s 'deficient performance' criterion.

To prove prejudice under Strickland’s second prong, Smith must demonstrate a reasonable likelihood that the result would have differed absent counsel’s error. The Superior Court bypassed assessing deficiency, focusing solely on prejudice and ruling that general witness credibility instructions sufficed, rendering Smith unharmed. It deemed the given instructions legally sound and adequate for the jury’s role, dismissing the claim.

The conclusion that Smith was not 'prejudiced' by the lack of a specific instruction on accomplice testimony credibility is a legal determination we review de novo. The State notes that this Court previously found the jury had enough information to assess DeShields' reliability and credibility, and Smith's counsel had ample basis to argue bias. However, jury arguments alone cannot replace a formal instruction from the judge on accomplice credibility. The jury was told that attorneys' closing remarks are not evidence and that only testimony and exhibits constitute evidence for their verdict.

While the Smith jury had enough details to evaluate DeShields' testimony, it lacked guidance from the judge on how to legally assess an accomplice's credibility. Decades ago in Bland, this Court acknowledged the need for a special instruction on accomplice testimony due to its inherent unreliability. Post-Bland rulings allowed flexibility in wording but never eliminated the requirement for such an instruction. A general credibility directive cannot compensate for the absence of a specific accomplice credibility instruction, as established in Bland.

Bland's ruling emphasized two key principles: accomplice testimony warrants unique jury scrutiny distinct from other witnesses, and while Delaware law doesn’t mandate corroboration, its absence deserves special attention. In Bland, despite upholding the uncorroborated testimony rule, the Court stressed the need for juries to exercise extreme caution when relying solely on accomplice testimony. The approved instruction warned against conviction without corroboration unless the jury was thoroughly convinced of the testimony's truthfulness.

In Bordley, this Court endorsed a pattern jury instruction aligning with Bland’s principles, highlighting the need for special scrutiny of accomplice testimony and consideration of corroboration. However, we now clarify that the Bland instruction is preferable to the Bordley pattern. For Smith, we reaffirm Bland, stating a general credibility instruction cannot substitute for a specific accomplice credibility directive. The Superior Court’s failure to provide this instruction left Smith’s jury inadequately guided in evaluating DeShields' uncorroborated testimony.

The court's credibility was undermined because Smith's lawyers failed to request it. Consequently, the jury in Smith's case was never informed, as per Bland, that accomplice testimony requires special attention and should be scrutinized more carefully. These points could have been included in a Bland-style jury instruction without revealing DeShields' case outcome. It is agreed that Smith did not kill Coverdale, as the State confirmed DeShields fired the fatal shot. The prosecution argued Smith was accountable as DeShields' accomplice for all crimes, including Coverdale's murder. The jury was told to determine if Coverdale's death was a foreseeable result of the first-degree robbery. The jury's decision on whether Smith and DeShields were accomplices hinged on whom they believed regarding the initial intent of their meeting with Coverdale. Smith claimed there was no plan to rob or kill, while DeShields testified they had agreed beforehand to

rob Coverdale at gunpoint. DeShields' account lacked corroboration. When a defendant's involvement in a crime relies on an accomplice's testimony, specific instructions about accomplice credibility are necessary. However, the failure to request such instructions isn't always inherently prejudicial. The impact depends on the case's specifics. In Smith's trial, the lack of a Bland instruction meets the prejudice requirement under Strickland's second prong. The record shows this error raises doubts about the reliability of Smith's convictions. Thus, we conclude that, under Strickland, Smith demonstrated prejudice due to his trial counsel's ineffective assistance.
