(12) Vick has not identified any specific due process violations, failing to demonstrate beyond speculation that his rights were infringed. See United States v. Valenzuela-Bernal, 458 U.S. 858 [102 S.Ct. 3440, 73 L.Ed.2d 1193] (1982).

(13) The appellant has also not proven that the trial outcome would have differed absent his counsel's alleged mistakes. See Strickland v. Washington, 466 U.S. 668 [104 S.Ct. 2052, 80 L.Ed.2d 674] (1984). Consequently, his claims of ineffective legal representation lack merit. (14) Lastly, because Vick was already serving sentences from the Court of Common Pleas for other convictions, the Superior Court correctly denied him credit for time served. The court also properly rejected his mandamus petition compelling the Department of Corrections to award him 143 days of credit for his Superior Court convictions. NOW, THEREFORE, IT IS ORDERED that the Superior Court's rulings are hereby AFFIRMED. BY THE COURT: /s/ Joseph T. Walsh Justice In the Supreme Court of the State of Delaware Herschel W. Vick, Plaintiff, Appellant, v. Karl Haller, Defendant, Appellee.

No. 149, 1986 Court Below—Superior Court of the State of Delaware, in and for Sussex County: Civil Action No. 85C-AU-20 Submitted: November 6, 1986 Decided: March 2, 1987 Before CHRISTIE, Chief Justice, HORSEY and MOORE, Justices. ORDER This 2nd day of March, 1987, after reviewing the parties' briefs, including the appellant's pro se submission, the Court notes: (1) This civil case arises from a criminal proceeding that resulted in Herschel Vick's 1984 convictions. Vick filed this suit on August 14, 1985, seeking damages and equitable relief against his public defender, Karl Haller, as well as the judge and prosecutor from his trial. While this civil case was ongoing, Vick's criminal convictions were upheld on appeal.

Vick v. State, Del.Supr. [504 A.2d 573], Nos. 289, 1984 and 19 and 76, 1985 Walsh, J. (December 20, 1985) (Order). On April 29, 1986, the Superior Court dismissed this civil action against all defendants, ruling the complaint failed to state a valid claim. Superior Court Civil Rule 12(b)(6). Vick then appealed. On August 22, 1986, this Court upheld the dismissal for two appellees—the judge and prosecutor—due to their immunity under 10 Del. C. § 4001 and the complaint's failure to state a federal claim. Supr.Ct. Rule 25(a). The current issue is whether the Superior Court erred in dismissing the complaint against the remaining appellee, Mr. Haller.

(2) When evaluating a motion to dismiss under Superior Court Civil Rule 12(b)(6), all well-pled allegations must be taken as true. Spence v. Funk, Del.Supr., 396 A.2d 967, 968 (1978). The motion will be denied if the plaintiff can potentially recover under any plausible scenario supported by the complaint. Id. While official immunity could justify granting such a motion, it is rarely granted when the immunity is qualified. 2A Moore's Federal Practice para. 12.07 [2.-5] n. 22 (1986), citing Scheuer v. Rhodes, 416 U.S. 232, 94 S.Ct. 1683, 40 L.Ed.2d 90 (1974). Pro se complaints, even if poorly drafted, are held to a less rigorous standard than lawyer-prepared pleadings and are dismissed only if no possible claim for relief exists.

(3) The plaintiff's claims against Mr. Haller span the entire criminal process, from charges to conviction. The complaint and attached documents allege that on February 28, 1984, the plaintiff was charged with traffic violations, resisting arrest, and drug-related offenses. At a March 8, 1984 preliminary hearing, Mr. Haller advised the plaintiff to accept a plea deal and waive the hearing to obtain a police report. When the plaintiff refused, Mr. Haller grew frustrated and suggested self-representation. The plaintiff then asked for a hearing transcript, but Mr. Haller declined, citing cost and his own notes. Later, upon learning of the plaintiff's intent to represent himself, Mr. Haller mentioned in a letter that the plaintiff might be entitled to a transcript.

(4) The plaintiff then filed an in forma pauperis request for the transcript, which the court forwarded to the public defender's office. Mr. Haller ordered part of the transcript just before the June 12, 1984 trial. The plaintiff also submitted four pretrial motions to the court, which were sent to Mr. Haller but not immediately filed. Correspondence shows Mr. Haller repeatedly attempted to advise the plaintiff while preparing for trial. He filed one motion, to suppress evidence, shortly before trial. The plaintiff alleges Mr. Haller misled him about the filing date, claiming in an April 30 letter that it was already filed, then stating in a June 5 letter that he served the prosecutor. Mr. Haller also confirmed the June 5 filing in a letter to Judge Stiftel.

(5) The plaintiff further claims Mr. Haller failed to request a jury trial, caused a witness to turn hostile, slept during part of the suppression hearing, joked with the prosecutor and police about sentencing, and did not use the preliminary hearing transcript to challenge an officer's testimony. (6) The plaintiff's claims allege violations of federal constitutional rights under 42 U.S.C. § 1983.

Under common law negligence (malpractice), the appellant's federal claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 is barred. A state public defender does not act under state authority unless conspiring with state officials to violate federal rights, as established in Tower v. Glover. The appellant did not provide specific allegations of such conspiracy involving Mr. Haller. Additionally, the Superior Court found the negligence claim barred by Delaware's official immunity statute, 10 Del. C. § 4001, which protects state employees from liability unless constitutional or federal law explicitly requires otherwise.

The statute specifies that no claims shall arise against state officials or employees if: (1) the act or omission occurred during official duties involving policy decisions, statutory interpretation, or discretionary actions; (2) the act was done in good faith for the public interest; and (3) there was no gross negligence. Judges, the Attorney General, and legislators enjoy absolute immunity, while plaintiffs must prove the absence of these immunity elements in cases against state employees.

The court ruled that Haller, as a public employee exercising discretion, was immune because Mr. Vick failed to disprove any immunity criteria. Haller argues for absolute immunity for public defenders, but the court declined to extend statutory immunity beyond legislative intent, citing Giuricich v. Emtrol Corp. Such policy changes must come from the General Assembly.

The Superior Court's decision was affirmed, holding that public defenders qualify for immunity under § 4001 if their actions meet the statute's three criteria. Citing Tower v. Glover, the court noted common law support for this immunity, contrasting Reese v. Danforth. As a state employee, Mr. Haller is immune unless the plaintiff alleges specific facts negating the immunity requirements in a dismissal motion context.

The three legal standards for immunity require the appellant to present facts suggesting that Mr. Haller's representation: (1) was unrelated to an official duty involving discretion; (2) lacked good faith and public interest intent; or (3) was severely negligent. The appellant fails to provide specific facts proving Mr. Haller's actions were outside his duties or discretionary scope. However, allegations include misinformation about a suppression motion filing date and other acts not assessable under current immunity criteria. Given the attached evidence and issues of good faith and negligence, the immunity ruling appears premature.

Given this case's context, resolving immunity via a dismissal motion was improper. A summary judgment motion under Superior Court Civil Rule 56 would be more appropriate. The appellant submitted substantial evidence, while the appellee provided none, leaving the pretrial record incomplete. The trial court should have treated the dismissal motion as a summary judgment motion, allowing the appellee to expand the record. The Superior Court's ruling is reversed, as the dismissal motion should have been handled as a summary judgment, and the case is remanded for further proceedings.

The case was put on hold awaiting the result of the federal lawsuit. The District Court dismissed the federal case, citing GreaL-West Life & Annuity Insurance Co. v. The court noted the Fund was attempting to reframe a monetary claim against the Brewsters as equitable, which Greatr-West deemed a legal remedy. Subsequently, the Court of Chancery dismissed the parallel case due to a lack of equitable jurisdiction, leading to its transfer to Superior Court under 10 Del. C. § 1902. There, both parties filed cross-motions for summary judgment. The Superior Court ruled in favor of the Brewsters, denying the Fund's motion and stating the claim 'relates to' an ERISA plan under § 514(a), leaving the Fund without a legal avenue to recover the funds paid for Mrs. Brewster.

The Fund appealed, arguing against federal preemption of its state subrogation claim. It claimed the Superior Court misapplied the term 'relates to' in ERISA § 514 and erred by ruling the suit wasn’t equitable under § 502(a)(3) yet could still be preempted by § 514. The appeal reviews the summary judgment de novo, including jurisdictional questions. The Brewsters maintain the Fund’s claim is entirely preempted by ERISA. As outlined in Moore's Manual on Federal Practice, complete preemption occurs when Congress intends to replace state law with an exclusive federal remedy, even if the claim is based on state law. This doctrine is exceptionally rare, applying only to statutes like the LMRA, ERISA, and the National Bank Act for usury claims.

Some courts clarify that this exception isn’t purely about preemption but federal jurisdiction. Removal and preemption differ, and preemption alone doesn’t guarantee federal jurisdiction. A more precise term might be 'jurisdictional preemption,' as it not only overrides state law but also establishes federal jurisdiction regardless of procedural context. Ordinary preemption, in contrast, is merely a defense against state law claims conflicting with federal law. Complete preemption, however, isn’t a defense but a jurisdictional rule for assessing removal when a complaint alleges only state claims. It examines whether the case is fundamentally federal, creating the basis for federal question jurisdiction and removal.

The present case centers on jurisdictional preemption under ERISA, which has a sweeping preemptive intent. Congress designed ERISA to create uniform administrative standards for benefit plans. Section 514 states ERISA supersedes all state laws 'relating to' employee benefit plans. Even if a state claim doesn’t explicitly fall under § 514, it may still be preempted if it aligns with ERISA’s civil enforcement provisions. This broad scope ensures consistency in benefit administration, reinforcing ERISA’s role as the exclusive framework for such disputes.

Under § 502, the case remains preempted and eligible for transfer to federal court. The U.S. Supreme Court has interpreted congressional intent behind § 502, stating that any state-law claim replicating, augmenting, or replacing ERISA's enforcement mechanism clashes with the goal of keeping ERISA's remedy exclusive, thus warranting preemption. This preemption aims to preserve consistency in federal oversight, as the Court noted: ERISA's preemption arose from the need to streamline complex plan administration. Fragmented regulations would disrupt efficiency, potentially causing employers to cut benefits or avoid establishing plans. Preemption guarantees uniform regulatory governance. Section 502's unified enforcement supports this, such as § 502(a)(1)(B), which lets participants claim owed benefits, enforce plan terms, or clarify future entitlements.

Section 502(a)(3) permits participants, beneficiaries, or fiduciaries to halt violations of ERISA or plan terms or seek equitable relief. In Great-West Life & Annuity Insurance Co. v. Knudson, the Supreme Court clarified that § 502(a)(3)'s 'equitable relief' demands restitution targeting specific assets held by the defendant, not personal liability. The Court did not decide whether ERISA preempts state-law contract claims against respondents. Pre-Great-West, courts widely held ERISA preempted state claims like contract breaches under subrogation agreements. Post-Great-West, divisions emerged on whether § 502(a)(3) let fiduciaries enforce subrogation.

In 2006, the Supreme Court resolved this in Sereboff v. Mid Atlantic Medical Services, Inc., a case akin to ours. There, ERISA plan beneficiaries injured in a car accident were required under the plan’s 'Acts of Third Parties' clause to reimburse medical benefits from third-party recoveries. After the plan paid their expenses and the beneficiaries settled with the tortfeasors, they refused reimbursement. The plan sued under § 502(a)(3), securing a lien on the settlement. The district court and Fourth Circuit ruled for the plan. The Supreme Court granted certiorari to address circuit splits and upheld the decision, deeming the relief equitable under § 502(a)(3).

The Fund, following Sereboff, could pursue an equitable lien or constructive trust over the Brewsters’ settlement via § 502(a)(3). That a state-law subrogation claim might overlap doesn’t negate ERISA’s exclusive federal jurisdiction. As stated in Metropolitan Life Insurance Company v. Taylor and Aetna Health Inc. v. Davila, Congress intended § 502(a) claims to be removable to federal court, reinforcing ERISA’s exclusive remedy nature under § 502(a).

The Plan and Agreement explicitly outlined the relief the Fund could pursue under ERISA, specifically the assignment of settlement funds equivalent to the benefits paid. While state law offers a means to enforce subrogation rights, ERISA has overridden Delaware courts' authority over the Fund's equitable claim to these proceeds. We concur with the Superior Court that Mrs. Brewster's agreement with the Fund also pertains to the Plan under ERISA § 514(a). The Plan mandated reimbursement of benefits from any third-party payments for expenses covered by the Fund, and Mrs. Brewster signed the required Agreement. We further agree that the Superior Court incorrectly implied the Fund lacked enforcement options; Sereboff confirms an ERISA remedy exists, allowing the Fund to pursue subrogation via § 502(a)(3) through a constructive trust or equitable lien. This remedy's availability justifies jurisdictional preemption here, as Congress intended ERISA's remedy to be exclusive, preempting the Fund's state subrogation claim. The Superior Court

OPINION GLASSCOCK, Vice Chancellor: Corporate success hinges on competent leaders, who wouldn’t serve if exposed to unchecked liability. Delaware’s indemnification laws address this. Pending issues involve statutory provisions and a contractual indemnity agreement. DGCL mandates indemnity for officials succeeding in proceedings but bars it for bad-faith actors. Between these extremes, corporations may define terms via charter or contract...

their service, provided they succeed. Conversely, indemnity is barred for bad-faith failures. Delaware law balances deterring meritless claims with attracting qualified leaders. Permissive indemnity between these bounds lets corporations tailor terms, enforceable unless violating mandatory statutes. Here, the parties’ contract governs absent statutory conflict.

The Plaintiff, a former executive, is suing the Defendant, his previous employer, for advancement and indemnification related to various legal proceedings stemming from regulatory and criminal investigations at the Defendant's company. Both parties are bound by an Indemnification Agreement that converts discretionary indemnification terms under the DGCL into obligatory ones. The core issue is whether the Plaintiff prevailed in any of the proceedings, warranting indemnification by law, or if further discovery is needed to assess his good faith, which would qualify him for indemnification under the Agreement. The parties have submitted briefs, and the case is now under review for cross-motions on partial summary judgment. For claims needing more discovery on the Plaintiff's good faith, I outline the pertinent evidence scope. Lastly, I address the outstanding advancement issue.

Marc S. Hermelin, who was CEO of K-V Pharmaceutical Company ('KV') from 1975 to 2008 and served on its Board until 2010, is pursuing indemnification or advancement for multiple legal and regulatory issues tied to KV's distribution of oversized morphine sulfate tablets. The facts behind these proceedings are more pertinent to discretionary indemnification, which hinges on meeting a 'good faith' standard. While a decision on discretionary indemnification isn't feasible now due to insufficient evidence, a summary of agreed-upon facts is helpful. In May 2008, KV was alerted by two pharmacies about oversized morphine tablets it had produced and distributed via its subsidiary, ETHEX Corporation. During its internal probe, KV found other oversized pills, including propafenone and dextroamphetamine sulfate. While KV reported the morphine issue to the FDA, it withheld information about the other pills.

Following employee complaints, KV's Audit Committee launched an internal investigation, leading to Hermelin's termination as CEO. This disclosure in KV's Form 8-K triggered investigations by the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Eastern District of Missouri, the FDA, and the Department of Health and Human Services' Office of Inspector General. Hermelin seeks advancement and indemnification for proceedings linked to these investigations. In his Verified Amended Complaint, Hermelin initially sought indemnification for six concluded proceedings, though two are no longer contested. The remaining four—the Audit Committee Matter, Criminal Matter, FDA Consent Decree Matter, and HHS Exclusion Matter—are summarized with focus on the charges and outcomes, which are key to determining if Hermelin achieved success on the merits.

KV argues that Hermelin's alleged successes in these matters are Pyrrhic victories—wins so costly they equate to losses—and thus don't qualify for mandatory indemnification under Delaware law. However, most of Hermelin's claimed successes aren't Pyrrhic but resemble losses like Lee's at Appomattox, where surrender on favorable terms averted greater sacrifice. For instance, in the Audit Committee Matter (August 2008), KV's Audit Committee investigated claims that Hermelin failed to act on reports of oversized tablets. The Committee, aided by independent counsel, conducted over 50 interviews and reviewed extensive documentation. Hermelin, represented by his own counsel, participated in the process.

During the investigation, he chose to rely on his own advice. After the investigation concluded, the board opted to end Hermelin's employment for cause in December 2008. KV announced this decision in a Form 8-K filing on December 5, 2008, which drew scrutiny from the USAO and other federal agencies. Shortly after Hermelin left his role as KV's CEO, the USAO launched an inquiry into KV's distribution of oversized pills. Due to Hermelin's role as a responsible corporate officer at KV and ETHEX, the USAO charged him with two federal strict liability misdemeanors, to which he admitted guilt. The District Court imposed a $1.9 million criminal fine and forfeiture, along with a sentence of at least 30 days in the St. Louis County Jail. Hermelin served 15 days, during which his private conversations were recorded, leading to the Jail Records Matter discussed later. Hermelin claims the USAO could have pursued more severe charges, and by pleading guilty to the misdemeanors, he avoided those harsher penalties.

Hermelin asserts that his guilty plea to the two strict liability misdemeanors allowed him to evade more serious charges, making him 'successful on the merits or otherwise' in the Criminal Matter. He seeks reimbursement for his $1.9 million fine and legal fees. KV argues that his jail time and substantial fine prove he was not successful. The FDA Consent Decree Matter stemmed from an FDA investigation between December 15, 2008, and February 2, 2009, into whether KV's manufacturing adhered to cGMP standards. The FDA sought an injunction to halt KV, Hermelin, and others from producing or distributing drugs until cGMP and quality controls were met. Though Hermelin was no longer KV's CEO when the FDA filed its complaint, he remained on the board. On March 18, 2010, the FDA, KV, Hermelin, and others entered a consent decree agreeing to destroy certain drugs and cease manufacturing until cGMP compliance was achieved.

The Consent Decree explicitly stated its terms did not apply to Hermelin as long as KV's board upheld his termination and he had no involvement in KV's decision-making or operations affecting compliance with the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. If these conditions changed, the decree would immediately apply to him. Hermelin argues the FDA's investigation found no misconduct by him, and the decree's inapplicability signifies his success. KV contends the decree's bar on his return to KV negates any claim of success. The HHS Exclusion Matter involved the OIG's decision to exclude Hermelin from federal healthcare programs. In May 2010, the OIG notified Hermelin of its intent to exclude him due to his ties to ETHEX, a convicted KV subsidiary. This exclusion would prevent him from receiving federal healthcare payments for services rendered.

The OIG based its decision on federal law allowing exclusion of individuals with ownership or control interests in sanctioned entities or those serving as officers or managing employees. Despite Hermelin's defense submissions, the OIG formally excluded him for 20 years in October 2010. Unlike Hermelin, KV faced mandatory exclusion by state Medicaid agencies due to its potential ownership of an excluded entity. Hermelin maintains that his exclusion was unjust, while KV argues it reflects his lack of success in the matter.

The entity (ETHEX) was under the control of an excluded individual (Hermelin). To prevent exclusion, KV negotiated with the OIG, which agreed to postpone ETHEX's exclusion if KV dissolved ETHEX promptly. By dissolving ETHEX before its exclusion, KV avoided mandatory exclusion for owning an excluded entity. KV also risked exclusion due to Hermelin's controlling stake. Hermelin claimed he faced a 'Hobson's Choice': either sell his KV shares and accept his exclusion without appeal, or let KV be excluded. He chose to sell his shares and waive his appeal rights, and the OIG agreed not to pursue KV's exclusion. Hermelin now argues he shouldn't bear his legal costs for sacrificing himself and that KV should cover his expenses related to the HHS Exclusion Matter. He also claims success, as the OIG found no misconduct on his part, attributing his exclusion solely to his ties with ETHEX. KV counters that Herm

elin was unsuccessful, as the OIG imposed the severest penalty: a de facto lifetime ban from federal healthcare programs. KV also contends that while Hermelin's stock divestiture may have spared KV from exclusion, this shouldn't alter the outcome, as the OIG handled Hermelin's exclusion separately from his agreement to divest and waive appeal rights. B. Advancement for the Jail Records Matter Beyond his indemnification claims, Hermelin seeks coverage for legal fees in pursuing injunctive relief against the St. Louis County Jail, where he was held after his conviction in the Criminal Matter. After pleading guilty on March 10, 2011, to two federal strict liability misdemeanors, the District Court fined him $1.9 million and sentenced him to '30 days or less' in jail. Hermelin served 15 days starting March 14, 2011. During his incarceration, he met with visitors, including his wife, other

family members, friends, clergy, and his assistant. Hermelin avoided discussing KV or its business, focusing instead on private matters like medical, religious, and legal issues. These conversations were recorded per jail policy. On April 25, 2011, a St. Louis Post-Dispatch reporter, citing the Missouri Sunshine Law, requested records related to Hermelin's jail time, including visitation logs and recordings of his calls and visitor conversations. The jail released most records on May 5 but planned to release the recordings unless barred. Hermelin sued to block their release, arguing they were private. On December 6, 2011, the Circuit Court of St. Louis County permanently barred the jail from releasing the recordings, deeming them 'purely private matters.' Hermelin's Indemnification Agreement excludes coverage for self-initiated actions. He claims he deserves advancement because he didn't initiate the Jail Records Matter but acted defensively to protect sensitive information. He also argues his injunction was akin to a compulsory counterclaim, which the Agreement doesn't exclude from advancement. KV disputes this, asserting the injunction falls under the Agreement's exceptions for advancement. KV also argues that even if compulsory counterclaims qualify, Hermelin's lawsuit didn't meet the definition under federal or Chancery Court rules. C. Procedural Posture The parties briefed and argued whether Hermelin qualifies for advancement in the Jail Records Matter, and
the court heard oral arguments on the issue.

Regarding the matter dated January 5, 2012, I conclude, based on the reasons provided, that the Indemnification Agreement explicitly denies advancement for the Jail Records Matter because Hermelin initiated the injunctive relief action. Additionally, I address Hermelin's eligibility for mandatory indemnification and the extent of pertinent, discoverable evidence concerning permissive indemnification. As detailed, the court can assess an indemnitee's claim to mandatory indemnification—dependent on whether they prevailed in a proceeding on the merits or otherwise—using a far narrower record than needed for permissive indemnification, which evaluates the indemnitee's good faith. Due to this evidentiary difference, I asked the parties to brief whether Hermelin was 'successful' in any proceedings for which he seeks indemnification, thereby qualifying for mandatory indemnification under 8 Del. C. § 145(c), and to define the scope of relevant evidence for permissive indemnification under 8 Del. C.

§ 145(a). After reviewing the briefs and record, I determine that Hermelin is not legally entitled to mandatory indemnification for the Criminal Matter and HHS Exclusion Matter but is eligible for the FDA Consent Decree Matter. Concerning permissive indemnification for the Criminal, HHS Exclusion, and Audit Committee Matters, discovery is restricted to the conduct related to those proceedings. I elaborate on these conclusions below. II. STANDARD OF REVIEW Neither party has claimed material factual disputes preventing a decision on advancement, mandatory indemnification, or the scope of evidence for permissive indemnification. Both parties also agreed during the January 5, 2012 Oral Argument that their briefs should be treated as cross-motions for summary judgment. Thus, I consider these issues ready for resolution based on the existing record. Summary judgment is warranted when no genuine factual disputes exist and the movant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law.

Partial summary judgment is suitable if only part of the case can be resolved with the submitted record. Hermelin and KV are bound by an Indemnification Agreement, which primarily governs KV's indemnification duties. The Agreement states that in any enforcement proceeding for Hermelin's indemnification rights, KV 'must, to the fullest extent permitted by law, bear the burden of disproving the presumption.' Furthermore, if a proceeding involving Hermelin concludes without an adverse judgment against him, it is presumed he succeeded on the merits. Overcoming this presumption requires clear and convincing evidence. III. ANALYSIS A. Advancement for the Jail Records Matter Delaware law allows corporations to advance expenses for officers or directors defending actions where indemnification is permissible. KV's Bylaws, Article IX, Section 1(e), mirrors this provision, permitting KV to advance expenses. Under these permissive sources

of indemnification and advancement rights, the Indemnification Agreement requires KV to advance Hermelin's expenses for specific matters. Since the Agreement is the sole source imposing mandatory advancement duties on KV, its terms govern this analysis, unless they conflict with KV's Bylaws or the DGCL. Section 4(a) of the Agreement states: (a) Unless Section 3(b)(iv) applies, the Company must advance Expenses to Indemnitee to the fullest extent allowed by the [DGCL] if Indemnitee is or may become a party to any Proceeding due to their Official Capacity or actions taken therein. Section 3(b)(iv) creates a critical exception: 'Indemnitee is not entitled to indemnification for Expenses in any Proceeding (or part thereof) they initiated unless the Board authorized it.'

Hermelin contends that this clause does not prevent advancement for the Jail Records Matter, as he did not 'initiate' the proceeding; instead, the Post-Dispatch started it by requesting information from the Jail's Custodian of Records. Similarly, he claims his injunctive relief request resembles a compulsory counterclaim, noting that Section 3(b)(iv) does not explicitly bar advancement for such claims. However, his interpretation that the Post-Dispatch or Custodian initiated the matter by threatening to release his private recordings misreads Section 3(b)(iv), which excludes not only proceedings Hermelin started but also any 'parts' (including claims or permissive counterclaims) he initiated. Even if the Custodian or Post-Dispatch 'initiated' the Jail Records Matter and Hermelin's lawsuit was a 'defense,' he cannot seek advancement for any 'part' he initiated. Thus, his 'counterclaim' falls under Section 3(b)(iv)'s exclusion, which the parties agreed upon.

From Hermelin's perspective, his 'counterclaim' in the Jail Records Matter clearly falls under Section 3(b)(iv)'s exclusion, a provision the parties negotiated. Whether this arrangement reflects sound corporate policy is not for me to decide. Alternatively, Hermelin argues his injunctive relief claim constitutes a compulsory counterclaim exempt from Section 3(b)(iv)'s bar. Even assuming Section 3(b)(iv) allows advancement for compulsory counterclaims, his injunctive relief claim does not sufficiently resemble one to qualify. Court rules require a party to assert as a counterclaim any claim arising from the same transaction as the opposing party's claim. Hermelin claims his injunctive relief arose from the jail records request and that failing to file would have forfeited his rights, but this reasoning overlooks the framework for compulsory counterclaims.

Hermelin's argument disregards the foundational requirements for a compulsory counterclaim. Neither the Custodian nor the Post-Dispatch filed a claim necessitating a response from him, so there was no 'subject matter of the opposing party's claim' to base a compulsory counterclaim on. His situation mirrors anyone seeking injunctive relief due to rights infringement. Courts only grant injunctions for irreparable harm, meaning plaintiffs must act or lose their rights. Hermelin's interpretation would exempt all injunctive relief claims from Section 3(b)(iv), but the clause plainly bars indemnification for such claims. His broad definition of 'compulsory counterclaim' lacks contractual or legal support, and cited case law does not expand the term beyond court rules.

Since Section 3(b)(iv) applies to Hermelin's injunctive relief claim, he needed KV Board approval to pursue it for advancement. He requested but did not receive permission, so his advancement claim for the Jail Records Matter is denied. Regarding fee reimbursement, Hermelin must repay KV for advancements tied to the Jail Records Matter. The parties should agree on what portion of 'fees for fees' covered this matter; if they cannot, they must inform the court. For indemnification, Hermelin seeks mandatory coverage for the Criminal, HHS Exclusion, and FDA Consent Decree Matters, hinging on whether he was 'successful on the merits or otherwise.'

Elin achieved success solely in the FDA Consent Decree Matter, qualifying him for mandatory indemnification. For the Criminal Matter, HHS Exclusion Matter, and Audit Committee Matter (where Hermelin isn't seeking mandatory indemnification), permissive indemnification may apply; however, this Opinion later explains why the current record prevents a definitive ruling on that issue. Under DGCL Section 145, corporations typically have discretion over indemnifying officers, but Section 145(c) requires it when a director/officer succeeds 'on the merits or otherwise' in legal proceedings related to their role. KV's Bylaws mirror this language, as does Section 1(c) of Article IX.

Section 5 of the Indemnification Agreement, titled 'Indemnification for Expenses for Successful Party,' aligns with DGCL §145(c) and KV's Bylaws: If the Indemnitee succeeds in any Proceeding (even partially), they must be reimbursed for all reasonable expenses. This includes dismissed cases or settlements where indemnification is later deemed appropriate. The parties agree the three matters Hermelin cites qualify as 'Proceedings,' but the pivotal question is whether he was 'successful on the merits or otherwise.' Absent such success, indemnification hinges on KV proving Hermelin acted in bad faith under DGCL §145(a).

The Indemnification Agreement defines 'success on merits or otherwise' broadly in Section 7(e)(iii): Settlements or non-adjudicated resolutions that avoid burdensome litigation constitute success, creating a presumption in the Indemnitee's favor. Challenging this presumption requires clear, convincing evidence. The parties dispute whether courts should assess the specifics of a proceeding's outcome under Section 145(c) or simply accept the result as indicative of success.

Both parties initially argue Hermelin's success can be judged purely by each proceeding's outcome but alternatively propose discovery into his criminal plea, FDA Consent Decree, and HHS Exclusion negotiations if their primary stance fails. KV even suggests governmental intent behind the results should matter. This overcomplicates Section 145(c)'s mandate: success is determined by the result itself, not underlying motives. If the outcome shields the indemnitee from liability, probing the 'how' or 'why' is unnecessary—regardless of prosecutorial or agency intent.

The notion of being 'successful' is clearly irrelevant. An indemnitee would struggle to obtain testimony from a prosecutor stating they intended the defendant to 'succeed' during plea negotiations. Delaware law avoids such abstract considerations, focusing solely on the outcome rather than the reasoning. Under Section 145(c), this Court evaluates only the result of the action, aligning with the DGCL's language and minimizing costly discovery into dismissals or settlements. Here, I assess Hermelin's charges and compare them to the actual outcome. a. Hermelin Is Not Entitled to Mandatory Indemnification for the Criminal Matter Hermelin clearly did not succeed in the Criminal Matter. He faced two federal misdemeanors, pled guilty to both, and was fined $1.9 million.

Hermelin was also sentenced to up to thirty days in jail. He claims a guilty plea is not an adverse judgment and that avoiding 'expense, delay, and uncertainty' qualifies as 'success' under Section 7(e)(iii) of the Indemnification Agreement. While DGCL § 145(c) often deems any non-conviction a 'success,' Hermelin pled guilty to all charges, paid a hefty fine, and served jail time—hardly a favorable outcome. His reliance on Section 7(e)(iii) is unconvincing, as it merely acknowledges that some pre-judgment resolutions may qualify as success. Delaware precedent holds that 'success' under § 145(c) means avoiding adverse judgment, not moral exoneration. For instance,

in Merritt-Chapman & Scott Corp. v. Wolfson, the Court ruled that indemnitees were successful for dismissed charges, even as they pled guilty to others. Hermelin fails to draw a valid parallel, as he pled guilty to all charges without any dismissals. He argues the USAO could have charged him more severely, citing ETHEX's case, but claims negotiations limited his charges to two misdemeanors. Such negotiations, if they occurred, are irrelevant under Section 145(c). This Court does not assess potential charges but evaluates the actual outcome against the filed claims.

In criminal cases, dismissal usually means success, while a conviction—even via guilty plea—means failure. Hermelin pled guilty to all charges, paid a large fine, and served jail time. Though he may have avoided some burdens, this does not constitute 'success.' Allowing guilty pleas to qualify as success would undermine DGCL § 145(a)-(b), rewarding those without any defense. Hermelin achieved no success on his charges and thus is not entitled to mandatory indemnification for the Criminal Matter. b. Hermelin Is Not Entitled to Mandatory Indemnification for the HHS

In the HHS Exclusion Matter, Hermelin did not prevail on the merits. On May 19, 2010, the OIG notified Hermelin of its intent to exclude him from federal healthcare programs and allowed him to present a defense. After reviewing his submissions, the OIG imposed a 20-year exclusion, which Hermelin admits amounted to a lifetime ban due to his age. Given the disparity between the potential lifetime exclusion and the actual 20-year exclusion, Hermelin clearly did not succeed on the merits. Hermelin argues that he achieved success because the OIG did not require monetary payment and claims his settlement protected KV from exclusion, making it unfair to deny his indemnification rights.

The OIG's settlement, where Hermelin waived his appeal rights in exchange for KV's exclusion being waived, allegedly saved him from 'expense, delay, distraction, disruption, and uncertainty,' which he claims qualifies for indemnification under the agreement. However, these arguments obscure the central question: Did Hermelin succeed when the OIG excluded him for 20 years (effectively for life)? The answer is no. Hermelin’s waiver of appeal and divestment of KV stock in exchange for the OIG sparing KV are irrelevant. His indemnification rights stem from statute and contract, not equity. While his divestment may have been necessary to avoid KV’s mandatory exclusion, the record suggests the OIG only demanded his appeal waiver in return for not excluding KV permissively.

Although sound corporate policy might justify indemnifying officers who sacrifice themselves for the company, my role is to determine legal entitlement, not evaluate corporate practices. Hermelin’s claim hinges on whether he 'succeeded on the merits,' which is confined to the OIG’s action against him. The OIG’s exclusion decision was independent of its actions toward KV, rendering Hermelin’s voluntary sacrifices irrelevant. Even if considered, 'taking one for the team' does not equate to legal success. In such cases, the company benefits, not the indemnitee, and indemnification becomes a corporate policy matter under DGCL § 145(a)-(b).

I conclude Hermelin was 'successful on the merits or otherwise' in the FDA Consent Decree Matter. The decree imposed no new penalties or restrictions on Hermelin, meaning he avoided an adverse outcome, constituting success. The FDA’s complaint sought an injunction barring KV, ETHEX, Hermelin, and others from drug manufacturing until compliance with cGMP and FDCA was achieved. However, the final decree did not enforce these restrictions on Hermelin personally, thus meeting the standard for indemnification under Section 145(c).

Section 145(a). In Stockman v. Heartland Industrial Partners, L.P., former Vice Chancellor Strine recognized that the wording of § 145(a) and (b) primarily applies to cases where the indemnitee has been found to breach a legal or ethical obligation, admitted fault, or resolved a case through payment. The first two scenarios suggest the indemnitee acted against corporate or societal interests, making indemnification counterproductive to enforcing legal and fiduciary responsibilities. Additionally, these cases typically involve a detailed judicial record from a full trial, aiding in assessing compliance with § 145(a) and (b)’s good faith standard. Settlements, however, often lack such records, necessitating further investigation to evaluate the indemnitee’s conduct.

Despite this, the Stockman Court observed that § 145(a) and (b) are seldom applied in settlements because indemnitees usually collaborate with corporations, legal teams, and insurers to resolve disputes. Neither party in Stockman could cite prior cases where this Court assessed whether a settling indemnitee met § 145(a) and (b)’s good faith requirement. As the Vice Chancellor noted, settlements aim to conclude disputes, not prolong litigation. Hermelin’s indemnification claims face similar hurdles, as none of the cases involved findings of bad faith or admissions of guilt. The Criminal Matter ended with a guilty plea to strict liability misdemeanors, which, under Section 7(e)(iii) of the Indemnification Agreement, does not automatically imply a non-indemnifiable state of mind, leaving Hermelin’s conduct unclear.

The HHS Exclusion Matter also lacked a bad faith determination, as Hermelin’s exclusion stemmed from his ties to ETHEX. Similarly, in the Audit Committee Matter, while Hermelin was terminated 'for cause' due to alleged willful misconduct, the record offers little evidence to support this claim. Thus, additional evidence is required to determine if Hermelin acted in good faith under § 145(a). A full trial is needed to assess whether Hermelin reasonably believed his actions aligned with KV’s best interests or had no reason to suspect his conduct was unlawful. The scope of discovery is confined to Hermelin’s behavior in the proceedings for which he seeks indemnification.

For the Criminal and HHS Exclusion Matters, discovery is restricted to facts concerning KV’s and ETHEX’s production of oversized tablets, including specific medications, and Hermelin’s responses. In the Audit Committee Matter, discoverable evidence includes allegations by KV employees that prompted Hermelin’s investigation, as well as other misconduct influencing the Board’s decision. Irrelevant facts are excluded. The Criminal and HHS Exclusion Matters are straightforward, focusing on formal charges, while the Audit Committee Matter is limited to Hermelin’s conduct tied to the investigation and termination. There will likely be overlap between the Criminal and HHS Exclusion Matters and employee complaints, as these allegedly centered on Hermelin’s handling of the oversized tablet issue, which led to the legal actions.

HS Exclusion Issues. It seems the Audit Committee ended Hermelin's employment due to further misconduct, including previous conflicts with the FDA. However, unlike other cases, the Audit Committee Matter lacked formal charges or civil claims (aside from employee complaints that prompted the inquiry). Additionally, there’s no clear record of the Board’s reasoning for Hermelin’s dismissal. To deny Hermelin indemnification, KV must prove the Audit Committee acted based on an incident where Hermelin demonstrated genuine bad faith. The specifics of such incidents determine whether Hermelin qualifies for indemnification in this matter. By framing relevance this way, I dismiss Hermelin’s claim that discovery on good faith should be restricted to records from the indemnification-seeking cases. Hermelin’s proposed scope, largely confined to filed documents and transcripts, aligns more with what the Court will assess under 'success on the merits' under Section

145(c). Section 145(a), unlike Section 145(c), demands proof the indemnitee acted in good faith, a detailed inquiry likely requiring trial and credibility assessments. The differing evidence standards under Sections 145(a) and (c) explain my decision to handle mandatory indemnification summarily. Hermelin’s cited cases don’t back his limited discovery argument. While Stockman noted that a judicial record from a full proceeding can help evaluate § 145(a) and (b) good faith compliance, here, the lack of such records necessitates further discovery. Stockman didn’t restrict permissive indemnification discovery to prior judicial records; it merely stated that re-litigating good faith may be unnecessary if such records exist. Hermelin’s other cited cases similarly fail to support his position.

CONCLUSION For these reasons, I rule the Plaintiff isn’t entitled to advancement for the Jail Records Matter or mandatory indemnification for the Criminal or HHS Exclusion Matters, but is entitled to it for the FDA Consent Decree Matter. Evidence for permissive indemnification is confined to the Plaintiff’s conduct in the underlying proceedings. While KV prevailed on most indemnification issues, this victory may prove hollow. Delaware case law on DGCL § 145(a) evidence standards is sparse, likely because companies often settle such claims out of court due to the high costs of litigating good faith. This economic incentive is especially strong when indemnification agreements require the company to cover both parties’ costs initially. The parties may pursue discovery and trial on good faith, effectively litigating what they’ve avoided via settlements. I leave it to them to decide if the benefits outweigh the costs. Counsel must submit an order reflecting this Opinion.

The Insurance Commissioner’s original claim, filed in 1941, was challenged. To clarify legal issues, the Special Master ordered an amended claim. The receivers argued this was a new claim, barred by 1946 and 1948 orders against new filings without consent.

The original claim referenced an unsigned 'Treaty of Re-Insurance No. 820.' The amended claim attached a 'Memorandum of Agreement' from 1930, signed by both parties. The receivers contended the amended claim was a substantial departure, effectively a new claim. The original claim’s validity relied on the unsigned treaty, while the amended claim introduced a different agreement, raising questions about its admissibility under the court’s distribution orders.

The document was initially attached to the original claim by mistake. When the amended claim was required to be filed, the error was identified and corrected by attaching the correct agreement that supported the claim. The Special Master believed this was a valid amendment, and I concur. The motion to dismiss the amended claim is rejected. Motion to Disallow the Claim. To clarify the motion's foundation, a brief summary of the claim's underlying facts is necessary. The Exchange was an unincorporated group of subscribers involved in reciprocal or inter-insurance activities. Established in Pennsylvania in 1919, it operated until June 8, 1933, when it was dissolved by the Dauphin County Court of Common Pleas due to insolvency. The Pennsylvania Insurance Commissioner was directed to seize and liquidate its assets. Reciprocal insurance is a system where individuals underwrite each other's risks through a shared attorney-in-fact, with each subscriber acting independently.

None of the subscribers act jointly; they are both insured and insurers. The insurance exchange lacks corporate status, functioning as an unincorporated association of individual subscribers. The attorney-in-fact acts on behalf of each subscriber, handling all insurance exchanges and authorized to perform any related actions. Subscribers do not interact directly; all transactions occur through the common attorney-in-fact. Members pay a premium or fee, with a portion deducted as the attorney-in-fact's compensation. Subscriber liability is typically capped at an amount equal to the initial premium. Cases such as Long v. Sakleson and Neel v. Crittendon, along with legal references, support this structure.

Pennsylvania law mandates that subscribers exchanging indemnity contracts must be contingently liable for at least one additional annual premium. The Exchange's policies included a clause stating that if premiums and reserves were insufficient to cover losses, subscribers would be liable for an extra amount not exceeding their annual premium. However, Keystone Indemnity Company, as attorney-in-fact, was required to secure adequate reinsurance to protect subscribers from this contingent liability. The subscribers appointed Keystone Indemnity Company, a Pennsylvania corporation, as their common attorney-in-fact to manage their inter-insurance operations.

On August 15, 1930, the Exchange, via its attorney-in-fact, entered an agreement with International Re-Insurance Corporation, a California entity, to indemnify subscribers against assessment liabilities up to $1 million. On June 9, 1931, a Delaware corporation assumed these obligations. An endorsement on December 2, 1931, extended the agreement until cancellation with three months' notice. The Exchange paid all premiums, but on July 1, 1932, International terminated the agreement, effective immediately.

On October 1, 1932, receivers were appointed for International due to its insolvency. By September 12, 1938, the Court of Common Pleas in Dauphin County, Pennsylvania, mandated that Exchange subscribers with policies issued between April 9, 1929, and May 18, 1933, pay an assessment equal to one annual deposit premium per policy to cover liabilities. The Liquidator collected these assessments, filing a claim on behalf of subscribers, with proceeds to be remitted to those whose policies were exchanged during the re-insurance agreement. The receivers contested the claim, arguing the Exchange lacked authority to enter the agreement, as the attorney-in-fact's powers were limited by the power of attorney.

The power of attorney in a reciprocal insurance exchange serves as its charter, defining the attorney-in-fact's duties and powers. In Wysong v. Automobile Underwriters, Inc., it was established that the attorney-in-fact's authority is bound by this document. The Company's power of attorney allowed it to act on subscribers' behalf regarding policies and lawful business management. Pennsylvania law permits re-insurance agreements for subscriber protection, and policy Paragraph N required the Company to secure adequate re-insurance. The August 15, 1930, agreement aligned with Paragraph N and state law, making it a lawful business act. Thus, the Special Master correctly upheld the Company's authority to enter the re-insurance agreement.

The receivers also argued that the Liquidator lacked authority to pursue the claim on subscribers' behalf, insisting subscribers were indispensable parties. The Special Master sided with the receivers, recommending disallowance. This issue hinges on the Pennsylvania Insurance Commissioner's role as Liquidator. State law empowers the Commissioner, upon an exchange's insolvency, to take control of its assets, contracts, and rights of action. The Liquidator's duty is to liquidate assets, settle debts, and protect creditors, as outlined in 40 Purdon's Statutes, Sec. 206.

The Liquidator's role involves collecting and converting the defunct exchange's assets into cash to pay creditors. The primary assets are subscriber assessments, as seen in Donaldson v. Fortna. The Pennsylvania liquidation process aims to safeguard creditors, requiring insolvency for Liquidator appointment. The Liquidator holds title only to exchange assets available to creditors, not individual subscriber assets. The August 15, 1930, agreement stipulated International would indemnify subscribers, further distinguishing subscriber assets from exchange liabilities.

The Exchange protects against losses due to liability for assessments that policyholders are responsible for. Only the Exchange's subscribers benefit from this indemnification agreement, provided they are liable for such assessments. Subscribers act collectively through a shared attorney-in-fact. While the agreement with International was made in the Exchange's name, the attorney-in-fact solely represents individual subscribers and lacks authority beyond its power of attorney. The indemnification covers assessment liabilities, which only subscribers face, as the Exchange itself cannot be liable for assessments. The agreement thus primarily benefits subscribers, not the Exchange as an entity.

The indemnification agreement does not qualify as an Exchange asset transferable to the Liquidator by law, so the Liquidator cannot pursue this claim. International's liability under the agreement was to individual subscribers, not the group collectively. Each subscriber who paid an assessment could file a separate claim, either personally or via an agent. However, the Liquidator, lacking proof of agency, cannot act on their behalf. The Special Master concluded the Liquidator has no standing to advance the amended claim, a recommendation I endorse, resolving the matter. The receivers also raised two additional arguments against the claim.

The reinsurance agreement underlying the claim stipulated that International's liability would arise only after a court-ordered assessment caused subscriber losses. The agreement was canceled in 1932, but no assessment occurred until 1938, making subscriber liability effective then. The Special Master determined that losses occurred over six years post-agreement, outside its active period, thus absolving International of liability. I concur with this conclusion, as detailed in the Special Master's reports. The receivers' second argument concerned a time-barred claim.

The reinsurance agreement required claims to be filed within two years of its termination. The Special Master noted that a definitive claim for assessment-related losses couldn't be made without a valid assessment during that window. Since no assessment occurred within the two-year period, the filing deadline passed. I agree with this reasoning. The Special Master's recommendations are adopted, and the motion to disallow the amended claim is granted. An order may be submitted with notice. Affirmed on appeal. See poste p. 471, 86 A. 2nd 647. PER CURIAM. Respondent L. Vincent Ramunno appeals a Board on Professional Responsibility finding that he violated Delaware Lawyer's Rule of Professional Conduct 3.5(c) for undignified and discourteous conduct.

During a court hearing, addressed to the judge and opposing counsel, the Board issued a private admonition. Under Board Rule 9(e), we find this sanction insufficient for two reasons. First, the public nature of these proceedings undermines the idea of a private reprimand. Second, the severity of Mr. Ramunno's misconduct, along with his prior reprimand for similar behavior, demands a public censure. We uphold the Board's finding of unprofessional conduct but overturn the private admonition in favor of a public reprimand, with this opinion serving as the official rebuke. The facts leading to the misconduct finding are largely undisputed. During a January 16, 1990, conference, Mr. Ramunno used a vulgar term to describe opposing counsel in front of a Superior Court judge, who cited him for contempt.

At a pretrial hearing the next day, Mr. Ramunno sought to disqualify the judge, arguing the contempt citation showed bias. A key exchange followed: Mr. Ramunno acknowledged the contempt citation, calling it unreasonable and an abuse of discretion, and hinted at further consequences. The judge denied being angered, but when Mr. Ramunno insinuated the judge might retaliate, the court found him in contempt again, imposing a $150 fine for insulting the court's authority. The Superior Court upheld both contempt findings. Opposing counsel later brought the matter to the Board, charging Mr. Ramunno with violating Rule 3.5(c) by behaving in a manner degrading to the tribunal.

After a hearing, the Board dismissed the charges, citing insufficient evidence for additional sanctions. This Court remanded the case, ruling the Board's decision conflicted with Rule 9(f), which treats a criminal conviction as conclusive evidence, and that the Board erred by considering sanctions before determining misconduct. On remand, the Board found misconduct and issued a private admonition. Mr. Ramunno objected, leading to another remand where the Court clarified it had not directed a misconduct finding but required the Board to evaluate the issue properly, including defenses.

Following the second remand, the Board reaffirmed its finding of misconduct and again imposed a private admonition. Notably, the Board cited Mr. Ramunno's sincere testimony about his remarks as influential in their decision. The case highlights the tension between private discipline and public accountability in professional misconduct proceedings.

The initial contempt finding by the Superior Court stemmed from actions taken in frustration, without any intent by the Respondent to be heard by others... The Board also concluded that the behavior leading to the second contempt finding was more a clumsy handling of a sensitive motion (to disqualify) rather than a deliberate disrespect to the Court. In the Matter of L. Vincent Ramunno, Board on Professional Responsibility, No. 6, 1990, Report After Second Remand (August 28, 1992). In his appeal, Mr. Ramunno cites this language to argue that the Board's factual findings contradict its guilty verdict. He contends that if his remarks and subsequent exchange with the court were unintentional, as the Board noted, then he cannot be held liable for intentionally disruptive or demeaning behavior toward the tribunal under Rule 3.5(c). Thus, he asserts that the Board's factual conclusions logically demand an acquittal on both misconduct charges. On appeal, this Court evaluates whether substantial evidence supports the Board's findings.

In Matter of Higgins, Del.Supr., 565 A.2d 901, 906-07 (1989), it is undisputed that Mr. Ramunno used vulgar language toward opposing counsel, which—regardless of intent—reached the presiding judge. It is also agreed that he engaged in a disrespectful exchange with the judge the next day, implicitly questioning the court's integrity. Given these facts, Mr. Ramunno's intent to disrupt is irrelevant; the key issue is whether his discourteous behavior degraded the lower court under DLRPC 3.5(c). Rule 9(f) of the Board on Professional Responsibility clarifies that a conviction is conclusive evidence of the crime. Here, the defendant was convicted of two counts of contempt under

11 Del.C. § 1271(1), which requires proving beyond reasonable doubt that the defendant displayed disorderly, contemptuous, or insolent conduct in court, disrupting proceedings or undermining judicial authority. Given this conviction and no valid defenses, Mr. Ramunno's behavior clearly disrupted the court and diminished its respect. The Board's remark about unintentional conduct, made only in the sanction context, does not negate the degrading impact of his actions or create inconsistency in the ruling. Insulting opposing counsel and disparaging the court’s integrity are indefensible. Moreover, this was not an isolated incident;

Mr. Ramunno has a history of intemperate conduct in court. In 1983, this court privately reprimanded him for unprofessional behavior falling short of acceptable standards (Weber v. State, No. 197, 1981, slip op. (January 17, 1983), attached herein). We again find his actions wholly unacceptable. Further misconduct may result in harsher penalties than a public reprimand. PER CURIAM (not for official reporting): On October 12, 1982, the defendant's counsel tried to submit a reply brief that exceeded the page limit set by Supreme Court Rule 14(d). Overlength briefs had been a growing issue, prompting the Chief Justice to issue two administrative orders, as detailed in Appendix A. These orders explicitly state that briefs beyond the prescribed limits will be rejected. Following this attempt, a phone discussion occurred between the Chief Deputy Clerk and defense counsel, which led to a memo dated October 18, 1982, from the Clerk to the Court (Appendix B). This memo resulted in an October 26 order demanding a justification for not imposing sanctions on defense counsel (Appendix C). A hearing on this matter was conducted on November 12, 1982 (Appendix D), kept separate from the main case. Under Supreme Court Rule 102(b), attorneys must handle all court matters with utmost professionalism.

Supreme Court Rule 33 outlines sanctions as follows: RULE 33. SANCTIONS If a party fails to adhere to any rule or order, the Court may impose sanctions after providing notice and a chance to respond. These sanctions can include reasonable attorneys' fees or ruling against the offending party. Disciplinary measures, such as fines, may also apply to counsel. Rule 33 applies to both attorneys and litigants, allowing the Court to sanction attorneys directly. After the hearing, we were taken aback by defense counsel's oral arguments. Initially, we considered referring the matter to the Board on Professional Responsibility. However, we decided against burdening the Board with trivial disputes. We also recalled the principle that judges should exhibit resilience and avoid rash decisions, as noted in Craig v. Harney, 331 U.S.

367, 376, 67 S.Ct. 1249, 1255, 91 L.Ed. 1546 (1947), and opted for a thorough review of the appendices. After deliberation, we concluded that defense counsel's actions—submitting an overlength brief, the conversation with the Chief Deputy Clerk (per counsel's account), and their oral presentation—fell short of professional standards. Legal practice demands not only expertise but also respect for procedures and civility. A true professional is judged by their treatment of nonprofessionals. The appendices’ record is self-explanatory, and we find the conduct below acceptable standards. Defense counsel is hereby reprimanded. MR. RAMUNNO: Rest assured, Your Honor, I’ll speak—perhaps starting with the facts before legal arguments. On October 12th, we filed our brief in the Weber murder case, a grave matter. Mr. Taylor called, stating, 'Your brief breaks page limits; per the Chief Justice’s order, it’s rejected. Retrieve it or we’ll discard it.' I replied, 'Wait, what’s happening?' JUSTICE McNEILLY: Mr. Ra-munno— MR. RAMUNNO: I thought— JUSTICE McNEILLY: Before you elaborate— MR. RAMUNNO: Yes. JUSTICE McNEILLY: We’re not here to gather facts. MR. RAMUNNO: Then why are we here? JUSTICE McNEILLY: We seek your response to the rule. MR. RAMUNNO: I’m recounting events. Mr. Taylor’s memo describes them, and so do I. JUSTICE McNEILLY: Do you contest those facts? MR. RAMUNNO: Absolutely. JUSTICE McNEILLY: Proceed. MR. RAMUNNO: Thank you. He spoke mechanically, as if challenging the Chief Justice’s order was unthinkable—

I believe it’s a right if I follow the law. Will you revoke it over a harsh word to a clerk? JUSTICE McNEILLY: This Court grants the privilege and can revoke it. MR. RAMUNNO: If you deem my actions warrant it, then do so, Chief Justice—
I did not
in case of 'hell'
he was required to
Therefore, I do not

I won't surrender my right to speak or my freedom of speech, nor should I be prevented from expressing my views to you or a clerk simply because I'm a lawyer. For instance, in the 1973 case New York Justice of Appellate Division v. Erdman, decided by the New York Court of Appeals, an attorney wrote an article in Life magazine labeling judges as whores.
