In CERBCO, controlling stockholders, who were also directors, were found to have breached their duty of loyalty by pursuing a corporate opportunity without informing the corporation. The court affirmed this breach and distinguished between transactional damages and other damages from the fiduciary breach. Although no transactional damages existed, the stockholders were held liable for incidental damages, including payments received and expenses incurred by the corporation.

The Delaware Supreme Court emphasized that the scope of recovery for a breach of loyalty should not be narrowly defined. Penalties under Delaware law are strictly imposed to ensure fiduciaries are held accountable. In CERBCO, the court ruled that the controlling stockholders were liable for $75,000 received from a third party and any expenses the corporation bore due to their self-interested actions. This decision underscores that fiduciary breaches can lead to broad remedies, even in the absence of direct transactional harm, reinforcing the stringent standards of loyalty and accountability in Delaware corporate law.

Created to prevent disloyalty, Delaware law mandates that fiduciaries must not gain personally from their actions and that beneficiaries remain unharmed once disloyalty is proven. Counts I-VIII contest decisions by the defendant directors and Yucaipa Defendants regarding the annual meeting, record date, and Yucaipa Transaction, potentially violating their duty of loyalty. Under CERB-CO, defendants might face liability for breach-related damages, including Morgans' incurred and ongoing expenses, as well as potential disgorgement of the $9 million termination fee if recovered. The Parfi ruling examined an arbitration clause, which the Delaware Supreme Court termed 'a specialized type of forum-selection clause.' Carlyle, 67 A.3d at 384 n. 41. In Parfi, the Court held that the arbitration clause would not apply to claims unrelated to 'contract rights or performance' under the agreement containing the clause. Parfi, 817 A.2d at 155. It also ruled that this court erred by sending fiduciary duty claims to arbitration when the arbitration clause was in an underwriting agreement unrelated to the defendants' fiduciary status. Id. at 156-57. The clause covered 'any dispute, controversy, or claim arising from or related to' the underwriting agreement. Id. at 151 (internal quotation marks omitted). This court had deemed the clause applicable to both fiduciary duty and contract claims due to shared underlying facts. The Supreme Court agreed the claims stemmed from 'some or all of the same facts' but concluded the clause did not extend to fiduciary claims.

not encompass fiduciary duty claims merely because they shared factual origins with contract claims. The Court emphasized that the arbitration clause's scope was limited to disputes directly tied to the underwriting agreement's rights or obligations. Parfi, 817 A.2d at 156. This distinction underscores the principle that forum selection clauses, including arbitration provisions, are interpreted narrowly when applied to claims outside their contractual context. The ruling reinforces that fiduciary duty claims, even if factually overlapping, remain distinct from contract disputes unless the clause explicitly covers them. This precedent clarifies that Delaware courts will not extend such clauses to fiduciary matters absent clear language to the contrary, preserving the separation between contractual and fiduciary legal frameworks.

The argument does not apply as the defendant's fiduciary duties to the plaintiff are based on rights and obligations separate from any contract. Id. at 157 (footnote omitted); see also Reznik v. If Yucaipa's view prevails, it would resolve multi-forum litigation issues, though this would mark a significant departure from longstanding practices. Section 102(b)(7) Malone and Gault seek dismissal, arguing the Complaint alleges only a duty of care breach, which the Exculpatory Clause in Morgans's Certificate of Incorporation shields them from. The Clause states: Directors are not liable for monetary damages for fiduciary breaches, except as prohibited by Delaware law. Exceptions include disloyalty, bad faith, intentional misconduct, unlawful dividends, or personal gain (8 Del. C. § 102(b)(7)).

C. § 102(b)(7). In essence, Section 102(b)(7) shields directors from monetary liability for care breaches but not for bad faith or disloyalty (Stone ex rel. AmSouth Bancorporation v. Ritter, 911 A.2d 362, 367 (Del.2006)). Bad faith includes actions contrary to the corporation's best interests (In re Walt Disney Co. Deriv. Litig., 906 A.2d 27, 67 (Del.2006); Stone, 911 A.2d at 369). It covers both intent to harm and deliberate neglect of duty (Lyondell).

In Chem. Co. v. Ryan, 970 A.2d 235, 240 (Del. 2009), it was stated that the protection from liability under a certificate of incorporation provision under 8 Del. C. § 102(b)(7) functions as an affirmative defense. Emerald P'rs v. Berlin (Emerald I), 726 A.2d 1215, 1223 (Del. 1999) (footnote omitted) noted that defendants relying on such a provision typically must prove all its elements. The extent to which a court can categorize claims as solely under the duty of care and grant judgment based on Section 102(b)(7) immunity depends on the case's stage, standard of review, and procedural considerations. At the pleadings stage in a fiduciary duty case, under the business judgment rule, a court may swiftly apply Section 102(b)(7) to rule for defendant directors unless the complaint presents facts challenging the board's disinterest, independence, or good faith.

Under Section 102(b)(7), a court can dismiss claims at the pleadings stage if the complaint fails to rebut the business judgment rule by questioning the board's disinterested majority. Here, the plaintiff has alleged enough to cast doubt on the Board and Special Committee's independence, with only Malone not contesting these claims. The complaint's assertions negate the business judgment rule's presumptions, making entire fairness the applicable standard. This standard also applies because Yucaipa is considered to control Morgans, and transactions benefiting a controlling party warrant this scrutiny. Cases like Kahn v. Tremont Corp., 694 A.2d 422, 428 (Del. 1997), affirm that entire fairness applies when a controlling shareholder is involved on both sides of a deal.

Regarding Malone, the complaint claims he relinquished his lead negotiator role to Gross, whom he knew lacked independence due to his ties to Yucaipa. Malone allegedly misled another director, Kalisman, about the Yucaipa Transaction's timing and delayed notifying the Board and Special Committee about meetings on March 30, 2013. On March 26, he advised the Special Committee's counsel to delay scheduling until all issues were resolved and to withhold documentation until the commitment letter was signed. These allegations suggest Malone acted against Morgans' and its stockholders' best interests, supporting a pleadings-stage inference of misconduct.

Delaware's pleading standards for surviving a Rule 12(b)(6) motion are lenient. Courts must accept all well-pled facts as true, interpret vague allegations favorably if they provide notice, and dismiss only if no recovery is conceivable under any plausible scenario. Central Mortg., 27 A.3d at 536. The standard hinges on whether recovery is possible. Given the complaint's allegations and the entire fairness standard, dismissal is unwarranted.

There is a chance Malone may be found to have violated his duty of loyalty. The standard for pleadings is less stringent than the preliminary injunction standard, which demands the plaintiff demonstrate a likely success on the merits. The court's earlier remark that the plaintiffs failed to show a reasonable probability of success in proving Malone's breach of loyalty does not determine the outcome at the pleadings stage. Given the Complaint's overall content, the specific accusations against Malone, and the expected review standard, it cannot be conclusively stated that the claims only involve a duty of care violation. Thus, the Exculpatory Clause cannot be used to dismiss the claims against Malone at this stage. Gault did not contest the allegations against him in his dismissal motion but joined Malone's brief and later tried to argue separately in a reply, which the court struck down.

Gault failed to explain how the Section 102(b)(7) provision prevents recovery against him, so his motion is denied. The Complaint sufficiently alleges Gault's close connections to Yucaipa and that he disclosed the Special Committee's negotiating stance to Burkle. These claims support the inference that Gault breached his duty of loyalty at the pleading stage. The motion to dismiss Counts I-VII as moot is denied. Count IX's request to declare the Transaction Documents unenforceable due to alleged fiduciary breaches is also denied, though other aspects of Count IX are dismissed. The motions to dismiss based on the Exculpatory Clause are denied.

The Yucaipa Defendants argue they cannot be both fiduciaries and aiders of a breach simultaneously, which is correct on the merits. However, at the dismissal stage, the OTK can present alternative legal theories. The Complaint adequately alleges Burkle controls Yucaipa, which in turn controls the Yucaipa Funds and Holdings. Thus, for dismissal purposes, the Yucaipa Defendants can be treated as a single entity that either owed fiduciary duties or aided others' breaches.

Comparisons with cases like Del Monte Foods, El Paso, and Toys 'R' Us show that injunctions depend on the likelihood of aiding and abetting claims. Delaware Supreme Court cases affirming targeted injunctions, such as Paramount and Mills, involved viable aiding and abetting claims against third-party contract holders. These decisions highlight the importance of proving the counterparty's awareness and participation in fiduciary breaches.

In Inc. v. MacAndrews & Forbes Hldgs., Inc., 506 A.2d 173, 183-85 (Del. 1986), the court upheld a targeted injunction against an asset lock-up and termination fee, finding the counter-party received preferential treatment over other bidders and exploited this advantage to impose unreasonable defensive measures. Contrast Emerald I, 726 A.2d at 1223, where the court ruled that in a challenge to a transaction with a majority stockholder subject to entire fairness review, Section 102(b)(7) could not be applied summarily due to factual disputes requiring trial, with Malpiede v. Townson, 780 A.2d 1075, 1094-96 (Del. 2001), which held that in a challenge to a third-party, arms' length merger approved by informed stockholders, Section 102(b)(7) could be applied at the pleadings stage unless the plaintiff alleged insufficient director independence. See also Emerald P'rs v. Berlin (Emerald II), 787 A.2d 85, 93-94 (Del. 2001), stating that Section 102(b)(7) could not be applied without first assessing the transaction under the entire fairness standard.

Marvel, V.C.: The plaintiff appeals the dismissal of her uncontested divorce petition. Evidence showed the parties were married on January 12, 1957, and cohabitated in Delaware until July 1958, with no children from the union. After their final separation, the plaintiff resided separately in Claymont, Delaware, maintaining a home for herself and a daughter from a prior marriage. The petition, filed on July 7, 1961, sought divorce under Delaware's voluntary separation statute, alleging three consecutive years of separation without cohabitation and no reasonable chance of reconciliation. Summons was served on the defendant, Francis B. Maloney, a Delaware resident, on July 13, 1961, but he neither appeared nor responded, leading to an uncontested trial on October 13, 1961.

On October 16, 1961, the trial judge ruled that the plaintiff's evidence failed to establish grounds for divorce based on voluntary separation. The court denied the plaintiff's motion for reargument, clarifying that the defendant's silence did not constitute consent to the separation, and an affirmative act was required. Title 13 Del. C. § 1522(11), effective April 3, 1957, introduced new divorce grounds, permitting divorce after three years of voluntary separation without cohabitation and no expectation of reconciliation. This legislative shift was examined in Owens v. Owens, 149 A.2d 320 (Sup. Ct. Del.), which noted Delaware's evolving policy against forcing unwilling parties to remain married, even absent traditional fault-based grounds.

In 1957, the Delaware General Assembly amended Title 13 Del. C., reflecting a legislative shift toward recognizing voluntary separation as a valid divorce ground. The court in Owens v. Owens highlighted this change, emphasizing that Delaware no longer required fault to dissolve marriages where parties lived apart voluntarily for an extended period. The trial judge in the present case underscored that mere silence from the defendant did not meet the statutory requirement for voluntary separation, necessitating clearer evidence of mutual agreement to part ways. This interpretation aligned with the legislative intent to provide a no-fault divorce option while ensuring both parties' voluntary participation in the separation was demonstrable.

Section 1522 was amended to include living separately without any reasonable chance of reconciliation as a new ground for divorce. This change allows either spouse to seek divorce unilaterally, regardless of the other party's role in the separation. In Rolph v. Rolph, Chancellor Seitz ruled that the voluntary nature of § 1522(11) negated any claim of aggression by the husband, dismissing the wife's property petition. He noted that this provision introduced a divorce ground distinct from traditional 'aggression' concepts, relying instead on mutual voluntary action, whether explicit or implied. The trial court referenced Judge Herrmann's opinion in denying the divorce.

In Schmitthausler v. Schmitthausler, the court emphasized the need for a voluntary separation. The case involved a husband who moved to Delaware without providing a home for his wife or inviting her to join him. The wife testified she wished to reconcile, even writing to him in 1953. Contrastingly, in the present case, the husband, though served personally, neither contested the divorce nor sought reconciliation. His inaction over the statutory three-year period was deemed tacit agreement to the separation, with no hope of reconciliation, aligning with precedents like Buford v. Buford.

The court concluded that voluntary separation could be inferred from conduct or silence, not just explicit agreement. Thus, the plaintiff was entitled to divorce under Title 13 Del. C. § 1522(11). The order was reversed, directing a divorce decree nisi. Justice Herrmann then addressed a libel case, questioning whether the disputed newspaper publication was privileged.

On January 11, 1963, reporter Eugene Knoblauch obtained information from the IRS about a tax seizure, mistakenly naming C. Stanley Short, Jr. instead of Sr. The News-Journal published the story, correcting it later. The core issue was whether the error affected the publication's privileged status, given the IRS's role in providing the inaccurate details.

C. Stanley Short, Jr. filed this defamation lawsuit solely against the defendant newspaper publisher. The plaintiff argues that the news release was not part of the Director's official responsibilities, thus not privileged, and under the common law principle that 'tale bearers are as bad as tale makers,' the defendant is liable for disseminating false and damaging statements. The defendant claimed privilege as a defense, while the plaintiff acknowledged no malice or misuse of privilege. The Superior Court ruled the publication was privileged [205 A. 2d 6] and awarded summary judgment to the defendant, leading to this appeal.

Defamation law reflects a public policy that individuals should be shielded from harm to their reputations. Typically, those who publish or republish defamatory content are held strictly liable, with no defense based on good faith or error, though these may reduce damages. However, there are exceptions where a greater public interest allows free expression without fear of defamation claims, granting certain privileges. As Prosser on Torts (3d Ed.) notes, privilege exists to protect socially important interests, even if it harms the plaintiff's reputation. Privileges can be absolute (no liability regardless of truth or malice) or conditional (protection only without malice), as seen in cases like Klein v. Sunbeam Corporation and Pierce v. Burns.

We now examine the privilege questions, first concerning the Director and his subordinate, then the defendant publisher. As federal officials, the Director and his colleague's privilege is determined by federal precedent, established in Howard v. Lyons and compared in Carr v. Watkins. The federal standard for executive branch officials' privilege was clarified in Barr v. Matteo, expanding on earlier rulings like Yaselli v. Goff and Spalding v. Vilas, which granted absolute privilege to high-ranking officials.

In Barr v. Matteo, the Supreme Court significantly broadened executive privilege. The case arose when the Acting Director of the Office of Rent Stabilization issued a press release defending his decision to suspend two agency officers amid congressional scrutiny. The suspended officers sued for libel, but the Court majority, citing Spalding v. Vilas, ruled that absolute privilege should not be restricted to cabinet-level officials, extending it to lower-ranking executives as well.

The Chancellor ruled that complainants must first prove their claim that the ballots should have been counted, not discarded. If they fail, their case ends regardless of issues with Williamson's 45 shares or Snodgrass's 54 shares. Success in counting the 671 votes grants them office if Williamson's shares are included, making Snodgrass's shares irrelevant. Without Williamson's shares, only complainant Ch's case proceeds further.

To succeed, appel must overcome the defendants regarding the Snodgrass shares issue. The relevance of the Snodgrass shares hinges on the perspectives taken concerning the other two points: the rejected ballots and the Williamson shares. I now address these contentious matters, starting with the rejected ballots. Should these ballots have been dismissed entirely? They were cast under the assumption that cumulative voting was allowed. The election judges ruled that such voting was not permitted for this corporation, a correct decision. Although Delaware law permits vote cumulation, it is only valid if the certificate of incorporation includes such a provision, which this corporation’s certificate lacked. Evidence shows disputes arose during the meeting over cumulative voting, with complainants asserting their right based on Pennsylvania law, while the judges upheld Delaware law for this Delaware corporation, denying cumulative voting. The judges instructed voters to cast straight ballots if they wished to vote straight, but the complainants refused, leading the judges to reject the ballots, marking them as 'Rejected under corporation laws of Delaware.' While the judges rightly refused to count the votes cumulatively, rejecting them entirely was unjustified.

The statute does not specify ballot format; any form revealing voter intent is acceptable. Determining this intent requires examining the ballot itself. These ballots clearly indicate the stockholder’s intent to vote their shares. Each ballot begins with a statement like 'I, the undersigned, hereby vote 150 shares of stock for the following named persons,' followed by the complainants' names and Mr. Mcjunkin’s, with figures after each name. These figures, unexplained on the ballots, total seven times the voted shares, suggesting the voter intended to cumulate votes for the four named individuals. This demonstrates a clear intent to vote for these candidates, with the figures representing surplus instructions on vote allocation. The judges could not legally fulfill these instructions, but this does not negate the voter’s clear intent to vote their shares. Ignoring the votes entirely disenfranchises the shareholder based on a legal misunderstanding.

The voter’s mistaken belief about vote strength should not invalidate their shares’ voting power. If the law permits only one vote per share, and a voter, while clearly intending to vote for specific candidates, incorrectly seeks greater voting strength, it is unreasonable to strip their shares of all value. Voting and vote counting are distinct processes. Here, the shareholder could only cast 150 votes per director. The higher figures beside each name, if interpreted as voting instructions, should have been disregarded. The judges should have counted the shares’ legal voting strength, ignoring the voter’s erroneous instructions. The defendants’ cited cases do not contradict this conclusion. When voting can be done straight or cumulatively, mixing methods is not allowed.

Where cumulative voting is permitted, it must be explicitly stated in the certificate of incorporation. Since this corporation’s certificate lacked such provision, cumulative voting was invalid. The judges correctly rejected cumulative voting but erred in dismissing the ballots entirely. The ballots showed clear intent to vote, and the figures were merely surplus instructions. The law’s limitations on vote strength should not nullify the votes themselves. The judges should have counted the shares as legally allowed, disregarding the unenforceable instructions. This approach avoids unjust disenfranchisement while adhering to legal constraints.

If a voter casts a straight ballot but claims they intended to vote cumulatively, their intent is determined by the ballot itself. This principle was upheld in cases like In re P. B. Mathiason Mfg. Co. and Commonwealth v. Blatchford. The opposite is also true: if a ballot clearly shows cumulative intent, it cannot be counted as straight. Courts agree that a ballot allowing dual interpretations must reflect the voter's evident intent. A similar principle applied in Loubat v. Le Roy, where the start date of a director's term was determined by the ballot's clear indication.

When voters legally choose between two dates, the date shown on the ballot must be honored. However, if the law permits only one interpretation of the count, there's no room for extrinsic evidence to alter the intent. The issue here is whether the ballots reflect an intent to vote the shares as indicated and if they should be counted within legal limits. The court concluded they should have been counted as casting 671 votes for the four nominees. The next issue concerns the voting rights of Williamson's 45 shares, which were allegedly transferred too late for the election.

The relevant statute, Section 29 of the General Corporation Law, prohibits voting shares transferred within 20 days before an election. Williamson's shares were transferred on February 15, 1927, and the election was held on March 7, 1927. Defendants argue the 20-day period ends the day before the meeting, but this calculation is incorrect. Legal precedent, such as Simkin v. Cole, establishes that the first day is excluded, and the act's day is included. Applying this rule, Williamson's shares were transferred within the prohibited period, rendering them ineligible for voting.

The voting rights of Williamson's shares are also contested on the grounds of his stockholder status, despite his payment, certificate, and book entry. Complainants argue Williamson isn't a party to the proceedings, making it improper to rule on his rights. Voting rights are a critical aspect of stock ownership, and denying them requires the stockholder's presence. Cases like Talbot J. Taylor & Co. v. Southern Pacific Co. and General Investment Co. v. Lake Shore, etc., Ry. Co. support this, holding that injunctions against voting shares are invalid without the owner's participation.

50 F. 160. If an injunction should not be granted in such instances, it is equally valid that the vote, once received, should not be dismissed in a review proceeding if the stockholder who cast it is not involved. The complainants, who supported Williamson's claim, did not include him as a party. The defendants could have added him as a party and served him effectively, especially given the recent amendment to the General Corporation Law (33 Del. Laws, c. 104), which allows the Chancellor to rule on voting rights in corporate election reviews. The complainants had no need to involve Williamson, as no objections were raised about his stockholder status during the meeting, and his vote was rejected only due to how it was cast—a matter already addressed. Williamson could have been included by the defendants and properly served. Bouree, et al., v. Trust Francais,

etc., 14 Del. Ch. 332, 127 A. 56. Sending him a registered letter about the proceedings does not make him a party or serve as effective process. Without Williamson as a party, I refuse to discard the ballot representing his recorded stock. It should be counted for its full legal effect. Having ruled that the cumulative ballots must be counted as the law permits, and that Williamson's ballot belongs in that group, the outcome shows the complainants received these votes: Chappel 682, Daly 671, and Gammell 671. This result, regardless of the Snodgrass stock, gives them a majority, entitling them to a decree declaring their election as directors. Given this conclusion, there is no need to address the Snodgrass shares. Decree accordingly. Note—An appeal was filed, reversing the Chancellor's decree. The Supreme Court's ruling will appear in 16 Delaware Chancery Reports. See also 141 Atl. 191.

CAREY, Justice. Appellant Alexander G. Brinkley was convicted of second-degree murder in Superior Court and has appealed the sentence. He argues that (1) the evidence was insufficient for conviction, (2) the trial judge made improper comments on the evidence, and (3) the prosecutor's summation included prejudicial remarks. The appellant lived with the victim, Evelyn Jordon, in Wilmington. On April 20, 1966, after returning to their room, he told Mrs. Ray to call the police, admitting he had shot Evelyn. Officers arrived and found the victim dead on the bed. An autopsy revealed a bullet entered her right eye, with fragments in her brain and no powder burns. The doctor concluded the bullet ricocheted off her skull, likely fragmenting upon impact. A .38 caliber revolver, missing two rounds, was found in the basement, which the appellant admitted owning.

Mr. Ray testified for the defense, stating the iron bed in the appellant's room had a hole in its left leg, unnoticed until the trial. Photos of the bed were entered as evidence. The appellant testified that he and the victim had been arguing before the shooting, with her taunting him about her activities.

He confessed to shooting twice, intending to scare rather than kill her. The first shot went over her head and out the window, while the second was fired downward as she leaned over the bed. The small room, measuring 13 feet 8 inches by 13 feet 7 inches, was mostly occupied by a large bed. An officer later testified no bullet hole was found in the bed. The appellant argues the evidence doesn’t support the verdict, claiming the killing was accidental.

The defense contends the bullet may have ricocheted off the bed leg before hitting the victim’s eye, suggesting the killing was unintentional. They argue the close proximity and high-velocity bullet support this theory. However, the prosecution maintains that once malice was implied, the burden shifted to the defendant to prove justification or mitigation. The jury wasn’t obligated to accept the defendant’s version of events.

The judge instructed the jury that second-degree murder involves a killing without premeditation but with a wicked indifference to life. In this case, the defendant fired two shots in a confined space, knowing the risks of ricocheting bullets. Despite lacking intent to harm, his actions demonstrated reckless disregard for human life, justifying the jury’s verdict.

During deliberations, the jury requested testimony involving the term 'ricochet,' but the judge denied the request, noting uncertainty over whether the word was even used in testimony. This decision, along with the judge’s explanation, is now questioned by the appellant, though the court found no error in the refusal to acquit.

In the summation, there was testimony that a jury could consider regarding the possibility of a ricochet. The appellant claims this comment might have led the jury to believe the defense fabricated the ricochet theory without evidence. We reject this argument. The judge never stated there was no supporting testimony; his overall comments indicated the opposite. The final argument is that the prosecutor made unsupported claims in his summation, such as the hardness of the skull, bullet fragmentation, whether marks on the bed leg were rust or powder burns, and the distance between the appellant and victim during the second shot. The skull and bullet remarks were based on the doctor’s testimony, rust marks on common knowledge, and the distance was the attorney’s recollection. We cannot say these exceeded proper limits or that the judge abused his discretion by not striking them.

Given that the trial judge twice reminded the jury to rely on their own memory of the testimony, not the attorneys’ statements, we find no reversible error and affirm the judgment. VEASEY, Chief Justice: Two legal questions were certified by the Superior Court and accepted by this Court under Article IV, Section 11(9) of the Delaware Constitution and Supreme Court Rule 41. However, after accepting certification, new information led us to decline answering the questions and dismiss the case. The certified questions were: (a) Do Sections 2126 and 2127 of Title 19 of the Delaware Code violate the constitutional principle granting the Delaware Supreme Court exclusive authority over Bar governance by giving the Industrial Accident Board or General Assembly control over fees and creating potential conflicts for claimants’ attorneys? (b) If not, should Section 2126 require the Board to avoid arbitrary fee approvals and consider factors from General Motors Corporation v. Cox?

We accepted certification on July 7, 1995. The Industrial Accident Board moved to intervene, arguing an additional question was necessary for a proper decision. We granted their motion. The Board sought to argue that a commutation agreement submitted to them qualifies as an award under 19 Del. C. § 2127. The case was fully briefed and argued before this Court.

Due to post-certification developments, we dismiss the certified questions as improvidently granted. When accepting them, we were unaware that the Governor had signed Senate Bill 212 on July 6, 1995, amending the relevant statute. Thus, answers would likely only apply to this rare case. Therefore, 'important and urgent reasons' no longer justify addressing the certified questions under Supreme Court Rule 41(a)(i), and we decline to rule on the issues raised.

Before the amendment brought by Senate Bill 212, Title 19, Section 2126 stated that attorney fees for services under the Workers' Compensation Law required Board approval. Section 2127 previously capped attorney fees at $2,250 and barred attorneys from charging clients more than the Board-approved amount. The bill amended Section 2126 to exclude attorneys, limiting its scope to physicians. Section 2127(b) now stipulates that costs under Section 2127(a) will not be awarded if a claimant rejects a settlement offer matching or exceeding the post-hearing award. Senate Bill 212 is not under this Court's review, and we refrain from addressing its constitutionality.

We avoid assessing the bill's constitutionality but note its introduction stemmed from concerns over this Court's exclusive authority over bar governance, as highlighted in Simmons v. Delaware State Hosp. Rule 1.5 of the Delaware Lawyers' Rules of Professional Conduct, enforced solely by this Court, governs attorney fees. It mandates fees be reasonable, considering factors like time, skill, case complexity, local standards, results achieved, and fee structure. Compliance with Rule 1.5 fulfills a lawyer's fee-related obligations, while violations fall under this Court's disciplinary jurisdiction, as affirmed in In re Appeal of Infotechnology, Inc.

The certified questions and intervenor's arguments hinge on a repealed statute, which, while relevant to this case, holds no bearing on future matters. Its jurisprudential impact is minimal, though significant to the involved parties. Had we recognized the statute's limited applicability earlier, we would have declined certification. Thus, dismissing the certified questions as improvidently granted is now appropriate.

A commutation transforms periodic payments into a lump sum, as defined by Black's Law Dictionary. Here, the parties submitted a commutation agreement for Board approval, exchanging future payments for a fixed amount. Pre-amendment Section 2127 capped attorney fees at 30% of the award or $2,250, whichever was lower, and barred additional compensation for Board services, except for appellate work. The 1985 version of Section 2127(b) enforced these restrictions.

The relevant section now states: If a settlement offer for a case before the Industrial Accident Board is sent to the claimant or their attorney in writing at least 30 days before the trial date set by the Board, and the offer is equal to or exceeds the final award granted by the Board, subsection (a) of this Section will not apply. 19 Del.C. § 2127(b) (1995). The synopsis of Senate Bill 212 notes that in Simmons v. Delaware State Hospital, the Supreme Court found § 2127 potentially unconstitutional due to subsection (b)'s regulation of attorney conduct, traditionally overseen by the state Supreme Court. This bill resolves the issue by removing conflicts of interest and promotes settlements over trials when fair offers are made. The Board's claim that commutation agreements qualify as awards under the old statute conflicts with the usual interpretation of 'award' and would allow undue regulation of attorney-client relationships.

where the litigant is not formally before the Board. As the statute has been revised, we refrain from addressing this matter. However, we observe that statutes imposing attorney fees as costs against a party do not disrupt the attorney-client relationship. We withhold judgment on the retroactive application of Senate Bill 212 to this or other cases. See Hubbard v. Hibbard Brown & Co., Del.Supr., 633 A.2d 345, 354 (1993). DUFFY, Chancellor: This interpleader case involves Farmers Bank of the State of Delaware determining whether Mildred Howard or the Executor of Sadie Cooper Rust's estate is entitled to a savings account. The account was solely in Mrs. Rust's name. On July 8, 1967, she instructed the Bank to add Mrs. Howard's name but insisted Mrs. Howard not be informed until after her death. The Bank complied. Mrs. Rust

passed away on February 22, 1968, and the lawsuit followed. Initially, Mrs. Howard claimed Mrs. Rust gifted her a joint interest in the account, but this argument failed. Farmers Bank of the State of Delaware v. Howard, Del.Ch., 258 A.2d 299 (1969). The Supreme Court upheld this decision, 268 A.2d 870 (1970), but remanded to allow Mrs. Howard to argue she was a third-party beneficiary of the contract between Mrs. Rust and the Bank. To ensure fairness, this Court permitted briefing on that theory, leading to this ruling. (1) Delaware recognizes third-party beneficiary contracts, allowing a stranger to the contract to enforce promises made for their benefit. Bryant, Griffith & Brunson v. General Newspapers, 6 W.W. Harr. 468, 36 Del. 468, 178 A. 645

(Super. Ct.1935); 17A C.J.S. Contracts § 519(3); 2 Williston on Contracts (3 ed) § 347. (2) A donee beneficiary can enforce such a contract without prior knowledge or consent. Restatement, Contracts § 135(a); 4 Corbin on Contracts § 783. (3) Enforcement depends on the contract's terms, reflecting the parties' intent as expressed in their agreement. 17A C.J.S., supra, § 519(4) h (b). (4) Mrs. Howard asserts she was a donee beneficiary of the contract between Mrs. Rust and the Bank, arguing Mrs. Rust directed the Bank to pay her the account balance after her death, which the Bank accepted. She contends the Court must honor Mrs. Rust's intent to benefit her.
Following her passing, the evidence includes Mrs. Rust's signed signature card, her written note, the account records, and a letter from Mr. Richardson (summarized in the Appendix).

One could contend that this evidence indicates Mrs. Rust's intention to benefit Mrs. Howard through one of three legal mechanisms: (a) establishing a joint account with survivorship rights, though this argument has been dismissed by higher courts; (b) forming a contract with the Bank to designate Mrs. Howard as a third-party beneficiary upon her death, though this faces issues like lack of legal precedent and potential testamentary gift complications; or (c) creating a trust akin to a Totten trust, a concept recognized in Delaware but not fully briefed by counsel.

The Totten trust principle has been upheld in Delaware, as seen in Delaware Trust Co. v. Fitzmaurice. Deberry invited Beverly and Mark to his room to relax after the incidents, where they continued drinking and using drugs. Beverly stated that Deberry attempted to convince her to stay the night with him. Shortly after, she left to sleep in another bunkhouse with two men, one of whom Mark had fought earlier. Mark followed but slept outside due to the earlier conflict. Beverly alleged that Deberry woke her soon after she fell asleep, and she told him to leave. Later, he returned, trying to remove her pants while holding a knife to her throat, causing her to cut her fingers. They then moved behind a barn, where Deberry threatened her, forced her to undress, and had intercourse with her. After about thirty minutes, fearing detection, he made her dress and took her to a more secluded area at knifepoint.

To reach the secluded spot, they passed a guard station where a guard noticed two people leaving the track. At the second location, Deberry again forced Beverly to undress, and they had intercourse for over an hour before returning to the track complex. The guard checked their IDs, and Deberry warned Beverly to stay silent about the incident. She later woke her boyfriend to take her to the hospital for her hand injury, which needed stitches. On the way, she told him Deberry had raped her. Police arrived shortly after, and Beverly identified Deberry as her attacker when he was brought to the door of his bunkhouse under the headlights of a police car.

Deberry claimed that after accompanying Beverly and Mark to the bunkhouse, he and Mark slept outside her door. However, due to the damp ground, he returned to his own bunkhouse and fell asleep. He denied any involvement in the alleged assault, stating he was only awakened by the police. During pre-trial discovery, the defense requested evidence and Brady material, but the state claimed it had none. Before the first trial, the defense sought Deberry’s clothing, arguing it would likely have Beverly’s blood given the prolonged intercourse and her cut hand. They threatened to seek dismissal if the clothing wasn’t produced.

The prosecutor stated he knew of no blood on Deberry’s clothes, and the judge ruled that testimony about the absence of blood could suffice. The judge focused on the scope of testimony regarding Beverly’s injury rather than the potential exculpatory value of the missing clothing. The prosecutor was ordered to check for the clothing, but it was never found. At the second trial, a detective confirmed that evidence unit officers had taken both Deberry’s and the victim’s clothing, consistent with his earlier testimony.

The detective from the evidence unit testified that Deberry's clothing was neither seized nor sent to the FBI for analysis. Additionally, he was unaware of the whereabouts of those items. Deberry claimed that the police confiscated all his clothing from his room, and since his arrest, he had been incarcerated and never returned. He asserted that the police had complete control over his belongings since that night. The forensic evidence presented in court included blood and hair analysis. A black head hair of Negroid origin was found on the victim's jeans. While most structural features matched Deberry's hair, enough differences existed to prevent the FBI analyst from determining its source. A hair found in Deberry's pubic combings did not match the victim's, and no other hairs were discovered. Blood and semen stains on Beverly's clothes yielded inconclusive blood typing results, and no blood was found on the alleged knife used by Deberry. The examining doctor noted no signs of forced intercourse, though the lack of trauma could align with either consensual or non-consensual acts.

Deberry argues that under Brady v. Maryland and United States v. Agurs, the State was obligated to provide his clothing for examination. Given the inconclusive forensic results, his clothes might have challenged the victim's account based on potential stains or hairs. Moreover, the absence of such evidence on his clothing could have been crucial to establishing reasonable doubt about his guilt. The State counters that Brady and Agurs only apply if it possesses or can access the requested materials, citing Boyer v. State. Since the trial evidence was unclear about the State's possession of the clothing, it claims no duty to produce it. The State also argues, per Agurs, that the clothing was not obviously exculpatory enough to warrant disclosure under a general Brady request. It further contends that lacking blood, semen, or hairs on the clothes would not introduce reasonable doubt absent other evidence, rendering the clothing immaterial by Agurs' standards.

The parties framed their arguments around Brady and Agurs, focusing on whether the evidence favored the defense and was material. However, we see the issue differently. The core question isn't whether the clothing was discoverable but how to address the State's loss or destruction of exculpatory (or potentially exculpatory) evidence before or during the defendant's discovery request. While Brady, Agurs, and Stokes v. State—which outlines additional Brady considerations—may broadly apply, they don't resolve the dilemma we face: what remedy is appropriate when the State once had the evidence but lost or destroyed it? The State insists its Brady duty hinges on possession or access (per Boyer), but we believe it clearly had Deberry's clothing at one point before losing or destroying it, distinguishing this case from Boyer.

Brady and Agurs provide context for our decision but are analytically distinct and not directly applicable here. For instance, Government of the Virgin Islands v. Testamark illustrates this distinction. The State's duty under Brady arises only if it possesses or can access the evidence, yet we find it likely the State once had Deberry's clothing and later lost it. This scenario diverges from Boyer, where possession was unclear. While Brady and Agurs inform our analysis, they don't squarely address the issue of lost or destroyed evidence. Thus, we must determine the appropriate relief when exculpatory evidence is no longer available due to the State's actions or negligence.

F.2d 1162 (3d Cir.1978); United States v. Bryant, 439 F.2d 642 (D.C.Cir. 1971); Brown v. United States, D.C.Ct. App., 372 A.2d 557 (1977). Such claims must be evaluated by: 1) determining if the material would have been disclosable under Criminal Rule 16 or Brady if it existed when requested; 2) assessing whether the government had an obligation to preserve it; and 3) if preservation was required, deciding whether the duty was violated and what remedies apply. Brown, 372 A.2d at 559. See also, e.g., United States v. Grammatikos, 633 F.2d 1013 (2d Cir.1980); United States v. Loud Hawk, 628 F.2d 1139 (9th Cir.1979); United States v

Miranda, 526 F.2d 1319 (2d Cir.1975). Limiting the inquiry to what happened to the evidence and its trial impact is overly narrow. The State might argue the evidence was undiscoverable or not required to be preserved. See Super. Ct.Crim.R. 16(b). See also DeSalvatore v. State, Del.Supr., 163 A.2d 244 (1960); State v. Traenkner, Del.Super., 314 A.2d 202 (1973); Annot., 19 A.L.R.4th 509, 515-18 (1983). However, claims about lost exculpatory evidence must be resolved only after analyzing each element of the framework. B. Superior Court Criminal Rule 16(b) permits defendants 'to inspect and copy or photograph specified books, papers,

documents, tangible items, structures, or locations, or portions thereof, held by the State....' In State v. Winsett, Del.Super., 200 A.2d 237 (1964), the court mandated production under Rule 16 of the car linked to the victim's death and the alleged weapon. The court noted these items were tangible, obtained from the defendants, and crucial to the defense, necessitating disclosure. Id. at 238. Here, Deberry initially sought a list of disclosable materials, likely to refine a future discovery request per Rule 16(b). See State v. Traenkner, Del.Super., 314 A.2d 202 (1973); Super.Ct.Crim.R. 16(b). Regardless, Deberry's clothing was disclosable under Rule 16(b), consistent with

Winsett. Moreover, the State did not oppose disclosure based on immateriality or unreasonableness. See Super.Ct. Crim.R. 16(b). Thus, the State cannot now contend the clothing, if preserved, was exempt from disclosure under Criminal Rule 16. Supr.Ct.R. 8. C. The second analytical step—the State's preservation duty—is clear: failing to preserve evidence 'may deprive a defendant of due process and undermine valid convictions.' E.g., Government of the Virgin Islands v. Testamark, 570 F.2d 1162, 1165-66 & n. 7 (3d Cir.1978) (citing cases). While Brady v. Maryland, 373 U.S. 83, 83 S.Ct. 1194, 10 L.Ed.2d 215 (1963), and Superior Court Criminal Rule 16 do not explicitly mandate preservation, as noted in United States v

In Bryant, 439 F.2d 642, 651 (D.C.Cir.1971), it was established that the government's duty to disclose evidence begins once it has collected and secured such evidence. This ensures that critical evidence is not destroyed before prosecution starts or before defendants become aware of it. Proper preservation during early investigations is essential for later disclosure. We agree and affirm that the State's duty to disclose also encompasses preserving evidence, grounded in the due process clauses of the Fourteenth Amendment and Delaware Constitution, article I, section 7. This duty applies not only to the Attorney General but also to all local, county, and state investigative agencies. See Bryant, 439 F.2d at 650; Barbee v. Warden, 331 F.2d 842 (4th Cir.1964); Lewis v. United States, 393 A.2d 109 (1978).

We do not specify the exact administrative procedures needed for the Attorney General and law enforcement to preserve evidence. However, under Superior Court Criminal Rule 16(b), a defendant need only demonstrate that an item 'may be material to the preparation of his defense' to warrant discovery. Cf. United States v. Bailleaux, 685 F.2d 1105 (9th Cir.1982); United States v. Felt, 491 F.Supp. 179 (D.D.C.1979). To err on the side of caution, agencies should define discoverable evidence broadly to include any material potentially favorable to the defendant. See Bryant, 439 F.2d at 652 n. 21.

The final step in our analysis is determining whether the State failed to preserve evidence and the impact of such failure on the conviction. This involves balancing the State's conduct against the prejudice to the accused. The State must justify its actions, while the defendant must show how the lost evidence harmed their defense. Key factors include '(1) the level of negligence or bad faith, (2) the significance of the lost evidence, and (3) the adequacy of remaining evidence to support the conviction.' United States v. Loud Hawk, 628 F.2d 1139, 1152 (9th Cir.1979) (Kennedy, J., concurring).

When evaluating the State's conduct, courts should consider whether the evidence was lost or destroyed while in custody, whether the State disregarded the accused's interests, and whether negligence or deliberate actions occurred. Prosecutorial involvement in the loss of evidence may indicate motive to harm the defendant. Loud Hawk, 628 F.2d at 1152 (Kennedy, J., concurring). These factors are particularly relevant in assessing the State's adherence to its duty.

This inquiry examines statements from individuals who handled the material before and after its loss, evidence preservation protocols, case-specific practices, and recovery efforts. For example, Brown v. United States, D.C.Ct.App., 372 A.2d 557, 560-61 (1977); Johnson v. United States, D.C.Ct.App., 298 A.2d 516, 519 (1972). The defense's prejudice due to the lost evidence must also be considered. Prejudice analysis involves assessing the evidence's centrality to the case, its role in proving the crime's elements or the defendant's intent, the reliability of substitute evidence, and the likely jury impact without it. Loud Hawk, 628 F.2d at 1152 (Kennedy, J., concurring).

See, e.g., United States v. Grammatikos, 633 F.2d 1013, 1020 (2d Cir.1980); Government of the Virgin Islands v. Testamark, 570 F.2d 1162, 1167 (3d Cir.1978); United States v. Bryant, 439 F.2d 642, 653 (D.C.Cir.1971). After outlining the required judicial inquiry, we find no explanations for the evidence's loss. Deberry claims police took his clothing; one detective blames another, who denies it. Typically, we would remand for further fact-finding. See Bryant, 439 F.2d at 653; Johnson, 298 A.2d at 519. See generally 5 Am.Jur.2d Appeal & Error § 974, at 401-03 (1962).

However, remanding here would not improve the record. See Bryant, 439 F.2d at 653 (McGowan, J., concurring). Moreover, if lost evidence severely prejudices the accused, the State's culpability level becomes irrelevant. See Loud Hawk, 628 F.2d at 1152 (Kennedy, J., concurring); United States v. Miranda, 526 F.2d 1319, 1324, 1327 (2d Cir.1975); Cotton v. United States, D.C.Ct.App., 388 A.2d 865, 871 (1978). Thus, deciding based on the current record aligns with our analysis. Despite scant details on the clothing's loss, the State must bear responsibility.

Deberry, a transient racetrack worker, had all his belongings, including the clothes he allegedly wore during the attack, in his room. Upon arrest, he couldn't preserve this critical evidence, while the police could. One officer implicated another in taking the items. In such crimes, the victim's and perpetrator's clothing are often vital evidence, as the police's actions (seizing Beverly's clothes and likely Deberry's) confirm. The police had a duty to preserve this evidence. If such evidence is lost due to police negligence, the State must heavily justify overcoming the defendant's prejudice claim. A vague explanation is inadequate, as it hinders the defendant's ability to prove mishandling and seek relief. Though the track guard claimed to check an employee's pass.

At the time Beverly said she left and came back to the track complex, the only proof connecting Deberry to the rape was her testimony. The physical and medical evidence was unclear. If the clothes lacked Beverly's hair, blood from her hand injury, or semen, their absence would back Deberry's claim of no intercourse. While the guard's testimony and medical proof of intercourse weakened Deberry's denial, this highlights the clothing's potential significance. Scientific tests on the clothes could have strongly influenced the jury, making their loss highly prejudicial, especially given the police's duty to preserve evidence. The state's failure to produce De

berry's clothing or test it suggests any results would have favored him. The state's reliance on weak evidence implies stronger proof would have hurt their case. Given the lost clothing's impact on Deberry's defense, reversing his convictions is the only fair remedy. The state can choose to drop charges or retry him. In a retrial, the state must agree that Deberry's clothing would show no incriminating evidence, as they bear responsibility for its loss.

Deberry also disputes Beverly's identification, calling their on-site encounter overly suggestive and likely to cause misidentification, leading to an unreliable courtroom ID. The state argues the confrontation was not suggestive, as it was a natural result of the crime and arrest. Here, the quick identification wasn't unnecessarily suggestive. Beverly knew Deberry well, having spent much of the prior day with him. She identified him by name and where he lived, and the officer confirmed her immediate recognition. The defense emphasizes Beverly's lack of detailed description, but this wasn't crucial since she clearly knew Deberry.

Further description wasn't needed given Beverly's familiarity with Deberry. Her initial identification by his first name and residence, along with her quick confirmation, supports its reliability. The defense's focus on her limited physical description overlooks her prior relationship with him, making detailed features unnecessary for identification.

In 1284 (D.C.Cir.1969), the court assumed without deciding that reliability must be considered after determining the procedures were not unnecessarily suggestive. Based on the facts, the victim's identification of Deberry was deemed reliable, citing Neil v. Biggers, 409 U.S. 188, 199 (1972). Since Beverly's out-of-court identification was admissible, her in-court identification was not addressed, referencing Watson, 349 A.2d at 741 and Baker v. State, Del.Supr., 344 A.2d 240 (1975). After the opinion was issued on January 27, 1983, the State discovered clothing seized during the defendant's arrest, which had been in its possession despite court orders to produce them. The State had previously claimed the items were missing and continued to argue as if they were never found. The Court found this late discovery did not change its conclusions, instead reinforcing the need for rules on evidence handling in criminal cases. The Motion for Reargument was denied. An exchange between the trial judge and the deputy attorney general revealed the State's intent to avoid referencing blood on the clothing unless notified.

The State suggested the detective might have been mistaken about who had custody of the evidence, as the victim's clothing was initially taken by a hospital employee. However, testimony from a nurse indicated the clothing was bagged, labeled, and later given to a detective, supporting the detective's account. Rule 16 outlines the defendant's rights to inspect and copy relevant statements, reports, and grand jury testimony, including written or recorded confessions, autopsy reports, and physical or mental examinations.

Rule 16 further specifies that the defendant may request access to written reports of tests such as ballistics, fingerprints, and blood analyses, as well as medical examinations of the defendant or victim. The rule applies to materials within the State's possession, custody, or control, including grand jury testimony. This ensures the defendant can review evidence the State intends to use at trial, promoting fairness and transparency in the legal process.

Books, Papers, Documents, or Tangible Objects. The defendant can request the Attorney General to allow inspection, copying, or photographing of specified items in the State's possession, provided the items are relevant to the defense and the request is reasonable. This does not cover internal State documents, reports, or memoranda related to the case investigation, nor statements by State witnesses, unless specified under subdivision (a). At the time of the Winsett decision, Rule 16 allowed defendants to request access to certain materials after indictment, subject to court approval and a demonstration of relevance and reasonableness.

The requested items must be pertinent to the defense and the request must be reasonable. The court will outline the timing, location, and method for inspection and copying, and may impose fair conditions. Assessing whether the clothing would have been discoverable under Brady and Agurs is hypothetical since the clothing is unavailable. If Deberry's clothing lacked blood, semen, or hair stains, it could have supported his denial of involvement. The case relied heavily on the victim's testimony, with limited physical evidence, making the absence of such stains critical for raising reasonable doubt.

Since the defense only made a general Brady request, the clothing's materiality depends on whether its absence could create reasonable doubt in the context of the entire case. If the clothing had no stains or hairs, it would likely have been discoverable under Brady and Agurs. Referenced cases include Stokes v. State and Vouras v. HOLLAND, Justice: After a jury trial, defendant Jamour Pressey was convicted of Robbery in the First Degree and Resisting Arrest. Pressey appeals, arguing the trial judge improperly admitted a victim's hearsay statement under the excited utterance exception. The court found no merit in this claim and upheld the convictions. The incident involved three men robbing Anthony Calm at gunpoint, taking his belongings, and leaving him on a step. The third assailant also stole Calm's clothing before fleeing.

Calm obeyed. Once the third man disappeared, Calm hurried home. Since the thieves had taken his house key, he started pounding on the front door. About two minutes later, his sister opened the door. Calm explained to his sister and mother that he had been robbed. His mother, Kimberly Wallace, remembered Calm being 'terrified,' 'hysterical,' and 'in tears.' Wallace went out to look for the robbers. After driving two blocks, she met Wilmington Police Detective Michael Ballard and Officer Brian Vettori in their patrol car. She 'desperately' reported the robbery to them before driving off to continue her search. Ballard and Vettori trailed behind. Wallace soon spotted a man walking down the street. She got out of her car and informed the officers that he was one of the robbers. Ballard, wearing a tactical vest, stepped out and shouted, 'Stop, police!' but the man ran. Ballard pursued him on foot while Vettori followed in the car. When the man halted, Vettori exited his vehicle and commanded him to the ground at gunpoint. The man apprehended by Ballard and

Vettori was Pressey. Vettori noted Pressey wore a black-and-white checkered scarf. On Pressey, they found a cell phone, Calm’s school ID, and his house key. When Vettori dialed Calm’s number, the phone found on Pressey rang, showing Vettori’s caller ID. Wallace returned home and then drove Calm to the arrest site to identify the robber. Earlier, while Wallace was searching, Calm had changed into a t-shirt and sweatpants after being left in just his boxers and socks. Calm later testified he felt 'in shock,' 'nervous,' 'distraught,' and 'shaken.' Wallace added that Calm was 'still frightened.' When they arrived for the identification, Calm stayed in the car, 'hiding under his hood and slouching to avoid being seen.' Wallace recalled he was 'still crying' and seemed 'scared.' Both Wallace and Vettori testified that Calm

recognized Pressey as one of the robbers. Records show the identification occurred within twenty to sixty minutes of the robbery. Pressey was indicted for First-Degree Robbery, Second-Degree Conspiracy, and Resisting Arrest. The State dropped the conspiracy charge. The case went to a jury trial, where Calm, Wallace, Ballard, and Vettori testified. The jury convicted Pressey of First-Degree Robbery and Resisting Arrest. For the robbery, the judge sentenced him to ten years at Level V, with four years suspended for probation. For resisting arrest, he received one year at Level V, suspended for Level III probation. During Wallace’s testimony, the defense objected, calling Calm’s identification hearsay. The judge ruled:

Under Delaware Rule of Evidence 803, an excited utterance is a statement about a startling event made while under its stress. The declarant’s availability doesn’t matter. If the State proves it was an excited utterance, the questions to Calm are irrelevant. If the foundation is laid, the statement is admissible. Wallace then testified Calm was 'scared,' 'crying,' and 'hiding in the car' when he identified Pressey. The judge found the foundation sufficient and allowed the testimony. During Vettori’s examination, the defense objected again. The judge required the State to re-establish the foundation. Vettori described Calm as 'sitting in the back seat,' 'nervous,' and

The trial judge ruled that the prosecutor had established a sufficient foundation, allowing Vettori to testify that Calm identified Pressey as one of the robbers. Pressey contends that the judge improperly admitted Calm's prior statement under the excited utterance exception to the hearsay rule. Courts review such decisions for abuse of discretion. The Delaware Rules of Evidence generally bar hearsay but include exceptions like the excited utterance rule, which permits statements made under the stress of a startling event, even if the declarant is available. This exception is considered well-established, as it assumes the declarant's reliability due to their heightened emotional state.

The excited utterance exception relies on the idea that the declarant, overwhelmed by excitement, is unlikely to fabricate and will speak truthfully. In Gannon v. State, the court outlined three requirements for admission: (1) the statement must stem from a startling event, (2) it must be made while the excitement persists, and (3) it must relate to the event. Pressey concedes the first and third requirements were met but argues the second was not, claiming Calm's excitement arose from being forced back to the scene, not the robbery itself. In Culp v. State, the court noted that while elapsed time is a factor, it is not the sole determinant of admissibility.

The court in Culp acknowledged that prolonged time may reduce the likelihood of ongoing excitement but emphasized that if the declarant remains under the event's influence, even delayed statements can be reliable. The ruling distinguished D.R.E. 803(1), which requires contemporaneity, from D.R.E. 803(2), which focuses on the declarant's stressed state during the statement. The reliability of such statements hinges on the declarant's condition when speaking, not just timing. The court reiterated this principle in Dixon v. State and applied it in cases like Evans v. State, where statements made hours post-event were admitted due to the declarant's continued distress.

In this case, Wallace and Vettori described Calm as fearful, crying, and visibly shaken when identifying Pressey. The record supports that Calm's statement met all three foundational requirements for the excited utterance exception. His nervousness, shaking, and shaky voice indicated he was still under the stress of the robbery, justifying the admission of his out-of-court statement as reliable evidence under D.R.E. 803(2).

The 'excited utterance' exception under D.R.E. 803(2) applies here. The record fails to prove that Wallace forcing Calm back to the scene was an intervening event that caused Calm's excitement rather than the earlier robbery. Thus, Pressey has not demonstrated that the trial judge erred in allowing Calm's statement under the excited utterance hearsay exception. The Superior Court's rulings are upheld. See Purnell v. State, 979 A.2d 1102, 1106 (Del. 2009); Foster v. State, 961 A.2d 526, 529-30 (Del. 2008). D.R.E. 802 states hearsay is inadmissible unless permitted by law or rules. Refer to D.R.E. 803, 804. Dixon v. State, 996 A.2d 1271, 1276-77 (Del. 2010) notes these exceptions rely on circumstances ensuring trustworthiness.

State, 704 A.2d 272 (Del. 1998) are also relevant. Id. at 274. Additional cases include Dixon v. State, 996 A.2d at 1276; Foster v. State, 961 A.2d at 530; Bruce v.
