The Court deemed the case ineligible for a writ of error and dismissed it. Marvel, Vice Chancellor: Plaintiff requests annulment of an insurance policy issued to Milburn R. Ford on October 17, 1955, covering his life for $2,000 and including disability provisions irrelevant here. Ford died November 17, 1955, leaving his widow, the

The beneficiary listed on the policy is named as a defendant alongside the administrator of the deceased's estate. The plaintiff argues that it was misled into issuing the policy, a copy of which is included with the complaint, due to fraudulent misrepresentations made by Milburn R. Ford in his insurance application. These misrepresentations were deliberate, knowing, and significant to the risk Prudential undertook. The insurance plan covered the decedent and six coworkers, along with their employer, Joseph A. Smith, president of Silverside Dairy, Inc., with individual policies issued for each person. Premiums varied based on age, and payroll deductions were arranged for payment. No medical exam was required; policies were issued based on application statements and prepaid initial premiums. At trial, it was confirmed that Milburn R. Ford had misrepresented his medical history in his application.

Contrary to his application, Milburn R. Ford had been under a physician's care from July 30, 1952, until his death in November 1955. His blood pressure ranged from 154/102 to 200/120, averaging 190/100, and he was on constant medication for hypertension. He also suffered from bronchiectasis, and a September 1, 1955, bronchoscope exam revealed chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pulmonary fibrosis, and left ventricular enlargement. A blood pressure reading on October 15, 1955, showed 180/120. Ford died on November 17, 1955, from an aortic rupture. The plaintiff's assistant manager testified that had Ford's poor health, particularly his high blood pressure, been known, the policy would not have been issued. The plaintiff asserts that Ford concealed this medical history.

The complaint details how Ford falsely answered 'no' to key questions on his insurance application, including whether he had ever been treated for heart trouble or high blood pressure, or consulted a doctor in the past five years. The plaintiff claims it relied on these false answers and would not have issued the policy had it known about Ford's high blood pressure alone. While beneficiaries typically sue at law in such cases, precedent supports rescission under these circumstances, as seen in Equitable Life Assurance Society v. Wilson. At trial, the agent who handled Ford's application testified that he asked Ford the questions, recorded the answers, and had Ford sign after briefly reviewing the form. No witnesses were present except possibly another agent, though Ford's employer noted Ford was unloading his truck when approached about insurance.

The plaintiff bases its case on the agent's testimony about questioning Ford, as well as statements from Ford's employer, Smith, and another employee, McNulty, who confirmed being asked similar medical questions. The plaintiff highlights that no evidence directly contradicts the agent's account and argues that the consistent questioning of others at Silverside Dairy supports its claim. The plaintiff emphasizes that Ford's application omitted his serious medical history, further justifying the request for policy rescission.

It must be inferred that Ford was treated similarly. Defendants, however, highlight the lack of significant medical history on the Silverside Dairy applications and others solicited by the plaintiff's agent as proof of the agent's complete disregard for the health of potential insured individuals. With a long delay since the trial and defendants failing to submit their brief on time, the Court, when reviewing the case, faced the challenge of assessing King's credibility nearly a year after his testimony and opted to convene an advisory jury to evaluate the facts about King's interactions with Ford, particularly in a setting suitable for expert handwriting analysis. The jury determined that Ford did not disclose any prior treatment for high blood pressure to King when the application was completed. They also found that question 19(b) regarding high blood pressure was never posed to Ford, and the negative response on the form was added after Ford signed it. The jury reached a similar conclusion for other questions.

The jury also addressed question 20(c) about doctor consultations in the past five years. For the defendants to prevail, given the contract's nature and the clear relevance of Ford's health to the insurer's obligations, they must demonstrate fraud by the agent, King, as established in Prudential Ins. Co. v. Gutowski. The jury's responses, interpreted favorably to King, reveal a careless and unprofessional approach, indifference to Ford's health, and post-signing alterations to the application. Even if fraud by King were accepted (requiring disbelief of his testimony), the question remains whether defendants are entitled to the death benefits under the contested policy's circumstances. After Ford signed the application, it was returned to King.

The application was later reproduced and attached to a policy issued by the plaintiff's home office. The policy was delivered to Ford after October 17, 1955. The photostat copy of the policy clearly shows the negative responses to health-related questions and the word 'None' for illnesses listed in questions 19, 20, and 21. Additionally, the declaration above Ford's signature affirming the accuracy of the application's answers is legible and understandable. The policy explicitly states it covers the individual insured and includes a clause indicating it is issued based on the application's representations, which is attached and incorporated into the policy. Had Ford doubted the transaction's nature or believed his health was irrelevant due to a group insurance arrangement, reviewing the policy would have revealed that the medical answers were crucial to its issuance and were falsified.

The policy emphasizes that the insured's health, as stated in the application, is vital to the insurer's commitment. If the application process was rushed and neglected the agent's fiduciary duty to Ford, he had ample opportunity upon receiving the policy to review it, recognize any discrepancies, and report them to the insurer for corrective action, as supported by Standard Sewing Machine Company v. Frame.

In these consolidated asbestos cases, defendant Celotex Corporation ('Celotex') seeks partial summary judgment, arguing it cannot be held liable for punitive damages due to its acquisition of predecessor companies involved in asbestos production. Plaintiffs argue factual disputes about Celotex's connection to its predecessors' actions prevent summary judgment.

The factual basis for Celotex's motion stems from pleadings and limited discovery, with plaintiffs given the benefit of any inferences. Celotex entered the asbestos industry in 1972 by acquiring Panacon Corporation ('Panacon'), formed in 1970 through the merger of Philip Carey Corporation and Briggs Manufacturing Corporation. Philip Carey had long been involved in asbestos manufacturing and mining. Celotex initially bought 75% of Panacon's shares from Glen Alden Corporation, later acquiring the remaining shares. No shares were exchanged, and no Panacon shareholder became a Celotex shareholder.

The merger of Panacon into Celotex was finalized on June 28, 1972. Celotex, a subsidiary of Jim Walter Corporation, thus succeeded Panacon and its predecessors in asbestos product manufacturing, some of which allegedly harmed plaintiffs. Before acquiring Panacon, Celotex had no involvement in asbestos products. Post-merger, it continued distributing a limited line of asbestos products under the same brands but with added warnings. Panacon's notice to minority shareholders described its primary activities as manufacturing building construction products and mining asbestos fibers, mostly for construction use. Celotex also acquired vast Canadian asbestos deposits exceeding 68 million tons through the merger.

Celotex acquired assets related to asbestos production and retained some of Panacon's employees, including L.A. Pechstein, Jr., who may have known about asbestos hazards as early as 1963. While Celotex does not currently dispute its liability for compensatory damages, it questions whether a successor corporation can be held liable for punitive damages stemming from its predecessor's actions, which it did not explicitly endorse. The key issue is whether Celotex qualifies for summary judgment based on successor immunity, arguing that punitive damages policies don't apply to successor corporations.

Punitive damages aim to punish and deter wrongful conduct, but Celotex argues these goals are irrelevant when there's no shared identity or interests between successor corporations. Such damages must be proportionate to compensatory awards and serve to discourage future misconduct. Although Celotex accepts general liability for Panacon's actions, the legal basis for successor liability in tort cases remains undecided in Delaware, with only indirect precedents like Fehl v. S.W.C. Corp. touching on the issue.

In Fehl v. S.W.C. Corp., the court explored whether buying assets from a tortfeasor subjects the buyer to jurisdiction under Delaware's Long Arm Statute. The ruling noted a trend toward treating asset sales with business continuity as de facto mergers, especially in product liability cases. This logic applies even more strongly in de jure mergers, where statutory frameworks like 8 Del.C. § 259 reinforce successor liability, extending it to tort claims based on policy considerations, as seen in cases like Ramirez v. Amsted Industries.

Celotex contends that plaintiffs seeking punitive damages from successor corporations are not true creditors but rather pursuing excessive compensation, potentially harming other claimants' ability to recover. The debate over successor liability for punitive damages remains unresolved, with conflicting rulings in other jurisdictions, including cases involving Celotex itself.

In In Re Related Asbestos Cases, N.D.Cal., 566 F.Supp. 818 (1983), the court upheld Otex's argument against punitive damages. A Federal District Court, anticipating California law, ruled that successor liability did not extend to punitive damages in that context. The court examined the relationship between Celotex and Panacon's predecessor, Philip Carey, during the merger and found insufficient common ownership to hold Celotex accountable for its predecessor's misconduct. While the court dismissed the relevance of some Panacon employees' continued employment due to shareholder changes, it overlooked product continuity. The court also emphasized that plaintiffs' mere expectation of presenting evidence was inadequate to prevent summary judgment. Notably, California law does not tie punitive damages to compensatory amounts, a factor the court considered in assessing bankruptcy risks for successors.

In Delaware, the risk of bankruptcy from punitive damages is lower due to legal standards requiring such awards to be reasonably tied to circumstances and compensatory damages, as seen in Guthridge v. Pen-Mod, Inc., Del.Super., 239 A.2d 709 (1967) and Malcolm, supra. Conversely, the Pennsylvania Superior Court in Martin v. Johns-Manville Corp., Pa.Super., 322 Pa.Super. 348, 469 A.2d 655 (1983), held Celotex liable for punitive damages. The court recognized that punitive damages might not apply if the successor lacked shared leadership with the predecessor but concluded that successors could sometimes be penalized for predecessors' recklessness. The decision highlighted the role of punitive damages in punishment and deterrence, aligning with Restatement principles.

The Martin court ruled that punitive damages could apply to successors when there's enough identity between the two entities to ensure punishment of those responsible for reckless acts and deter future misconduct (469 A.2d at 667). Other cases, like Hanlon v. Johns-Manville Sales Corporation, 599 F.Supp. 376 (N.D. Ia. 1984), Frond v. Celotex Corp., Ill.App., 107 Ill. App.3d 654 (1982), and Neal v. Carey Canadian Mines, Ltd., E.D.Pa., 548 F.Supp. 357 (1982), also allowed punitive damages against Celotex for predecessors' actions, emphasizing deterrence. These rulings demonstrate that successor liability depends on case-specific facts, with some courts permitting punitive damages under deterrence theories despite varying corporate connections.

While one court interpreted the Celotex-Panacon merger differently under California law, others have imposed punitive damages on Celotex as a successor to deter harmful conduct. In this case, though there's no extensive overlap in leadership, disputed inferences suggest Celotex retained some Panacon and Philip Carey employees involved in asbestos distribution. Crucially, Celotex continued the asbestos product line post-merger, albeit with added warnings. However, the record lacks sufficient detail to evaluate these warnings, and neither party has addressed this gap. Given the summary judgment context and the need to favor plaintiffs in disputed inferences, these factors warrant further scrutiny regarding successor liability and punitive damages.

As the decisions show, deterrence is a policy objective that justifies allowing punitive damages. A successor company continuing a product line while aware of its risks, such as by adding warning labels, might engage in reprehensible behavior warranting punitive damages. In rejecting Celotex's summary judgment motion, this Court does not imply that punitive damages will necessarily be upheld at trial. Such damages in product liability cases require proof of egregious conduct, and even in strict liability jurisdictions, additional evidence of aggravated behavior is necessary. Given the uncertain stance on strict liability in this State, a solid foundation for compensatory damages must precede any consideration of punitive damages. However, assuming Celotex's implicit acknowledgment that both compensatory and punitive damages could apply to its predecessors' actions, factual disputes about Celotex's continuation of the harmful product line and retention of involved personnel prevent a legal ruling exempting it from punitive damages, thus denying its motion.

Cline v. Prowler Industries of Md., Inc. seems to bar strict liability claims in personal injury cases involving goods sales, but it remains unclear whether asbestos plaintiffs qualify as 'consumers' or 'bystanders.' This case involves a personal injury from a May 14, 1965, car accident. The plaintiff received treatment at Kent General Hospital and from several doctors in Dover, Wilmington, Richmond, and Baltimore. After filing the lawsuit, the plaintiff consulted additional doctors in Baltimore and a Wilmington-based expert witness retained by their attorney. The defendant has moved under Superior Court Rule 34 to obtain all medical reports, but the plaintiff resists producing post-suit reports, citing lack of 'good cause' and claiming some are privileged as attorney work product.

The plaintiff opposes the defendant's motion for production of post-suit medical reports, arguing no 'good cause' has been shown and that Rule 35 should govern such discovery. Additionally, reports sent to the plaintiff's attorney during the lawsuit are claimed as privileged work product. The case raises three issues: whether 'good cause' exists for producing all medical reports, whether Rule 35's envisioned exchange of reports affects the 'good cause' determination under Rule 34, and whether the attorney's post-suit reports are protected as work product.

Superior Court Rule 34 mandates document production upon demonstrating 'good cause,' with relevance alone being insufficient. The Empire Box Corp. case established that 'good cause' pertains to the need for the document, not just its content, requiring judicial discretion. Subsequent Delaware cases on Rule 34 'good cause' rarely address motions for doctors' reports, leaving this issue largely unresolved. The burden lies with the moving party to prove a necessity for the documents beyond their mere relevance.

4. In Ariff v. Powers, 479 Civil Action (Del.Super., 1966), Judge Quillen mandated the plaintiff to provide all medical, psychiatric, and psychological reports concerning the plaintiff's physical and mental state. In a subsequent letter opinion dated January 19, 1968, Judge Quillen noted that when injuries are complex and involve multiple medical experts from various specialties, requiring depositions before document production would impose undue time and cost burdens. He concluded that good cause could be established to allow defendants to form a comprehensive understanding of the claimed injuries. Greene v. Sears, Roebuck & Company, 40 F.R.D. 14 (N.D. Ohio E.D. 1966). The factual parallels between Ariff and the current case lead this Court to deem Ariff decisive on the 'good cause' matter at hand. Nonetheless, the plaintiff argues that Superior Court Rule 35

and federal cases addressing the interplay between Rule 35 and Rule 34 bar production under Rule 34 if the moving party hasn't decided whether to invoke Rule 35 for a physical examination. The Court finds this argument unconvincing. Judge Quillen's sole remark in Ariff on this point was: 'I am satisfied that there is no absolute bar to producing doctors' reports. Buffington v. Wood, 351 F.2d 292 (3rd Cir., 1965).' While Buffington didn't address Rule 34's 'good cause' requirement or the lower court's order to exchange medical reports, it suggests Rule 35 isn't the sole authority on such exchanges. Supra, 351 F.2d p. 297. Additionally, in Petition of Trinidad Corporation, 238 F.Supp. 928 (E.D. Va., 1965), the Court stated: 'If a party chooses to waive independent examination rights, a copy of the report

falls within the bounds of permissible discovery.' Although production was denied in Trinidad, the Court's rationale supports finding 'good cause' here, unaffected by Rule 35's language. Turning to the 'work product' issue, in Frank C. Sparks Company v. Huber Baking Company, 10 Terry 267, 114 A.2d 657 (Del.Super., 1955), the Court cited Scourtes v. Fred W. Albrecht Grocery Co., D.C., 15 F.R.D. 55, 58, defining 'work product' as including the insights, observations, and opinions of individuals hired by an attorney to assist in case investigation and trial preparation. This extends to technical or scientific knowledge gathered by experts employed by the attorney. The Huber Baking Company Court further stated

at p. 658 of 114 A.2d that an attorney's work product is generally shielded from discovery, not due to attorney-client privilege, but to protect attorneys' private files from opposing counsel's intrusion. Only in exceptional cases of significant hardship would a court compel production. Expert medical witness reports have been classified as privileged, as seen in In Re Bates, 167 Ohio St. 46, 146 N.E.2d 306 (1957). Thus, the report by the Wilmington doctor hired by the plaintiff's attorney is privileged and won't be produced. However, the Baltimore doctor's report, obtained by the plaintiff independently before legal representation, isn't privileged and must be produced. In summary, all reports are to be produced except those from the plaintiff's expert medical witness in Wilmington.

The order is hereby confirmed. It is so ordered. Boyce, J.: We believe the bill of particulars, given the facts of this case, is adequate. Hastings, J., presenting the court's opinion: A motion for nonsuit has been filed by the defendant's counsel, arguing that the suit is filed under the name of Madison Willin et al., trustees of St. John Methodist Episcopal Church of Seaford, Sussex County, Delaware, whereas the plaintiff's evidence indicates the church was incorporated on February 24, 1871, and remained so when the suit was initiated. Reference is made to Chapter 39 of the Revised Code, page 309, which states: 'Section 1. Any Christian religious group or congregation of fifteen or more members may incorporate by electing three to twelve trustees, adopting a name, and filing a certification with the deeds recorder.' 'Sec. 2. Such

trustees must be elected at a public meeting of the congregation, held at their usual place of worship, with ten days' notice posted at the entrance, and by a majority vote of attending members.' 'Sec. 3. The elected trustees and their successors form a corporation under the adopted name, with perpetual succession and the rights of a corporate entity, including the ability to acquire, hold, and manage property for the congregation, its ministers, members, or related purposes like schools or cemeteries. Decisions by a majority of trustees are binding.' 'Sec. 4. Any property held by the congregation or its trustees before incorporation transfers to the trustees upon incorporation, who may then manage or dispose of it.' Attention is also drawn to Chapter 275, Vol. 11, Laws of Delaware, enacted March 1, 1855, sections 1 and 2 of which state:

'Section 1. No grant, conveyance, devise, or lease of property to any individual or their successors in an ecclesiastical role shall confer any legal interest, nor shall such transfers to a person by office title benefit their successors. This section does not validate any prior such transfers. 'Sec. 2. No transfer of real estate intended for religious worship shall grant rights to any recipient unless made to a corporation formed under Chapter 39 of the Revised Code, titled 'Religious Societies.' It is argued that this section places land title exclusively with the corporation, requiring related lawsuits to be filed in the corporation's name, not its trustees'. Clearly, after this act, no property could be transferred to a religious group unless incorporated under Chapter 39, as Section 4 of Chapter 275 mandates escheatment to Delaware. The intent was to further restrict the mortmain act in Section 10 of Chapter 39. The issue is whether post-incorporation property title resides with the corporation or its trustees. Sections 3 and 4 of Chapter 39 are broad, while Section 9 specifically addresses the Protestant Episcopal Church, stating:

'The rector, wardens, and vestry of any Protestant Episcopal Church shall hold property for its benefit, with succession as provided by church canons.' The statutes' interplay raises questions about title vesting post-incorporation, particularly whether trustees or the corporation itself holds legal ownership. The broader language of Sections 3 and 4 contrasts with the specific provisions for certain denominations, highlighting the legislative intent to balance general incorporation rules with sectarian needs.

The clergy and vestry members of any Protestant Episcopal Church, upon verifying their name or designation as outlined in section 1, shall form a corporation, possessing the same privileges, rights, and authorities granted to trustees of other religious groups. Chapter 100 of Volume 11 and Chapter 599 of Volume 19 in Delaware's laws specify that the Roman Catholic Church may manage its religious corporation differently, adhering to its own faith's practices. Section 9, concerning the Protestant Episcopal Church, along with other statutes for the Roman Catholic Church, states these groups 'shall be a corporation, with the franchises, rights, and powers vested in trustees of other religious societies.' The term 'other religious societies' here likely refers to sections 3 and 4 of chapter 39, which govern religious societies broadly and stipulate, as per section 4, that all property rights held by such societies or congregations, whether directly or through trustees, shall transfer to the trustees upon incorporation, enabling them to manage or dispose of such property.

Chapter 39 exclusively addresses the incorporation of religious societies, which, like all corporations, can only operate through designated agents. These agents, specified by statute as trustees, hold the property rights. When chapter 275 of Volume 11 is interpreted alongside chapter 39's general provisions and its section 10, which incorporates the historic statute of montmain, it becomes clear that chapter 275 aims to enforce the statute of montmain, prohibiting land conveyances for religious purposes to individuals or ecclesiastical offices and preventing indirect transfers or trusts that violate section 10's intent. This interpretation preserves sections 3 and 4 of chapter 39 without altering pre-existing law. Since section 4 explicitly vests property titles in trustees, they are deemed appropriate parties to this lawsuit, and the motion for nonsuit is accordingly denied.

It must be witnessed and signed by at least two credible individuals in the testator's presence. The level of proof needed may vary based on factors like age, mental capacity, and context. LEGAL ANALYSIS InterDigital has filed to dismiss LG's complaint in favor of arbitration. InterDigital does not claim the court lacks jurisdiction over the dispute. Instead, it requests the court use its discretion under the McWane doctrine to dismiss this case in favor of the earlier arbitration. The Delaware Supreme Court ruled in McWane that 'a Delaware action will not be'

automatically stayed due to a prior case in another jurisdiction with the same parties and issues,' but 'a stay may be justified . by facts and circumstances that persuade the Court's discretion.' 263 A.2d at 283 (emphasis added). However, 'this discretion should generally favor a stay when a prior action exists in another competent court, involving identical parties and issues, capable of delivering swift and fair justice.' Id. Instead of a stay, a Delaware court following McWane may dismiss the later-filed case in favor of the earlier proceeding. See Donald J. Wolfe, Jr. & Michael A. Pittenger, Corporate and Commercial Practice in the Delaware Court of Chancery § 5.01 at 5-3 (2013). A. The Arbitration Qualifies as a First-Filed Action. The initial question under McWane is whether 'a prior action is pending elsewhere.' McWane, 263 A.2d at 283. While the arbitration predates this suit, LG claims an arbitration cannot

be considered a 'prior action' under McWane. There seems to be no precedent where a Delaware court applied McWane to dismiss a case in favor of an earlier arbitration. LG argues the absence of such cases proves McWane does not cover prior arbitrations. However, the scarcity of cases may stem from reasons other than McWane's inapplicability. Typically, in disputes with an ongoing arbitration, the defendant moves to dismiss the later case by asserting the dispute must be arbitrated. The court then decides on substantive arbitrability or, per the contract, dismisses the case for the tribunal to rule. If arbitration applies, McWane is irrelevant. If not, the tribunal cannot 'deliver prompt and complete justice,' making McWane inapplicable. Due to unusual circumstances, InterDigital's McWane argument escapes this dilemma. Both parties agree the Tribunal can determine arbitrability, and they also

acknowledge the current dispute stems from the NDA, which lacks an arbitration clause. Thus, this case uniquely involves both the tribunal and court having jurisdiction, allowing McWane to apply. In McWane, the Delaware Supreme Court highlighted two key policy reasons for the doctrine. First, it 'prevents wasteful duplication of resources when courts, lawyers, parties, and witnesses handle the same dispute simultaneously.' Id. Second, it 'avoids conflicting rulings and a race to judgment in preferred forums.' Id. These reasons equally support applying McWane to a first-filed arbitration. In other contexts, like issue and claim preclusion, this court has treated arbitration as a prior action. See, e.g., Meso Scale Diagnostics, LLC v. In the case of Dean Witter Reynolds, Inc. v. 537 U.S. 79, 84, 123 S.Ct. 588, 154 L.Ed.2d 491 (2002), it was stated that procedural issues are generally for arbitrators, not judges, to resolve. The Trustmark decision emphasized that arbitrators handling commercial disputes may address ancillary issues affecting their work. They can resolve procedural matters without judicial interference, as allowing courts to review such decisions would undermine arbitration's efficiency. Other circuits, like the Sixth in Savers Prop. & Cas. Ins. Co. v. Nat'l Union Fire Ins. Co., 748 F.3d 708, 722 (6th Cir. 2014), and the Second in Michaels v. Mariforum Shipping, S.A., 624 F.2d 411, 414-15 (2d Cir. 1980), agree that courts should avoid intervening in procedural arbitration disputes.

Permitting judicial review of every procedural ruling, or lack thereof, would disrupt arbitration. If the Tribunal errs, LG can challenge the final award later, as noted in SOC-SMG, 2010 WL 3634204, at *3. This court will not interfere with interim decisions. LG also claims the Tribunal cannot grant equitable relief under the License Agreement’s 'arbitrators at law' clause (PLA § 5.2(c)), arguing Delaware’s equity court distinction limits the Tribunal’s powers.

LG’s interpretation of 'arbitrators at law' is flawed. The phrase distinguishes arbitrators bound by legal principles from those with broader discretion, not the historical law-equity divide. The License Agreement chose the former but did not bar injunctive relief. The law-equity distinction stems from medieval England, where the Court of Chancery addressed common law courts’ rigidities, as explained by Quillen & Hanrahan in their history of Delaware’s Chancery Court.

The text delineates a boundary between two legal jurisdictions by contrasting law and equity, suggesting that any opposition between them is either completely or partially incorrect. Citing William Blackstone's Commentaries, it notes that while courts of law and equity followed the same fundamental rules, they differed in procedures and remedies. Blackstone emphasized that the key distinction lay in how justice was administered, including methods of proof, trial, and relief. English settlers brought these legal practices to the American colonies, as highlighted by Howard L. Oleck.

After gaining independence, several U.S. states, like Delaware, established separate equity courts modeled after England's Court of Chancery. Delaware's constitution granted its Court of Chancery the same equity jurisdiction as Britain's High Court of Chancery before colonial separation. Similarly, the U.S. Constitution allowed federal courts to handle cases 'in Law and Equity,' with Congress enabling federal judges to administer both, switching roles based on whether a case was a common law complaint or an equity bill. Federal courts exercising equity held jurisdiction comparable to England's high chancery court.

By the mid-19th century, most U.S. states had combined their law and equity courts, a change mirrored in Britain by the Judicature Acts of 1873 and 1875. The U.S. federal courts unified their procedures under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure in 1938, and Arkansas was the last state to merge its courts in 2001. Today, only Delaware, Tennessee, and Mississippi maintain separate equity courts, as the distinction between law and equity becomes a distant memory in most jurisdictions.

The License Agreement's mention of 'arbitrators at law' does not relate to the historical split between law and equity. Instead, it refers to arbitration under AAA International Rules, which differentiate between arbitrators applying legal precedents and those deciding cases as 'amiable compositeur or ex aequo et bono.' 'Arbitrators at law' adhere to a specific legal system's precedents, much like a court, while the latter approach focuses on fairness and equity without strict legal constraints.

An arbitrator serving as an 'amiable compositeur or ex aequo et bono' has the liberty to settle disputes using broader fairness principles, often without strict adherence to any specific legal system's laws. If equity were still viewed as Selden's 'roguish thing,' a stronger parallel might exist between equity courts and arbitrators acting ex aequo et bono, suggesting the term 'arbitrators at law' could draw interpretive significance from the law/equity divide. However, this notion of equity faded by the early 1800s, with Pomeroy and Story discrediting it in their works. See Pomeroy's, supra, § 56-67; Story, supra, § 1-37. Presently, as the maxim states, '[e]quity follows the law.' Wolfe & Pittenger, supra, at v. The function of an amiable compositeur or ex aequo et bono arbitrator differs markedly from contemporary equity courts. 'While equity rulings are considered part of legal doctrine, decisions ex aequo et bono are regarded as outside it.'

'Equity operates within the legal framework, whereas ex aequo et bono appeals to moral, social, or political ideals external to law.' The arbitrator's role under these concepts implies a discretion and divergence from legal precedent far exceeding what U.S. courts, even equity-focused ones like Delaware's Court of Chancery or federal courts exercising equitable powers, would allow. HORSEY, Justice: Defendant was found guilty by a jury in Superior Court on multiple drug-related charges. On appeal, defendant raises several alleged errors warranting reversal. We first examine claims of error in the Trial Court's refusal to suppress: (i) drug evidence seized during searches of his mobile home and safe deposit box; and (ii) his post-arrest oral statement made during an allegedly unlawful detention. On October 28, 1983, Delaware State Police secured a warrant to search defendant's home. Executed at 10:00 a.m. by a specialized drug 'Investigative Strike Force,' the search uncovered: significant quantities of drugs and related paraphernalia; a loaded firearm; numerous other weapons; over $1,000 in cash; coded documents; and a safe deposit box key. After seizing the items, defendant was arrested on-site and transported to the barracks by 10:30 a.m. for processing. The chief

The investigator and arresting officer stayed on-site until 5:00 p.m. to oversee the search and catalog the seized items. The evidence was later taken to the troop, where a thorough report listing over 150 confiscated personal items was reviewed and submitted to the magistrate by approximately 5:30 p.m. The lead investigator then went back to the troop to process the defendant, who had been detained without communication since that morning. Between 6:30 and 7:00 p.m., the defendant was read his Miranda rights, did not ask for a lawyer, and answered the investigator's questions, admitting ownership of one of the firearms found. On October 31, 1983, police secured a warrant for the defendant's safe deposit box, which held over $4,000 in cash. The defendant later argued that the premises search warrant lacked probable cause.

The defendant claimed the affidavit had flaws, such as unverified informant reliability, outdated information, and insufficient location details. However, the affidavit collectively provided enough evidence to reasonably suspect the defendant's residence was used for ongoing drug trafficking, as referenced in Jensen v. State. In Tatman v. State, the court adopted the 'totality of the circumstances' standard from Illinois v. Gates for assessing probable cause. This replaced the earlier Aguilar-Spinelli test, which required proving an informant's basis of knowledge and reliability. The new standard applies here, as the affidavit cited multiple corroborating sources: four independent informants, citizen complaints about frequent short visits to the defendant's home, and the affiant's own surveillance observations.

The affidavit demonstrated a strong likelihood of finding evidence of drug-related activity at the defendant's residence, meeting the 'fair probability' threshold set in Gates. The defendant's argument about stale information was dismissed, as the nature of drug trafficking allows for a broader timeframe when evaluating repetitive criminal behavior. Recent reports of suspicious activity, some as recent as two days before the warrant application, further supported the warrant's validity. The court also rejected the claim that the search location was inadequately described, as the affidavit clearly specified the rural address of the defendant's property.

The affidavit's detailed accounts, including multiple informants and consistent surveillance, established sufficient probable cause for the search warrant. The ongoing and repetitive nature of drug trafficking justified the timeframe of the reported activities, countering the staleness argument. The location was sufficiently identified, and the totality of circumstances supported the warrant's issuance. Thus, the defendant's challenges to the affidavit's validity were unfounded, and the search warrant was deemed legally sound under the applied standards.

The home was described with enough detail and supported by a photo identifying it as the defendant's residence. We don’t need to address the defendant’s claim that the warrant for his safe deposit box lacked probable cause, as no evidence from the box was presented at trial. Still, we acknowledge the Trial Court’s finding of probable cause and uphold the denial of the defendant’s motion to recover seized funds from his box and home. The origin of the money was disputed, with conflicting testimony from the defendant and sufficient evidence suggesting it was linked to illegal activity rather than lawful gains.

The defendant argues that his admission of gun ownership, made over eight hours after arrest, should be suppressed due to unlawful detention under 11 Del. C. § 1909. He highlights the nearly nine-hour delay between arrest and confession. While delays under 24 hours aren’t automatically unreasonable, they can be deemed so based on context. The admissibility of a statement under § 1909 depends on evaluating all circumstances, as established in prior cases.

The reasonableness of police delay in presenting an arrested person to a magistrate is a factual issue decided by the Trial Court and upheld on appeal if supported. Here, the nine-hour delay was due to the arresting officer’s involvement in a lengthy search and seizure. Given his expertise in drug-related cases and the volume of evidence, the delay wasn’t unreasonable. The officer was the most suitable person to interrogate the defendant, and an earlier interview would have been premature.

The defendant argues that the additional delay before being taken to the magistrate—sometime after 9:00 p.m.—should exclude his 7:00 p.m. statement. However, the critical period for assessing delay is before the confession, not after. The extra time may have been needed to prepare the multiple charges against him. The defendant also claims his statement was coerced, citing an officer’s threat to charge his companion with a gun offense as duress.

Among the numerous firearms discovered at the defendant's property (a prohibited individual), the defendant did not claim ownership of any seized weapon. The Trial Court dismissed this argument following an evidentiary hearing, with the voluntariness issue being a factual determination based on overall circumstances, as established in Schneckloth v. Bustamonte, 412 U.S. 218 (1973). Record evidence confirms the Trial Court's conclusion that the defendant's statements were voluntary, free from undue pressure or coercion. This aligns with Anderson v. State. Bellamy v. State, heavily cited by the defendant, is factually and procedurally distinct. The State acknowledges that the defendant's misdemeanor conviction for drug paraphernalia possession under 16 Del.C. § 4771 must be overturned and the indictment dismissed.

The indictment's failure to include a critical element of the charge necessitates dismissing the drug paraphernalia offense. The Trial Court incorrectly denied the defendant's motion to dismiss and improperly allowed the State to amend the indictment post-evidence. Other claims of reversible error lack substance. The Court acted within its discretion in restricting defense counsel's witness questioning, and the evidence, interpreted favorably to the State, sufficiently supports the findings: defendant possessed the seized contraband and weapons, intended to distribute controlled substances, and had a deadly weapon during felony commission. Refer to Ross v. State and Redden v. State. The judgment is PARTIALLY AFFIRMED, PARTIALLY REVERSED, and REMANDED. Under § 1909, an arrested individual must appear before a magistrate promptly, ideally within 24 hours (excluding weekends/holidays), unless a judge extends detention for up to 48 hours with valid cause, per Super.Ct.Crim.R. 5(a).

BIFFERATO, Judge. This case involves Delaware's criminal charges against Getty Oil Company (Eastern Operations) Inc. ('Getty') for allegedly releasing visible air pollutants/smoke in breach of DWARCR Regulation XV, Section 2.1, violating 7 Del.C. § 6013(a). Getty seeks dismissal under Rule 12(b). For this motion, the Court assumes: (1) on August 10, 1972, Getty activated a fluid coker emitting dark smoke; (2) complaints prompted a state investigation into the smoke's source and density; and (3) the emissions were a brief, non-continuous event. If these assumptions are inaccurate, a formal hearing can be convened. The Court will address Getty's arguments sequentially.

First, Getty contends that administrative procedures under 7 Del.C. § 6006 were obligatory due to §§ 6204–6205, and the State's failure to comply deprives the Court of jurisdiction. Section 6204 requires addressing ongoing air pollution or regulatory violations via § 6006. The statute's wording targets persistent pollution issues, not isolated incidents. Thus, Getty asserts the criminal proceedings under § 6013(a) are invalid without prior administrative resolution.

When there is an ongoing source of pollution, the appropriate approach is to follow sections 6204 and 6006. However, this case involves a one-time past action. Section 6204 does not require the use of section 6006 here. Section 6205 of Title 7 is also irrelevant, as it addresses measures to prevent or correct air pollution. The State is prosecuting based on an alleged past event, not a current issue. Even without a mandate, should the State adhere to Section 6006 before acting under § 6013(a)? Section 6006 states that the Secretary should seek compliance through conference, conciliation, or persuasion for ongoing violations.

The procedure in Section 6006 is clearly intended for ongoing issues. Once a violation is completed, compliance is impossible. Even if the violation occurred, no action can undo it. The Secretary might persuade Getty to avoid future violations but cannot change past actions. This section focuses on current problems, not past ones. Getty argues that 'shall endeavor' in Section 6006 mandates its use, but 'shall be fined' in Section 6013 is equally mandatory. The Conservation Act and Chapter 60 of Title 7 aim to manage water and air resources for the State's benefit.

Delaware Code § 6001(a)(2) emphasizes protecting and utilizing the State's water and air resources. Pollution prevention is vital for public health and safety, as stated in § 6001(b)(5). The law should be liberally interpreted to achieve its goals. Unless explicitly required, the State has discretion in choosing procedures. Environmental protection is the priority, and flexibility is often necessary. The statute specifies actions for ongoing pollution but allows flexibility for past violations. Once prosecution begins under § 6013(a), jurisdiction shifts to the Superior Court under § 6013(e).

Getty's motion to dismiss argues that no offense has been stated. First, Getty claims no violation of rules regarding a 'commercial type application' under § 6013(a) was alleged. Second, even if Regulation XV, Section 2.1 was violated, it wouldn’t constitute criminal conduct under § 6013. The Court agrees that § 6013(a) requires neglecting a rule for a 'commercial type application,' defined in § 6007 as requests for licenses or permits for systems or processes not classified as 'individual type applications,' or implementing statutes or rules for such systems.

An 'individual type application' involves Regulations II and XV of DWARCR. Regulation II focuses on permits, registration, and application requirements, aiming to outline reporting and approval processes for equipment that may release air contaminants. Regulation XV, Section 1.1, aims to manage visible emissions from stationary sources. Getty faces charges under Regulation XV for exceeding allowed smoke or contaminant density. The issue is whether violating Regulation XV, Section 2.1, constitutes neglect under a 'commercial type application'. Regulation XV exempts start-up and shut-down of certified continuous equipment under Section 3 of Regulation II.

If Getty had an operation certificate for equipment start-up, Regulation XV would not apply. However, lacking such a certificate, Getty was bound by visible emission standards. This appears as neglect under a 'commercial type application', specifically for an operating certificate. Section 3 of Regulation II supports this, requiring approval before constructing or altering emission equipment. Applications must detail start-up/shut-down methods and their emission impacts.

Section 3.2 mandates an operating certificate before using new or altered equipment. Section 3.3 requires owners to obtain certificates within 90 days of a written request or by December 31, 1973, if no request was received before September 30, 1973. Section 3.4 states certificates are issued only if equipment complies with Commission rules. Section 3.5 requires tests to assess emissions and compliance, ensuring equipment operation adheres to air pollution regulations.

The regulation addresses start-up, shut-down, and operation of emission-emitting equipment, including construction and alterations. Operating certificates, issued post-compliance testing, are mandatory. Applicants must apply within 90 days of a request or proactively by December 31, 1973. No violation occurs if no request is received before September 30, 1973. However, lacking a certificate does not exempt compliance with other regulations, like Regulation XV's emission standards, unless an operating certificate governs the equipment.

In response to whether breaching Regulation XV, DWARCR, constitutes neglect or failure to comply with a 'commercial type application' regulation, it seems that violating Regulation XV without an operating certificate does imply neglecting or failing to apply for such a certificate, i.e., a 'commercial type application'. Thus, the State has accused Getty of an offense related to a 'commercial type application', and the alleged breach of Regulation XV, Section 2.1, DWARCR, is a criminal act under 7 Del.C. § 6013(a). Getty's motion to dismiss on these grounds is rejected. Getty's final dismissal argument is twofold: (1) the State's filing omitted the statute criminalizing Regulation XV violations, and (2) the indictment's use of disjunctive language in Regulation XV is unclear, denying Getty a precise charge statement as required by Rule 7(c), Superior Court Criminal Rules, and its constitutional rights under Article I, Section 7 of the Delaware Constitution and the Sixth Amendment.

Defendant must receive a clear, concise written charge statement under Rule 7(c), Superior Court Criminal Rules, to prepare a proper defense, as established in United States v. Cruickshank (1876) and Demonia v. State (1965). The State's August 11, 1972 complaint charged Getty with violating Regulation XV, DWARCR, and 7 Del.C. § 6013(a), but the August 21, 1972 information omitted the statute, citing only the regulation. While Getty objects, Rule 7(c) does not mandate dismissal for omissions unless prejudice occurs. No prejudice in case preparation is evident, so the Court denies dismissal but permits the State to amend its information under Rule 7(e), Superior Court Criminal Rules.

Getty also contests the use of 'and/or' in Regulation XV, DWARCR, and the indictment, arguing it creates ambiguity. Although 'and/or' is often criticized in legal texts, its use is only problematic if it causes uncertainty. The phrase 'air contaminants and/or smoke' in Regulation XV, Section 2.1, can mean either, or both, without significant confusion. Thus, dismissal is unwarranted. The indictment and information are sufficiently clear for defense preparation, and the State may amend its filing to include the violated statute. Getty's dismissal motion is denied.

Harrington, Chancellor: The bill states, and the demurrer acknowledges: (1) Alice Boyle Hoey died intestate in Wilmington in 1939; (2) she owned a Vandever Avenue and LaMotte Street property with a laundry business; (3) Edwin E. Hoey and Anne M. Hoey Leary were appointed administrators on July 26, 1939, posting a $45,000 bond with Massachusetts Bonding and Insurance Company; (4) the estate included laundry machinery, trucks, and equipment, which Hoey and Leary took possession of as part of the estate's assets.

Acting as administrators, as previously mentioned'; (5) that 'from approximately July 26, 1939, until around August 17, 1943, Hoey and Leary, claiming to act as administrators, as stated, without any authorization from the Register of Wills or any other court with jurisdiction, managed the laundry, utilizing the buildings and personal property they held as administrators for this purpose'; (6) that on August 17, 1943, the defendants 'Hoey and Leary were dismissed as administrators, and the complainant was named administrator of the deceased’s estate. Subsequently, the complainant qualified and currently serves in this role'; (7) that 'Hoey and Leary have failed to submit an account of their administration of the deceased’s estate, despite orders from the Register to do so'; (8) that 'the complainant is informed, believes, and asserts that there are outstanding debts of the deceased and that the estate is insolvent, lacking sufficient assets to cover these obligations.'

The requested relief is evident from the facts. The issues presented by the individual defendants’ demurrer are (1) whether this court can hear a bill for an accounting against the former and removed administrators of Alice Boyle Hoey’s estate, and (2) whether an administrator de bonis non can file such a bill, especially when the estate is insolvent. The demurrer from the Massachusetts Bonding and Insurance Company raises identical questions. It also disputes whether it can be included as a defendant in the accounting bill alongside the prior administrators, the principals in the administration bond, or if the complainant’s sole recourse is a legal action. Executors or administrators must gather assets, settle the deceased’s debts, and distribute any remaining funds to rightful parties. Operating a business run by the decedent is neither their duty nor within their typical authority. If this occurs, interested parties may generally choose to demand an account of any profits earned or a full return of the assets used, with interest; if losses arise, the administrators may be held liable.

24 C.J. 55; see also 33 C.J.S., Executors and Administrators, § 189; Gilligan v. Daly, 79 N.J.Eq. 36, 80 A. 994; In re McGovern, Sur., 118 N.Y.S. 378. However, the issue is whether the parties’ rights can be resolved in this court via an accounting bill. Apart from other grounds for this court’s jurisdiction in complex mutual accounting cases (see Davis v. Davis, 1 Del.Ch. 256; Illinois Finance v. Interstate Royal Credit Ass'n., 11 Del.Ch. 349, 101 A. 870), it is acknowledged that the English Court of Chancery had at least concurrent jurisdiction over decedents’ estate administration and settlement during our separation from England, as the Ecclesiastical Court’s powers were quite restricted. Glanding v. Industrial Trust Co., 28 Del. Ch. 125, 45 A. 2d 553; 1 Pomeroy. Eq.

.Jur., (5th Ed.) § 346; 4 Pomeroy Eq.Jur., (5th Ed.) § 1127-1129, 1153. This jurisdiction applied whether the decedent died testate or intestate (4 Pomeroy, supra, § 1155), and typically rested on the fiduciary relationship between the personal representatives and creditors, legatees, or others entitled to a share of the estate. 1 Pomeroy, supra, § 346; 4 Pomeroy, supra, § 1127, 1155; In re Ortiz' Est., 26 Del.Ch. 240, 27 A.2d 368, 373. Discovery may play a key role in equity accounting cases, but it is not the fundamental basis for jurisdiction. Adams Equity, 74 Law Libr. *p. 220; 1 Pomeroy, Eq.Jur., supra, § 191. It is uncontested that, in most aspects, this court possesses largely the same authority as the

The English Court of Chancery in 1776 held certain powers, as noted in § 10, Art. IV, Const. of 1897, and § 4637, Rev. Code 1935, referencing Glanding v. Industrial Trust Co. The proviso in Section 4637 simply restates the longstanding equity rule on jurisdiction. Once a court of equity assumes jurisdiction, statutory grants of similar powers to another body rarely diminish its original authority, as seen in Glanding v. Industrial Trust Co. and other cases like State v. Wilmington Bridge Co. and Fox v. Wharton. The question of whether equity jurisdiction is overridden hinges on legislative intent, with such statutes interpreted narrowly.

To abrogate equity jurisdiction, statutory language must typically include explicit prohibitions or affirmatively grant exclusive jurisdiction to another court, as noted in 1 Pomeroy, § 281. Defendants argue this court lacks authority to compel executors and administrators to account, citing state constitutions that assign such jurisdiction elsewhere. However, prior to the establishment of the Court of Chancery in 1792, other Delaware courts exercised broad equity powers. The Register of Wills, a constitutional office since 1792, is addressed in § 17, Art. VI, and later in § 33, Art. IV of the 1897 Constitution, as referenced in Wilmington Trust Co. v. Baldwin. Section 34 of Article IV mandates executors or administrators to file accounts with the Register, who must review and settle them.

The Register of Wills must examine accounts and supporting proofs in the presence of the executor or administrator, adjusting them according to law. Settled accounts remain in the office for inspection, and notice must be given to beneficiaries within three months. Exceptions to the account may be raised by interested parties, with disputes heard in the Orphans' Court. This process, rooted in the 1792 Constitution, originally included guardians. Jurisdictional analysis also involves supplementary statutes, which typically allow executors one year from appointment to settle estates and file final accounts, though annual accounts are required unless the Register grants an extension.

Since 1806, the Register has held authority to initiate contempt proceedings against executors failing to comply with accounting duties, as seen in § 24, Chapt. 21, Vol. 4, Laws of Del., and later codifications. This provision also applied to guardians. While the Register exercises judicial functions in some contexts, in settling executor and administrator accounts, the role is primarily administrative. The historical Court of Errors and Appeals further contextualizes this jurisdictional framework.

The decision was established as early as 1842, and this court must adhere to it. Robinson v. Robinsons' Adm'r., 3 Harr. 433; see also Wilmington Trust Co. v. Baldwin, supra; Peckard v. Price, 5 Del.Ch. 239; Bodziak v. Theisen, Adm'r., 4 Terry (43 Del.) 487, 50 A.2d 409. However, the Orphans' Court may review and decide on the fairness of allowances granted to the accountants by the Register, or any additional valid charges, through proper exceptions. Since 1829, the Register of Wills has had the authority to entirely suppress inventories or debt lists or deem them incomplete after reviewing evidence. Witness testimonies must be documented, signed, and certified as depositions. In the event of an appeal, these must accompany the inventory or debt list to the Orphans' Court. § 3835, Rev. Code 1935; Rev. Code 1829, p. 22

3; Rev. Code 1852, p. 302. While the Constitution allows exceptions to executors' or administrators' accounts to be heard by the Orphans' Court, the statute also states: 'The same rule applies when witnesses are examined before the Register regarding any account.' Six complainants, all shareholders of the Home Life Insurance Company of America, a Delaware corporation, have filed a lawsuit against that company and the Home Protective Company, also a Delaware corporation, on behalf of themselves and other shareholders. The officers of both companies have been the same individuals for over nine years, including during the disputed transactions, and a majority of the insurance company's directors also served on the protective company's board. Until 1907, the Protective Company owned nearly all the insurance company's shares, controlling it. Later, until late 1913, the Protective Company sold shares of the insurance company at roughly twice their par value, often tied to insurance policies sold by the insurance company's agents, with policyholders given the option to purchase shares.

Some of these shares, along with others later acquired by the Protective Company, were issued under an option granted by the insurance company. This option originated from a decision by the insurance company's directors on October 29, 1906, giving Paul Bright the exclusive right to buy $100,000 worth of stock at par value, initially $100 per share, later reduced to $10. At that time, $100,000 of stock had been issued from an authorized capital of $250,000. On April 15, 1907, the Protective Company bought Bright's entire stake in the insurance company, including outstanding shares and goodwill, for $155,000, and Bright transferred his stock subscription option to the Protective Company. At a January 21, 1908, shareholders' meeting, it was resolved that surplus earnings, if any, would go to the Protective Company to finance the insurance company, and directors were authorized to increase the capital from $250,000 to up to $1 million, pending legal steps.

At a February 16, 1909, shareholders' meeting, a resolution was passed acknowledging the option granted to Bright, its transfer to the Protective Company, and the planned capital increase. It also noted that the Protective Company had provided funds and securities to help the insurance company maintain its legal reserves and grow its business, with the understanding that these advances would continue as needed and be repaid from surplus earnings. The resolution expanded the option to cover the entire capital stock. The Protective Company's answer explained that these funds were necessary to acquire new business, either through agents or by reinsuring other companies' risks, as insurance laws restricted the use of the company's regular income for such purposes.

For such a purpose, it was also clarified that a newly established insurance company must spend significantly more than the premiums it collects to cover agent commissions and other costs to achieve rapid growth. Once the business expands substantially, the income will surpass these expenditures. Essentially, a new company spends more to secure policies than it earns from policyholders. To support the Home Life Insurance Company's rapid expansion, the Protective Company provided several financial contributions. During the annual stockholders' meeting on February 19, 1915, a resolution was passed acknowledging the January 21, 1908, meeting and detailing the receipt of approximately $470,000 from the Protective Company, with around $81,000 repaid. The resolution authorized issuing obligations for these and future advances at 6% interest, payable only from surplus funds exceeding $10,000, without creating a lien or debt unless the company dissolved or ceased operations.

Against the Insurance Company, these obligations were not to be treated as a liability or due unless the company was dissolved or retired. Until 1912, the Protective Company owned a majority of the Insurance Company's stock. Afterward, while it no longer held a majority, it retained the power to regain control by exercising its stock option. Currently, the Protective Company holds about 6,000 of the 16,000 outstanding shares, with 8,500 unissued shares remaining. It holds the exclusive right to purchase these unissued shares at par value. Between 1907 and late 1913, the Protective Company exercised its option to buy shares at par and sold them alongside insurance policies at two to three times their face value. From 1913 to 1916, it acquired no shares. However, in June 1916, after some stockholders expressed dissatisfaction and threatened legal action, the Protective Company purchased 3,700 shares at par under the option.

Until recently, the Insurance Company's officers and directors held very few of its shares but were significant shareholders in the Protective Company, where they also served as officers and directors. The complainants allege that the Protective Company's financing plan for the Insurance Company was inherently fraudulent and deceitfully executed. The complainants also claim that the officers of both companies, who were the same individuals, engaged in deceptive practices, including misleading book entries and reports, and paid dividends from non-earning sources, impairing the company's capital.

The complainants argue the option was illegal and void for two reasons: (1) it violated stockholders' pre-emptive rights to equal access to unissued shares and maintaining proportional control, and (2) it contravened the rule against perpetuities. Was the Protective Company's financial aid to the Insurance Company illegal or unfair? Evidence showed that accessible working capital is vital for a life insurance company's growth, especially in industrial insurance. Success hinges on policy volume, but new companies often face initial costs exceeding premiums. State law prohibits using capital stock for working capital, requiring surplus funds from stockholders or earnings. These earnings, derived from mortality gains, interest, or lapses, belong to shareholders but are insufficient for rapid expansion, necessitating additional contributions.

The Protective Company, a holding company, provided roughly $470,000 in advances, with $80,000 repaid. In exchange, it secured exclusive rights to the Insurance Company's unissued stock at par. Shareholders approved this arrangement in January 1908. Earnings from mortality gains, excess interest, and lapses—reported to the Insurance Commissioner—could fund new business, but rapid growth demanded extra capital, typically sourced from contributions. The Protective Company's role was to supply this surplus, ensuring the Insurance Company's expansion.

A portion of its surplus was to be paid to the Protective Company for financing purposes. Later, repayments were to come only from surplus exceeding ten thousand dollars, or in case of dissolution, from the Insurance Company's assets as a debt. Essentially, the Insurance Company received funds from the Protective Company to grow its business, agreeing to repay only from surplus over ten thousand dollars, unless dissolved, in which case the amount would be treated as a debt. Was this arrangement unfair or illegal? The core issue is whether an insurance company can legally borrow money to expand its business, repaying only from surplus earnings unless dissolved, where it becomes a standard debt. A broader question is whether borrowing for business expansion is inherently wrong. The answer is clear: if such borrowing demonstrates sound management and efficient use of funds, it is not wrong. Properly spent, the money generates future profits, enhancing the company's value even before new business arrives. Borrowing under these terms cannot harm the company, as repayment depends on profitability.

Investing in new business is like planting seeds for a guaranteed future yield. If the funds are used effectively, the company benefits without risk of insolvency, as repayment is tied to profits. The Insurance Company's capital remained intact because the debt was payable from surplus, which represents net earnings. Even if repayable generally, each dollar spent on new business increased the company's value, balancing the loan liability. This logic is both sound and practical. The validity of this approach was further supported by calculations of the company's liquidating value, as seen in Schedule C of Defendants' Exhibit No. 23 and Huggins' testimony. Given these principles, the Protective Company's arrangement—advancing funds for new business, repayable only from surplus (or surplus above ten thousand dollars later), and treated as a debt only upon dissolution—was neither unfair nor invalid. It posed no harm to the Insurance Company or its stockholders. The same would hold true if the lender were the company's president, officers, directors, or even stockholders.

The arrangement would also be acceptable if the lender were another corporation with overlapping leadership or majority ownership of the Insurance Company. Since the contract terms were fair, the source of the funds was irrelevant. In fact, loans from stakeholders might be more advantageous, as their vested interest would likely ensure efficient and profitable use of the money. Therefore, the complainants cannot seek relief solely because the Protective Company provided funds under this repayment plan. The outcome would not change even if the Protective Company held exclusive rights to purchase the Insurance Company's unissued shares at par, securing long-term control.

Nor would the situation differ if the Protective Company had exclusive rights to acquire the Insurance Company's unissued stock at par, thereby maintaining permanent influence. The fairness of the contract terms remains the critical factor, not the lender's identity. Stakeholder involvement could even enhance the likelihood of prudent fund usage, benefiting the Insurance Company and its shareholders. Thus, the complainants' objections based on the lending arrangement or the Protective Company's privileges hold no merit.

Additionally, if the $360,000 in advances from the Protective Company are treated as debt, the Insurance Company's capital would be entirely depleted. The evidence strongly supports the complainants' claim that the real estate was significantly overvalued. While property valuation is challenging, $183,000 is clearly excessive, and a more accurate figure would be at least $20,000 lower, closer to $100,000. The exact extent of capital impairment is irrelevant here, but it does not automatically justify liquidating the company via receivership.

state laws grant the Insurance Commissioner broad authority and responsibilities over insurance companies operating within the state. The issue of capital impairment falls under his purview, including determining its consequences. This court should not interfere with his official duties, especially before he has acted or declined to act. However, refusing to intervene now does not mean the court is relinquishing jurisdiction. Testimony from the actuarial expert suggests the Insurance Company's liquidation value could repay the Protective Company's advances and still leave each share worth $22 to $24, despite a par value of $10 (see Schedule C of Defendant's Exhibit No. 23). Other evidence indicates the relationship between the two companies has been advantageous rather than harmful. While this doesn't address all allegations in the complaint, it may reasonably influence the court's choice of remedies. Should the Walsh contract be annulled,

the court must weigh the broader implications. The Insurance Commissioner's role is central here, and judicial restraint is advisable to avoid preempting his decisions. The actuarial evidence highlights the company's potential to settle debts and retain shareholder value, suggesting that immediate receivership may be unnecessary. The beneficial ties between the two companies further complicate the matter, as they may mitigate some claims in the complaint. Ultimately, the court's discretion in selecting remedies should account for these factors, balancing legal accountability with practical outcomes.

The complainants alleged that Basil S. Walsh, the company's president, secured an unfair commission contract in 1905, which was hidden in reports to the Insurance Commissioner. Walsh swore under oath that no officers received commissions, later claiming the unprofitable contract justified his answer. This explanation is inadequate. He accepted a valueless debt to improve the company's reports, receiving substantial premiums in return. While the contract doesn’t clearly benefit the company, it isn’t unjust enough to warrant court intervention. Walsh even offered to cancel the contract if deemed unfair, but his misleading statement remains problematic.

His false report is the most concerning aspect. Testimony shows he abstained from voting when the board approved his proposal, and no breach of trust is evident. The contract doesn’t justify appointing a receiver, nor is there a specific request for relief. Despite deceptive bookkeeping, misleading reports, and questionable dividends, these issues—though reprehensible—don’t warrant court action against the company. Exposure or the Insurance Commissioner may address some problems, but the court shouldn’t take over the company’s management. The stock option’s validity and the Protective Company’s financial arrangement were deemed fair.

Since the Protective Company’s financial support to the Insurance Company was legal and fair, the court can only prohibit dividends not from surplus or net profits. Both defendants willingly allowed full access to their records. Without grounds for dividend-related relief, the case should be dismissed. However, the Insurance Company’s deceptive reports likely caused the litigation, so both defendants should share some costs due to shared managerial responsibility. Note: The Supreme Court upheld the Chancellor’s decree in June 1918. See post p. 428.

HOLLAND, Justice. Defendant John R. Smith appealed his denied request to lower his sex offender tier from III to II, arguing his common name could cause misdirected registration notices. The State countered that Tier III is mandatory for his conviction under Del-Code Ann. tit. 11, § 4121(e)(1)(a). The Superior Court agreed, denying his request. On appeal, Smith claims the court misapplied the statute and that Tier III violates the ex post facto clause. We reject these arguments and affirm the judgment. Background: In June 1996, Smith was arrested and charged with five sex offenses in the Justice of the Peace Court.

Smith faced charges including Unlawful Sexual Contact in the Second Degree, followed by additional sex offenses. In March 1997, as part of a plea deal, he pleaded guilty to one count of Unlawful Sexual Intercourse in the Second Degree and one count of Unlawful Sexual Contact in the Second Degree. Smith acknowledged the registration requirements and agreed to re-register upon release. On June 27, 1997, he received a 22-year sentence, suspended after ten years, with twelve years of supervision. The State dropped fifteen other charges, and the court ordered the Department of Correction to notify upon his release.

Delaware's sex offender registration law, DeLCode Ann. tit. 11, § 4120 et seq., was updated in July 1998 to mandate registration for offenders convicted under Section 4121(a)(4) upon release from Level V or IV facilities. The amendment introduced three Risk Assessment Tiers, with offenders assigned based on their conviction. Section 4122(a) applied the law to convictions between June 21, 1996, and March 1, 1999. Unlawful Sexual Intercourse in the Second Degree fell under Tier III.

Smith argued his Tier III classification was incorrect, claiming he should be in Tier II since he was initially charged with Unlawful Sexual Contact in the Second Degree. However, the plea agreement included Unlawful Sexual Intercourse in the Second Degree, and Smith knowingly accepted the terms. The record shows he was aware of the Tier III requirement and benefited from the plea deal. The Superior Court rightly upheld his Tier III classification.

Smith's second claim alleged an ex post facto violation, but the court ruled Delaware's registration law is not punitive, rejecting his argument. The Superior Court's judgment was affirmed, requiring Smith to register every 90 days for life under Tier III. On September 28, 2005, his sentence was adjusted to clarify these terms.

Modify the work release program for the Level IV segment of the sentence and adjust the hold level from Level III to Level IV. The risk assessment tier issue was not resolved. Super. Ct.Crim. R. 11(e)(1)(C). The Superior Court noted in its sentencing order, 'The requirements of 11 Del. C. § 4120 and 4336, Sex Offender Registration and Community Notification, are applicable to this case.'
