It’s also notable that Mrs. Langmeier’s initial examination, requested by Marlene Holland and Judge Gallo, took place on June 15, 1981.

Dr. Weintraub mentioned meeting Judge Gallo at Mrs. Langmeier’s home on August 6, 1981, and observing her as Judge Gallo reviewed the will he was preparing. Judge Gallo disputes this, denying any discussion of the will that day and claiming Dr. Weintraub’s memory is faulty. At trial, Judge Gallo testified that he explained Delaware’s testamentary capacity laws to Dr. Weintraub over the phone. Dr. Weintraub, however, stated he was unaware of these laws even during the trial. In his deposition, Judge Gallo assumed Weintraub knew the requirements due to his 30 years of experience. Judge Gallo also testified that on August 13, 1981, after reviewing the will with Mrs. Langmeier, everyone except Dr. Weintraub left the room.

Dr. Weintraub then privately went over the will with her. According to Judge Gallo, they returned after Dr. Weintraub called them back, confirming Mrs. Langmeier was fine for the signing. Dr. Weintraub’s account differs; he insists he never reviewed the will’s terms privately with her on August 13, 1981. Judson Ryon, another will witness, stated he only realized he was witnessing a will upon arriving at her home. As her hearing aid provider, he assumed his role was to ensure she could hear. By signing, he merely confirmed her signature in his presence and admitted he couldn’t assess her competency, relying on Dr. Weintraub’s presence.

Mr. Linarducci, assigned to represent Mrs. Langmeier in the guardianship case, visited her on July 9 and 16, 1981. Initially concerned about her competency, he wouldn’t have called her as a witness. By the second visit, she seemed more responsive, leading him to believe her condition varied daily. Notably, on July 16, Mrs. Langmeier expressed her wish to leave $25,000 each to Marlene Holland and Frank Bolden in her will, noting Marlene’s short tenure. Mr. Linarducci had no involvement in drafting the will or employment contract and only saw them after Mrs. Langmeier’s passing.

Regarding his death, he was not involved in signing these documents on August 13, 1981. Considering these factors, I must conclude that Marlene Holland's testimony cannot be fully trusted. Additionally, the evidence presented by the will's supporter shows inconsistencies concerning Mrs. Langmeier's mental capacity on that date and whether her decision to leave most of her estate to Marlene Holland was truly voluntary. Combined with the opposing evidence, I find it sufficient to rule that the opposing party has met its burden in this case. The complexity arises from the legal requirement that the party challenging the will must prove incapacity and undue influence at the exact time the will was signed.

Six individuals were present either during or around the time Mrs. Langmeier signed her will on August 13, 1981. Judge Gallo, his office's notarizing attorney, Dr. Weintraub, and Judson Ryon were present during the signing. Marlene Holland and her lawyer, Mr. Flynn, were with her shortly before and after. All except the notarizing attorney testified in favor of validating the will. Since no one from the opposing side was present, they cannot directly refute this testimony. However, circumstantial evidence about the testator's state of mind at the critical moment can still be considered, as established in legal precedents.

The presence or absence of testamentary capacity or undue influence can be proven through both direct and circumstantial evidence. However, such evidence must ultimately demonstrate the testator's mental state and freedom of will precisely when the will was executed. Circumstantial evidence involves inferring a fact from other proven facts, and it holds equal weight to direct testimony in legal proceedings, as supported by case law and legal scholarship.

While only the will's supporter provided direct evidence about the testatrix's condition on August 13, 1981, this does not solely determine the outcome. Established rules for will contests allow evidence of the testatrix's mental and physical state before and after the will's signing to be considered. Medical experts' opinions generally carry more weight than those of lay witnesses. Additionally, the witnesses who signed the will, due to their role, are presumed to offer credible testimony regarding the execution process.

Legal regulations concerning the testator during the will's execution, particularly for assessing his mental capacity, allow witnesses to share their opinions on whether his mind seemed sound or unsound at the time. If these witnesses are deemed intelligent and truthful, their views carry significant authority. Rodney v. Burton, supra; Ethridge v. Bennett's Executors, supra. However, the credibility of a subscribing witness's opinion hinges on their chance to observe and evaluate the testator's mental state and how they utilized that opportunity. If they lacked or failed to use this opportunity, their opinion loses its special legal weight, as the law values such testimony based on the witness's observational access and likelihood of using it due to their involvement in the process. In re Miller's Will, supra. In this jurisdiction, testamentary capacity means the testator must, at execution, be able to think, reflect, and judge, understanding their actions and property disposition.

He must possess adequate memory and comprehension to grasp the nature of his actions. In re Estate of Bandurski, Del.Ch., 281 A.2d 621 (1971); Rodney v. Burton, supra; Pritchard v. Henderson, supra. Could the individual comprehend that they were distributing their estate via a will and to whom? In re Miller's Will, supra; Smith v. Day, supra. Was he capable of recalling the property he was distributing and its beneficiaries? Steele v. Helm, supra. If so, the will stands valid, irrespective of whether the distribution seems unwise to others or the testator's mental state before or after execution. Regarding undue influence, the law is clear: it refers to excessive influence given the case's context. For influence to be undue, it must dominate the testator's mind, override their free will, and compel them to draft a will reflecting another's intentions, not their own.

This can occur through persuasion, pressure, flattery, intimidation, or other means. Regardless of the method, the undue influence must have affected the testator's mind during the will's execution. Key elements include a vulnerable testator, the chance to exert influence, an intent to do so improperly, the actual application of such influence, and a resulting impact. Nardo v. Nardo, supra; Conner v. Brown, Del.Super., 3 A.2d 64 (1938). Applying these criteria to the evidence, I conclude the caveator has proven Alice Langmeier lacked the capacity to execute a will on August 13, 1981, and that the will resulted from undue influence as legally defined. On testamentary capacity, the caveator presented expert testimony from three medical professionals,

one who examined her six weeks before the will and two who treated her five days after. Their expertise is undisputed. All agreed, with reasonable medical certainty, that on August 13, 1981, Alice Langmeier could not make complex decisions, understand will-making, or devise a rational property distribution plan. The opposing medical opinion comes only from Dr. Weintraub, who, despite being hired to assess her capacity, asked no questions about her property, heirs, testamentary intentions, or reasons for a new will. His closest inquiry was asking if she knew why Judge Gallo sent her for evaluation; she reportedly did not. Furthermore, he never evaluated her against Delaware's legal standards for testamentary capacity thereafter. This is for the

The simple reason was his lack of awareness. L. Kent Wyatt, the attorney Dr. Hayes consulted, concluded on June 26 that Mrs. Langmeier lacked testamentary capacity. She couldn’t answer questions about her property intelligently—she only recalled owning a house and a car—and didn’t grasp the idea of a trust or trustee. That same day, she couldn’t remember her housekeeper’s name, even though Marlene Holland had accompanied her to Dr. Hayes’s office. The record shows no clear evidence that Mrs. Langmeier fully understood the extent of her estate in the summer of 1981. This was evident at the August 13 signing when, after executing her will, she questioned Judge Gallo about whether she could afford a $400 weekly payment to Holland, only signing after his reassurance.

Judge Gallo assured her she had ample funds. Another notable event on August 13, though previously unmentioned, involved Thomas Posatko. Appointed by the court on July 30, 1981, to monitor Mrs. Langmeier’s well-being, Posatko met her around August 7 to introduce himself. Their meeting was friendly, with Mr. Flynn also present. On the morning of August 13, unaware of the will signing later that day, Posatko visited her to read a letter from a Missouri relative. Despite their recent meeting, Mrs. Langmeier didn’t recognize him, mistaking him for a relative of Arthur Langmeier—just hours before she signed the will.

During the August 13 signing, Marlene Holland’s credibility as a witness is questionable due to her vested interest. The notarizing attorney from Judge Gallo’s office didn’t testify, and Gallo’s account conflicted significantly with others’, casting doubt on his recall. Mr. Flynn wasn’t present when the will was explained or signed, so he couldn’t attest to Mrs. Langmeier’s state of mind at that time. However, he confirmed that shortly after signing, she couldn’t even write her name, raising concerns about her capacity during the execution.

Only Judson Ryon and Dr. Weintraub, the subscribing witnesses, provided testimony. Dr. Weintraub believed Mrs. Langmeier could make a will if given slow, supportive explanations and thought she was competent on August 13. However, he admitted he didn’t re-examine her that day, relying instead on her lack of questions or objections to Judge Gallo’s explanations. Judson Ryon testified he noticed nothing amiss with Mrs. Langmeier, but his account lacks the depth to fully counter the doubts about her testamentary capacity.

On August 13, Meier admitted in his testimony that he barely noticed Mrs. Langmeier during the will's explanation. He believed his role as a witness was solely to confirm her signature, so he moved away to avoid intruding on Judge Gallo's discussion with her. He later testified that he stayed by the doorway to avoid eavesdropping, as he felt it was not his concern. When questioned about assessing Mrs. Langmeier's mental competence, he outright stated he was unqualified to do so, further admitting he couldn't judge her capacity to sign legal documents that day. Thus, his testimony holds little weight.

The credibility typically given to Judson Ryon as a witness is effectively nullified. As the fact-finder, the Court must weigh the evidence and determine its reliability. Factors such as witness impartiality, their firsthand knowledge, memory accuracy, and other relevant details are considered, as established in legal precedents like Benson v. Wilmington City Ry. Co. Applying these principles here, the evidence strongly suggests Alice Langmeier lacked the mental capacity to execute a will on August 13, 1981. Similarly, the circumstantial proof of undue influence is compelling, particularly given Marlene Holland's sudden involvement in Mrs. Langmeier's affairs.

Marlene Holland's entry into Mrs. Langmeier's life led to several suspicious occurrences, indicating the testatrix's vulnerability and Holland's undue influence. These included cash gifts exceeding $9,000, mostly processed by Holland, and a $5,000 check taken out of sequence when a relative planned to visit—an act without justification. The gradual isolation of Mrs. Langmeier from her neighbors, friends, and Missouri relatives further raised concerns. Additionally, the cashing of Series H bonds and the alleged $34,500 gift to Holland were orchestrated entirely by Holland, with Mrs. Langmeier remaining silent during bank interactions despite staff attempts to engage her directly.

The employment agreement ultimately removes any uncertainty regarding undue influence. The guardianship was meant to safeguard Mrs. Langmeier from exploitation, with Delaware Trust Company appointed to oversee her finances and prevent unwise transactions. Despite this, Holland arranged periodic payments for her role as a companion while secretly pursuing additional financial gains. This blatant overreach underscores the manipulation at play, violating the guardianship's protective intent and demonstrating Holland's exploitation of Mrs. Langmeier's vulnerable state.

Mrs. Langmeier secured a more favorable arrangement by dealing directly with Mr. Flynn, her attorney, without informing Delaware Trust Company. She provided him with specific instructions, and he prepared the agreement as testified, which I find credible. The employment contract was only drafted the day before signing, and neither Mrs. Langmeier nor her attorney, Judge Gallo, had reviewed it until Mr. Flynn presented it on August 13. Her lack of awareness of its terms is evident when she asked Judge Gallo if she could afford $400 weekly, suggesting no prior intention to pay Marlene Holland that sum. The agreement and will, leaving her $1 million estate to Holland, were presented together under questionable circumstances, with Holland’s chosen lawyer and doctor present.

Mrs. Langmeier signed the employment agreement against her own interests, likely without understanding it, after being assured she could afford it. Given the guardianship and Holland’s awareness of it, this reveals Holland’s intent to exploit their relationship for personal gain. The timing and execution of the will further suggest undue influence, supported by Mr. Linarducci’s testimony. On July 16, 1981, Mrs. Langmeier appeared competent yet expressed a wish to leave Holland only $25,000, contradicting the later will. This discrepancy underscores that the agreement reflected Holland’s intentions, not Langmeier’s, demonstrating Holland’s control over her by August 13, 1981.

The employment agreement unmistakably represented Marlene Holland’s interests, not Alice Langmeier’s. Combined with other evidence of Langmeier’s subjugation to Holland’s influence, the will of August 13, 1981, was unduly influenced. Despite any initial goodwill between them, Holland’s actions were self-serving. Consequently, I rule in favor of the caveator on both undue influence and testamentary capacity grounds. This case paints a troubling picture of exploitation in a vulnerable relationship.

This case presents a tragic scenario. Alice Langmeier, once a dignified and educated woman, faced an undeserved end. In her final months, isolated at 85, she found comfort in someone she could assist, but the situation devolved into legal and medical chaos, severing ties with her few acquaintances. Her deposition revealed a broken, incoherent figure, a stark contrast to her former self. Such misfortunes are timeless, yet no less regrettable. Credit is due to both legal teams for their professionalism in handling this complex case, as seen in similar precedents like Ethridge v. Bennett’s Executors.

Case Overview Prior Proceedings Key Rulings This appeal from the Court of Chancery's final judgment involves combined lawsuits: an initial Delaware statutory appraisal case (the 'appraisal action') and a subsequent shareholder suit for rescissory damages due to alleged fraud and unfair dealings (the 'personal liability action') filed by plaintiffs Cinerama, Inc. ('Cinerama'), a New York-based firm, and Cede & Co. ('Cede'), the registered owner. The disputes arise from a 1982-83 cash-out merger where Technicolor, Incorporated ('Technicolor'), a Delaware company, was acquired by MacAndrews & Forbes Group, Incorporated ('MAF'), a

Delaware corporation, via a merger with Macanfor Corporation ('Macanfor'), a fully owned MAF subsidiary. The tender offer and subsequent merger proposed $23 per share in cash to Technicolor shareholders (excluding MAF and affiliates). Cinerama owned 201,200 Technicolor shares, representing 4.405% of outstanding shares. It declined the initial MAF acquisition offer starting November 4, 1982, and opposed the second-stage merger finalized on January 24, 1983. After dissent, Cinerama sought a share appraisal in March 1983 under 8 Del.C. § 262. During pretrial discovery, Cinerama uncovered testimony suggesting director misconduct in the company's sale. In January 1986, Cinerama filed another suit in the Court of Chancery against Technicolor

, seven of the nine Technicolor board members during the merger, MAF, Macanfor, and Ronald O. Perelman ('Perelman'), MAF's Chairman and primary shareholder. The personal liability action included claims of fraud, fiduciary breach, and unfair dealing, seeking rescissory damages among other remedies. Cinerama also argued the merger was void from inception due to lack of unanimous director approval for repealing a Technicolor charter supermajority clause. Defendants moved to dismiss, claiming Cinerama lacked standing after pursuing appraisal. The Chancellor denied dismissal but ruled Cinerama must later choose which claim to pursue. Cinerama appealed, and this Court reversed. Cede & Co. v. Technicolor, Inc., Del.Supr., 642 A.2d 1182 (1988) ('Cede I'). In Cede I, we found the Chancellor erred legally by requiring an election of remedies.

Prior to the trial, we ruled that the plaintiff shareholder could pursue both its appraisal claim and personal liability claim simultaneously through the trial process. The case was sent back for a combined trial on these matters. After a lengthy trial and additional discovery, the Chancellor chose to address the appraisal case first, despite this Court's implied guidance in Cede I. In an unpublished decision on October 19, 1990, the Chancellor set the fair value of the dissenting shareholders' Technicolor stock at $21.60 per share as of the merger date, January 24, 1988. Later, in June 1991, the court issued another unpublished decision, finding strong evidence of fiduciary breaches by the defendant directors but ruled that Cinerama failed to prove its case, resulting in a judgment for the defendants. The court also dismissed Cinerama's additional claims.

Cinerama's other arguments—that the merger was void from the start, that Technicolor's directors violated disclosure duties in their 14D-9 filing and proxy statement, and that MAF and Perelman breached fiduciary duties as controlling shareholders—were also rejected. Cinerama appealed both rulings. Regarding the Personal Liability Opinion, we see no validity in Cinerama's claims for rescissory damages. While we agree with the Chancellor's materiality standard for duty of loyalty, we disagree with his reasonable person analysis but leave the loyalty issue unresolved. The trial court did not consider the impact of Technicolor's charter requirement for unanimous director approval (for mergers with less than 95% shareholder support) on the presumed 'material' disloyalty of directors Sullivan and Ryan. The court also overlooked the relevance of Delaware Code § 144's interested-director provisions.

These provisions pertain to: (1) the business judgment rule's loyalty requirement; (2) Technicolor's charter stipulations; and (3) Cinerama's rescissory damages claim, should it succeed under an entire fairness review. We further find the trial court erred in redefining the business judgment rule's duty of care standards for an arm's-length transaction without evidence of bad faith or self-dealing. The Chancellor incorrectly placed an unprecedented burden on Cinerama to prove board negligence to rebut the rule. Additionally, the court wrongly limited damages for wrongfully cashed-out shareholders to the difference between fair appraisal value and the tender offer price. Beyond the unresolved loyalty issues, we find the business judgment presumption rebutted due to the board's lack of due care.

Consequently, we reverse and remand the personal liability action with instructions to apply the entire fairness standard to the merger. This decision makes Cinerama's appeal of the Appraisal Opinion irrelevant. As background, Technicolor, a leader in film processing since 1970, faced declining competitiveness by the late 1970s. CEO Morton Kamerman described its main lab as 'totally out of control,' incurring significant losses. Despite its industry dominance, Technicolor struggled to maintain its position, prompting restructuring efforts.

The CEO launched initiatives to cut costs at Technicolor's film labs and address inefficiencies. By the late 1970s, Kamerman's efforts boosted market share and profits, but growth stalled in the early 1980s. Recognizing limited long-term potential in theatrical film processing, despite its 50% net income contribution, Kamerman proposed 'One Hour Photo' (OHP)—a rapid consumer film service. Approved in 1981, the plan aimed for 1,000 stores and a $150M investment, briefly lifting stock to $22.13.

The market responded poorly to Technicolor's OHP announcement, with shares dropping nearly $4. Concerns arose over the $150M investment versus $78M equity. Store openings lagged, and early locations reported losses. As competition hurt core film processing and other divisions struggled, only 21 of 50 planned OHP stores opened by 1982, with a projected $5.2M loss. Kamerman remained optimistic, calling OHP a growth opportunity.

Technicolor's 1982 financials showed an 80% net income drop, from $17.073M to $3.445M, blamed on division write-offs and declining film processing profits. By September 1982, shares hit a low of $8.37. Meanwhile, MAF's Perelman saw Technicolor as a takeover target, despite MAF being smaller. After failed bids elsewhere, he pursued Technicolor discreetly, aware of financial and hostile-bid constraints.

Perelman, unknown to Technicolor's management, faced lender opposition to hostile bids and a 95% supermajority merger requirement. In September 1982, he sought advice on accessing Technicolor, learning Bear Stearns' Tarnopol had ties to director Sullivan. Tarnopol relayed Perelman's interest, leading to a secret lunch meeting. Sullivan disclosed nothing to fellow directors about the discussion or planned meeting.

The board members of Technicolor. On Monday, September 13, Sullivan asked his secretary to contact his stockbroker and buy ten thousand shares of Technicolor stock at market price. Brown ('Brown') from Debevoise & Plimpton as external legal counsel. in the coming weeks. Isham, who was retired and often traveled, remained on standby. The court noted the parties disputed these details, with Brown testifying he supported the release while Kamerman did not.

In New York, Goldman assembled a valuation package, and three days later, on October 21, they informed Kamerman via phone that a price range of $20-$22 was worth exploring. However, Goldman also recommended that Kamerman evaluate other potential buyers for Technicolor. Goldman developed an LBO model, assessing Technicolor's value and MAF's financial status. Beyond this, Goldman conducted no additional financial analysis for Technicolor's sale to MAF, aside from a fairness opinion for the October 29 board meeting. Goldman also updated its October 21 LBO analysis for the board presentation. On October 27, six days after Kamerman received Goldman Sachs' fairness opinion, he and Perelman agreed on a price over the phone. Perelman initially proposed $22.50 per share, but Kamerman countered with $23, stating he would recommend it to the board, which Perelman accepted. That evening, Kamerman

directed Technicolor's general counsel, Oliphant, to draft a notice for a special board meeting scheduled for 10:00 a.m. on October 29 in New York City. Technicolor asked the New York Stock Exchange to suspend trading of its stock. The meeting notice did not reveal its purpose, and only a few directors were informed before October 28. All nine directors attended. Three—Lewis, Isham, and Bjorkman—had limited awareness of the proposed sale, with Bjorkman and Lewis only knowing what Kamerman had shared beforehand. Three others—Simone, Frye (former head of Technicolor's Consumer Processing Division), and Blanco (CEO of its Government Services Division)—were unaware of the sale until the meeting. Ryan, the President and COO,

knew little beyond what he had gathered indirectly from Davis of Gulf & Western. Before the meeting, Kamerman had only cryptically told Ryan on October 27, 'Something is going on. I'm negotiating with someone...' The Technicolor board met on October 29 to discuss MAF's proposal. Kamerman detailed Bear Stearns' involvement on MAF's behalf and summarized his negotiations with Perelman. He mentioned receiving an initial offer of $20 per share, countering with $25, and finally agreeing to $23. Kamerman advised the board that $23 was 'good' as it represented ten times core earnings of $2.30-$2.50 per share. He recommended accepting MAF's offer, citing Technicolor's low market value and a projected $1 per share loss on the One Hour Photo business. He argued the company was vulnerable to a takeover due to its depressed stock price.

Kamerman asserted that accepting $23 per share was 'prudent rather than gambling' on the One Hour Photo venture's success. He outlined the deal's structure: a tender offer by MAF at $23 per share for all outstanding shares, followed by a merger converting remaining shares at the same price, making Technicolor a wholly owned MAF subsidiary. Kamerman detailed MAF's option to buy 844,000 unissued shares and its stock purchase agreement with him, Bjorkman, and their wives. He also summarized his proposed employment contract with MAF and noted Technicolor would pay Sullivan a $150,000 finder's fee, acknowledging their financial stake in the deal. Kamerman then handed the meeting to outside counsel Brown, who was unaware that Sullivan, Bjorkman, Lewis, and Isham had limited prior knowledge of the sale, while Blanco, Simone, and Frye had none.

Brown outlined the proposed transaction's structure, summarized the merger terms, and reviewed key documents. He informed the board they weren't required to accept Perelman's offer or seek alternatives. Goldman delivered an oral presentation using a 78-page 'board book,' covering Technicolor's financial projections, stock data, and ownership details. Their LBO analysis concluded that $23 per share was fair, pending further review. Some directors proposed negotiating for a higher price, but Perelman was firm. Director Simone suggested seeking other offers, but the board favored certainty, rejecting the idea. Meeting minutes and court records show the board unanimously approved the merger with MAF, recommending shareholders accept $23 per share and repeal the supermajority provision.

The board also approved the Stock Option Agreement, Sullivan's finder's fee, and Kamerman's employment contract. Post-meeting, Technicolor announced the acquisition terms via press release. In November 1982, Technicolor filed SEC forms 14D-9 and 13D, endorsing MAF's $23 per share tender offer. By December 3, MAF acquired 82.19% of Technicolor shares, closing the offer on November 30. A special shareholder meeting was scheduled for January 24, 1983, with proxy statements including Goldman's November 19 fairness opinion. At the meeting, 89% of shareholders voted to repeal the supermajority amendment and approve the merger.

The central issue is whether the Technicolor board's October 29 merger approval with MAF is protected by the business judgment rule or subject to judicial review for fairness. The Chancellor found no collective breach of loyalty by the board, though Directors Sullivan and Ryan may have acted disloyally. The court also suggested all directors might have breached their duty of care. Despite Sullivan's conflict of interest, the Chancellor ruled Cinerama failed to prove the board's independence was compromised, upholding the business judgment presumption.

Regarding duty of care, the court stated Cinerama must prove monetary loss from the board's breach and quantify it. The Chancellor doubted the board met its care obligations in approving the merger but emphasized negligence alone wasn't sufficient without demonstrated harm. The business judgment rule's presumption of due care required Cinerama to show tangible losses, which it failed to do.

The injury does not warrant legal action. The court further explained that a judicial determination of a director's good faith and loyalty in an independent, third-party transaction should mitigate the impact of a board's failure to exercise due care in a company sale. The Chancellor's reasoning for downplaying the due care aspect of the business judgment rule in such transactions stemmed from a concern that the rule, unaltered, could produce severe outcomes. The Chancellor explicitly referenced this Court's ruling in Smith v. Van Gorkom, Del.Supr., 488 A.2d 858 (1985), noting the plaintiff's argument for revisiting the precedent set in that case. Personal Liability Opinion at 3. This appeal addresses three key questions related to the Delaware business judgment rule, including the Chancellor's interpretation of the duty of loyalty in claims involving director self-interest or lack of independence.

Cinerama argues that the Chancellor made significant legal errors in interpreting and applying the business judgment rule's requirements for director loyalty and care. They claim the Chancellor imposed unreasonable proof burdens on shareholders for breaches of these duties, which are inconsistent with equity and Delaware law. Even under the court's revised loyalty standard, Cinerama contends the record lacks sufficient evidence to support the finding that most directors did not breach their duty of loyalty. Cinerama has dropped its claim of bad faith by the directors, except for Director Sullivan, and is appealing other unfavorable rulings by the Chancellor.

The court found no convincing evidence of bad faith among the directors, except for Director Sullivan, concluding they acted in good faith during the merger approval. Personal Liability Opinion at 36-37. The remaining contested rulings, mentioned earlier and appealed by Cinerama, will be addressed later. Defendants acknowledge the Chancellor's innovative approach to the duty of care, requiring proof of harm for a breach to be actionable, but defend it as sound despite lacking precedent. They argue the Chancellor's 'material interest' standard for the duty of loyalty is not new but a rephrasing. Defendants seek affirmation on all appealed issues and challenge the Chancellor's findings on the directors' duty of care breaches as erroneous.

We identify reversible errors in the Chancellor's handling of both the duty of loyalty and duty of care. The cross-appeal by the defendants lacks merit. The core issues involve the interpretation and application of the business judgment rule's loyalty and care standards, which are legal questions subject to de novo review. Kahn v. Household Acquisition Corp., Del.Supr., 591 A.2d 166, 175-76 (1991); Waggoner v. Laster, Del.Supr., 581 A.2d 1127, 1132 (1990). If the rule's elements are correctly defined, the trial court's factual findings on loyalty or care are given considerable deference unless clearly wrong.

result of a systematic and analytical thought process. Citron v. Fairchild Camera & Instrument Corp., Del.Supr., 569 A.2d 53, 64 (1989); see also Levitt v. Bouvier, Del.Supr., 287 A.2d 671, 673 (1972). Foundational Principles and Components of the Delaware Business Judgment Rule Our foundation lies in the core tenet of Delaware law that corporate operations and decisions are overseen by or under the guidance of its board of directors. 8 Del.C. § 141(a). In fulfilling these responsibilities, directors bear a steadfast fiduciary obligation to safeguard the corporation's welfare and prioritize shareholder interests. Guth v. Loft, Inc., Del.Supr., 5 A.2d 503, 510 (1939); Aronson v. Lewis, Del.Supr., 473 A.2d 805, 811 (1984); Van Gorkom, 488 A.2d at 87

2; Mills Acquisition Co. v. Macmillan, Inc., Del.Supr., 559 A.2d 1261, 1280 (1988). The business judgment rule stems from these foundational concepts. The rule prevents courts from unjustifiably interfering in corporate governance. See Mills, 559 A.2d at 1279; Unocal Corp. v. Mesa Petroleum Co., Del.Supr., 493 A.2d 946, 954 (1985); Sinclair Oil Corp. v. Levien, Del.Supr., 280 A.2d 717, 720 (1971); A.C. Acquisitions Corp. v. Anderson, Clayton & Co., Del.Ch., 519 A.2d 103, 111 (1986). Though established long ago, the rule was recently reaffirmed by this Court as follows: It functions both as a procedural framework for litigation and a substantive legal standard. As an evidentiary principle, it

establishes a presumption that corporate directors acted with due diligence, in good faith, and with sincere belief that their decisions served the company’s best interests. Aronson v. Lewis, Del.Supr., 473 A.2d 805, 812 (1984). This presumption applies to board-approved transactions within their authority unless evidence of fraud, bad faith, or self-interest arises. Grobow v. Perot, Del.Supr., 539 A.2d 180, 187 (1988). See Allaun v. Consolidated Oil Co., Del. Ch., [16 Del.Ch. 318] 147 A. 257, 261 (1929). Citron, 569 A.2d at 64 (applying the rule to a third-party sale without self-dealing); see also Unocal, 493 A.

2d at 954. The rule strongly presumes director actions are valid unless they lack any reasonable business justification. Sinclair Oil Corp., 280 A.2d at 720; see also Unocal, 493 A.2d at 954. Thus, shareholders challenging a board decision must first overcome this presumption. Aronson, 473 A.2d at 812; Van Gorkom, 488 A.2d at 872; Citron, 569 A.2d at 64. To do so, plaintiffs must demonstrate directors breached any aspect of their fiduciary duty—good faith, loyalty, or due care. See Citron, 569 A.2d at 64; Van Gorkom, 488 A.2d at 872; Aronson, 473 A

At 812.2d, if a shareholder plaintiff cannot meet this burden of proof, the business judgment rule applies to shield corporate officers and directors and their decisions, preventing courts from questioning these judgments. See, e.g., Citron, 569 A.2d at 64; Van Gorkom, 488 A.2d at 872; see also 8 Del.C. § 141(a). If the rule is overcome, the burden then shifts to the defendant directors to demonstrate the 'entire fairness' of the transaction to the plaintiff. Nixon v. Blackwell, Del.Supr., 626 A.2d 1366, 1376 (1993); Mills, 559 A.2d at 1279; Weinberger v. UOP, Inc., Del.Supr., 457 A.2d 701, 710 (1983). Under the entire fairness standard, directors must prove to the court's satisfaction

that the transaction involved both fair dealing and a fair price. Nixon, 626 A.2d at 1376; Mills, 559 A.2d at 1279; Weinberger, 457 A.2d at 710. Additionally, in cases involving a company sale, directors must show that the price was the highest reasonably attainable. Mills, 559 A.2d at 1288; see also Citron, 569 A.2d at 67-68 (the board must secure the best possible deal for shareholders) (citing Revlon, Inc. v. MacAndrews & Forbes Holdings, Inc., Del.Supr., 506 A.2d 173 (1986)). IV. DIRECTOR DUTY OF LOYALTY/BOARD DUTY OF LOYALTY Presumption of Loyalty/Duty of Loyalty This Court has consistently defined the duty of loyalty in strict terms, requiring officers and directors

to avoid using their trusted positions for personal gain. A longstanding public policy, rooted in an understanding of human behavior, mandates that corporate officers and directors must rigorously uphold their duty to protect the corporation’s interests and avoid actions that could harm it or deprive it of potential benefits. The principle of undivided loyalty requires no conflict between duty and personal interest. Guth, 5 A.2d at 510; see also Ivanhoe Partners v. Newmont Mining Corp., Del.Supr., 535 A.2d 1334, 1345 (1987). Essentially, the duty of loyalty requires prioritizing the corporation’s and shareholders’ interests over any personal interests of a director, officer, or controlling shareholder.

Pogostin v. Rice, Del.Supr., 480 A.2d 619, 624 (1984); Aronson, 473 A.2d at 812. Typical instances of director self-interest include a director being on both sides of a transaction or gaining a personal benefit not shared by shareholders. See Nixon, 626 A.2d at 1375; Gilbert v. El Paso Co., Del.Supr., 575 A.2d 1131, 1146 (1990); Weinberger, 457 A.2d at 710; Aronson, 473 A.2d at 812; Sterling v. Mayflower Hotel Corp., Del.Supr., 93 A.2d 107, 110 (1952); see also Ernest L. Folk, Delaware General Corporation Law: A Commentary and Analysis § 141.2 at 141:17 and § 14

1.33 (3d ed. 1992). An independent director is typically defined as one whose decisions are solely based on the corporate merits of a transaction, free from personal or external influences. See Aronson, 473 A.2d at 816; Pogostin, 480 A.2d at 624. Conversely, a director who gains significant benefits from endorsing a transaction cannot be considered impartial. See Folk, Delaware General Corporation Law § 141.2 at 141:33. This principle limits our evaluation of the Court of Chancery's duty of loyalty framework. The Chancellor's Approach to Proving Director Self-Interest in Cinerama The Chancellor determined that proving a director's self-interest in an arms-length third-party transaction requires stronger evidence than in traditional self-dealing cases where directors are on both sides. Without clear self-dealing, the court held that evidence of personal or special benefits to a director does not

automatically undermine independence under the business judgment rule unless the benefit is deemed 'material.' The Chancellor defined material self-interest in third-party transactions as needing to meet two criteria: (1) it must likely influence the judgment of a reasonable person in the director's position, and (2) it must affect the board's collective decision. Applying this test, the Chancellor found Cinerama's evidence met the first criterion for Director Sullivan and possibly Director Ryan but failed the second. The court ruled that Sullivan's and Ryan's interests did not compromise the board's overall independence. Breaching Director Independence to Rebut the Business Judgment Rule The issue is whether the Chancellor's standard for proving director independence aligns with Delaware precedent. Unfortunately, defendants have not presented convincing case law from Delaware or elsewhere supporting the

trial court's decisions. Neither party has addressed relevant Delaware statutes. As a result, we refrain from ruling on some issues, deeming them premature for appeal. The Chancellor's Two-Part Test for Material Self-Interest The Chancellor established a two-part test to determine if a director's self-interest is significant enough to challenge the presumption of independence. Shareholders must prove: (1) the self-interest's materiality to the director's impartiality, and (2) its materiality to the board's collective independence. Materiality under either part requires showing the interest could reasonably sway a reasonable board member's decision. We find no Delaware case law endorsing this interpretation of the business judgment rule in third-party transactions, and the parties cite no supporting authority. Additionally, the parties neglected key questions, such as whether the Chancellor's second criterion aligns with Delaware law and whether

the Chancellor properly applied it here. While we uphold the first part of the materiality test as consistent with Delaware law, we remand unresolved issues regarding the second part. Cinerama's Challenge to the Chancellor's Test Cinerama argues the Chancellor's standard for rebutting the business judgment rule is legally flawed. It claims any director benefit not shared by stockholders should suffice to overcome the presumption of independence. Cinerama cites Aronson and Pogostin, but we find these references taken out of context. In Aronson, this Court stated that to prove a loyalty breach, a plaintiff must show a director was on both sides of a transaction or gained a personal financial benefit through self-dealing, not just a general benefit.

The responsibility falls on the corporation or all stockholders collectively.' Aronson, 473 A.2d at 812 (citations omitted) (emphasis added). Therefore, Aronson's condition that personal financial gain must amount to self-dealing aligns with and reinforces the Chancellor's interpretation. Cinerama also misinterprets this Court's remark in Pogostin, which states that '[d]irectorial interest arises when a director gains, or is set to gain, personal financial advantage from the disputed transaction not equally available to stockholders.' 480 A.2d at 624 (emphasis added). Cinerama misreads Pogostin. Our statement does not imply that a single director's self-interest, or even disloyalty, taints the entire process to the extent that the board loses the protection of the business judgment rule. This Court has never ruled that a director's plausible interest in a contested transaction alone is enough to strip the board of the business judgment rule's presumption of loyalty. As long as 8 Del.C. § 144's conditions are satisfied

self-interest alone does not disqualify a director. For rule rebuttal, disloyalty must be proven. See Citron, 569 A.2d at 65-66; Unocal, 493 A.2d at 958; Cheff v. Mathes, Del.Supr., 199 A.2d 548, 554 (1964). Such misconduct includes, but is not limited to, entrenchment motives, see Gilbert, 575 A.2d at 1146, Polk v. Good, Del.Supr., 507 A.2d 531, 536-37 (1986), Unocal, 493 A.2d at 954-56; fraud against the corporation or board, see Mills, 559 A.2d at 1283; neglect of directorial duties, see Lutz v. Boas, Del.Ch., 171

A.2d 381, 395-96 (1961); or selling one's vote. Neither Aronson nor Pogostin supports Cinerama's claim that a single director's disqualifying self-interest alone suffices to rebut the business judgment presumption of board loyalty; no Delaware precedent from this Court endorses such a view. This Court has avoided rigid rules for determining when a director's breach of independence due to self-interest provides enough evidence to rebut the business judgment presumption. We concur with defendants that whether director self-interest amounts to board disloyalty is fact-specific and varies by case. See Citron, 569 A.2d at 64; Grobow v. Perot, Del.Supr., 539 A.2d 180, 186 (1988). Trial courts need flexibility to assess if an officer's or director's interest in a disputed transaction is significant enough to breach loyalty and corrupt the board's decision.

Therefore, we dismiss Cinerama's argument that 'any' director self-interest, without proof of disloyalty, is enough to rebut the business judgment rule's loyalty presumption. Cinerama also challenges the Chancellor's use of a reasonable person standard to gauge the materiality of a director's self-interest in a disputed transaction. We find this standard unhelpful and confusing, so we reject its use in assessing whether director self-interest rebuts the rule. The Second Part of the Chancellor's Materiality Test: Proving Interest Material to the Entire Board's Independence The Chancellor ruled that, to rebut the business judgment rule, any director self-interest impairing independence must also be shown to have compromised the board's deliberation. The Chancellor defined the test's second part as follows: The initial question of independence is factual: does the financial interest, under all circumstances, create a reasonable likelihood it adversely influenced the directors' actions to the corporation's detriment?

In certain cases, a debatable or confirmed personal financial gain might, when considered in context, be deemed insignificant in reality to the exercise of judgment driven solely to attain the optimal outcome for the corporation and its shareholders in a sale scenario. Personal Liability Opinion at 23-24 (emphasis added). Under this framework, it remains unclear what exactly a shareholder plaintiff must demonstrate to show a reasonable probability of compromised board independence. Apart from the burden of proof issue, the Chancellor's stipulation that a director's self-interest must translate into board self-interest seems to draw from concepts in 8 Del.C. § 144(a). Enacted in 1967, section 144(a) formalized recognized corporate governance principles to offer a limited safeguard for boards, preventing director conflicts from invalidating corporate actions. 56 Del.Laws, ch. 50 (1967); see Beard v. Elster, Del.Supr., 160 A.2d 731, 738 (1960) (a pre-section 144(a) case applying these principles).

Section 144(a) safeguards corporate actions from being nullified due to director self-interest if: (1) disclosed and approved by a majority of disinterested directors; (2) disclosed and approved by shareholders; or (3) the transaction is deemed fair to the corporation. 8 Del. C. § 144(a)(1)-(3); Folk, The Delaware General Corporation Law § 144:5. Section 144(a)(1) effectively mandates that approval by a majority of informed, disinterested directors eliminates any taint of self-interest. See Fliegler v. Lawrence, Del.Supr., 361 A.2d 218, 222 (1976). The Court of Chancery concluded, with little elaboration, that Sullivan's finder's fee, while influencing his judgment, did not materially affect the transaction overall since the board approved it after disclosure. This finding may align with section 144(a). See Fliegler, 361 A.2d at 222. However, neither the lower court nor the parties incorporated section 144(a) into their reasoning. Another unresolved issue is the relevance of Technicolor's charter requirement for unanimous director approval in cases of self-interest.

Technicolor's charter mandates unanimous director approval for a company sale ratified by less than 95% of outstanding shares. Article Tenth states: (2) A 95% supermajority vote is required for mergers... (5) No amendment to the charter can alter Article Tenth unless approved by 95% of shares, except amendments unanimously recommended by the board. Here, the supermajority clause likely served as a takeover defense, ensuring no merger or sale proceeds without each director's disinterested vote. The question arises whether the Chancellor's finding of board approval by an 'overwhelming' disinterested majority suffices to meet the duty of loyalty, given Technicolor's unanimity requirement.

The supermajority provision in Technicolor's charter appears designed to prevent mergers or sales without unanimous, disinterested director consent. This raises doubts about whether the Chancellor's reliance on an 'overwhelming' disinterested vote alone satisfies the duty of loyalty, especially when the charter demands unanimity. Neither the parties nor the lower court addressed this critical issue, leaving unresolved how Technicolor's unique governance structure impacts the board's fiduciary obligations in this context.

We choose not to answer this question initially, pending the lower court's examination of section 144(a)'s implications. We refer this matter back to the Court of Chancery for further consideration, with these points in mind: Does a director's self-interest or lack of independence invalidate a unanimity requirement? Does section 144 supersede a charter's unanimity clause? Can full disclosure to a disinterested board meet Technicolor's unanimity standard? Key issues for remand concerning the duty of loyalty include: (1) the exact proof standard under the materiality test (see note 32); (2) whether this standard aligns with Delaware law and section 144(a); (3) how Technicolor's unanimity requirement affects the duty of loyalty in this case; and (4) the impact of upholding the lower court's finding of no disclosure breach on director self-interest. Director Duty of Care and Board Presumption The Delaware business judgment rule stems from shareholders entrusting directors with corporate management. This delegation is codified in 8 Del.C. § 141(a) and, for mergers, in 8 Del.G. § 251. See Singer v. Magnavox, 367 A.2d 1349 (1976), partially affirmed and reversed.

In Del.Supr., 380 A.2d 969 (1977), the business judgment rule's judicial presumption favoring director and board actions is deemed crucial in derivative lawsuits. Aronson, 473 A.2d at 812, notes that this presumption applies only if directors are disinterested, well-informed before voting, and act with due care. The court emphasized that directors must gather all reasonably available material information and exercise appropriate diligence in their duties. Id. at 812. The duty of care, as repeatedly defined by this Court, is a core component of the business judgment rule, alongside the duty of loyalty, both essential for fiduciaries serving a corporation and its shareholders.

a company and its stockholders. Lutz, 171 A.2d 381, highlights that these duties are equally important. This Court's rulings, both before and after Van Gorkom, consistently treat the duty of care and loyalty with equal importance. Cases like Aronson, 473 A.2d at 814, Unocal, 493 A.2d at 955, and Moran, 500 A.2d at 1356, reinforce this principle. The duty of care has been interpreted in various contexts, such as requiring directors to actively engage in corporate decisions, particularly during significant events like mergers or sales.

Directors must play an active and hands-on role throughout a company's sale process, as stated in Citron, 569 A.2d at 66, and Unocal, 493 A.2d at 954. Before approving a merger or sale, directors must ensure they and their peers are fully informed of all material facts. Aronson, 473 A.2d at 812. The business judgment rule assumes directors have fulfilled their loyalty obligations (see Section IV) and collectively met their duty of care. Barkan, 567 A.2d at 1286, and Moran, 500 A.2d at 1356, affirm this. A court will only rule a board breached its duty of care if directors failed to thoroughly and deliberately prepare before voting on major transactions like mergers or sales.

Van Gorkom, 488 A.2d at 873, and Aronson, 473 A.2d at 812, clarify that a board loses the business judgment rule's protection only if it fails to meet the duty of care, triggering an entire fairness review. Cases like Van Gorkom, 488 A.2d at 893, and Shamrock Holdings, 559 A.2d at 271, illustrate this. The Chancellor in this case dismissed due care concerns, stating that even with negligence, the plaintiff lacked grounds for judgment. Personal Liability Opinion at 6. By assuming the Technicolor board was grossly negligent but requiring proof of injury, the court added an extra hurdle to rebutting the business judgment rule.

The court determined the requirement was unmet and injury could not be proven, given its prior conclusion of fair value in the statutory appraisal. Thus, it sidestepped deciding whether the board had neglected its duty to take reasonable steps to stay informed before approving the merger. The court cited a decades-old case, unmentioned by either party, to justify requiring proof of injury. It ruled that since the board acted disinterestedly and in good faith, the plaintiff must demonstrate that any oversight likely caused harm. Without such proof, the court dismissed all claims, noting the plaintiff's failure to establish injury from the alleged negligence.

In my view, merely proving a breach of the board’s duty of care in a third-party merger does not automatically warrant a plaintiff’s victory. Instead, as with any negligence claim, the plaintiff must prove the breach directly caused harm and specify the injury. Citing cases like Barnes v. Andrews, the court emphasized this burden. On appeal, Cinerama argues the directors’ gross negligence placed the case under Van Gorkom and Revlon’s precedents and that the Chancellor wrongly applied tort principles from Barnes to dismiss the claims.

Cinerama’s arguments are legally sound and supported by the record. Defendants admit no prior Delaware ruling required shareholders to prove injury from a breach of duty of care or loyalty at the rebuttal stage. This case uniquely imposed such a demand, contrary to precedent. The entire fairness standard shifts the burden to directors to prove a transaction’s fairness, yet requiring plaintiffs to show injury via unfair pricing would absolve negligent directors of this duty. The Chancellor’s ruling stood despite his 'grave doubts' about the board’s due care.

In Cede I, it was acknowledged that proof of a breach of fiduciary duty could allow Cinerama to claim rescissory damages. The court noted that if fraud or fiduciary breach nullified the merger, Cinerama's appraisal action would become moot, entitling it to rescissory damages. Cinerama also contested the trial court's ruling that Technicolor's directors did not violate their disclosure duties, arguing omissions in tender offer and proxy filings were material under Delaware's fiduciary disclosure standards.

The Chancellor correctly held that Cinerama bore the burden of proving material nondisclosures under Rosenblatt. The record supported the court's finding that most alleged omissions were immaterial and lacked factual basis. However, the case must be remanded to reassess the materiality of Ryan's undisclosed self-interest, as the Chancellor's conclusion that it was immaterial due to the board's unanimous approval raises questions. The decision implied that undisclosed self-interest might be deemed immaterial based on collective board approval, a premise requiring further scrutiny.

This issue involves mixed questions of fact and law, warranting deference to the factfinder. The trial court's immateriality finding may hinge on whether a director's undisclosed self-interest can be rendered immaterial by a unanimous board vote. Alternatively, it might rely on a Rosenblatt analysis of how nondisclosure affects a shareholder's 'total mix' of information. The concern lies with the former premise—that a unanimous vote can legally nullify the materiality of a director's undisclosed interest—necessitating remand for clarification of the ruling's basis.

The Chancellor's materiality test for director self-interest was upheld, but the reasonable person standard was erroneous. The correctness of the second part of the materiality test remains undecided, pending review of §144(a) and Technicolor's unanimity requirement. The duty of care element was misstated, as requiring shareholder injury to rebut the business judgment presumption was a legal error. On remand, the court must reassess the transaction for entire fairness, with jurisdiction reserved solely on the materiality issue.

Under Weinberger's tenure, we uphold the Chancellor's decisions regarding Cinerama's remaining claims but send back for further explanation his ruling on the duty of disclosure concerning Director Ryan's assumed material self-interest.
