Cinerama argues that the Chancellor's materiality test for assessing director self-interest is a novel and subjective approach, replacing an objective standard. They claim it sets an impractical benchmark, demanding proof that a director's financial stake was substantial enough to influence their actions against the corporation's interests. Cinerama also maintains that director loyalty should not be evaluated using the reasonable person standard from tort law, while disregarding Technicolor's unanimity requirement for company sales.

Defendants contend that the Chancellor correctly applied Delaware's business judgment rule, emphasizing director disinterest and independence. However, they admit no prior Delaware case has directly addressed the burden of proof issue. They defend the Chancellor's decision to place this burden on Cinerama but fail to discuss its implications for duty of care claims. Notably, they omit any analysis of whether requiring proof of harm aligns with legal standards for duty of care breaches.

The Chancellor concluded that the board, as a collective body, faced no independence issues in approving the MAF merger. He found no material conflicts of interest among board members except for Fred Sullivan, an outside director. This ruling was supported by credible evidence, reinforcing the board's unimpaired decision-making process. The reasonable person standard was not deemed applicable in this context.

The standard is imprecise. While it seems to shield only director actions not involving simple negligence, in reality it covers all actions except those amounting to gross negligence. Refer to Graham v. Allis-Chalmers Mfg. Co., Del.Supr., 188 A.2d 125, 130 (1963) (using a 'prudent man' standard for duty of care); contrast with Aronson, 473 A.2d at 812 (applying gross negligence for duty of care) and Van Gorkom, 488 A.2d at 873 (same). The Graham ruling is ambiguous and unclarifying. Though it appears to employ a 'prudent man' standard, it later mentions director liability in terms of reckless behavior. Notably, we have clarified that Graham does not pertain to business judgment cases. See Aronson, 473 A.2d at 813 n. 7. We have also asserted that the Graham standard, whatever it may entail, is irrelevant in cases involving a breach of

the duty of loyalty. See Mills, 559 A.2d at 1284 n. 32. The Chancellor's opinion presents multiple interpretations of the plaintiff's burden in proving the second element of the materiality standard. One approach suggests materiality exists if a director's financial interest could reasonably influence an impartial person's judgment to shareholders' detriment. Personal Liability Opinion at 36 (emphasis added). A stricter approach, illustrated by an example, involves two directors (a board majority) approving a lock-up sale that doubles their salaries. The Chancellor deems this self-interest immaterial, leaving the transaction under business judgment protection. This implies that even significant self-interest among a majority may not affect the board's overall decision-making under the second part of the materiality test. The shareholder plaintiff's burden for this test remains unclear.

Section 144(a) states: (a) A transaction between a corporation and its directors, officers, or affiliated entities will not be invalidated solely due to such relationships, or because the director/officer participated in the approving meeting, or their vote was counted, provided: (1) Material facts about the relationship and transaction are disclosed to or known by the board or committee, which approves it in good faith by a majority of disinterested directors, even if less than a quorum; or (2) Material facts are disclosed to or known by voting shareholders, who approve the transaction in good faith; or (3) The transaction

is fair to the corporation when authorized, approved, or ratified by the board, committee, or shareholders. As explained later, section 144 clears the 'interested director' issue through three avenues, allowing such transactions to qualify for business judgment rule protection. See Marciano v. Nakash, Del.Supr., 535 A.2d 400, 403-05 (1987); Fliegler, 361 A.2d at 222. Under this statute, approval by a fully-informed disinterested board (8 Del.C. § 144(a)(1)) or disinterested shareholders (8 Del.C. § 144(a)(2)) grants business judgment protection. Marciano, 535 A.2d at 405 n. 3. Alternatively, an interested director failing disclosure can eliminate the conflict by proving the transaction's overall fairness. Id.; 8 Del.C. § 144(a)(3).

Methods to limit the influence of a conflicted director include: excluding them from board meetings, as seen in Ivanhoe, 535 A.2d at 1343; Puma v. Marriott, Del.Ch., 283 A.2d 693, 695 (1971); stepping down from the board, Rosenblatt v. Getty Oil Co., Del.Supr., 493 A.2d 929, 938 (1985); or forming a committee of impartial directors to assess the proposal, Weinberger, 457 A.2d at 709 n. 7; Zapata Corp. v. Maldonado, Del.Supr., 430 A.2d 779 (1981); Citron v. E.I. Du Pont de Nemours & Co., Del.Ch., 584 A.2d 490 (1990). These methods are noted without suggesting they would have resolved the conflict in the Technicolor board's actions.

In the October 29th decision, the Barkan case emphasized that board actions must be assessed based on context to ensure they were made with due care and loyalty. Absent a breach of duty, such actions are protected by the business judgment rule. Barkan, 567 A.2d at 1286, citing Mills, 559 A.2d at 1286-88. The Moran case further clarified that this rule presumes directors acted informedly, in good faith, and in the company's best interest. Moran, 500 A.2d at 1356, citing Aronson, 473 A.2d at 812.

The Chancellor noted that claims of inadequate care and Revlon duties both hinge on directors being poorly informed about alternatives or merger consequences. Auctions provide information, while market-check mechanisms are less effective but lower-risk. Lock-ups are problematic as they hinder information by deterring higher bids. Personal Liability Opinion at 39-40 (footnotes and citations omitted). Cinerama questioned the court's reliance on the obscure Barnes case, which was unmentioned in briefings and rarely cited since 1924. Defendants offered no sufficient rebuttal.

In Barnes, a director, Andrews, was sued for negligence due to minimal involvement in key meetings. The court found him negligent but not liable, as the plaintiff couldn't prove his inaction caused the company's failure. Judge Learned Hand ruled that while Andrews failed in his duties, the plaintiff needed to show his active involvement would have prevented the loss. Barnes, 298 F. at 616. As noted earlier, Technicolor's charter required unanimous board approval to repeal its anti-takeover clause, mandating 95% shareholder approval for mergers. Rodney, J., highlighted three key questions arising from the facts.

1) Is a husband eligible for marriage annulment due to fraud if the wife was already pregnant by another man before marriage, even if the husband had prior sexual relations with her before marrying? 2) Can either spouse testify about the husband's lack of access during conception? (a) Without any applicable statute. (b) Under Delaware law. 3) Has the marriage been validated? Before addressing these questions, it's prudent to exclude certain unrelated issues that some courts have vaguely referenced in relevant rulings. Cases involving false pregnancy claims or false chastity assertions, which typically result in denied relief, are not considered here. Also excluded are instances of undisclosed premarital pregnancy where the husband had no prior relations with his wife, as American courts usually grant relief in such scenarios, unlike in England.

These cases are relevant only to demonstrate that premarital pregnancy by another man qualifies as fraud under the Statute. In Williams v. Williams, the court ruled that fraud must fundamentally undermine the marriage contract. I believe such fraud occurs when the wife, pregnant by another at marriage, cannot fully fulfill marital obligations. This leads us to the first question: (a) Can a husband annul a marriage for fraud if the wife was pregnant by another man before marriage, despite having prior relations with her? Some respected jurisdictions deny relief in such cases, warranting closer scrutiny. Foss v. Foss and similar cases exemplify this stance.

Decisions denying the husband relief typically fall into two categories: (1) those citing the husband's unclean hands, and (2) those citing his failure to investigate the truth of the woman's claims. The first group includes New Jersey cases like Seilheimer v. Seilheimer. This reasoning is questionable, as the husband's prior misconduct doesn't negate the wife's fraud, which prevents her from fully entering the marriage. The parties are not equally at fault. The second group, led by Massachusetts cases like Foss v. Foss, holds that a man who marries a pregnant woman after having premarital relations with her cannot claim relief if he didn't properly investigate her condition.

Massachusetts courts consistently refuse relief in such cases, emphasizing the husband's lack of due diligence. This doctrine underscores the expectation that a man who engages in premarital relations should verify the woman's claims before marriage. However, this approach overlooks the distinct nature of the fraud, which lies in the wife's inability to fulfill marital duties due to her pregnancy by another. The focus should remain on the fraudulent essence of the marriage contract, not solely on the husband's prior actions or investigative failures.

Her accusation regarding his responsibility for her situation did not reach a level that would warrant judicial approval. In reality, these cases do not support the idea that a husband's premarital actions legally prevent him from seeking redress after marrying a pregnant woman based on her false claim of his paternity. Courts focus on the insufficiency of his inquiry, implying that a thorough investigation would have justified relief despite the premarital relationship. However, the Massachusetts rule is flawed because the case hinges on the woman's deliberate fraud. Allowing her to argue that the deceived party failed to investigate thoroughly contradicts legal principles, even in straightforward transactions like vendor-purchaser disputes. Often, identifying reliable sources of information would be impractical.

An inquiry might reveal a lack of chastity, but this is not the lawsuit's foundation. The woman alone knows the unborn child's true parentage. As noted in Winner v. Winner, imprudent behavior with a lover does not necessarily mean a woman has lost all credibility. A man may reasonably trust her assertions. Notably, no relevant case since 1892 has denied the husband relief; all recent rulings have granted it. Contrary to older precedents, more modern decisions, such as Lyman v. Lyman and Wallace v. Wallace, reflect sounder logic.

Cases like Gard v. Gard, Winner v. Winner, Jackson v. Ruby, and others, including Ritayik v. Ritayik and Di Lorenzo v. Di Lorenzo, align with this trend. Additional references include Short v. Short and annotations in A.L.R. I will not analyze each case's reasoning, but their conclusions resonate with me. Often, a man with premarital involvement, believing he caused a pregnancy, seeks to rectify the situation through marriage. Denying him legal recourse for being deceived punishes his honorable intent, not his prior misconduct.

I believe premarital relations alone should not legally bar a man from annulling a marriage due to fraud, especially when the fraud involves pregnancy by another man at the time of marriage. There is no logical basis for such a restriction, as recent rulings demonstrate a shift toward granting relief in these circumstances.

There is no valid reason to deny a husband the chance to establish the parentage of a child conceived prior to marriage, especially when courts permit investigations into paternity for children conceived after marriage. This issue primarily revolves around the availability of valid and lawful evidence. The State should not uphold a marriage that exists merely in name and is founded on a deceitful misrepresentation of a fundamental human relationship. The basis for this annulment case is that the defendant was already pregnant by another man when she married the plaintiff. As noted by Morse, J., in Sissung v. Sissung, the core of the marriage contract is absent if the woman knowingly carries another man’s child at the time of marriage, regardless of the husband’s awareness. The focus now shifts to the question of proof, which leads to the second point.

2. 'Is either the husband or wife permitted to testify about the husband’s lack of access during conception?' (a) In the absence of relevant statutes. (b) As influenced by Delaware law. A logical examination of this issue requires dividing it into two distinct scenarios: first, when the child is conceived and born within marriage, and second, when conception occurs before marriage but birth happens during marriage. This discussion focuses on the latter. In 1777, Lord Mansfield ruled in Goodright v. Moss that, based on principles of decency and policy, neither spouse could testify about the husband’s lack of access during conception. Subsequent English rulings, including Russell v. Russell (1924), reaffirmed this stance.

6, which upheld Lord Mansfield’s principle. In the U.S., most jurisdictions have consistently followed the 'Mansfield Rule.' Bancroft v. Bancroft is no exception, as the court ignored parental testimony and relied on other evidence. Kansas initially dissented but later adopted the rule in Martin v. Stille. Similarly, in Loudon v. Loudon, a divided court (eight to six) saw the majority reject the Mansfield Rule, while the minority, including five Supreme Court justices, supported it. Notably, the majority included judges who may not have had formal legal training.

have such qualifications. The majority (eight), comprising three justices and five judges, rejected the Mansfield Rule, while the minority (five justices and one judge) upheld it. Professor Wigmore strongly criticized the rule in his Evidence treatise, arguing it lacks precedent and rationale. Despite his persuasive analysis, judicial practice in England and America overwhelmingly supports the rule. Given its deep entrenchment in legal tradition, changing it would likely require legislative action. Detailed discussions of these cases can be found in annotations at 60 A. L. R. 380; 68 A. L. R. 421; 89 A. L. R. 911; and 13 Br. Rul. Cas. 312.

In Jones on Evidence (4th Ed.), Section 733, page 1316, and 7 Am. Jur. 640, Section 21, it is noted that when a case concerns a child born in wedlock but conceived before marriage, the admissibility of spousal testimony regarding 'non-access' hinges on whether the husband had pre-marital relations with his wife. If the husband had no such relations and a child is born shortly after marriage, barring his testimony on 'non-access' appears unreasonable. This rule stems from the principle preventing a parent from disowning their own child, rooted in public policy.

The refusal to allow a husband to testify about lack of pre-marital relations when a child is born soon after marriage forces him to implicitly accept a false assumption of prior illicit intercourse. Lord Halsbury in the Poulett Peerage Case (1903) A.C. 395 supports this view, as does Re Duckworth, 55 Ont. L. Rep. 272. This logic underpins many U.S. rulings permitting marriage annulment if the wife was pregnant at marriage without the husband's knowledge and without pre-marital relations. See L.R.A. 1916E, 650; Ann. Cas. 1914C, 1291. This distinction is highlighted here not for direct relevance but because adopting the full rule is unnecessary in this case, as the plaintiff admits pre-marital intercourse.

The Mansfield Rule applies when a child is born in wedlock after pre-marital conception and intercourse, barring either spouse from testifying about the husband's 'non-access' during conception. Wallace v. Wallace (137 Iowa 37) states that antenuptial conception does not weaken the presumption of legitimacy post-birth. Cases like State v. Shoemaker (62 Iowa 343) affirm that legitimacy is presumed even if birth follows marriage closely, indicating pre-marital conception.

As noted in Dennison v. Page (29 Pa. 420) and other cases, the presumption of paternity remains strong whether conception occurred before or after marriage, requiring equally strong evidence to disprove it. The court in Dennison emphasized that proof of 'non-access' must be conclusive to challenge paternity. In the current case, the only evidence of the plaintiff's 'non-access' is insufficient to override this presumption.

The plaintiff's own testimony and the defendant's admissions marked the time of conception. Both are inadmissible under the Mansfield Rule unless a statute modifies it, which leads me to examine Section 3534 of the Revised Code (1935). This section, part of the chapter on desertion and support, originated in 1913 and states that no additional evidence is needed to prove marriage or parentage beyond what is required in civil cases. It also nullifies confidentiality rules between spouses in prosecutions under Sections 2 to 14, making both competent to testify on relevant matters, including marriage and parentage.

The statute explicitly applies only to prosecutions under Sections 2 to 14, preserving existing laws except for those specific cases. Since this proceeding falls outside that scope, the statute is irrelevant. Analogous cases are cited in 60 A.L.R. 390, 68 A.L.R. 421, and 13 Br. Rul. Cas. 323. In Hicks v. State, a similar statute was interpreted, excluding a husband's testimony, though the ruling went further than necessary, as it involved no pre-marital relations. The statutes create an anomaly that requires acknowledgment.

The exclusion of spousal testimony regarding non-access originated to prevent parents from bastardizing their children, initially applied in filiation cases and later extended broadly. Statutes like the one cited lift this restriction for direct cases, leaving the rule intact where it wasn't originally intended. The anomaly, if any, stems from legislation and can be resolved by it. The third preliminary question was whether the marriage was confirmed, which necessitates dismissing the petition. The marriage occurred on June 16, 1937, with marital relations continuing until the child's birth on December 14, 1937, and resuming until January 18, 1938, after a separation. These acts confirmed the marriage, and the statute permits dissolution only for fraud unless confirmation occurs.

Herrmann, J.: The Court must determine if defendant Benjamin Seidel can challenge the Sheriff's return of service. The action began on October 13, 1954. The Sheriff's return stated summons was served on Seidel personally on October 25, 1954, with copies of the writ and complaint. On November 12, 1954, plaintiffs filed an amended complaint and issued another summons. The Sheriff's return for this summons noted service on Seidel, also known as Ben Seidel and Isaac Krigstein, with copies of the amended writ and complaint.

On November 17, 1954, Seidel appeared specifically to challenge jurisdiction over himself. He sought to nullify the Sheriff's return of service from October 25, 1954, arguing he was not served before the complaint was amended and the second writ issued, making the return false. Plaintiffs argued the return is binding between parties and cannot be disputed by Seidel, who countered that while presumed accurate, the return's validity can be challenged. The Sheriff's return from October 25, 1954, appears proper, with no fraud claims, yet judicial views differ on whether such returns are incontestable.

Some jurisdictions uphold the common law rule that a sheriff's return, if proper on its face, is final and cannot be disputed by the defendant in the same case. Others have moved away from this strict doctrine, allowing the return to serve only as preliminary evidence that can be challenged with external proof, especially before judgment. References include Annotation 124 Am. St. Rep. 756 and related legal texts. Delaware lacks a definitive ruling on this issue, though Smulski v. H. Feinberg Furniture Co. suggested the common law rule applies post-judgment.

Seidel argues the Smulski case is irrelevant because (1) the rationale for upholding returns after judgment doesn’t apply here, where the challenge occurs beforehand, and (2) Smulski predates Delaware’s Civil Rules, which modernized procedural practices. Common law treats all challenges uniformly, deeming a proper sheriff’s return final unless fraud is involved, even pre-judgment. Cases like Vaughn v. Love support this view, emphasizing the return’s binding nature unless statutory or rule changes override it.

The common law remains Delaware’s standard unless altered by statute, court rule, or established contrary practice. No such statute exists, and no opposing practice is evident. Seidel cites Civil Rule 12(b)(2) as overriding common law, but since the rule doesn’t explicitly modify it, any change must be clearly implied. Courts hesitate to assume common law shifts without explicit language, as seen in Hazzard v. Alexander. Implied repeal of common law is disfavored, requiring clear intent.

Modifications can only be declared in unambiguous situations. Rule 12(b)(2) should be interpreted in relation to the pre-existing common law on the matter. Whether the Court Rule overrides prior common law, without explicit repeal, hinges on whether there is an irreconcilable conflict between them, unless it is evident that the newer rule is meant to replace the older law entirely. State v. Donovan, 5 Boyce 40, 90 A. 220, 224; State for use of Davis v. Adams, 3 Terry 54, 27 A. 2d 401, 403. I believe Rule 12(b)(2) did not implicitly abolish the common law principle of the absolute accuracy of a sheriff's return, which is part of this State's legal tradition. The Court Rule and the common law are not fundamentally incompatible. Compare Woods v. Zellers, D. C. E. D. Pa., 9 F. R. D.

6. Additionally, it is not evident that the Rule was intended to replace the common law on this issue. Various challenges to the court's jurisdiction over the defendant, previously raised under common law through motions to vacate the return, appear permissible under Rule 12(b)(2) without conflicting with the common law principle of return accuracy. See 1 Woolley on Delaware Practice, Secs. 212, 213. Other jurisdictional challenges under Rule 12(b)(2) could also coexist with the common law rule on return conclusiveness. Since Rule 12(b)(2) and the common law can operate together, it cannot be assumed that the common law was implicitly repealed. I must conclude that Rule 12(h)(2) does not satisfy the criteria for repealing common law, and the absolute verity rule remains in effect in Delaware despite the adoption of civil procedure rules. I reluctantly reach this conclusion, as most other jurisdictions have adopted a more lenient approach.

The common law rule is outdated and no longer aligns with modern procedural principles, with its original purpose long forgotten. See Sunderland 'The Sheriff's Return', 16 Col. L. Rev. 281-298; 2 Moore's Federal Practice (2d Ed.) p. 1040; Vaughn v. Love, supra. However, this Court cannot simply choose between rules based on preference. Its role here is limited to declaring the law as it stands. Nonetheless, I suggest that the common law rule should be repealed to remove Delaware from the shrinking group of jurisdictions still upholding this archaic and discredited doctrine. The Sheriff's return of service on the defendant dated October 25, 1954, is binding between the parties, and its accuracy cannot be challenged in this case. The motion to vacate the return is denied. Due to the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause, it has been ruled

that the common law rule of conclusiveness applies only to state residents. See Vaughn v. Love, supra. Civil Rule 12(b)(2) states: '(b). Defenses and Objections: How Presented. Any defense, legal or factual, to a claim in a pleading must be included in the response, except for specific defenses that may be raised by motion, including (2) lack of personal jurisdiction. The defendant here followed the old practice of moving to vacate the return rather than using the Rule. No decision is made on the motion's form. The Chancellor's response on November 26, 1822, noted a significant difference between the Statute of Distribution, 22 & 23 Car. II, c. 10, and Delaware's intestate estate law, [1 Del.Laws 284,] particularly in relevant sections.

The distribution to collateral heirs. Under English law, any surplus not allocated to the wife, in the absence of children or their legal representatives, is divided equally among the nearest relatives of the same degree and their legal representatives, without specific mention of siblings or their descendants. For instance, when a man with three brothers died intestate, and each brother had predeceased him leaving varying numbers of children, it was decided that the distribution should be per capita, ensuring all children received equal shares, as they inherited directly as next of kin rather than through representation. However, under our Act of Assembly, if there are no children or their representatives, the remaining estate after the wife's portion is divided equally among the deceased's siblings or their legal representatives, not the next of kin, unless no siblings or their representatives exist. In such cases, siblings' descendants inherit by representation, not as next of kin, as stipulated by the Act.

The phrase 'or their legal representatives' pertains to the descendants of siblings who died before the intestate, not those who died afterward. If a sibling had died after the intestate, their share would vest in their estate, passing to their executors or administrators, and their children would not inherit directly from the intestate or per capita. Instead, they would inherit as heirs of their deceased parent. Unless the siblings' descendants inherit per stirpes, the term 'legal representatives' in the Act would be meaningless. Judge Milligan delivered the court's opinion, addressing whether the plaintiffs inherited by descent or purchase. The term 'heirs' can function as either a limitation or a description, depending on context. Here, it served descriptively, identifying who would inherit after the widow's death.

Helen Sloane, the plaintiffs' mother, predeceased the testator, rendering the devise to her void. Consequently, her children could not claim through her but inherited directly from the testator, acquiring a fee simple estate by purchase. Had Helen Sloane survived the testator, she would have received only a life estate, as the initial fee simple was later restricted. However, her premature death nullified the devise to her, allowing her children to inherit equal shares in fee simple directly from the testator, not through her by descent. Attorneys Raybold and Comegys represented the plaintiffs, while Layton acted for the defendant. The court ruled that each plaintiff was entitled to an undivided half of the estate originally devised to Helen Sloane and ordered judgment accordingly.

Memorandum Opinion by Vice Chancellor Noble. Petitioner Explorer Pipeline Company ('Explorer') operates a petroleum pipeline system from the Gulf Coast to the Midwest. Its board approved a major capacity expansion costing over $100 million, financed via an operating lease to bypass a corporate provision requiring supermajority (75%) shareholder approval for borrowing exceeding $15 million. Three shareholders, owning over 33% of Explorer's stock, oppose the project, insisting on supermajority approval. Explorer filed a declaratory judgment action against its eight shareholders, all major oil companies or affiliates, to determine whether supermajority approval is necessary for the financing arrangement.

The project requires shareholder approval of the operating lease format to move forward. The Respondents and their respective shares in Explorer's common stock are: Chevron Pipeline Company ('Chevron') 16.90%, CITGO Pipeline Investment Company ('CITGO') 6.80%, Conoco Pipeline Company ('Conoco') 7.71%, Equilon Pipeline Company, LLC ('Equilon') 26.00%, Marathon Oil Company ('Marathon') 17.36%, Phillips Investment Company ('Phillips') 6.07%, Sun Pipe Line Company of Delaware ('Sun') 9.40%, and TRMI Holdings, Inc. ('TRMI') 9.97%. The Opposition Respondents—Marathon, CITGO, and Sun—oppose the expansion. Explorer has sought summary judgment. In this opinion, I find that Explorer is entitled to partial summary judgment, ruling that the operating lease format, as approved by the board and detailed in draft lease documents, does not require supermajority shareholder approval under its certificate of incorporation. However, I defer ruling on certain equitable claims raised by the Opposition Respondents.

the Opposition Respondents, leaving them for future resolution. II. STATEMENT OF FACTS A. Explorer. Explorer, a Delaware corporation founded in 1967, is headquartered in Tulsa, Oklahoma. It operates a 1,400-mile interstate pipeline for transporting petroleum products, running from Port Arthur, Texas, to Tulsa, Oklahoma, and Hammond, Indiana. The pipeline has been operational since the 1970s. Explorer's board consists of eight directors, seven of whom are affiliated with Chevron, Conoco, Equilon, Marathon, Phillips, Sun, and TRMI. CITGO lacks a voting board member after its representative was not reelected; its former member now attends meetings in a non-voting role. The president of Explorer serves as the eighth director. The corporate structure is unique, as Explorer competes with its shareholders, who also compete among themselves. These shareholders and their board representatives are highly experienced in the pipeline industry. B. Explorer's Certificate of Incorporation. Explorer's summary judgment motion hinges on the interpretation of

Article EIGHTH, paragraph (d) of Explorer's certificate of incorporation, which states in part: EIGHTH: The Board of Directors, with a three-fourths majority vote, is authorized to: (d) Incur, create, assume, or guarantee debt, including securing it with mortgages or liens on corporate property, provided the total debt does not exceed $15 million. If the debt reaches $15 million, further indebtedness requires approval from 75% of voting shareholders. However, if a single shareholder holds over 25% and votes against or withholds approval, the consent of all other shareholders suffices. This clause mandates supermajority board and shareholder approval for certain financial obligations. Another section of Article EIGHTH grants broad powers to the board: The Board may exercise all corporate powers, subject to Delaware law and the certificate of incorporation. Unless otherwise specified, the Board can act by a majority or quorum vote. The certificate also includes standard provisions, such as Article THIRD, paragraph (b)(2), which authorizes the corporation to acquire, hold, and manage real and personal property through various means.

purchase, grant, lease, or other methods, and to own, operate, and manage such property. The certificate further outlines the board's authority to engage in these activities, provided they comply with Delaware law and the corporation's governing documents. These provisions ensure the board has the necessary flexibility to manage Explorer's assets while adhering to legal and structural constraints.

Article THIRD, paragraph (b)(4), also authorizes the acquisition of any property, whether real or personal, tangible or intangible, through purchase, lease, or other means, including goodwill and various rights from other entities. Additionally, paragraph (b)(1) explicitly allows the board to construct, purchase, lease, or otherwise obtain and manage pipelines, storage facilities, and other necessary infrastructure for handling crude petroleum and its derivatives. With these provisions in place, the discussion now shifts to the project's history that led to this dispute. C. Mainline Pipeline Expansion.

For nearly seventeen years, the expansion of Explorer's mainline pipeline has been intermittently considered. As a common carrier, Explorer must proportionally reduce shippers' volumes when demand exceeds capacity. Since 1984, and especially over the past two and a half years, prorating capacity has been necessary. At a 1999 stockholders' meeting, the board was directed to revisit expansion plans. Over the next year, Explorer tackled engineering and regulatory challenges, presenting options to the board. By October 12, 2000, the board was ready to approve the expansion, proposing financing through short and long-term notes. However, the plan failed to secure the required 75% stockholder approval, prompting the board to explore alternative methods, including an operating lease.

On December 12, 2000, the board revisited the expansion plan, revoking the earlier approval and endorsing a scaled-down $100 million project. Funds were allocated for engineering and permitting, while financing decisions were postponed pending a meeting with financial representatives. By February 8, 2001, options like debt, leasing, and equity were reviewed, with traditional debt and operating leasing emerging as top choices. On March 8, recognizing the impossibility of securing supermajority approval for debt, the board opted for an operating lease. Management was tasked with negotiating lease terms that met accounting and tax standards, pending further board approval.

At the March 21, 2001 meeting, the board approved a Term Sheet outlining the operating lease framework for financing the expansion. It became clear that at least one shareholder believed supermajority approval was also needed for this format, leading the board to seek a declaratory judgment. Meanwhile, Explorer progressed with the transaction, nearing completion despite unresolved final documents. D. Operating Lease Structure. Explorer pursued this method due to anticipated shareholder resistance to traditional debt. Management engaged The CIT Group, Inc., to structure funding, actively negotiating terms like interest rates, as typical for such transactions.

Explorer, as the entity responsible for building and managing the improvements, will assume the final risk that these improvements meet its operational objectives. It will also handle payments, which are the only funds available to repay equity and debt investors, and has been deeply engaged in the entire process. A basic overview of the operating lease concept might be useful. While construction is ongoing, the project will be held by a dedicated trust (the 'Trust'). Through a construction agency agreement, Explorer will commit to building or overseeing the project's construction. The Trust will secure the required funding, including both debt and equity. It will also be the borrower for construction loans. Once construction finishes, the financing will shift to an operating lease model. The Trust will remain the project owner but will lease it to Explorer, who will make 'triple net' rent payments, covering operating costs, insurance, and taxes. The lease terms are binding, meaning Explorer must pay rent regardless of circumstances.

Rent payments will be split between debt servicing for lenders and returns for equity investors. Under specific conditions, Explorer may choose to buy the Trust's stake in the project and take over its debt. The lease will last 30 years, with Explorer's rent being the sole funding source for investors and lenders. Since the operating lease is the only funding mechanism, Explorer must agree to the rent structure, including the interest rate or its calculation method, before proceeding. III. THE PARTIES' ARGUMENTS Explorer seeks a ruling via summary judgment that its operating lease doesn't require supermajority board or stockholder approval under its Certificate of Incorporation. It argues there are no factual disputes, the supermajority clause is clear, and its interpretation should stand as law. In essence, Explorer claims it doesn't need 75% shareholder approval to proceed with the operating lease.

Opposition Respondents argue the motion is premature, the supermajority clause is unclear and needs external evidence for interpretation, and it should block Explorer's proposed lease. They also raise equitable claims, questioning the lease's adoption process, and assert the lease's economic risk mirrors what the supermajority clause was meant to protect. They contend 75% shareholder approval is mandatory for Explorer to use an operating lease. IV. ANALYSIS A. Legal Standard Explorer moved for summary judgment under Court of Chancery Rule 56(c), which permits judgment when no material facts are disputed and the movant is legally entitled to win.

B. Ripeness Opposition Respondents have consistently claimed the case isn't ready for adjudication, as the transactional documents weren't finalized when filed and remain incomplete. However, the board had approved the transaction, and the Term Sheet outlined its framework. The validity of the board's action (or whether supermajority approval was needed) was already in dispute, presenting a corporate governance issue. Delaying until all documents were final would undermine the Declaratory Judgment Act's purpose and unnecessarily postpone the project's implementation or cancellation. Moreover, with draft documents available, the court could address the core issue without waiting for every detail to be finalized.

With the necessary information now accessible, there is a substantial framework to evaluate the proposed transaction. In summary, Explorer's application raises significant issues ready for resolution. Additionally, Opposition Respondents have requested a temporary restraining order and a preliminary injunction to halt the operating lease transaction. If they argue that the process has reached a stage requiring injunctive relief and that supermajority approval should have been secured, then judicial review of Explorer's operating lease method is warranted, even without final documents, to address the concerns raised in their motion for interim relief. C. Principles of Interpretation. Certificates of incorporation serve as contracts between a corporation and its shareholders, as well as among shareholders themselves. Consequently, Delaware courts apply standard contract interpretation principles when analyzing these certificates. The Court examines the contract's wording to discern the parties' intent from their explicit language or to identify any ambiguities. Unless the language is unclear, extrinsic evidence cannot be used to interpret, alter, or introduce ambiguity into the contract.

The Court can only deem a contract ambiguous if it is 'reasonably or fairly open to multiple interpretations.' If ambiguity is found, all relevant extrinsic evidence is considered, including the parties' statements, business context, prior interactions, and industry practices. The Court must interpret the contract, such as the certificate of incorporation, as a complete document to harmonize its provisions where possible. Delaware corporations are governed by their boards of directors, with shareholder approval typically decided by a majority vote. Supermajority provisions, which allow minority shareholders to block majority decisions, must be explicit and unambiguous due to their deviation from majority rule principles. These provisions should be interpreted strictly to honor their intent without broadening their scope through liberal interpretation.

Without the supermajority clause, Explorer's board could proceed with the project via an operating lease. Article THIRD, paragraph (b)(1) of the certificate authorizes the board to lease pipelines, pump stations, and storage facilities. The project, structured as an operating lease, involves leasing pump stations and storage facilities, which would typically require only board approval. The key issue is whether the operating lease arrangement would result in Explorer incurring, creating, assuming, or guaranteeing borrowed money debt exceeding $15 million, triggering the supermajority requirement. While the transaction involves borrowed money, Explorer itself is not the borrower; the Trust is. However, the Trust's ability to repay depends on Explorer's lease payments. Opposition Respondents contend that the lease structure amounts to 'indebtedness' due to Explorer's binding payment obligations.

They argue that, despite being classified as a lease for accounting purposes, the arrangement functions as debt in practice. Dr. Stewart C. Myers, a finance expert retained by the Opposition Respondents, asserts that the lease is 'debt in disguise,' noting that credit agencies treat such obligations as debt because they reflect a company's true financial position. Explorer will face long-term cash flow commitments, bear the risk of project failure, and experience effects akin to a significant debt burden. Although Explorer maintains that the lease does not constitute indebtedness, its general counsel acknowledged during deposition that the lease obligations could be equated with long-term debt under certain interpretations.

The Opposition Respondents contend that terms like 'incur, create, assume, or guarantee' should be interpreted broadly. The Court agrees that narrowly focusing on individual words risks misconstruing the provision's intent, necessitating a broader analysis. However, even a broad interpretation cannot extend to liability for borrowed money unless Explorer directly assumes it. The phrase 'for borrowed money' ultimately undermines the Opposition Respondents' argument. The Court cannot ignore that Explorer will not be liable for borrowed money in the proposed transaction.

Consequently, I find that the operating lease arrangement, as proposed, does not involve Explorer incurring, creating, assuming, or guaranteeing any borrowed money debt. The Opposition Respondents further argue that the supermajority provision's $15 million debt limit applies to the transaction. They highlight the clause: [The Board may incur... borrowed money debt...] provided the outstanding balance does not exceed $15 million, beyond which supermajority approval is required. They assert this applies broadly to 'indebtedness,' not just 'borrowed money debt,' raising two questions: whether the proviso's 'indebtedness' is restricted to 'borrowed money debt,' and whether it applies if the transaction doesn't involve such debt.

The first question is whether the proviso's 'indebtedness' is tied to 'borrowed money debt' at the start of the supermajority provision. The second is whether the proviso applies if the transaction doesn't involve borrowed money debt. The provision authorizes the board to 'incur, create, assume, or guarantee' such debt, with the $15 million limit introduced by 'provided.' A proviso limits the scope of the provision and must be read in context. The $15 million cap refers only to debt approved under Article EIGHTH, paragraph (d), not to obligations outside it.

The proviso restricts the board's authority to incur borrowed money debt, which Explorer isn't relying on. Article EIGHTH, paragraph (d) grants this authority but imposes limits under certain conditions. These limits aren't standalone restrictions on the board's power. If no borrowed money debt is involved, the proviso is irrelevant. Thus, the supermajority provision is unambiguous, and the Court has interpreted Article EIGHTH, paragraph (d) within the transaction's context. No supermajority approval is required for the operating lease. However, this ruling is limited and doesn't assess whether the transaction complies with accounting, tax, or UCC requirements.

With no disputed material facts and Explorer legally entitled to interpret the supermajority provision as inapplicable to the operating lease, partial summary judgment is warranted. E. Extrinsic Evidence. While contract interpretation, here the certificate of incorporation, can proceed without extrinsic evidence, a brief review of such evidence may support the Court's conclusions. In this case, the extrinsic evidence is inconclusive.

Long-term payments are unavoidable, impacting cash flow and other project opportunities. Failure to meet payments or project success would lead to severe outcomes. Credit agencies view operating leases as akin to long-term debt. Opposition Respondents contend that their supermajority rights, protecting minority shareholders from Explorer's debt obligations exceeding $15 million, are relevant. Their argument aligns with consistent corporate governance but would require reformation, not just interpretation, of the certificate. Article EIGHTH, paragraph (d) was amended in 1990, with meeting minutes and participant recollections providing insight. Pre-amendment, the provision stated: EIGHTH. The Board, by a three-fourths vote, could incur, create, assume, or guarantee borrowed money debt, including mortgages and liens on corporate property, with long-term debt (over 12 months) requiring 75% shareholder approval.

Before the 1990 amendment, the restriction focused on debt duration, not amount. Short-term debt (under one year) avoided supermajority approval, while longer-term debt required it. The 1990 amendment stemmed from a 1988 controversy when Explorer planned a $19 million project funded by short-term debt, likely to be rolled over. Shareholders feared being locked into recurring short-term debt or forced into longer-term obligations without input. One shareholder's counsel argued: A $19 million project shouldn't bypass shareholder approval via short-term financing. The policy's key phrase was 'short-term financing of approved capital projects,' which this wasn't. If markets shifted, 75% approval would be needed for long-term financing, but the decision would already be made by the Board. The concern was whether the funding policy's intent was honored and if such a major expenditure should proceed as proposed.
The objecting counsel now claims their clients' stance applied only to borrowing money, not other funding methods. Such belated interpretations (over a decade later) are of limited value.

The value was limited. The Explorer's advisors and shareholder attorneys reviewed and modified the problematic wording, leading to the shareholders accepting the changes. The directors' meeting notes, which approved these adjustments, clarify that the amendment aimed to determine if Board or Stockholder approval was needed for issuing commercial paper that might be extended beyond a year or refinanced with long-term debt. These minutes suggest the amendment targeted conventional borrowing via commercial paper. A participant in the 1990 amendment process recalled that no one involved—directors, shareholders, or their representatives—indicated the amendment would alter the interpretation of 'indebtedness for borrowed money' as used in Paragraph (d) prior to the amendment.

Another participant recalled that during the months of discussions about amending Paragraph (d), no director, shareholder, or their legal or financial advisors ever suggested that the amendment, either before or after 1990, was meant to include operating leases. A different participant remembered the amendment as ensuring that major capital projects required approval from 75% of shareholders, aligning with Explorer's joint venture structure. However, this participant acknowledged that operating leases for financing capital projects were never considered. Both accounts agree that operating leases were not discussed at the time, which may imply the supermajority provision was not designed to restrict them.

The extrinsic evidence, though inconclusive, would have supported Explorer's position that the supermajority provision was not meant to limit operating leases. Operating leases, while long-used for capital projects, had not been employed for pipeline expansions. Delaware law prevents courts from rewriting contracts, but it allows interpreting omitted terms based on likely intent. The court could view Explorer's lease payments as 'indebtedness' under the supermajority provision, as the drafters' intent aligns with the term's plain meaning and context.

Although the rental obligations under operating leases may not strictly qualify as 'indebtedness,' they likely fall within the drafters' intent. The 1990 amendment addressed commercial paper for capital projects but retained the phrase 'for borrowed money.' The court cannot expand the provision to include operating lease payments explicitly. While such a restriction might suit Explorer's venture, the court must adhere to the language agreed upon by informed shareholders and cannot impose its own interpretation.

Ten years ago, F. Other Matters. The opposing parties have presented arguments not directly related to the interpretation of the supermajority clause as reasons to deny Explorer the relief it requests. These points, some more detailed than others, encompass: equitable constraints allegedly applicable to Explorer or the majority shareholders; improper director elections; the irrationality of using a costlier operating lease to bypass the supermajority requirement; misuse of voting rights; withholding critical information, including confidential data, from the board; board member conflicts of interest; unclean hands; and violations of implied good faith covenants. This Memorandum Opinion resolves a legal question about interpreting a corporate charter provision, concluding that a board resolution can proceed despite potentially restrictive charter language. The remaining issues are largely equitable, questioning whether a technically legal transaction should be permitted, a matter tied to the opposing parties' pending request for interim injunctive relief.

To the degree that the application extends beyond interpreting Article EIGHTH, paragraph (d) of the charter, the Court views it as a suitable procedural framework for evaluating these claims. Additionally, the Court is not currently convinced, absent further argument from parties more focused on the supermajority provision's interpretation, that these equitable issues lack significant factual disputes. VEASEY, Chief Justice: This appeal addresses defendant-appellant Ronald McNulty's argument that insufficient evidence supports his convictions for Trafficking in Cocaine, Possession with Intent to Deliver Cocaine, Use of a Vehicle for Keeping a Controlled Substance, and Conspiracy Second Degree. For the reasons below, we: (i) uphold McNulty's convictions for the possession offense.

and crimes related to trafficking; (ii) overturn and send back the vehicle offense charge for a not guilty verdict; and (iii) return the case for a new sentencing. I. BACKGROUND On October 15, 1992, New Castle County Police officers were monitoring the home of McNulty's mother, Charlotte Cooper ('Cooper'), to confirm reports of her selling cocaine. Cooper organized a drug deal over the phone, appointing Tillery as the courier. Around 5:00 p.m., Detective Joseph Schofield ('Schofield') saw McNulty, Cooper, Debra Lewandowski ('Lewandowski'), David Jones ('Jones'), and Marion Tillery ('Tillery') outside Cooper's apartment. Shortly after, everyone except Cooper entered Lewandowski's car, with Lewandowski driving, Tillery in the front passenger seat, and Jones and McNulty in the back. They began driving to the delivery location. McNulty was the sole person in the car who could identify the buyer, but all knew Tillery was carrying cocaine for the deal. Scho

field, in an unmarked car, along with a marked police unit, began trailing Lewandowski's car as it departed Cooper's residence. Schofield noticed Jones and McNulty 'moving around and glancing back at [him],' prompting Schofield to order the patrol unit to pull the car over. The unit complied. Tillery fled, evading capture after a 30-minute pursuit. During his escape, he dropped cash and tore open bags, scattering a white powder (later confirmed as cocaine) on the street. Schofield and another officer gathered 6.40 grams of cocaine but found no additional drugs in the car or on McNulty. Lewandowski, Jones, and McNulty were arrested and questioned at the station. McNulty admitted knowing Tillery had drugs and was making a delivery but claimed he asked to be let out before reaching the destination. A jury trial began on July 11, 1994, featuring testimony from Schofield and Lewandowski. McNulty moved for acquittal on all counts

except conspiracy. The Superior Court rejected the motion. McNulty offered no defense and did not renew his acquittal request. On July 13, 1994, the jury convicted McNulty on all charges. This appeal challenges the Superior Court's denial of his acquittal motion regarding his convictions for possession, trafficking, and vehicle use. II. THE POSSESSION CHARGE McNulty contends the State did not prove he was an accomplice to Tillery's cocaine possession. The State argues sufficient evidence existed under accomplice liability theory to uphold the possession conviction. The relevant law, Title 11, Delaware Code, Section 271 ('Section 271'), states: 'A person is guilty of another's offense if[,] intending to aid or facilitate the crime[,] they assist, advise, or agree to help in planning or committing it.' 11 Del.C. § 271(2)(b). The State can obtain a possession conviction using

accomplice liability under Section 271. See Glendon v. State, Del.Supr., 461 A.2d 1004, 1005 (1983). Section 271 mandates the State provide evidence aligning with: 'Defendants need not specifically intend the outcome. If the result was a foreseeable consequence of the criminal act, their intent as accomplices includes facilitating that result.' Martin v. State, Del.Supr., 433 A.2d 1025, 1029 (1981) (quoting Hooks v. State, Del.Supr., 416 A.2d 189, 197 (1980)), cert. denied, 454 U.S. 1151, 102 S.Ct. 1018, 71 L.Ed.2d 306 (1982); see Glendon, 461 A.2d at 1005-1006 (rejecting

Under Section 271, a claim of insufficient evidence fails because the State provided some proof—such as the defendant accepting $25 for involvement in a drug deal—showing intent to assist the principal's actions. Once the State meets the accomplice liability standard, it doesn’t need to prove the defendant physically possessed the cocaine. Glendon, 461 A.2d at 1005. McNulty contends that evidence identifying him as the sole person who could recognize the buyer only supports facilitating delivery, not possession. However, the indictment explicitly charges McNulty and Tillery with possessing cocaine with intent to deliver. Combined with testimony about McNulty’s suspicious behavior during police pursuit, this evidence sufficiently supports the possession conviction under accomplice liability.

McNulty seeks reversal of the trafficking conviction, claiming insufficient evidence. The State counters that constructive possession was proven, as McNulty could control the cocaine’s fate by identifying the buyer. To uphold a possession conviction, the State must present enough evidence for a jury to find actual or constructive possession. 16 Del.C. § 4753A(a)(2); 28 C.J.S. Drugs & Narcotics § 158 (1974 & Supp.1994). Constructive possession requires proof of the defendant’s 'dominion and control' over the drugs, as established in cases like Potts v. State, 458 A.2d 1165 (1983), and statutory definitions under 16 Del.C. § 4701(28).

Dominion and control are essential for constructive possession, as noted in 28 C.J.S. Drugs & Narcotics § 157 (1974 & Supp.1994). A vehicle custodian is presumed to have such control, per Holden v. State, 305 A.2d 320 (1973), and Marvel v. State, 290 A.2d 641 (1972), though this presumption can be rebutted. Mere presence or awareness of drugs in a car isn’t enough for possession; the State must prove conscious dominion and authority, as emphasized in Holden, which overturned convictions based solely on proximity to drugs.

Constructive possession requires the State to demonstrate the defendant’s knowledge of the drugs’ location, ability to control them, and intent to direct their use, as outlined in Speight v. United States, 599 A.2d 794 (1991). Proximity to drugs may establish a prima facie case if tied to an ongoing criminal operation. Without such links, mere awareness or closeness is insufficient for conviction, reinforcing the need for evidence of active control and intent.

United States, D.C.App., 515 A.2d 1108, 1113 (1986); United States v. Hubbard, D.C.App., 429 A.2d 1334, 1338, cert. denied, 454 U.S. 857, 102 S.Ct. 308, 70 L.Ed.2d 153 (1981). In Wells, the court dismissed a defendant's claim of insufficient evidence because he fulfilled one of three key roles in a narcotics operation, specifically handling illegal substances alongside two others. Wells, 515 A.2d at 1114 (defendant transported water needed to dilute heroin and clean syringes). The court ruled this participation amounted to constructive possession of heroin. Id. Suspicious behavior by a defendant can also support a constructive possession claim. Fleeing in a car with illegal drugs when spotted by police 'provides strong circumstantial proof that [the defendant] collaborated with his companions for a shared criminal intent. The visible drug paraphernalia further suggests their aim was [constructive] possession.' United States v. Covington, D.C.App., 459 A.2d 1067, 1071-72 (1983). Even evasive actions less extreme than

flight can serve as circumstantial evidence of constructive possession. Potts, 458 A.2d at 1167 (defendant fled from the kitchen, where drugs were found, to a bedroom when police arrived); see also Thompson v. United States, D.C.App., 567 A.2d 907, 909 (1989) (defendant concealed himself behind a divider during a search while officers interrogated another suspect). However, vague 'furtive movements' alone are inadequate for a conviction. In re T.M., D.C.App., 577 A.2d 1149, 1153-54 (1990) (defendants hiding under bedcovers during a police raid did not prove constructive possession of a firearm and ammunition). Here, the prosecution demonstrated McNulty, a non-owner, was near the cocaine in the car and knew of its presence. Alone, this evidence would not uphold a trafficking conviction. See, e.g., Holden, 305 A.2d

at 321. Therefore, the conviction can only stand if additional proof ties McNulty to a 'broader criminal scheme involving possession,' as in Earle, 612 A.2d at 1265-66. The 'criminal scheme' here is the possession charge, backed by sufficient evidence, as detailed earlier. The 'additional proof' connecting McNulty to this operation includes two factors. First, McNulty alone could identify the buyer (Hubbard, 429 A.2d at 1338), making him a critical, though not sole, link in the drug distribution chain (Wells, 515 A.2d at 1114). Second, Schofield testified McNulty acted suspiciously—'ducking and glancing back' when noticing police pursuit. These 'furtive gestures' alone cannot justify his conviction (T.M., 577 A.2d at

In 1153-54, these actions do not meet the threshold for suspicion of guilt based on flight, as noted in Covington, 459 A.2d at 1071-72, or concealment, per Potts, 458 A.2d at 1167; Thompson, 567 A.2d at 909. However, when combined with the previously mentioned evidence, a jury could reasonably conclude that McNulty had constructive possession of the cocaine. IV. THE USE OF VEHICLE OFFENSE McNulty contends there was insufficient evidence to support the use of vehicle charge. The State presents two theories for accomplice liability: first, McNulty's alleged key role in identifying the buyer during the drug transaction, and second, his involvement with Lewandowski. The indictment describes the offense as '[D]EBRA LEWANDOWSKI, RONALD MCNULTY, AND MARION TILLERY... knowingly keeping a vehicle used to store controlled substances, violating Chapter 47, Title 16 of the Delaware Code.'

The only evidence for this charge was Lewandowski's ownership and operation of the vehicle, and Tillery transporting the cocaine to the car and attempting to discard it after the police stopped them. McNulty's ability to identify the buyer was irrelevant to whether he 'facilitated the offense,' per 11 Del.C. § 271(2)(b), as the relevant offense under accomplice liability was Lewandowski's (or Tillery's) 'knowingly keeping a vehicle,' under 16 Del.C. § 4755(a)(5). Therefore, the use of vehicle conviction is overturned and sent back to the Superior Court for acquittal. See Monroe, 652 A.2d at 567-68 (requiring remand for acquittal when evidence is insufficient).

V. CONCLUSION Due to the State's failure to provide evidence for the use of vehicle offense, the Court REVERSES and REMANDS FOR ENTRY OF A JUDGMENT OF ACQUITTAL on that count. For the possession and trafficking charges, the Court AFFIRMS the convictions based on accomplice and constructive possession theories, respectively, and REMANDS for resentencing. Jurisdiction is not retained. . 16 Del.C. § 4753A(a)(2)a. . Id. § 4751. . Id. § 4755(a)(5). . 11 Del.C. § 512. McNulty does not contest this conviction. . Lewandowski later told police more cocaine was at Cooper's apartment, leading to its discovery along with drug paraphernalia. However, the charges here do not relate to that search. . Lewandowski testified otherwise at trial. . The State does not claim that failing to renew the motion waived the issue, so we assume it did not for this appeal.

As a preliminary matter, our review of McNulty's claims follows these guidelines: de novo scope and the standard being 'whether any rational trier of fact, viewing the evidence favorably to the State, could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.' Monroe v. State, Del.Supr., 652 A.2d 560, 563 (1995). . Given this ruling, we do not address the State's alternative constructive possession argument. . The State provided no proof of McNulty's actual possession of the cocaine. .See also State v. Schmidt, 110 N.J. 258, 540 A.2d 1256, 1260-65 (1988) (discussing 'possession' history). . The State does not argue McNulty was a custodian. . Given this decision, we need not address the State's alternative accomplice liability theory or its oral argument claim that the conspiracy conviction requires further proof.

The court determined that McNulty had constructive possession of the cocaine as a legal matter. Rice, J., instructed the jury: 'Ladies and gentlemen of the jury, the plaintiffs in this case, Ida Ponder and James W. Ponder, are seeking compensation from the Maryland, Delaware and Virginia Railway Company for damages caused by a fire that destroyed their timberland. The plaintiffs allege that the defendant operated a steam railway near their property and failed to remove brush and other flammable materials from its right of way, violating Section 3448 of the Revised Code of 1915. This negligence, they claim, led to a fire that spread to and damaged their timber. The defendant denies these allegations, asserting it did not leave combustible materials on its land and is not liable for the plaintiffs' losses. The plaintiffs' case hinges entirely on'

'the defendant's alleged violation of Section 3448 of the Revised Code. The issue before you is straightforward, with limited questions to resolve. Section 3448 states that if a railroad company allows brush or other flammable materials to remain on its land and a fire results, causing property damage, the company is liable for such damages. If you find that the defendant failed to remove such materials and this led to the plaintiffs' property being damaged, your verdict should favor the plaintiffs. In that case, the only remaining matter would be'

'determining the extent of the plaintiffs' damages based on the evidence. If you rule for the plaintiffs, your verdict should reflect fair compensation for their losses, considering the property's value before and after the fire, including both young and mature timber. When evidence conflicts, your duty is to reconcile it if possible. If reconciliation is impossible, weigh the credibility of witnesses, their knowledge, and their opportunity to observe the facts. You alone must judge the reliability of the testimony presented. Should you conclude that the plaintiffs' damages resulted from causes other than the defendant's failure to comply with the law, your verdict must be'

'in favor of the defendant. Your decision should align with the preponderance of evidence. Verdict for the plaintiffs. HERRMANN, Justice: In this workers' compensation case, the Industrial Accident Board found that the employee, a laborer, sustained a back sprain from an accident, resulting in two months of total disability. The Board ruled that a skin condition, scleredema, was unrelated to the accident. It awarded compensation for the back sprain but limited it to the two-month period. The Superior Court upheld the Board's findings, citing sufficient evidence for the back sprain and the employee's failure to prove the skin condition's connection to the accident. However, the Court rejected the Board's classification of the award as temporary total disability under the statute. We affirm both rulings. General Motors Corporation v. Freeman, Del.Supr., 164 A.2d 686 (1960); Ernest DiSabatino & Sons, Inc. v. Apostolico, Del.Supr., 26'

In the 1970 case cited as 9 A.2d 552, the Superior Court directed the Board to reconsider the matter as a petition to end total disability benefits, placing the onus on the employer to prove suitable employment options for the employee, referencing Stikeleather v. Zappacosta, 293 A.2d 572 (1972). The burden-of-proof standard was later refined in Franklin Fabricators v. Irwin, 306 A.2d 734 (1973), which clarified that this rule applies solely to 'displaced' or 'odd-lot' cases. The court outlined that if an employee’s physical and circumstantial factors (like education or age) clearly place them in the 'odd-lot' category, the employer must demonstrate available work matching the employee’s abilities.

If the evidence does not clearly classify the employee as an 'odd-lot' case, the employee must first prove they unsuccessfully sought suitable work due to their injury. Only then does the burden shift to the employer to show available employment. The current case, involving a back sprain, falls into the latter category, meaning the employee must initially demonstrate failed job-seeking efforts before the employer’s burden applies. The employee argues he lacked medical clearance to work before the hearing, but this is irrelevant now, as he has access to the employer’s medical opinions and discovery materials for the remand.

The employee’s claim that he had no prior medical approval to return to work before the Board hearing holds no weight in the current proceedings. He now possesses the employer’s medical assessments and can act accordingly during the remand. Additionally, under 19 Del.C. § 2322(d) and Board Rule 9, he was entitled to all medical reports and pretrial disclosures, ensuring full discovery rights. The lower court’s decision is adjusted, and the case is sent back for further review, referencing M. A. Hartnett, Inc. v. Coleman, 226 A.2d 910 (1967), and Ham v. Chrysler Corporation, 231 A.2d 258 (1967).

Judge GEBELEIN addresses whether the Superior Court has jurisdiction over a defendant accused of crimes committed as a juvenile but charged as an adult. The indictment includes four felony counts from early 1985, with the defendant born on April 1, 1967. The defense argues that since the alleged offenses occurred before he turned 18, the Family Court holds exclusive jurisdiction, warranting dismissal. However, the Superior Court retains concurrent jurisdiction over crimes unless explicitly assigned elsewhere, per 11 Del.C.

Section 2701(c). See also Brasure v. State, Del.Supr., 291 A.2d 287 (1972). The question in this motion is whether Family Court has exclusive jurisdiction over the alleged offenses. The statute granting Family Court authority in delinquency cases states: The Court shall have exclusive original civil jurisdiction in all state proceedings involving: (2)a. Any child accused in this State of delinquency by violating any state law. 10 Del.C. § 921(2)(a). The intent behind establishing Family Court includes the principle that one court should have original statewide civil and criminal jurisdiction over family and child-related matters. 10 Del.C. § 902(a). The statute granting Family Court jurisdiction applies to 'any child' charged with delinquency, defined as a person under 18. 10 Del.C. § 901(3). This implies no delinquency jurisdiction exists for non-children.

over non-minors. Additionally, the act includes specific rules for Family Court handling of individuals charged with delinquency before turning 18 but adjudicated after. See 10 Del.C. § 937(b)(17). This would be unnecessary if the Court had exclusive jurisdiction over all offenses committed before age 18. A key principle of statutory interpretation is that the General Assembly does not act without purpose. Thus, § 937(b)(17) must have been included for a reason, likely to address the loss of delinquency jurisdiction once the respondent turns 18. This Court finds that Family Court's jurisdiction depends on the defendant's age when charges are filed, aligning with its purpose to treat juveniles differently from adults. See Fletcher v. State, Del.Supr., 409 A.2d 1254 (1979); the availability of non-amenability proceedings, 10 Del.C. § 938; and prior rulings that jurisdiction hinges on the offender's age. See State v. Anderson, Del.Super., 385 A.2d 738 (1978). For these reasons, the Court concludes that if a child commits an offense but becomes an adult before charges are filed, Superior Court has jurisdiction. Motion denied. IT IS SO ORDERED. The statute granting Family Court criminal jurisdiction does not apply here. See 10 Del.C. § 922. Similarly, the general jurisdiction provisions of 10 Del.C. § 925 are irrelevant.

Court Below: Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware, C.A. No. 9686-CB AFFIRMED. OPINION CHRISTIE, Judge. Falcon Tankers, Inc., a Delaware corporation, entered into a contract with Litton Systems, Inc., also a Delaware corporation, for Litton to design, build, and sell Falcon a tanker named the 'Falcon Lady.' Litton designed the ship, Falcon approved it, and construction was completed. Upon delivery, Litton fulfilled the contract terms. However, issues arose with the ship's ballast and cargo discharge system during its initial voyages. Disputes over system failures led both parties to submit two preliminary questions to arbitration. These issues can be summarized as: 1. Did the cargo and ballast discharge system, as designed and installed (including pump modifications due to breakdowns), meet the Construction Contract and Specifications without needing an additional auxiliary 'stripping' system? 2. If the separate stripping system installed exceeded contract requirements, what portion of its cost, if any, should Falcon Tankers, Inc. bear? Note that resolving these arbitration issues would not address all disputes in this lawsuit, as many were not submitted to arbitration. Falcon seeks broader resolution in this case.

the arbitration process. Only in this lawsuit does Falcon attempt to recover damages beyond the scope of the arbitrated issues. The arbitration panel's decision would not have resolved all contractual disputes between the parties, as many claims were excluded from arbitration. Falcon's broader grievances, including potential breaches of contract and design flaws, remain unresolved and are the focus of this litigation. The arbitration was limited to specific technical questions, leaving other legal and financial matters for judicial determination. Thus, this suit addresses unresolved disputes that were not part of the arbitration agreement.

The extra losses it claims resulted from the malfunctions, beyond the expenses of fixing the supposed flaws. Regardless, the arbitration panel only considered the initial issue, ruling that the cargo and ballast discharge system failed to comply with the contract's terms. The second issue remained unresolved as Falcon opted to file this lawsuit, and Litton dropped its argument that Falcon was bound by the mandatory arbitration clause in their agreement. Falcon now aims to recover significant consequential damages allegedly caused by design flaws in the system Litton installed in the 'Falcon Lady'. The complaint includes three claims: Count I alleges Litton breached implied warranties regarding the ship's merchantability and fitness; Count II asserts Litton violated an express warranty that the vessel would meet Grade 'B' petroleum transport standards and MSC requirements; Count III accuses Litton of negligence in design and construction.

Choosing or designing the cargo pumps improperly and failing to test and inspect them thoroughly. Initially, Litton raised two defenses, the first citing an arbitration clause in their contract with Falcon, which mandated disputes be resolved through arbitration in New York under state law and AAA rules. However, Litton has since withdrawn this defense. The second defense relies on a 'guarantee clause' in the same contract, stating the seller provides no warranties for the Pielstick System and limits liability for defects discovered within six months of delivery to replacement or repair, excluding consequential damages for vessel, cargo, or personal injuries. This clause also extends to subcontractors' materials and workmanship.

Litton argues the guarantee clause bars Falcon's claim for consequential damages, asserting the clause's express warranty restricts remedies to defect repairs and excludes other warranties. Additionally, Litton claims the clause precludes negligence-based consequential damages. Litton also filed a third-party complaint against Worthington Corporation, accusing them of designing and manufacturing the faulty pumps installed in the 'Falcon Lady'. Beyond addressing Falcon's claims, Litton seeks compensation from Worthington for repairs to the Falcon Lady, issues with pumps on Hulls No. 1163-1165, pump design for the 'Marine Chemist', and damages related to equipment for Hulls No. 1168-1171.

Worthington has moved to dismiss both Falcon's complaint and Litton's claims. The dispute centers on whether the guarantee clause absolves Litton of liability for consequential damages and whether Worthington bears responsibility for the alleged pump defects. Litton's position is that the clause clearly limits its liability, while Falcon seeks to recover extensive damages for design and operational failures. The outcome hinges on interpreting the contract terms and assessing the parties' adherence to their obligations.

third-party grievance. The motion's basis involves Litton's defenses against Falcon, citing the arbitration and guarantee clauses in the contract, along with an alleged improper joinder of claims in the third-party complaint. This opinion addresses Worthington's motions to dismiss. Worthington contends that the arbitration clause is irrevocable, cannot be waived, and can be invoked to compel Falcon and Litton back into arbitration. It supports Litton's stance on the guarantee clause and argues for dismissing the third-party complaint's additional claims due to improper joinder. The motions raise three key issues: Worthington's standing to enforce arbitration despite Falcon and Litton's reluctance, the guarantee clause's limitation on damages for design defects versus material defects, and whether the third-party complaint's counts should be dismissed for improper joinder.

negligence. The third issue is whether Worthington's motion to dismiss the third-party complaint's extra counts should succeed due to improper joinder. These issues will be addressed in order. Before delving into them, it's important to note the contract's choice-of-law clause, specifying that U.S. and New York laws govern. On such clauses, Chief Justice Layton remarked that parties have limited freedom to choose the jurisdiction governing their contract, provided the selected jurisdiction has a material connection to the transaction. This principle was upheld in Wilmington Trust Co. v. Wilmington Trust Co., and Delaware's Uniform Commercial Code also permits such choice-of-law provisions in sales transactions.

1-105(1). This Court will honor the contract's choice-of-law clause, applying U.S. and New York laws. The first issue is whether Worthington can enforce the arbitration clause to compel Falcon and Litton to arbitrate, despite their mutual agreement to litigate. Worthington argues it has standing because: (a) arbitration agreements are irrevocable under U.S. and New York law; (b) Falcon and Litton waived their right to avoid arbitration by submitting one issue to arbitration; (c) Worthington is a third-party beneficiary, having relied on the contract; and (d) under Civil Rule 14, Worthington can assert Litton's defenses against Falcon. These points will be examined in sequence.

the term 'irrevocable' in the New York Arbitration Act requires clarification. Worthington claims that once parties agree to arbitrate disputes, they cannot revoke this agreement. This interpretation lacks legal or logical support. While the agreement may be irrevocable in the sense that one party cannot unilaterally revoke it, mutual consent can rescind it. Corbin explains this clearly: a valid arbitration agreement can be terminated by mutual rescission at any stage, as arbitration statutes do not strip parties of this power. Thus, the right to arbitration can be extinguished by mutual agreement, even after arbitrators are appointed.

Section 1443 of the Contracts bin at 432 notes a comparable outcome in Zimmerman v. Cohen, 236 N.Y. 15, 139 N.E. 764 (Ct.App.1923). The court explicitly ruled that the Arbitration Law facilitates enforcing arbitration agreements but does not preclude parties from opting for alternative dispute resolution methods. The law permits parties to pursue litigation if mutually agreed, treating arbitration clauses as any other contractual term, modifiable or waivable by mutual consent. The term 'irrevocable' here implies that unilateral revocation is barred, but mutual agreement can alter the clause.

The term 'irrevocable' signifies that the arbitration agreement cannot be terminated by one party alone but requires grounds like those invalidating any contract. Mutual consent can revoke it, as clarified in Zimmerman, supra, at 765-766. The Court affirms that arbitration agreements can be revoked by all parties' mutual assent. Worthington argues that Falcon and Litton waived revocation rights by arbitrating some issues, but no direct legal precedent supports this. Corbin's view that parties can mutually rescind arbitration clauses mid-proceeding is deemed correct, and Falcon and Litton's partial arbitration does not constitute waiver.

Worthington's standing to enforce the arbitration clause hinges on its relationship to the contract and parties. It claims third-party beneficiary status, citing reliance on the clause when contracting with Litton. General contract principles dictate that only parties or privies to an arbitration agreement can invoke it (17A C.J.S. Contracts § 515(4)).
