There is no evidence of fraud by her or anyone else, nor any reason to think she had knowledge of the estate’s condition beyond what the petition disclosed.

Did the widow, by choosing to accept the will’s terms and waiving her dower rights, forfeit or provide equivalent value for the interest on $3,333.33, which she now requests be invested or secured to pay her semi-annual interest for life, as directed in the will? In Chancery cases involving election between two interests or revoking a prior election, courts have consistently ruled that a party must be fully informed about their rights and the estate’s status before being compelled to elect. This includes obtaining accounts in court. Under English law, and likely here in similar equity cases, a widow must understand the comparative value of her dower rights versus a will’s provision before being forced to choose. This principle is so fundamentally fair that no contrary ruling exists. Other factors, such as original intent, acquiescence, or third-party impacts, may also bind a party, but these vary too widely for a universal rule; each case must be judged on its specifics.

In Wake v. Wake, 1 Ves. Jr. 335, it was held that receiving benefits under a will could bind a party to their election. However, the circumstances must clearly show intent or acquiescence. The fairness of ensuring informed decisions in such matters is undisputed, and courts have consistently upheld the need for transparency and full disclosure when parties face choices affecting their rights. Each case must be evaluated based on its unique facts, as no single rule can cover all possible variations in intent, action, or consequence.

The legacy and annuity provided under the will for three years did not preclude her right of election from being presumed as not acting with full awareness, which would otherwise bind her. It is established law that actions taken by a party before fully understanding their rights typically do not constitute an election. In this case, where the election was made without complete information or the means to obtain it, it would be unjust to hold the widow to such a decision if revocation is the only remedy available. Furthermore, if revocation is permissible under appropriate conditions, as supported by legal precedents, it should be granted by the same court where the election was originally made. No other court possesses the jurisdiction to authorize such a revocation, nor does the Court of Chancery have the authority to compel this court to permit it.

The refusal of this court to allow the revocation of an election, despite equitable circumstances warranting it, would leave the Court of Chancery unable to provide relief. This court is the sole venue where such a revocation can be granted, and the right to revoke under fair conditions is well-supported by consistent judicial rulings. Here, the widow exercised her statutory right of election in this court, which also issued the order for the sale free of dower. The sale has been reported to the court, revealing that the widow acted without full knowledge of the estate's condition or the opportunity to acquire it, relying instead on the administrator's petition, which was presumed accurate at the time. The sale proceeds remain with the administrator. Shouldn't the widow's equitable claims apply to these funds, protecting them from creditors during her lifetime?

If so, this court could order the administrator to set aside a portion of the sale proceeds to satisfy the widow's equitable lien, using only the remaining balance to settle the deceased's debts during her lifetime. The reserved amount would, after the widow's death, revert to the administrator for paying any outstanding debts or distributing to the rightful beneficiaries under the will. While the administrator and the widow might seek guidance from the Court of Chancery on managing the reserved funds, this court could also direct the administrator to safely invest the sum to provide the widow's annuity during her life, with the remainder distributed according to legal requirements.

There is no statutory provision explicitly authorizing this court to mandate such an investment, but as a court with equitable jurisdiction, it can apply fair principles to matters within its purview. Given the state's legislation safeguarding the widow's rights in her husband's estate proceeds—especially when she waives dower for a share of the sale interest—this court would not overstep its authority by ordering a proper investment. Instead, it would align with the law's intent by granting the petition's request in this regard. The Latin maxim 'Qm hwret in litera, hwret im, oortieeP' underscores the importance of adhering to both the letter and spirit of the law.

When a court has jurisdiction, it possesses the authority to adjudicate every issue arising in the case, and regardless of whether its ruling is correct, its judgment remains binding in all other courts until overturned. However, if the court acts beyond its authority, its judgments and orders are considered null and void, not merely voidable, and do not prevent recovery even before reversal. As established in Elliott v. Peirsol, 26 U.S. 1 Pet. 340, 7 L. ed. 170, the principle holds that when a court has subject-matter jurisdiction and the right to decide all issues in the case, its decisions can only be challenged through a writ of error or appeal. In this instance, no writ of error is applicable, and an appeal, limited to the Superior Court for the county, could only be pursued if the judges' opinions conflicted. This underscores the need for careful consideration of the propriety and correctness of our decision.

It should also compel us to exercise the jurisdiction we rightfully hold and avoid deferring questions to another tribunal with no or uncertain jurisdiction, whether original or appellate. If a widow can revoke her election to accept her husband's will's provisions in lieu of dower, and if such revocation must occur in the court where the election was made, then she should either revert to her legal rights or receive fair compensation from the proceeds of the estate's sale for debt payment. Consequently, the court where the election was made should determine the compensation's amount, which would not be an absolute lump sum but rather annual interest, preserving the principal for future beneficiaries once the widow's interest ceases.

If the Orphans' Court handled the real estate sale proceedings and possesses equitable powers, as well as jurisdiction over the case, then it logically follows that this court is the appropriate body to decide on safeguarding the principal sum. Should the court deem it necessary or proper to invest the principal for security, it would have the authority to order such an investment. If the petitioner is entitled to interest on her share of the sale proceeds as a dower equivalent, not barred by her election, she would fall within the equitable scope of the Act of March 26, 1869, granting this court the authority outlined therein.

The Act of March 26, 1869, comprises a single section (Code, 55'T), stating that upon the return of a real estate sale by an executor or administrator to settle debts, the purchaser may either secure the widow's share as per statutory provisions or pay it into the Orphans' Court. In such cases, the court would direct the investment or security of the share for the benefit of interested parties. Here, why shouldn’t the administrator, who became the purchaser with court approval, pay the court-determined equitable sum into the court for investment or security, as indicated in the sale return?

The administrator was informed that the real estate sale totaled $11,946.00, with one-third being $3,982.00, yielding annual interest of $238.92. This amount would exceed the $200 annual interest on $3,333.33 that the petitioner seeks. The widow's petition claims the deceased's estate was unencumbered, except for a $2,214 recognizance with under a year's interest. Deducting this from the sale total leaves $9,598.54, one-third of which is $3,199.51, with annual interest of $191.97.

The annual interest falls $8.03 short of the $200 the widow claims. The deceased also willed her a Dover house as part of her dower relinquishment. The fair rental value of the property is unclear, as is whether two-thirds of it or the recognizance should factor into the reserved amount. These issues require further proof, but the court sees no fraud or injustice in the widow's devise.

The widow should amend her petition to include the deceased's creditors as co-defendants, served with a rule to appear and show cause against investing $3,333.33 as requested. The court reserves judgment on revoking her prior election, unless equitable alternatives exist.

The indictment alleges that on August 8, 1954, Charles Clarence Allen drove recklessly on Route 30, violating multiple statutes. His vehicle struck Richard Garrison Booth's car, causing it to overturn, catch fire, and trap 17-month-old James Christopher McPhail, who died in the blaze. Count one specifies the reckless driving charge.

The phrase 'failed to maintain a proper lookout' is not claimed to violate a statute, but it is a well-established legal principle that drivers on public roads must always keep a proper lookout for other vehicles or pedestrians. The obligation to look includes noticing what is clearly visible, unless there is a valid reason for not seeing it. State v. Elliott, 1 Terry 250, 8 A. 2d 873. However, it is argued that the charge does not adequately detail the defendant's failure to maintain a proper lookout and the surrounding circumstances. Under Delaware’s Chapter 239, Volume 34 of the Laws of Delaware, an indictment need not follow common law or statutory precedents but must clearly outline the crime in simple terms to inform the defendant of the accusation. The specifics of when and where the defendant failed to keep a proper lookout are essential.

The damage to Richard Garrison Booth’s car and the death of James Christopher McPhail are evident. Drivers on public roads must maintain a proper lookout at all times and under all conditions, with a consistent standard of care required. This duty applies to any situation that may arise. State v. Kreuger, 1 W. W. Harr. 118, 111 A. 614. The first count’s allegations are sufficient. The third count accuses the defendant of driving with 'wilful or wanton disregard for safety,' citing 21 Del. C., Sec. 4123, but lacks details on the acts constituting the offense. While indictments for statutory offenses are usually valid if phrased similarly to the statute, this rule does not apply if the statute’s wording fails to clearly define all elements of the crime.

The accused must be informed of the charges in clear terms to prepare a defense or use the verdict in future proceedings. Evans v. United States, 153 U. S. 584, 14 S. Ct. 934, 38 L. Ed. 830; Id., 153 U. S. 608, 14 S. Ct. 939, 38 L. Ed. 839; State v. Lassotovitch, 162 Md. 147, 159 A. 362, 81 A. L. R. 69; People v. Green, 368 Ill. 242, 13 N. E. 2d 278, 115 A. L. R. 348; State v. Moran, 99 Conn. 115, 121 A. 277, 36.

This principle is supported by Delaware cases: State v. Donovan, 5 Boyce 40, 90 A. 220; State v. Burris, 6 Boyce 166, 97 A. 427; State v. Kreuger, 1 W. W. Harr. 118, 111 A. 614; State v. Morrow, 1 Terry 363, 10 A. 2d 530; State v. Boyle, 5 Terry 414, 61 A. 2d 121. Article 1, Section 7 of the Delaware Constitution guarantees the accused the right to be fully informed of the charges. To ensure the defendant can prepare a defense, the count should describe the conditions or actions showing the accused drove with wilful or wanton disregard for safety.

for the safety of individuals or property. The fourth count alleges, 'He operated the vehicle at a speed exceeding what was reasonable and prudent given the conditions and considering the actual and potential hazards present.' This count mirrors the wording of the first sentence in Section 4125(a) of Title 21 of the 1953 Code and faces the same issue I noted for count three. It does not specify the conditions or hazards at the time of the incident. As previously stated, this is essential to fully inform the defendant of the charges. The State v. Kreuger case is especially relevant here. The motion to dismiss the third and fourth counts is approved. The sixth count closely follows the second sentence of Section 4125(a), stating: 'He failed to adjust his speed to prevent a collision with another vehicle on the road.' This count aligns with the first count, which I have already addressed. Just as drivers must maintain constant vigilance, they must also consistently manage their speed to avoid collisions with others on the road, adhering to legal standards and the duty of care. The motion to dismiss the first and sixth counts is denied, while the motion to strike the third and fourth counts is granted.

a motor vehicle operator on public roads must always maintain proper awareness and adjust speed as needed to prevent collisions with any person, vehicle, or object on or entering the roadway, in line with legal obligations and the responsibility to exercise reasonable caution. The motion to dismiss the first and sixth counts is rejected. The motion to strike the third and fourth counts is approved. Pennewill, C.J., delivering the court's opinion: This case seeks compensation for a significant amount of toluol allegedly lost during transport from Johnstown, Pennsylvania, to Hercules, California. The claim states the goods were handed over to the defendant on November 16, 1917, in Johnstown, and the defendant failed to transport them safely or deliver them to the plaintiff in Hercules. The lawsuit was filed on November 16, 1920. Along with three general responses to the claim, the defendant submitted three specialized pleas. The fourth plea, the first specialized one, asserts that the shipment was handled under the terms of the uniform bill of lading, which stipulated that legal actions for loss, damage, or delay must be filed within two years and one day after delivery or, if delivery failed, within two years and one day after a reasonable delivery period passed.

under the terms of the uniform bill of lading, which included a clause stating: 'Claims for loss, damage, or delay must be filed within two years and one day after the property's delivery, or if delivery was not made, within two years and one day after a reasonable delivery time has passed.' This plea also claims the tank car reached its destination around February 4, 1918, which was a reasonable delivery timeframe, and the lawsuit was not filed within the required period. The defendant's fifth plea, the second specialized one, argues that the shipper provided the car used for transport, and the alleged loss occurred due to the car's defective state when loaded, specifically because the heater coils were not properly drained. The sixth plea, the third specialized one, is nearly identical to the fourth. The plaintiff objected to the first and third specialized pleas, raising two main points: (1) The bill of lading's terms were invalid during federal oversight. (2) The conditions in the fourth and sixth pleas are illegal and unenforceable. These arguments will be reviewed in reverse order.

We believe the carrier's liability under common law or state statutes before federal regulations is irrelevant to this case's pleadings and will not be examined. Under the Carmack Amendment to the Hepburn Act, Congress mandated that carriers issue bills of lading and held them accountable for any loss, damage, or injury to the property, regardless of which carrier caused it. No agreement or rule could exempt the carrier from this liability. Due to federal oversight, all state laws became ineffective for interstate shipments. The plaintiff's demurrer challenges the validity of the bill of lading's terms during federal control and asserts that the conditions in the fourth and sixth pleas are unlawful. These issues will be addressed in reverse order. The broader question of carrier liability under pre-federal statutes is not pertinent here and will not be discussed.

When goods were transported from one state to another under federal law, it was claimed in the declaration that the shipment occurred on November 16, 1917, while the plea stated some goods arrived by February 4, 1918. On December 26, 1917, the President, using authority from the Army Appropriation Act of August 29, 1916, seized control of the nation's railroads, including the defendant's lines. The federal oversight was later reinforced by an act on March 21, 1918, and ended on March 1, 1920, per the Transportation Act of February 28, 1920. The duration of federal control thus spanned from December 26, 1917, to March 1, 1920. Section 206f of the act specified that the time under federal control would not count toward statutory limitations for claims against carriers.

The Transportation Act (Section 206a) further stated that lawsuits against carriers could be filed within existing state or federal limitation periods, but no later than two years after the act's passage, in courts that would have had jurisdiction absent federal control. These provisions, along with the Cummins Act, addressed the plaintiff's first demurrer. The court found no illegality in the defendant's bill of lading under federal law. The defendant argued the bill complied with the Cummins Act of March 4, 1915, which prohibited carriers from setting a suit-filing period shorter than two years.

The bill of lading in question did not violate the Cummins Act, as it allowed a slightly longer filing period than mandated, benefiting the shipper. The Carmack Amendment required bills of lading but did not set a limitation period. Before the Cummins Act, carriers could impose reasonable contractual limitations, provided they did not negate liability for negligence. Cases like Missouri, Kansas & Texas R. R. Co. v. Harriman and Texas & Pac. Ry. Co. v. Leatherwood supported this principle. The Cummins Act barred shorter limitations but permitted longer ones.

The second demurrer challenged whether the bill of lading's terms remained valid during federal control. The Lazarus Case (D. C.), 271 Fed. 93, cited by both parties, was deemed irrelevant because no bill of lading was issued there. The court ruled that the carrier's filed limitation period qualified as federally prescribed, but noted a valid contract with a longer period might not fit that description. The statute's applicability here was uncertain, given the bill of lading's extended timeframe.

The period of federal control is excluded from the limitation period, even with a contract like a bill of lading, but the statute only applies if the cause of action arose before federal control. This case lacks evidence on when the cause of action began, and without a delivery agreement, a reasonable time for delivery is assumed. Determining what is reasonable depends on circumstances and may require jury deliberation, as it cannot be decided without trial evidence. The pleadings suggest the cause of action could have arisen before or during federal control, though the defendant claims delivery occurred reasonably by February 4, 1918, despite the goods being received earlier on November 17, 1917.

A recent appellate court decision reversed the Lazarus Case, ruling that the two-year condition in the bill of lading was part of the transportation agreement. The time to file an action was contractually fixed, not statutory, and the Transportation Act’s extension does not include the federal control period or alter the carrier-shipper contract terms. Contractually agreed time limits for filing actions are binding, and Congress cannot override them without violating the Fifth Amendment. The court clarified that Section 206(f) of the Transportation Act applies only to statutory limitations, not contractual ones, aligning with the definition in paragraph (a).

The appellate court’s reversal in the Lazarus Case favored the defendant, but the plaintiff argues the plea is flawed for not alleging the suit was filed within two years of written notice of claim disallowance. This argument references Section 438 of the 1920 Transportation Act, which specifies the two-year period starts from the carrier’s written notice of claim denial. This provision amended the 1915 Cummins Amendment, which prohibited carriers from setting shorter limitation periods but did not specify when the period begins. The Transportation Act addressed this omission.

The shipment contract under the Cummins Amendment states suits must be filed within two years and one day after delivery or a reasonable time for delivery has passed. This contract was valid, with the limitation period being a key term. The Transportation Act, enacted over two years later, aimed to clarify the computation of limitation periods but did not override the contract’s terms. The contract’s provision for a reasonable time for delivery remains enforceable, and the Act’s amendments do not apply retroactively to alter agreed-upon terms.

Two years following the carrier's notification to the claimant that their claim was denied, the contract stipulates the timeframe for action. While the plaintiff correctly asserts that 'the limitation of an action pertains to remedy rather than right' (36 Cyc. 1142; Lewis' Sutherland, Stat. Const. (2d Ed.) § 668; Terry v. Anderson, 95 U. S. 628, 24 L. Ed. 365), a subsequent statute extending the time to file suits may only affect the remedy. However, when the limitation is integrated into the contract, as here, the later statute does not apply. The plaintiff has demurred to the defendant's fifth or second special plea, citing that the plea fails to show the consignor provided the car for adequate consideration, that the defects were noticeable upon ordinary inspection, that the consignor knew of the defects, or that the consignor released the defendant from liability.

The cited cases on this issue are more perplexing than clarifying. Nonetheless, it is clear that a carrier remains liable for goods damaged due to a defective car, even if the shipper supplied the car. In Frohlick v. Pa. Co., 138 Mich. 116, the shipper had an inspector, and in Ala. G. So. R. Co. v. Morris & Co., 249 Fed. 312, the defect was not detectable by the carrier despite reasonable care. Most cases referenced by the defendant suggest the shipper may have waived the carrier's duty to inspect. We conclude that even if the shipper provided a defective car, the carrier is responsible for losses preventable through diligent inspection, unless evidence shows the shipper explicitly waived liability (Ala. G. So. R. Co. v. Morris & Co.; Ala. & V. Ry. Co. v. Amer. Cot. & Oil Co., 249 Fed. 308).

Exceptions exist if the facts imply the shipper absolved the carrier of liability (Cleveland, C., C. & St. L. Ry. Co. v. Louisville Tin & Stove Co., 33 Ky. Law Rep. 924). The plaintiff's demurrer is overruled for the defendant's fourth and sixth pleas (or first and third special pleas) but sustained for the fifth (or second special) plea. See Cook v. Gray, 2 Houst, 455, and Gray v. Cook, 3 Houst. 49.

After arguments, Grubb, J., delivered the Court's opinion: Defendants George W. May and Frank J. May in Maria C. Hartman's libel suit should be released on common bail. The alleged libel arose from pleadings in a pending Chancery Court case, and this Court's interference would disrupt justice there. Thus, on public policy grounds, the defendants are discharged on common bail. Woolley, J.

Presenting the court's opinion: The declaration in this matter includes a single count, where the plaintiff states he was a laborer hired by the defendant manufacturing company. He was assigned to assist in lowering an 800-pound barrel down a steep staircase. He raised concerns about the danger of the task to his employer, who assured him proper tools would be provided. The plaintiff claims he was told to proceed down the stairs to help with the task, trusting the defendant’s promise. However, the defendant allegedly failed to supply the necessary equipment and began moving the barrel without warning, leading to the plaintiff's injury. The defendant filed a general demurrer, arguing the declaration did not establish a valid cause of action.

The defendant also cited contributory negligence by the plaintiff, as well as his awareness of the working conditions. They argued the plaintiff did not qualify for negligence protections that excuse employees from assuming risks after reporting unsafe conditions. Instead, they claimed the plaintiff fell under a different negligence rule, where a worker performing obvious manual labor cannot avoid risk by citing a promise of safer tools. The court found the pleadings did not sufficiently present this negligence issue, as the declaration failed to outline a clear cause of action or scenario where the argued legal principle would apply. The plaintiff described being assigned the task, reporting the hazard, and receiving a promise of tools, but the specifics of his injury and involvement in the incident were unclear.

The declaration did not clarify how the plaintiff was injured, what he was doing at the time, or whether his participation directly caused the harm. Without these details, the court concluded no actionable claim was presented to evaluate the legal arguments raised in the demurrer. For these reasons, the demurrer was upheld.

OPINION BY STEELE, V.C.: This ruling addresses a petition to appoint a receiver for managing property during mortgage foreclosure and deficiency proceedings. The issue is whether interim relief should be granted to safeguard the mortgagee’s interests post-foreclosure but before resolving the deficiency claim. On June 21, 1996, respondents William P. Ingram and Margaret A. Ingram executed a mortgage agreement with petitioner Dover Associates Joint Venture, securing a $1,150,000 loan on Delaware property. After defaulting, the mortgage terms allowed Dover Associates to seek a receiver. A foreclosure action was filed, and on November 25, 1998, the parties agreed to a stipulated judgment.

Dover Associates agreed to accept $1,390,000 as full payment for the mortgage. The Ingrams were required to transfer their property rights to Dover Associates if they failed to pay the amount within 90 days. Instead of providing the cash, the Ingrams found a buyer willing to pay $1,390,000, but the sale couldn't close immediately, leading Dover Associates to take control of the property. The Superior Court foreclosed on the property, and Dover Associates acquired it for $1,000,000. Later, Dover Associates requested a receiver to manage the property during litigation, citing equitable power and contractual terms as justification.

Have Dover Associates sufficiently justified their equitable claim for a receiver? The Ingrams argued that equity shouldn't intervene because Dover Associates acted unreasonably by foreclosing instead of negotiating with a $1,390,000 buyer. They claim Dover Associates' actions—rejecting a $1,390,000 offer, buying the property for $1,000,000, then selling it for $1,200,000—undermine their deficiency claim and equity's intervention. The Ingrams contend that fairness requires Dover Associates to pursue only the deficiency claim in court.

The Ingrams suggest the court can resolve the parties' claims and award damages. Dover Associates argues that the Ingrams' mortgage default and failure to provide cash as agreed justify removing their control over the property. They imply the Ingrams might misuse rental income, reducing funds for a potential deficiency judgment. However, the court finds no compelling reason to appoint a receiver, given the disputed facts and Dover Associates' questionable conduct after acquiring the property for $1,000,000.

Despite the lack of equitable justification, the mortgage terms mandate a receiver's appointment upon default. The agreement explicitly allows for a receiver to manage the property during foreclosure proceedings. The court must enforce this contractual right, as equity follows the law. The Ingrams' default triggered Dover Associates' right to a receiver, and equity principles require upholding this legal provision, regardless of the Ingrams' objections to Dover Associates' actions.

Unfairly handling the property's disposal makes it unjust to enforce the contractual right to collect rents and manage the property. Equity cannot, as the Ingrams argue, nullify a legally contracted right. While a receiver may be appointed to prevent significant harm when no contract exists, this standard doesn't apply here, as the contract explicitly allows for immediate receiver appointment upon default. The parties agreed that default justifies this equitable remedy, and equity must uphold the law when contractual rights are clear. Dover Associates' equitable claim for a receiver falls short, but their contractual right grants them the remedy.

Despite the lack of a comparable legal remedy, balancing the parties' competing interests is necessary. Appointing a receiver to manage the property and collect rents during litigation won't harm the Ingrams, as losing rental income isn't detrimental. Conversely, equity enforces Dover Associates' contractual right to a receiver, a remedy the Ingrams agreed to when securing funding and triggered by their default. Thus, Dover Associates' petition for a receiver is granted under these conditions: (1) The receiver will manage the property and collect rents; (2) Collected funds, after expenses, will be held in escrow pending litigation; (3) The receiver must account for funds at the end of the receivership, applying any balance to the judgment; (4) Dover Associates must submit an Order reflecting these findings.

The record shows the Ingrams operated 1101 Stone Associates, LLC, which manages the property and collects rents, though it's unclear if they are also tenants. The Mortgage, Security Agreement, and Assignment of Rents signed by the Ingrams grants Dover Associates control over the property. Dover bought the property for $1,000,000 and sold it for $1,200,000 to a buyer procured by the Ingrams. A deficiency action is pending in Delaware Superior Court, Kent County, under case Ingram v. 1101 Stone Associates, LLC, et al., C.A. No. 99C-09-006-HDR.

Referencing the Mortgage, Security Agreement, and Assignment of Rents, Section 7.04 allows the Mortgagee or receiver to manage the property, make repairs, collect rents, and preserve its value. They may operate in the Mortgagor's name or otherwise. Legal precedents like 27A Am.Jur.2d Equity § 113 (1996) and Delaware Trust Company v. Partial, Del.Ch., 517 A.2d 259 (1986) support this. The Ingrams' default activates these contractual rights, justifying the receiver's appointment to protect Dover Associates' interests.

The Ingrams contend that Dover Associates' inability to handle the property sale in a commercially reasonable way completely prevents them from claiming a deficiency. Wilmington Trust v. Conner, Del.Supr., 415 A.2d 773 (1980). I discuss this point briefly as it is irrelevant to this case and doesn't influence the Court's decision to appoint a temporary receiver. In Wilmington Trust v. Conner, the Supreme Court overturned the Superior Court's ruling, preventing the creditor from securing a deficiency judgment in an auto repossession case due to their failure to give the debtor proper notice about the collateral's disposal. Id. The 'absolute bar' concept arises from a creditor's non-compliance with notice obligations. This ruling doesn't apply here. Dover Associates foreclosed on the property and is now pursuing a deficiency judgment. The Superior Court might determine that any alleged mishandling of the property sale impacts the deficiency judgment, but there are no notice-related issues here that would invoke the 'absolute bar' theory. Thus, I reject the Ingrams' argument. . Moore v. Associated

Producing & Refining Corp., Del.Ch., 121 A. 655, 656 (1923) (citing Gray v. Newark, Del.Ch., 79 A. 735, 739 (1911)). . Beal Bank, SSB v. Lucks, Del.Ch., C.A. No. 14896, mem. op., Steele, V.C., 1998 WL 778362 (Oct. 23, 1998). In Beal, appointing a receiver to ensure rent payments wasn't contractually stipulated, unlike the current case. . See The Estate of Magaral, Del.Ch., No. 81150, Brown, C. (Oct. 18, 1984) (despite potential unfair outcomes, Chancellor Brown adhered to 'equity follows the law' to decide estate beneficiaries). . 30A C.J.S. Equity § 93 at 289. . Unless they or

an entity under their control attempts to evade rent payments. This could justify their resistance to the order—a scenario equity would not support. HOLLAND, Justice: This appeal raises novel questions regarding Delaware's Truth in Sentencing Act. The appellant, Ronald L. Robinson ('Robinson'), requested a 'resentencing' under the Act, but the Superior Court denied it, ruling the Act applies only prospectively. Robinson argues this was a legal error and, alternatively, that the Act violates his constitutional right to equal protection if applied prospectively. The State moved to affirm the Superior Court's decision. Supr. Ct.R. 25(a). We find both arguments unpersuasive. Facts After a Superior Court jury trial, Robinson was convicted of Possession with Intent to Deliver a Narcotic Schedule II Controlled Substance under 16 Del.C. § 4751, Possession with Intent to Deliver a Non-narcotic Schedule I Controlled Substance under 16 Del.C. § 4752, and Maintaining a Dwelling for Keeping Controlled Substances under 16 Del.C. § 4755. Due to prior federal drug convictions, he received an enhanced sentence under 16 Del.C. § 4763(a).

Robinson was sentenced to a mandatory 18-year prison term followed by 20 years of probation. He didn't appeal initially but later filed for post-conviction relief under then-existing Superior Court Criminal Rule 35. The Superior Court denied his motion, and this Court upheld the decision on appeal. See Robinson v. State, Del.Supr., 509 A.2d 94 (1986) (ORDER). Robinson then sought a federal writ of habeas corpus, which was also denied. On August 8, 1990, Robinson sent a letter to the Superior Court. In his

In his letter, Robinson claimed that Delaware's Truth in Sentencing Act, specifically 67 Del.Laws, ch. 130, nullified the two statutes—§ 4751 and 4752—under which he was sentenced. He sought suitable redress. The court interpreted his letter as a motion under Superior Court Criminal Rule 61, seeking a sentence adjustment. The State countered, arguing his request was time-barred per Rule 61, leading the Superior Court to reject his claim. Two key issues arise: first, whether Robinson's claim is procedurally barred due to untimeliness under Rule 61, and second, whether he qualifies for resentencing under the Truth in Sentencing Act rather than Chapter 16 of the Delaware Code. An affirmative answer to the latter could exempt his claim from Rule 61's time bar.

Rule 61 took effect on January 1, 1988, superseding Rule 35 for post-conviction remedies. Rule 61(i)(l) imposes a three-year limit for filing post-conviction relief, starting from the final conviction judgment or, for newly recognized retroactive rights, from their recognition by Delaware or the U.S. Supreme Court. This three-year window became active on January 1, 1989, applying even to pre-Rule 61 convictions, as confirmed in Boyer v. State. The limit is jurisdictional and inflexible under Super. Ct. Crim. R. 45(b).

Robinson was convicted on May 17, 1985, giving him until May 17, 1988, to file a Rule 61 motion for sentence correction. However, he filed only on August 8, 1990, missing the deadline. While Rule 61's time bar is strict, exceptions exist. Robinson could bypass it by proving his case fits one of Rule 61's exceptions, as noted in Boyer v. State. He argues the Truth in Sentencing Act repealed his sentencing statutes, rendering his sentence illegal and eligible for correction under Rule 61(i)(l), potentially exempting him from the time bar.

Robinson contends the Truth in Sentencing Act provides a retroactive right, newly recognized, that should shorten his sentence. If valid, his motion would avoid the time bar, as Rule 61 permits filings within three years of such a right's establishment. The Act's Section 3 applies to crimes committed after June 30, 1990, while Section 4 preserves repealed statutes for earlier crimes. Though Robinson correctly notes the Act repealed 16 Del.C. § 4751, 67 Del.Laws, ch. 130, § 15, maintained its applicability for pre-June 30, 1990, offenses.

to make it illegal to possess Schedule I or II Narcotic Controlled Substances with the intent to distribute. Compare 16 Del.C. § 4751(a) (1983) with 16 Del.C. § 4751(a) (Supp.1989). The savings clause in Section 4 of the Truth in Sentencing Act, along with the ongoing prohibition of the specific conduct involved, demonstrates the General Assembly's clear intent to retain the offenses for which Robinson was convicted. See Wicks v. State, Del.Supr., 559 A.2d 1194, 1195-96 (1989). The Truth in Sentencing Act only became effective at 12:01 a.m. on June 30, 1990. Robinson was arrested on June 18, 1984, and sentenced on May 17, 1985, well before the Act was implemented. Although the Truth in Sentencing Act modifies the statutes under which Robinson was convicted, the General Assembly's intent remains evident. An examination of the Truth in Sentencing

Act reveals that it does not grant retroactive rights to Robinson. Compare United States v. Stewart, 865 F.2d 115 (7th Cir.1988). The Delaware General Assembly never intended the Truth in Sentencing Act to apply retroactively. Therefore, Robinson's motion for post-conviction relief does not meet the exception to the three-year filing requirement under Rule 61. Truth in Sentencing Act/Equal Protection Alternatively, Robinson argues that if the Truth in Sentencing Act applies only prospectively, it violates his constitutional rights. Specifically, he claims it denies him equal protection under federal law. Robinson asserts that the U.S. Constitution forbids states from implementing two sentencing systems for the same crime, resulting in unequal sentences. When a state legislature establishes differing sentencing schemes for identical offenses, there is a presumption of constitutionality. Clements v. Fashing, 457 U.S. 957, 962-3, 102 S.Ct. 2836, 2843-44, 73 L.Ed.2d

508 (1982). The equal protection clause allows states flexibility to pass laws that may seem to treat similar individuals differently. Id. 'Traditional equal protection standards require only that distinctions have a rational connection to a legitimate state objective. Classifications are invalidated only if they are entirely unrelated to the state's goals and no justification can be found.' Id. See also Schweiker v. Wilson, 450 U.S. 221, 230, 101 S.Ct. 1074, 1080-81, 67 L.Ed.2d 186 (1981). While this Court has not yet examined the implications of the Delaware Truth in Sentencing Act on repealed statutes, other courts have addressed similar issues. In Foster v. Wash. St. Bd. Of Prison Terms And Parole, 878 F.2d 1233 (9th Cir.1989), the petitioner was convicted in Washington for rape and kidnapping two years before a

change in the state's penal laws. In 1981, Washington enacted a Sentencing Reform Act ('SRA'), effective July 1, 1984, applicable to crimes committed on or after that date. Id. at 1234. The petitioner was convicted in July 1982. Id. He argued that the SRA denied him equal protection by treating pre-July 1, 1984 offenders differently from those convicted afterward. The Ninth Circuit upheld his sentence, applying the rational basis test and concluding that sentencing improvements served a legitimate government purpose. Id. at 1235. See also Mistretta v. United States, 488 U.S. 361, 109 S.Ct. 647, 102 L.Ed.2d 714 (1989); and Swinson v. U.S. Parole Comm'n, 682 F.Supp. 29 (E.D.N.C.1988), aff'd, 84

In 9 F.2d 606 (4th Cir. 1988), the court noted that the Sentencing Reform Act (SRA) was implemented to standardize prison terms by removing parole discretion, which aligns with a legitimate governmental objective. In Frazier v. Manson, 703 F.2d 30 (2nd Cir. 1983), the Second Circuit affirmed a Connecticut sentencing law applicable to post-October 1, 1976 cases, rejecting an appellant's 1973 sentencing challenge. The court upheld the legislature's classification, stating that identical sentences for the same crime are not mandated and that prospective penalty reductions are permissible despite disparities for pre-act offenders. Id. at 36, citing Williams v. Illinois, 399 U.S. 235 (1970).

The court found prior rulings convincing, acknowledging that the Truth in Sentencing Act creates disparate sentencing for crimes committed before and after June 30, 1990, but deemed the General Assembly's rationale valid. Consequently, Robinson's equal protection claim for sentence reduction was denied. The State's motion was granted, and the Superior Court's denial of post-conviction relief was affirmed.

In United States v. Stewart, 865 F.2d 115 (7th Cir. 1988), the defendant pleaded guilty to federal conspiracy and possession charges on September 16, 1987, and was sentenced on November 16, 1987. He argued for sentencing under the SRA, effective November 1, 1987, but Congress later clarified it applied only to post-effective-date offenses. The Seventh Circuit noted some SRA provisions would disadvantage the defendant, framing the issue as an ex post facto concern. The court ruled Congress intended non-retroactivity, upholding the original sentencing provisions.

In a negligence case appeal, the court reversed the plaintiff's judgment due to an incomplete jury instruction on brake statutes (21 Del.C. § 4304). The defendant, driving downhill, encountered brake failure at a red light, colliding with the plaintiff's truck. The brake malfunction stemmed from a ruptured hose. The case was remanded for a new trial.

that the defendant did not maintain proper control of her vehicle; that she breached the Statutes regulating speed and traffic-light-controlled intersections; and that she contravened the Statutes mandating sufficient brakes, specifically 21 Del.C. § 4303 and 4304. The defendant's only argument was that the accident was unavoidable. The Trial Court directed the jury on these matters. Regarding § 4304, the jury was told: 'The subsequent statute defines Delaware’s standard for adequate brakes.' 'To meet Delaware’s requirements, service brakes must halt a vehicle moving at 20 mph within 30 feet on dry asphalt or concrete, while the hand brake must do so within 55 feet under the same conditions.' 'Clearly, this instruction omitted a key part of § 4304.'

critical condition: 'where the slope is no more than 1 percent.' This phrase is part of § 4304(a) and applies to § 4304(b) and (c). Accurately interpreting the brake Statute was essential for resolving this case. The Trial Court’s failure to provide the jury with the full Statute was a serious mistake. Consequently, the judgment is overturned, and the case is sent back for retrial. We reject the defendant’s claim that she deserved a directed verdict due to insufficient evidence of negligence. The jury, in our view, rightly considered her negligence. While other appeal grounds need no ruling here, we offer these clarifications for the retrial: The plaintiff, as owner, was allowed to testify about his truck’s post-accident value under the established before-and-after method for assessing property damage in auto negligence cases.

However, the plaintiff lacked expertise in valuing damaged trucks. Thus, allowing his testimony on this damage aspect was incorrect. An owner may estimate their vehicle’s pre-accident value—based on the assumption that familiarity implies general knowledge of worth. See State v. 0.15 Acres of Land, etc., 3 Storey 372, 169 A.2d 256 (1961). No similar principle allows an owner to estimate post-damage value without expert input, which must be direct, not hearsay. Refer to Alber v. Wise, 3 Storey 126, 166 A.2d 141 (1960); Teitsworth v. Kempski, 11 Terry 234, 127 A.2d 237 (1956). Regarding jury instructions: The jury was told it could compensate the plaintiff for

anticipated future income loss.' In our assessment, the evidence was inadequate to justify this instruction: The plaintiff had a neck sprain. He missed eight workdays post-accident and another 15-16 days over nine months before trial. He attributed this to headaches and sleep loss affecting his focus. His doctor stated the headaches might continue. This was the entirety of the future earnings loss evidence. Precedent holds such evidence insufficient for jury consideration. Coles v. Spence, Del., 202 A.2d 569 (1964); Henne v. Balick, 1 Storey 369, 146 A.2d 394 (1958). The judgment is reversed, and the case is remanded for proceedings consistent with this ruling. 21 Del.C. §

Section 4304 states: Ҥ 4304. Brake performance standards '(a) Service brakes on any motor vehicle or combination must be capable of stopping the vehicle within 30 feet when moving at 20 mph on dry, clean asphalt or concrete with a slope not exceeding 1%. '(b) Under the same conditions, the parking brake must stop the vehicle within 55 feet and hold it stationary on any incline. '(c) For vehicles with only two-wheel brakes, service brakes must stop within 40 feet and the parking brake within 55 feet under these conditions.' 21 Del.C. § 4303 adds: Ҥ 4303. General brake requirements '(a) All highway-operated vehicles must have brakes sufficient to control, stop, and hold the vehicle and any attached trailer, with two independent braking systems each affecting at least two wheels. Motorcycles need only one brake. All brakes must be well-maintained and comply with Commissioner regulations, adjusted to work equally on both sides.

Trailers must have brakes meeting these standards, with two separate braking mechanisms each acting on at least two wheels, designed so no single failure affects both systems. This portion of the charge was flawed as it merely stated the law without connecting it to the facts, unlike Beck v. Haley, Del., 239 A.2d 699 (1968). Carey, J. Before Delaware adopted new procedural rules, statutes of limitations required affirmative pleas and couldn’t be challenged via demurrer, even if the claim was time-barred. 1 Woolley’s Del. Prac. 373.

The new rules adopted Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 9(f) and 12(b) verbatim. Rule 9(f) treats time allegations as material for pleading adequacy, while Rule 12(b) allows dismissal motions for failing to state a claim. Most federal cases permit raising limitations via motion if the complaint reveals the action is time-barred. 2 Moore’s Federal Practice (2d Ed.) 2257, Sec. 12.10. When state and federal rules align, federal interpretations should guide unless compelling reasons exist otherwise. Thus, a dismissal motion is appropriate here, a point the plaintiff doesn’t dispute. Her brief concedes the applicable limitations period began when the harmful substance was prescribed (March 26, 1946), not upon injury discovery.

The key issue is whether the one-year limit for personal injury actions applies or the general three-year rule. The statute here isn’t tied to specific action forms or injury causes, unlike some state laws limiting it to certain misconduct. It broadly covers all personal injury damage claims, rendering many plaintiff-cited cases irrelevant due to their reliance on narrower statutes. The plaintiff’s argument hinges on distinguishing between injury types, but the statute’s plain language encompasses all personal injury claims, regardless of cause or legal theory.

The courts have ruled that malpractice does not qualify as the type of assault addressed by the statute, as seen in cases like McClees v. Cohen, 158 Md. 60, 148 A. 124; Burke v. Maryland, 149 Minn. 481, 184 N.W. 32; Francis v. Brooks, 24 Ohio App. 136, 156 N.E. 609; and White v. Hirschfield, 108 Okl. 263, 236 P. 406. Additionally, cases referenced in annotations such as 1 A.L.R. 1313 and 62 A.L.R. 1417, which hinged on the type of legal action, are irrelevant here. These cases focused on whether the suit was contractual or tort-based, whereas our statute imposes limitations on all personal injury claims without such distinctions. The statute’s wording explicitly applies regardless of whether malpractice stems from contract breach or negligence, or whether the plaintiff can choose between these legal avenues.

Courts interpreting statutes similar to ours have aligned with the reasoning above. I concur with the rulings in Bodne v. Austin, 156 Tenn. 353, 2 S.W. 2d 100, 62 A.L.R. 1410, and Klingbeil v. Saucerman, 165 Wis. 60, 160 N.W. 1051, 1 A.L.R. 1311, where the statutes were nearly identical. The plaintiff heavily relies on Menefee v. Alexander, 107 Ky. 279, 53 S.W. 653, but the Kentucky case may not be directly applicable due to differences in its statute. To the extent it conflicts with this reasoning, I reject it, as it contradicts the majority of legal authority, including Klingbeil v. Saucerman, 165 Wis. 60, 160 N.W. 1051, 1 A.L.R. 1313; 41 Am. Jur. 232; and 34 Am. Jur. 84.

In Lewis v. Pawnee Bill's Wild West Co., 6 Penn. 316, 66 A. 471, 474, 16 Ann. Cas. 903, our Supreme Court emphasized that the statute’s language is clear and requires no interpretation. The court stated that judges cannot introduce exceptions for specific cases or individuals when the statute itself provides none, and no perceived hardship justifies deviating from its plain terms. While legislative intent can be elusive, it is reasonable to assume that the reduced limitation period for personal injury claims was due to the nature of such evidence—often oral and susceptible to loss from witness death, fading memories, or other factors. These reasons do not suggest any intent to differentiate between directly inflicted injuries and those arising indirectly from torts or contract breaches.

Until the legislature revises the statute to reflect changed priorities, this Court cannot impose exceptions on its unambiguous text, regardless of individual hardships. The complaint clearly seeks damages for alleged personal injuries and was filed over a year after the liability arose, placing it under the one-year statute of limitations. Thus, the motion to dismiss is granted. SHORT, Vice Chancellor: This case was filed under 8 Del.C. § 225 to determine the validity of an election for certain directors of the Burr Corporation. Both parties have requested summary judgment, and this ruling addresses those motions. The plaintiffs, collectively holding a significant portion of Burr Corporation’s stock, are involved in the dispute.

The plaintiffs collectively hold 30% of the issued and outstanding shares and serve as directors of the corporation. Before the dispute, Donald Burr was president and CEO, Robert Hartman was executive vice-president, and Eugene Tracey was vice-president of sales. Understanding the case requires examining Burr Corporation's certificate of incorporation and bylaws. The restated certificate specifies that the number of directors is set by the bylaws and elected at annual shareholder meetings. Section 3.02 of the bylaws states the board can have one to nine directors, elected annually unless Section 3.04 applies, which addresses filling vacancies due to death, resignation, or removal, as well as new directorships from increasing the board size.

The authorized number of directors can only be filled by a majority vote of the remaining directors. Following these rules, the board set the number of directors to five, and in May 1971, the plaintiffs, Richard Steadman, and Henry Keller were elected. In June 1971, the board expanded to six directors, appointing George Pratt to the new position. Pratt, Keller, and Steadman represented the majority shareholders. On September 9, 1971, the majority shareholders amended Section 3.02 to increase directors to nine, revised Section 3.04 to let majority stockholders fill new directorships, and updated Section 3.08 to allow special board meetings with two days' notice.

On the same day, three new directors were elected by majority shareholders. A special board meeting was called under the amended Section 3.08, resulting in a 5-3 vote to remove the plaintiffs as officers, though they remained directors. The plaintiffs dispute the validity of the new directors' election, arguing that the amended bylaws allowing shareholders to fill vacancies conflict with the certificate's requirement for annual director elections. They claim this restriction means directors can only be elected annually, making the bylaw void unless the certificate is amended.

Plaintiffs correctly assert that bylaws conflicting with the certificate are invalid, citing relevant case law. However, the court disagrees that the documents conflict. The certificate's provision mirrors 8 Del.C. § 211(b), mandating annual director elections. Precedent holds that such statutes govern regular elections but don’t bar special elections for new directorships, as seen in Moon v. Moon Motor Car Co. and Campbell v. Loew's, Inc. Richman v. De further supports this interpretation.

Val Aerodynamics, Inc., 40 Del.Ch. 389, 183 A.2d 569 (1962); In re A. A. Griffing Iron Co., 63 N.J.L. 168, 41 A. 931 (1898), affirmed by memorandum, 63 N.J.L. 357, 46 A. 1097 (1899). This situation closely resembles Moon v. Moon Motor Co., supra. In that instance, shareholders expanded the board by revising the by-laws and promptly appointed new directors to the additional seats. Soon after, the restructured board convened and replaced specific officers. The Moon plaintiffs contested the majority shareholders' actions, claiming that holding an election outside the annual meeting stipulated in the by-laws breached Section 30 of Delaware Corporation Law. The court dismissed this claim, ruling that the term 'annual meeting' in legislation pertains to electing directors to replace outgoing ones in the standard corporate cycle.

The court determined that Section 30 of the Delaware Corporation Law at the time did not prohibit shareholders from holding special elections to occupy newly established director roles. The Court's reasoning was grounded in the idea that if the majority owners believed the corporation needed a larger board—whether due to prudent management needs or poor administration by the current board—it would be unreasonable to force them to wait nearly a year to implement their decision. 151 A. at 302. I find the plaintiffs' attempt to differentiate Moon unconvincing, even though, when Moon was decided, directors lacked the authority under Delaware law to fill new director positions. See remarks by the Chancellor in Campbell v. Loew’s, Inc., supra. The court's stance that urgent management needs or majority board misconduct may justify immediate action by the majority owners remains relevant here, despite current Delaware law allowing directors to fill such vacancies.

Following Moon, I conclude that Section 211(b) of the Delaware Corporation Law, the successor to Section 30, applies solely to regular elections, not the scenario at hand. Thus, Burr Corporation’s amended by-laws, enabling shareholders to elect directors for newly created positions, do not contravene this statute. Furthermore, there is no basis to assume the certificate of incorporation’s annual meeting clause is stricter than Section 211(b). The plaintiffs have not provided a compelling reason to interpret the certificate provision unusually. Anyone advocating such an interpretation should identify explicit charter language supporting it. Investment Associates, Inc. v. Standard Power and Light Corp., 29 Del.Ch. 225, 48 A.2d 501 (1946), affirmed, Del.Supr., 29 Del.Ch. 593, 51 A.2d 572 (1947). Consequently, I find the certificate’s annual meeting requirement aligns with Section 211(b).

Given this, the by-laws, which comply with the statute, also harmonize with the certificate. Therefore, amended Section 3.04 of the by-laws is valid. The plaintiffs further argue that even if Section 3.04 is valid, its wording does not grant shareholders unrestricted authority to elect directors. Section 3.04 states: 'Vacancies on the Board caused by death, resignation, or removal of directors, as well as new directorships from an increase in board size, may be filled by a majority vote of the remaining directors or by a majority of outstanding shares; however, if the vacancy involves a director designated under a stockholder agreement per subsection (c) of section 218 of Delaware General Corporation Law, and the designating party retains that right, the directors may only appoint another nominee from that party.'

If a majority vote cannot fill the vacancy within 60 days of its occurrence, the President or Secretary may convene a special shareholder meeting to address it. Directors elected this way will serve until the next annual election and until successors are properly elected, unless removed earlier. If no directors are in office, an election may follow statutory procedures. Plaintiffs argue Section 3.04 allows stockholders to fill vacancies only if remaining directors fail to do so within 60 days, but this interpretation is unsupported by the provision's clear wording. Section 3.04 distinguishes between vacancies from death, resignation, or removal and newly-created directorships from increasing director numbers. The plaintiffs' cited sentence only addresses vacancies, not new directorships, a distinction long upheld in Delaware courts.

Johnston, 31 Del.Ch. 469, 64 A.2d 416 (1949), and Campbell v. Loew's, Inc., supra, support this view. Additionally, 8 Del.C. § 223 treats vacancies and newly-created directorships as separate concepts. The Burr Corporation bylaws were meticulously drafted, likely with awareness of Delaware’s distinction between vacancies and new directorships. Had the drafters intended to redefine 'vacancy' to include new directorships, they would have explicitly stated so, deviating from established legal meaning. They did not. Thus, 'vacancy' in Section 3.04 refers only to openings from death, resignation, or removal, excluding newly-created directorships. Consequently, Burr Corporation’s shareholders acted in compliance with the amended Section 3.04.

I conclude that the amendment to Section 3.04 of the bylaws was valid and did not conflict with Burr Corporation’s certificate of incorporation. The majority shareholders acted in accordance with the amended section, which allowed them to elect directors to newly-created positions. Therefore, the defendants’ motion for summary judgment is granted, and the plaintiffs’ motion is denied. An appropriate order may be submitted with notice. The defendant, a Colorado resident, owned nearly all attached stock, now valueless due to a federal receivership, preventing bail posting. He asserted no debt existed to the plaintiffs and argued appearance could occur without discharging the attachment, as its purpose was to secure judgment and compel appearance. The statutes, if interpreted to mandate bail for appearance, would violate the Fourteenth Amendment by enforcing arbitrary and unreasonable distinctions among defendants. The defendant argued that appearance and plea filing should proceed without disrupting the attachment's security function, ensuring fair trial rights while preserving the plaintiffs' claim on the property for potential judgment.

Demanding a thousand dollars to secure the dissolution of the attachment and release of the seized stock shares, as a prerequisite for allowing the defendant's appearance and plea submissions, is unjust, excessive, and undermines core judicial principles. This summarizes the defendant's counsel's argument in their brief. The plaintiffs counter nearly every point raised by the defendant, asserting that he cannot participate or defend without posting special bail, as no appearance is valid otherwise. They base their stance on statutory wording and over a century of consistent practice, claiming no prior instance where an individual defendant in a foreign attachment case appeared without special bail. They argue that although the statute lacks explicit prohibition, the implication is as binding as a direct ban, and permitting such an appearance would nullify the plaintiff's attachment benefits, contrary to legislative intent.

Entering an appearance without special bail transforms the case into an in-personam action, voiding its in-rem nature, and any subsequent judgment would be general, eliminating the attachment's lien. The plaintiffs assert that allowing the defendant to appear without bail would strip them of all attachment advantages. They also argue that, as this is the second term, an appearance and trial would force a continuance, barring any judgment under the statute. Additionally, they contend that the statute allowing corporations to be summoned as garnishees is irrelevant here. To the defendant's claim that requiring special bail violates the Fourteenth Amendment by denying due process, the plaintiffs respond that the defendant can still defend by posting security matching the attached property's value, a reasonable and common legal requirement in in-rem actions.

The plaintiffs' argument, as presented, notes the unprecedented nature of the defendant's claim that an individual can appear in a foreign attachment suit without special bail. While this lack of precedent doesn't outright invalidate the claim, it carries significant weight. The defendant counters that this case presents a novel issue, with the sole distinction being the exorbitant bail amount, which they cannot meet. The court, however, finds this distinction irrelevant, as bail feasibility always depends on a defendant's finances. The inability to post large bail doesn't exempt this case from established rules. The court firmly holds that in foreign attachment cases against individuals, appearance requires special bail—indeed, bail submission constitutes appearance. No conflicting precedents were cited, and while the defendant's statutory interpretation is compelling, it fails to persuade.

The court concludes that the statute serves dual purposes: compelling appearance and securing a plaintiff's lien on attached property. These aims are interdependent, as allowing appearance without bail would undermine the attachment's benefits—a result the legislature surely didn't intend. The defendant argues that appearance needn't dissolve the attachment, but the court disagrees. The statute's construction is a state matter, rendering external case law minimally helpful. The defendant's reasoning, though robust, doesn't alter the court's view that special bail is indispensable for appearance, preserving the attachment's integrity and legislative purpose.

He acknowledges that the defendant's appearance would shift the case from in rem to in personam. Consequently, the attachment valid in an in rem action would dissolve unless preserved by statutory provisions, such as those for foreign corporations. The defendant cites this statute to argue the attachment's persistence post-appearance, but the court finds this reasoning flawed. The statute’s explicit language for foreign corporations implies its absence in individual cases would not save the lien. Moreover, a general judgment post-appearance would nullify the attachment's lien, as it wouldn’t specifically bind the seized property. The defendant references prior rulings to counter this, yet those involved post-judgment motions that didn’t undermine the judgment's lien.

In the cited cases, the court allowed defendants to contest claims post-judgment, preserving the lien unless the defense failed. The court treated these as default judgments under a state statute permitting reopening if the defendant lacked prior suit knowledge and had a valid defense. The court likely acted either under the statute’s terms or by analogy, aiming for fairness without harming the plaintiff’s lien. While not endorsing these rulings, the court clarifies they don’t address pre-judgment appearances without bail. Another concern is that a trial would delay judgment, conflicting with the statute’s mandate for judgment by the second term without bail. Continuance might not outright bar judgment, but the statute’s strict wording casts doubt, aligning with longstanding legal opinion.

The defendant argues that filing a declaration and pleading rules grant him the right to appear and plead. Plaintiffs’ counsel stated the declaration was filed cautiously due to new pleading rules. However, this filing doesn’t alter the statute’s interpretation. The defendant further claims that even if his appearance is dismissed, the court lacks jurisdiction because the garnishee, a Delaware corporation, never operated in the state. Revised Code Section 4120 subjects corporations doing business in the state to attachment laws, but the garnishee wasn’t attached or summoned here.

The court notes that permitting a defense post-judgment in attachment cases doesn’t address pre-judgment appearances without bail. Plaintiffs argue a trial would delay judgment, contrary to the statute’s requirement for judgment by the second term without bail. While the court might still enter judgment post-continuance, the statute’s imperative language makes this uncertain. The defendant’s reliance on the declaration’s filing is misplaced, as it doesn’t override the statute. His jurisdictional argument hinges on the garnishee’s lack of in-state activity, but since the corporation wasn’t attached or summoned, the attachment laws don’t apply.

The defendant's shares in the corporation were seized according to Section 2009 of the Revised Code, which states that shares in any incorporated company can be attached for debt. Under this law, the corporation itself is not garnished; instead, an officer provides the sheriff with a certificate of the debtor's shares. This longstanding statute is broad and not restricted by the later Section 4120. Additionally, Section 1986 specifies that the legal location of stock ownership for state corporations is within the state, making it unnecessary to interpret Section 4120's 'doing business' clause in this context.

Regarding the defendant's claim that the statute violates the Fourteenth Amendment by denying due process, we disagree. The statute does not prevent a defense but requires security equal to the attached property's value. This condition replaces the seized assets and is no different from requirements in other legal actions like rent disputes. The rule is neither arbitrary nor excessive and aligns with due process standards. The plaintiffs have not presented any conflicting precedents to challenge this conclusion.

We further find no merit in the defendant's argument that the statute creates an unlawful classification. This point was barely emphasized during arguments, so we see no need for extensive discussion. After thorough review, we uphold the statute's constitutionality and affirm that special bail is required for appearance. This ruling is supported by overwhelming legal authority, and we have addressed all key issues without unnecessary elaboration.

The Superior Court ordered the removal of the defendant's improper filings and entries, directing a default judgment collectible only from the attached property. Before the judgment amount was finalized, the defendant petitioned to reopen the case, citing reasons similar to those later presented. A rule was issued for the plaintiffs to respond, with the return date subsequently adjusted.

The court expanded the order, instructing the sheriff to deliver the writ to the plaintiffs' attorneys of record, without affecting the legality of the service. The sheriff's return noted that the writ was personally delivered to Saulsbury, Morris, and Rodney on May 18, 1916. The plaintiffs' attorneys requested a special appearance to challenge the service as illegal, which the court allowed. They moved to void the service and dismiss the petition to open judgment, arguing insufficient grounds, with the legal issues referred to the Court in Banc.

The judgment in question was not final but a default judgment, as defined in Citizens' Loan Association v. Martin. Serving the rule on the plaintiffs' counsel constituted valid service, and formal service might not have been necessary. Notice to the attorney sufficed for pending matters, as Sections 4089 and 4169 of the Rev. Code 1915, which address final judgments, do not specify notice requirements. Superior Court Rule 6 treats notice to counsel as standard practice, supported by statutory rule-making authority under Section 3730.

Courts commonly allow service of rules or processes on the plaintiff's attorney of record when opening judgments, even if entered as final pro forma. This practice, upheld under common law to ensure justice for nonresident plaintiffs, lacks statutory mandate but is widely accepted. Cases like Beach v. Beach and Pick v. Glickman illustrate this principle, alongside references in legal digests and rulings such as Phelps v. Heaton and Branch v. Walker.

Sections 4089 and 4169 of the Rev. Code 1915 govern proceedings to open judgments that would otherwise remain final. Section 4089 requires affidavits denying notice and asserting a valid defense, while Section 4169 demands a sufficient cause and security for potential costs. Courts retain broad authority to modify judgments during their term or at any stage before final judgment, ensuring flexibility in judicial proceedings.

Statutes do not regulate these matters at all. It is clear from reviewing the Delaware Reports that the Superior Court possesses broader authority over its judgments than what the cited statutes specify. Examples include Lofland v. McDaniel, 1 Pennewill, 416, 41 Atl. 882; Woodward, Baldwin & Co. v. Arlington Mills, 2 Pennewill, 188, 44 Atl. 620; Janvier v. Culbreth, 5 Pennewill, 505, 63 Atl. 309. Courts with general jurisdiction inherently hold the power to modify or vacate judgments, a capability not granted by statute but essential to their function. Statutes addressing specific aspects of this power do not restrict the court's broader authority. 1 Black on Judgments, § 297. Supporting cases include Kemp v. Cook, 18 Md. 130, 79 Am. Dec. 681, 694; Bradley v. Slater, 58 Neb. 554, 78 N. W. 1069.

In Donnelly v. McArdle, 14 App. Div. 217, 219, 220, 43 N. Y. Supp. 560; Kiefer v. Grand Trunk R. R. Co., 55 Hun. 604, 8 N. Y. Supp. 230; Ladd v. Stevenson, 112 N. Y. 325, 19 N. E. 842, 8 Am. St. Rep. 748, similar principles are upheld. In this state, a petition and rule to show cause have been established as the correct method for requesting to open a default judgment in foreign attachment cases, as seen in In re Levy, 3 Pennewill, 5, 50 Atl. 540. The judgment in question is interlocutory. Courts retain full control over interlocutory judgments until a final judgment is issued. Motions to open such judgments are not restricted to the term in which they were entered but can be filed anytime before final judgment. 1 Black on Judgments, § 308; Kitchen v. Strawbridge, 14 Fed. Cas. 692, No. 7,854.

Additional references include Starke v. Woodward, 1 Nott & McC. (S. C.) 259; Hastings v. Cunningham, 35 Cal. 549; Mowatt v. Cole, 59 Ill. App. 345; Matthews v. Cook, 35 Mo. 286, 289; Burnes v. Burnes, 61 Mo. App. 612; 30 Cent. Dig. § 300, 'Judgments'; Blythe v. Hinckley, (C. C.) 84 Fed. 228, 239. When uncertainty arises about whether a judgment should be reopened, the court should lean toward granting the motion. Black on Judgments, § 354; Vermont Marble Co. v. Black (1894) 4 Cal. Unrep. Cas. 901, 38 Pac. 512, 961; Watson v. San Francisco, etc., R. Co., 41 Cal. 17, 20; Westphal v. Clark, 46 Iowa, 262, 264.

This appeal relies on the court's equitable discretion. Plunkett v. Dillon, 3 Del. Ch. 496, 509, 510; Townsend v. Townsend, 5 Harr. 20; Hickman's Adm'r. v. Hickman, 3 Harr. 511, 512. The Superior Court's equitable authority is affirmed by both statutory and constitutional provisions, such as Section 3726, Rev. Code 1915, and Article IV.

Section 24 of the 1897 Constitution outlines equitable powers, distinct from a court's general legal authority, as detailed in 1 Pomeroy's Eq. Jur. § 67. The court's equitable discretion, which is boundless, hinges on the injustice or prejudice to the party seeking to overturn a judgment. As noted in 1 Black on Judgments, § 318, the Superior Court has consistently used this power to reopen default judgments in foreign attachments, allowing defendants to contest claimed debts, as seen in cases like Taylor v. Rossiter and In re Warthman. While surprise was a factor in those cases, the current situation equally demands the court's equitable intervention.

The court's equitable discretion applies just as strongly here. The defense asserts no debt is owed, and the hardship matches prior cases where relief was granted. This hardship is worsened because the plaintiffs' actions against a corporation—whose stock was seized—have temporarily nullified its value as bail security.
