The case involved a charge of selling alcohol on an election day. Clubine initially pleaded not guilty but later admitted to the crime in court records. His lawyer attempted to remove these admissions, but the request was denied. The court's authority to handle the case was questioned, but the challenge was dismissed. Initially, the judge refused a trial, citing the records as proof of guilt, leading to Clubine's conviction. An appeal was filed, and later, the judge reversed the conviction on his own initiative, ordering a new trial. Clubine then sought a review of the conviction. The Oregon Supreme Court ruled that a justice's court could overturn a void judgment, treating it as if it never existed.

Legal texts like 51 C.J.S. and 35 C.J. discuss the authority of justices of the peace to reopen or vacate judgments. Some jurisdictions deny this power, while others allow it in specific cases, such as when a judgment is void due to lack of jurisdiction. The cited cases consistently involve void judgments or statutory provisions granting such authority. After reviewing these sources, I found no broader recognition of this power beyond these circumstances. This raises doubts about whether justices of the peace can generally vacate judgments—civil or criminal—without statutory backing, unless the judgment is legally invalid.

The Oregon Supreme Court's decision in Clubine v. City of Merrill is reasonable, as justices of the peace should correct void actions in their records. To assess this further, we must examine Delaware's statutes to see if justices of the peace have such powers. Delaware's Constitution allows the General Assembly to grant jurisdiction to lower courts or justices of the peace over certain criminal matters, including assaults, concealed weapons, and other misdemeanors. The Assembly can regulate this jurisdiction, determining procedures and appeal rights, with mandatory appeals for severe penalties.

Under Title 11 Del. C. § 2701(a), justices of the peace have original jurisdiction over misdemeanors only when explicitly authorized by law. Beyond this, there is no clear legislative framework governing their criminal jurisdiction or procedural rules. However, Title 10 Del. C. § 950 may provide additional context. The General Assembly has not extensively regulated this jurisdiction, leaving uncertainties about the scope of a justice's power to vacate or reopen judgments outside statutory exceptions.

5. Over time, through various laws, the General Assembly has given Justices of the Peace authority over specific crimes. However, no statute exists that allows them to overturn or reopen judgments in criminal cases or grant new trials. This differs from civil cases, where Title 10 Del. C. § 9542 permits Justices of the Peace to vacate default judgments within 15 days, as seen in State ex rel. Rockey v. Hatton. Additionally, Title 10 Del. C. § 9549 allows them to grant trials in civil cases if a defendant disputes the claim, with the judgment remaining intact until a trial concludes.

or levy on it is overturned until after a trial rules against the obligation. The statute also outlines further protections, including the need for security, after which the judgment and execution are nullified. Title 10 Del. C. § 9550 enables Justices of the Peace to order new trials in civil cases if requested within 15 days of judgment, with notice required. The absence of similar provisions for criminal cases suggests the General Assembly intentionally withheld such powers from Justices of the Peace, as implied by Appon et al. v. Belle Isle Corp. et al.

a conviction or authorize new trials in criminal cases. If the General Assembly had intended to grant such authority, it could have easily passed laws similar to Title 10 Del. C. § 9549 and 9550. Delaware precedent holds that Justices of the Peace derive their jurisdiction solely from statutes and lack authority unless explicitly granted. Cases like Carey v. Russel, Draper v. Draper, and Hawkins v. Mendenhall reinforce this principle, as do later rulings such as Jones v. Charles Warner Co. and Lawson v. Layton.

& Layton, which emphasized that consent cannot confer jurisdiction on a Justice of the Peace. Other cases, like Farrell v. Maryland Credit Finance Corp. and Howell v. Eastburn, further clarify their limited authority. In State ex rel. Rockey v. Hatton, the Court affirmed that Justices of the Peace are not courts of general jurisdiction, while Townsend v. Harmon categorized them differently.

Courts with restricted authority, along with cases like Farrell v. Maryland Credit Finance Corporation, 2 W. W. Harr. 569, 127 A. 879, and Howell v. Eastburn, 9 W. W. Harr. 588, 2 A. 2d 899, describe the jurisdiction of these courts as purely statutory. Additionally, Williams v. Singleton, 2 Storey 488, 160 A. 2d 376, affirms that Justices of the Peace Courts have limited jurisdiction. In State ex rel. Rockey v. Hatton, Chief Justice Layton noted (10 Terry at 266, 114 A. 2d at 652) that Magistrates' Courts, though constitutionally established, have only the powers granted by statute. These cases primarily address civil jurisdiction but underscore the constrained authority of these courts.

The Supreme Court and Superior Court's stance on Justices of the Peace emphasizes that their jurisdiction and actions must be backed by statutory authority. Given the courts' scrutiny over civil matters, even greater caution is warranted in criminal cases, where state and defendant rights are at stake. Without explicit statutory power, such as Title 10 Del. C. § 9542, 9549, and 9550 for civil cases, Justices of the Peace lack authority to overturn criminal convictions or grant new trials post-guilty plea. Doing so would undermine Title 21 Del. C. § 708, which mandates appeals within 15 days of conviction.

Defendant's reliance on State v. Insley, 1 Storey 196, 141 A. 2d 619 (1958), as precedent for the Justice of the Peace's 1961 actions is misplaced. The Insley case reflects concerns about a fair trial for the defendant under specific circumstances but does not support overturning a criminal conviction post-guilty plea or after the statutory appeal period under Title 21 Del. C. § 708. Comparing Insley's facts with the current case shows no relevance to the Justice of the Peace's actions.

A review of the briefs in the Insley case reveals its irrelevance to the current matter. Mrs. Insley claimed a State Trooper advised her to plead guilty to avoid harsher penalties, as stated in her affidavit during certiorari proceedings. This scenario differs entirely from the case at hand, where the Justice of the Peace's actions lacked statutory basis and contradicted established legal procedures.

She disputed the accuracy of the Justice of the Peace's transcript, arguing it failed to reflect the Trooper's advice on her rights, which she claimed coerced her into a guilty plea. Her counsel requested a hearing to address the transcript's alleged inadequacies and sought permission to withdraw her plea, citing State v. Martin and State v. Brown. The State countered that the record was accurate and the certiorari should be denied, asserting the Court lacked authority to permit plea withdrawal.

The Court upheld the Justice of the Peace's record as sufficient but ruled under 10 Del. C. § 542 that it could allow Mrs. Insley to withdraw her guilty plea and replead. The State appealed, arguing § 542 did not grant additional jurisdiction, as the Justice of the Peace was not implicated in any misconduct. The Court's order permitting plea withdrawal was challenged as beyond its authority.

The State emphasized that the Superior Court lacked power under § 542 to order plea withdrawal, as the Justice of the Peace's actions were uncontested. The Supreme Court later ruled the Superior Court overstepped by considering the Trooper's unrecorded statements and lacked authority to entertain plea withdrawal applications from Justice of the Peace cases.

No briefs raised the Justice of the Peace's power to vacate convictions or alter pleas pre-conviction. The Supreme Court's decision in State v. Insley clarified the procedural limits, emphasizing redress for misconduct by the Trooper or Justice of the Peace should occur within their jurisdiction, not through the Superior Court's intervention.

If he had properly used his authority, in line with his duty to safeguard the constitutional rights of the accused, that was the limit of the Supreme Court's suggestion. Given the facts here, it's evident the defendant's rights weren't harmed; the outcome stemmed from his own decisions, with no external pressure. It appears the defendant sought to retry his case on December 27, 1961, citing illness as grounds for a new trial to appeal on merit. The Insley case doesn't broadly alter statutes on Justices of the Peace's jurisdiction or grant them new powers, as clarified by Chief Justice Southerland in Williams v. Singleton.

Under 10 Del. C. § 561(a), procedural rules 'do not override statutes' or modify existing law, as seen in Stockman v. McKee et al and Curran v. Wooley et al. These cases affirm that the Court's rule-making authority doesn't extend to altering substantive law. Notably, these procedural rules don't apply to cases before Justices of the Peace. An Order may be submitted accordingly.

The Attorney General's Motion to Dismiss the Appeal should be granted, and the appeal dismissed. The Justice of the Peace must also correct records from the defendant's August 18, 1961 arrest, removing the December 27, 1961 proceedings. As noted in legal texts, continuances in Justice of the Peace Courts are statutorily regulated, with Delaware's law (10 Del. C. § 9504) allowing adjournments only to specific dates, not indefinitely.

First Federal Savings and Loan appeals the Superior Court's denial of its summary judgment motion and the grant of Nationwide's cross-motion. The Court ruled First Federal's claim was time-barred by Nationwide's 12-month suit clause. First Federal argues Nationwide is estopped from enforcing this clause due to its conduct, or that the limitation should run from the claim denial date, not the fire loss. Alternatively, it contests the Court's decision.

First Federal argues that if Nationwide is not legally barred from enforcing its policy limits, the Court incorrectly granted Nationwide's summary judgment motion by overlooking a disputable estoppel issue. Additionally, First Federal appeals the Superior Court's refusal to reconsider its motion, citing this Court's ruling in Allstate Insurance Co. v. Spinelli, Del.Supr., 443 A.2d 1286 (1981). The key details are as follows: On February 9, 1980, a fire partially damaged property insured by Nationwide, which First Federal was foreclosing as the mortgagee. Nationwide's policy includes a clause limiting lawsuits to one year after the loss. In March, First Federal and Nationwide discussed the fire claim, with Nationwide assuring coverage despite an ongoing arson probe. By May, First Federal had acquired the property and sought a claim update.

First Federal and Nationwide agreed that the bank was eligible for fire damage proceeds, and First Federal requested a claim status report. By late May, Nationwide hired Delaware counsel for negotiations, and First Federal followed suit in September. Subsequent communications were handled by attorneys. In July, Nationwide asked First Federal for a detailed claim statement, expressing hopes for a quick resolution. In September, First Federal proposed specific settlement options based on property ownership. On November 11, Nationwide countered with an $18,485.78 offer, which First Federal implicitly rejected on December 2, insisting on its $25,000 demand and emphasizing urgency.

Nationwide did not reply to First Federal's December 2 letter or subsequent follow-ups on January 8 and February 9, 1981. In the February 9 letter, First Federal's attorney warned of impending legal action due to the lack of response. However, the lawsuit wasn’t filed until May 11, 1981—15 months post-loss. The Superior Court rightly denied First Federal's summary judgment motion, as this Court's decision in Closser v. Penn Mutual Fire Insurance Co., Del.Supr., 457 A.2d 1081 (1983) nullifies First Federal's policy limitation argument.

In Closser, we interpreted a nearly identical suit limitation clause as starting from the loss date, rejecting the claim that it should begin only after the insurer denies coverage. First Federal admitted during oral arguments that Closser resolves its policy interpretation dispute. Its estoppel argument—based on Nationwide's silence after the December 2, 1980 offer—also fails. The letter was sent over two months before the 12-month deadline and followed Nationwide's November settlement offer. First Federal's December 2 response included a contractor’s $28,000 estimate but reaffirmed its $25,000 settlement demand.

We are maintaining our demand of $25,000 and will not adjust it. First Federal remains committed to settling for $25,000. I urge you to discuss this with your client, as time is critical. Please reply promptly. The December 2 response from First Federal's attorney clearly rejects Nationwide's offer and reaffirms their $25,000 settlement proposal. By raising estoppel against Nationwide's limitation defense, First Federal bears the burden of proof, as established in Brandywine One Hundred Corp. v. Hartford Fire Ins. Co. This burden persists despite Nationwide's summary judgment motion. The issue is whether a reasonable fact-finder could identify grounds for estoppel.

The court accurately applied estoppel law in this case. Estoppel, concerning insurers, involves misleading actions by the insurer that the insured relies on to their detriment, as seen in Ottendorfer v. Aetna Insurance Company. Essentially, estoppel bars a party from enforcing a contractual term if their conduct suggested they wouldn’t assert it. This principle is supported by cases like Closser v. Penn Mutual Fire Insurance Co. and Betty Brooks v. Ins. Placement Facility, as well as annotations in A.L.R.2d.

In Employers' Liability Assurance Corp. v. Madric, Chief Justice Southerland emphasized that estoppel conceals the truth for fairness. The party claiming estoppel must prove they were unaware of the truth and justifiably so. First Federal's argument that Nationwide's silence created estoppel lacks Delaware legal backing. Ottendorfer v. Aetna Insurance Company clarifies that the insured must demonstrate the insurer's misleading conduct and their reliance on it to avoid policy limitations.

Gribble v. Royal Insurance Co. and Murray v. Lititz Mut. Ins. Co. reinforce that an insurer’s silence doesn’t estop them from asserting policy limitations. First Federal’s reliance on the Delaware Unfair Trade Practices Act is misguided. Even if the statute applied to attorneys representing insurers, there was no evidence Nationwide’s lawyer routinely ignored correspondence to indicate a general business practice.

Under 18 Del.C. § 2304(16), a single transaction may violate the Act, so Nationwide's lack of response does not imply estoppel. First Federal claims the Superior Court incorrectly made unfavorable inferences against it, including mislabeling Nationwide's November 11, 1980 letter as a 'firm offer.' First Federal argues that actual cash value was not policy-defined and first appeared in the letter, suggesting ongoing negotiations. It also asserts no evidence shows its attorney knew of the policy's suit limitation. The record lacks justification for these inferences, as the correspondence clearly shows First Federal rejected Nationwide's offer and made a final counteroffer, indicating a deadlock. Additionally, First Federal's attorney referenced policy provisions by September 1980 and was directed to file suit by the fire's anniversary. Nationwide's actions post-December 2 letter could not have misled First Federal, nor could a reasonable fact-finder conclude its counsel was unaware of the suit limitation. Ottendorfer v. Aetna and Closser v. Penn Mutual support this. First Federal failed to prove estoppel, so the Superior Court rightly deemed the suit time-barred and upheld Nationwide's summary judgment.

The Superior Court's rejection of First Federal's reargument motion, citing Allstate Insurance Co. v. Spinelli, was not an abuse of discretion. Affirmed. Note that different attorneys represented both parties during this period; current counsel were retained months after the initial filing. Since First Federal sought summary judgment in Superior Court by claiming no material facts were disputed, it cannot now contradict that stance. Thus, no issue exists regarding Nationwide's burden to prove the absence of factual questions, per Moore v. Sizemore and Baoust v. Kraut.

Seitz, Chancellor: North European Oil Corporation ('corporation') seeks court approval for a reorganization plan due to its inability to locate majority stockholders, preventing majority-vote actions. Notice was given to all shareholders, and an Amicus Curiae was appointed to review the petition. One shareholder objected at the hearing. Undisputed facts reveal the corporation, chartered in Delaware in 1929 with 1,692,291 outstanding shares, became inactive in 1942 for unpaid taxes but was revived in 1954. Its sole income derives from German oil interests. Since 1954, no shareholder meeting has achieved a quorum, and directors were elected only via court intervention. Despite extensive efforts, the corporation had contacted only a fraction of shareholders by the hearing date.

remaining shareholders by the time of the hearing. The corporation's inability to convene a majority vote has persisted since its revival, necessitating judicial assistance for director elections. The proposed reorganization aims to address this impasse. The Court, after considering the Amicus Curiae's report and the sole objection, must determine whether the plan is fair and equitable under the circumstances.

Owners of approximately 650,000 shares. Consequently, the company cannot proceed with any action needing majority approval. During a special stockholder meeting on June 21, 1956, a proposed reorganization plan to address the issue received strong support from attending stockholders. Yet, with less than a majority present, no action could be taken. The corporation then filed a petition seeking court approval to finalize its proposed reorganization plan. The amended reorganization plan can be outlined as follows: 1. A new corporation would be established (a draft Certificate of Incorporation and bylaws were provided). 2. The assets of the petitioning corporation would be transferred to the new entity in exchange for 1,692,291 shares of its stock. 3. The petitioning corporation would dissolve, and its shares in the new corporation would be distributed to its stockholders on a one-to-one basis, except for shares belonging to missing stockholders, which would be held by a court-appointed trustee as non-voting shares.

These non-voting shares would not receive dividends or other distributions. However, any missing stockholder who came forward could claim their non-voting shares from the trustee and convert them into voting shares in the new corporation. They would also be entitled to any unpaid dividends or distributions tied to those shares. 4. Once the process was completed, the new corporation would no longer be under the court's jurisdiction for this matter. Notably, the Treasury Department confirmed the reorganization would be tax-free. This case involves a solvent corporation seeking court approval for a plan allowing known minority stockholders to become the sole voting stockholders, with missing stockholders retaining the right to claim voting shares if found. This situation is unprecedented, with no existing legal precedent or Delaware statute directly applicable. The court's authority to grant relief must rely on its traditional power to intervene in cases lacking adequate legal remedies. The petitioner has no legal recourse, so the question is whether the Court of Chancery can provide relief by approving the petition.

No jurisdictional objections were raised, but the court still sought clarity on this issue and appointed an Amicus Curiae to report on it, among other matters. As noted by the Amicus Curiae, the Court of Chancery has acknowledged its authority to appoint a receiver for a solvent corporation without statutory backing in compelling cases. While not exercised, this principle was acknowledged in cases like Drob v. National Memorial Park and Lichens Co. v. Standard Commercial Tobacco. In the Lichens case, the court recognized that equity courts could appoint a receiver for a solvent corporation in cases of fraud or mismanagement accompanied by exceptional circumstances. The court observed a growing trend to recognize this inherent power under special or urgent conditions. In examining related precedents, the case of S. E. C. v. Fiscal Fund is noteworthy, as the U.S. District Court for Delaware affirmed the broad authority of equity courts to address issues not foreseen in corporate statutes.

The court can intervene to appoint a receiver for a solvent corporation without statutory basis if stockholder or executive actions (or inaction) risk significant harm to the corporation's stakeholders. By similar logic, the court may also appoint a receiver to protect stakeholders in cases of corporate deadlock, such as the inability to secure a majority vote for essential actions. The potential harm to the corporation in such scenarios can be as severe as in cases of mismanagement or evenly split votes. Thus, the court has jurisdiction to consider the petition. Since a receiver acts as the court's agent, the court can forgo appointing one and directly oversee the relief process once justified. This approach will be adopted here. The next consideration is whether the petitioner has presented sufficient grounds to warrant approval.

To address the general relief requested, it must first be acknowledged that the current corporate operations are not significantly harmed by the inability to reach a majority of the stockholders. However, this doesn’t fully resolve the issue, as other scenarios could endanger the corporation without being immediately urgent. Efforts to contact the majority stockholders have been unsuccessful, and this outcome is unlikely to change soon. This lack of connectivity prevents the corporation from taking essential actions requiring majority approval, which is particularly critical given its reliance on a depleting asset—German oil properties. Without the ability to diversify or sell assets, the corporation faces severe limitations due to the missing stockholders.

The nature and location of the sole income source make it impractical to delay judicial action until a specific crisis arises. The evidence suggests that contacted stockholders share the same interests as the missing ones, supporting the need for equitable relief. The proposed reorganization plan, with added conditions, adequately protects missing stockholders’ interests by allowing them to claim voting rights and accumulated dividends if they reappear. The risk of conflicting votes is minimal, as no evidence indicates divergent interests between known and missing stockholders. Thus, the plan, including provisions for adjusting authorized stock, is approved.

The implementation process outlined in the petitioner’s brief will be followed, including hiring a firm to locate missing stockholders with 50 or more shares, excluding defunct entities. Since the petitioner already acts on behalf of missing shareholders, appointing the new corporation as trustee will minimize costs. The trustee will report annually to the court and handle cases where stock certificates are unavailable. While the objecting stockholder argued for more extensive efforts to locate missing stockholders, the efforts made were sufficient to demonstrate the remoteness of reconnecting with the majority holdings. The approval conditions should address these concerns, warranting the overruling of the objection.

The Chancellor’s first question concerns whether trustees have discretionary investment authority or are limited to 'legal' investments. The court must determine whether Pennsylvania or Delaware law governs the trust, as argued by the parties. The facts presented highlight the potential jurisdictional ambiguity in administering the trust.

The issue is whether Pennsylvania or Delaware law applies to the current trust administration. However, since both states' laws seem identical regarding trustees' freedom to deviate from prescribed 'legáis' in trusts like this one, I won't address the conflict of laws question. Instead, I'll analyze whether the trustees are limited to 'legáis' as defined by Pennsylvania and Delaware law. The pleadings include relevant Pennsylvania constitutional and statutory provisions (admitted as facts) about trust fund investments. Pennsylvania's Constitution (Section 22, Article 3) bars the General Assembly from passing laws allowing trustees to invest in private corporation bonds or stocks. Several Pennsylvania statutes permit trustees to invest in specific securities called 'legáis,' none violating this constitutional restriction.

These statutes—enacted on April 5, 1917 (P.L. 46, 20 PS § 802), June 7, 1917 (P.L. 447, 20 PS § 801), June 29, 1923 (P.L. 955, 20 PS § 801), and July 11, 1923 (P.L. 1059, 20 PS § 802)—don’t mandate investments in the listed securities but authorize trustees to do so. The trust under review explicitly grants trustees discretion to invest in 'good investments' as they see fit, without restrictive language.

The Pennsylvania Supreme Court has ruled that when trustees have investment discretion, the state's constitutional and statutory 'legáis' provisions don’t apply. This was established in Barker's Estate (159 Pa. 518), where the discretion was less clear than here, and reaffirmed in In re Detre's Estate (273 Pa. 341), stating that discretionary powers exempt trustees from legal investment rules. In re Taylor (277 Pa. 518) doesn’t contradict these precedents but clarifies that the discretionary power must be unambiguous to override statutory restrictions.

This trust’s settlors clearly intended to grant investment discretion, as shown by phrases like 'to invest... in good investments' and a later clause allowing trustees to change or retain investments without liability, except for willful default or negligence. The language explicitly absolves trustees of responsibility for errors in judgment or fact, reinforcing their broad discretionary authority.

The trust instrument clearly grants trustees discretion over investments, and this intent is further supported by the settlors' actions, as they initially included non-legal securities under Pennsylvania law. Additionally, the settlors, who were also trustees, participated in reinvesting in non-legal securities, which, though not definitive proof of their intent to bypass legal investment restrictions, still serves as evidence of their broad discretionary approach.

The language used by the settlors in granting discretionary power was intentionally broad, as evidenced by their actions and legal precedent. Consequently, the trustees of this trust are not bound by Pennsylvania's legal investment rules. Under Delaware law prior to April 3, 1931, trustees could invest in specified securities unless the trust instrument stated otherwise, but this did not apply to trusts like the one in question, as the trustees were not appointed by a will or the Chancellor.

Delaware's Section 3875 was revised in 1931, allowing trustees to invest according to the trust instrument's terms or, absent such provisions, in specified securities. The law emphasizes the fiduciary duty of due care in selecting investments and permits trustees to retain non-conforming assets acquired before May 1, 1931, if they were lawful at the time, provided they exercise prudent judgment in holding or disposing of them.

Trustees are permitted to acquire and retain non-conforming assets from any source, provided they act in accordance with the trust instrument's terms. They may hold such assets until it is no longer prudent to do so, without liability for losses. Additionally, securities acquired before May 1, 1931, under prior Delaware law may be retained under the same conditions, ensuring fiduciaries are not penalized for past lawful investments.

Property held under sub-division (D) or (E) must be invested according to sub-division (A) or (B), as applicable. The statute's wording is permissive, not mandatory, allowing trustees to invest trust funds as specified. By staying within the statute's approved investment categories, trustees gain protection against surcharges for losses. However, subsection (C) limits this protection, as such statutes primarily guide trustees, offering safety if they adhere to permitted investment classes.

The trustee is shielded from liability even if the investment fails, but these statutes do not override the trust creator's right to choose their preferred investment guidelines. The amended statute explicitly allows trustees to follow the trust instrument's investment provisions. Here, the settlors intended trustees to invest freely, judged by equitable standards rather than statutory rules. The trustees' broad discretion reflects the settlors' chosen guidance.

The trust agreement grants trustees significant discretion, making its provisions the governing rule for investments. When the trust instrument includes such provisions, subsection (A) permits investments under its terms, just as subsection (B) does for its listed securities. Thus, investments aligned with the trust instrument are as valid as those under subsection (B). Trustees may safely invest as they deem fit, provided they follow the trust's directives.

Trustees have full authority to invest and reinvest as they see fit, without liability for losses unless due to wilful default or negligence. Their discretion in investment choices is broad, and no statutory classification restricts them under Pennsylvania or Delaware law. The case does not require examining their general discretion but confirms they are not bound by statutory investment limits. The Wilmington Trust Company, as a successor trustee, retains this conferred discretion.

Do the successors have the same discretionary authority as the original trustees under the trust agreement? I believe they do. The Supreme Court of this State resolved this issue in Jacobs v. Wilmington Trust Co., 9 Del. Ch. 400, 80 A. 346, 349. The key factor is the intent of the trust's creators. In the Jacobs case, the Court endorsed a principle from In re Smith, [1904] 1 Ch. 139, 73 L. J. Ch. 74, stating that powers granted to trustees to manage trust property are typically tied to their office and transfer to successors unless clearly specified otherwise. The wording of the trust document is crucial, and broad discretion alone does not override this presumption.

In this case, the trustees are explicitly empowered to manage the trust property, including holding title and making investments. This differs from scenarios like Lockwood v. Stradley, 1 Del. Ch. 298, where the power was unrelated to property ownership. The agreement clearly assigns these powers ex officio, transferring title to the trustees and their successors. There is no indication that the trust was intended to be personal to the named trustees. On the contrary, the agreement allows trustees to fill vacancies or appoint a trust company as co-trustee, with the option to replace it later. This flexibility underscores the non-personal nature of the trust.

The agreement also specifies that if a trust company serves as sole trustee, it must distribute all net income to beneficiaries without discretion. However, co-trustees retain discretion over income payments. This distinction highlights that the settlors only restricted a trust company’s discretion in this specific area, implying it retains all other discretionary powers. The document does not otherwise differentiate between corporate and individual trustees, suggesting equal authority in matters like investments.

Given the agreement’s detailed provisions, it is reasonable to conclude that the Wilmington Trust Company, as co-trustee, holds the same discretionary investment powers as the original trustees. While the agreement is lengthy, further analysis supports this interpretation. A decree should reflect this conclusion.
